Country of publication: India.
Ṭ.ṇo. 934: *Kriyāsāratattvaprakāśinīvyākhyā*, copied from a manuscript belonging to ṇārāyaṇankunju ṇambūdiripad.
The *Kriyāsāra*, with the commentary *Kriyāsāratattvaprakāśinī* composed by Śrī Nārāyaṇa of Ernakulam.
[The *Kriyāsāra*]
Beginning from the third chapter,
Hari [now] states the method for purifying the site (*sthalaśuddhi*), starting with the words "palāśaśākhā" and ending with "kuryāttālatrayam," using *palāśa* branches and *darbha* grass.
Having swept the ground, the pavilion, the altar, and the area for the sacrificial pits with the *vāyu* mantra,

and having smeared them with the *gāyatrī*, one should scatter mustard seeds with the *astra* mantra; then, having swept and smeared [the area] as before, one should meditate upon the pavilion as being of the nature of *śakti* and [proceed] by that same path.

"Having sprinkled with the Astra-mantra, one should scatter the *vikira* offerings from the root"—this is the connection with the [preceding] separated word. "Having recited the *vikira* offerings with the Mūla-mantra, one should place the products of the cow (*gavya*) therein"—this intermediate sentence is for the purpose of reminding one to collect the materials required for the preceding rites. Water.

Having sprinkled everywhere with the mantra "punantu," and having scattered *darbha* grass, flowers, and unbroken rice grains with the mantra "iṣe tvā," one should then worship the world-protectors in the center with the root mantra and in the directions by their names, using perfumes and other offerings. Then...

Having placed incense and lamps for the purpose of dispersing minor obstacles, one should perform the triple clapping of the hands (*tālatraya*) and so forth. Here, the mention of "with water consecrated by the *astra* mantra" during the purification of the temple (*prāsādaśuddhi*) and so on is intended to demonstrate alternative mantras, not to demonstrate a difference in the subject matter.
It should be observed.
In this regard, another mantra from the Pāśupata Tantra is recited here.
"One should smear [the ground] with filtered cow-dung water using the Varuṇa-mantra.

Having thus described the purification of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), he speaks of the purification of the site (*sthalaśuddhi*)—preceded by the recollection of what has been done—for the sake of its protection, namely the worship of the Lord of the Pitcher (*kumbheśapūjā*). Thus...

Having performed the purification of the site, one should perform the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*) in a lotus diagram in the northeast according to the rules; then, following the procedure for the consecration of the jar (*kuṃbhasaṃskāra*), the filling with the mental [mantras], and so forth,
one should place the Lord of the Jar (*kuṃbheśa*) in the side [of the mandala] along with gold, gems, and fragrant water, consisting of both the subordinate and primary qualities.
Or, when the state [of the ritual] has been attained, one should fill the *karkarī* on the left side;

in that context, the meaning is "the Lord of the Jar" (*kumbheśa*), referring to the worship of the lotus-form of the letters and so forth as prescribed by the power of the injunctions. In that [jar], the *ātmatattva* is below at the *mūlacakra*, and above at the heart-lotus.
Having assigned the *vidyā-tattva* above and the *śiva-tattva* at the center of the brows,

and having invoked and worshipped them in sequence, one should meditate upon Śiva— who is permeated by all the *tattvas* and consists of the totality of the three *tattvas*— and worship Him after performing the ritual reception (*pratipatti*) according to the method prescribed in one's own ritual manual (*kalpa*).
Having propitiated Vardhanī with the Aghora-weapon, those [waters], by means of that weapon, form an unbroken stream adhering to the wall on all sides.

One should sprinkle [the vessel] while circumambulating it by that path— that is, along the path of the *vardhanī* situated in front— having led the jar (*ghaṭa*) to the Lord of the Jar (*kuṃbheśa*). Then,
having placed the scattered offerings (*vikira*) that were swept up at the time of the cleansing upon the seat, one should set [the jar] on top of them.
Having propitiated [the deities] with perfumes and flowers, having properly worshipped them at each respective place preceded by offerings,
one should wrap the primary jar with two cloths. Afterwards, the other—
the weapon-jar— should be placed upon mustard seeds prepared on one's own seat.

The meaning is that the worship consisting of the placement (*nyāsa*) and the completion (*pūraṇa*) brings joy. Then, the Guru should wrap [the vessel] with a single cloth and subsequently generate the fire in the manner to be described;
he explains the generation of the fire as follows: "having sprinkled," etc., meaning having smeared the ground, which is the site of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Having smeared [the ground] with cow-dung water prepared in the common manner, and having purified it by means of methods for the purification of the site such as sweeping and so forth, this is stated to be performed after the recitation; then,
having sprinkled [it] with the *praṇava*, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) preceded by the respective seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the limbs.

Having gradually purified [the body] by means of *samādhi*, and having repeatedly incinerated the consonants (*ca*), flooded them with the seed-syllables (*bīja*), dried them, and performed the abandonment according to the method mentioned within, one should cook [the elements] after performing the sequence beginning with burning and ending with the second drying. Here, "by means of the seed-syllables" refers to this process.

4) By the multiplicity of mantras, the multiplicity of tantras is indeed indicated; furthermore, at the beginning, with the *astra* mantra, one should draw a line called a "vajra" pointing upward (*udagagrā*) from the front of the previously drawn vajra-line.

On the eastern side, one should gradually draw three lines from the base, middle, and tip of the vajra-line using wood sticks of equal size; having sprinkled them with the *varman* mantra and cast away the wood shavings,
one should [proceed] with the *praṇava* alone, using the *praṇava* itself along with *kūrca*, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and water.
One should prepare a seat with grass-blades, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), which have been sprinkled with the arghya water.

"Having worshipped" (abhyarcya): this means having worshipped the prepared seat—that is, having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā). Then, having worshipped the Goddess with scents and other offerings using the heart-mantra of Bhuvaneśvarī, one should meditate upon her, who possesses the luster of a blue lotus.

One should meditate on her as one who has bathed after her menses and desires sexual union, according to the manner described. Having taken up the fire with the Astra-mantra and having cooked it with the Varma-mantra, at the end of the removal of the portion for the flesh-eaters (kravyād),
one should place the fire— which is the form of Śiva’s seed and is golden-hued— into her [the vessel] by circling it with the Hṛdaya-mantra, and divide it threefold within her.
One should cast [the offering] into the womb [of the fire-pit] according to the method stated in another scripture— either with the *prāsāda* mantra or with the *mūla-hṛdaya* mantra. Then,
immediately after the kindling and other rites, [one should worship] with perfumes and so forth.

Having worshipped [the deity], one should perform the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception). He explains this conceptualization with the passage beginning with "garbhādhānam" and ending with "vyomavidyayā. [The rite of] *garbhādhāna*...

One should perform the *puṃsavana*, the naming of the newborn, and the first outing (*niṣkrāmaṇa*) in sequence with the five Brahma-mantras, offering eight oblations of clarified butter for each and performing the rites accordingly; one should offer eight oblations of clarified butter with the *Puruṣasūkta* mantra for the naming, and eight oblations of clarified butter with the *Īśa* mantra for the first feeding (*prāśana*).

One should perform [the rite]. Thus it should be understood in all cases. Regarding these two, Puruṣa and Īśa, the phrase "by Īśa alone" means that the *samāvartana* (return home) is performed by the fifth, Īśa, and not by any other method. The meaning of "with the heart [mantra] and the Prāsāda [mantra]" is that the *agnyādhāna* (establishment of the sacred fires) is performed with those.

The rest is easy to understand. Having offered fuel-sticks with their respective mantras, one should then offer eight oblations of clarified butter separately for each rite, either with this [mantra], or with the *pūrṇāhuti*, or with the ninefold self-mantra (*navātman*). One should perform the meditation and the offering of water with the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*) alone; such is stated in other scriptures.

He explains its specific details here in a concise sequence; he formulates the subsequent procedure (*uttarakṛtya*) by means of a sūtra preceded by a restatement of what has already been done, beginning with "Thus" (*evam*). He elaborates upon the sūtra [beginning] with "On the altar" (*vedyādi*): "on the altar" means on the altar of the pavilion (*maṇḍapavedyām*), and "also on the right" means even in the southern half.

Having prepared the altar (vedi) either in the eastern half or—as indicated by the word "vā" (or)—in the western half, and having divided it, [one should act] in the section of Agni or the section of Nirṛti; such is the meaning.

Alternatively, having prepared the site for the mandala to be described hereafter in the center of the sacrificial ground (vedī) for the purpose of worshipping the Supreme Deity, [one should act] either to its east or to its south.

This is the meaning. Here, the mention of [the specific items] is for the purpose of illustrating the stages beginning with childhood, since the injunction is common [to all]. There, having drawn a svastika, one should place grains—namely rice, husked rice, and white mustard seeds—covered by a cloth upon this.
Having scattered [flowers] there, one should spread out an excellent bed provided with pillows and so forth.

Regarding the word "bed" (*śayyām*): having worshipped the bed according to the rules—performing the worship of the pedestal and other rites endowed with the tenfold procedure—and according to one's capacity for worship.
One should place the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala) around me; thus one enumerates the auspicious symbols.
The "Eight Auspicious Ones" (maṅgalāṣṭaka), beginning with the conch and ending with the pair of fish, have been described here;
having placed them in the directions starting from the east, one should likewise place the jars (kalaśas) in their proper order.
The meaning is that the sequence for worshipping the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) is as follows. Within those [jars]...

One should properly offer the Vidyeśvaras, beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin, according to the sequence of worship established by the Siddhas that will be fully described; having brought them into proximity, one should worship them. Regarding "the great pitcher":
at the location of the head, one should place a large pitcher—a *droṇa* pitcher—with the mantra *āpo hi ṣṭhā*.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and then completed [the preliminary rites], the word *atha* here signifies the immediate succession following the invocation of the principles (*tattvāvāhana*).
Thereafter, one should worship properly with the root mantra— this being the implied meaning— and then [recite] *āpo hi ṣṭhā*.

The construction is: "Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the mantra, one should worship. Regarding the feet, one should offer water for the *arghya* and *pādya* with the mantra beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*. On the two sides, one should place milk and honey with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*); this is how it should be applied. As for the phrase "in bowls and so forth," the sense is that [these items] are outside of that.

One should scatter white mustard seeds mixed with honey and clarified butter in the form of a rampart for the sake of protection, using the Astra-mantra. Having thus performed the consecration of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa-saṃskāra*)— the rest being easy to understand—
one should [proceed] to the northeast for the purpose of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the image-vase (*biṃba-kuṃbha*).

For the purpose of draining the water from the *kalaśa* consecration, one should construct another pavilion in the middle of the altar (*vedikā*). Then, in another pavilion in front of that, one should fill ninety-nine *kalaśas*. He explains the method of filling them as follows: "In the cardinal directions..."

Regarding the passage beginning with "kaṣāyam" (the astringent), [it is said] "by the lords of the left limbs in due order. Here, the phrase "unilaterally" (*ekāntena*) implies that although the filling of the central jar—concerning which it was stated at the end—that "the fragrance is in the center," it is more appropriate to perform it at the very beginning.
The Master has already explained the constituent parts, such as the astringents and so forth, previously. Thus, it is said "in due order."

The statement regarding the sequence of the meaning of the mantra is made by way of restating what has already been established, because the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the substances was explained separately (p.

"One should perform the *adhivāsa-homa*," he says; having filled [the vessel] again after the offering of the remnants (*saṃpāta*), and having worshipped and consecrated it, one should place another pedestal upon the *svastika* on the central altar within the bathing pavilion (*snānamaṇḍapa*).

The meaning is that one should install and worship the *upapīṭha*. Then, the construction is as follows: one should collect the skin, cow-dung, and *darbha* grass, together with scents, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth.
Now, he says "vṛtra... to describe going for the purpose of bringing the *liṅga*; here, [the *liṅga*] has been resolved upon.

The meaning is that one should duly withdraw all the mantras residing in the image into the *liṅga* and contemplate its manifestation as the *liṅga*. Likewise, one should extract [the deity] from the *liṅga*. Alternatively, having removed the cloth, rubbed it with *darbha* grass and other materials, and washed the *liṅga* with water—

One should draw [the deity] forth from the causal water—that is, one should properly raise it up and generate it—this is how it should be applied; or alternatively, having performed some worship of the body [of the deity] fashioned by the root mantra and having adorned it with perfumes and other offerings, one should lead it to the bathing pavilion; thus he says, "with perfumes and flowers. [He places it] upon the bathing throne.

Facing the temple, O auspicious Karṇa, one who is engaged in the appropriate rites such as the recitation of mantras should perform the placement [of the deity] in sequence and then bathe it according to the sequence of mantras prescribed for the filling; this is the summary.
Regarding what is to be done prior to the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), he says "having rubbed" (*parighṛṣya*). Now, as for the word *kaṣāya*:
The skins, which serve as the cause for the extraction of the essence (*rasa*), are observed here;

having rubbed them with an astringent (*kaṣāya*), one should bathe them with pure water—that is, ordinary water—and then, having rubbed them with cow dung, one should bathe them with water; thus, the act of rubbing should be applied to each [ingredient] individually. Furthermore...

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: immediately after the *mūla-sakalīkaraṇa*, one should properly bathe [the deity] with the jars of *kaṣāya* and so forth, using the mantras previously mentioned in their prescribed order. Having thus duly consecrated [the deity] according to the rule and in accordance with the ritual procedure—

Following the channel that carries the root-consciousness (mūlāśraya-sākṣicaitanya), one should meditate upon Mahādeva—who is eternal, fixed, and immutable—within that *liṅga*, and offer [worship] preceded by the presentation of water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings; thus it is said by Bhīma. By Bhīma.

The connection with the distant [words] is as follows: "Having smeared the scent with Aghora, one should worship with scents using Īśa. The intermediate sentence, "One should indeed give the garment with Vāma," depends on what precedes it; the particle *vai* is for the purpose of establishing its own specific time, [namely] "with Vāma."
Alternatively, "veṣṭayet" (he should wrap) is the reading; "vaktrakaḥ" (the mouth-piece) should give the incense for the *arghya* offering.
The word "daded" (he should give) is carried over [from the previous verse]. Here, it should be understood that after the incense, the lamp should also be offered with the root mantra (*mūla*).

Having worshipped, saluted, and propitiated the Lord God with perfumes and other offerings, one should [offer] with one hand or with both hands in three portions, namely the portions of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.

One should touch [the directions] in the four quarters according to rule with one's own Gāyatrī, preceded by the recollection of the respective deities. Those Gāyatrīs are written here in brief for the sake of conciseness; they are provided out of regard for brevity.
The meaning is that they were not recited. "They are written down in brief" (*likhyante tāḥ samāsataḥ*) is the correct reading.

Regarding the reading "they are written down in summary" (*tāḥ samāsena likhyante*), one should understand that the absence of the letter *n* in the word *likhyate* is an archaic (Vedic) usage, employed out of fear of violating the meter, according to the Lord [the author].
It should be understood that one should merely place the floral remains (*nirmālya*) upon the head, or else, according to the procedure prescribed by the *Pāśupata* and other traditions,

having invoked [the deity] with the root mantra, worshipped it, performed the lustration (*nīrājana*), and together with the image-keepers (*mūrtipāḥ*) performed the auspicious day rite (*puṇyāha*), one should present the water offering (*arghya*). Then:

With the mantra "Arise" (uttiṣṭha), one should lift the Liṅga from its pedestal; with the mantra "Stand upon the chariot" (rathe tiṣṭha), having carefully and vigilantly placed that deity upon the chariot, one should lead it around the pavilion in a clockwise direction. Upon reaching the gateway, one should descend [the deity] from the chariot.
One should cause [the disciple] to enter within, preceded by the ritual washing of the feet, while reciting the two verses beginning with "udutyaṃ jātavedasam" and "ākṛṣṇena".
Again, having led the bed around clockwise and placed it upon the bed in such a way as to face the palace, one should have [the deity] lie down with the Vāmadeva mantra.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Kriyāsāra commentary. || 3 ||
Having thus described the gross purification consisting primarily of ritual actions such as the preliminary consecration (*jalādhivāsa*) and so forth, the author,

beginning the subsequent chapter (*uttarapaṭala*) in order to explain another form of purification centered on bathing (*snāna*), provides a summary of the chapter's contents with the following aphorism: "The preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*)."

"One should act accordingly, O Lord of Sādhakas"—the analysis of this compound is as follows: "after the gross purification beginning with the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsa), and after the evening observances.
A *sādhaka* is one who meditates upon identity with the Lord attained through the power of *samādhi*. That is the meaning. He...

The meaning of the aphorism is that one should perform the most closely integrated *adhi-vāsana* (infusion) of the Supreme Lord, whose nature is consciousness (*cid-ātman*), by means of His presiding presence within the *mantra-liṅga*, establishing Him there eternally. In this regard, first [is described] that of the practitioner as set forth in the aphorism.

He explains the meditation on identity with the Lord (*īśvaratādātmyabhāvanā*) with the passage beginning "having washed his feet" and ending with "having meditated upon himself as Śiva. Regarding "having washed": the Guru, being pure and having performed his ablutions and other rites, [ensures] bodily purity; by implication, he is also wearing new garments. Furthermore—
Having arranged his garment like the sacred thread (*upavīta*), having washed both his feet and hands, and having sipped water according to the rule (*vidhi*).
Restraining his speech, he should lie down facing west in the western part;
it should be understood that he lies facing east in the south-western direction from that *liṅga*,
and in its south-eastern part he sits facing north.

One should properly perform the purification of the self (*ātma-śuddhi*) and the purification of the vital principle (*jīva-śuddhi*) by means of the *praṇava*, breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "seated, facing north" (*āsīna udaṅmukha*), the word division is "seated" (*āsīnaḥ*) and "facing north" (*udaṅmukhaḥ*). [The cloth should be] neither white nor yellow; the dust... [is not to be used].

The sandhi here is archaic, as in the case of *viti* and other examples; alternatively, by the phrase "having washed his feet" (*prakṣālya pādau*), purification of the body is intended, and by the phrase "with speech restrained" (*vāgyataḥ*), purification of the mind is intended.
Thereafter, having dissolved one's own individual self (*svajīvātman*) into the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and having rendered it supreme (*paramīkṛtya*), immediately thereafter—
One should withdraw the principles— the earth and the others which constitute their substratum—

by properly uniting them with the Supreme Lord through non-separation from Him; thereafter, for the sake of purifying the physical body, which is insentient by nature and merely phenomenal, [one should proceed].

Dhāraṇā, which has other names such as "drying" (śoṣaṇā), one should perform—that is, one should effect—after having produced the principles (tattvas) and [performed] the stages of flooding, flaming, hardening, and perforating. (p. 13)
Having joined one’s own self-consciousness [with the deity], having generated and then disposed the principles (*tattva*) that constitute its substratum,

and having performed the ritual placement of the principles (*tattvanyāsa*), one should perform the ritual placement of the mantras (*mantranyāsa*), specifically the placement of the root mantra (*mūlamantranyāsa*). One should perform this correctly, following the sequence beginning with the contemplation of the foundational support (*ādhāra-bhāvanā*).

It should be understood that one should perform self-worship (*ātmārādhana*). Now, "self" (*ātman*) refers to one's own individual soul (*jīvātman*), which is all-pervading and has made the entire manifold universe (*prapañca*) its object through the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) perfected by the realization of all things. All...

Having meditated upon Śiva himself as the Supreme Lord— the Master who pervades his own effects and is capable of the creation of the universe and so forth by mere will— and having cast off the state of being a limited individual soul (jīva),
one should remain established in the nature of the Supreme Lord, who is filled with the aforementioned multitude of qualities; thus:

One who is endowed with meditative absorption (dhyāna) and has realized the state of the Supreme Lord previously described, while still awake, should first perform the union of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna) and other preliminary rites; then, by means of the Tāraka-mantra, having joined the individual soul (jīva) residing in the subtle body (liṅga) with the Self (ātman), which is the Supreme Self (paramātman), for the sake of its supreme unification, he should subsequently withdraw the constituent principles (tattvas).

He explains the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) therein with the passage beginning with "the sense of smell" and ending with "in due order within the [vidyā-]kalās and so forth. [The goddess] is conjoined with the breath (*prāṇa*) and the organ of generation (*upastha*), her own specific sense organs having dissolved into herself, [namely] the sense of smell and the organ of generation.

One should dissolve the earth— which is endowed with the qualities of the elements and the five qualities beginning with smell— into its own cause, the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*), by means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) using the mantra to be described later.
And that subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*) within the water, one should dissolve into the water by means of the pervasive [mantra] of its own seed-syllable (*svamantra*).

Then, that water—endowed with the qualities of its letters and the four qualities beginning with taste (*rasa*)—one should dissolve into its own cause, the subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*). The word "should dissolve" (*saṃharet*) applies everywhere [in the subsequent stages].

In fire (*pāvaka*), by implication, there is the subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*). Fire, likewise, is endowed with its own cause—the subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*)—and is possessed of three qualities (*triguṇa*) and four parts (*pāda*). And that [fire], together with skin and hands, is joined with two qualities. Wind is in touch; in the subtle element of touch (*sparśatanmātra*), it is in touch within space (*vyoman*).

One should dissolve the single quality of space, which is conjoined with the ear and speech, into its own cause, the subtle element called sound; that sound-subtle-element into the mind—here "mind" is a synonym for *manas*;
that mind into the ego (*ahaṃkāra*); and that ego into the intellect (*buddhi*).

In that which has another name, Mahat; likewise, in that intellect (*buddhi*) which is called "the quality" (*guṇa*), namely the principle of qualities (*guṇatattva*); in the unmanifest (*avyakta*), which has the synonym *prakṛti*; likewise, in that unmanifest; and in passion (*rāga*), which has the synonym Puruṣa—here [referring to] the twenty-sixth principle whose nature is described as "the limb of Kauśika" and so forth—in that [passion]. Taṃ.

Passion (*rāga*) resides in the [tattvas] beginning with *vidyā* and ending with *aśuddhavidyā*; *aśuddhavidyā*, *niyati*, *kāla*, *akāla*, and *māyā* reside in the *māyā-tattva*; *śuddhavidyā* resides in the *śuddhavidyā-tattva*; *sadāśiva-śakti* resides in the *sadāśiva-tattva*; and *śiva* resides in the *śiva-tattva*.

In due order, by way of a succession that does not bypass the intermediate steps, one should dissolve [the elements] into the supreme Śiva, who transcends the thirty-six principles (*tattva*). One should dissolve that sound-tanmātra into the mind (*citta*);
the mind, which has another synonym, *manas*, into the intellect (*ahaṃkāra*); and that *ahaṃkāra* into the intellect (*buddhi*).
In that which has another name, "the Great" (mahat); likewise, in that intellect (buddhi), in the constituent of the qualities (guṇa)—that is, in the principle of the three qualities (triguṇatattva);

that principle of the three qualities [resides] in the Unmanifest (avyakta), which has "Prakṛti" as its synonym; and that Unmanifest likewise [resides] in Attachment (rāga), which has "Puruṣa" as its synonym; and here, O Kauśika, the Puruṣa is the twenty-sixth.

In that nature described by these and other [verses], one should understand that passion (*rāga*) resides respectively in *vidyā* and the others— namely, *aśuddhavidyā*, *niyati*, *kāla*, *māyā*, *śuddhavidyā*,
*sadāśiva*, *śakti*, and *śiva*— without transgressing the stated order.
One should dissolve [the elements] successively into the Supreme Goddess, who transcends the thirty-six principles (*tattva*).
He teaches the dissolution of the principles and their withdrawal, along with their mantras: *hāṃ* and *hvīm*, joined with *haṃ* and *hasa*;
and with these—*hrāṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *hyaūṃ*, *hyaiṃ*, *hauṃ*—together with the *Tāra* (Oṃ).
One should withdraw [the elements] into the supreme Śiva according to the proper rule.

16) In this regard, it should be understood that the dissolution of the five seeds, [represented by] the syllable *TĀRE*, and of the mind (*citta*) and so forth, must be performed by means of the five elements. [The sequence is] from the feet, to the navel, to the heart.
Having mentally projected the five elements at the palate and the space between the eyebrows, and above those, in each successive joint,
the mind and the other [tattvas], one should recite twenty-five times the mantras beginning with "Hāṃ namaḥ śivāya pṛthivyātmane huṃ phaṭ."

Having performed breath-control (prāṇāyāma) according to the number of those respective qualities, and having accumulated [the energy] during those respective measures (mātrās), one should pervade from the aforementioned locations up to the respective locations with the mantra: "hlāṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the self of Nivṛtti; obeisance. Then, [one should place it] in the subsequent principle (tattva) for each respective measure.

The meaning of the words according to the rule is: "having repeatedly withdrawn [the elements] in their proper order, one should dissolve them into the Supreme Śiva, who is endowed with the thirty-six principles. Thus, having dissolved the individual soul (jīva) residing in the *liṅga*, as well as the principles (tattvas) residing therein, into the Supreme Śiva, and having rendered it supreme;
One should clarify the *liṅga*, which is of the nature of pure insentience, through processes such as drying;

thus he says, "by means of air. One should dry that *liṅga*, whose nature is merely its appearance, by means of "air"—that is, through breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) using the seed-syllable of air—and burn it away by means of fire.

One should flood [the universe] with the Vāruṇa [mantra]. Immediately after the flooding, one should meditate upon the entire world without exception as consisting of water alone. "In that" means: subsequently, after the flooding, on page 17.

After the meditation on the state of the world as a single ocean, one should place—that is, project—the earthly power known as "bīja" (the seed) within that flooding water; this is because [the earth] is the seed for the sprout of the world, and by implication, this is done through the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) of the seed-syllable of earth. Then, upon that [power]:

Having meditated upon the bubble, which is the nature of all effects, as having arisen from the utterance of the *tāra* (Om) within the Śakti that consists of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and having meditated upon the *liṅga* as being identical with and of one essence with that [bubble], [one should worship] in that *liṅga* by means of the *tāra*.

One should unite the individual soul (jīva) residing within the self. Then, after the placement of consciousness along with its objects (*sārtha*), one should contemplate the principles (*tattvas*) which serve as their substratum.
The Lord explains the contemplation of the principles, including the expansion of all the paths, beginning with the words "by Śakti," and so forth.

Having prostrated before the two [deities], the Lord— the Supreme Lord who transcends the thirty-six principles (tattvas), whose nature is described in such passages as "transcending the thirty-six principles," and who is the witness and the performer of the fivefold cosmic acts beginning with creation— is [the object of worship].
Immediately after the arrangement of consciousness, desiring to emanate the principles (*tattva*) that serve as its substrata,

Śambhu— by means of his power (*śakti*), that is, by his own capacity— agitated the ether (*nabhas*). By that [power] through which he is capable of [bestowing] enjoyment (*bhukti*) upon the ether— which is heard in the Vedas as "Brahmā is the supreme ether of speech" and so forth— he [proceeds].
And regarding liberation, [there is the state] "the single [nature] of the multitude of bound souls" (p.
18), and so forth; this refers to the sky of consciousness (*cidgagana*) which transcends the thirty-six principles (*ṣaṭtriṃśattattva*), as recorded in the *Smṛti*.

Causing agitation— that is, transformation— of Śakti, whose synonym is *kṣobha*, he brought forth, or generated, Ānāda, the thirty-sixth principle (*tattva*) known by the alternative name Śivatattva. Here, the statement is made because the creation of the universe, being entirely beyond direct perception, is accessible through scripture alone (*āgama*).

"From *nitya* was born" is the application of the term *bhūtapracaya*. Thus, from *nāda*, *bindu*—which is synonymous with *śakti* and consists of thirty-five principles (*tattvas*)—was born. From that, *sadāśiva* was born; the word "and" (*ca*) indicates that his letters, words, and mantras also end in *nāda*.
The word "svayam" (itself) is intended to include both the nature of being sound (*nāda*) and the causes such as color (*varṇa*) which will be described later.
And likewise in the Pāśupata [scripture]:
"Desiring to emit the entire creation, that eternal Lord, presiding over the power of action through his nature of knowledge, stirred the sky by means of his power, which is indeed the causal state."
"It produced the subtle *nāda*; from *nāda* came the *bindu*, possessing the splendor of a thousand suns;
from that, Sadāśiva was born, consisting of the gross *nāda*; from him, manifold creation was pierced forth.
Regarding "from him" (*tataḥ*), it means from that Sadāśiva, in due order, consisting of that [gross *nāda*] or otherwise.

The principles (*tattva*) and so forth, the *kalās*, and the worlds (*bhuvana*) would be the *pātas*. From the *nāda* of the *Sadāśiva-tattva*, from the limbs of the *nāda*, there arise the phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and mantras.

Thus they would be born. These are declared to be the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvāna*). O Śiva, because they are differentiated, those best of teachers [perform] upon the *liṅga* the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to rule: the creation of the principles (*tattva*), the years, the maturation, the manifestation, the letters, and the principles.
Following the established procedure without deviation, one should sequentially perform the placement of the mantras on the seats (*pīṭha-nyāsa*), the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and so forth;
thereafter, the principles (*tattvas*) should be placed according to the sequence previously described.
The installation of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvanyāsa) has indeed been stated by us as well in the *Tantrasamuccaya*, and thus it is not elaborated upon here.

Having thus conceptualized the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra), which is established through the purification of the principles (tattvas) and consists of the expansion of the well-known six paths, within that [body]...

Having invoked the form [of the deity] into the common substratum through the five Brahmans and the Vyomavidyā, one should empower it; thus, "having invoked with the [mantras] beginning with Īśāna" means having invoked by means of the Brahmans unified [with the deities], and by means of the Brahmans in the form of threads and so forth, which are the *raṅga-mantras*.

Having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with [the mantras] beginning with *Sarvajña*, one should worship correctly according to the method of one's own *kalpa*. Immediately thereafter, having invoked [the deity] as Vyomavyāpi Śiva, one should worship him along with his limbs.
And in the invocation, one should perform it both individually (*vyaṣṭi*) and collectively (*samaṣṭi*) by means of these two.
20) Having thus described the bringing together of these two, the Vedic and the Tantric, which are so greatly desired, [he proceeds] with the daily worship that is about to be explained.
He says, "by means of the six-syllabled [mantra]," meaning that one should also perform the current worship with that very mantra which is accepted among the five Brahmans as the Prāsāda-mantra.

"One should worship the Lord of Gods with the six-syllabled mantra, or with the *nāda*, or with the *brahma-mantras*"; the phrase "one should worship" is understood from what was stated previously. He now sets forth the extraction of the six-syllabled mantra (*ṣaḍakṣara*), preceded by an assessment of its excellence, saying: "The six-syllabled..."
He extracts the mantra: "Tāra" means that there, the first syllable of the sequence is *tāra*, which is the syllable *oṃ*;

the second is *śūnya*, the syllable *na*; the third is the object of emission (*sargīviṣaya*), the poisonous syllable (*viṣākṣara*) ending in the visarga, the syllable *ma*; and the fourth is endowed with the subtle (*sūkṣmasamanvita*).
The letter *śa* is joined with the ejected letter *i*; the fifth is *kuṃ*; *bhānantā* means *kuṃ* followed by *bha*;
and because it is the support of nectar (*amṛta*), *ananta* refers to the letter *ā*, that is to say, the letter *va*. Thus is the meaning.

The sixth [syllable] should be *marut* (the letter *ya*). Thus, it is the essence of the Vedas, the essence of the Śrī Rudra Upaniṣad; for this very reason, it is the unsurpassed six-syllabled mantra—this is the remainder [of the sense].
Having thus explained the six-syllabled root mantra, [he speaks of] Īśāna and so forth...

This is for the purpose of establishing that the five forms consist of the transformation of the syllable *na* and so forth—the first syllables of those [names]—which themselves are transformations of the *praṇava*.

He demonstrates its nature as the seed-syllable (*bīja*) with the words "by the letters beginning with *na*" (*nādyarṇaiḥ*). [This is seen in passages such as: "In some cases, joined with the *bindu*, it attains the state of a *vipra*," and so forth. This means that by the letters of the mantra beginning with *na* (*nakārādi-mantrārṇaiḥ*), which are properly uttered together with the *bindu*—which is the form of the transformation of the aforementioned power—it [attains that state] because of their status as the causal factors.

One should fashion the effects, beginning with Īśāna, by means of [the mantras] that have entered the state of seed-syllables (*bījabhāva*). Having thus stated the five form-mantras (*mūrtimantra*), he describes the method of fashioning the forms of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) with them, starting with the words "on the head" (*mūrdhni*). Those [mantras], beginning with Īśāna, [are assigned] to the head, the face, and the heart.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) according to the prescribed order upon the secret place, the two feet, the [three] faces, and the mouth, as well as upon those situated in the east, south, north, and west. By the phrase "according to the rule" (yathānyāyam), it is meant that one should use the names beginning with Īśāna and so forth—
excluding the letter *ya*— joined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*, and joined with the names of the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) and the others, together with the *bindu*.
The practitioner should know that the name is joined with the *jāti* vowels— namely *svāhā* and so forth— and that the final letter *ya* is accompanied by the *visarga*. Here,
because the term "practitioner" (*sādhaka*) specifically mentions the extraction of only the *bindu* and *visarga*, [it refers to] the name.

It is illuminated that [the mantra] is not to be extracted. Now, he extracts the temple-mantra (prāsāda-mantra) along with its formal promise, beginning with "nādaśca. "Joined with the human vowel" means joined with the fourteenth vowel;
"āmbara" refers to the syllable *ahaṃ*.
One should extract this six-syllabled root mantra together with the nasal bindu;
it is the unsurpassed essence of the Vedas, as stated in the Vedic tradition. The meaning is that while this is supreme, it belongs to the Tantric system.
Now, for the purpose of extracting the mantras of the forms and so forth, he extracts their seed-syllables [with the verse beginning] "suṣire".
O Lord, it is joined with the ninth vowel *suṣira*, the seventh vowel *a*,
the fifth element *e*, the third fire *u*, the first *ṣa*,
and the syllable *a* together with the *bindu*.

One should extract the syllable *ha*. The word "should extract" (*uddharet*) is understood from the preceding context. Furthermore, in the extraction of the Root Mantra (*mūlamantra*), the count is intended to include the neutral vowel (*napuṃsakasvara*), whereas in the extraction of the Form Mantra (*mūrtimantra*), it is intended to exclude it; thus it is stated in the Pāśupata [Tantra].

"Know that the seed-syllables of the five forms, beginning with Īśa, are joined respectively with the thirteenth vowel, again the eleventh, the fifth, the third, and the first vowel. He states the method of placement (nyāsa) with the words "by that": "by that extracted seed-syllable."

One should first install the Brahmās, beginning with Īśāna and ending with Satya, who possess beautiful forms and the forms of faces, joined with their respective names as before; subsequently, one should install the [five] elements in order, joined with the long vowels, the bindu, the letter *ha* (vyoman), and the [respective] classes of consonants (*jāti*).

One should worship the deity with this *prāsāda* mantra, or with the *brahma-mantras*. Here, in this text, the worship is explained; [the author] elucidates it as being performed with water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth. One should invoke the deity according to the prescribed rule.
Having preceded this with the ritual procedures such as the sakalīkaraṇa appropriate for that [deity], and having worshipped him profusely with water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings,
with perfumes using the *gandhadvārā* mantra and so forth, with abundant flowers,
incense, lamps, and milk-rice (pāyasa) and other such foods.

One should worship the deity with offerings according to the prescribed rule, without transgressing the ritual procedure for propitiating the maṇḍala. The word "one should worship" (arcayet) carries over from what was stated previously.
Having placed neuter stones and substances here upon the bed, one should perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*);

thus he says, "jewels" (*ratnāni*), meaning precious materials. In the phrase "medicinal herbs" (*oṣadhayaḥ*) and so forth, the nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative; the meaning is "medicinal herbs such as *śāli* rice."
It is said that after the worship, one should perform the *bali* offering as a remnant of that; thus [the text says] "lāja":
with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with parched grains (*lāja*) and other ingredients, one should offer the *bali* in the eight directions outside the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) while reciting this mantra.

Roasted rice is *dhāna*; when that same rice is ground into powder, it is *saktu*. He indicates the mantra for the offering (*bali*) with the words "mamikram"; having given the offering with this [mantra], immediately thereafter—
(On page 24:

Having worshipped Śiva in the pavilion, the liṅga, and the maṇḍala, and having performed the *prasannapūjā*— this is the meaning— one should thereafter purify both the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the neuter stone (*napuṃsakaśilā*).
He explains the purification: "With the bark-sheaths" means having scrubbed with the bark-sheaths of *darbha* grass and earth, one should wash it with pure water;
immediately thereafter, having thoroughly washed it with "waters of Varuṇa"—that is, with waters presided over by the deity Varuṇa—using the Varuṇa mantras.

Having washed [the site] preceded by the withdrawal of the elements (bhūtasaṃhāra), the practitioner, being "one who knows the procedure" (vidhānavit)— by which it is indicated that he is one who knows the procedures for the withdrawal of the elements and so forth to be performed during the consecration (adhivāsa)— should purify [it] through meditative concentrations (dhāraṇā) consisting of drying and other such methods. Thus.

Having purified [the site] according to the rule, and having performed the seed-syllable of Śakti, breath control (prāṇāyāma), the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the pedestal, the worship of the pedestal, and so forth without transgressing the proper method, one should worship the Goddess who is the very essence of the pedestal—namely, Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī; this is the implied meaning. Furthermore, this is an indicative mark for the "neuter stone" (napuṃsaka-śilā) as well.

"One should subsequently purify the pedestal (pīṭha) as well as the neuter stone (napuṃsaka-śilā)," because they are treated equally in the context; there, worship is performed with the *tāra* [syllable]. Having covered those two with a cloth immediately after the worship, one should then purify the temple (*prāsāda*) as well and perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*).
During that worship, one should scatter *darbha* grass and unbroken grains (*akṣata*);
this also serves as an indication for other offerings. Having recited the mantras beginning with "kṛṇuṣva," (p.
25) [one should proceed].
O twice-born ones, having performed the protection rite (*rakṣā*), one should go outside from this [place];

after the worship, they should touch the *liṅga* in all directions and recite the Vedas; by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that they should recite the *Śivasaṃhitā* and so forth in the corners, as previously stated.
The purpose of this collection of Tantric mantras is as follows: now he says that one should perform the *pratiṣṭhā-homa* (consecration oblation).

"And the liṅga"—thereafter, the Guru, immediately following the aforementioned rites, in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) produced near the head of the liṅga, in that fire for the *tatva-homa*, [should offer] the four *vyāhṛti*s.

Gradually, one should offer eight thousand fuel-sticks (*samidh*) each of *palāśa*, *udumbara*, and *aśvattha* trees, smeared with milk, clarified butter (*ājya*), and honey; likewise, one should offer eight thousand sesame seeds (*tila*) smeared with milk, clarified butter, and honey—the meaning being "sesame seeds" for each. These should be offered separately.

One should offer the first substance here with the first *vyāhṛti*, the next substance with the next *vyāhṛti*, and so forth; this sequence is to be understood. After this, following the oblations of substances, one should offer with these [mantras] beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *svāhā*: "O Śarva, O Rudra..."

With these and other mantras of the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti) currently under discussion, along with the worship mantras, one should offer clarified butter (sarpiḥ) once each. "Then he should conclude" means that he should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and so forth.
Now, he describes the *adhivāsa-homa* [consecration oblation] beginning with the words "having distributed," etc. One should know...
By the passage ending with the word "manūn," [it is shown that] after the offering of the *pratiṣṭhā-homa* and the subsequent presentation [of the deity],

Having distributed— that is, divided and taken— that fire by means of the [five] Brahmās, such as Vaktra and the others, which are established in their respective directions, one should deposit it in the cardinal directions,
beginning with the east; and in the corners, beginning with the southeast, one should deposit the fire by means of the limbs (aṅgas), namely the limbs of the Brahmās, such as Sarvajña and the others.
"One should cast" (*vinikṣipet*) means "one should deposit" (*nikṣipet*); this follows from what was stated previously.

Here, the description of the division of the directions and intermediate corners is for the purpose of demonstrating the division of the mantras, not for the purpose of demonstrating the ritual tracing (*viharaṇa*). Furthermore, the non-tracing (*aviharaṇa*) is performed according to the clockwise sequence (*pradakṣiṇakrama*).

Those who know this remember [it thus]. As for the division of directions for the mantras, he will state later that "the assignment of directions for the mantras is proclaimed according to the sequence of worship. Having thus described the ritual movement of the fire (*agniviharaṇa*), he speaks of the preliminary consecration oblation (*adhivāsahoma*) with the passage beginning "and having performed the mouth of the fire" and ending with "one's own mantras."
All the image-protectors (mūrtipās), having brought all [the offerings] near the mouth of the fire, should offer what has been cooked with the mouth [mantra].
They should offer with the names of Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta, and Vāmadeva, beginning with the face-mantras, and with the limb-mantras (aṅgamantras) of the heart, crest, and armor.

They should offer fuel-sticks (*samid*) and other materials separately one hundred and eight times each, using the names of the heads and their respective limbs established in their corresponding directions.
He enumerates the fuel-sticks and other items with the words "fuel-sticks, clarified butter," etc.; as for the fuel-sticks, they will be described in the Chapter on Ablution (*snapanapaṭala*).
The disciples should receive the mantra of the preceptor’s sacrificial pit (*ācāryakuṇḍa*).
27) "The Guru should offer oblations with [the mantra of] Īśāna"—thus it is stated that the pacifying fire-sacrifice (*śāntihoma*) must be performed right there.
At the end, after the ten substances have been offered and prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering,
they should all offer curd, honey, and clarified butter separately one hundred and eight times each;
having thus performed the *mṛtyuñjaya-śānti* according to the stated method and completed the oblation, [they should proceed].

Having touched the *saṃpāta* [the residue of the oblation], one should perform worship; by stating "tataḥ" (then), he reminds one of the previously mentioned procedure for the propitiation of the mandala and so forth, in order to demonstrate its immediate sequence following the consecration of the *liṅga*. With the word "nṛtta" (dance), he concludes the ritual procedure for the day.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Tattvaprakāśinī*, a commentary on the *Sāra* composed by Nārāyaṇa.
Now, he describes the method for the installation of the consecrated image (*saṃskṛta-liṅga*) with the words "having bathed" (*snātvā*).
Having bathed at dawn, having bathed according to the sequence prescribed in the *Pāśupata* and other systems,
and having performed the meditation on the Self (*ātmabhāvanā*) and so forth in accordance with the rules appropriate for that purpose, [one should worship] Maheśvara.

Having performed the prescribed rites upon the *mantra-liṅga* and the *maṇḍala*, and having worshipped and installed the deity, one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with curd, clarified butter, and honey— and by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), turmeric and other such substances— as well, for the sake of achieving the potency (*vīryavattā*) of the deity.

At the present time of worship, he says "deva" etc., because the gods, planetary spirits (grahas), elemental spirits (bhūtas), and so forth, stationed in the directions starting from the east, desire offerings (balis).

"To them" means to those [deities] located in the eight directions around the pavilion, starting from the principal door-deity and the [other] planets; having offered the *bali* with the remnants of that [offering], one should perform the "depositing of jewels" (*ratnanyāsa*). Therein, first, by means of the plastering of the temple, one should perform the installation of the Temple-Person (*prāsādapuruṣa*).

By the words "it indicates by implication" (*sūcayati sāmarthyāt*) and so forth, it means: just as that [is], so too is the word of the authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*). Having consecrated the temple (*prāsāda*), preceded by the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*), one should recite the *praṇava* offerings, the root mantra, the five principles (*pañcatattva*), and the temple mantra (*prāsādamantra*).

The sense is that, having installed the deity of the temple, performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, and worshipped it, one should contemplate [the deity] as being identical with the temple itself. And thus it is said in the Pāśupata [tradition]: "Having first performed the domestic sacrifice (gṛhayāga), the preceptor should subsequently install [the deity] in the temple. Having reflected in this way...

Having measured according to the method to be described, one should fashion the site for the foundation; "five more" means that the hundred-and-fifth part of the width of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha),
extending from east to west, is divided into one hundred and five parts.
Once [the site] has been divided, one should bring that single [portion] from the center of the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*);

having led it back by that same distance toward the rear, one should there establish the laying of the thread running from south to north. In this way, one should establish the arrangement at the rear.
Regarding "bhuvaṃ gamasya": one-sixteenth part of the width of the door— that is, the twenty-sixth part out of one hundred and twenty-six— of the lower plank of the door of the *bhuvangama* [temple].

Whatever portion [of the total area] corresponds to the devotee's share, one should lead that same portion from the center of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) toward the north; there, one should lay out a cord extending from east to west, with the deity situated facing the northern direction. Thus it is.
At the intersection of the established north-south line and the east-west line,

one should determine a diagonal line; then, from that diagonal line, having moved a barley-grain portion toward the northeast (aiśānī) within the diagonal section, one should designate the location— indeed, one should designate the location.

The previously mentioned [procedure] applies here as well. Having properly placed that neuter stone (*napuṃsakaśilā*)— which has been worshipped with the *praṇava*— in that location, one should install it, that is, establish it, with this mantra beginning with "sthirī" which will be stated immediately below, in the designated place.
The meaning is that one should arrange it so that the central point becomes the "neuter stone" (napuṃsakaśilā).

He indicates the mantra for installation with the words "sthitaṃ" (established); he indicates the mantra of supplication with the words "tvam eva" (you alone); having thus supplicated with the previously mentioned mantra, the meaning is that after the installation, one should worship with the *praṇava* (OM) and then offer supplication.
Immediately after that (p.
30), he filled the pit above the *napuṃsaka-śilā* with scented water; and because of the word "and" (*ca*), [he did so] prior to that as well.

With great care, one should diligently purify [the site] by means of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for the sake of achieving stability in the consecration; having removed any fragments of stone or other debris within it, one should then place the gems (*ratna-nyāsa*) in that pit—this is the summary. Regarding that, the following is what must be performed prior to it.
Having offered oblations with the verse "cchāyā" and having offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the Gāyatrī,
and after further offering the remnants of that [butter], he should consecrate those jewels with that same Gāyatrī; that is, he should touch them and recite the mantra over them.

With the eight *kalās* of Sadyojāta, one should place those [substances]—the jewels and so forth—to be described immediately hereafter, beginning from Indra (the east) and proceeding clockwise starting from the east, according to the method of yoga. Regarding the word "one should place": one should place a ruby (*padmarāga*) in the center.

Therefore, having drawn [the following] together, it should also be applied here: "He counts the jewels, [namely] the diamond. *Nīla* refers to the sapphire (*indranīla*), meaning the gem of Śatarkatu; *gāruḍa* means emerald (*marataka*). And thus it is said in the Pāśupata: "Vaiḍūrya is called by the name marata."

Gāruḍaka, marataka, aśmagarbha, and harinmaṇi— thus Amarasimha enumerates the minerals of that second enclosure; "with manaḥśilā" refers to the eight [deities] of Vāmadeva, beginning with the syllables *oṃ* and ending with *bala*, which is the meaning.

"Likewise honey" (p. 31). By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), it is intended to refer either to the substances and mantras mentioned in other scriptures or as a restatement (*anuvāda*). The remainder is easy to understand. [The term] "auspicious day" (*puṇyāha*) [is used] because of the depositing of jewels (*ratnanyāsa*).

The word "puṇyāham" (auspicious day) indicates that this must be performed beforehand, preceded by the determination of the proper time; the particle "ca" (and) implies that one should perform it after having established [the ritual site]. The phrase "having thus laid it down very level, one should worship the pedestal again" includes the worship of the pedestal as taught in the *Pāśupata* and other scriptures; this is indicated by the word "tataḥ" (then).

Having reached the pavilion, one should dissolve the consciousness residing in the jewel and situated within the mandala into the deity; having properly joined them through complete unification, one should then unite [the deity] with the arches, banners, and other external elements, ending with the jar of the Vidyeśvara, in due order.

Having sprinkled the Maheka vessel of the Vidyeśvaras according to the rules, preceded by the performance of the protection with the Astra-mantra and other rites, having offered the Arghya water and prostrated, one should raise it with a concentrated mind;
having raised it with the *uttiṣṭha*-mantra and mounted it upon the vehicle with the Vāmadeva-mantra. (2)

Having circumambulated the sacred image (Aṅga) together with the Mūrtipas carrying the water-vessel (nīraja), the pitcher (nakarkarī), the large jar (droṇa-kuṃbha), the main vessel (kuṃbheśa), the parasol (chatra), the fly-whisks (cāmara), and other ritual waters, as well as with the Mūrtipas supporting the vehicle, one should lead it toward the temple.
He describes the sequence of the ritual procedure, beginning with "With the *arghya* in hand," and so forth. At the two doorways, [he should perform the rite] at the location of the gates (p.
Having offered *arghya* water to remove the fatigue of the journey, and having given it with effort and vigilance,

he should cause the deity to enter within; there, upon that neuter stone (*napuṃsaka-śilā*) for which the worship of the pedestal has been performed, the Guru, having mastered the tradition, should install [the deity] according to the rule.

Having taken that liṅga with the Sadyojāta mantra according to the tenfold procedure beginning with the invocation (parāvāhana) and the visualization of the form (mūrtibhāvanā), and having carefully established it with the Vāmadeva mantra,
one should likewise install it according to the procedure that will be recalled by oneself.
Having established [the deity], having meditated upon the union of the support and the supported,

and having performed the propitiation of the mantra, one should take it up with the *Sadyojāta* mantra for the sake of realizing its universal nature (*vaiśvātmya*), enter by means of the *Vāmadeva* mantra after first performing the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*).
Having firmly established [the deity] with the Śivāghora-vidyā, having prostrated with the Vajra-mantra,

and having worshipped thoroughly with perfumes and flowers while meditating, one should conceive of oneself as [the deity]; thus, having first performed the nyāsa of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) as prescribed in another Smṛti.

Immediately thereafter, one should invoke the supreme reality, which is characterized by immovability and other such qualities, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), and whose sole essence is pure awareness (*caitanya*); the meaning is that one should perform the invocation of the individual soul (*jīvāvāhana*).
One might ask: "Is the consciousness of the Lord also like the consciousness of those such as ourselves?"
Because it is capable of coming and going through its contracted mode of activity, it is fit for being mounted; therefore, he says:
"It is immovable," for, due to its perfection, it lacks the cause for entering into a location not yet reached.
"Immovable" means delimited by space; "fixed" means eternal, that is, undelimited by time; "bliss of the Self" (ātmānanda) means that whose bliss is the Self.

The meaning is: the supreme bliss that is established solely by its own inherent power and essence, and is not established by anything else. It is incomparable because it possesses extraordinary and unique sovereignty; thus, there exists no comparison for it.
Likewise, it possesses the radiance of many tens of thousands of suns; "many tens of thousands of suns" serves as the metaphor for its form.

The intended meaning is that it is of an exceedingly luminous nature. That Supreme Self, which is the reality transcending its own effects and is the ultimate reality—the supreme divine consciousness in the form of *cit*—one should invoke into the *mantra-liṅga*, which is established as the individual soul (*jīva*). This is the intended meaning.

The Lord of Practitioners (sādhakeśvara)— the practitioner himself being the lord— explains the invocation of the vital breath (jīvāvāhana) with the words "having taken" (ādāya). From his own heart-lotus (svahṛdayapuṇḍarīka),
he takes that which is directed toward the internal resonance (nāda), ending with the phrase "the bliss of sound" (nādānanda).
That Goddess constantly sounds forth with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) whose nature has been described as "the sound of living beings" (*prāṇiśabda*),

and with the temple (*prāsāda*) known by the name Ānanda, whose nature has been described as "the resonance of musical performance" (*saṃgītakadhvani*) and so forth, which belongs to the Lords of the Worlds (*bhuvanapati*).

It should be understood that [the universe] is swallowed by the five Brahmans, which are determined by the eight-syllable mantra grasped through the apprehension of its constituent parts (pratīka). By means of that [mantra], it is so perceived.

One should perform this rite of invocation (āvāhana) by means of the five Brahmamantras themselves— enclosed at the beginning and end by the Praṇava (Oṃ), and illuminated by Bindu and Nāda— in the manner to be described; thus,
one brings the Supreme Consciousness, which has been described in its true form, together with the vital breath.
Having taken [the breath] as it enters through the nostrils exhaled at that moment,

and having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) upon all six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) so as to make them complete, one should join [it] very closely with the body in the manner of the relationship between the body and its inhabitant; then, within that, the inner liṅga.

Having meditated upon the Supreme Lord— who consists of knowledge and bliss, who is composed of knowledge and likewise composed of bliss, who is the cause of all causes, and who is the direct cause even of Prakṛti, the cause of all causes— one becomes identical with Him through the infusion of that consciousness.
Having meditated upon the mantras—the life-installing (jīvanyāsa) and other mantras—one should sequentially assign the limbs and non-limbs.
Then, one should visualize him in the form of the desired gross mantra, surrounded by his retinue and encompassed by all [deities]; thus he says, "one should meditate upon him," and so forth.

Having thus visualized [the deity] in the form of the desired mantra-body up to the words "revered by all the gods," one performs the invocation with a hymn for the sake of attaining his complete sovereignty.

He says that one should act as follows: "Having meditated thus. Having meditated on all this in this manner and prostrated, the wise one, who knows the self and the ritual of invocation, stands before [the deity]; then, preceded by a hymn of praise—namely, these mantras to be described beginning with the hymn starting "Siṃha"—[he should say], "May he come."

"One should invoke [the deity] with the mantras beginning with 'Bhagavān' and so forth. By implication, this means that one should perform the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) through the root-mantra, the limb-assignments (*aṅganyāsa*), and other such rites. Having thus described the procedure for installation at the conclusion of the hymn of praise and the invocation, [the author now sets forth] a portion of the ritual as indicated by the words of the verse, according to the rules.

One should manifest that *liṅga*— which is renowned for its supreme invocation (*parāvāhana*) and so forth, and which possesses the nature of the manifest Lord (*prakaṭeśvara*)— by means of the *Sadyojāta* mantra. Having raised it with effort and vigilance through the method of invocation, one should then, by means of the *Vāmadeva* mantra, firmly establish it as the essence of the Supreme Brahman.

Having installed that image upon the *napuṃsaka-śilā* (neuter stone) in its formal aspect so as to remain until the end of the eon (*ākalpānta*), [one performs] the confinement with the *aghora-bhīma* [mantra], the protection of one's own power,
and the presence until the end of the eon through the *mukha-vidyā* in the *mantra-liṅga*.

And having requested Īśāna for the presence of the specific deity according to the rule— namely, the binding of the respective mudrās and so forth, in order not to transgress the proper method— one should offer a handful of flowers as an oblation until that presence is attained.

Having performed the installations of the jewels and so forth, having prayed without transgression, and having placed gold upon the head in the upper portion of the locus of the mantra, [one should regard it] as the supreme self with the nature of excellent gold.

Having performed the ritual placement according to the rules, and having consecrated the deity with water from the *droṇa*-pitcher jar accompanied by the rites beginning with the consecration of the Lord of the Jar (*kumbheśa*), one should perform the procedure according to the rules starting from the invocation of the vital breath (*jīvāvāhana*) up to the end of the hymn of praise (*stotrāvāhana*) for that *liṅga*.

Having performed the sakalīkriyā upon the Liṅga by means of the invocation with the root mantra and other rites, one should place the deity— who has been provided with water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), and so forth, prepared near the bed— at the time of bathing, using clarified butter, scents, and milk, or those substances commonly available, while reciting "thou art firm" (sthiro 'si) and the previously mentioned [mantras].
Having held [the vessel] for the purpose of serving oneself or others, with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), or with perfumed milk—
meaning milk in which fragrance predominates— one should perform the entire ritual procedure for that *liṅga* using perfumes,
flowers, and so forth; "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to perfumes, flowers, and other such items.

Having worshipped with incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth, and having placed his hand— the "Hand of Śiva"— upon the head, that is, the top of the *liṅga*, he should cause Śiva, along with His limbs (*sāṅga*), to pervade the void,
as well as the five Brahmans and the ancillary mantras (*aṅgas*). [He should likewise perform this] for the desired root mantra along with its limbs.

And one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times; beyond that, one should diligently recite the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, the Pāśupata, the Rudra, and the Śrīrudra, by means of this word "diligently."

37) By the statement "having repeated [the mantra] for the sake of increasing the presence" (*sānnidhyādhikaye*), an increase in proximity is indicated; and by the expression "having prayed and placed the golden [image] on the head according to the rule" (*yathānyāsaṃ hemaṃ vinyasya mūrdhani*), the phrase "according to the rule" (*yathānyāya*) implies—

Having filled the pedestal with gems, gold, sand, and the nine Śaktis while reciting "Aum, O Nātha, and with the left [hand], 'dhruvā dyauḥ'," one should then bind it very firmly and without gaps using a vajra-paste,
while muttering "dhruvā dyauḥ" over the head of this image.

Some maintain that the term "kāñcana" (gold) refers to the installation of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and so forth as taught in the *Pāśupata* and other traditions. [However,] everything is indeed to be understood through the instruction of one's own guru with effort; thus, at the conclusion of the rites described here, the pedestal and the *liṅga* have been installed with care.
Having applied effort to avoid agitation and the like, and having placed and firmly established that pedestal with the pedestal-mantras, and having worshipped it with Bhuvaneśvarī,
one should worship the Lord who is present within the mantra-liṅga, having wrapped him at that time with two garments.

Having diligently performed the preparation, such as strengthening with jewels, gold, silk, and so forth, and having cast the immovable eight-fragrance [powder] therein, one should then worship together with the limbs and the enclosures, following the mantra-invocation and the union of the support and the supported.
Having worshipped the deity with offerings beginning with water and perfumes and ending with food offerings, one should exit and perform the supreme rite for the fire.

Immediately after propitiating the Fire, one should arrange the attendants of the sacrificial offering, such as the door-keepers and others, by means of their respective mantras; that is, one should arrange them so that they remain intent upon protecting [the deity], persisting for as long as the presence of the deity's mantra-signs endures.
He states the sequence for arranging the retinue: "The two gatekeepers," and so forth. In this manner, one should arrange all the attendants of Rudra in their respective places;

having arranged them and worshipped them according to the rule—having worshipped them with the ritual procedures such as the *diśāhoma* and others, and having offered the *bali* and paid homage—[one should proceed].

Having sipped water for purification (*ācamana*) according to the procedure beginning with "until the end" (*yāvadanta*), and having entered within, the preceptor (*ācārya*) should mutter the root mantra (*mūlamantra*)— the very same offering as that performed by the guru— and having praised the deity with various hymns and,
by the force of the word "and," with mantras such as the *Śivasaṃkalpa*, he should propitiate the Lord.

Having prayed for the accomplishment of his desired goal, he should ask for forgiveness with the verses beginning "mā tvā somasya māne" (Do not [abandon us] at the measuring of Soma), either to remove the fault of the prayer or to remove the fault of ignorance; and having performed the directional oblation (diśāhoma) according to the rules, [he should worship] the Deity.

"One should ask for forgiveness"—this is the connection with what precedes. Having thus described the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), he indicates the duty of the patron (*yajamāna*) who causes it to be performed: "one should worship" all [the deities], etc.
One should honor the members of the three [upper] castes, the Śūdras, the Pāriśavas, and others in due order with wealth, grain, and the like, as well as abundant clothing and gifts of food; therein,
the "wealth" for the Brāhmaṇas should be understood as gold and so forth, as well as land and the like.
Thereafter, immediately following that, one should worship the Guru together with the image-keepers (mūrtipās);
by implication, one should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to him and to them according to one's capacity.

"Nirātram" means having spent three nights— that is, three days and nights— performing the worship of the maṇḍala, offerings, oblations (*homa*), feeding of Brahmins, giving of gifts, and so forth; then, on the fourth day,

one should follow the sequence beginning with the propitiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*), the peace-offering (*śānti*), the ritual bath with the water-pot (*kalaśasnāna*), and other such procedures for the Deity.

One should perform the ritual bath with seventeen substances according to one's capacity; by the word "according to capacity" (*śaktyā*), it is indicated that the use of the [seventeen] jars is mandatory, and thus even a bath with twenty-five substances is not considered a transgression— this is the *pratiṣṭhā*.

Regarding the phrase "he who desires to act," it is explained that the primary subject under discussion is *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration), which refers to the eternal establishment of the Supreme Lord— who is a mass of consciousness and bliss— through his own representative form as a *liṅga*, out of a desire to favor his devotees, for as long as *saṃsāra* endures.
The selection of a preceptor (*guru-varaṇa*), the preparation of the ritual implements (*tantra-liṅga-saṃpādana*),

the consecration (*saṃskāra*), the installation (*sthāpana*), the placement of the vital breath (*jīva-nyāsa*), and so forth, have been clearly explained in their proper sequence. This [is the procedure].

This establishment has been declared by the wise who are adept at discerning the good from the bad; it must be refined by those of supreme intellect whose minds are not corrupted by defects such as envy.
It is to be purified by thoroughly pacifying faults through the removal of what exceeds the correct measure. These very [principles] are ours.

The meaning is that this is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Having thus concluded the exposition of the first part— which is also known by the name "Section on the Foundation" (*pratiṣṭhābhāga*)—
and in order to prevent the dullness of intellect in those who might otherwise expect liberation through that alone, [the author] intends to state what follows immediately.
Understanding that this chapter describes the subsequent sections concerning the interruption of worship and so forth, he concludes the chapter with the words "worship and so forth" (*pūjādyam*).
This means that in the five subsequent chapters mentioned above, "worship and so forth" will be explained in brief and in sequence.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Tatvaprakāśinī, a commentary on the Kriyāsāra.

Having thus described the installation of the *mantra-liṅga*— which serves as the substratum for the daily worship and other rites heard in the scriptures such as "the worshipper" (*evam arcaka*) and so forth— the author now promises to explain the worship that must necessarily be performed during daily worship, festivals, and other occasions, which share the same purpose as that [installation]. Now...
p.
41) "Now I shall speak"—that is, I shall speak briefly of the worship that does not fall under the first category of ritual actions known from the scriptures; thus, "I shall speak briefly."
Since what was stated in brief has been followed by an acceptance of a further summary,

it is implied that there is no contradiction here even with the detailed accounts found in other scriptures, such as the filling of the conch, the worship of the Self, and the preparation of offerings.

This statement—that there is no fault in performing only this much because some other scriptures also provide a method of concise exposition—is made thus. Since we have already demonstrated that procedure in the *Tantrasamuccaya*, it will not be demonstrated here; such is the case for the worship (*pūjā*).

To address the point regarding "primacy," he says: "All [these] grant success. Regarding the word "having bathed": there, the worshipper, having bathed according to the injunctions and having performed the libations to the gods and ancestors, remains restrained in speech; and with his mind fixed internally upon Mukunda—according to the principle beginning with "by the remembrance of Mukunda"—he worships Śiva for the sake of that purification.

Remembering [the deity] while recollecting [him], after performing bathing and other rites for the purification of body, speech, and mind, one should go to the worship pavilion (*pūjā-maṇḍapa*)—this is the remainder of the sense—for the purpose of worship.
"Having washed" means having gone there and washed one's feet; then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should honor the two doorkeepers.

Having first obtained permission for that, one should enter properly, beginning with the right foot (p. 42), meaning into the interior of the worship pavilion (*pūjāmaṇḍapa*). Then, [one performs] the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) by means of the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
Having performed the purification of the hands with that weapon-mantra,

and having performed the binding of the directions (digbandha)— which begins with three claps (tāla)— one should then, after the construction of the fire-walls (agniprākāra) to be performed immediately thereafter, [proceed] in the various directions.

Having meditated upon the lords of the directions, he should thereafter sit upon a seat of darbha grass and perform the purification of himself— that is, the purification of his individual soul (jīva) and its subtle body (sūkṣmadeha).
In that regard, he first describes the method for purifying the channels (*nāḍīśuddhi*), beginning with the words "one should exhale" (*recayet*) and "having exhaled" (*racayitvā*).

For the purpose of purifying the channels, one should exhale the air held in *kumbhaka* through the various channels by means of their specific regulation; then, immediately following that, after the *praṇava-prāṇāyāma*, the subsequent practice is to be performed.

One should purify the elements—the subtle elements that constitute one's own body—by means of the process of dissolution; having dissolved them into their own cause, the Supreme Self (Paramātman), according to the order of withdrawal, one should effect purification.
This is because, in such scriptural passages as "From the Self, space was produced," it is the elements themselves [that are intended].

The intention is that, because their creation is heard [in scripture], one should dissolve them back into those very [elements]. He explains the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) with the passage beginning "at the tips of the feet" and ending with "according to the rule. The phrase "the heart and so forth" refers to the *prāsāda* mantra accompanied by the heart and other [limbs].

(43) [The deities] who constitute the heart of the palace, characterized by their respective seed-syllables such as *hāṃ* and so forth, residing in their own maṇḍalas, and supported by the maṇḍalas of the elements beginning with earth;
With the seed-syllables of barley (*yava*) consisting of the syllables *hnāṃ*, *hvīṃ*, *hrūṃ*, *hyaiṃ*, and likewise *hauḍ*,

combined with *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, one should [perform the practice] according to the previously described forms— by means of five, four, three, two, and once respectively— through the repetitions of the upward strike (*udghāta*).
