Having purified those elements situated respectively at the tips of the feet, the base of the navel, the heart, the throat, and the palate— by means of the stages of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), breath-restraint (*prāṇāyāma*), and meditative absorption (*āpatti*), according to the previously mentioned procedure— one should dry up the body with the vital air.

The connection is with what will be stated hereafter. Here, by means of the sentence ending with "purification through sound" and "in the expanse," [it is shown that] when the body is motionless due to being firmly established in posture (*āsana*), and the *apāna* wind is pressed down and turned upward by the cessation of its voluntary movement;

And when there is this upward-moving power of breath (prāṇa-śakti), by means of the strength of that breath, this practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma)— which is designated by the term "upward thrust" (udghāta)— proceeds higher and higher toward the station of the principles (tattva); therefore, this prāṇāyāma is celebrated as "udghāta."

According to the doctrine of the dissolution of the five elements, and by the rule of the conjunction of the seed-syllables of the limbs, there arises the fault of the undesirable consequence of obtaining two *ha*-sounds.
"He removes by means of the resonance (*nāda*)," meaning by means of the resonance [and] the palace (*prāsāda*), that is, by means of the letter *ha*;

the remainder is that by this the purification of the ether (*vyoman*) is prescribed. Thus, through the simultaneous withdrawal of the sequence of elements which constitute its own substratum, he [performs] that which precedes it.

Having performed *prāṇāyāma* with the utterance of the *praṇava*, one should, by means of the path of yoga and the method of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), conceive of oneself— the individual soul— as abiding in the Supreme Self, which is the ether (*vyoman*) whose other name is the Supreme; as it is heard in the Upanishads, "Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman," and so forth.
Having elaborated slightly within the context of the incidental discussion, he shows the remainder of the subject matter with the words beginning "by the wind" (*vāyunā*), etc.

The term "divine" (*divyam*) refers to the divine deity [who arises] through the sequence of creation and so forth, consisting of the solidification and the perforation of that [substance] immediately following its dissolution.

Having meditated upon the deity who has arisen— being like the form of the Supreme Lord because merit alone is his essence— and having first dissolved himself into the Supreme Self through the process of withdrawal, one should unite one's own individual self (*jīvātman*) with that [deity] by way of presiding over it.
The word *ca* indicates the touching [of the body] following the transformation of the year and so forth;

having performed [this], one should carry out the ritual according to the rule of the mantra. Therein, he shows the visualization of the hands: "the two palms"—meaning the two palms of the hands joined together—and by the word *ca*, the sides as well, one should purify with the *astra-mantra*.
Again,
on both hands, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) with the root mantra and the *prāsāda* mantra, arising from the nature of the blazing hand-gesture.

The word "root" (*mūla*) continues to apply here. Having done so, after the placement of the written letters (*lipitatva*), one should then begin the placement of the "play of the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇavilāsa*), which is the arrangement of the five Brahmans that constitute the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*). He divides that [placement] with the verse beginning "those [are] the face," and so forth.
Immediately after that, he says that one should also install the limbs (aṅgas) for the sake of accomplishing omniscience and so forth,

with the words "having installed the hearts" (hṛdayāni) and "having installed" (nyastvā). Having thus installed them in the manner described, and having meditated upon the Lord of Devas in the heart according to the ritual rule, [one should proceed] from the sun-lotus, from the middle of the sky, and even from the position above.

One should remember Gaṅgā as she descended upon the head of the Blessed One; by means of that nectar-water, one should perform the auspicious visualization of all offerings, beginning with the *arghya*. Having worshipped according to the sequence of the prescribed rules and having recited the mantra, one should then [attain] identity with That.

Immediately after the meditation, being composed, the master of supreme samādhi should commence the worship—the self-worship and the worship of the deity—using the *astra-mantra*. With the *astra-mantra*, he should wash the vessel along with its stand and the conch shell; having filled it with water using the *mūla-mantra*, [he should proceed].
One should again envelop [the object] with the Kavaca mantra; having purified it with the Śikhā mantra, inspected it with the Netra mantra, and protected it with the Astra mantra (p.

Immediately after that, one should install and invoke the mantras— the Soma-mantra, the Mūla-mantra, and the Gaṅgā-mantra. Having thus briefly described the filling of the conch and the self-worship, here,
having worshipped and meditated for a day upon the installed mantra-liṅga, [one should perform the rites] on the ground prepared before it.

He demonstrates the present-day worship on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) representing that [divine] locus with the words "the foundational power" (*ādhāraśakti*). Regarding that, he describes the worship of the seat (*pīṭhapūjā*) with the passage beginning with "the foundational power" and ending with "one should arrange in due order. Furthermore, after the self-worship (*ātmārādhanā*),...
And the *ādhāra-śakti*; by the word "and" (*ca*), [one includes] the *mūla-prakṛti*, the tortoise (*kūrma*), and so forth;

furthermore, immediately thereafter, [one should place] the earth—this being the implied meaning—one should arrange them one above the other within this single pentad, mentally conceive them, and then worship them, that is, one should perform the sacrifice.

What is about to be described is also adopted here. Furthermore, immediately thereafter, he states that one should worship Dharma and the others in the form of the legs of the pedestal (*pīṭhapāda*) in the corners beginning with the southeast (Agni), and Adharma and the others in the form of arrows (*iṣu*) in the directions beginning with the east; thus he says "Adharma" and "Adharma and the others."

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the inclusion of the qualities (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*); therefore, the meaning is "non-dharma, ignorance, non-detachment, and lack of sovereignty. Furthermore, it is in the form of a thread clinging to the seat (p.

Above Māyā and Vidya, one should worship the lotus as the seat of the deity; the nine Śaktis in the form of the petals, filaments, and pericarp; and the triad of mandalas in the form of the pericarp itself—thus he says with the words beginning "satvam," and expresses the nine Śaktis with the words beginning "vāmā."
With the words beginning "tārārṇaiḥ" (by means of the syllables of the seed-mantras), he divides the threefold nature of the mandalas;
the meaning is that they are situated in their respective places within the mandalas without distinction.
Having thus described the worship of the seats (pīṭha-pūjā), he speaks of the mounting [of the deity] there by means of the form (mūrti) in the passage beginning with "kalpayitvā" (having fashioned).

By the end of [the section] "one should practice," the meaning is that one should then visualize the deity in the form of the mantra-body of the temple (prāsāda), situated upon the pericarp; having visualized him as endowed with four arms and so forth, by means of the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva. Internally...

The phrase "the arrangement of the instruments" (karaṇavinyāsam) is connected with the distant [word]. One should perform the arrangement of the internal instruments (antakaraṇavinyāsa)—that is, the arrangement of the pentad beginning with Īśāna—within the lotus-center (karṇikā) of the divine form. Then, [one should contemplate] the deity in the form of a gross, imagined body.

Having meditated upon [the deity] as distinguished by four arms and other attributes by means of the Prāsāda mantra, one should invoke and establish therein that witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya), which is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), from the lotus of the heart; thus he says, "of the nature of consciousness."

(p. 48) Now, after the invocation of the form (mūrty-āvāhana), the Guru, having invoked the light whose nature is consciousness (cid-rūpa-jyotis) from the lotus of his own heart— the lotus of his heart— should deposit and establish it.

"Gradually" means one should perform the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) in sequence—such as by displaying the mudrās for invocation and so forth, and the application of the principles of the letters (*lipitatvanyāsa*).

Having thus invoked and performed the ritual of integration (*sakalīkṛtya*), one should offer the guest-water (*pādya*) and other articles to the deity; this is what he states with the words beginning "the guest-water," etc. "Thus" means in this manner.

Having performed the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, one should then worship the thread, cloth, and other items upon that deity as being the very body of the Lord Śambhu. He explains this with the words beginning with "the head," etc., and the word "and" (*ca*) [in the phrase] "the heart and so forth."

The word "paścāt" (afterwards) has the sense of a collective [inclusion] of the unmentioned [elements] such as the speaker and the weapon; it means that immediately after the section on Śambhu, one should worship the section on the Mūrtis—that is, one should worship the group of deities beginning with Abhīta and Sadyojāta as the retinue of the Mūrtis. He now divides the worship of the Mūrti-pakṣa.

With the passage beginning with "in the west" and ending with "one should worship that lotus on the outside," one should worship the limbs— the *hṛdaya* and so forth up to the *netra*— in the cardinal directions starting from the east,
and the *astra* in the intermediate directions starting from the north and ending with the northwest.
The meaning is that one should worship by circumambulating [clockwise]. With perfumes, flowers, and so forth, exactly as received from the Guru’s tradition and other sources. (p. 49)

The meaning is that it should be provided with the flower-enclosure and so forth. Having worshipped in this manner and performed the intermediate ritual of worship (*antarapūjā*), one should subsequently offer oblations—that is, perform the *pūjā-homa*.
Then, one should offer to all the spirits (*bhūtas*), such as Nandin and others, according to the previously stated method.
Having visualized [the deities] together with Fire right there, one should offer the *bali* offering; then, having sipped water (*ācamya*),

and having offered the water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamanīya*)— which is also known by the name *pānīya*— as well as the water for the *āvidhānīya* (due to the word "and" [*ca*]), one should dismiss the food.
He offered the *nirmālya* (remnants of the offering) and caused it to be accepted;

then, having again given water for rinsing the mouth (*gaṇḍūṣa*) and water for sipping (*ācamana*), he subsequently offered five types of offerings in sequence: perfumes (*gandha*), flowers (*puṣpa*), and—as indicated by the word "and" (*ca*)—incense (*dhūpa*) and so forth, as well as mouth-perfumes (*mukhavāsa*) and other items.
One should worship with betel leaves, sandalwood paste, cakes, and so forth; having thus honored him,
and subsequently having worshipped slightly with the root mantra, one should offer one's entire being to the deity in the form of the *brahmārpaṇa* sacrifice, and then praise and propitiate him.

Having first offered the *prasannārghya* (the water of grace) and having consecrated [the deity] with the water of grace, one should— by implication— offer the final *arghya*, bid farewell (*visarjayet*), and dismiss (*udvāsayet*) [the deity]. While remaining in that very place, one should either dismiss the installed *manna-liṅga* or dismiss it into one's own self.
Having thus described the worship with the palace-mantra (prāsādamantra),
he now describes the worship of the six-syllable mantra (ṣaḍakṣarapūjā), preceded by a restatement of the placement of the vital breaths (prāṇanyāsa).

The remainder [of the meaning] is that by means of the six-syllable mantra, there is a slight difference in the placement of the hands (*nyāsikara-nyāsa*), in worship (*arcana*), in the ritual of the deity’s form (*mūrti-pūjā*), and so forth. "In sequence" means [placing] the syllables of the mantra conjoined with the *bindu*, following those syllables of the *Māra* mantra and their corresponding *bindus*.
One should sequentially join the mantras of Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, and Īśāna— namely "Oṃ Tatpuruṣāya Namaḥ" and so forth— with the fingers of both hands simultaneously:
on the index, middle, little, and ring fingers, as well as on the two thumbs, in their respective order.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*). Here too, the meaning is that the limbs (*aṅga*) are to be placed as before, from the thumb to the palms. Having thus declared the various types of *nyāsa*, he describes the various types of worship (*saparyā*) with the words beginning "prāk" (*previously*), and concludes the worship with an explanation that is self-evident, stating: "this is the adoration enjoined by the scripture."
The sense is that this has been stated briefly in the root scriptures; its detailed exposition should be sought there.

Thus, one should perform this daily and in due order, beginning with the purification of the self (*ātma-śuddhi*) and following the prescribed sequence, as an obligatory rite like the *agnihotra* and other such rituals.
The meaning is that it must certainly be performed; once the mantra-liṅgas have been installed, one should perform [the rites] constantly and in their entirety.
Otherwise, because of the failure to dispel the spirits, there would be the risk of provoking the wrath of the Supreme Lord.

The sense is that a transgression occurs. Demonstrating the consequence when a fault arises regarding one worthy of worship, he concludes the chapter with the words "animitte" (in the absence of a cause). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "In the absence of a cause, because of the lack of fault, the worship would be nullified. If, however, a cause should arise, then it is appropriate.
"Only after performing the expiation (niṣkṛti) should one worship the Deity.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Tattvaprakāśinī*, a commentary on the *Kriyāsāra*.
Having thus described the daily worship (*nityapūjā*), [the author now addresses] the occasion for worship that arises due to occasional rites (*naimittika*) and the contingency of its omission.

In order to provide a remedy, he begins another chapter that sets forth the atonement for those [incidents], starting with the words "The causes," and so on. In the Śiva-āgama, many causes such as falling and other such ill omens (*durnimitta*) have been proclaimed. Here, by the word "falling" and the like, [the author refers to] the [loss of] the mantra-sign (*mantra-liṅga*).

The falling by chance, the perception of measurement, the falling from the self-established stone of the neuter, the falling from the vehicle of Kautuka, and the fall at that very moment and so forth are intended to be explained by means of the *tantra*. Who are those deities for whom there is falling and so forth? They are the "falling-and-so-forth" ones (*patanādyāḥ*). Who [is he]?

O best of instructors, when the causes such as phlegm, blood, and so forth arise within the body— having touched the objects of touch and other sensory domains— the relative strength or weakness of each respective humor (*doṣa*) is determined. Furthermore, O supreme one, [the teacher should consider] the intensity of the burning radiance and the nature of the primary and secondary symptoms.
p.
52) A teacher skilled in discernment should perform the pacification of that [transgression];
for in this matter, although the fault of both the locus and the occupant is transmitted to one another.

Nevertheless, it is said that when the locus (*sthāna*) is defective, purification must be performed for both; when the occupant (*sthānin*) is defective, purification of that [occupant] alone must be performed, because by the purification of that alone, the purification of both is accomplished. Thus, "in the locus" means in the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) and so forth.
When the area around the enclosure wall is defiled by the occurrence of death or birth, or corrupted by defects such as the spilling of blood,

one should perform the purification of the ground in the form of digging, the purification of the site, and the purification of the *liṅga* and the mantra in the form of washing and so forth. [Regarding the *liṅga*:]...
If [the site] is defiled, then immediately after the purification of the *liṅga*, purity will be achieved for the location as well merely by means of sprinkling and pouring out;
this is the remainder [of the sense]. He shows the sequence of the purifications under discussion:

Regarding "purification of the site" (*sthānaśuddhi*): the construction of the sentence is that first the purification of the site must be performed, and immediately after that, the purification of the *liṅga* must be performed;
this applies when the purification of the mantra and the *liṅga*—whether accompanied by digging and other rites or performed alone—has been completed.
Then, immediately thereafter, for the sake of purifying the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*),

one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites according to the prescribed rules for pacifying its defects, following the injunctions proclaimed by Śaṅkara and others; the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the specific procedures for that [purification].

53) One should perform that [rite] beginning with the water-pot; it enumerates the purification of the site for the preliminary work as "digging," and then analyzes it, stating "one should bring [the earth]" up until the end with the words "having fed the Brahmins."
Or, by means of the Abhirathya weapon, upon the utterance of the mantra,
one should dig a wicked spot measuring one man’s height or half of that (one cubit) deep.
Having cast the dust produced by the digging toward the southwest, one should burn it with *kuśa* grass.

The word "with the Astra-mantra" (astreṇa) is understood to carry over [from the previous verse]. Having cast fire there with the Astra-mantra and having consecrated it as a Mahilā, the intention is that one should place that fire in a pit. Regarding the phrase "with cow's urine" (gomūtraiḥ):
after the burning, having removed the ashes and so forth from that site, one should fill it with cow's urine; the particle "tu" (but/then) indicates this.
The proponent of division (Bhedavādin) maintains that there is a dissolution of the collyrium; however, when [the vessel] has been filled with cow urine and that has dissolved,

one should fill it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) accompanied by the Brahma-mantras, and having sprinkled everywhere— whether in that very place or elsewhere— with those [mantras], one should fill it again five times.

Having performed the ritual treading with cows, one should fill [the area] with cow-dung from the riverbank, from a field of *kuśa* grass, from an anthill, and so forth; and with eight kinds of dung produced from the middle of the river, from both banks, from the roots of *kuśa* grass, from an anthill, from a mountain, and from fire, as indicated by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*).
And with the two [mudras] born of the sacred ford and the ocean, one should fill [the vessel] thoroughly and most firmly with these ten types of earth. Thus (p.

Thus, according to the original layout, one should perform the procedure beginning with excavation as appropriate for the image (*bimba*), the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and the temple (*gṛha*) in their respective courtyards (*indrāṅkaṇa*).
Having performed everything from the excavation to the filling— without overstepping the principles regarding the relative strength or weakness of various defects— and having made [the site] firm;
One should fill the pit with earth using the feet of sacrificial elephants;

having pounded it while sprinkled with cow urine and likewise strengthened with the water from the feet of Brahmins— according to the method to be described later— and by the use of the word "ca" (and), [one should perform] the filling and the "dwelling for cows," which is the excellent *gonivāsana*.

And having performed it in that manner, he himself will state regarding the portion for Viṣṇu: "He should feed the Brāhmaṇas. Having thus acted and fed the Brāhmaṇas—at least eleven Brāhmaṇas, according to the Smṛti texts beginning with "ghee and milk-rice"—he should do these things.

Having fed [the guests] according to the rule by means of the word used by the proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*), and having fed them elsewhere in a place unfit for such a meal, the mere touching of their leavings and so forth is indicated;
and having constructed a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) there, it is called a "pavilion" according to the aforementioned method.
Having performed [the ritual] and smeared it with the *kavaca* mantra, immediately after purifying the remnants,

one should smear that spot with cow-dung water using the *kavaca* mantra for its protection; then, in the pavilion purified by the *gavya* and *aghora-astra* mantras, [one should proceed] with the products of the cow (*gavya*).

When [the site] has been purified by the Aghora-weapon mantra, this is an illustrative indication; for the purification of the location includes everything from the sweeping and so forth up to the worship of the Mantra-form, and likewise:

In the Pāśupata rite, having cleansed with the Aghora-weapon mantra and smeared with cow dung, one should scatter white mustard seeds; having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow, one should draw a lotus there and worship Śiva along with his limbs. Thus, having performed the purification of the site.
The linga should be purified according to the sequence of washing and so forth— namely, washing and immersion—
in accordance with the order that will be described immediately hereafter, performing the ritual washing with *darbha* grass,
clay, and cow-hair, and silently with water.

Having thoroughly purified [the site] according to the rites to be described immediately hereafter, such as *mārjana* (sprinkling) and so forth, one should cause the *śāntihoma* and other rituals— specifically those for pacifying defects of the location— as well as the *homa* prescribed by Śaṅkara, to be performed; the word "by the image-bearers" (*mūrtipaiḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

The purification of the *liṅga* through washing and other means is enumerated; he explains "washing" with the passage beginning with "washing" and ending with "the procedure for consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is thus remembered.
Regarding "washing," the connection is that it consists of silent washing with *darbha* grass, clay, cow-hide, and water.

The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Purification (*śodhana*)—meaning washing (*plāvana*)—is performed with scents, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), using non-mantric [substances], that is, without reciting Vedic mantras; this is the purification mentioned previously on page 56.

The previously mentioned [procedure] follows: with water containing *kūrca*-grass, as prescribed for the placement of vessels (*pātrasādana*), and with water combined with substances such as fruits, gold, and other common materials, one performs the worship of the bathing throne (*snānapīṭha*) accompanied by mantras, following the sequence beginning with the *agnīkaraṇa* rite, wherein the *kūrca*-grass has been placed according to the ritual order.

Preceded by the ritual procedures such as *sakalīkaraṇa*, at the time of bathing, one should perform the bath with the *praṇava* accompanied by the five *brahmans* and other [mantras] according to the rules; that which occurs here is the "bath," as established by the remainder of the sentence beginning with "yat tad iha snānam bhavet" through the syntactical structure of the second half of the verse, referring to the vessel of accomplished purpose (*siddhārtha-pātra*).

That which was stated in the *Uttamasādana*— namely, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites for the final preparation (*uttaśikaraṇa*)— is performed by not overstepping the logic prescribed in one's own ritual manual (*svasamṛti*), having first filled [the vessel] with water scented with perfumes, flowers, and unhusked rice (*akṣata*), according to the sense of the mantra "āpaḥ" (O Waters).
Then, having performed the preliminary part of the bath with the *kūrca* grass-bunches, one should again perform the *mārjana* (sprinkling) which is a constituent part of the bath;

for it is by the very statement "one should perform the *mārjana*, which is a constituent part of the bath" that the [verses] beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā* are joined with the traditional injunctions (*smṛti*).

The mantras for wiping have been indicated; having thus explained the purification, he explains the pouring of the stream with the passage beginning with "saṃsthāpya" and ending with "udvāsya varuṇaṃ punaḥ.
Regarding the word "saṃsthāpya," it refers to a vessel made of metal, belonging to Varuṇa—that is, having Varuṇa as its deity.
Having likewise placed the forms of cauldrons and so forth situated upon a heap of grain in the northeast (p. 57), one should install them accordingly.

Having properly established the water-vessel after performing the preliminary rites such as the worship of the *pīṭha* and the consecration of the vessel, and having filled it with auspicious waters purified by straining and other means along with a tuft of grass (*kūrca*),
[one should place] within this water two golden and silver fish and two tortoises.
Likewise, one should place a lotus pond complete with lotus stalks and flowers; and two fish and two tortoises,
both made of gold and silver— wherein, according to the double use of the particle "ca," the males are golden and the females are silver, and the pair of fish consists of one golden and one silver.

They collect [the materials]. Therein, having invoked Varuṇa at the sacred ford (tīrtha) by reciting the mantra beginning with "dhruvāsuti" and others, [one places him] upon three feet made of Palāśa wood or other such trees as have been procured from among the Palāśa, Pippala, and so forth.

The vessel made of iron with golden holes refers here to the fact that when gold is the primary material, silver is secondary; whereas when silver is the primary material, the state of having golden holes is secondary—the sense being that the golden vessel alone is primary. Having filled that vessel, one performs the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha) above the image.

At the time of the second bath obtained through the sequence beginning with the sakalīkaraṇa, one must perform an unbroken stream [of water] for the duration of a watch (yāma) day after day. He explains this with the words "having filled": *āpūrya...* etc.

"Accompanied by mantra" means: having taken water from the Varuṇa vessel with half a verse, one should fill this "stream-vessel" with the five tattvas while accompanied by mantra, preceded by the recitation of the root *praṇava*. He describes the method for the recitation during the stream [of water] with the words "pañca... [and so on], meaning "with darbha grass in hand."
With pavitra-grass in their hands, touching the vessel and the stream-vessel with darbha grass, remaining silent, their speech restrained from all that is not prescribed by mantra,
undisturbed, withdrawing their mental attention from other objects, they meditated upon the imperishable God.
The five mantras are, in sequence, the five Brahmans or the five principles (tattvas),
as taught in the scriptures according to the order of recitation; they are Vedic, as taught in the Śrīkaṇṭha-pāvamāna-mañjarī and other Āgamas.
And the Tantric mantras should be recited in their proper sequence— namely, the *Anuvāka*, the *Rudrasūkta*,
the *Śrīsūkta*, the *Pāvamāna*, the *Pauruṣasūkta*, the final *Anuvāka*, and so forth— without deviating from this order;
provided that the occasion for doing so arises until the end of the stream [of recitation].
"Having performed the appropriate expiation (*niṣkṛti*), one should then worship the deity," according to such injunctions,
the worship [performed] prior to the occurrence of the cause for interruption is prescribed to last until the end of the *dhārā* [offering] (p.

One should worship [the deity] again at the end of the stream on the first day; furthermore, since it is stated that "one should not [perform] the Vāruṇa vessel on the first day, but where it is recited for three nights," one should dismiss Varuṇa at the end of the stream on the third day, and thereafter perform his worship.

Immediately thereafter, one should perform the immersion (*avagāha*). He explains this immersion with the passage beginning with "the vessel" and ending with "the twice-born. Having determined the measure of the internal space according to the size of the *liṅga*, and having made the vessel the receptacle for immersion;
Having completed the worship of the *liṅga-pīṭha* and so forth, once again, when the rite of bathing is accomplished,

one should carefully and without negligence cover the *liṅga* with cloth and *darbha* grass; then, having placed a vessel that is free of cracks, one should fill it with the products of the cow (*gavya*), both individually and collectively, at the time of immersion.
He prescribes the mantras to be recited with the words beginning with "pañca" and ending with "śobhanam. The twice-born ones,

having sat down all around the *mantraliṅga*, [should recite] the five Brahma-mantras and the Śiva-mantras, along with their ancillaries (*aṅgas*), during the filling with cow-products and the filling with the individual and collective fragrances.
Or, within the five Brahmans, the limbs are likewise Vyomavyāpi Śiva; the meaning is that these are the limbs.
The ten-syllable [mantra] is Vyomavyāpi, the ten-syllable [mantra] is Śrīkaṇṭha, the three-syllable [mantra] is Nīlakaṇṭha, and Rudra is Śrīrudra. Furthermore, food is Śiva.
They should recite these [verses] beginning with *saṃkalpa*; here too, the phrase "one should worship the deity" is understood to follow. Thus, for seven days.

Having described the worship consisting of immersion for one *yāma* at a time, he explains the seventh purification, which takes the form of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), with the passage beginning "five" and ending with "is remembered.
[He describes] the five jars [to be filled] with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and so forth.

Having properly filled [the vessel] with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and the other items indicated by the word "etcetera," as well as water— preceded by the consecration of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), worship, and the ritual of the jar (*kumbha*)—
and having worshipped the Deity with perfumes and so forth along with the *brahmamantras*, one should consecrate it with the *brahmamantras*; the word "tu" (but/however) [indicates this].

This illuminates [the view] beginning with the Lord of Brahmā (Īśāna). Alternatively, the word "tu" (but/rather) indicates a different position; it illuminates that some authorities also remember the filling and worship (*pūraṇapūjā*) and so forth by means of the five *tattvas*. One should bathe the Deity with those very mantras that have been recited.

At the time of the second bath, one should bathe [the deity] in the reverse manner; having thus purified and worshipped according to the stated method, one should perform the prescribed expiation as proclaimed by Śaṅkara, and subsequently carry out the peace-offering (śāntihoma) which will be described immediately hereafter. Then, seven...
Immediately after purification, there is the recitation of the entire text (*pārāyaṇa*) according to the signs and according to the meaning.

By the statement, "One should perform the recitation of the entire Veda according to one's means," it is indicated that there would be the consequence of the Supreme Lord’s wrath if the *pārāyaṇa* were performed without a sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇa*). He then explains the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the production of the sacred fire (*sāgnijanana*) as previously taught by Śaṅkara, beginning with the words "of the house," and so forth.

Having completed [the ritual] up to that point, one should construct a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) resembling a crescent moon on the southern side— that is, the right side— of the house or palace; and having purified it through cleansing and so forth, as well as drying and so forth, one should [proceed] with the *vajra* mantra.

Having engraved [the seat] with the Vajra-mantra as taught in the Pāśupata and other traditions— "Hūṃ Phaṭ Kaṃ"— which is situated in the middle of the Tāra (Oṃ), one should sprinkle it with the Astra-mantra.
After the sprinkling upon the seat (viṣṭara), when the seat has been placed [there] with the Praṇava, [the deity] is installed upon that seat.

And on the yogic seat, one should visualize the goddess Umāśakti together with Bhuvaneśvarī, indicated by the word "and" (ca) in the left [hand]; the sense is that, having invoked her and performed the ritual identification (*sakalīkṛtya*), one should contemplate her according to the manner described in the passage beginning with "desiring pleasure" (*ratyarthinī*). One should also worship her with the *hṛdaya* mantra and the *aghora* mantra.

Having taken up the fire with the *sadyojāta* mantra and having recited the *śiva* mantra to expel the flesh-eating spirits (*kravyāda*), one should then recite the *śiva* and *īśāna* mantras for the sake of the refinement of the remaining [deceased], and combine them with the *aghora* mantra.
p.

62) Then, having cast [the fire] with the *sadyojāta* mantra, one should unite it with the *hṛdaya*, *aghora*, *śiva*, *īśāna*, and *varman* mantras; thus, in the ritual arrangement of the five limbs, there is the composition of the five mantras beginning with *īśāna*.

Having performed the five rites beginning with conception and ending with the naming ceremony— by means of the one called Vamadeva who has attained the state of all beings, by Aghora and Purusha, by Shiva, and by Ishana— and likewise [performed] the Shankara rite in the Pashupata system;

Having begun with the words "one should generate the fire," one should perform the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception) by means of the five [mantras] called Īśa, Vāma, Praśānta, Puruṣa, and Īśāna. Having thus performed the generation of the fire (*agnijanana*), one should proceed up to the end of the *agnimukha* (invoking the mouth of the fire).

Having performed [the preliminary rites]—as indicated by the word "and" (ca)—one should offer oblations of cooked food with the mouth, using fuel-sticks (*samidh*) made of *udumbara* and *mārga* wood, along with clarified butter as the sacrificial offering (*havis*).
One should perform the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) one thousand and eight times in sequence with these mantras: the Aghora, Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, and others.

Afterwards, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with these— sesame, mustard, mung beans, and *śāli* rice— using the face-mantra (*vaktramantreṇa*). Then, one should offer one thousand oblations with *dūrvā* grass using the face-mantra,
and one hundred and eight oblations of curd, honey, and ghee with the *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra.

"He brings it together" (*upasaṃharati*) means that one should conclude [the rite]; the meaning is that one should perform the ritual action ending with the consecration from the jar of its completion (p. 63). He shows the scope of the aforementioned expiation: "this" (*eṣā*).

In the case of death and other such events occurring in a temple dedicated to Madirā, and when defects such as birth, death, or bloodstains exist, this expiation is prescribed; and by the use of the word "ca" (and), it indicates that the pacification of dogs and so forth is also included. The term "liṅge" (in the liṅga) shows another form of purification concerning the *mantra-liṅga*. "Liṅge" means in the *liṅga*.

When there is contact with sweat and so forth— where "and so forth" refers to weeping, laughter, and the like— as well as when there is contact with a dog, a staff, or other such impurities, one should perform the purification of the *liṅga* through washing and other means in due order, and also perform the *śānti-homa*, as previously mentioned by Śaṅkara (indicated by the word "ca").

One should perform the *nandiprokta* and other rites; the preeminent teacher explains the *śāntihoma* with the passage beginning with "having performed" (*kṛtvā*) and ending with "for the pacification of all defects" (*sarvadoṣapraśāntaye*). In the northeast (*aiśānyām*), there is a square (*turyaśrakam*) and, as required by the sequence, an octagon (*aṣṭāśram*), ending with the removal of fear (*aśaṅkāśamanāntā*) and the square.
Having constructed such a specialized pit (kuṇḍa), one should properly generate the fire through the sixteen rites; subsequently, after the worship of the ritual jar (kalaśa) and so forth,
one should perform the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha) rite prior to the cooked oblation (pakvahoma).

It is cooked with the *pīṭha-mantras*, clarified butter, and the *vaktra-mantra*, and [consecrated] with the mantras for the worship of Brahmā and the others, as well as the *śambhu-pakṣa* and so forth.

One should offer ghee once with the prescribed *brahmans* (mantras) beginning with the word "Brahman. The fuel-sticks (*samidh*) produced from the *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, and *vaṭa* trees—meaning those made of *pippala* wood; the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is used here according to Vedic usage—and these should be offered one hundred and eight times with the first *vidyā*.

The phrase "the primordial knowledge" (*ādyavidyā*) is connected to each sentence: "non-food," "dūrvā grass sprinkled with honey," "parched grains" (*lājādi*), and so on; specifically, parched grain, mustard seeds, sesame, barley, rice, flour, and again clarified butter—these seven substances are [offered] with the primordial knowledge.

"One should perform the oblation thereafter" means that after the aforementioned oblations of the fourteen substances have been performed, one should offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation and complete the remainder of the *homa*. He concludes with the word "peace" (*śānti*). Thus [ends the section] concerning the locus and the presiding deity.

Having set forth the expiations, he now shows some expiations for those acts being performed that arise from negligence or unintentional causes, beginning with the verse "bhinne": when the full jar, having been consecrated for the ritual bathing, is broken.
Others, having filled a vessel and prepared another jar in its place, should fill it as before with the water from the shards of the broken jar, or in the absence of that, with other water,
and then perform one hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra, followed by the residual clarified butter (saṃpātājya).
Having touched the *kalaśa* (vase),
and having touched it while reciting the *huta-mantra*, one should mutter it as many times as the number of oblations; this is [the procedure].
The wise have prescribed expiation for the common jar (kalaśa) in the doctrine of the jar;
however, for the proponent of difference, it is taught that in the case of the destruction of the Brahma-jar and so forth, there is no [expiation] by means of sound alone.
Here, the performance of the five tattvas, the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), and other rites of atonement are indicated by the term "mantric calamity" (mantrotpāta).

Regarding the portents caused by mantras—such as the performance of deficient or excessive minor mantras—the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas), beginning with Ananta, are to be offered oblations; the meaning is that one should perform an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*) eight times eight in number for each of those beginning with Ananta. [The rest is] as before.

In the case of objects such as ritual offerings or other materials, or when there is an adverse omen, the oblation (*homya*) is to be performed on the left; in the absence of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the oblation is to be made with the *vajra* [mantra]. When clothing is burned, ten thousand (*ayuta*) oblations are to be offered with the *siṃhākṣurikā* mantra. This has been explained in the prose commentary (*nigada*).
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Tattvaprakāśinī*.
Having thus stated the incidental definition of atonement (*niṣkṛti*),

he makes his formal promise regarding what he intends to say— namely, the restoration of the worn-out (*jīrṇoddhāra*)— by means of half a verse that is self-explanatory; [he thereby establishes] the necessity of the restoration of the worn-out.

He says: "By the rite" (*vidhinā*) means characterized by the rite—namely, the means for achieving the Lord’s eternal and firm presence through meditation, consecration (*adhivāsa*), the ritual placement of life-force (*jīvanyāsa*), and so forth; it is that which has been established [as such] by this rite.
If the installed *liṅga* of Īśvara— which is of the nature of the *liṅga-śarīra*— or the *mantra-liṅga*,

which is of the nature of the gross body (*sthūla-śarīra*), or the temple (*geha*) or palace (*prāsāda*), should decay, then at that very moment, without wasting time, one should act according to the manner to be described immediately hereafter.
One should extract that [liṅga] from its sanctuary according to the prescribed rite; one should dig it up and replace it with another in that same location according to the rite.

For a mantra-liṅga installed by the Lord, there should be no removal without the prescribed rite, because in the absence of such a ritual separation, the liṅga becomes defiled and its unstable condition becomes the cause [of misfortune].

The sense is that the extraction [of the deity] must certainly be performed for the sake of pacifying anger. In this regard, he first demonstrates the extraction during the decay of the temple with the passage beginning "In the directions of Indra and Īśāna" and ending with "one should perform the ritual bath," [specifying] from the outside of the enclosure wall and from the outside of the central gateway.

In a house previously constructed with spacious chambers divided in proportion to the main temple, one should fashion a new small shrine using the same proportions as the elements (bhūtāṃśaiḥ); according to this principle,
its door should face the door of the main temple.
The door facing the main sanctuary is for that very reason of a different origin;
in front of it is a small wooden house, auspicious and square in its center.

Having constructed the pavilion according to rule, complete with a railing, banners, arches, sacrificial pits, and so forth— ensuring that it does not deviate from what is proper or improper— and then, following the rites of sowing the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), the preliminary consecration of the small image (*alpa-bimba*), and the ritual bathing (*jalādhivāsana*), one should duly prepare the house, which is a small temple.

Having purified the pavilion— whether it be a *maṇḍapa* or a *mallamaṇḍapa*— together with its enclosure, beginning from the wrapping of threads up to the conclusion of the *vāstu-juṣṭi* rite, and including the procedures for the water-pot and the ascetic, as well as the ritual for the destruction of demons (*rakṣoghna*) and so forth in the main temple;
Having established the presence of the Lord as a *liṅga* at the root of Śiva,
and having thoroughly purified him through the seven purifications, expiatory rites, ablutions, and the consecration with the jar of nine substances, one should worship him.
Having worshipped the attendants in each respective main temple and offered them oblations,
and having made a request with the words "May they listen" and so forth,
the Guru should prepare a svastika in a small pavilion there and spread out a bed upon it.

Having fashioned the *liṅga* or a small *liṅga* according to the rules, characterized by the prescribed rites such as the preliminary immersion in water (*jalādhivāsa*) and so forth, [one should perform the consecration] with the jars and other vessels, specifically those jars for the purification of the image (*bimba*).

Having purified it with the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) and other rites indicated by the word "and so forth," and having placed it upon the bed according to the rules, one should cause the previously mentioned combined inner-liṅga to lie thereon; [this refers to] the deity.

The supreme practitioner, with great effort, having propitiated the deity residing in the main temple— characterized by efforts such as the preparation of abundant offerings in order to ensure that future worship will not be interrupted for a long time— should [place] an image made of iron, gold, or the finest gold before the deity.

One should prepare a vessel made of iron that has been purified through washing with mantras and the like, as well as properly consecrated by drying and other rites, and by the placement of *darbha* grass; therein, one should place a bundle of *kūrca* grass consisting of *dūrvā* and *kuśa*, along with precious gems.
One should fill [the vessel] with filtered [water] using the root mantra;
first, having cast into the jar— which is of the nature of the Suṣumṇā and the form of the deity— the unbroken *kūrca* with the syllable Om (*praṇava*),
and having cast *dūrvā* grass, *kuśa* grass, and gems while regarding them as the living soul (*jīva*).
The sense is that immediately after fulfilling the mental [offering], one should fill [the vessel] with filtered water while reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).

By the word "should fill" (*pūrayet*) itself, the present well-known procedure—including the worship (*pūjā*), the invocation of the form (*mūrti-āvāhana*), the invocation of the mantra (*mantra-āvāhana*), and so forth—is merely restated here. "In this way" (*evam*) means in this manner.
Having performed the placement of the water-pot (kalaśa-sādana) for the purpose of dismissal, one goes outside (p.
proceeds to the front pavilion of the small shrine (bālālaya) constructed outside the temple, and [approaches] the Liṅga.
One should purify that small liṅga which has been shadowed [with sandalwood paste] through the sequence of the withdrawal of the principles (tattvasaṃhārakrama);

having purified it again by means of drying and other rites, having established the principles, generated them, and performed the placement (nyāsa), and after performing protection, the invocation of the mantra, worship, and so forth—
Having performed the protection ritual, one should go outside. Then, regarding the commencement of the dismissal (*udvāsana*), it is said:

"The performer" means he should ask the performers about the time limit; what is told by them, he should report that to the deity—this is the ellipsis. He now indicates the mantra for requesting permission for that:

Saying "O Blessed One," and having informed the Lord of Gods with the passage beginning with "he states the manner of dismissal" and ending with "one should worship," one should give gold, garments, and so forth to them according to one's capacity;
then, with effort, as in the statement beginning with "just as in the worship of the deity," one should apply diligence.
Relying on the request of the Brahmins in the form of the words "Let it be done with your permission," and then,

together with the deities such as the guardians of the field (*kṣetrapāla*) and the retinue of offering-deities (*baliparivāra-devatā*), having withdrawn the *tattvas* by means of the fire-oblation (*homa*) of the withdrawal-*tattva* (*saṃhāra-tattva*) and so forth;
Having placed the entire collection of principles that constitute the body of the mantra, together with the retinue of deities, into the *liṅga*,
and having preceded this with the sprinkling from the vessel of the principle of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-tattva*);

Having contracted this [universe] within the *liṅga-śarīra*, one should know that the Supreme Lord residing in the *liṅga* is of the nature of the Śiva-tattva, [recited] with the *praṇava* at the beginning and end, and encapsulated by the *praṇava*.
"Enlightened by Bindu, Nāda, and Anta" means: by Bindu, which is the Lord of the Worlds (*bhuvanapati*) in the form of the *bindu*; by Nāda, which is the *prāsāda* mantra;
and by Ananta, which is the five-syllabled mantra situated within the *prāsāda* of the power of the *praṇava*—that is to say, by the eight-syllabled mantra of Śiva. By these, they are enlightened.
The meaning is "by those [mantras] joined together. By means of such five Brahmans, one should perform the rite of invocation;

the intention is that one should invoke [the deity] from the root-liṅga into the frontal kalaśa and so forth, according to the principle of invoking the *jīva* (life-principle). Here, by the word "rite" (*vidhi*), the traditional method is intended.

The specific procedure for that is indicated: having invoked [the deity] into the jar in this manner, and having performed the traditional placement of the five mantras (*pañcamantranyāsa*) and so forth, the Guru should worship it after performing the ritual integration (*sakalīkṛtya*) preceded by the invocation of the mantras; thereafter, following the protection of the primary image (*mūlabimba*), he should perform that [ritual].
Having dressed [the deity] in fine garments and wrapped the pitcher with two cloths, he should take it up, remain silent, and remembering Śiva, go outside the temple.
Having circumambulated the main shrine and the small pavilion, he should lead it there.
Then one should place the *kalaśa* upon the bed, and subsequently install the Lord of Devas in the previously consecrated *liṅga*, whether it be a small *liṅga* or a *kalaśa*.

Having worshipped in due order at the *jīvakalaśa* and, by the force of the word "and" (*ca*), at the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the guardians of the images (*mūrtipās*) and the preceptors (*ācāryas*) should all perform the *adhivāsa* oblation.
He describes the procedure for the installation of a small *liṅga* with the verse beginning "the house" (*geham*) and ending with "not indeed thus" (*naiva tviti*).

Having purified the small house according to the rules together with the fire-oblation (*homasaṃyuta*), and having performed the ritual procedure ending with the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day) rite for the site (*vāstu-puṇyāha*), then,
immediately after the consecration of the pedestal (*pīṭhapratiṣṭhā*) and so forth, [one should install] the Deity in that small house.
One should cause the form consisting of the *lapa*, *liṅga*, *jīva*, *kalaśa*, and so forth to enter; at the auspicious moment (*muhūrta*), one should install and consecrate the *liṅga*.

One should unite that which resides in the *kalaśa* with that *liṅga*; and at the time of the invocation of the life-force (*jīvāvāhana*), one should sprinkle it with the waters of life (*jīvādbhiḥ*). In this manner, one should perform the union according to the stated procedure.

Then, at the conclusion of the rite for the invocation of the life-force (*jīvāvāhana*), having performed the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*), the invocation of the mantras (*mantrāvāhana*), their subsequent placement (*tannyāsa*), and so forth, one should worship again,
including the arrangement of the retinue (*parivārakalpanā*) and other rites up to the ceremonial bath on the fourth day.

He states that one should perform [the rite] according to the principle of the first consecration (*prathamapratiṣṭhā*) in the passage beginning with "the retinue" (*parivārān*) and ending with "but by the very rule" (*vidhinaiva tu*), a text which is self-explanatory (*nigadavyākhyāna*).
Having thus described the procedure for the exit (*niṣkrāmaṇaprakriyā*), he now demonstrates the method for leading [the deity] to the primary abode (*mūlālayapraṇayanaprakāra*).
By the phrase ending with "according to the household practice" (p.
it means that the house should be constructed by artisans according to the rules, starting from the previously determined site, shape, and so forth.

Not deviating from the principle of conceptualization, having established that [mind] as "the liberated one," and without wasting time on minor distractions such as entering [the dwelling], he should— with effort—
avoid fragments of potsherds, rags, and so forth as prescribed by the Teacher, and perform cleansing and other such acts.
Having thoroughly purified the primary residence— the main temple— through activities such as washing, and having cleansed the *liṅga* through washing, immersion, and so forth,

as well as the deity residing in the small shrine by means of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), the bathing of the image (*biṃba*), the consecration with the ritual jar (*kalaśābhiṣeka*), and other rites of cleansing and flooding; and having likewise purified the deity in the small temple...

In due order— namely, the purification of the temple (*prāsada-śuddhi*), the purification of the image (*bimba-śuddhi*), the sequential purification (*krama-śuddhi*), the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the principles of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-tattva*), and the cutting of the thread (*sūtra-ccheda*) according to the sequence to be described hereafter— one should invoke [the deity] into the jar (*kalaśa*), and by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), also into the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) and the original temple (*mūla-prāsāda*), as well as the mantra-liṅga of the vital principle (*jīva-kalaśa*).
Having accepted [the invitation], on the following day, after performing the preliminary rites such as the dismissal [of the deity],

and following the visualization for the installation of the primary *liṅga*, one should consecrate the deity residing in the *jīva-kalaśa* with *jīva*-waters, according to the prescribed method at the time of the invocation of the *jīva*.

One should apply [the ritual] to the primary liṅga. Then, having performed everything— including the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) as proclaimed by Śaṅkara and so forth (the word "and so forth" indicating the *tattvahoma* and other rites)—
for three nights with oblations, gifts, and the like;
Having led [the deity] forth on the fourth day in due order, one should perform the bathing of the God with power (*śakti*) using seventeen substances;
thus it is said that one should carry out the ritual ablution (*snapana*). In this manner—

Having described the restoration of a dilapidated temple (*prāsādajīrṇoddhāra*), he now demonstrates the restoration of a dilapidated image (*biṃbajīrṇoddhāra*) with the passage beginning with "the *liṅga*" and ending with "by means of salutation, prayer, and so forth.
If the *liṅga* should become dilapidated, even in that state, by means of the procedure for cutting the thread (*sūtrachedavidhāna*), [one should act].

Having also offered oblations to all the *tattvas*— the word "also" (*api*) implying that one should likewise offer to Vāstoṣpati and others— and having performed [the rite] in this manner, namely by following the procedure described for the consecration of a temple (*prāsāda*), one should perform the installation of the small liṅga (*alpa-liṅga-pratiṣṭhā*) beginning with the worship of the Jīva and ending with the consecration of the Jīva-vessel (*jīva-kalaśa-abhiṣeka*).

And this [phrase] "having made it equal to the previous" is connected with the subject whose rite has not yet been commenced; the intermediate sentence beginning with "having invoked into oneself" and ending with "by oneself alone" is intended to show a specific method for cutting the thread. Regarding the word "having invoked," that reality [is to be invoked] into that *liṅga*.

Having first performed the rites of the *dūrvā* grass, the peace-vessel (*śāntikalaśa*), and the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one should invoke that form which consists solely of the impressions of the established reality (*sthitatattvāvāsanāmātrarūpa*) into one's own essential nature (*svasvarūpa*) abiding within the orb of the sun; then, having become Caṇḍeśvara himself, [one should worship] that *liṅga*.
Having produced [the water] according to the prescribed rite and placed it in a cart, he had the water carried by two bulls;
then, after performing the worship of Pīṭhāra and other preliminary rites, [he installed] Caṇḍeśvara.
Reciting that mantra, one should then cast [the items] into the water. Thereafter, following the ritual bathing, libations, and so forth, having bathed, one should go to the house—the primary temple.
There, one should either personally offer the gems that were placed there, or [they may be offered] by oneself. Thus it is said. Now:

One should demonstrate the consecration, installation, and the restoration of the life-force (jīva-pratyarpaṇa) for the manifested root-liṅga according to the previously stated method, by performing the rites beginning with "having made the liṅga equal to the former," and one should also cause all the remaining expiations to be performed.

By the passage beginning with "with effort" and ending with "thus explained by the recitation," he shows the restoration of a worn-out seat (*pīṭha-jīrṇoddhāra*) through the section starting with "when the seat is worn out" and ending with "by means of prostrations, prayers, and so forth. When the seat is worn out, [one should restore] that which resides therein...

Having performed the ritual for the dissolution of the pedestal (pīṭhasaṃhāra) by following the prescribed procedures— including the oblation of the principles of withdrawal (saṃhāratattva) as taught in the *Prāsādajīrṇa*, the consecration of the jar (kalaśābhiṣeka), meditation, and the contraction [of the deities]— one should [offer] the five principles ending with *huṃ phaṭ* individually.
Having first performed the offering of the descent of the Siddhas (*siddhasaṃpāta*), one should unite the Śakti residing there on the pedestal with the Deity;

then, having invoked the Deity into that jar, worshipped Him, and performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) in the pavilion—and by the word "and" (*ca*), following the abandonment of the dilapidated pedestal—thereafter... *ga* [the ritual continues].

Having purified this seat by means of washing and other rites, and having consecrated it—whether through water-consecration (*jalādhivāsa*) or without such consecration—it is rendered ritually prepared.
Having carefully and with vigilance established a new pedestal according to the method prescribed for consecration, one should perform the consecration with that *jīvakalaśa* (life-pitcher),
thereby [consecrating] the Śakti residing in the pedestal according to the rules, without deviating from the previously mentioned procedure for the consecration of the pedestal.

Having established [the deity] through the lineage and having performed the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandha*), one should worship according to the ritual procedure (*kalpavartman*). Then, preceded by the statement of the logic of consecration (*pratiṣṭhitanyāyokti*), there is the concluding propitiatory oblation (*upasaṃhārakaśāntihoma*) and so forth. Thus...
Having presented the act of exiting as independent of the consecration of the child's abode,

he now demonstrates the procedure for the temple-palace (*prāsāda*) which pertains to the commencement [of construction] and is independent of the exit, beginning with the words "when the house is old. Now, when the house is old, O Lord of Gods, the deities— the attendant deities— [depart].

Having properly joined all the principles (tattvas) together, and having drawn them in through contraction and other means by performing the fire-oblations of the principle of reabsorption (saṃhāra-tattva), one should either join them and then perform the ritual of contraction (saṃkoca).

He brings it together [under the heading] "the restoration of the decayed. Here, the mention of "in brief" (samāsena) is for the purpose of indicating that the [details regarding] the words, the essence, the fire-oblation, the meditation, and the contraction are to be understood from other scriptures. Regarding what should be done after that in the case of a *liṅga* installed in a small temple, he says:

Regarding "in a small shrine": even if it is located in a small shrine, if the *liṅga* is made of stone, one should cast it into the water; if it is made of wood, one should burn it. In this case as well, p.

He states that the activity consists precisely in pleasing the Guru and so forth: by the half-verse beginning with "the Guru," he demonstrates the superiority of the restoration of an old [temple] over its initial consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) in order to incite one toward that undertaking; thus, it is prescribed by the root scripture (*mūlāgama*).
Having described the restoration of dilapidated temples and other structures,

he now demonstrates the procedure for the eight types of binding (*aṣṭabandha*), which is to be inferred by an analogous method, through the composition of the text from here until the end of the chapter. Thus, [the eight].

Just as the destruction of the binding (bandha) leads to the occurrence of bile-fever, he states the necessity of that [binding] through the context of the omission of worship, by means of such statements as:
"The eightfold binding is the cause of causes for the omission of worship," and so forth.

He says that for one whose worship is being brought to completion by the wearing away of the eight bonds, the state of being asura—the root of all misfortune—would follow due to the lack of acceptance by the Lord; thus he says, "When that has disintegrated.
In the phrase *tadviśīrṇe*, the suffix *kta* denotes the state (*bhāve*), meaning "in its disintegration. This demonstrates the eightfold bond.

From the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) up to the end of the passage "and one should perform the ritual bathing" (*snapanaṃ ca samācaret*), the meaning is as follows: "Therefore" means because such an occurrence arises from the *rakṣas* and the *praṇava*, etc. In that regard, however, according to the *Aṣṭabandha-nibandhana*, there is partial destruction (*ekadeśanāśa*) by means of the appropriate [remedy], and total destruction (*sarvanāśa*).

The meaning is that [the defect] would be subject to destruction over a long period of time. Regarding the word "nālam": having thoroughly purified it with effort—effort consisting of the removal of the eight ancient bonds (*bandha*) and so forth—preceded by the offering of the oblation of the power of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-śakti-homa*) and its dedication.
77) "Therefore, having dissolved [the deity] and purified the stalk (*nāla*), should one begin the fire-offering (*homa*) rite?

Here, the statement regarding the commencement of the *homa* immediately after the purification of the stalk is intended to indicate that the *homa* must be performed following that specific sequence.
In order to declare that the separate performance of the *sṛṣṭi* (emission) and *saṃhāra* (reabsorption) oblations is primary,
he explains the oblation with the words beginning with "having performed" (*kṛtvā*) and ending with "the *sviṣṭakṛt* and so forth.
He demonstrates the procedure for the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandha*) with the word "the seat" (*pīṭham*), [referring to its worship] with scents, flowers, and other offerings.
Having recited the mantras in sequence from Ādhāraśakti up to the Universal Aggregate (Samaṣṭi),

and immediately after the formal worship of the pedestal (pīṭha), having envisioned the totality of Nature (Prakṛti) as the manifest Śakti invoked upon the Śakti-pīṭha, and having worshipped her according to the prescribed rites beginning with the water for the feet (pādya) and ending with the bath (snāna).

Having invoked the deity and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should worship up to the conclusion of the bath; then, having performed the *nāndīmukha* rite according to one's capacity, and having placed the eight-fold bond (*aṣṭabandha*), sand, cloth, and so forth— where "and so forth" refers to gems, gold, and the like— in close proximity, one should set them down.
One should perform the *puṇyāha* rite as part of the bathing ceremony;

after the *puṇyāha*, having offered the remaining offerings such as garments and so forth, one should worship [the deity]. This is stated by the passage beginning with "with scents" (*gandhaiḥ*) and ending with "together with gold" (*sasuvarṇakaiḥ*). One should [worship] the stalk—the opening of the pedestal—with the root mantra, together with gold.
Having filled it with sand, one should consecrate the pedestal and the *liṅga* with perfumes—the eight fragrances—using the root mantra and the six-syllabled *śakti*-seed mantra.
Having respectfully anointed [the seat], one should cover the pedestal and the deity with two unwashed garments;

this is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) that includes the offering of all remaining articles from ornaments up to the lamps, and it demonstrates the preparation of the materials for the eightfold binding (aṣṭabandha).

Up to the words "it might be so in the case of conch," [the text explains]: conch, gold, and *abhayā* lac are, respectively, six, four, and one part. "Six parts" means that of which there are six parts; thus, gold is four parts, and *abhayā* is two parts.

Lac is one part. Cotton, stone, and sand—each of these is equal in measure to the lac. *Dhātrī* is equal to one part of lac; this means it consists of a single portion. Having made all the aforementioned substances into a paste, one should grind them together with oil.

One should know that this collection of substances for the oil consists of the nine powers (*nava-śakti*), combined with the *saṃpāta* [offering]. Having purified this by means of *dhāraṇā* and other practices, and having worshipped it with the *praṇava*, one should offer this *saṃpāta* along with the powers (*śakti*).

Having recited [the mantras] with the nine powers, the root mantra, the root of Prakṛti, the Lord of Beings as the root of the God, and the six-syllabled mantra, and having given gifts according to his capacity, the person and Prakṛti— both of whom are eternal— as well as Time, [should worship] the God and the Goddess according to the rule and according to their own nature.
Having meditated upon the God and likewise the Goddess according to the prescribed rules beginning with "sattama" (p. 79), and recollecting the God and the Goddess with his intellect;

Recalling them as being mutually integrated through the relationship of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the object to be supported (*adhiṣṭheya*), by means of the powers (*śakti*) and the root mantra—the previously mentioned [procedure] is understood to follow here. The meaning is that one should deposit this [mudrā] during an auspicious moment (*sulagna*) with those [mantras]. Reciting "That [is] Dhruva... up to Dyaus," one should make it very firm.
Then, having performed the gentle rites, followed by the pervasive *praṇava*,

the visualization of mutual union, the invocation of the mantra, the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*), and so forth, one should properly install the deity together with his retinues and attendants.

One should worship the Brahmins according to the method shown in the *Pratiṣṭhāsamaya*, and feed all castes, including those possessing all knowledge; [this is done] for one's own sake, with the suffix *taddhita*. The phrase "one should feed food" (*annādyaṃ bhojayet*) is understood to carry over. Again, by the rule of the *Pratiṣṭhā*.
He says that one should perform the bathing and other rites on the fourth day with the words "prāyaścittādikam" (expiatory rites, etc.).

He states that these are not required with the word "etad" (this). With the words "kuṇḍānām" (of the sacrificial pits) and so forth, the wise one [the author] states that there is no requirement for the definitions of the sacrificial pits and other such details that were not mentioned due to brevity or omission.
With the words "itthantena" (up to this point), he concludes the procedure for the eightfold binding with the phrase "aṣṭabandham" (the eightfold binding).
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Tattvaprakāśinī*, a commentary on the *Kriyāsāra*.
Having thus explained the incidental rites of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and the restoration of a dilapidated temple (*jīrṇoddhāra*),
one should spend three nights performing fire-offerings (*homa*), gifts (*dāna*), and so forth, and on the fourth day, proceed in due order according to one's capacity.

Intending to state the summary of the subject matter already introduced— beginning with "one should prepare the bath for the deity with seventeen substances" and so forth— he reveals what he wishes to say by first making a formal promise, from the words "Now,
as for the bath" up to "with seventeen substances. Now, as for the bath:

The connection here is as follows: having made the formal promise "I shall explain," on the fourth day— the day of the bathing ceremony for the trident-bearing God of gods who has been installed— one should perform the ritual bath according to the rules with seventeen substances, using one's capacity regardless of whether it is sufficient or not.

By the word "śaktyā" (according to one's capacity), the necessity of performing the ritual bathing on the fourth day is indicated. For this very reason, it is implied that even for one who possesses the requisite capacity, the bathing with twenty-five substances here is not to be considered a transgression. He introduces the general principle of filling the jars with the words beginning with "kramāt" (in sequence).
Up to the words "the jars as well," one should sequentially clean the pavilion starting from the wrapping with thread and ending with the cleansing of the jars;
then, having laid out the squares (padāni), one should prepare a pedestal (pīṭha) in these squares using grains. One should [also purify] the jars and the ritual substances with the Astra-mantra.
Having purified [the site] by means of the sprinkling of weapons (*astraprokṣaṇa*) and other rites (p.
one should establish it within, then externally for the human [level], and likewise in the middle for the divine [level], in due order.

One should properly fill the jars according to the sequence to be described, filling them preceded by the rites such as the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the consecration of the jars (*kumbha-saṃskāra*). He begins to state the specific procedure for the bathing with the seventeen substances, starting with the words "yadā" (when). Therein, [he refers to] that which was previously introduced...

He states the arrangement of the squares: "In the twenty-fivefold city," that is, in a field consisting of twenty-five compartments, one should draw six lines each running eastward and six lines each running northward, thereby forming twenty-five squares; there, in the center...

Likewise, having laid out a *nāṭaka* (checkerboard) and an *aṣṭaka* (octagon) on all sides— by arranging one square each in the eight directions outside the *navaka* (nine-square grid) and collectively forming an *aṣṭaka*— one should erase the remaining eight intermediate squares; in those squares, [one should place] rice grains.

Having prepared a pedestal, one should arrange the *darbha* grasses. Having thus explained the words "I shall describe the steps," he introduces the explanation of the words "the materials" with the statement, "one should fill the jars afterwards. Therein, he first demonstrates the consecration of the jar (*kuṃbha*).

From the words "washed" (*kṣālitāni*) up to "one should place the brushes in sequence" (*kūrcān nyaset kramāt*), the meaning is self-evident; now he summarizes the filling of the substances with the word "then" (*tataḥ*). "Then," having had the substances to be described brought by the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipaiḥ*).

82) One should fill [the vessel] with water that is both fit and unfit for use. Then, regarding the method for procuring water in order to complete what remains of that, he says—from "In the northeast" up to "one should recite the mantra."

One should consecrate [the water] with the mantra beginning with "imā āpaḥ" (these waters), etc.; this is the implied meaning. Regarding the phrase "with that": one should fill the jars while reciting the aforementioned mantra, reciting the mantra mentioned in another Smṛti which states: "For filling and for the arrangement of substances, the five-syllabled mantra is prescribed. One should thus fill the jars while reciting that mantra.
Īśāna, Sāvitrī, Rudra, Hutāśana,

Skanda, Dhanada, the seven Ṛṣis, Jambhaka, Antaka, and Varuṇa— these are indeed proclaimed as the deities of the oceans; they should be remembered in their respective order during the arrangement of ritual materials.

Some say that one should fill the jars while reciting the mantras of the deities mentioned for the purpose of arranging the ritual substances, beginning with "the deities in the jars," etc.; [one should use] either the five-syllabled *prāsāda* mantra or any one of the five *brahma* mantras as the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) prescribed for stability.
Some say it is Japan.
Then, having placed the "sleep-pitcher" (nidrākumbha) at the location of the head, one should fill it with water using the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā";
others say this refers to the previously mentioned mantra. In this matter, one should adhere to what is explicitly stated in the text.
Having thus summarized the filling [of the pitchers], he summarizes the worship with the words "pūritāni" and so forth.
With the words ending in "pūjayet," he explains the filling of the Brahma-vase; with the words ending in "madhye naivedyakaiḥ kramāt," [he explains the subsequent rites].
Having first placed an excellent *kūrca* (seat-grass bundle) woven with twenty-five blades of *darbha* grass,
one should place it in the center of the area of the central jar, which is filled with gold, jewels, and scented water.

Situated in the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus, consisting of all mantras for the sake of one's own purification, it is composed of the threefold energy (tejas) and the four-syllable solar mantra and others—
all being of the nature of every mantra; therefore, it is mobile and supreme among all.
The meaning is that it has a form consisting of a body contrary to the Supreme Lord.
One should fulfill that [mandala] according to the rules, without deviating from the procedures for fulfilling the mental [aspects] and so forth.

Regarding the word "tasmin" (in that): it refers to that which has the yogapīṭha and so forth as its beginning; the suffix -tasi is used here in the sense of the locative case, meaning "in that which has the yogapīṭha and so forth as its initial [element]," wherein the yogapīṭha is first worshipped as one's own support.

Alternatively, the meaning is: having performed the drawing of the lotus-seat (*lipikamalamaya-yogapīṭha*) prescribed immediately after the filling (*pūraṇa*), as well as the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, by means of the form (*mūrti*) indicated by the word "and the rest" (*ādi*).
In that sense, the suffix *-tasi* is used in the sense of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) with the elision of the ablative particle (*lyap*). In such a *śiva-kuṃbha* (auspicious jar), [one should act].

Having worshipped the God of gods with offerings beginning with perfumes and ending with food oblations, and having recited [the mantra] while touching the water-pot, one should recite the root-mantra one thousand and eight times; then, having obtained permission from the Lord of Gods, one should fill the other pots in sequence.
He explains this with the passage beginning "pañcagavyam" (p. 84) and ending with "pūrayet kramāt. Here, by the word "krama" (sequence), both the external and the internal [are intended].
The clockwise sequence beginning with the east is intended; thus, in the *Pāśupata* [tradition]:

"Outside, in the east, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and in the southeast, milk," and so on, starting from "sweet water" up to "water with *darbha* grass," [is arranged] in a clockwise direction.

With the portion of the text ending with "pūrayet" (he should fill), it was stated; now, by the verse beginning with "kṣāram," he causes one to remember the worship preceded by the counting of the oceans. Having made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpya*) regarding the waters of the ocean—which are difficult for ordinary people to procure—he [should perform the rite] with the water of Varuṇa as a substitute for them.

The intended meaning is that one should worship after having filled [the vessel]; he states that one should employ auspicious sprouts and so forth therein with the words "Then the path" (*tato vīthī*). While introducing the arrangement of substances, mantras, and so forth not previously mentioned, he [concludes] the current topic of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) and the fire-oblation (*homa*).
He elaborates [the ritual] from the words "Then he performs the oblations" (*prapañcayati tato homān*) up to "are proclaimed" (*parikīrtitā*). Then the Guru,
surrounded by the *mūrtipas* (guardians of the forms) in the directions starting from the east,
[should worship] with the *Tatpuruṣa-sūkta* and those [mantras] denoted by the word "etcetera," namely Aghora and Sadyojāta.

And with the Vāmadeva hymns in the corners—in the corners starting from the southeast—and with the heart-mantra and those indicated by the word "etcetera," namely the crest (*śikhā*), armor (*kavaca*), and head (*śiras*) mantras, [one should worship] everywhere.
One should cause the oblations (*homa*) to be performed with the limbs of Brahman, beginning with *Sarvajña*, after having performed the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*) in sequence;
the preceptor himself should perform [the rite] with the *Īśāna* [mantra] and the *Īśāna-sūkta*.
According to the meaning of another Smṛti text stating "in the fire-pit of the Guru or of Nāgeśa," this refers to the fire-pits in the various directions.

Regarding the question of how the directional arrangement is established when only the indicative marks—the Tatpuruṣa and others in the corners, and the Hṛdaya and others—are mentioned, he says: "The worship... [is as follows]. The directional arrangement of the mantras is proclaimed according to the sequence of worship; this has been clearly stated in the Muktāgama—this is the ellipsis. In whichever direction...

The meaning is that whichever mantra is prescribed for the worship (pūjā), that very same one is proclaimed for the fire-oblation (homa) in that direction.
