"Cooked" means having offered the cooked food with the Gāyatrī; then, after the aforementioned worship and oblation performed with clarified butter using the mantras for the worship of Brahmā and the others once each, [one should proceed] with these.
One should shake [the vessel] in sequence with the substances to be mentioned according to the order of recitation; he enumerates the substances, beginning with *samit*.

He arranges the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) in the directions starting from the east, beginning with *pālāśī*. Here, it should be understood that the *pālāśī* fuel-stick is for the teacher’s fire-pit (*ācāryakuṇḍa*). He states the number of oblations (*homasaṃkhyā*):

"One hundred and eight" means: one should perform [the rite] separately one hundred and eight times, offer oblations separately, and present the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). He recalls the mantra for the final oblation:
"Vyoma"—that is the *pūrṇāhuti*; it is proclaimed to be performed with the ten-syllable mantra of Vyomavyāpin.
(As stated on p.
86) "by us previously" is the ellipsis to be supplied. He describes the correspondence between the oblations and the pitchers:
"of the pitchers," etc. When there is a multiplicity of pitchers, a multiplicity of oblations is desired; in this regard—
In the present case, whether there are seventeen or twenty-five [deities], one should prepare only a single water-pot (*kalaśa*).

He abbreviates the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*): having offered the *sampāta* oblation, having unified the pots, and having purified them through the sequence beginning with the collection of the principles (*tattvasambhāra*), they become pure.

Having sprinkled [the deity] with the *saṃpāta* ghee using the mantra beginning with "bhavantu," and having again worshipped that deity— whether he has returned to his inner main temple or is present there before one’s own face or in a portable image (*kautuka*)—
and having bowed to him while characterized by the *añjali* mudrā, [one worships] the deity...

One should make a formal request (*vijñāpayet*). Regarding the mantra for the request, he says: "Having made the request to the Lord of Gods with the words 'O Adhivāsa' and so forth, and having performed dance and song outside, one should pass the night while remaining awake," according to the stated method; then, having passed the night, at the conclusion of the kindling of the sacred fuel (*samidh*) on the following morning—

Having obtained the permission of the twice-born— the reciters of the *pārāyaṇa*, the astrologers (*mauhūrtika*), and others— the learned man, together with the *mūrtipas* (image-keepers) who carry the lamps and the consecrated water-pots, and being fully cognizant of the sequence of rites to be performed on the day of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) and the day of the ritual bath (*snapana*).
One should begin the ritual bathing.
87) Regarding the word "anna": having entered within, [one should obtain] permission from the doorkeeper.
Having first opened the door by means of muttering the seed-syllable of the "knowledge-wind" (*jñānavāyu-bīja*),
he entered openly within, removed the floral offerings (*nirmālya*), and then,
having anointed [the image] with a jar of appropriate oil and washed it, he performed the application of *śirīṣa* powder and other ointments.

Having first thoroughly washed and worshipped [the image], and having offered milk-rice (pāyasa)— this being the implied meaning— thereafter, one should perform the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha) and so forth according to the rules,
accompanied by the appropriate rites; then, having respectfully performed the placement of the principles (tattva-nyāsa), one should perform the placement of the mantras (mantra-nyāsa) in due order.

Having prepared the water for washing the feet (pādya) and the respectful offering (arghya), one should present them; then, having given the water for sipping (ācamana), one should place dūrvā grass and unbroken rice grains on the feet and the head with the Tāra mantra; then, having respectfully performed the lustration (nīrājana) with the Astra mantra, one should subsequently [bathe the deity] in due order with the jars containing the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances.

One should perform the bathing according to the sequence stated by Pūraṇa, using the five Brahma-mantras and so forth, ending with "the middle [mantra] by means of the *vyomani-dyuti*. The meaning is that among the substances such as the *pañcagavya* and others, the *pañcagavya* is the first.

"One should bathe the oceans with the group beginning with Samudrajyeṣṭha" means that one should state the group beginning with Samudrajyeṣṭha for each individual ocean and then bathe them. He describes the arrangement of the bathing [mantras] as being in fragments.

Having worshipped each fragment piece by piece, the word "tu" (but/and) indicates that one should perform an intermediate bath with the mantra dedicated to Maheśa; thus, the "intermediate bath" has been described.
And having done so, one should bathe [the deity] with other jars containing the remaining portions;

having poured the residue from each jar into a single vessel, one should [bathe] the attendants of the deity, such as Indra and the others who receive the offerings, as well as the deities of the directions, starting from the east, using that [liquid].
Having sprinkled water over those [images] that have been consecrated and established, one should then worship the deity thoroughly;

one should worship with offerings, attendants, and other pleasing elements. Afterwards, the patron (yajamāna) should worship the preceptor (ācārya), the guardians of the images (mūrtipās), and the members of the assembly (sadasyas), using seventeen types of materials such as jars, baskets, and so forth.
He shows the extent [of the ritual] with the passage beginning "by twenty-five" and ending with "one who desires expansion.
By the term "free from anger," it is indicated that this [practice] is relegated to the lowest category.
He concludes the bathing with seventeen substances with the word "this."

This bath, enjoined by scripture and prescribed by scripture, has been fully indicated and correctly expounded by us; though it belongs to the secondary alternative, its power is swift in accomplishing the fruit ordained for the primary alternative on the fourth day.

"Even elsewhere, such as in the case of penance (*prāyaścitta*) and so forth, one should perform [the rite] with devotion. Now, beginning to state the procedure for the twenty-five substances, he says "atha" (now). Now.

I shall now describe the supreme ablution (snapana), as enjoined by the scriptures, characterized by twenty-five substances and performed in the sequence beginning with the *asama* [arrangement]. He indicates the vases for the inferior category with the passage beginning with "twenty-five" and ending with "or up to one hundred and eight. This is as follows:
Now, first of all, this one hundred and eightfold [rite] is being heard;

therein, it should be understood that the procedure for the one hundred and eight jars—which is both inferior and superior—is presented first in order to demonstrate the status of the supreme method as the most desired object. Regarding the conceptualization of that field:
He demonstrates this with the passage beginning with "sixteen" and ending with "in the *bhṛśādi* group. Regarding the word "thus":

having thus conceived the field (*kṣetra*) according to the stated sequence, one should perform the worship of the seat (*pīṭha*), the consecration of the jar (*kuṃbha-saṃskāra*), the arrangement of the ritual substances (*dravya-vinyāsa*), the mental fulfillment (*mānasa-pūraṇa*), and so forth, without transgressing the proper rule (*nyāya*).

One should fill the Śiva-pitcher, which has Śiva as its presiding deity, and the Brahma-pitcher as before; one should first fill the central one, which consists of all mantras and is supreme, and so forth—
having filled the Brahma-kalaśa according to the previously mentioned method, one should then [fill] the others.

One should fill twenty-four water-pots with the twenty-four substances for the *pādya* and other offerings. The substances for the *pādya* and so forth are as follows: [p. 90]... [list of substances].

He enumerates each [item] according to its respective location, from "pādya" up to "in due order"; the phrase "mixed with flour" is the ellipsis. He speaks of the twenty-five deities beginning with the Śiva-kumbha, from "Īśāna" up to "the deities. This is the *vāk* (speech).
Sarasvatī, Rudra, the eleven Rudras, the first-born, the eldest, the sages,

the seven Ṛṣis, the Viśvedevas— the Viśvedevas— thus he enumerates the constituent parts of the collection of substances beginning with the water for the feet (*pādya*). [He continues with] *dūrvā* and so forth.

By the passage ending with "ratnamīritam," [the author] recalls the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) and other rites for the worship of the vase; by the passage beginning with "etair" and ending with "samārabhet," [he recalls] the bathing mantras and so forth.
Therefore, immediately after the summary statement of the procedure for the ablution (*snapana*), I shall explain the bathing mantras.

The Guru himself, having worshipped [the deity] five times in succession with the mantras to be recited hereafter, and having performed the lustration (nīrājana), should bathe the Lord according to the prescribed rite using the remaining water from the pitcher,
following the sequence of pouring and filling, with the mantra beginning with "tanmaheśāya."

One should perform an intermediate bath; he states the mantras for the bath beginning with "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" and ending with "vyomavyāpikrameṇa tu. Regarding "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," [he gives] the water for washing the feet (*pādya*).

"Successively, [one performs] the middle [ablution] with the Vyomavidyā. Because the Śiva-kumbha possesses fixed mantras, it should be understood that the intended sequence of bathing—from the *pādya* (water for the feet) up to the Śiva-kumbha—is what is meant.
He concludes [the section] with the words "by these," because they are the least inferior among the desired [options].
Below, I shall describe the arrangement of the inferior field (*adhamakṣetra*) starting from "What is the singing?

(*kā gītī*) up to "in some places it is prescribed" (*kvacid iti vihitaṃ*), [which indicates] that there might be an incapacity on the part of the performer; if that is the case, then one should perform the bath with twenty-five jars devoid of pure water elsewhere.

The meaning is that in some cases there may be the occurrence of even a slight trace of power; the sense is that in such a case, because an unenjoined act has been performed, there would indeed be the wrath of the Lord. He explains the procedure for the central pitcher (*madhyakalaśa*), along with its various divisions and elaborations, in twenty verses beginning with "pañcaśataṃ" and so forth.

The textual passage ending with "is remembered" (smṛtam) [refers to] not [just] twenty sūtras; rather, it refers to two hundred [sūtras] characterized by twenty sūtras. In the outer human [mandala], there are four groups of six in the cardinal directions and four groups of six in the intermediate directions; in the inner divine [mandala], there is a group of eight in the intermediate space.

Eight and twelve—these, by the collection of the cardinal and intermediate directions, make eight sets of twelve within the ninefold [mandala]; the remainder is that one should fashion the lotus in the Brahma-ninefold;
thus he speaks of two hundred and seventeen as "the group of six."

(The phrase) "by twenty threads" is understood [from the previous context]. In that inner divine field (*antardaivika-kṣetra*), one should [draw] a hexagon and a square respectively according to the sequence of directions and intermediate points; and outside of that, in the human field (*mānuṣa*), [one does so] in the cardinal and intermediate directions.

In sequence, one should make groups of twelve, twelve, sixteen, sixteen, and eight within the intermediate spaces; whether one should do so or not is also drawn here from what will be stated later. By those previously mentioned lines, twenty—
By forming twenty-five groups of nine through the *sūtras*, it is established— depending on the context— that one should make either two hundred and twenty-five or two hundred;
for it was previously stated that "the first group of six" and so forth would subsequently amount to seventeen more.

I shall describe the arrangement of the remaining two hundred and fifty-three [squares]. Regarding the "twenty-one-fold" [mandala]: in the twenty-one-fold [mandala], there are eight lotuses for Brahmā and nine for the Devas respectively within; and externally, in the human region, there are nine [lotuses] in the corners and the cardinal directions.

"Three sets of twelve" means there are twelve [deities] in the cardinal directions and twelve in the intermediate directions; thus, two hundred and fifty-two are proclaimed. He speaks of the arrangement of three hundred in the field (*kṣetra*) within the *gotrapuṭa*.
He speaks of the arrangement of five hundred and five words in the field called *dhīrapuṭa*;
finally, in the inner *daivika* [section], there are eight [verses].
The meaning is that there are seventeen [units] in each of the directions and in the outer corners; among these,
one should arrange three [units] and twenty-five [units] in the middle of those seventeen located in the outer corners.
He concludes the procedure for the twenty-five substances alone with the words:
"Thus it is remembered as being by means of twenty-five substances.
Now, [the procedure] with the aforementioned twenty-five substances when combined with other substances such as oil, etc.:

Intending to explain the supreme ritual of the *kalaśa*, he introduces it with the half-verse beginning "by other substances" (*dravyair anyaiḥ*). Therein, first, he explains the ritual consisting of two hundred and fifty-three [verses] with these very words beginning "one hundred and eight" (*aṣṭottaraśatam*).
By the word "thus" (*tviti*), [it is meant] in a field characterized by twenty-four sūtras as "one hundred and eight.

The term "in the field" (*kṣetre*) follows from what was previously stated. There, having made one hundred and eight [squares] in the center and sixteen groups of nine outside of that, from the middle...
In the center, having filled [the space] with one hundred and eight [units] as previously described,

one should place outside of that, in the cardinal directions and intermediate corners, substances ranging from oil to water using the eight-form (aṣṭamūrti) mantras beginning with Śarva, in uneven numbers.
Having completed [the verse] with the first, third, fifth, and seventh syllables being equal,
and the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth being even-numbered, [one applies this] to the group beginning with *bhṛśam*.

In the intermediate spaces, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the mantras whose essence is the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*), beginning with Ananta, Sūkṣma, and the others— using these very mantras as previously described— in due order, [one should place] the earth belonging to the Śaiva lineage.

"One should establish [the deities] in the sequence beginning with the water for the feet (pādya)"— thus, in that very context, he describes the arrangement of three hundred positions with the words "in the field, in the enclosure of the lineage," and so forth, ending with "with three hundred jars. Furthermore, in that same place,
he demonstrates a specific distinction through the application of other substances with the words "having made one hundred and twenty," and so on.

Up to the words "three hundred jars," [the description continues]: in the very field of the *gotrapuṭa*, in the center, it is provided with nine-squares situated in the corners—that is, in the nine directions and the eight corners—as well as provided with the two sets of eight previously mentioned corners. Thus.

And in the Brahma [mandala], having prepared one hundred and twenty— that is, one hundred and twenty— consisting of a central ninefold [array] situated upon the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus, surrounded by twenty-nine such groups,
and having filled the twenty-nine groups with scented water, [one should lay] the thread for the eastern direction.
With substances containing scented water located in the segments immediately following the thread starting from the right side and so forth, using the previously mentioned materials ending with clay,
and ending with the root-mantras applied with scented water.

One should perform the ablution with three hundred jars using the previously mentioned mantras ending with the Śikhāṇḍinīs and those ending with the Śivakumbha, along with the aforementioned substances in a particularly elaborate manner.

The wise teacher, skilled in reasoning and refutation, explains the procedure of three hundred and twenty [deities] with the passage beginning "In the field, in the Mitra-puṭa" and ending with "three hundred are proclaimed.
Having first stated that one should place two hundred in the middle within the field (kṣetra) in the center of the Mitra-puṭa...

Having made one hundred and twelve [squares] by excluding the *dalakalaśa* (petal-vase), there is a group of twelve in the outer directions; in the middle of the sixteen, there are three groups of four—
meaning three sets of four squares each— and those are...

One should perform [the rite]. Then, having filled the vessels— beginning with the Śiva-vessel and ending with the jar of earth from the well— using the previously mentioned substances and mantras according to the rules, without deviating from the application of their respective substances, deities, and so forth,
one should place them on both sides of the earthen [vessels] without distinction.
Having filled four vessels with scented water using the root mantra,

being composed and joined with the meditative concentration on the respective mantras of the deities for the water for the feet and so forth, one should consecrate the deity with those scented waters using that root mantra, performing all four circumambulations in a clockwise direction.

"One should fill" means that one should fill all four sets of earth situated on both sides— which are the subject of the previously mentioned fragrant water— in the order of clockwise progression starting from the Satya, Antarikṣa, and so forth, with the statement placed in the very middle regarding the fragrant water prescribed for both sides of the earth.

The meaning is that one should fill [the vessel]; the remainder is easy to understand. Now, he begins to describe the most excellent ablution (*snapana*) with the half-verse beginning "with four," and explains it in the section on the field (*kṣetra*).

From the words "kapālapuṭa" and so forth, up to "the guru should bathe," [it is explained as follows]: in the field of Kālapura, which consists of twenty-one squares (*puṭa*), there are one hundred and eight [deities] in the center; outside of that, by way of the collection of the cardinal and intermediate directions, there are nine groups of eight;
and in the middle of those nine groups established in the cardinal and intermediate directions, there are three.

One should prepare three sets of three here; having filled them as before with materials ending in clay in the form of the Śiva-pitcher and so forth, one should fill the three on each of the two sides of the clay with fragrant water. The Guru should arrange twenty-eight groups of nine outside of that.

He describes the twenty-eight methods of filling with camphor in the passage beginning with "karpūra" and ending with "pradakṣiṇam. In the phrase "aṃburuhāya sāmi," there is an elision of the suffix, as in the case of "maujavāsvākṣa"; and in "sātvatāṃ patiḥ," there is an absence of the *nuṭ* augment, which is an archaic (ārṣa) usage.
"Having filled [the vessel] with milk, *palāśa* leaves, and so forth"— having thus filled it, the Guru,
having worshipped and offered oblations, should bathe the deity with those [substances]. Having thus described the duties of the Guru,
he states the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the patron (*yajamāna*) who undertakes that [rite], beginning with the words "the deity," referring to the Guru and others.

By the statement regarding [the deity's] worthiness of worship, the patron (*yajamāna*) who is implied by that meaning is [described as one] who has caused the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) to be performed for the sake of attaining all his own desired goals.

[He beheld] the Lord, whose form was radiant from the fourth-day ablution (cāturthika-snapana), intent upon bestowing grace, together with his companions who had assumed physical forms; the Guru who performed that [rite];
the scholars, experts in the concentration required for each specific action being performed; and the recitation...
He [honored] the Brahmins who were his ultimate refuge, those devoted attendants intent on carrying out his commands,
and all other assistants such as the Pāraśavas and others,
with food and other gifts common to all people, at the conclusion with food and so forth.

With devotion toward all those whom one worships— beginning with the performance of daily worship using substances appropriate for the deities denoted by sacred words, such as offerings of flowers, and toward gurus and others with specific gifts of cows, land, gold, and other suitable sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā)— [one should perform worship].

One should worship [the deity] endowed with a mental disposition consisting of the contemplation of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) and joined with perfect faith; thus he concludes the procedure for the ritual bathing, reiterating the statement from the fourth chapter: "The attendants of the God are said to be non-substantial."

He explains the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) for the retinues whose bathing and installation have not been specified by means of the remainder of the chapter, beginning with "the fire-oblation of the directions" (*diśā-homa*) and so forth.
Having placed the fires in the eight directions, the officiating priests perform the preliminary rites beginning with the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*).

Having performed [the preliminary rites], they should offer the cooked oblation according to the rules with these mantras to be recited immediately hereafter, accompanied by the ritual procedures for the five Tārās and other such darbha-grass rites.

He states the mature mantras with the passage beginning with *indrakṛtam* and ending with *tryambakam*. In the north-western corner associated with Vāyu, having recited each of the five *tārās* individually in front— that is, starting from the east, the eastern direction— one proceeds in this manner in sequence.

Once they have become cooked, they should then offer oblations with the mantras beginning with Indra, as previously enjoined in their proper order, using sacrificial wood, clarified butter, parched grain, and so forth, which were previously prescribed for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), or else with the four substances; here,
by the statement "from the east in sequence," [this applies] at the eastern gate and the western gate.

It is indicated that the *diśā-homa* (directional oblation) in the temple should be performed starting from the east; having completed the oblations, one should install the pitchers filled with the residual ghee (*saṃpāta-ājya*) upon the pedestals according to the rite and worship them in sequence.
For the offering-pedestals, there is the cleansing with *darbha* grass and so forth, and their placement.

Having established [the deities] according to the ritual procedure for the worship of the Seat of Purification (śuddhipīṭha), one should worship Indra and the others in due order; the intention is that one should also offer the bali-oblation with the remnants of the sacrificial oblation (havis).
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Tattvaprakāśinī*, a commentary on the *Kriyāsāra*.
Thus, having described the time for the performance intended to establish the retinue,
[the author now describes] that which consists in pleasing the Supreme Lord surrounded by his entire retinue (p. 99).

Intending to describe a specific form of worship (saparyā) which is synonymous with a festival (utsava), he reveals his intended meaning by stating "the festival" (utsavam). Then, after the installation of the entire retinue, there is an abundance of food offerings (annādya-bali) for all living beings, beginning with the twice-born (dvija) and ending with the gatekeepers (dvāstha).

It was a place where the entire circle of attendants had gathered in great numbers for the offering, crowded with various musical instruments— filled with five kinds of instruments such as the *ānaka* drum and others—
and likewise accompanied by dance and song.

And one should perform such a festival; therein, first, one should perform the planting of the sprout and the installation of the flag. Thus he says: "Having prepared the seed-sprout (bījāṅkura) everywhere—in the great flagstaff, the fort, and so forth, at the places of the deities of the offering, at crossroads, and the like."

Having installed auspicious banners everywhere in sequence and having placed beautiful flags, one should worship them with perfumes and flowers. Regarding the mantra for the installation of the great banners and flags, he says "namaste" (salutation to you). Therein, "everywhere" refers to the interior and exterior of the enclosure walls, as well as the streets, crossroads, and so forth.

And at all places where the procession of the deity halts, having swept and smeared [the ground], one should scatter flowers and unbroken rice grains (akṣata), along with offerings such as *ayaṃpūra*, and incense such as *aguru* and *gulgulu*.
Then, after fumigating and following the purification of the site, one should worship Śiva;

[the text] demonstrates the perfection of the worship by means of the passage beginning with "having consecrated and bathed" and ending with "one should ask for forgiveness," [including] the ritual worship of the pedestal and so forth, accompanied by the appropriate procedures.
At the time of bathing, having bathed [the deity] with pure waters, milk, curd, clarified butter, products of the cow, scented waters, and coconut water,
and again at the time of bathing with jars, having anointed [the deity] beautifully with perfumes and the eight fragrances (aṣṭagandha), and having clothed [the deity] in garments;

Having performed worship— this entire wealth of the retinue being the very essence of worship— and having offered food consisting of various kinds of eatables and the like, saying only "I offer," and then having performed the fire-oblation (homa) and given the bali-offering, the Guru himself, intending to describe the remainder of the worship, speaks in the middle of the discourse as an incidental point.

Having introduced the procedure for the offering to the mouth (*mukhanivedya*), he demonstrates it with the passage beginning "In the mouths of Īśa and the others" and ending with "all thus. Having first connected it to the subject at hand—rice mixed with milk and sesame (*kṛsara*)—he states the remainder of the worship with the word "having offered" (*nivedya*). Thus, having offered the pleasing food to the mouth, then...

Having displayed the *dhenumudrā* and established protection in all directions— as prescribed in other Smṛtis— and having offered oblations after the presentation of the nectar-moon (*sudhāṃśu*) and so forth, one should worship the fire,
perform the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*) with the root mantra, and offer either one thousand and eight [oblations].
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations;
then, with the limbs of the Mūrtis, one should offer a tenth part of that, and with the Vidyeśvaras and others, one by one.

Having sprinkled [water] around, recited [the mantra] again, and completed the remainder of the *homa*, one should offer the remaining sacrificial oblation (*nivedya-śeṣa-havis*) into the fire according to the principle established in other *smṛtis*. Then, having offered the *bali*,
one should present the *bali* appropriate for the door upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*) in the new fire, according to the stated rule regarding the *bali*.

Having given [the water] and performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), the Guru himself— having attained the state of the Supreme Lord through the realization that he has attained it— the Preceptor, having first offered the water known by the name *paranāma* (which, as indicated by the word "tu," serves to cleanse the mouth) according to the rules of *ācamana*, [offers] the food.
One should release [the remainder] again with the leftover food; one should offer the *nirmālya* (remnants of the offering) to Caṇḍeśvara.

Immediately thereafter, having given water—known by the other name *gaṇḍūṣa*—as well as mouth-perfume (*mukhavāsa*) in the form of the five-fold betel (*pañcatāmbūla*) and so forth, and having worshipped [him] slightly, [one should worship him] properly.

Having performed the dissolution of the primordial nature (*prakṛti-vilāpana*) and other rites properly, having worshipped with abundant handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), and having recited the mantra; then, having placed the "Hand of Śiva" (*śivahasta*) upon one's head and recited according to the method prescribed in another *Āgama*; and having praised and prostrated, one should ask for forgiveness.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Lord as abiding in his prior state.

One should recite the ritual service for the retinue of offerings; first, having brought down the *bhūta*-offering, he explains it with the passage beginning with "at night" (*niśi*) and ending with "in due order" (*yathākramam*). Regarding the term "kautuka":
Having worshipped the deity residing in the primary *liṅga* within the *kautuka* and *balibiṃba*, and having invoked and honored him,
one should place [the deity] upon the head of the disciple; then, having recited the *svasti* mantra, one should go outside with him,
exit from the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), and [dismiss] the door-keepers and others.

One should offer the *bali* to the deities of the *bali* sacrifice ending with the *kṣetrapāla*. The deities of the *bali* sacrifice, beginning with the door-keepers (*dvāstha*) and so forth, are enumerated; one should worship them in sequence up to the end of the passage beginning with "Nandin" and ending with "one should worship in order.
Here, in the phrase "Nandin and the others" (*nandyādīni*), the word "others" (*ādi*) denotes the retinue outside, ending with the *kṣetrapāla*.
He describes the procedure for the offering (*baliprakriyā*): "Having performed and caused to be performed instrumental music, dance, and song"—and as he will say later:
"Having thus completed the offering there, one should cause dance, song, and so forth to be performed. Thus [is] the offering.
The connection is that one should perform the *bali* mudrās and display them. In that regard, he shows the specific procedure for the festival *bali* with the words "of those," and so forth.
Of those aforementioned attendants, such as the door-keepers and others, [one should offer] previously in their respective side-maṇḍalas.

Having offered the *bali* to the assembly [of deities] on the sacrificial mound (*sthāṇḍila*) situated at the left side, one should then offer the *bali* with the *mālā-mantras* beginning with "Oṃ namo bhūtebhyaḥ" and so forth, to the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*) and their assemblies, and subsequently outside of that, in the cardinal directions and intermediate corners. Thus, [it is said]: "in the cardinal directions and intermediate corners."

103) It should be understood that the separate placement [of offerings] in the corners is for the purpose of indicating a deficiency in the *bali* mantras, and not for the purpose of demonstrating the sequence of the cardinal and intermediate directions; this applies to the *bali* offerings for the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*) and others.

He states the distinction: "The guardians of the directions" (dikpān) means the guardians of the directions and their vehicles; by the word "and" (ca), it includes the previously mentioned gatekeepers immediately thereafter.
Having performed the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) with the attendance mantras prior to the worship, one should then perform the worship. Thus he says, "according to the *Āgama*."

I shall write— briefly, for the sake of a concise summary— the mantras extracted from the Āgamas, such as "sphura sphoṭaya huṃ" to be uttered at the end of the [mantras] called Tāra and Śakti, as well as those extracted from other Smṛtis; from these, namely from Nandī and the others, here.

Having offered the *bali* in the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should offer the *bali* in the respective peripheral maṇḍalas according to the ritual procedure, by means of the application of the mantras for the twenty Gaṇas beginning with Mahākāla, without transgressing the prescribed method; thus one enumerates the twenty classes of spirits, beginning with "Mahākāla," and so forth.

With the words ending in "pātālās te namo namaḥ," one should offer the *bali* on the *balipīṭha* using the mantras beginning with "svāhā" and those beginning with "bhūtidā," as taught by the masters of the *pīṭhas*.
First, having enumerated the group beginning with Bhūtidā, the author describes the arrangement of their respective positions, stating "Bhūtidā."
He writes the specific mantras (p. 104), beginning with "Oṃ, homage to Mahābala," and so forth; thus, by these [mantras] which have been written.

Having offered the *bali* on the pedestal with the five mantras, one should offer the *bali* outside of that, in the enclosure of the ritual procedure (*prakriyā-āvaraṇa*), once around with these three mantras to be written immediately below, beginning with "Oṃ, salutation to all beings! May they accept [this]," and so forth.

Outside of that, one should also offer an oblation (bali) to the planets. He mentions the planets with the words "the gods" and so forth, and concludes the oblation. Regarding the passage beginning with "of these," having offered the oblation to the Kṣetrapāla in the northern direction among the quarters of these planets, and having thus completed it there—

"One should cause dancing, singing, and so forth to be performed before the Kṣetrapālas. Regarding the outer offering (*bahirbali*), he states an alternative view with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). Previously, in the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*), [the offering was made] with the *mālāmantras*, namely the three mantras beginning with "Oṃ namo bhūtebhyaḥ" and so forth; immediately after that, subsequently...

In the second, third, and fourth enclosures, one should respectively offer oblations (*bali*) to the twenty *gaṇas* beginning with Nandin, to the *bhūta*-groups, and to the planets— the word "having offered" being understood from the context.
Having done this, [one should worship] with the *bhūtidā* and others recited in the section on the *balipīṭha*.

"One should complete [the rite]"—the word "by day" (*divā*) is understood; and regarding the remaining days, that is, on the days immediately following the day of commencement, one should offer the *bali*—namely, the festival *bali*—both by day (indicated by the particle *ca*) and at night.

"Or one should offer the *bhūtabali* on the day before," [it is said]. On the night before the pilgrimage, the preceptor (*ācārya*), having offered the great offering (*mahābali*) and the village offering (*grāmabali*), and having obtained the consent of all living beings, thereafter performs that which consists of the dispersal of minor spirits.
Immediately after hunting and other such activities, having entered within, one should pray to the Lord;

he states the mantra of prayer as "tīrthayātrā" (the pilgrimage). Having prayed thus, and after performing the bath, sipping water, self-contemplation (*ātmabhāvanā*), and so forth, [one should worship] with vessels containing sprouts (*aṅkurapātra*), lamps, and the eight auspicious symbols (*aṣṭamaṅgala*).

Having decorated the pavilion and spread the bed, and having worshipped it, the preceptor enters within; then, according to the prescribed rule, he performs the offering of clarified butter (*ghṛtāropaṇa*) by means of the *bhūr* and other mantras, without deviating from the ritual procedure for the sprinkling of clarified butter, dūrvā grass tips, and so forth, which are placed upon an *aśvattha* leaf.

Having dissolved the universal pervasion into the Lord of the Universe, together with the image-protectors, one should place a golden coin with pearls upon a linen cloth while reciting the *Puṇyāha* mantra; then, with both hands, one should perform the binding of the *kautuka* (protective thread) on the right arm of the Deity using a multiform woolen thread while reciting the *Aghora* mantra.

One should perform [the rite]. Then, following the purification of the ritual image (*karmabimba*) through meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*), one should invoke the deity into the ritual image; having established the deity in the pavilion accompanied by all auspicious items and every kind of musical instrument, [one should place it] facing the temple.
Having established [the image] and worshipped it, and having performed the appropriate worship with suitable offerings,
one should spend the night without sleeping; by the very phrase "one should spend that night without sleeping," this is intended.
"That which is day for all beings is night for the sage who perceives"—
in accordance with this other traditional teaching (*smṛti*), one should bring this "great night" consisting of worldly activity to its own cause,
the Supreme Brahman, and contemplate it as dissolved therein; this is what is suggested.

The meaning is that, having dissolved the three states— waking and the rest— by means of the five mantras, the root mantra, and the *praṇava* which pervade them, one should contemplate being intent upon the experience of one's own true nature as the form of eternal bliss-consciousness (*sadānandacidrūpa*).
Then, the Guru, having bathed in the morning and performed the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*) according to the rules, [proceeds].

The pervasion of the five mantras rooted in the *praṇava*, the awakening and raising [of the deity], the auspicious offering of the sight and the *arghya*, the dismissal from the bed (*śayyodvāsana*), the worship of the throne (*pīṭhapūjā*), the invocation (*āvāhana*),

the ritual integration of all parts (*sakalīkaraṇa*), the presentation of water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, the cleansing of the teeth (*dantadhāvana*), the scraping of the tongue (*jihvollekhana*), the giving of mouthfuls of water (*gaṇḍūṣadāna*), and the ceremonial bathing (*snapana*).

The pouring of honey and clarified butter, anointing with unguents, bathing again, the offering of garments, dūrvā grass, flowers, sandalwood paste, collyrium, and agallochum; the presentation of ornaments, the mirror, and fodder; the listening to the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth; and the daily giving of gifts and worship.
Having prepared everything appropriate for that time and endowed with the knowledge required for it, one should worship Śiva;

having brought the deity from the primary image (*mūlabimba*) into the house of the marriage-thread (*kautuka*), one should [unite] the deity residing in the primary image with the deity residing in the *kautuka*.

And having directed [the disciple], he should also worship him—by the word "and" (ca), it is implied that he should worship. The phrase "he should worship" (saṃpūjayet) is understood from what was stated previously. Now, he says "in the mortar" (ulūkhale) regarding how one should have powders prepared for the purpose of anointing (udvartana).

One should have the powders of black gram, *śāli* rice, barley, and so forth, mixed with turmeric and cow dung, ground in a clean, new mortar; then, having combined those various powders with the materials for the *homa* and other rites,
one should place them in a vessel and worship the deity residing in the primary image (*mūlabimba*) by means of the respective root-mantras of each powder.
At the time of bathing, having bathed [the image] with waters and anointed it with ghee and oil,
one should sprinkle it again at the time of bathing with that same powder.

By the phrase "with the five mantras," it is implied that one should sweep the *mantra-liṅga* on all sides with that powder and cause it to be placed upon the heads of the devotees; having bathed [the deity] again and worshipped according to the rules, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the processional oblation (*yātrā-homa*) according to the prescribed ritual.

He explains the *yātrā-homa* (the fire-sacrifice for a journey) with the passage beginning with "having performed the *agnimukha*" and ending with "he should offer the *pūrṇāhuti*. Here, the meaning is that he should offer oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the two hymns, the *śākuna* and the *svasti-sūkta*; the word "should offer" (*dadet*) is to be construed with each subsequent statement.
The meaning is "with the heart and with the temple"; having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited,
and then, having removed and subsequently produced the *kautuka* (wedding bracelet).

After the prayer for the purpose of the journey to the ritual image (*karmārcā*) and the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), and after the completion of the *yātrā-homa* and its dedication, one should invoke [the deity] from the primary image (*mūlabimba*) into the ritual image, perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), wrap it with two garments, and— by the use of the word "and" (*ca*)— [perform the remaining rites].

Having protected the primary image (mūlabimba) and touched it with the remaining *saṃpāta* clarified butter— this being the implied meaning— the preceptor (deśika), taking that deity residing in the *kautuka* [vessel], should go outside from the inner sanctum; at the door of the temple, he should recite auspicious words (*maṅgalavāda*).

Having performed the recitation of the *Rūpamaṅgala* hymn beginning with "jagannirmāṇa," and having gone out and offered the *bali*, one offers the *bali* once around both inside and outside, from the gatekeeper (*dvāstha*) to the *balipīṭha*; then, having gone outside the *gopura* and mounted a vehicle such as an elephant, one [proceeds] toward it.
Furthermore, having meditated upon the bull, who has become the vehicle of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara),

and having offered the flag-oblation (dhvajabali), one should join the bull situated there to the vehicle; the meaning is that one should contemplate the vehicle as being of that same form, and having done so, one should mount the Supreme Lord upon it.
Surrounded by all kinds of musical instruments and provided with offerings such as water and perfumes,

one should go within a *yojana* to a river or another reservoir; having prepared a well-concealed sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) on its bank or on the shore of the sacred site (*tīrtha*), one should offer [the oblation] upon it.

109) One should place Śiva upon the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha). Having placed Śiva and worshipped him with water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings, preceded by the invocation of the mantra and so forth, one should then invoke the sacred waters (tīrtha).

The meaning is as follows: having consecrated the sacred site (*tīrtha*) with the *dhāraṇā* and other rites, one should invoke the *Gaṅgā-tīrtha* by means of the *Gaṅgā-mantra*, cause it to become present, and then immerse the deity in that sacred site. Then, after the application of scented powder (*cūrṇodvartana*), the bath, and so forth, one should [place] that deity upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).

Having engaged [the priests] and honored them with food and other offerings, one should present there the great cooked oblation (havis) provided with such items; then, after the consecration of the sacred water (tīrtha), having offered it,
he reminds [the priest] of the homa that must be performed even before that, for the sake of the residual drops (saṃpāta) and so forth.

"One hundred and eight" refers to the number. Now, he reveals the powder, massage, and so forth mentioned by the word "atha" (now) in the phrase "puṇyāham" (auspicious day). Having designated it as an auspicious day together with virtuous people, and having massaged [the body] respectfully with powders, one should recite the *Aghamarṣaṇa* and other hymns (*sūkta*); such is the meaning. Likewise...

"Having bathed and worshipped, and taking [the deity] according to the rule"— this is a restatement of the previously mentioned worship. Having done this, having taken the deity along with the mantra-prayers for the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) and the dismissal (*udvāsana*) of the *tīrtha*, and having placed [the deity] upon a vehicle, [one proceeds] very quickly.
"He should go to his home, the primary abode"—this indicates the intent of proceeding with the utmost speed, namely that it is indeed a journey (*yātrā*).

According to the rule, this refers to the sequence established for the offerings during the journey (*yātrā-balikṛta-krama*), in order to avoid [the ritual] being performed within the womb (*garbha*) [of the house].

Following the sequence previously indicated and without deviating from the proper method, one should offer the *bhūtabali* at night; then, on the following day when the sun has risen, for the sake of pacifying the defects of the journey, one should perform the ablutions in the superior and other grades according to the prescribed order. This is merely an illustration; [the ritual] should be performed according to one's means.

Having thus described the duties of the preceptor (*guru*) to be performed immediately after the selection—namely, the worship of Maheśvara and the honoring of the assembly that has been sprinkled with water—he now states the duties of the patron (*yajamāna*):
"To the Preceptor and the Protectors of the Images," and so forth; one should perform that according to the rule.
When the rite prescribed as concluding with the ritual bath at the sacred ford (tīrtha) has been completed,

one must certainly give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor (ācārya) and the image-protectors (mūrtipāla); otherwise, by the maxim beginning with "For [if] the performer's rite is devoid of faith, it surely leads to malevolent magic (abhicāra)," and so forth, it would result in misfortune.

The letter *e* indicates that the destruction of one's lineage and other such faults arise from the wrath of the Supreme Lord; therefore, one should, endowed with devotion, worship all others—such as the ritual attendants (*parikarmī*), those who recite the *pārāyaṇa*, and the *vārīśava*, etc.—according to one's capacity. Thus he concludes.

By means of showing the contradiction with his own composition, he hopes that this work will have the learned as its audience through the first half of the verse beginning with "etad"; and by the second half beginning with "rakṣitavyam," he prays that it may not fall into the hands of the wicked. [The term] "dasyubhyaḥ" refers to those who are proficient in the science of thieves.
p.
111) The sense is that in this very way one attains Śiva. I have here, according to the method adopted by the excellent Guru, explained in some detail the state of being Śiva within this Tantra.
Let the skillful [commentator] explain the remainder by this very method; I shall strive regarding that portion as well, which is difficult to grasp in its detailed classification.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Tattvaprakāśinī*, the commentary on the *Kriyāsāra*.

Salutation to Śiva. Now, having thus expounded the Śiva-tantra according to the Pāśupata tradition, he makes a formal promise to explain the Viṣṇu-tantra, which follows next in sequence, according to the Pañcarātra tradition:

Having paid homage to Hari, I shall describe the sequence of ritual actions (kriyākrama) in brief; thus, by stating "having paid homage to Hari," he clarifies his formal promise (pratijñā) while making known the purpose [of the work], on the grounds that it is rooted in the Smṛti.
This is expressed in the passage beginning with "by the gods" and ending with "concluding with the bath at the sacred ford (tīrthasnāna). Here, "by the gods" refers to Vāsudeva and others.
Although it has been clearly stated by sages such as Nārada and by teachers such as Śrī Bhagavatpāda,

nevertheless— because this [objection] is accepted even in the subsequent section— the word "yadyapi" (even though) should indeed be employed in the statement of the doubt; thus, although it has been clearly stated, nevertheless...

For the sake of recollection by the foremost of practitioners during the performance of ritual acts, I [shall describe] the sequence of rites, beginning with the worship of the Guru and ending with the ritual bath at a sacred ford (tīrtha). (p. 112) This is the sequence of rites.

The previously mentioned [passage] follows here; in the reading "I shall describe that, beginning with the worship of the Guru and ending with the ritual bath at a sacred site" (*tīrthasnānāvasānika*), it constitutes a single sentence and includes the selection of the Guru obtained first. [The word] "purified" (*śodhita*) explains [the status of] the patron (*yajamāna*).

The construction is as follows: "Having taken hold of [the hand] with the right hand, ending with the words 'in the right hand,' while reciting this mantra, one should choose [the bride]. In this context, among the mantras for the limbs and the forms (aṅgamūrtimantra), one should use those very same mantras by which the worship of the presiding deity of the form (mūrtipa) is performed.

To make known that the consecration of the *arghya* and other offerings must be performed, it is prescribed as an option to consecrate them with the root mantra, the [deity] forms, or the limbs; that preceptor,
having examined the earth according to what is appropriate by means of clay and so forth described in other ritual manuals, [should proceed].

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: having understood [the site], having demarcated the earth up to its perimeter wall, and having worshipped it here in the center and in the directions according to rule with perfumes and other offerings, one should give the *bhūtakrūra* bali with this mantra. "Having done thus" refers to such an acquisition of the site (*bhūtaparigraha*).

Having performed [the rites] many times for the sake of general purification, one should dig the desired ground at an auspicious moment; here, the word "ground" (*kṣitim*), which is to be mentioned later in the phrase "one should dig the ground," should be drawn back and applied [to this point as well]. Now, nine...
113) The Guru himself, adorned with new garments and other ornaments, [should perform the rite] by means of the mantra according to the ritual procedure;
since the word *mantrataḥ* is used in the sense of all case endings, the term *mantrataḥ* functions as a word ending in the third case.
The remainder is easy to understand. With the words "at an auspicious moment" (*sumuhūrte*), he summarizes the foundation in the netherworld (*pātālapratiṣṭhā*).

With the words "one should place the tortoise-stone" (*kūrmaśilāṃ nyaset*) up to the end [of the verse], he explains the procedure first encountered there. Then, with the verses beginning with "jewels" (*ratna*) and ending with "one should pray with this mantra" (*prārthayen manunāmunā*), he explains [the procedure] in the center.
In the center of the pit, according to one's capacity—that is, as far as one is able—one should place jewels, gold, and so forth with the root mantra;

the meaning is that one should perform the placement within the jars, preceded by the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the consecration of the jars (*kumbha-saṃskāra*). The remainder is easy to understand.

Having first completed the ritual for depositing the treasure (nidhi), he brings down the lotus of letters (lipipañjara) for the purpose of laying the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā), beginning with the words "with perfumes and so forth" (gandhādyaiḥ). Distinguishing the lotus of letters, he extracts its mantras starting from "KṢA ĀDITYA... and ending with "...joined with Śakti in the center."

The letter *kṣa* and those beginning with it—namely, the letters from *la* to *śa*, which constitute the *kṣādi* group—are a *bahuvrīhi* compound with *guṇasaṃvijñāna*. Thus, "that whose forms (*mūrti*), roots (*śiphā*), stalks (*nāla*), sap-channels (*sarā*), thorns (*kaṇṭaka*), and cavities (*randhra*) consist of the *kṣādi* [letters]" is what is meant; for this very reason...
*Kṣaṃ namaḥ parāya mūrtyātmane namaḥ*— these are the mantras for the extraction [of the syllables], their properties, and so forth (p.

"Sahitāntasthā" means the *dharmas* (phonemes) situated at the end of "a" and so forth; "dharmādyantasthābhiryuktāḥ" means joined with those [phonemes] situated at the end of "a" and so forth; "dharmādyantasthayujas" refers to the knots (*granthi*) which are joined with those [phonemes] situated at the end of "a" and so forth—thus it is. Here, the word "knot" (*granthi*) generally denotes the eight knots beginning with the Āgneya and the others.
If that is so, how then is the establishment of the seed-syllables (*bīja-varṇa*) in the knots of the east and other directions intended?
To this he says: "With *adharma* and so forth, the neuter. This means:
the neuter [terms] together with *adharma* and so forth are "the neuters beginning with *adharma*"; [they are established] together with those neuters beginning with *adharma*.

The present [deity] is non-dharma and so forth, the neuter; the mantras for those [petals] begin with "Obeisance to the supreme Dharma" and "Obeisance to the one whose self is the Āgneya-knot," and so on, using three petals at a time in the form of leaves, starting with the letter *ka* and ending with the letter *bha*.

"Endowed with colors" means followed on all sides by those [letters] whose end is the *karṇikā*; that is, those beginning with *ka* whose final letter is *ma*, which functions as the *karṇikā*. Their respective mantras are: "Obeisance to the Supreme One, the essence of the eastern filament, *kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ namaḥ*," and so forth.

The final *sparśa* (consonant), which has become the seed (*bījabhūta*), possesses the seed-syllable *a*; thus, among the eight vowel-letters (*svaravarṇa*)— which are divided into short and long by the *visarga* immediately following the leaf— the tips [of the *sparśas*] are marked with the *visarga* included within the short vowels and the *bindu* included within the long vowels.
That whose filaments (kesara) are the vowels beginning with *p* (as on page 115)— that is so [described]. *Aḥ*, *Āṃ*, *Namaḥ* to the supreme self whose nature is the eastern filament.

The mantras beginning with "namaḥ" are here [the petals]; because the final vowel 'a'— which serves as the seed-syllable of the leaf— is the seed of the tactile sense (sparśa), there is the worship of the lotus of letters for the pericarp, even though it has descended from the flavor inherent in the leaf, due to the external sequence of forward and reverse order.

Having thus described the attainment of the phonemes beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*, which are joined by the sacrificial rites following the *kesara* [syllables] as understood through the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*), he leads them inward with the syllable *oṃ*;
for the nature of the cause has been stated as "the word *prati* for every living being," and so forth.

He describes the pervasion of the *praṇava* (OM) by means of the phonemes and forms with the words "by the parts of Tārā": "Endowed with the three parts of Tārā through the sequence of Ātman, Vidyā, and Paratattva; [the mantra] is declared to be pervaded everywhere upon the petals, filaments, and pericarp by the parts of Tārā beginning with the letter 'A', which constitute the principles of Ātman, Vidyā, and Paratattva."
The meaning is "endowed with. The mantras beginning with *īṃ ātmatattvātmane namaḥ* (Salutation to the Self-principle, the letter *īṃ*) and so forth are those mantras.

Here, by the force of the statement "endowed with the triad of *tārā* syllables," [it follows that] prior even to the worship of the three principles (*tattva*), [the worship] of their constituent parts [is required].

Some also remember the worship of the three mandalas as being within themselves; here, in the center of the pericarp, [one worships] that which is joined with the power of sound (*nādaśakti*). In this context, by the two terms *nāda* and *śakti*, one refers to the *nāda-śakti* which is a constituent part of the *tārā* (the syllable *oṃ*), and its seed-syllable, the letter *ha*.
The two syllables *hrīṃ* are also stated as a pair in the Tantra: *hṛn namaḥ parāya nādātmane namaḥ* and *hrīṃ namaḥ parāya śaktyātmane namaḥ*; these are their respective mantras.

"The letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, the *bindu*, the *nāda*, the *śakti*, and the *śānta*—thus the *praṇava* is remembered as sevenfold," and so forth. Among these parts of the *praṇava* as recorded in the Smṛtis, the first part consists of the *bhūtātman* and so on; for the triad [of *ātman*s], the penultimate part [is the *jñānātman*].

It should be understood that by the very apprehension of the two—the *nāda* and *śakti*, which constitute the manifest portion—there is also necessarily included the apprehension of the other portions, namely the *bindu* and *śānta*. This is indicated by the mantras: *saṃ namaḥ parāya bindvātmane namaḥ* and *oṃ namaḥ parāya śāntātmane namaḥ*.

With their respective mantras. The connection is that one should thus visualize the lotus of letters (lipipaṅkaja) as distinguished by the specific attributes such as the syllables beginning with *kṣa* and the [deity] forms. Upon that lotus of letters, one should place the tortoise-slab (*kūrmaśilā*). This explains the consecration of the tortoise-slab.

"Having washed" means: then, having washed that tortoise-stone (*kūrmaśilā*) which has been consecrated (*adhivāsita*) there in that lotus-diagram (*lipipadmaka*), and having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
one should place it with the mantra "akūbāra," worship it again, and make a request preceded by the performance of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The filling of that pit for the propitiation of Gaṇapati, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and the Supreme Deity (p.
The phrase "he says" refers to the section beginning with "the eastern [direction]" and ending with "he should satiate the fire.

Now, following the worship of Gaṇapati and Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and having worshipped the Lord of Gods at the doorway, he should satiate the fire; this is the preliminary rite, supplied by way of the "lion's glance" (siṃhāvalokana) principle.

He collects [the materials]. He gathers the *vāstubali* offering which serves as the preliminary part for the laying of the bricks; then he should worship the site-deity (*vāstu*) in the northeast with *kuśa* grass, flowers, unbroken rice, and cooked rice. In that regard, first—
He shows what must be taught regarding the arrangement of that *tatpuruṣa* [mantra] by stating the arrangement of eighty-one words.

The connection is that "in the middle" means that in the outer row there should be one word for each of Īśa and the others; he then speaks of the deities to be worshipped with the aforementioned words, beginning with "to be worshipped," and so forth.

Up to the word "vicakṣaṇaḥ," Brahmā is to be worshipped in the nine squares. Furthermore, in the previously mentioned eastern group of six, in the two pairs of corners of the fire (southeast), Ārya by name, Savitṛ, and Sāvitra are to be worshipped; the term "to be worshipped" carries over [from the previous context]. Vivasvān is situated in the Viṭ square.

By implication, "in the south" means Indra and Indrajaya; likewise, "the pair in the direction of Nairṛta" means [those two]. "Measured" means situated in the western direction. "Rudrajaya and Rudra" likewise means the pair in the Vāyavya direction. The remainder is that there is a group of six in the north (saumya). In that regard:
The Mountain (Mahīdhara) and Āpavatsa are in the two directions of Śarva;
likewise, Water (Āpas) is to be worshipped in due order—this is the remainder [of the instruction]. Outside of Īśa and the others is Kaṃ.

The deity residing in each individual word of the line says: "Then, however" (*tatas tu*) and so forth, ending with "situated in the northern direction" (*kauberyāṃ diśi saṃsthitā*). Having thus described the division of the words for the forty-five deities beginning with Brahmā, he states the location of the remaining eight:

With the passage beginning with "Śarva-skanda" and ending with "vicakṣaṇa," he states here as well that [the offering] should be performed outside of that: "Then one should offer the bali to the planetary spirits (devagraha) and so forth in due order.
This means according to the stated sequence, by way of circumambulation; thus he recites the planets and then the gods.

To indicate the necessity of the *vāstu-bali* (the ritual offering to the site-spirit), he recounts a traditional narrative beginning with "There was once...": Long ago, immediately after the creation of the world, there was a most terrifying Asura named Vāstu;
tormenting the world, he was struck down upon the earth by the gods. By those gods...
For the purpose of rousing him, one should worship the Lord with these fifty-three deities stationed upon the limbs of that Vāstupuruṣa,
using offerings consisting of clarified butter and other sacrificial materials as described in other ritual manuals.
One should worship them with their respective names. He concludes: "Having offered the bali-oblation to them in sequence with devotion and having bowed, one should ask for forgiveness.
This establishes the sequence of the bali-oblation mentioned in both alternatives, beginning with the words "from the middle."

119) The description of the *vāstubali* offering after the excavation in the portion of Śiva and after the leveling in the portion of Viṣṇu is for the purpose of indicating that it must be performed in both cases and in both places.
It should be understood that this does not refer to the grasping of either one [of the two].
By first providing a resolution, he introduces what must be done immediately thereafter with the word "thus" (evam).

"He collects the bricks and should place them on the right side of the door according to the rule"— this statement explains the fire-oblation (*homa*), which constitutes a portion of the aforementioned ritual procedure,
from the words "there, in the north" up to "one hundred and eight," or [the offering] to Indra and the other deities.
Having drawn the lines with the *vyāhṛtis* and [the names of] Indra and the other deities— the word "lines" (*rekhā*) being understood to follow from the previous context—

thereafter, following the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*) and so forth; or else, having stood behind the fire on its western side with palms joined in reverence (*kṛtāñjali*), facing eastward and thus facing the fire.

One should mutter the eight-syllabled mantra; having muttered it thus, bowing with excessive devotion—his head being bent low—while remembering Nārāyaṇa, the Lord who is the source of manifestation through his manifold form, he should mutter it eight times in this manner, having obtained His permission, as is implied by the context. Thus...
Having performed these rites upon those bricks, having offered the clarified butter from the remnants of the oblation, and having dismissed the fire,
the Guru, bowing down and facing eastward toward the site of the bricks,
[regards] that fire as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

Having meditated upon the Lord who is the subject at hand, one should understand that the eight bricks are pervaded by the Blessed One in the form of the Virāj-body, by means of the designation of the eight *prakṛtis*.

The meaning is "having conceived [them] in this way. Having thus meditated, one should place those eight bricks—each marked with one of the eight syllables—from Agni to Indra within the planned squares;
specifically, in the four-square diagram, they are to be placed in the squares of Agni and Vāyu.

Having divided the field into four quadrants by marking two lines each— one from the north (saumya) to the east (pūrva), and likewise one from the southwest (nirṛti) to the northeast (īśa)— in accordance with the sequence prescribed in other scriptures.

The meaning is that one should place [the syllables] starting from the section named Āgneya (the southeast) up to the two words located in the northeast cell (Īśa) ending with the word of Indra (Indra). And so it is stated in the *Prayogamañjarī*: "One should duly [place] the eight Satya-kalās with the eight..."

"One should lay down the bricks according to the rule of circumambulation, numbering one hundred, from the east (aravāt) up to the northeast (īśānta), in all the directions. Thus, the reading "from Agni to Īśāna" (agnyādīśāntam) is correct; and so it is stated in the Viṣṇu-saṃhitā:
One should place those eight bricks starting from Agni and ending with Īśāna; therein, with respect to the four squares mentioned as being within the square [mandala], (p.

The procedure for the ritual placement (vinyāsa) extends from Agni to Īśāna; this should be understood as the "bricks" (iṣṭakā). Having thus prepared the bricks, [one should perform the rite] with pure jars—those purified by straining and other means, refined with cloth, and previously filled and arranged.

Having filled the pit in the center of the bricks with fragrant waters rich in the scent of *saṃpāta* and gems, and having placed auspicious flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) upon it while reciting the *Tāra*, one should observe the whirlpool (*āvarta*). Regarding the result of observing the whirlpool, he says: "The whirlpools here are both auspicious and inauspicious."
"The southern and northern [sides] are to be known. Regarding "rice and so forth":

thereafter, following the propitiation of the deities residing there, one should cover the pit with soil from fields such as those growing rice. And thus it is said in the *Prayogamañjarī*: "And one should fill it completely."
"By means of rice and so forth, with the soil produced from the field"—the remainder is easy to understand.
He states the purpose of the "sleep-killer" (*svapnaghna*) by means of the rest of the text beginning with "In an auspicious [dream], there is gain," and so on.
He introduces what must be done next, preceded by the resolution of the present topic, by means of this [verse].
He describes the arrangement of the womb-vessel (garbhapātra) with the passage beginning with "of the palace" and ending with "those who know it":
starting from a size of four cubits corresponding to the palace, up to seventy-one cubits for the final palace, and beginning from one cubit [for smaller ones].

(122) The temple [should be] from one cubit up to nine cubits; the *liṅga* and the womb-vessel (*garbhapātra*) should be four finger-breadths in length, and it is taught that these three [measurements] should end at one cubit.
"One should calculate by means of the triple-proportion (trairāśika)"—thus it is said in the *Pāśupata*:

"The vessel for the highest [grade] should be eight finger-breadths wide and half that in height, with the height at the top being three-quarters of that; it should be one cubit in length. Here, the height is determined by the triple-proportion."
Regarding what is to be fashioned,

it is stated in the *Prayogamañjarī*, in the *Sumatisaṃhitā*, and in other Āgamas: "The [canopy] is eight finger-breadths [in width], half of that less [for the middle], and one-quarter less for the upper covering."

One should fashion the inner vessel (*garbhapātra*) according to the proportions of the temple, characterized by density and other such qualities; furthermore, one should purify it according to the prescribed rules, such as washing with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), without deviating from the ritual procedure. Regarding the measurement of the vessel in another manner, he says "well-concealed" (*suguptam*), which is as follows:
The wall should be well-concealed; likewise, by means of this [measurement], the arrangement of the altar (*vedi*) shall be formed from the wall.

Regarding the wall, he says in the remainder of the text: "The wall, the pillar," and so forth. That measurement falling upon the portion of the wall is one-third of the fourfold space of the wall-pillar.
Having divided the length of the wall and pillar into four parts,
and having further divided one of those parts into three, the wise know that one of those [subdivisions] to be [the measure].

The meaning is that it is one-twelfth of the height of the wall or pillar. Having divided the width of the pillar by the [three] qualities (guṇas), the measurement of two parts is stated for Śiva; however, according to the Bhāga-śāstra, the wall is one-fourth of the pillar, which amounts to one part.

"Regarding that, it is stated in another Smṛti: 'It is said to be four finger-breadths in measure, and having made it up to the end of the hand [of the door], it is thus prescribed,' and so forth; this is for the most part the same. Having thus described the arrangement of the womb-vessel (garbhapātra), he now states the location for placing the womb (garbha) with the words beginning with 'of the door'."
On the right side— that is, the side other than the left— of the door of the future palace, having divided the width of the wall into three parts and set aside two parts toward the outside,
one should [place it] there in the remaining third part. Even that third part [is further divided].
Having divided the third part into three and set aside two parts within,

one should divide the width of the wall in the remaining outer part into nine parts; having set aside six parts outside and two parts inside, when the remaining outer part has been smeared with cow-urine...

On that [altar], one should place [the materials] by joining the base of the door-posts to the side of the base of the doorway; "the womb" (*garbha*) is the understood subject. Regarding the method of depositing the substances there in the womb-vessel (*garbhapātra*), he says, beginning with "washed" and ending with "golden."

When this vessel has been washed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and purified by means of the *dhāraṇīs*, and when the worship of the seat (*pīṭha-pūjā*) has been performed upon that seat— which is fashioned from rice and other materials— [one should place it] upon unbroken grains (*akṣata*).

Having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*)— that is, having extracted the ocean according to the principle stated in the *Śivabhāga*— and once this vessel has been placed upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*), one should first extract the ocean from it; then,
having meditated upon the lotus of the syllables (*akṣarāmbhoja*) according to the rule, [one should place] the earth with its mountains and oceans within that.

Having meditated again and again upon the world-sphere (bhūmaṇḍala) situated within the world-elephants (diggaja), one should place the earth-clods struck from the mountains and other sources in the middle and at the corners [of the mandala] with the Gāyatrī and other mantras; "in the form of a tortoise" (kūrmarūpam) means the image of a tortoise, that is to say, the tortoise itself. The rest is easy to understand.
One should bring all that together and, having gathered it, place it within the vessel of the womb.

He describes the *garbha-homa* with the textual sequence beginning with "having done thus" (*kṛtvaivaṃ*). "Having done" means having performed the arrangement of the substances; the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) implies this. Having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) using the twelve-syllable mantra (*dvādaśārṇavidyā*), one should place it to the south of the fire.

The meaning is that one should perform the oblation in sequence as before, according to the previously mentioned procedure for the *iṣṭakā-homa*, including the rites from the cooked offerings up to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. In that regard,
it is stated that the *iṣṭakā-homa* for the eight types of knowledge (*aṣṭavidyā*) and so forth is performed with the eight syllables individually.
Regarding the establishment of specific mantras (p.
he states the other mantras to be offered with the twelve [verses] beginning with *varṇarīti* and so forth, accompanied by clarified butter.

"Ending with 'vṛṣabhāstara' and ending with the *vyāhṛtis*": after that, following the specific mantra-homa, one should offer the *vyāhṛtis* ending with the *vyāhṛtis*. Then, one should offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*), as well as clarified butter, one hundred and eight times with the *gāyatrī* mantra.

Having offered the previously mentioned *vyāhṛtis* along with the four substances and so forth, and having offered the clarified butter as a *saṃpāta* oblation, one should present that *saṃpāta* clarified butter; then, visualizing the earth beneath that vessel standing before one, one should mutter the mantras— the mantras prescribed for the *homa*.
At night, during an auspicious moment and accompanied by favorable omens, having obtained the permission of the twice-born,
that preceptor— facing east and endowed with supreme devotion—
meditated upon his own body as Hari and [placed] the Śakti upon a consecrated seat within the sanctum.
Having meditated and worshipped this vessel of the womb situated in the foremost hand,
and recollecting the white earthly Brahmāṇḍa which has become the womb of this Śakti,
[one should place] within this vessel, as before, the terrestrial sphere resting upon Ananta, along with its mountains and oceans.
Having meditated upon the Earth in the manner previously described as the "World-Elephant" (diggaja), slowly reciting the mantra to be stated hereafter,
one should act according to the rule for the birth of the House-Form (gṛhamūrti) and the manifestation of the Person of the Temple (prāsādapuruṣa).

The connection is: "one should deposit the embryo (garbha) without deviating from the stated rule" (p. 126). He states that mantra for the deposition of the embryo (garbhanyāsa) with the words beginning "sarva-".

He concludes the description of the results with the word "evam" (thus). Thereafter, one should have the form of the transformation of the *garbha* placed within the temple constructed by artisans; this is the ellipsis.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Tattvaprakāśinī*, a commentary on the *Kriyāsāra*.
Having described the procurement of the materials for the consecration of the image of Śrī Viṣṇu,

[the author], now commencing the exposition of the collection of rites beginning with the sowing of auspicious sprouts— which constitute the preliminary stage of the consecration— first describes the offering of the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*).

He promises to speak: "Now I shall explain. Now, after explaining the accomplishment of the temple and so forth, he says, "I shall explain the planting of the auspicious sprout in brief. By the inclusion of the word "in brief," he indicates that the intended purpose is for the enjoyment of Śiva.

Having resolved upon that time— such as a seven-day period or more— in view of the day of initiation for the great sacrifice (*mahādhvara*) of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the mantra-image, which consists of the form of the initiatory rite (*dīkṣaṇīya*) and the sowing of the seeds of auspiciousness,
and by virtue of it being the remainder of the preparatory fast (*vāsaśeṣatayā*).

Just as with the *niddhyā* and other rites that must be completed according to their respective rules, one should not begin [the main rite] until those preliminary ones are fully accomplished; this is the rule. However, once the temple has been built and the auspicious moment (*muhūrta*) determined, the excellent preceptor (*ācāryavarya*), being wise and possessing a mind purified by the rituals of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*abhiṣeka*), should perform [the main rite].

(127) A *prāsāda* is so called because the Lord (*īśvara*) is pleased (*prasīdati*) while seated therein; it refers to a temple for a deity, a mantra-image, or both. When that [site] has been prepared at the auspicious moment (*muhūrta*), one should perform the rite once it has indeed been properly prepared.
The phrase "planting the auspicious sprout" (maṅgalāṅkuraropaṇam) refers, by implication, to the procedure as intended; thus, he states one specific time:

"in the northern [solstice]" (uttare). In that regard, it means during the first half of the year, when it is perfectly pure and not defiled by defects such as the guru being in retrograde motion (māuḍhya), specifically at the time of the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa).

At that time, specifically during the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), on an auspicious day characterized by a favorable weekday, lunar date (tithi), and asterism (nakṣatra)—here, by the word "day" (dina), the asterism is intended—the quality of being auspicious is common to all three, namely the weekday and the others; or alternatively, by the word "day," the solar day (ahar) is meant, and thus... [the passage continues].
In that regard, they first enumerate the asterisms suitable for it, namely Punarvasu and Bharaṇī;
the word "and" (ca) indicates that Revatī and the others, which are listed in the latter half [of the sequence], are inferior, while Bharaṇī, which is listed last of all, is the most inferior.

It indicates the lunar days (tithis) and multiplies them, beginning with the first day (pratipad). It mentions the weekdays starting with Monday (Soma), and speaks of the auspiciousness of the ascendant (lagna) through the phrase "observation of the rising" (udayanirīkṣaṇa).
By the portion of the text stating "situated in the twelfth house," it indicates a momentary defect (muhūrtadoṣa) that must necessarily be avoided; [it refers to] a weak Mars (bhauma).

"One should observe the Sun situated in the twelfth house"— the meaning is that [the practitioner] would become blind after a long time. "Having examined" means having thus examined the auspicious moment (muhūrta) prior to that.
"Before a day and a moment" means before the seventh, ninth, or fifth day;
the word "before" (prāk) is to be understood separately and connected with each of the terms "seventh" and so forth, and this "seventh" is relative to that [day].
The use of the fifth case ending for the seventh day and so forth is likewise stated in the *Sumatisaṃhitā*:
"On the seventh or even the ninth day, or indeed on an auspicious day prior," and so on; and Śiva himself declared this regarding the eighth day following the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
