"One should perform the offering of sprouts beforehand"—thus it has been stated; therefore, prior to the seventh day and so forth, on an auspicious day, one should perform the planting of the auspicious sprouts (*maṅgalāṅkurāropaṇa*). He states "on an auspicious day" because the sowing of seeds (*bījāvāpa*) must also be accomplished at an auspicious time, or else this [statement] is intended for that purpose.
Regarding the procedure for the alternative timing [of initiation], having established the time of sowing, he states the task for the day of initiation connected to that:
"In this case, the procedure for the seed and the sprout is accompanied by worship as prescribed for the three times."

He elaborates upon the procedure for sowing the seed (*bījāvāpa-vidhi*) preceded by the description of the vessel (*pātra*) and other implements, in the textual passage beginning with "threefold" and ending with "the attentive Guru," [pertaining to] all ritual acts (p.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: in all auspicious rites, such as the consecration of a deity (*pratiṣṭhā*), the festival of the ritual jar (*kalaśotsava*), and so forth, one should purify the seeds after having prepared pedestals with bundles of rice (*vrīhikūrcaka*), placed vessels filled with clay and other materials upon them, and arranged [the seeds] with the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*).
"Priyaṅgu, mustard, śyāmā, rāja-māṣa, āḍhakī, yava, mudga, paśiṃbuka, and kulattha"—these are separate words; "they shall be the seeds" is the completion of the sentence.
The rest is easy to understand. He states the mantra for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*): "jitanta" and so forth.

He describes the procedure for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*)—beginning with "tritāra"—and the procedure for worship (*pūjana*)—beginning with "devatā"—by means of half a verse. Those seed-syllables (*bīja*) are [associated] with the names of the deities:
Brahmā, Rudra, and Hari are to be worshipped respectively in the barley, mustard, and mudrā; and Vāyu is to be worshipped.
Skanda is to be worshipped in *niṣpāva* beans; Śakra in *priyaṅgu*; Agni in *māṣa* beans;
Arka in *kulattha*; Yama in *śāli* rice; Varuṇa in sesame seeds; Śrī in *rājamāṣa* beans; Rādhakī in *śyāmāka*; and the Moon in [other grains]—thus it is stated in another Smṛti.

The meaning is "with the mantras of the deities"; the intention is that one should worship those seed-syllables (*bīja*) at each of the three libations (*anusavana*). Likewise, in another scripture it is said:
"Every day, the worship of the deity of the seat (*pīṭha*) together with the vessel containing the seed-syllables."
"He is to be worshipped at the libations (savanas), being unshakable, with water and other offerings at the conclusion of the sprinkling" (p.
One should perform those [offerings] with the names of the deities, with the syllable *caṃ*, and with the root mantra (*mūla*), using perfumes and flowers.

"One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth"—with these words he describes the procedure for the *bali* offering, from the verse beginning with "In the mandalas" up to the end of the verse ending with "uttering the respective mantra. He describes the *bali* substances from the verse beginning with "Palala" up to the end of the verse ending with "and likewise the nine jewels"; here, *palala* refers to roasted sesame seeds.

Roasted rice, *uḍumba*, buds, parched grains (*lājāḥ*), and blossoms of roasted *śāli* rice; with the remainder of the text beginning with "at dawn" and so forth, he states the time for the final daily offering and describes the installation of the banner (*dhvaja*) preceded by the performance of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

"Thus" means performed according to the rules through the *dhāraṇās* and so forth; "purified according to the rules" refers to the vehicle (*vāhana*) preceded by the extraction of its mantra. He describes its worship: with the vocative "Tārā," followed by the word "King of Birds" (*pakṣirāja*) ending in the suffix for the vocative case, [he addresses] the King of Birds.

Having established [the deity] with the mantra consisting of the words "Come, come," one should worship with perfumes and other offerings using that very eight-syllable mantra of the King of Birds (*pakṣirāja*).
Then, as it is stated in the *Grantha*: "The seed-sprout has arisen again," he extracts [the mantra] from the portion belonging to Śiva; this is its root.

This has been explained word-for-word by the remainder of the text beginning with these words. Having thus performed the sowing of the seed-syllables and so forth, and having established [the deity], he summarizes the consecration of the image (bimba-saṃskāra) with the word "atha" (now).
Now, p. 131.

After the commencement of the sowing of seeds and other such appropriate rites, and in accordance with the prescribed rules, the artisans— without deviating from the established method for the production of the image—
should fashion the image, adorned with its characteristic marks, from the neck down to the navel and the private parts.
One should fashion [the image] according to the measurement of the face, and so forth; it should be characterized by the previously mentioned marks.
It may be purchased, provided it is free from defects such as stone fractures or other flaws.

An image that has not been purchased solely for the taking of materials from the artisan should be used when the time arrives; [if it is made of] stone, it should be kept for three nights, and if of metal, for one night.

When the time specified for each particular type of gemstone has arrived—as indicated by the passage beginning with "maṇinigām" and so forth—one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) in water. Regarding the phrase "endowed with characteristics," he describes the formulation of the primary characteristics among those already mentioned as "the opening of the eyes. And by the artisans...
By the use of the word "ca" (and), it is indicated that the teacher himself should first adopt a common gaze;

for those who are trembling, the opening of the eyes should be performed according to the method taught in other scriptures— that procedure [is explained] by the teacher himself in the ritual for the *biṃba* and the jar.

He will speak of the acceptance of the image; he explains that one "takes hold of the image" by means of the *praṇava*. Immediately after the absence of an agent [of consecration], he states the contemporary purification:
"having washed," meaning having first washed it on all sides with water using *darbha* grass.
Having rubbed [the body] with earth, *darbha* grass, and bark, and having washed it with cow-hair [brushes],...

Having touched this [image] which has been smeared with ghee, one should then wash it after the application of lentil powder (*masūra-cūrṇa*). He states that one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) for the purpose of manifesting the form of the Virāṭ of that [image], beginning with the words "śamī-pallava" and ending with "should offer the *saṃpāta* clarified butter."

Having mentally conceived the image as the object to be consecrated in the fire in front of one, and having directed that fire toward it— in that sense— it says "nīrāñjanam" (the rite of waving lights) and "by the Brahmins," meaning that for its protection, one should perform the nīrāñjana rite by means of the Brahmins. Then, in the afternoon, following the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) and so forth—

Having worshipped Varuṇa upon the ocean-slab of the Yoga-pīṭha, and while recollecting the Yoga-pīṭha itself, one should withdraw the image from the path of the ocean according to the procedure to be described— beginning with "endowed with the nose and the organ of generation"— and having meditated upon it as consisting of fire, [one should extract it] from the luminous orb.

One should place the luminous form of the *bimba* within the water; having meditated externally on the five mantra-flames and externally on the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) situated in the directions starting from the east with the five mantras of Vāsudeva and the others, and with the final one situated in the remaining direction— and by implication, with the *astra* mantra— [one should perform the rite].

The meaning is that after the conceptualization of the five forms (mūrti-pañcaka), one should protect [them] and, outside of them, one should conceptualize the world-protectors (lokapāla) as being intent upon their protection; this is understood through the relative gradation of the ritual substances.

He states the duration for the ritual immersion (*jalādhivāsa*) as "for three nights" (*trirātram*). Because one's own self is conceived as the infinite specific form of the image of Śrī Viṣṇu, it is likewise conceived [to remain] for three nights;
whereas metal [images] are [conceived] for one night—that is, for only a single day and night—in the water, both by day and by night.

The word "should consecrate" (*adhivāsayet*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. He concludes with the words "with the head to the east. Having thus described the preliminary consecration of the image and the water, he introduces the purification of the temple—which is to be performed simultaneously with that [consecration]—with the word "now" (*atha*), using the term "unwearied" (*atandrita*).
When the image of Viṣṇu has been installed and the sequence of purification has begun, and the temple has been properly constructed—
meaning the architectural work has reached completion—
the gross body of the temple, which serves as the substratum for that installation, is also [prepared].

It is indicated that he caused [the image] to be defiled by means of the entry of minor protective spirits (*kṣudrarakṣa*) with a view toward the [proper] time; this he explains with the words "together with the *mūrtipas*," and so forth. Having approached the temple (*prāsāda*) together with the *mūrtipas*, performing a circumambulation (*sapradakṣiṇa*), [he went] to the right of the house—that is, to the south of the temple.

Seated at the side, the Guru should perform, in due order, the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and so forth— the worship consisting of the placement of mantras, the propitiation of Gaṇādhīśa, the means of purification,
the installation [of the deity], and so on— and furthermore, the temple that has just been released from the carpenters, as soon as it is released.
One should purify; [the author] explains the purification with the sūtras beginning with "with the sūtras" (p.
134) and ending with "the state of *tāla* and so forth," which refers, for that purpose, to the inner sanctum (*garbhāgāra*).

Having gazed all around outside with the weapon-vision (*astradṛṣṭi*), and having encircled it with threads and a garland of *darbha* grass, one should again sweep it, sprinkle it with cow dung, wash it,
and smear it with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).
And one should scatter mustard seeds, unbroken rice grains, and dūrvā grass.

Having swept the area, smeared it with cow dung, and anointed it with fragrant waters— and by the use of the word "and," having sprinkled it with products of the cow— one should scatter *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice, *kuśa* grass, and so forth, everywhere with the eight-syllable mantra, using the five powers beginning with Parameṣṭhin.
One should offer incense along with a lamp; then, regarding the grains:

next, in any one of the corners—namely the northeast, southeast, or northwest—having performed the ritual service (*caryā*) there and having scattered the grains, one should place a full jar and the weapon-jar (*astrakalaśa*).

Having sprinkled [the area] on all sides with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the remainder of the *pañcagavya*, using the mantra beginning with "kṛṇuṣva" and the wheel-mantra (*cakramantra*), one should perform the triple clapping of the hands (*tālatraya*) and so forth. It should be understood that here, the subsequent sprinkling with *pañcagavya* is according to the traditional practice (*sāṃpradāyika*).

He describes the oblation for the destruction of demons (*rakṣoghna-homa*) with the words "In the southeast" (*āgneyyām*). One should offer cooked food with the two mantras beginning with *rakṣohaṇam*, then with those beginning with *kṛṇuṣva*, and with the five [mantras] beginning with *ye devāḥ*; likewise, one should offer clarified butter (*ājya*) with the [five] Durgā-mantras and the *vyāhṛtis*.

The connection is that "having offered [the preliminary oblation], one should offer the four substances. He explains the oblation of the four substances with the words beginning "apāmārga": with the *cakra*-mantra, the fuel-sticks of *apāmārga*, the sacrificial food (*havis*), and the clarified butter (*ājya*).
The remainder [of the sentence] is that one should complete the homa after having offered one hundred and eight oblations for each [deity];

this includes the offering of the *saṃpāta* (the remnants of the oblation) and so forth. Regarding the specific details beginning with "apāmārga" and ending with "and he should fill the *śvaśra*," it means that one should fill the *śvaśra*—that is, the foundation pit—with grains.
The remaining portion introduces the Vāstuhoma with the words "evam" (thus). Regarding "tameva" (that very same):

having established that very fire which was already accepted for the Rākṣoghna-homa, one [performs the rite] on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) prepared to the east of it with rice grains, strewn with cloth, and covered with Kuśa and Dūrvā grass.
One should place two jars filled respectively with rice and water, each containing a bunch of *śamī* leaves.
Then, having placed gold in the jar of rice— that is, in the jar filled with rice—
one should [worship] with the verse beginning "gaṇānāṃ tvā," which indicates exclusivity (*evakāra*) by implying independence from anything else.

Having performed the "twice-revolved" (dvirāvartita) rite with his own feet and limbs, he should worship Śānti with the verse *śanno devī* and with water-offerings (*vārghya*) and so forth in due order, prior even to the installation of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
Having done this, he should then [offer] the cooked [oblation] with the two mantras beginning with *atha vāstoṣpate*.

One should perform the oblation with the six verses beginning with "vāstoṣpate dhruvaḥ" and so forth, followed by the five [verses] beginning with "jñāta," and again with the groups of nine auspicious verses (śannavarga).

Likewise, one should offer oblations of clarified butter with the *vyāhṛtis*; one should perform [the rite] with the verse "śanno devī" using *śamī* fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and boiled rice; then, one should offer oblations with the root mantra and with *dūrvā* grass smeared with cow-products; having offered one hundred and eight oblations thus.

What was stated by Śivabhaga applies here as well; the ellipsis is that one should "complete the fire-oblation" (*homam samāpayet*). Then, he says "at the conclusion of the oblation," and so forth, ending with "one should cause [the officiant] to recite 'Obeisance to the Vastu of Śiva' (*śivāṃ vāstu*)," to indicate that one should perform the offering of the *haviḥ*, the *vāstu-bali*, the *saṃpāta*, and so on.
This is explained by the [preceding] statement itself.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Tattvaprakāśinī*, a commentary on the *Kriyāsāra*.
Now, with half a verse beginning with "tathā," he announces the consecration of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).

He summarizes the characteristics of the pavilion with the words "the pavilion. He describes its consecration with the passage beginning with "the threads" and ending with "one should perform the three claps, etc. Having sipped water, restrained his speech, performed self-purification, and adorned himself according to the rule—
Having gathered all the ritual materials such as the thread and so forth therein, and having wrapped it all around with a thread and a cord of *darbha* grass,

one should place archways made from *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *vaṭa*, and *plakṣa* wood at the gateway locations in the four directions— namely, the four cardinal directions starting from the east— in their proper sequence.

137) One should drive [the stakes] in sequence, not deviating from the order of the feet, using the mantra "May the earth be pleasant" (*syonā pṛthivī*) at the end of the names of the deities of the arches (*toraṇa*), which have been well-adorned with [epithets] such as "beautiful" (*suśobhana*).
The connection.

All five [arches] are two cubits in width; this is the description of the characteristics of the arches (*toraṇa*), which should be stated separately. He enumerates the deities of the arches as "the very beautiful ones" (*suśobhana*). He enumerates the deities of the banners (*dhvaja*) as "the clay of that" (*tanmṛda*).

He states the characteristic of the banner with the word "temple" (*prāsāda*). He states the location for the banner with the phrase "inside the archway" (*toraṇābhyantara*). He describes the worship of those two with the word "archways" (*toraṇāni*). Regarding the term "oblation" (*bali*), having offered the oblation and entered within, at the doorway—that is, at the eastern and other doorways—
On both sides— the right and left sides— in pitchers adorned with jewels, such as rubies and corals, as enumerated in other scriptures,
[he placed] these: Pūrṇa and Puṣkara, as well as Ānanda and Nandana, and Vīrasena.
One should likewise worship Suṣeṇa, Saṃbhava, and Prabhava.
Regarding the worship of the arches and the jars, he says "then at the bases of the arches" with the mantras;
that is, with the specific mantras of their own names, for the purpose of indicating the absence of deities in the intermediate directions.

138) He states that one should worship Indra and the others as objects of sacrifice, saying "Indra," etc.; he describes the purification of the site with the words "with tooth-sticks," etc.; the remainder [of the ritual] is performed with the *Nṛsiṃha* mantra ending in *phaṭ*.

Having conceived of the pavilion as being of the nature of Śakti, one should sprinkle it with the mantra of Vāsudeva; this is the connection with the word "Vāsudeva" which occurs later in the text. The injunction "one should scatter [the grains]" and so forth, beginning with "Vāsudeva," is a separate sentence that serves as a reminder of the rules for the ritual placement (sādana); standing facing the east, one should perform it with that [mantra].

With the aforementioned Vāsudeva, one should scatter the *vikirāḥ* three times with the palm turned upward; the rest is easy to understand. He describes the worship of the Lord of the Pitcher (*kumbheśa*) with the words "In the northeast" (*aiśānyām*). Now, in the northeast, the Lord of the Pitcher—situated upon a heap of grain and accompanied by jewels, gold, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*)—should be [worshipped] in whatever manner is appropriate.

One should fill [the vessel]. Within that, one should worship Hari together with the limbs (*aṅga*) and the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), according to the well-known rites for the worship of the syllables (*lipi*) and the lotus (*padma*).
Having performed that worship as the presiding lord (*īśatva*) and the worship of the *tāri* and so forth, one should circumambulate the Lord of the Vase (*kumbheśa*).

Having established the single sentence beginning with "Now, having filled... and ending with "...or in the western [fire-pit] of one's own pit," and having protected [the site], he says that one should generate the fire, using the passage beginning with "One should worship at the side... and ending with "...or in the western [pit] of one's own pit."
Then, with an unbroken stream [of water], the practitioner, having moved around starting from the northeast sector and ending at the northeast, [should perform the rite].
Having carried it around [the fire], one should place the "Trika-amvardhani" in front;

according to the method stated in another Āgama, one should place it upon the mustard seeds—[referring to] the fire. Afterwards, following the circumambulation of the Lord of the Jar (Kumbheśa), [one should act] in one's own pit (kuṇḍa).

One should kindle the fire in the Guru-kuṇḍa, or in the western circular kuṇḍa (the *pratīcīna-kuṇḍa*); the meaning is that, in the absence of the Ācārya-kuṇḍa, one should kindle the fire in the western kuṇḍa. And so it is stated in the *Nāradīya-paddhati* regarding rites for many deities:

First, having consecrated the fire at the portion of Hari-Hara and established that fire which possesses a dual nature, one should bring forward the eastern fire located in the sacrificial pit with the verse, "We choose Agni as our messenger. Then, [one should proceed] with the verse, "From that fire, wealth... and the verse, "O Agni, you by your days..."
One should lead the southern *pāvaka* [fire] with the mantra "Agnimagnim havīmabhiḥ"; one should lead the northern *pāvaka* [fire] likewise.

This is the specific rule for the four-sided (*catuṣṭapakṣa*) pit: it is equal in extent to the base of the face of the original [pit]. In the middle of its neck (*kaṇṭha*), there are two depressions (*nimna*).
And one should construct the two [pillars] in the middle of that, having the form described as "entering the circular pit," at the region of the neck (p.
The hollow space should be in the form of a channel for as long as it takes for the little finger to enter;

the remainder is generally twelve special finger-breadths (viśiṣṭāṅgula), and furthermore, its handle should be one-third of that, beautiful like a cow’s tail, according to the stated requirements and without exceeding the prescribed beauty.
The handle should be decorated.

In this manner, one should fashion the *sruk* endowed with the proper characteristics, measuring one *aratni* in length; the *sruva* should be made circular, with a mouth two finger-breadths wide, and shaped like a cow’s hoof-print, such that it sinks slightly into soft mud.

Having fashioned the *sruva* ladle—endowed with the characteristics previously described beginning with "it should be"—and by the word "and," the *juhū* ladle as well, one should properly commence the rite known as the generation of the ritual fire (*karmāgni*). He explains this in detail with the passage beginning "having purified" and ending with "one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra. In that [rite], Lakṣmī is in her menses.
Having meditated and worshipped, and having worshipped with the Śrī-bīja accompanied by the limbs beginning with the *āśrama*, [one performs] the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*—
namely, *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, *sīmanta*, *jāta*, and *nāma*.
Likewise, having accepted the sequence— namely *annaprāśana*, *caula*, and *vratabandha*—
one should worship each [rite] individually with the *tāra* (the syllable Om),
and having offered sixty-four oblations of clarified butter with the eight limbs beginning with the Heart-mantra at intervals between them.
One should perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra, as previously stated, using the "twelve-fold self" (*dvādaśātman*) root mantra according to the prescribed rule.
The connection is that, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should perform the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*.
Having thus performed the consecration of the fire (*agnisaṃskāra*), one should invoke [the deity] and worship it;
furthermore, one should offer clarified butter (*ājya*) one hundred and eight times with the root mantra consisting of eight syllables.
Regarding the phrase "the bed": after wandering around Kumbheśa once more, one should prepare the bed.

He explains this with the passage beginning with "previously" and ending with "by means of the twelve-syllable mantra," [describing] the ritual preparation of the bed according to rule, such as the worship of the bed by means of the Śrī-bīja.
Having propitiated [the deity] according to the prescribed rites for that purpose, one should place the water-pots all around.

Regarding the arrangement of the wheel and lotus, he says, starting with "five cubits" and ending with "the remaining parts are like those of the Bhadraka. Alternatively, [the area] may be five cubits, or reduced by one-third, or divided into four parts of one cubit each.
Having divided that [area] into three parts and taken a square field measuring either one-quarter less than those three parts or four cubits (sapāda-catuṣkara), or otherwise five cubits,
one should again [mark] the east-west and north-south lines.
Having stretched seventeen threads and divided them equally into sixteen parts, one should set aside two outer rows for the sake of the door-ornaments (*dvāraśobhā*) and so forth; then,
starting from the outermost [row], one should draw a row all around with that same width, beginning from the fourth [row].
One should divide [the area] into seven equal parts; (p.
142) that which is joined with three parts [of these] is the outer square, joined with a single row.
The third row outside of that should be the pathway (*vīthikā*); this is the remainder [of the instruction]. Having divided that fourth row into five parts, one should join one part to the pathway;
this joining with the fifth part mentioned immediately before is prescribed for a five-cubit [structure].

The other [measurement] previously mentioned consists of seven parts and three parts; it is recorded as being at the end of the fourth part, less one-third and plus one-quarter. Here too, there is a Vedic (ārṣa) sandhi; the remainder is the field within the path (vīthī), which, having been divided and made circular, [is placed] in its center.
In the center of the circular field, between the pericarp and the central circle,
one should rotate [the line] such that the internal portion and the external portion are equal;
one should divide the middle section into four parts, as is the case here with the central region.
Within those four parts, using three of them,
one should draw an eight-petaled lotus; then, with the remaining fourth part,
one should divide the navel— which is circular in form— equally into three parts by means of three concentric circles.
And one should draw it as follows: having drawn an outer circle on the lamp-stand (dīpadīpikā) and divided its center equally,
one should conceive three other equal quadrangular fields within the inner half,
and having so arranged them, one should fashion a lotus in the central triad.
p.
143) "The wise one should draw three naves within the inner space of three and a half [parts]. Regarding the word "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*):
after thus completing the arrangement of the parts up to the naves, the spokes and the outer [circumference] are divided into three.

"Equally" means that in the division under discussion, having drawn the spokes equally within the outer portion by means of two inner portions, one should divide that third part— which consists of the rim (*nemi*), the middle rim (*marā*), and the circumference (*paridhi*)—
into two perfectly equal parts, and then rotate the thread situated there according to the internal and external divisions.

One should divide it into two parts. He explains the arrangement of the spokes with the words "at the joint of the spokes" and so forth: at the joint—that is, in the interval—of the spokes, one should cast five threads;
one should also divide the crosswise line into twelve parts.

Having demarcated twelve spoke-fields according to the method taught by the learned, beginning with the rule: "One should divide [the circle] into three parts from the junctions of the lines extending toward the directions established upon its circumference, down to the center, and along the two sides, using the lines fixed at the middle," and so forth;
The meaning is that, having established the twelve lines of the beginning and middle,
one should cast five horizontal lines each within the intervals of the spokes and the middle lines; that is, having rotated that spoke-field three times.

The root and tip of the spokes—the two at the root and the two at the tip—along with the line through the middle of the spokes, are each joined by a single step on both sides; thus, the middle [of the spokes] is endowed with two steps each. (p. 144) Of the spokes...

Having made the middle part such that it is increased by one-fourth through the method of placing two pairs of units on both sides of the central line, one should fashion the spokes according to the analogy and their proper form; as for the rim, one should divide the location of the rim into two parts.

The extensions (*prathayaḥ*) situated on the original rim (*prakṛtanemi*) are to be made as primary extensions (*pradhayaḥ*). Among these, the primary extensions (*pradhayaḥ*) have their front joints (*āgrānyasandhayaḥ*) located internally; twelve of the extensions have their front joints located externally, while the other joints are the central joints of the spokes (*arālamadhyasandhayaḥ*).
And so it is said in the *Dīpadīpikā*: "The spokes, their tips, their middles, the threads arising therefrom, and the twelve internal joints;
as well as the external [spokes] and their expansions, which are divided according to the lines of those joints."
Because they are of such a nature, they should be numbered at twenty-four.

The remainder—the outer path (*bahiṣṭhavīthī*) and so forth—should be constructed as it is well-known elsewhere, as described in the *Bhadraka* and other texts; this is the implied meaning. He states the specific detail for filling that space: "one should fill it with colored powders (*rajas*)."

The remaining parts [of the ritual] are as described for the Bhadra [type of pavilion], up to the end; having thus concluded the description of the circular [pavilion] by means of this self-explanatory passage, [the text now describes] the portion concerning the purification and bathing of the image (*biṃba*) within the pavilion to be constructed.
(145) By the words "all this, beginning with the construction of the pavilion," and so forth, [it refers to] the jars. Now,
having laid out squares in front of the bathing pavilion, upon all of them on every side...

The construction is as follows: having prepared the pedestals (*pīṭha*) with grains according to the rules, one should fill the jars (*kalaśa*) accompanied by the rites appropriate for that, such as the worship of the pedestal and the consecration of the jars (*kuṃbhasaṃskāra*).
He summarizes that filling [of the jars] in the verse beginning with "eighty-one" (*ekāśīti*), etc., in the cardinal and intermediate directions.

By the phrase ending with "one should fill," it is meant that one should fill the central group of nine [vessels] in the field of eighty-one squares with substances beginning with sprouts and ending with earth; the meaning is that one should fill the remaining external nine vessels surrounding the central nine after having filled the central nine.

One should divide [the materials] according to the rules for substances such as sprouts, beginning with "Brahmā" and ending with "taking the earth from the center. Here, *brahma* refers to the *palāśa* tree; *śrīvṛkṣa* means the *vilva* tree;
and *candana* refers to white sandalwood and red sandalwood. *Jāti* refers to the *jāti* flower; and likewise—

In the manual (paddhati), white and red sandalwood, jasmine, and kunda flowers are mentioned; this connects with the passage beginning with "vrīhi" and ending with "he should fill the jar located in the northwest. And in the north, there is "maṅgala" on top.
The concise statement beginning with *sahadevī* and ending with *tat punaḥ* is a separate sentence intended for the enumeration of the auspicious medicinal herbs (*maṅgala-auṣadhi-gaṇana*).

Regarding "seven": having procured earth produced from seven anthills, one should place it in the central pitcher situated upon the pericarp with the mantra, "Obeisance to Soma, who dwells within the Lord of Forests. Alternatively, having taken earth produced from the aforementioned seven anthills, one should place it in the center.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: having prepared these aforementioned items, from the sprouts up to the auspicious medicinal herbs, one should place them in those very [vessels]. In that regard, with the exception of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the decoction jars, one should fill all [the other vessels] with pure water.

The remainder is easy to understand. Having thus accomplished and prepared the vases, one should meditate externally upon the world-protectors (lokapālas) and protect [the area] with the five mantras.
Having gathered the previously employed mantras and properly dissolved them into oneself, [one should dissolve them] into water.
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: having removed the worship that was accepted, one should wash it with auspicious waters.
Holding darbha grass in his hand, he stands before it—[the image] which has been held by the *mūrtipas*, established in its own place, and situated facing him—and says: "Salutations to you..."
With these two verses in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, one should worship while making the request; then, having had [the thread] held by one who has conquered his senses,
one should empower the protective amulet (*kautuka*) or talisman (*pratisara*) made of silk cloth or similar material seven times with the eight-syllable mantra for the pacification of obstacles.
One should bind it with the eight-syllable mantra.
Then, one should place that image in a pavilion adorned with canopies and other ornaments, accessible by the Brahma-path.

"One should have another made," and so forth; one should lead [the deity] to the pavilion under discussion. Here, by the force of the qualification "adorned with canopies and the like," the substantive "pavilion" (*maṇḍapa*) must be supplied. In that place, on the auspicious seat (*bhadrāsana*), which is the bathing throne (*snānapīṭha*), [the deity] is joined together.

Having properly superimposed [the mantra] upon the subject at hand, while muttering the mantra "trīṇi," he should place the *samīcī* facing eastward; having recited the mantra "bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ," he should [anoint it] with clarified butter (*ājya*) produced from a cow, using the mantra "tejo 'si."
Likewise, one should anoint it; thus it is stated in the *Sumatisaṃhitā*:

"Having placed the three [vessels] on the pedestal, the practitioner should recite 'bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ' and, having smeared it with cow-ghee, recite 'tejo'si'. This refers to that which has Nārāyaṇa as its essence.

Having placed it on the pedestal with the mantra "Three," one should recite "Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ"; then, having smeared it all over with ghee using the mantra "Tejo 'si śukram," one should rub it with lentil flour.
Having rubbed it with water so that the coating may be properly removed,
he should wash it, smear it with clay from an anthill, and then fill the pitcher situated upon its pericarp with that very clay from the anthill.
p.
148) One should bathe [the deity] with water using the *samudrajyeṣṭha* mantra.
He states the sequence for bathing the vases on the petals starting from the east, together with the mantras, beginning with the words "kaṣāya" and so forth.

With the mantra beginning with "divyā" and ending with "ityantena," [he should perform the rite] with the roots together with their root-parts (samūla), meaning with the eight [herbs] starting with Sahadevī; this is the sense of "with the necks" (galaiḥ). He introduces the opening of the eyes with the words "the wise one should open the eyes. He explains [this] with the passage beginning with "ājyam" and ending with "budhaḥ."

In the phrase "citram devānām iti ca," the word "ca" (and) indicates that one [offering] is with the verse "citram devā," and another is with "āpyāyasva," and so forth; this is an illustration from the *Viṣṇu-saṃhitā* and other texts.
He collects the mantras for opening the eyes with the words "dhenur iti," having removed the cloth from the face.

The meaning is that the cow shown [as a gift] shall be the teacher's fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the opening of the eyes. Regarding the phrase "one should bathe": one should bathe [the deity] with the pitchers located in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast (*āgneya*), following the sequence previously mentioned and the sequence prescribed for the filling.

The meaning is that, just as with the pitchers located at the cardinal directions, there is no difference in the sequence for the filling and the bathing regarding the pitchers located at the intermediate directions. He explains this in two verses beginning with "Haṃsa":
one should perform the rubbing of the lower body of the image with the mantra beginning with "drupadādī".

On the head, one should apply an emblic myrobalan (*āmalaka*) treated with the mantra "mānas toke" and combined with *muramāṃsī*; thereafter, [one should apply] fragrant water to the cardinal and intermediate directions.
O wise one, one should bathe [the deity] with fragrant waters filled in the central jar of the *khaṇḍa* using the mantra "viṣṇorarāṭam"; thereafter,
one should bathe it with pure water from jars and its surrounding jars while reciting the verse "tadā tadedamāpaḥ pravahata."

By this much, it has been indicated that the knower of logic [should act] by pronouncing [the mantra] in the central jar with "to all except the middle one" (*sarvebhyo madhyamaṃ vinā*); thus, having consecrated the *bimba* in sequence through the jar-consecration (*kalaśābhiṣeka*), one should cause the deity to become present. Therefore, he says: "Then, one should invoke."

"Recite that mantra," he says. He describes the manner of offering that oblation with the passage beginning "golden" and ending with "one should cause [it] to be made with an upper garment. Having thus presented the oblation, he states some manifestation of its form and so forth with the words "all-seeing."

The meaning is that by means of the mantra "viśvataścakṣuḥ," one should pervade [the deity] from the hair to the feet and from the soles of the feet to the hair, thereby making it both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala). Then, for that [deity] whose majesty has slightly begun to manifest, there is the offering of oblations.
He states the procedure with the words beginning "The herbs together" and ending with "for long life and for splendor";
the meaning is that [the action is performed] with the mantra beginning "O tree, not from your flower" and ending with "for long life and for splendor."

150) He introduces the praise of that [deity] with the word "tataḥ" (then). Having stood before him, one should praise the Lord of Gods (*Deveśa*) with these *sāman* chants; he shows the *sāmans* with the words "by that called Rathantara."

One should praise Puruṣottama with the Rathantara [Sāman] beginning with "abhitvā śūra nonumaḥ," with the Vairāja [Sāman] beginning with "pibā somam indra," with the Gāyaka Sāman beginning with "agna āyūṃṣi," and [one should praise] the Image with [the hymn] beginning with "uttiṣṭha."

Having raised him up with the words, "Rise from the auspicious seat," and having placed the Brahmin—the one who has accomplished his purpose—upon the auspicious Brahma-chariot, he should lead him there by human effort; the word "to the pavilion" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Having offered the *arghya* at the door, [he should lead them] through the doors.

"One should cause [the deity] to enter with the mantra 'viśvataścakṣuḥ'. The meaning is as follows: having pervaded the offering just described—whose majesty has been made manifest—with the mantra "viśvataścakṣuḥ," and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the assignment of limbs), one should imagine the deity's limbs to be complete and then cause [the deity] to recline.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Kriyāsāra-vyākhyā*. 13.
Now, he begins to explain the "acceptance" (adhivāsa) that has immediately followed: "Now, as for 'acceptance'—

the meaning is that I shall speak according to the determination of the treatises (*śāstra*), in the form of 'this must be done thus,' and so forth, without transgressing the intent of the treatises."
151) He praises the *adhivāsana* (consecration) for the purpose of indicating its necessity with the words "by connection with which" (*yadyogāt*).
By connection with which—meaning by connection with, relation to, or application of that ritual action of *adhivāsa*.
In the worship of the image (arcā), Hari remains ever-present from the beginning of that ritual time until the end of the world's duration.
Here too, he first demonstrates the contemplation of the Teacher (ācārya-bhāvanā) by saying "he [visualizes] himself," and so on;
having meditated upon himself as Śiva, etc., these purposes of the deity are as described in the section on Śiva.

The meaning is that even when there is the destruction of the effects and causes such as sleep and so forth, this [Self] remains imperishable. Now, he demonstrates the method of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which is to be practiced through the *mantra*-image, beginning with "by means of the *praṇava*" and ending with "is born."

Regarding the phrase "with the *praṇava*": here too, according to the method previously stated, one should unite the individual soul (*jīva*) who identifies with the image by means of the *praṇava*; having drawn it in from all its limbs and joined it within the heart, and then having caused it to ascend even from there, one should place it within oneself—in the Lord of All, whose nature is one's own inner self (*pratyagātman*).

Having brought about oneness with Hari— the Supreme Brahman, whose other name is Śrī Vāsudeva— who causes the manifestation and dissolution of the entire universe which is His own reflection, and having attained identity with the Supreme Self through breath control (prāṇāyāma) and other means;
The meaning is "having made supreme. Having done so, the body— which is an image whose nature consists solely of the appearance of earth— is the drying up of the earth of the worlds by the wind.
Having thoroughly dried [the body] with the great wind produced from the seed-syllable of wind (vāyu-bīja) touched by *prāṇāyāma*,
like a sapless gourd;
and having burned it with the great fire produced from the seed-syllable of fire (vahni-bīja) touched by *prāṇāyāma* together with the fire accompanied by the seed-syllables.

Having thoroughly inundated [it] with waters produced from the seed-syllable of nectar (amṛtabīja) which have been touched by the sprinkling and breath-control (prāṇāyāma), [the text says] "having inundated it here with waters";
by this very phrase "having inundated it with waters," [it means] with the waters that constitute its own cause, in a state of complete oneness.
The meaning "having flooded" (plāvayitvā) is indeed revealed as "having dissolved" (vilāpya); likewise, in the *Viṣṇusaṃhitā* it is said: "the dry earth, when burnt, is dissolved in water.
Thus, having withdrawn the earth into the waters, this [dissolution] is an indicative mark for the period of wind (*vāyuṣkā*), by way of its own nature.

Having dissolved those waters— which constitute the cause of the earth— into fire as before, once they have reached the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) with it and have been dried by the wind and burned by the fire; and having likewise withdrawn the fire into the wind through the sequence beginning with its own dissolution into its cause and so forth, until it reaches the state of equilibrium with the wind.

In the same way, one should lead the wind into the state of space. Having thus dissolved the elements in brief—with a slight variation for each—and having brought them into meditative absorption, [one performs] the remaining dissolution of the elements.

From the passage beginning with "He shows the internal" up to "the unity of the undetermined," it should be understood that this arrangement and configuration of the earth and other elements— along with their presiding deities— is characterized by a specific capacity belonging to each, which constitutes its respective *adhibhūta* (pertaining to the elements) and *adhidaivata* (pertaining to the deities).
The internal nature of the mantras presiding over those [senses] is thus ordained. Thus,

by means of the divine causes and objects associated with the inner self as described in the Śrīsātvata, one [perceives] the earth together with the nose and the generative organ, accompanied by the hosts of elemental beings.
By means of these and other [mantras] thus stated— along with the instruments of cognition such as the sense of smell, the instruments of action such as the organ of generation,
the objects of the cognitive senses such as odor, and the objects of the organs of action such as bliss— one should recite: *lāṃ namaḥ parāya pṛthivyātmane huṃ*.
Having joined [the elements] with their respective mantras through *prāṇāyāma* starting with "phaṭ," and having established them in the *tanmātras*,

one should unite them with the *ātmatattva* by means of the pervasion (*vyāpaka*) of their respective mantras, such as "Oṃ namaḥ parāya sarvātmane namaḥ. In this regard, the division of Durgā according to the *adhidaiva* [aspect] is explained by [the author] himself.

This will be explained hereafter and is not elaborated upon now. Having thus withdrawn [the elements] according to the stated sequence, one should bring about the state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*) with the subsequent principle by means of the *praṇava* breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*),
and then, by means of the breath-control of one's own mantra, withdraw [it] into the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*).
Having withdrawn [the senses] into the mind by means of the pervasive [breath], and having withdrawn the mind and ego-sense according to the stated method;
Having withdrawn that ego into the Great One (mahat), one should lead the Great Self—
which is synonymous with the principle of intellect (buddhi)— to unity with the unmanifest (avyākṛta); and that unmanifest,
by the gaze of Māyā for the purpose of creating the world, [is merged] into the embodiment of knowledge (jñānavigraha).

Even if there is some lack of clarity regarding the Self, which is of the singular nature of consciousness, one should lead [the mind] toward that very conscious Self as qualified by attributes such as tranquility; thus, by saying "tranquil," he pacifies the suspicion that the faults alleged by our own and other schools might arise.
In that which is peaceful, endowed with illusion, and exists as its own reflection;

which, though being the witness of all worldly transactions, is devoid of passion and other afflictions directed toward those objects; which is infinite and imperishable even while appearing as the reflection of the world-form that is momentary and fragile; and which [remains so] throughout time.

Alternatively, [the Self] may be of a limited nature, or it may be another [Self] in the form of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) of the entire continuum of living beings; although its function is contracted, like the great ether (*mahākāśa*),
it pervades all its own effects and is spatially undivided and inactive.

Even though it pervades one's entire body, one should lead [the mind] into the conscious self (cidātman), which— though liberated from all karma such as merit and demerit established through those very channels— is of an immutable and eternal nature due to its freedom from transformation and other such changes.

(155) Regarding "the body of the bath": in this way, having withdrawn that unuttered [form] within the conscious self (cidātman) which is somewhat permeated by *māyā*, one [withdraws] even that conscious self which is the body of knowledge (*jñānavigraha*).

Having performed *prāṇāyāma* with the *praṇava*, and having preceded this with the withdrawal of the powers such as *icchā* (will) and so forth, she is established— meaning she dwells perfectly and exclusively in her own nature, which is the most pure, a mass of existence-consciousness-bliss (*saccidānanda*), and is proven by such scriptural passages as "Bliss is Brahman" (*ānando brahmaṇaḥ*). This [nature] is the supreme bliss.

"One should meditate. Thus, having described the dissolution of the effect (*kārya*), he speaks of the dissolution of the cause (*kāraṇa*) with the word "peaceful" (*śānta*). Here, one should either take up the word "that" (*tam*) ending in the accusative case—referring back to "supreme bliss" (*paramānanda*)—and connect it as being intent on referring to the uncreated Self (*akṛta-ātman*); and so it is:

The meaning is that he has not brought his father— the self-realized one, who is devoid of activity, whose activity has been cast off, who is free from his own functions because the limiting adjunct (upādhi) produced by the play of *māyā*— the cause of the entire cycle of existence— has been removed;
[he has entered] into that which is peaceful, in which passion is extinguished, from which the perception of the seed of the play of *māyā* has departed, and which is eternally pure.

This is the meaning: in the infinite, imperishable, and unlimited supreme ether (*para-vyoman*), which is the substrate of sleep; which, due to the absence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is characterized by its own essential nature; which, like the great space (*mahākāśa*), is more pervasive and undivided in terms of location; and which is defined solely by pure existence and has the form of knowledge (*jñāna-vigraha*).
One should lead [the mind] into the conscious self;
one should not [lead it] even into that conscious self which is peaceful in form and in which all limiting adjuncts have been stilled.

The meaning is that he is established in supreme bliss. One should meditate upon that peaceful form—the conscious self (cidātman) for whom all limiting adjuncts (upādhi) have been stilled—as being likewise established in supreme bliss. Having thus described the dissolution of the universe along with its causes, [it continues: "when this world has thus dissolved..."

Furthermore, according to the stated principle that "the Supreme Lord proceeds toward creation again for the sake of benefiting living beings out of sport," [the author], desiring to describe the creation of the world,
cites the passage beginning with "He thought" (*tadaikṣata*), which prescribes the creation of the world and so forth.

By means of the observation of *māyā* established by scripture, he reflects upon the conscious Self (*cidātman*), who is slightly permeated by *māyā*, whose nature is immediate presence, and who is the Lord of the creation and other processes of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
He does so with the words "In whom," referring to that in which the unmanifest root-cause (*avyākṛta-mūlakāraṇa*)— slightly permeated by its own *māyā*— resides.
That which is dissolved within the conscious self (cidātman), remaining perfectly absorbed therein,
awaiting the ripening of the karma of all living beings for the sake of a future creation, and abiding as latent impressions (vāsanā)— that is its true nature as it exists.
Because the conscious self (cidātmā) cannot be established as a separate entity in its own right— just like a mirage— it is that very nature of the conscious self, when conjoined with *māyā*,
which constitutes the power (*śakti*) of the supreme, most pure Brahman for the creation and other activities of the universe.
They know the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*), whose nature is capacity (*sāmarthya*), as the lower Brahman.
Yet he who is this Supreme Lord, though having *saṃjñāna* (consciousness) as his cause, is of such a form.

Because it is a transformation (*vivarta*) of Brahman whose nature is pure consciousness, it has that as its cause; for this very reason, its own essential nature consists of the conceptualization of "higher" and "lower. Through the observation of its own specific characteristics, one thinks, "This is the higher," or through the observation of the nature of *māyā*, one thinks, "This is the lower"—this conceptualization is indeed one and the same.

He whose self is form (rūpātman)— the Supreme Lord (parameṣṭhin) known by the alternative name Vāsudeva, the Sovereign who, independent of any other cause, performs the creation and so forth of the universe—
is the creator of all, according to such scriptural passages as: "Having created that, He entered into it Himself."
He is to be known as the creator of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the self of all, and the form of the life-force (*jīva*) of the entire world.

Thus, having characterized him as the supreme creator, he shows the sequence of his creation with the words "that" (*tām*): that Vāsudeva, through the desire to create, [possesses] appropriate will and so forth.

Endowed with the three powers, having presided over Māyā— which is essentially non-different from himself, which is his own unmanifest state merged within him, and which constitutes the entire phenomenal world— he exists as the essence of Nāda, having the subtle element of sound (śabda-tanmātra) for his body.
He produced a form characterized by touch, consisting of the principle of the Person (puruṣatattva), which is the Pauruṣī [Mūrti];
that created Person is to be known as Saṃkarṣaṇa—thus it should be understood.
Furthermore, that Lord, the Master of the World, existing in the form of Saṃkarṣaṇa,

having agitated the manifest Māyā, created Pradyumna— the universal form consisting of the essence of all things, whose nature is the subtle element of form (rūpatanmātra), and who is composed of splendor (tejomaya).

Furthermore, existing in the form of Pradyumna, that Lord, having churned his own primordial nature— which consists of the subtle element of form and is composed of light— with [energies] that delight the universe,
both male and female, which are peaceful, tranquil, and present in minute proportions;

He created another body composed of mind, characterized by cessation and known by the other name "the reality of cessation. They know that Hari, who lies upon the waters, reclining on the serpent Śeṣa, as the one called Aniruddha; furthermore, he exists in the form of Aniruddha.
The illustrious Hari, having agitated the unmanifest Māyā consisting of the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra),
[produced] the Lord Prajāpati— whose body consists solely of the subtle element of smell, who is the self of all and the form of all principles (tattvas),
whose other name is Nārāyaṇa, and who is the natural source for the creation of all beings.

Because it was completed, he made it known by the name Prajāpati; here too, the previously mentioned word "he made" (akarot) is understood. As for the "five," these are the five powers in the form of Parameṣṭhin and so forth, belonging to the Supreme Self; by these, this supreme deity [is manifested].

Established in the supreme state of the Lord, as recalled by the Smṛti in the passage beginning "He abides in the supreme ether" (p. 159), they remain there with fixed order, that is, without confusion.

They are said to be established as the support of the entire world; because they consist of the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) which is the substratum for all living beings— the manifold expansion (*prapañca*) manifested through the distinctions of gods, humans, boars, and so forth— and because they exist in the form of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), they are declared to be the foundational locus of the entire universe.
He confirms this very point through the consensus of the learned:

"The five powers pertaining to the internal self," and so on, as stated by the exponents of the Vedas. These five powers are [classified] by the Vedic scholars as pertaining to the internal self (ādhyātmika), the elements (ādhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaivata).

The distinction [is as follows]: the internal (ādhyātmika) pertains to that which exists within the self in the form of the ear, speech, and so forth, or in the form of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth; the elemental (adhibhūta) pertains to those existing among their own respective elements in the form of space (ākāśa) and so forth, or in the form of the objects of hearing, speaking, and so forth; and the divine (adhidaiva) pertains to the deities.

The five [subtle elements] designated by the term *tanmātra* are proclaimed as the causal factors for the various distinctions— such as those of Sadāśiva and other forms, or the directions and so forth— existing among the gods; now,
[the text describes] the manner of the universal creation of Prajāpati once he has arisen.

For he indeed shows [this], as Prajāpati who consists of all selves; thus, immediately following, the previously mentioned Brahmā, who consists of all selves and desires to create the manifold world, [creates] the common [element].

That which is the common material cause of all effects, unmanifest, and designated as "the unprecedented" (*apūrva*), differentiated the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the karma of all living beings; it brought them forth by means of those [subtle elements] as its own first unmanifest effect, through those subtle elements (*tanmātra*) which are its own causes.
"By those waters which are the effects of the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra) and are under discussion, it is called 'unassociated';
then one should subsequently place the power known as the seed-syllable of earth," and so forth— this refers to the period immediately following the entry of the aforementioned power of earth.
"He created that egg. That created egg consists of the five elements;
it is composed of the great elements in their quintuplicated form (*pañcīkṛta*).
Precisely because of the nourishment by the seed-vigor (*vīrya*), it is golden; for that very reason, it is auspicious and radiant.

The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Here, by means of this textual passage beginning with "that [is] her own unmanifested *māyā*" and ending with "half of that consists of the five elements," [the author teaches] the *praṇava* and breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) for the purpose of creating the triad of powers beginning with Will (*icchā*), and so forth, up to the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*).

For the purpose of creation, the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) of the five elements arose; for the purpose of creating primordial water, the breath-control of the *praṇava* arose; and for the purpose of its solidity and so forth, the breath-control of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of earth and the rest arose as the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
The nature of the five elements, the five principles of reality (*tattva*), and the breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) have been indicated in sequence (p.
"It should be understood that therein" means: therein, within that image consisting of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), which is one's own self;
"withdrawn" means having ascended and brought [the elements] to oneness with the Self according to the stated sequence, they have been dissolved into one's own self;
[this refers to] those whose support is the five subtle elements (*tanmātra-pañcaka*) and who consist of the eternal primordial body.

Therefore, the individual power (*jīva-śakti*), which takes the five subtle elements as its object, whose various functions have been entirely withdrawn, which exists in a state of internal absorption, and whose functions are produced by union with the Supreme Reality—that [power] migrates into that [state]; the meaning is that one should cause such a function of the individual soul to migrate there. At that time—
Immediately upon the transition of the soul (*jīva*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), presided over by that soul,
acquires its activity and manifests its tenfold functions, such as the upward-moving function and so forth.
For it is that very subject under discussion which leads [the soul] to oneness with the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*).

The internal [prāṇa] is that which exists within the body; it is intended as "prāṇa" by another name when it has the Supreme Self (paramātman) as its support, and it is intended as having the nature of "prāṇa" when existing with the individual soul (jīva) as its support—this is the meaning. Therefore...

From this principle of *prāṇa*, the intellect (*buddhi*)—which consists of the three *guṇas*, is characterized by luminosity and so forth, and possesses eight functions—is born; it is for this very reason that it is said to have eight functions, such as *sattva* and the rest, beginning with virtue (*dharma*). Then, immediately after its own function, from that [intellect]...

From the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva), the power of agency belonging to the Self arises; from that, the ego (ahaṃkāra)—possessing the capacity of māyā which produces the conceit of being an agent—is born as its function. Of that ego...
The function [of the senses] consists of sound and other objects, and it is that which sets one toward sound and other objects.

But the mind (manas) arises immediately after that ego-sense (ahaṃkāra); thus, the mind is composed of volition and the like, having volition and conceptualization as its functions. From that mind, sound, touch, and form [arise].
And taste and smell—these five objects (artha) were produced as the five categories (padārtha).

By means of those objects, the sense organs (indriya), which possess both the power of cognition and the power of action—namely, those characterized by cognitive power and those characterized by active power—were originated; these constitute the two classes.

He shows this with the passage beginning "the ear" and ending with "are designated as objects. Following this, the remainder is that the five elements are originated by those [qualities]; they recite the elements starting with space (*vyoma*). This [recitation] is an illustration for the ear and the other senses by means of these elements. And so it is said:
Sumati says:

"The sixteen-fold effect is gross; that which arises from the subtle elements such as the intellect (buddhi) and so forth is subtle," and so on, referring to the ear and other senses; [the Self is] the support of all those, and of all karma earned by oneself.
From these, the gross body, which is the support of enjoyment, is produced; indeed, the gross body is produced as the support of all.

By this very concluding statement, the sequence for the purpose of creating the reality— the respective mantras, breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), ripening over a year, the piercing of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍabheda*), and so forth— is indicated. Here, first of all:

"Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and ego—thus is My nature divided eightfold. Thus, according to the Lord’s teaching on causality, the mind has primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) as its unevolved cause; the seven beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) are both evolvents and evolved effects (*prakṛtivikṛtayaḥ*).

The group of sixteen is a modification (*vikāra*); the *puruṣa* is neither nature (*prakṛti*) nor a modification—thus it has been stated. Lest there be a suspicion that [the *puruṣa*] might be included within the category of effects (*kārya*), [it is said that] from the *ahaṃkāra* characterized by transformation (*vaikārika*) arise the five sense organs (*buddhīndriya*), the five organs of action (*karmendriya*), and those five which have action as their purpose.
From the *taijasa* [ahaṃkāra], the mind (*manas*) is born, which is of two forms; from *bhūtādi*, the means for the accomplishment of volition (*saṃkalpa-sādhana*) arise.

In the manner previously stated—namely, that the five gross elements (*pañca-bhūtāni*) and the subtle elements (*tanmātrāṇi*) emerge respectively from these—the entire range of principles beginning with the Self (*ātman*) is accepted as proceeding from *ahaṃkāra*. It is not otherwise.
This is appropriate. For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of different causes for creation (*sarga*) and dissolution (*visarga*).

If this [unity of cause] is accepted, then it is stated that the senses, along with their objects, are withdrawn into the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), as they abide within those very elements. Thus, the withdrawal of the senses into the subtle elements is established.
Regarding the statement "having withdrawn space into the mind," the withdrawal of space—
which is merely space— into the mind is utterly inconsistent.
From that point onward, it is established that causality alone is logical; thus,
he makes a formal promise (*pratijānīte*) to explain the aforementioned seeds of reality (*tatvabīja*) and so forth, beginning with "of these" (*eteṣām*),
which is joined with the statement regarding the locus of the ritual placement (*nyāsasthāna*), namely the letter *ma* extracted from that [syllable], the letter *ma*.

Because of the designation of non-difference between the signified and the signifier, one should place the *jīvatattva*—which consists of the letter *ma*—as pervasive throughout all parts of the body by means of the mantra: *oṃ annam̐ḥ parāya jīvātmane namaḥ*. One should likewise place the letter *bha*, which is signified by the seed-syllable *bha*.
One should mentally place the Praṇava as the adjunct of the individual soul (jīva), pervading all limbs;

he states that its locus is characterized by the triad beginning with the intellect (buddhi) and so forth, and by saying "the letter Va," he indicates the locations for the mantras of the five measures (mātrās), while by saying "the letter Na," [he indicates the next].

One should sequentially place the ten sense organs, beginning with the ear and ending with the organ of procreation, which consist of the ten letters starting with *ṇa* and ending with *ca*, in their respective locations as the designators (*abhidhāna*) and the designated (*abhidheya*). Such is the intended meaning. And thus says the Āgama:

Having established that the group of sense organs beginning with the ear has the self as its object, and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) using the specific vowels and consonants starting from space (vyoman) and ending with earth (avanip), one should fashion the gross body.

165) He states the locus for that placement as "the head" and "the placement of emanation. This is joined with the letters beginning with *ḍa* and ending with *ka*, and consists of [the elements] starting from space (*vyoman*) and ending with earth (*avanī*).

In some cases, there is the Sṛṣṭinyāsa. One should place the Brāhma seed-syllable, which is the embodiment of the Tattva, on the head; the first and second [syllables] on the mouth, and the third in the region of the navel.

In some other scripture (*āgama*), there is such a form. Otherwise, it is said that the seed-syllable (*bīja*) begins with *ṅa* and ends with *ka*; and indeed, it is proclaimed as being in the sequence of letters from *ṅa* to *ka*.
By the word "indeed" (*kila*), the consideration of its logical justification (*upapatti*) therein is indicated. Thus...
Having introduced the placement (*nyāsa*) of the primary principles (*tattva*), he mentions the heart-lotus (*hṛtpuṇḍarīka*) and so forth as a relevant digression:
"The heart-lotus... Here, by the word "heart" (*hṛd*) itself, its locus for placement is indicated. [He says:
"Haṃ, the sun, twelve-fold, by its own radiance..."

One should know that there are seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍīs) situated within the heart-lotus; seated in its very center, one should meditate upon the moon, the seed-syllable *saṃ*, within the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*) in the middle of that [lotus]. Within that—

In the center of the lunar mandala is the radiant *bindu*; it is said that Agni and Soma, Prakṛti and Puruṣa, as well as *bindu* and *nāda*, are eternally one with each other. This mutual identity is the intended meaning of the term "seed" (*bīja*), which is indicated by the word *bindu*—namely, the seed-syllable of Fire (*vahnibīja*). Such is the sense.

166) One should contemplate the fire-mandala; the letter *vai* is for the purpose of indicating its well-known nature as consisting of ten digits (*kalā*). Thus is the union with the conscious self (*cidātman*).

Having manifested through the placement of the respective mantras both the body— which consists of the principles beginning with *prāṇa* and ending with *pṛthivī*, which are transformations of the neutral (*avyākṛta*) and their effects— and also the heart-lotus and other organs within it, which serve as its specific and permanent seats of abode.

He says that one should also perform the *nyāsa* of the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*) and so forth for the sake of accomplishing the perfection of all qualities, such as supreme sovereignty, of the Self presided over by that [mantra]; thus he says "the living soul" (*jīva*), meaning not merely that which dwells within the midst of a body that is already fully formed and predominantly material.

Having imagined the individual soul (jīva) as abiding in the state of the Lord (Īśa), awakened in its innate, perfected supreme sovereignty, one should unite it with the Supreme Being (Parameṣṭhin) by means of the seed-syllable joined with the *ṣoṃ* syllable;
the meaning is that one should contemplate it as being awake in supreme sovereignty through the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Parameṣṭhin.
Then, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) by means of the seed-syllable *yaṃ*— which is conjoined with the seed-syllable *yaṃ* and constitutes the principle of the Puruṣa—

one should meditate upon the state of the Puruṣa (*pauruṣaṃ bhāvam*), that is, the state pertaining to the Puruṣa, which is based on the conceit of being the Puruṣa through a slight glancing-over by Māyā.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the seed-syllable *vaḥ*, which ends in the *visarga* and is accompanied by the *visarga*, one should [place] that which bestows grace—grace consisting in the granting of the fruits of various actions—above [the elements such as] passion, hatred, and so forth.

One should meditate on that which is dependent upon the state of consciousness (*saṃjñābhāva*). The phrase "one should meditate on that which is dependent" is understood to carry over from what was previously stated. Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the seed-syllable *lāṃ*, one should meditate upon the creator of all manifestations, who possesses the aforementioned characteristics as the impeller of *māyā* and its effects.
One should again remember with one's whole being the creator of the continuity [of the lineage], its enjoyments, and the abundance of material wealth,
as well as the locations for the placement of the *parameṣṭhi* and other mantras— these five powers are declared to belong to the Supreme Self.
"By the term *pañcatanmātra*, they are proclaimed by the exponents of the Vedas"— since this states their non-difference,
it should be understood that [the elements] are described precisely by means of stating their locations (*sthāna*).
Thus, for the sake of the self-recognition of the true nature of the Self, which has attained the state of being the inner witness (*pratyagbhāva*):
And he says that one should place the *kopatattva* (the principle of wrath): "Then," [meaning] the cause for the withdrawal of prior existence,
the cause for the withdrawal of the entire phenomenal world superimposed by itself, the seed-syllable *kṣaṃ kṣaṃ*,
the *kopatattva* which is the cause for the restraint of all things, and the movement of *māyā* which has its own support.

One should contemplate the cause for the pacification of all things for the sake of restraining all the senses; by this, it is implied that one should contemplate the aforementioned meaning as pervading all limbs. With the words beginning with "the agent" and ending with "by the powers of knowledge," he summarizes the point: [one should contemplate Him] whose body is subtle and whose form is formless.

[One should meditate upon] Śrī Hari himself as Viṣṇu—the manifestation of knowledge, whose nature is consciousness, the Lord of the gods, the witness of the entire universe, and the most pervasive. (p. 168)

In the manner described, having presided over that [individual] agent— which is its own unmanifested *māyā*— and by means of the impelling of *prakṛti* as previously stated, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), presided over by the individual soul (*jīva*) and having attained its functional activity, then becomes the agent and the transformer.

Thus it was said: by means of the door of the *prakṛti* presided over by Him—who undergoes transformation through His own observation—the transformer and the support of all [is perceived]. It has been stated that the gross body indeed arises as the support of all, by way of the principles (*tattvas*) ending with earth, which take the form of its effects.

The entire maṇḍala, which is the support of all, is differentiated by these aforementioned powers— beginning with Parameṣṭhin— that consist of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and the power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*), through the differentiation of the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*), by way of the principles (*tattva*), the arts (*kalā*), and the worlds (*bhuvana*).

Having thoroughly pervaded, through identity, his own Virāṭ body— which is the nature of the undivided maṇḍala yet divided into all the maṇḍalas by means of the distinctions of the denoter (vācaka) in the form of phonemes, words, and mantras— and having rendered it conscious, he remains established in the state of being awake to his own true nature.
One should contemplate [the deity] up to the point where it says, "the entire maṇḍala, divided according to the fusion of the signified and the signifier.
Thus, by means of the sixfold deposition (*ṣaḍadhvanyāsa*) upon the manifested image of the mantra (*mantrabimba*), [one contemplates] the sixfold phenomenal expansion (*ṣaḍvidhaprapañca*).

And it is indicated that one should "imagine the state of being a planet" by the word "having meditated"; then he says "thereafter" (*tataḥ*) that one should "arouse him by means of offerings. "Well-disposed" (*subhāhitaḥ*) means one whose devotion is perfectly accomplished. Now, because a mantra-image (*mantrabimba*) that is not yet established is unfit for the arrangement of an entourage (*parivāra*), [the text proceeds].

He says that one should perform the worship of the mandala for the manifestation of its splendor: "With abundant [offerings]," meaning with those worthy of worship according to the ritualists; having propitiated [the deity], he describes the method of meditating on the substratum:
"The seat," and so forth; therein, in that circle of the lotus-mandala, together with the limbs, here...
The term "limb" (*gātra*) is an elliptical expression for the feet and so forth; likewise, the seat (*āsana*) consists of the powers of support (*ādhāra-śakti*) and others,
upon which shine merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and so on, joined by the feet and limbs, together with its appurtenances,
and provided with a covering in the form of *māyā*, *avidyā*, and so forth, which shine above the categories beginning with *sattva*.

Having meditated upon and worshipped it, one should visualize upon the chest of that [deity] and above that pedestal a beautiful wheel with three naves, twelve spokes, and two rims, endowed with all principles (*tattva*),
consisting of the twenty-four principles, and possessed of twenty-four peripheries.
One should contemplate the wheel; one should contemplate the sacrificer and then sacrifice again—this is the intended meaning.

He then explains that [point] with the words "starting from the east" (*pūrvādi*). The wise Guru [should contemplate] within the directions starting from the east, which are arranged from bottom to top.

The principles beginning with *prakṛti* and ending with *pṛthivī*, starting from *prāṇa*, [are arranged] according to their sequential order: the principle of *prāṇa* is at the lower limit, and the principle of *buddhi* is at the upper limit; immediately below that [is the principle of *ahaṃkāra*].

First, relying on the sequential method beginning with "the principle of ego (ahaṃkāratattva)," one should perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) and worship in a single circuit. Regarding the word "Sūrya" here, by the term *sūrya*, both the Sun as the essence of the deity and the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), which serves as the seed-syllable (*bīja*) for that mantra, are expressed. Therefore, the application is as follows.
The sun, which is correctly divided twelvefold by the twelve vowels— beginning with *a* and ending with the *visarga*, excluding the closed (*saṃvṛta*) vowels—
is the letter *ha*, appearing in forms such as *haṃ*, *ham*, and so forth; likewise, the sun is divided twelvefold.

One should place the Sun-god, whose essence consists of twelve forms divided by the names Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, Bhaga, Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, Parjanya, Tvaṣṭṛ, and the twelfth, Viṣṇu, within the spokes. [With the mantra: *Oṃ haṃ, salutation to the supreme Sūrya, whose nature is Aries*.

The meaning is that one should worship by placing [the deities] within the spokes using the mantras beginning with "dhāna * * * nnamaḥ" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "ending with the bindu": in the bright fortnight (*śukle pakṣe*), on the white [spoke], one should worship with the fifteen [syllables] beginning with 'ra' and ending with the *bindu*, as recited in their sequential order.
In the alternative case, [the mantra is formed] with fifteen [syllables], beginning with the *visarga* and ending with the letter *ā*, arranged in reverse order.

One should contemplate the Soma, whose essence is the deity, as divided by the vowels; one should contemplate the Soma-seed, the letter *sa*, which is divided according to the distinction between the white and the non-white, and which is the Soma divided by all the digits (*kalās*) in the form of lunar days (*tithis*), within each interval (*tantara*) on both sides by means of an ascending process (*ārohavṛtti*).

"Gradually," and so forth: by means of the reasoning set forth in the *Dīpadīpikā* and other works, one should divide [the channel] from the root to the tip and from the tip to the root, and contemplate it with the mantras beginning with "Oṃ, salutation to the essence of the first day of the bright fortnight, salutation," and so on; with the first vowel, one should contemplate the *akalās*, and in the middle, the *aras*.

And one should meditate with the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ parāyāmākalātmane namaḥ" upon the three navel centers, beginning from the inner navel. In the form of "Oṃ namaḥ parāya prātaḥsavanātmane namaḥ" and so forth, one should meditate upon the three *savanas* by their very names. Likewise:

With the mantra "Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, salutation to the Self whose nature is Wrath," one should contemplate one's own name as Wrath (Kopa), the principle of Wrath (kopatattva), situated upon the pericarp of the lotus. In its center— that is, in the middle of that well-worshipped lotus, within the region of the navel— [one should meditate].

"Paṅkajā-māram" (the destroyer of the lotus-born) is an elliptical designation for the remainder of the *pīṭhas*, beginning with Padma and ending with Samastha; one should meditate upon that here. In the midst of that—that is, in the center of the lotus—is the power (*śakti*) of Puruṣa, [expressed by] "Namaḥ" (salutation).
