Soma, whose seed-syllable is the letter *sa*, is divided by the vowels; according to the division between the white and the other [colors],
Soma— the very self of the deity— is divided by all the digits (*kalās*) in the form of lunar days (*tithis*).
One should contemplate *soma* in each successive interval by way of ascent on both sides, proceeding in turn according to the method described in the *Dīpadīpikā* and other texts;
having divided [the path] from the root to the tip and from the tip to the root, one should recite: *saṃ namaḥ śuklapratipadātmane namaḥ*.
One should contemplate [the deity] with these and other mantras. With the first vowel, one should contemplate the *akalā* (the partless) in the middle of the spokes and in the center with the mantra:
*saṃ namaḥ parāyāmākalātmane namaḥ*. And in the three navel-regions, starting from the interior of the navel, one should contemplate with: *annamaḥ parāya prātaḥsavanātmane*.
One should contemplate the three daily libations (savanas) by means of one's own name in the form "Namaḥ" and so forth. Likewise,

with the mantra "Oṃ Namaḥ Parāya Kopatattvātmane Namaḥ," one should contemplate one's own name as the element of anger (kopatattva), situated upon the seed-syllable (akṣa) and located in the position of the pericarp (karṇikā).

In the midst of that—in the center of that well-worshipped lotus, within the region of the navel—one should meditate upon the "source of the lotus" (*paṅkajābhāram*); "lotus" here is an elliptical designation for the remainder of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), beginning with the lotus and ending with the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*). Within that, in the middle of the lotus, [one should meditate upon] the *pauruṣī*.
Having meditated upon the power of the individual soul (*jīvaśakti*) with the mantra "Śaktiṃ maṃ namaḥ" and "Parāya jīvātmane namaḥ," [one should proceed].

Having worshipped in due order, beginning with the Support-Energy (Ādhāraśakti) and ending with the principle of the individual soul (Jīvatattva), according to their respective rites through recitation and other means, the wise one— following the specific ritual manual for the mantra consisting of one hundred and eight repetitions or more—
should cause that [deity] composed of mantra, which has been infused into the image consecrated by the mantra during the preliminary rite (adhivāsana), to enter [it].

Having meditated upon the form there, one should gradually conceive of it with its limbs and its enclosures (*sāṅga-sāvaraṇa*). Regarding the conception of the enclosures, he shows a specific sequence for the enclosures by means of the twelve-syllable seed-mantras.

The meaning is: "even though there are different types of root mantras, such as those with six, eight, or twelve syllables. He demonstrates the arrangement of the mantra-deities (*māntrika-āvaraṇa-yoga*) by saying "Vainateya and the others. Having thus worshipped, either the Guru or the submerged Ācārya...

Having offered the principles (tattvas)— beginning with the individual soul (jīva) and ending with the ego (ahaṃkāra)— into the fire produced in the sacrificial pit according to the sequence of birth and so forth, and having performed oblations for each principle with clarified butter in the number prescribed, one should [offer] the water of pacification (śāntitoya).

Taking consecrated water, one should sprinkle it upon the head of the image; "water for pacification" is mentioned as an illustration, as it also includes the residual drops (*saṃpāta*). Having thus described the primary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the image, which is the principal element, [the author now describes] the secondary...
Regarding the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth, [the text] says (p.
"Having purified the seat with barks and earths, and then having sprinkled it with *darbha* grass..."

The meaning is: having purified [the site] according to the method stated in the passage beginning with "one should wash it with water" and so forth; likewise, having consecrated the pedestal (pīṭha) and so on, the preceptor should perform the fire-oblations (homān) according to rule in the directions for those bearing the forms (mūrtidharān), and also in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍe)—this being the meaning indicated by the word "according to rule" (vidhivat).

He explains [the passage] with the word "then" (*tataḥ*) and states the leading forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*). With the word "then," he mentions the optional nature of the leading forward in the western direction.
He explains the oblation (*homa*) with the verse beginning "Agni is the messenger" (*agniṃ dūtam*). He explains [the procedure] with the word "having performed" (*kṛtvā*);
the principal oblation is "Oṃ Tat," and the cooked oblation (*pakvahoma*) is at the end.
Having performed that ritual action— beginning with the placing of the fuel-sticks (*idhmādhāna*) and ending with the *pīṭhamantra* oblation,
up to the end of the principal oblations (*pradhānahoma*)— which constitutes the "cooked oblation" (*pakvahoma*), meaning having completed the rites subsequent to that;
[one should worship] Agni with the Vedic verses beginning with "Iṣe tvā," "Ūrje tvā," "Vāyava stha," "Upāyava stha," and "Eṣo 'gne."

One should [worship] with the Sāman mantra "āyāhi," with the Atharvan mantra "śanno devīḥ," or with the Vedic opening mantras; or with the mantras of the limbs (aṅga-mantras) such as "vāk," "akruddha," "utkrānta," and "dyutkrānta";
or sequentially with the forms (mūrtis) beginning with Vāsudeva and Aniruddha.

With any one of these three types of mantras, they should offer sacrificial materials such as *samidh* wood and so forth, using the mantras associated with the guardians of the directions beginning with the East. The phrase "sacrificial materials" and so on, ending with "eight hundred of rice," constitutes a single sentence. This is [the meaning of] "this."

The Guru, in his own fire-pit, [offers] fuel-sticks and so forth with the root mantra. Here, in this [pit] whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, [he offers] with the mantra "O Agni, you by the days... and likewise for the southern and western [pits] with "O Agni, come hither... (agna āyāhi).

Having offered the nine substances as intended— since it is stated that for the Agni [rite] one uses "Agnim agnim atha uttare," for the Sārasvata "Tvam agne dyubhiḥ," for the Vāruṇa likewise [the same], for the Saumya the verse "Agniṃ dūtam," and for the [next] "Agnim agniṃ havīmabhiḥ"— one should perform the oblation.
Then, immediately thereafter, one should perform the *śānti*-oblation with ghee, curd, honey, milk, and—by virtue of the word "ca"—all other substances, in their proper order.
Regarding the place for depositing the remnants (*saṃpāta*) of that [oblation], he says "one should touch": having offered ghee, [one should touch] the foot.

"He should touch [the navel]"—the remainder of the sentence being "with the residue deposited by the *sruva* ladle. Thus, Sumati has declared that touching is performed with the *sruva* joined with the substance; therefore, after having offered curd and immediately thereafter having offered curd, he should touch the interior of the navel with honey.
Having offered the oblation, one should touch the head with the five Upaniṣads. Thus,
having performed the peace-offering (*śānti-homa*) with the five Upaniṣads in due order,
and having touched [the disciple] with the entire collection of ashes produced by the previously performed consecration-offering (*adhivāsa-homa*), [one should proceed].

One should worship the deity with flowers; having thus described the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), he describes the ritual service (*saparyā*) preceded by the pouring of oblations (*havissampāta*) with the verse beginning "four," and so forth, [stating] that its guardians stand individually at the doorways facing north.
p.

175) The Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, and Sarasvatī—these four, bound in knots [as effigies], are to be established as the four cows and worshipped by their respective names; such is the implied meaning. And likewise:
"They are to be worshipped with names, perfumes, and flowers in due order," thus it is said. He states the mantra for milking and so forth:
"And one should milk with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī. By that very Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī [one should perform the rite].
One should offer the *caru* oblation to the Lord of Devas, who has been made present through both the mantra and the maṇḍala.

Outside the pavilion, one should first offer the *bali*—accompanied by fragrance, flowers, and water—in the cardinal directions; then again in the intermediate directions, and subsequently in the eight directions starting from the east.

One should take [the offerings]. Regarding the mantra for the bali-offering in the cardinal directions, he says "The first... and so forth. Regarding the mantra for the intermediate directions, he says "In the trees... and so forth. Regarding the mantra for the eight directions, he says "May the Vināyakas... and so forth; the remainder is easy to understand. He concludes with "Having done thus... and so forth.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the commentary on the Kriyāsāra. || 14 ||

Now, preceded by the resolution of the ritual procedure (*vṛttasamādhāna*), he introduces the placement of the jewels that serve as the foundation for the consecration (*pratiṣṭhādhiṣṭhāna*) which is about to be performed, with the half-verse beginning with "having consecrated" (*adhivāsya*).
The preceptor, having thus consecrated [the site] through the prescribed arrangement beginning with the emergence of the deity (*devodbhava*), etc.,...
Then, having risen at dawn, bathed, and performed his customary morning rites, he should adorn himself and perform the deposition of jewels (*ratnanyāsa*) according to the path prescribed by rule.

Regarding the arrangement of the placement of jewels, he says "upon the neuter stone" (*napuṃsakaśilāyām*). Then the Guru, having fashioned and purified a pit in the center of the neuter stone and in the cardinal directions, should place substances such as seeds within those pits; the word "pit" (*gartam*) is used in the singular to denote the class.
He states that the *napuṃsaka-śilā* (neuter stone) should be consecrated even before the placement of the jewels (*ratnanyāsa*),

saying "having been washed" (*kṣālitām*). Therefore, at dawn, the Guru should wash it— which was already washed on the previous day for the purpose of the preliminary water-consecration (*jalādhivāsa*)— with abundant water, according to the method previously described.

Having washed it like a pedestal, having washed it over the image at the time of its consecration, and having worshipped it with the Tāra mantra— that footstone (pādaśilā), which is the neuter stone (napuṃsakaśilā)— then,
in the very place where the installation is to take place in the morning, the neuter stone as well [is to be placed].

Having said "having established," he says "going" (gamanam), meaning by resorting to the portion belonging to the lord of the back and the north. When the inner sanctum (garbhāgāra) is divided into seven parts each [along the length and breadth], [the measurement is taken] by that division of seven by seven.

Starting from the center with effort, the positions for Brahmā, the gods, humans, and Piśācas should be arranged on all sides; the portion for Brahmā shall be one-fifteenth, and in the divine [section],
there are thirteen parts.
There are eleven and nine *navāṃśas* remaining from the back portion of the two [sections]; in the *brahmāṃśa*,
having omitted the middle one, the second is also from the back.

The third location for the image of the standing single-form (ekavībera) is desired when the width of the doorway is divided into three; in the middle of the twenty-one parts, one should arrange the northern cord with half of the middle portion for the purpose of movement,
having arranged the diagonal cord at the junction of the west and north.
One should cause [the deity] to enter by means of the *bimba*, the *aṅgula*, or the *yava* for the Lord, or by means of two *yavas*. Having performed these three types of entry as described,

one should place and establish that which has been determined for installation— the installation of the mantra-image— using the *tāra* (the syllable Om) at that location, and thus establish it once it is installed.
Having worshipped her with incense, flowers, and other offerings while reciting the mantra *tāreṇa*, one should offer this prayer.

Regarding the prayer, he says "annam": "O Goddess, by the command of the Lord, you alone are the supreme power (*paramā śakti*), and you alone are the sustainer of the seat (*āsana-dhārikā*). In some places, such as the *Sumatisaṃhitā*, it is said: "You alone are present. You alone are the supreme power; you alone are the sustainer of the seat, O Goddess, by the command of the Lord.

"Thou must always remain here. Having thus informed her, and having first worshipped her with scents and flowers, the preceptor, meditating upon the Earth, should place her in the pit with this mantra:
"O Thou who art the inexhaustible treasure of jewels..."
"O Earth, remain firm here in the form of the Brahma-stone"— by such a composition of words as "you yourself," and so forth (p.
The installation of the *napuṃsaka-śilā* (neuter stone) has been prescribed, and the sense is that it should be done in that very manner—the meaning is:

having prepared the *napuṃsaka-śilā* within the pit and in the cardinal directions, and having purified them therein; he now explains that purification by stating, "one should purify with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)."

Regarding the phrase "oblations for the [eight] names": having offered one hundred oblations of clarified butter with the Gāyatrī and other verses under the name of Viṣṇu, and after offering the residue of that [butter], one should consecrate the jewels with that [mantra] and,
according to the sequence starting from the east, [place them] in order using the individual syllables of the eight-syllable [mantra].

Within that [mandala], one should place the seed-syllables, jewels, and minerals in their entirety and in their respective pits, following the sequence of the enclosures as previously stated, beginning with "the seed-syllable in the first enclosure," without deviating from that order.
Following the sequence of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one recites the seed-syllables (*bīja*) beginning with "yavāni" and ending with "hiraṇyakam.
Having performed the placement in all directions, the remainder is that one should place "hiraṇyaka" in the station of Brahmā.

To determine the auspicious time for that purpose, the knower of mantras—specifically one who knows the specialized mantras for the propitiation of the eight deities of the jewels—having prepared the "eight-jewel binding" (*ratnāṣṭabandha*) and other rites, [performs them] together with Vaiṣṇavas acting as the presiding forms (*mūrtidhara*), [reciting]: "May the deities of the eight jewels be pleased; it is an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*)."

Having caused the *puṇyāha* (declaration of an auspicious day) to be recited together with the *viṣṇugāyatrī*, one should touch that pit while circumambulating it clockwise by means of the *saṃpāta* [offering]. Then, upon the *napuṃsakaśilā* (neuter stone)...

The connection is that one should perform the "deposition of jewels" (*ratnanyāsa*). Then, having examined it with the feminine gender— that is, having determined by the female stone-mark that this is indeed a female stone—
one should worship the foot-stone (*pādaśilā*) preceded by the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), using the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī.
Having covered [the image] with two garments and performed the protection rite, one should go outside the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*).

Having thus performed the ritual procedure up to the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhārādhanā*), one should prepare the temple and so forth in order to bring about the fitness for the installation (*praṇayana*) of the venerable Viṣṇu image.
Having purified [the site], one should decorate it; thus he says: "* * * with saṃvalākas.

For the purpose of the fire-oblation (*homārtha*), one should [prepare] around the temple on all sides [altars] made of sand, two *vitastis* in width, [and] provided with a *prādeśa*, a *kāla*, a *gokarṇa*, and so forth, up to the thumb, in sequence.

A *vitasti* is to be known as twelve *aṅgulas*, as it has been stated; one should have sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*) constructed with a length and width of two *vitastis*, the implication being that they are to be made by the *mūrtipas*. Having done this likewise in the eight directions, [one should act] at the side of the fires established there.
One should place eight water-pots (kalaśas) in order, starting from the east, along with Vaiṣṇava flowers and sprouts corresponding to each respective [deity]. (p. 180)

One should consecrate the vessel containing the Viṣṇu-remnants with the eight-syllable mantra. He describes the method for that oblation, preceded by the recollection of the bringing forward of the fire (agnipraṇayana), with the root mantra beginning with "praṇīya."

The meaning is that one should bring forth the Vaiṣṇava fire from the preceptor’s pit (*ācāryakuṇḍa*) after it has been rendered potent; having thus prepared the fire, one should collect the *śāntitoya* (water for pacification), the water from the *praṇītā* vessel,

and the water from the *saṃpātādi* (the poured remnants) along with the water from the *samekṣa-kalaśa* (the jar containing the *mekṣaṇa* stirring-stick), from their respective locations into the front pavilion (*agramaṇḍapa*).

One should bring together that water collected from all the jars; having filled a Vaiṣṇava copper vessel— prepared for the worship of the *pīṭha* and other rites— in due order with the one hundred and eight syllables while circumambulating clockwise, one should invoke [the deity] with the *praṇava* and perform worship.

Having taken [the image] together with its clothing, ornaments, and so forth, one should sprinkle it with the twelve-syllable vidyā over the head of the *adhivāsa* pavilion during the rite of pacification (*śāntikakarman*) in the case of a multi-bera [image]; in the case of a single-bera [image],
one should sprinkle it while uttering "Oṃ" over the head of the principal image (*mūlārcā*) lying there.
[The ritual] with its implements [is performed] at the door for the image.

He describes the method for bringing forth the temple with the easily understood textual passage beginning with "situated in the sacrificial pit" (*kuṇḍastham*) and ending with "one should cause it to enter with effort" (*yatnāt praveśayet*).
p.

181) Regarding the term "pīṭha": then the Guru, having meditated upon the deity without transgressing the prescribed rules—such as the invocation of the supreme [form], the invocation of the state, and the invocation by mantra—according to the ritual procedure;
Taking the mantra-image and circumambulating the pedestal three times with it,
while reciting the Trailokyamantra beginning with "O you who have stepped across the three worlds," and so forth— the mantra to be mentioned immediately below— as well as the five Upaniṣadic mantras.
One should install [the deity] while recollecting the mantra-form, that is, the desired form beginning with the eight-syllable [mantra].
Likewise, one should establish it; as stated in the Sumati-saṃhitā:
"Then, having circumambulated the pedestal, one should place [the deity] with the entire [mantra]."

And in the case of the Nārāyaṇa-form, one should utter the five Upaniṣadic mantras associated with their respective forms, beginning with "Oṃ, to the one who strides through the three worlds, to Trivikrama"; and one should cause gifts of cows, gold, jewels, garments, and so forth to be bestowed upon the Brahmins.
Having established a separate statement intended to satisfy the astrologers and others— adopted according to the maxim of the lion’s glance— he says "having examined" (*parīkṣya*),
meaning that one should stabilize [the matter] after examination. In the phrase "the teacher himself" (*guruḥ svayam*), by the word "himself" (*svayam*), [it is implied] not by another.
It is indicated that for the stabilization of the *bimba*, there must be its "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhitatva*);
thus, first, one should contemplate the grace of the established deity by recollecting its own majesty.

He says that one approaches for the purpose of performing the ritual: "one should recite," and here the word "recite" includes the *āgama* mantras for the sake of favoring the world and so forth. Then, having bathed the Lord of the Jar (*kumbheśa*) with the waters from the water-pots (*kalaśodaka*), specifically the waters from the sleep-pot (*nidrākalaśa*), and having performed the ritual of making him complete (*sakalīkṛtya*), one should worship him. Now...

In that context, intending to describe the invocation of the life-force (*jīvāvāhana*), he recalls the invocation of the substratum and so forth with the passage beginning "having meditated" and ending with "all of this":
"Space shall be his form; earth shall be his pedestal."

This statement— beginning with "having meditated" (dhyātvā)— is intended to establish, by means of the "lion's glance" (siṃhāvalokana) logic, that the time of consecration (pratiṣṭhāsamaya) is beginningless; it is a separate sentence focused on the connection between the sacred seat (pīṭha) and worship, and it refers to the eightfold binding (aṣṭabandhana) to be performed immediately following the rite of installation (pratiṣṭhāpana).

The Guru, the best among those who know the mantras, having obtained from the mouth of his own Guru the invocation of the vital breath (*jīvāvāhana*) and other rites, and being foremost in understanding their meaning, [worships] Viṣṇu— the supreme, unconditioned, partless, transcendent beyond the aggregate of causes and effects, whose essential nature is pure existence.

Having meditated upon and recollected the Supreme Self— who is more pervasive than all else and whose other name is Śrī Vāsudeva— by means of a handful of flowers as the seed for the invocation of the present living soul (*jīvāvāhana*), one should consider where to meditate; in this regard, [the text says] "Space is *yaṃ* Brahman," and so forth.

The ether, heard of in the Vedas, would be the form— that is, the body— of that conscious Self characterized by the aforementioned attributes; and the earth, which serves as its substratum, would be the pedestal.
It may be so. That being the case, one should meditate upon the support consisting of heaven and earth—the pedestal for the image—and the pedestal which is the substratum of the form;
immediately thereafter, one performs the invocation by means of Parameṣṭhin and the others, either individually or collectively.

One should conceive of the eternal subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) as the form that serves as the substratum for that Supreme Self during its future state as a living being, [conceived] through the sequentially acquired [mantras]. Then, [one should conceive of it] as appropriate to the chosen mantra-form (*mantra-mūrti*).

One should fashion the gross body, which arises from the subtle body as its substratum, by means of the placement (*nyāsa*) of the root mantra; thus he says, "consisting of light" (*tejomayam*). Regarding that, he describes the placement of the mantra according to the arrangement of the *bimba* (the reflected image) with the words "being situated" (*sthita*); when the *mantra-bimba* is situated, one performs the placement of stability (*sthitinyāsa*).
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) ending with the *sthiti* placement. This should be understood to apply similarly when seated and so forth.
The meaning is that during travel, such as when mounted on Garuḍa, one may perform everything according to one's desire.
Now, he states the invocation of the life-force (*jīvāvāhana*): "Having thus performed the placement and meditated accordingly..."

In that [form], there is both the *sakala* (with parts) and the *niṣkala* (without parts); therein, the *sakalaniṣkala* is fit for the invocation of the individual soul (*jīva-āvāhana*), being a subtle body characterized by both the manifest and the unmanifest.

Then, having meditated, the Guru [should contemplate] Mahāviṣṇu, the witness of all the world, who resides within the lotus of his own heart, seated in the very center of the lotus of his heart; he is the powerful one, Mahāviṣṇu, and he is Sadāviṣṇu.

Having taken up that Kṣetrajña— the individual soul (jīvātman) which is the reflection of the conscious self, subtler than the subtlest, and whose other name is the Great Viṣṇu as established by the Smṛtis— by means of the mantra for invoking the soul beginning with "Parameṣṭhin" and so forth.

Having separated [the deity] according to the instruction and taken it from one's own heart, one should join it with the previously conceptualized subtle form in the heart of the image. Having restrained it with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and well-protected it by means of the all-pervading *praṇava*, then— [this] being indicated by the word "then" (*atha*), which denotes immediate succession—
The ellipsis is that one should perform the subsequent rites, such as the *jīvanyāsa* (infusion of life) and so forth.

From that, the ellipsis is that [the image] becomes endowed with life (*sajīvā*). Here, the phrase "not even again" implies that after having performed the eight-fold binding (*aṣṭabandha*) once more, preceded by the invocation of the mantra (*mantrāvāhana*), [one should proceed].

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and displayed the mudrās for the ornaments, weapons, and so forth, one should worship Puruṣottama, together with his limbs and retinue, in due order; thereafter, one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground for the sake of atoning for defects such as omissions or excesses. Then...
Having visualized the attendants, such as the doorkeepers, in their respective places and having offered the *bali* oblation, one should perform the protection of the deity.

And he says "one should pray" with the words beginning "Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa," etc. By the word "always" (*sarvadā*), having concluded the previous section, he states the remainder of the present ritual procedure, ending with the phrase "by means of the [mudrās] such as Nīti, Dyotana, and so forth. Thus, it is generally stated as arising from the Devas.

Having described the consecration of a single image (*ekabera*) through a series of textual passages, he begins to state the distinctions regarding the multi-image (*bahubera*) form by concluding that section:
"In the case of a single image," [the phrase] "I shall now declare the consecration for the multi-image" is to be understood as the ellipsis; thus he states the distinction regarding the multi-image.

Regarding the term *bahubera*: in the case of a *bahubera* [image], there is a ritual worship (*karmārcā*), for which a name has been assigned based on its specific qualities; such a statue is to be fashioned, and for it, one should perform the bathing and other rites, including the offering of unbroken rice-grains (*akṣata*) and oblations (*homa*), the presentation of the final offerings, the preliminary consecration of the water (*jalādhivāsa*), the purification of the image (*biṃbaśuddhi*), the bathing with the auspicious jars (*kalaśasnāna*), and the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*).

One should perform the entry into the pavilion and so forth. Then, being well-purified and possessing a concentrated mind, one should apply this which is characterized by the deposition of the principles (*tattva-nyāsa*) into the garland-worship (*mālārcā*), which was previously established in the form of the deposition of jewels (*ratna-nyāsa*). Having joined [the mantra] with the *praṇava* (OM),...

One should perform the rite of *mūlācārya*— the primary officiant— predominantly through the ritual of meditation and consecration (*dhyānādhivāsa*), beginning with "the living one who identifies with the image" (*jīvam arcābhimāninam*) and ending with "according to the path prescribed for one's own kalpa," by means of the distinctions between the limbs and sub-limbs (*aṅga-pratyaṅga-bheda*). This should be done in whatever manner is appropriate, such as through the dissolution of the principles (*tattvasaṃhāra*).

The consecrated ritual worship (saṃskṛtāṃ karmārcāṃ) [is performed] by means of the fire-oblation of reality (tatvahoma), the preliminary consecration oblation (adhivāsahoma), the pacification oblation (śāntihoma), the offering of the remains (saṃpātasamarpaṇa), the thorough worship (samarcanā), and so forth. (p. 186)

Having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) according to the previously stated procedure, on the following day one should enter the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) in the proper sequence and unite that ritual image (*karmārcā*) with the primary image (*mūlārcā*).
The meaning is that one should apply to the primary image those purificatory rites, such as the *tattva-homa*, which were performed upon the ritual image; it is thus.

Having thus performed the rites according to the prescribed method and having meditated upon the installed primary image (mūlārcā), when the time for the bathing of the Lord of the Kumbha and other rites has arrived, he should say, "This is that very deity, this is the form," while placing his feet upon the pedestal (pīṭha) before him, or upon a pedestal suitable for the placement of his feet.

Having performed everything in its entirety and having established [the deity] with the fivefold reality (tattvapañcaka), then, immediately after the bathing of the Lord of the Jar (kumbheśa) and other rites, one should perform the ritual of complete identification (sakalīkaraṇa) as before and worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. Having thus described the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), that...
To ensure stability, while describing the restoration and re-consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of an old image of the same class,

he states the procedure for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā-vidhi*) for the purpose of manifesting the supreme consciousness alone— the presiding deity who first arrived— by way of its internal nature: "Having installed," and so forth, ending with "one should worship."
By the phrase "up to the path of the aeon" (kalpavartmanā), it is meant that an image which was formerly installed—

whether by those of one's own lineage or by those of another lineage— in accordance with the prescribed rites, yet has become ancient and, due to being without a protector, has had its pedestal and worship removed; nevertheless, [it is still honored] by its constituent parts.

Although a complete and auspicious splendor is seen, it is nevertheless devoid of consecration (*adhivāsa*), being lacking the perfuming of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-adhivāsa*) and the fire-offering (*homa*).

In this way, the procedure is declared in the manner that will be described immediately hereafter; he demonstrates the procedure by means of what was previously stated: "with the substances prescribed," "having designated the water for consecration (*adhivāsa*)," "one should wash with abundant water," and so forth, according to the form previously mentioned.

Having bathed [the deity] according to the prescribed rite with the pitchers for the purification of the image (*bimba*), one should dissolve the *tattvas*. The meaning is that, having united them with the *praṇava*, one should dissolve the individual soul (*jīva*) and the presiding ego of the image (*arcābhimāna*) according to the method previously stated. Here, the purification extends up to the consecration following the aforementioned purification of the image.

"In the middle, one conceptualizes purification by means of washing and so forth" means that one should perform the purification with washing and so forth, as will be described in sequence— namely, washing (*kṣālana*), immersion (*plāvana*), bathing (*snāna*),
and wiping (*mārjana*). The word "again" (*punaḥ*) implies that these [actions] are to be performed repeatedly.

Having dissolved the principles (*tattvas*) into the Supreme Self and purified them, that principle is thereafter declared to be common to all— both for the rites of pacification (*śāntika*) performed for the aforementioned purposes and for the ritual of consecration (*saṃskārakarman*). Now, regarding the longevity of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the mantra, the image (*bimba*), and so forth:

He states the procedure: "When" (yadā)— that is, when the image has been defiled by other fires and so forth, or its limbs have been separated— then, upon that *bimba* which has been consecrated by the previously mentioned seven purifications and so on;

Having well-cultivated the path of reality by meditating on it through the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and the path of creation, one should then meditate on it as gradually dissolving into the supreme [Self] and one's own self via the path of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*); then, having again generated the image, [one should perform the rite] therein according to what was previously stated.

According to the procedure prescribed for the consecration of an image, at the time of invoking the living spirit (jīvāvāhana), one should sprinkle it with "living waters" (*jīvādbhiḥ*), as stated in the aforementioned method;
thus, at the time of invoking the living spirit, one should unite that consciousness which has been superposed upon one's own self [with the image]. This is the ritual procedure.

Having [perceived] the consciousness superimposed upon one's own self as being of the nature of the Supreme (pāra) and so forth, and having [realized] the Self through one's own self, the Guru—having assimilated the Deity into himself—should perform the rite of extracting the reflection (*bimboddhāra*) either in the water-pot (*kalaśa*) or [in the mirror]. This refers to what was stated immediately prior: "or, having invoked [the deity] into the water-pot."
The externalist, belonging to the side of darkness, argues that the same logic applies whether the temple is dilapidated or not;

thus, he says "in the image" (*bimba*). That is, when the image—or the house—is dilapidated, one should construct a wooden structure either in the region between Indra and Īśāna, or even in the space between Soma and Īśāna.
Having purified that area in front of the temple according to the prescribed method for purifying the temple,
one should place a copper pedestal there.

189) This rule for the directions is to be understood as applicable to a temple with a western entrance, in accordance with that [rule];
and likewise in the *Viṣṇusaṃhitā* regarding Parjanya, Jayanta, Diti, and Aditi.
Saṃ... [incomplete] Blank Folio Śrīḥ.

He recites the introductory verse (*om vṛttam*) in order to establish the connection: "This world, which consists of name, form, and action, was previously unknown as being identical with the inner Self and so forth; it is known [only] through differentiation, like a snake [superimposed] upon a rope. This is the meaning of the phrase "tad bhedam" (that differentiation).

Regarding the statement "it was declared concerning him," it has been said that the world, though unknown, becomes known through the inner self (pratyagātman) like a snake [superimposed] on a rope; thus, he cites an authoritative statement (*āptavākya*) as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to illustrate this point:
Just as a rope, when not clearly ascertained in the darkness, is conceptualized [as a snake].
In the same way, the self is conceptualized through states such as the appearance of a snake or a stream of water.
If it is asked, "Why was it stated that the world is an evil (anartha) because it is a transformation (*vivarta*) of the unknown inner Self (*pratyagātman*)?

[the author] replies: "In order to establish the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*). He says this because one becomes exceedingly afraid of the inner Self, thinking, "Ignorance is the cause of evil, and the entire world arising from it is an evil."
[The text] says:

"He desires to liberate. Now, if the entire world beginning with Brahmā is not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), then what is the human goal? It is the cessation of that [world]; thus he says: "The human goal is the cessation of all misfortunes..."

"Perishing [in relation] to the inner self"—for it is thus said that knowledge alone is the wealth situated in the goal of man (*puruṣārtha*): "The thorough knowledge of reality is the cause of the goal of man.
Here he states the reason: "[It is] that whose true nature is the attainment of all joy and the removal of every evil."
Since this transmigrating being is [defined] by its own nature as one possessing a perverted vision regarding what has been taught,
he says that ritual action and the like are not the means to liberation;
for there is nothing other than knowledge— which destroys ignorance— that serves as the obstacle to the human goal, because that goal is obstructed by ignorance alone.
Furthermore, its means of accomplishment is stated to be the reversal [of ignorance], as it was previously declared that the aphorism of this knowledge is "The Self, indeed.
Likewise, its introduction (upodghāta) has been previously explained along with its purpose; thus, one should meditate [upon it] as "The Self, indeed."

Thus, the knowledge of the Self has been aphoristically stated by the words beginning with "They say," and the purpose of that aphoristically stated knowledge of the Self has been declared following an objection. If one asks what that purpose is, he says:
When the inner Self (pratīc) is directly realized, all that is to be known is completely and exhaustively accomplished;

likewise, the supreme human goal is fully accomplished when [the Self] is superimposed as equal [to all]. Alternatively, this is established even through the sublation of the distinctions of the non-self.
"What is the use of the knowledge of the Self? To this he replies with the word "the inward" (*pratīcī*). For this very reason, it is said that "one should meditate [on the Self] as the Self alone.
Since this is so, one should perceive the non-dual Self within the Self; the Self alone [is the reality].

"The subject matter of the knowledge of Brahman is understood from the scripture"— thus he restates another previous occurrence with the words, "Now, [the soul] in another womb. Having thus restated that perishable knowledge, its result was clearly explained at the conclusion of the first chapter.

The internal, the elemental, and likewise the divine; the past, the present, and the future; the goal to be attained and the means of attainment—all this has arisen from ignorance. This has been set forth in brief at the conclusion of the chapter, and that same matter is presented once again.

The triad consists of the anus, as well as name and action; the summary of these three is the conjunction of the subtle body with the Self. Thus, by the phrase "then [it enters] another womb," the author draws forth that very ignorance of the inner self (pratyagavidyā) along with its appearances, which was previously indicated in the aphorism "its distinction."

At the conclusion of the third chapter, that which was to be done has been stated both in brief and in detail. Having thus drawn upon what has occurred [in the previous section], he demonstrates the connection by means of three *vārtikas*: "This one, whose body is the three worlds, is the universal form (*viśvarūpa*)."

Prajāpati, whose true nature as the Self remains unknown, possesses an ego-superimposition upon that very Supreme Being who is the embodiment of Prāṇa and within whom all infinite things are subsumed. (p. 192) From that [Supreme Being], he [arose].

This person, who has desisted from worldly activity and whose true nature as the Self has been directly realized, is the subject matter of this knowledge; he is presented by means of scripture through the words of Gārgya, who desires to impart the knowledge of Brahman. This is the meaning.
Gārgya is one whose body is the very self of the three worlds; for this very reason, that Gārgya is called Prajāpati, the one whose form is the universe.
He, whose body is the vital breath (prāṇa) containing within it all infinite deities, is the goal of the universe;

through the power of worship, he has realized that the entire product of ignorance is his own self. And therefore, by his grace alone, one who is dispassionate is raised up to the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman.

Alternatively, by the first [verse] Prajāpati is mentioned, and by the second and third, Gārgya. Now, one might object: "Since he is a knower of Brahman, why is he raised up as one qualified for the knowledge of Brahman? To this he replies: "Because he is not a knower of Brahman in its primary sense," due to his incomplete knowledge of Brahman.
"He is arrogant and insignificant; for no one who possesses complete knowledge ever becomes arrogant, as he is beyond duality. The meaning is that arrogance is a sign of not knowing Brahman.
He states that the principal knower of Brahman is the teacher Ajātaśatru:
p.
193) "The entire, complete object of human endeavor, as well as the other [the unmanifest], is conceived by Gārgya Ācāra through identity with Ajātaśatru. Thus it is said.
Having explained the connection with the Brahmana through its removal of the knots, he now states the connection with the chapter:
"Now that ignorance has been explained, the clear exposition of the Sutra 'The Self alone' (Ātmaiveti) for its eradication is commenced. Thus, by means of the Śruti.
The presentation of Gārgī and others is by way of the nature of disciple and teacher.
The meaning is that the subsequent text is for the purpose of explaining the Vidyā-sūtras. He states the purpose of teaching the Vidyā in the form of a narrative:
"This narrative has been told for the sake of achieving easy comprehension. Thus [he describes] his own...

Having shown the [standard] connection, he now demonstrates the connection as stated by Bhartṛprapañca, for the purpose of refuting it, by means of three and a half Vārtikas. Furthermore, other wise ones explain the connection here in this way: "That very one" (sa eṣa) is what has been introduced.
For that which was previously described through the historical narrative of Gārgya and Kāśya as having consciousness as its essence—
the one who determines [objects] and the enjoyer within this body— is indeed the deity and nothing else;
thus, this Śruti, under the guise of Gārgya, stated the prima facie position regarding the existence of the Self.
For the purpose of establishing agency and enjoyership, and for the sake of proving the final conclusion, the form of Kāśya is postulated by the Śruti.
194) Thus [it is said]. This is the meaning: among the five sūtras, this sentence "this has entered here" is the *vijñānātma-sūtra*; Maitreyī was not [intended] for its definitive determination.
Some say that because the word "brāhmaṇa" occurs earlier in the text, this refers specifically to the *Ajātaśatru-brāhmaṇa*.
This refutes the aforementioned connection:

"Because it is stainless, that [connection] is improper, as there is no application to the subject at hand"— the meaning of this is that [the connection is improper] because the agency and enjoyership of the vital-deity (prāṇadevatā) have been set aside in favor of the Self (ātman).

It is said that the next three Brāhmaṇas are commenced in order to establish [the self's] status as agent and enjoyer; however, this connection is not tenable because it lacks relevance to the subject matter at hand and because it would be fruitless. How is there an impossibility of relevance to the subject matter? It is explained:

"Liberation results from the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self. This [which was] under discussion—that "he knew himself as the Self alone"—is not established [if one holds otherwise]. For if agency and so forth were real (pāramārthika) for the cognizing self (vijñānātman), then there would be no connection with what is under discussion.

He establishes the fruitlessness [of the opponent's position] with the words "Even in the view that there are deities," beginning with "Is there anything... and so forth. The meaning is this: if it is desired that the cognizer be distinct from the deity, then the effort is fruitless; for [the opponent] does not accept the existence and agency of a self distinct from the gross body.
If only the state of being an enjoyer is intended [to be proven], then that is for the purpose of refuting the position of the Cārvākas; [therefore, it must be] distinct from the body.
Even on the view that the vital deity exists, since it is precisely that vital deity who,
by virtue of being the object of consciousness, can logically possess the status of agent and enjoyer,
the sequence of arguments establishing an entity distinct from the vital deity is fruitless.
He states that neither of the two types of defects applies to our proposed position regarding the relationship [between the two]:
"But when one whose true nature of oneness is unknown is intended here, he—
being established in the effects of ignorance— is addressed by the Śruti through the body of Gārgya."

At that time, for the sake of pacifying all causes of suffering through the refutation of opposing views, and for the purpose of understanding the meaning of the entire Vedānta by cutting away the roots of the prima facie arguments,
even Kāśyapa— who was himself a proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī)—
was produced by Śruti itself. All of this [occurred] then.
"It shall be fruitful through effort and not otherwise"—thus it was stated previously that the narrative (ākhyāyikā) is for the sake of easy understanding; now he states another purpose:
"Or rather, let this narrative be for the sake of enjoining faith, conduct, and so forth."

Thus, the narrative is meaningful according to its literal sense. Having stated the connection with the Brāhmaṇa, he begins the explanation of the meaning of the words: since it has been established that there is nothing other than the object attained through the vision as previously described, one becomes exceedingly arrogant; "vijñāta" refers to the ground for the cause of such pride.
"Having approached one who is faithful, endowed with a disciplined mind, and seeking the highest good, I shall speak to you of Brahman," thus did Kāśya address Gārgya.

There is no enemy born nor will there ever be one, because of the perception of ultimate unity; thus, O Gārgya, you have been made one whose intellect is turned away from what is contrary to that realization. Since there is no reality higher than Brahman, and since there is nothing beyond it, I shall speak of that which is to be meditated upon here.

"These [verses] destroy all [objections] regarding the cause; they are easy to understand. Now, one might object: "The Sage acted contrary to the rule that 'one should not speak to anyone unless asked. To this he replies: "Not [when asked].
Indeed, the Sage did act contrary to this when he said, "I shall tell you, O Brahmin," even though he had not been asked.
By saying "he spoke of the task," one implies "he said 'let us speak'" in the sense of "I ask"; therefore, there is no contradiction with the Smṛti. This is what he states:
"Surely, because of the observation of pride and so forth, [it is] the perception of incomplete reality."
"Therefore, for the sake of completeness, he questioned Kāśya, who was endowed with wisdom.

He states that even according to the position that the meaning is exactly as heard, there is no fault whatsoever: "Knowledge should not be spoken even when unasked to one who is faithful, qualified, desirous of knowledge, and possessed of humility."
Regarding the term "to the wise" (*vipaścite*), he states the authoritative proof for this:

"Where neither dharma nor artha are found, nor even a corresponding desire to hear [them], there it should be said that 'this is not knowledge'. It is thus indicated by the very prohibition, even without an explicit question.
The remainder of the sentence should be understood as follows: "Otherwise, there would be no connection with the subject matter at hand.
197) Thus, they state the reason for speaking again by means of a further question.
Relying on the maxim of "the lost horse and the burnt chariot," he spoke of the stages [of yoga],
being rich in human wealth and endowed with divine wealth. Since a person is qualified for all ritual action by means of these two types of wealth, Bālākṣa declared it himself.
The phrase "from Kāśyama" is an elaboration of what preceded;

[the author] explains the meaning of "a thousand in this [cow]" and so forth by means of four *vārttikas*. [He says: "I shall speak to you that Brahman which is easily understood," thus [he speaks] merely with words.

"I give away a thousand cows today even without the definitive realization of the one Self. Regarding the occasion for this gift of a thousand cows, the Śruti clearly declared through the repeated expression of his name, "Janaka,
Janaka," that he was the progenitor among those born of Śūdra women, and indeed the sole one who desired the welfare of all people.

Desirous of speaking and wishing to grasp him, they rush toward him, disregarding the well-known reputation that "this Gārgya has come to me"; and thinking, "He honors me as one who desires to give joy and wishes to listen," what kind of Brahman did he speak of?

Regarding this, he says: "The conscious one, all-pervading and eternal, who resides in the eye as the sun—him alone, situated in the midst, I always worship as Brahman. Thus, I [worship] Brahman of such a nature, distinct from that verbal expression.
(198) "I know [this]; therefore, you must not speak," he said. To Gārgya, who was speaking thus, the King of Kāśī replied, "No, no! Your statement has resulted in a mere conversation with me."
"But you have not asserted a cognition of an unprecedented object; therefore, do not say,
'I know [Brahman] even without your word,' for that would show the defects of your practice of saying 'I am [Brahman]'—
the claim of one who professes to have known Brahman through such practice."
"By one whose intellect is uncontradicted, [the truth] was practiced because Gārgya did not speak"—this is what you said.

"Brahman was known by me even without your speaking"—one who has the habit of speaking thus at length is a "vijñātabrahman" (one who has known Brahman); this [statement] of that disputant Jātaśatru was directed toward Gārgya.

The repetition of the negations is for the purpose of demonstrating the distraction of the intellect, because [the nature of] Brahman—which was intended to be spoken of by him—has not been stated; or else, Gārgya was a proponent of Brahman who did not know Brahman, and thus Ajātaśatru [negated] him regarding that propounding of Brahman, the genitive case being used in the sense of the accusative. Him.

Alternatively, the repetition of the negation serves to indicate that the plural number in the second case refers to the "proponents" (pravādinaḥ) from Gārgya's perspective; if it is asked how their state of being known is understood apart from those words, he says in response:
It is well known to us that even apart from your teaching,
that [system] does not require your word for its establishment, as it was already established previously.

"You know only Brahman alone, but not the qualities of worship or their fruits; however, you should not entertain such a doubt," he says: "Do not harbor the suspicion that 'I do not know its worship,' for one must also know the worship along with its qualities and its very fruit."

He explains the quality of *atiṣṭhā*: "Because he stands surpassing all beings by virtue of his preeminence, his name is *atiṣṭhā*; thus it belongs to him whose self is the Sun. He states the meaning of the term *rāja* as follows:

"And because he is radiant in his eyes, he is called 'King' (Rāja). Thus, for that person who meditates upon him as specified day and night, the fruit is exactly according to their meditation and not otherwise; for the sun's [power] was destroyed by Kāśya through the fault of a discrepancy in his understanding.

The two *vārtikas* beginning with "Gārgya began to explain another [instance of] Brahman to the King" state the meaning of the passage starting with "And he [is] that person in the moon," for the sake of easy understanding: [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the intellect (*vijñāna*), and he who is yonder in the moon as the bright (*sukra*), these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the self (*ātman*), and he who is yonder in the sun as the brilliant (*tejasvin*), these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the shadow (*chāyā*), and he who is yonder in lightning as the shining (*vidyut*), these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as sound (*svara*), and he who is yonder in thunder as sound, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as warmth (*uṣṇa*), and he who is yonder in fire as warmth, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the heart (*hṛdaya*), and he who is yonder in the quarters as the heart, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the breath (*prāṇa*), and he who is yonder in the wind as the breath, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the body (*tanmātra*), and he who is yonder in the ether (*ākāśa*) as the body, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as semen (*retas*), and he who is yonder in water as semen, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the right eye (*dakṣiṇākṣi*), and he who is yonder in the sun (*āditya*) as the right eye, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the left eye (*savyākṣi*), and he who is yonder in the moon (*candra*) as the left eye, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the right ear (*dakṣiṇaśrotra*), and he who is yonder in fire (*agni*) as the right ear, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the left ear (*savyaśrotra*), and he who is yonder in the quarters (*diśaḥ*) as the left ear, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the mind (*manas*), and he who is yonder in the moon (*candra*) as the mind, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as speech (*vāk*), and he who is yonder in lightning (*vidyut*) as speech, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the breath (*prāṇa*), and he who is yonder in the wind (*vāyu*) as the breath, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the body (*tanmātra*), and he who is yonder in the ether (*ākāśa*) as the body, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as semen (*retas*), and he who is yonder in water (*āpaḥ*) as semen, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the shadow (*chāyā*), and he who is yonder in darkness (*tamas*) as the shadow, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the self (*ātman*), and he who is yonder in the space within the heart (*hṛdyākāśa*) as the self, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the intellect (*vijñāna*), and he who is yonder in the ether (*ākāśa*) as the intellect, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the breath (*prāṇa*), and he who is yonder in the ether (*ākāśa*) as the breath, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the body (*tanmātra*), and he who is yonder in the ether (*ākāśa*) as the body, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the body (*tanmātra*), and he who is yonder in the ether (*ākāśa*) as the body, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as semen (*retas*), and he who is yonder in the ether (*ākāśa*) as semen, these two are one single being. He who knows this becomes a consumer of food, and his offspring does not perish. [The text continues: "He who is here in a person as the shadow (*chāyā*), and he who is yonder in the ether (*ākāśa*) as the shadow, these two are one single
"I meditate upon Brahman as the moon, the mind, and the intellect, which is without fear"— thus he explains the meaning of the word *bṛhat* (great):
because the lunar orb is twice the size of the solar orb, it is "great."
Thereafter, the moon is designated by its measure.

200) He explains the meaning of the three words "pāṇḍaravāsāḥ sauro rājā" with the following two verses from the *Uttaravārttika*: "She whose garment is white like the ocean... (ambhodhipāṇḍaraṃ vāso yasyāḥ).
One who possesses that [knowledge] and takes pride in the umbrella should be the one clad in white garments; he is Soma because of his gentle nature (*saumyatva*).
Soma shines exceedingly with moonlight and is the king of the Brāhmaṇas; therefore, one says "Soma, the King" out of a desire to prescribe meditation upon him.
By the word "soma," the *latā* (the creeper) as well as the [deity] Soma is included; he states the reason for this:
because they share the same property of being denoted by the same name. Both the creeper and Soma are grasped because the deity of both is one;
therefore, that pair is to be worshipped. Thus, the name "Soma" belongs equally to both of them.

Furthermore, Dharma increases through the waxing and waning of the moon; even the *latā* (creeper) and the *soma* (moon-plant) grow by means of their leaves, becoming two-leaved and so on during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), while they diminish leaf by leaf through the decrease of heat during the dark fortnight. Since the deity of both is the Moon (*himāṃśu*), it is said that there is "one deity. What, then, is her form? It is that of a *ruru* deer.
Regarding this, he says:
"Know that this is the one deity who determines each individual object; she is the enjoyer and the agent everywhere. Therefore, there is nothing other than her that is to be enjoyed; she is Brahman."
He states that the explanation is uniform across all the synonyms: "We worship this as the Self because it pervades everything. (p.

"The explanation is to be understood as identical in all sentences, as before"—this reveals the identical method. "And where [the suffix] *guṇa* occurs" is also possible here; however, in all sentences, the determination would be that it belongs to a deity ending in a consonant (*halanta*). Now, [one might object]: "Is it not brilliance (*tejasvitva*)?"

To the objection that since the sun and others also possess brilliance, why is luminosity considered a specific quality of lightning alone, they reply: "The light of the sun and the moon is eclipsed by the clouds; even there, lightning is preeminent in its brilliance, and thus it is called 'lightning' (vidyut) [from the root *dyut*, 'to shine'], [representing] the Brahman of space."
The two qualities, "full" (*pūrṇam*) and "non-functioning" (*apravarti*), have been indicated; he explains both of them as follows:
Just as the physical sky is not full in parts, [the Self] is full because it does not function (*apravartanāt*).
It is called "non-functioning" because, unlike jars and other objects, it is undivided; thus, space is said to be full.
The meaning is that because there is no proceeding and because it is immovable, it is called "non-proceeding" (*apravṛtti*).
He states another meaning of the word "non-proceeding":
it may mean "inactivity," for all activities [cease] in space; thus, activity does not proceed by itself.

The meaning is that, because space (*ākāśa*) is the substratum for that which consists of the *śukriya* [mantras], it is said to "proceed" (*pravarti*). If the reading is *akriyāvat*, the interpretation is even more straightforward. He explains the threefold fruit beginning with "victorious" (*jiṣṇu*):

He is *jiṣṇu* because of his victorious nature, or because he is not conquered by others; thus he is called *apājiṣṇu*. Those born from one [father] but belonging to another [mother] are designated as *anyatastyā*.

"Furthermore, one may become the husband of another's wife, the crusher of a stepbrother, or the conqueror of enemies; thus, 'victorious' (jiṣṇu) is the first fruit, 'unconquerable' (ajaiṣṇu) is the second, and 'crusher of foes' (śatrumardana) is the third. By means of the practice of the three qualities, he joins these three fruits [to the practice]."
Viṣṇu worships the Supreme Lord, whose qualities are those of Indra and who possesses the quality of Vaikuṇṭha.

Because his army is "invincible" (*parājita*), there is the defeat of rival forces; thus, the quality of being "overpowering" (*viṣāsahi*) is appropriate for Agni. He says that because Agni endures even the world when it is cast into him, he is therefore [so named].
"Because he reduces everything to ashes, he is called Viṣāsahi by the lords. Thus it was said.

Regarding the instruction to "meditate on this Puruṣa, who is Brahman and consciousness, in the waters, in the semen, and in the intellect," [the text] says "as before" in response to Kāśya. In this way, it is easily understood that the quality of the deity is the one who identifies with water.
The effect characterized by the arising of a reflection belongs to its worshipper, and the fruit is likewise similar;

this he states: "Since the effect is the arising of a reflection and the reflection itself [is the cause], therefore the object of worship must be a counterpart (pratirūpa), and its fruit in the waters is also of that same nature. Indeed.

To the objection that the attainment of the result follows from the literal meaning of the prefix *prati*, he says: "No; this prefix *prati* has its literal sense [only] because the result is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*)."

"But in the reverse order, however, it should be known that there would be misfortune; thus [the word] 'anurūpa' means 'conformable'. He explains the meaning of the word *anurūpa*: "One who is always diligent in accordance with the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and the conduct of the virtuous (*sadācāra*); because he conforms to the *Śruti* and so forth, let him therefore be called *pratirūpa* (conformable)."

"Such is he": the meaning is that for one who meditates upon him as possessing such qualities, sons and other offspring are born in accordance with the Vedas and other authorities. The word *rociṣṇu* means luster or brilliance.
That secret quality (*upaniṣad*) belongs to the person who is perceivable in a mirror and the like, and is endowed with it.
"O you who worship Brahman"— this is what he says.
When "worship" is mentioned in relation to the intellects such as the mirror-self (*ādarśātman*) and others that have transcended the *rociṣṇu* state,
Kāśya replies, "As before," of his own accord.

The meaning here is that one becomes radiant. Furthermore, the fruit pertaining to progeny is heard in the case of both the lightning and the Self-injunctions. To the question "How is that so?", he says:
"Where there is a multiplicity of objects of meditation, there the fruit extends even to progeny."

Since many objects such as "seeing a hundred lightning flashes" are well-known [in scripture], it might be thought that a plurality of fruits does not apply to the meditation on the *sektṛ* (the sprinkler) because of its specific adjuncts; to this, he says:
"In whatever [meditation] a fruit possesses certain qualities, the meditation there should possess those same qualities, according to the inference from the fruit."
"The fruits [are obtained] without having performed worship."
The meaning is that when there is a multiplicity of fruits, there must be a multiplicity of objects of meditation; or else, the word *anu* is heard as if it were outside [the compound], like a sound.
"One should designate [the sound] as internal, divine, and in the intellect"—this is easy to understand;
proceed. If one asks what the cause of the resonance is, he says "vital breath" (prāṇa):
"The vital breath, struck by the various parts of the body of a man running swiftly..."
"By means of a particular function, sound makes [itself] appear as if external; 'this person is Asura' is its quality, and for one who worships it, long life is the fruit. Thus he says:
"Through the projection of its function, this [breath] is called Asura; and because it is dependent upon that [quality], one becomes possessed of a hundred-year lifespan."
"One does not die by untimely death"—thus he states that for the God, having the quarters as his pride, having a second and yet being without a companion is his nature:
"In the quarters, he has no second companion; he is always alone, for [a second] is indeed difficult to conceive."

"Having abandoned the eastern direction and others, one should worship the western [direction] with ointments"—thus, he now states the fruit of the worship of the two qualities: "One should be a worshiper of all things, having removed the circle of wicked people; there shall always be stability in the lineage of sons and other kinsmen," [as stated] in the *Chāyāmaye*.
Likewise, it is easily understood that in both ignorance and knowledge there is but one single deity;
and [it is stated] that death is the attribute and the fruit of this deity.

Longevity, the absence of disease and so forth, and excellence—this is what he states: "Before the time of death, even disease does not approach him," and so on, beginning with the words "in the body which is opposed [to it] and in the intellect. This is easily understood in the case of such a Brahmin.
The quality of being "possessed of self" belongs to the worshiper; that very state of having a self under one's control is the fruit.
Furthermore, the progeny of the worshiper becomes possessed of a self under their control, because there are many notions regarding the object of worship.
Thus he says: "and being possessed of self, the progeny becomes possessed of self. One should sit facing the east.

Thus, in this final section, the meditation upon the vital breath (prāṇa) both collectively and individually is taught; whereas previously only the individual [aspects] were mentioned, he clarifies the intention there:
"The previous mention was of the individual [parts], but here that which is taught is intended as the collective."
"Gārgī, it being so, this is logical. What does he reveal by his intention?
Having had his instruction rejected, he repeatedly spoke of one Brahman after another with great reverence until the end of the section on the Self, because of the infinity of specific attributes.
"He said, 'The entire Brahman,' and when that too was rejected, Gārgya became silent.
This statement does not lose its intended meaning even as he speaks of the "entire Brahman.

All particularities can be expressed; therefore, he spoke of Brahman as a whole, because all particularities are included within it. When even that [Brahman] is negated, since there is no further activity, one has transcended [the world], just like Brahman. Now, all this—

If it is suspected that Brahman might be something other than existence (bhava), and that because of such difference it would follow that even that [existence] is non-Brahman, he says in response: "That which was previously described as the entirety of Brahman—
that very same thing is imagined by the deluded, through ignorance, as being both one and many."

The meaning is that this is what was stated in the passage, "One should meditate on the Self as 'just this' (ātmaiveti)," [using] the analogy of a rope-snake. He states the intention of the king when he said, "Only this much":
having looked at Gārgya with his head hanging down, the unsurpassed king said to him, "Only this much."
"I shall remove the remaining doubt. This means that he spoke thus—"only this much"—in order to make known that the Brahman which remains is not seen as something known.
Therefore, he says that there is an "overflowing" (āpluti) of meaning, signifying: "By this, you have been grasped."

And in the case of the "restrained" (*nigṛhya*) yoga, one should here point out the *pluti* (protracted) vowel; [the text says] "speaking Brahman," which indicates the status of a seer (*ṛṣitva*), and "this much is the Brahma-cosmos. If all this is not Brahman, then what is that Brahman? To this, he says:
"When it is unknown, the world is unknown; when it is known, the world is known accordingly.
That alone is Brahman because of its fullness, but not that which you have described, due to its incompleteness"—this is the elaboration of that [verse].

The word *brahman* has its primary meaning in the reality of the Self, which is established by itself as neither excluded nor followed by anything else; however, it does not have that same [primary] sense in what is other than that. Since the sun and so forth are not *brahman*, he says that the statement "it is not merely this much" is appropriate.
Since this is so, the King said to Gārgya, who had declared, "It is only this much," "That is not all," clearly because [the latter's knowledge] was insufficient for the state of Brahmanhood; for,
since he did not refute their status as Brahman, it is certain that he knows the primary Brahman.
Having understood that for this purpose [the king] had begun to approach him for instruction, he said this:
"This speech is characteristic of one who does not know the true nature of Brahman; it is not merely this much.
Then, having inferred from signs that the King was indeed Gārgya, Kāśya realized this.

"Expertise in the knowledge of Brahman is the means," he said to him for the sake of awakening to the Supreme Brahman. He elaborates on this: "Desirous of thoroughly knowing the Supreme Brahman, I have approached you with reverence; please instruct me."
"Regarding 'the state of being as-it-is' (yathāvattva): when this was said, [the king] replied that he did not understand how to perform the formal approach (upasadana).
To the king, the Kṣatriya, who spoke in this manner...
If a Brāhmaṇa should, when not in distress, enter upon a conduct that is contrary to his caste—

that is, a practice forbidden by the treatises on Dharma— then "acquisition" (yoga) is the attainment of what has not been attained, and "security" (kṣema) is the preservation of what has been attained; for the sake of these, it is the duty of the Brāhmaṇa to go to the king.
He says that it is understood as follows:
going for the sake of the fruits of *yogakṣema* (acquisition and preservation) is not forbidden;
however, approaching a king is forbidden for the purpose of merely beholding Brahman.

"Therefore, I shall instruct you in Brahman while you remain uninitiated, like a bilva fruit placed in the palm of the hand—knowing which one becomes all-knowing. Having said this, the king took him by the hand and raised him up; and the two of them approached the sleeping man, intending to examine his vital functions. This is the story.

The two *vārtikas* are easily understood. This [verse] clarifies that [the King] went to where [Gārgya’s] sleeping [son] was, thinking: "I shall teach Bālāki that Brahman spoken of by Gārgya is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), and likewise demonstrate to him the non-selfhood (*anātmatā*) of these [five elements]. Thus, [it is established] that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the enjoyer.

It establishes that the person intended by Gārgya is not an enjoyer. By means of two Vārtikas, which address the failure to recognize the name used for the purpose of calling out, [the text] shows how one should act with the names of deities when addressing a sleeping person, as has been explained.
Although he was being addressed in this way with words such as "O Bṛhan," he who was asleep did not wake up at all; therefore, [the person] intended by Gārgya—

"It is understood that [the Self] is not the enjoyer"—surely, by setting aside the waking state, the departure of the sleeping person is not perceived in order to speak of and demonstrate the Self; for in that [waking state], all objects are clearly apprehended. Therefore...

The self intended by Kāśya cannot be demonstrated by distinguishing it from the self intended by Gārgya while one is asleep, because all worldly activity has ceased. Therefore, he says that going to a sleeping person is not purposeful:

"Having abandoned the state of waking, why did they go to sleep? The clarity of all states is intended to be described during the time of waking. Thus, he says [the following] because the Self intended to be shown cannot be demonstrated while one is awake: "Of the vital breaths..."

Due to the intermingling of the new-born and the person, it is not possible to effect a discrimination between the enjoyer and the enjoyed in the state of awakening; for although all objects are perceived in the waking state,
nevertheless, it is impossible to effect the intended discrimination of the Self therein.

"Because all things are intermingled like milk and water"— starting from this point up to "the established conclusion," some [hold this view]. To show what that intended discrimination of the Self is, he says:
The person possesses only the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*); even in the slightest degree, he does not possess the state of being an object of enjoyment (*bhojyatva*).

According to the intention of Kāśī, for any other [entity], there is only the state of being an object of enjoyment and not the state of being an enjoyer; thus, the Self is indeed the witness (*sākṣin*).

"The Self cannot be the witness, for the witness is indeed non-Self"—this is the distinction. He says that such a distinction is difficult to find there because of its confusion; yet, upon awakening, it is not doubtful, for one is able to distinguish between the enjoyer and the enjoyed.

Therefore, because it has been said that "he approached the sleeping person with care," it is clear for this reason that you [the Self] are not the cause of objective entities; thus he says: "Therefore, although there is proximity of the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth during the waking state, it is difficult [to distinguish them] because of their mutual confusion."
"Thus there may be discernment. Now, one might object that even in deep sleep (suṣupta) the state of being mixed is the same;
to this he says "no"—because the Self has departed [to its own nature], experience is not presented to it, and all [the powers] remain indifferent.
Since it is Kāśya’s intention that "the deities, along with their causes, are asleep," [the question arises: what enjoyment of objects could belong to him there,
which would be employed in the cognition of objects?
Because the deities associated with the instruments [of action] are indifferent and have been withdrawn, he states the cause for this withdrawal:
"Having woken from the exhaustion of karma impelled by the pursuit of enjoyment, they lie down."
"The instruments [of action] together with the experiencing self are in the Self. Now, one might object: "But is not the Self intended by Gārgī also withdrawn?

If it is argued that, for this reason, enjoyment belongs to no one at all, he says "no": "The connection of wealth with the vital breath (prāṇa) is improper because of their distinctness; moreover, the one called 'other' is not the vital breath, but rather the single waking enjoyer who is accepted by Gārgya. On this point:
He states the proof: "Protecting by means of the vital breath," and likewise it is declared further on:
"The fires of the vital breaths"—this is clear; and likewise from the scriptural text concerning that which never sets. Therefore, he concludes that the vital breath remains awake during sleep.
"Unwearied, the vital breath alone remains awake here day and night"—what is it that arises from this? To this he says:
"Just as the vital breath was previously the enjoyer in the waking state, so too is it in the dream state."

"If the knower remains just as he is, let him be awakened by this [name]. Now, it may be argued that it is improper for the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to have a connection with names such as "Moon" because they are different;
yet, if even another name is used to awaken the *prāṇa*, then the *prāṇa* could likewise be awakened by names such as "Sun" and so forth.
One might suspect that because there is no distinction [between them], the act of addressing is merely a name for that [breath] and not an awakening,

since it is consciousness; however, having raised this doubt, [the author] states that because unity was declared when the Self was revealed as being both the breath and the moon, therefore the breath is awakened.
