"By means of names beginning with 'Candra'": alternatively, because of the functional equivalence between the thread (*sūtra*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there is also an address by means of names such as "Unspoken" (*anukta*), "Thread-portion" (*sūtrāvayava*), and so forth.
He states that [the Self] has performed [this action]: "Or, by implication, its apprehension" (sāmarthyāt tadgrahaḥ).

Alternatively, it means by the power of establishing that the conscious being is the enjoyer. Having thus stated the reason for awakening [the vital breath] by means of the names of the moon, he says "if" (yadi) to show that the vital breath is not the enjoyer because it does not grasp those names.

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) would be the enjoyer [of sound] as it is in the waking state; had it not heard the sound that reached it, it would not be the enjoyer, for it would not have heard it, like a stone. Thus, the one intended by Kāśya is the Self (*ātman*), while the one intended by Gārgya is the sleeping [vital breath]; therefore, this [address] is for the purpose of awakening him.

It was stated that because the name of the one who is addressed is not mentioned, the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—and no other—is the enjoyer, since it is the latter that is asleep; to this, the proponent of the prima facie view replies: "But surely, when this person who is asleep is awakened and addressed by his own name, he himself—the enjoyer—is made to hear the sound, and not some other non-enjoyer."

The meaning is this: even from the dull-witted, no discrimination would arise as to which of these two has awakened. Although the Self intended by Kāśī is asleep while the other is awake, nevertheless, when addressed by their respective names, it is the enjoyer alone who responds to the sound.
The insentient is not the self; therefore, at the time of awakening, it received the name employed for the purpose of addressing the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Alternatively, he addresses the objection that there would be no certainty as to which [object] Kāśya intended, since even for one who is not asleep, it is observed that at times,
due to the influence of causal conditions (*nimitta*), there is no perception of a nearby object. He refutes this as follows:

It is not so, because Gārgī’s position has not been specifically determined; since the Brahman intended by Ajātaśatru has not previously been established through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can there be a specific determination? He demonstrates that [determination] with the following six verses of the Vārttika.
"It does not perish" means that here, the setting of speech and the other senses is immortality;
Indra is the perfected one whose body is the year, who has withdrawn name and form, and who stands pervading the entire universe of the internal self and so forth,
in whom the world is woven as warp and woof.
By means of the illustration of the fish,
it is shown that even when one is asleep, the vital breath (prāṇa) remains performing its own functions entirely while making a tumultuous sound,
just as when one is awake; furthermore, Gārgya does not admit any other enjoyer here apart from the vital breath.

Whether at that time or at another time, since something other than the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is being experienced as an object of enjoyment, it must necessarily be understood that the object of cognition (*bodhya*) is directly present; for, by its very nature as an object of cognition, it is like fire which burns both the fuel and the burner. Yet, even while being made an object of cognition, it was not itself awakened.
"That [name] is the vital breath (prāṇa), the enjoyer; therefore, it is established as its own name because of the lack of awakening to it."
The meaning is this:
you admit that even in the state prior to awakening, there is the specific quality of being non-sleeping.

Therefore, when one whose vital breath (*prāṇa*) has fallen asleep does not perceive nearby sounds, no cause other than its being non-self (*anātmatva*) can be imagined; for if it were otherwise, it would be perceived by the whole self. Thus, the vital breath is non-self. [Objection: But surely this "non-perception" refers to the non-perception of a relationship.
He states that the basis [of the misconception] is not the basis of selfhood:

"If it is argued that [the deity] did not perceive [it] because of the failure to grasp the connection with its own specific name, he says that such a failure to grasp the connection with the deity is impossible; thus, there can be no doubt regarding the non-grasping."

He says that the fault of being non-self (*anātmatva*), which arises because [the self] is not grasped as being distinct from everything else, applies equally even to the self intended by you; he states this in response to the objection:
"If the fault is equal in your position too because of non-apprehension. He then says that it is not equal.
It is not so, because of the conceit of totality regarding that which lacks the "I-sense" in a single part; he elaborates this very point by way of an illustration:
"Upon the utterance of the designation 'finger' and so forth, [the child] awakens because of its being placed [therein]."

"One who possesses the identification with the entire body alone does not experience the identification with a single part. This is the meaning: just as when "the finger" is mentioned, Devadatta does not rise [from his seat], because he possesses the identification with the whole body; likewise, because [Kāśī] possesses the identification with the totality of the body and its instruments (karaṇa), it is intended as Kāśī.

215) Because there is no sense of identification (*abhimāna*) with the mere vital breath (*prāṇa*), which stands in the place of the thumb for one who regards it as the Self, its name is not mentioned; it is not, however, because it is non-Self. [Objection: But the moon is but a single part of the vital breath.

Therefore, having raised the objection that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not grasped by being addressed with those names because it is not the Self, [the author replies] that the vital breath is present everywhere among all things, like "cowness" (*gotva*), and thus it is not excluded in each respective instance.

He states that non-apprehension is untenable because the conceit "I am" arises: "But because the vital breath (prāṇa) is fully present in all things both collectively and individually, one who possesses a self would not be without consciousness, owing to his identification with everything. This is because it has been stated that there would be no lack of consciousness.

In this regard, the following objection is raised: "If you do not admit a real relationship between the self and the non-self, nor a real relationship with knowledge, and [if] the states of agency and so forth are merely adventitious, then the self as intended by you cannot be established. To this, he replies:
"Awakening and non-awakening are not appropriate for [the Self], because it consists solely of immutable consciousness.
Now, one might ask: "If it is self-luminous, how can its knowledge be dependent on another? To this he replies:
"By means of awakening dependent on another," referring to this Self's eyes and other [senses].
The meaning is that [the self] possesses knowledge dependent upon instruments. Now, [an objection is raised]: "Is it not that very [self] which is the primary Self? To this he replies:
"From the vessel of water...
The phrase "as another" means that just as the primary sun is distinct from the reflection of the sun in water, so too,

due to the absence of sentience [in the former], the immutable consciousness (kūṭasthabodha) is distinct. Having thus resolved an objection arising incidentally, he now raises an objection regarding the subject at hand.
Just as you yourself have observed that there is no awakening even by one's own name when [the body] is not conscious,
so too is there no awakening from the vital breaths despite the existence of an enjoyer.
Just as Devadatta is conscious as a self, yet the self intended by you does not awaken even when addressed by its own names in this manner.

"Sometimes it does not arise. Thus, he addresses this objection—that the enjoyer, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), likewise does not arise—by stating that because the logic of the distinction between "asleep" and "sleeping" is possible, the apprehension of the sevenfold [breath] is indeed appropriate, whereas it is not fitting for one who is not sevenfold; this is the meaning of "remember what has been said."

Now, one might object that the sense organs do not grasp their own names because they are composite entities, and not because they are non-self; anticipating this, he states that the very composition of the sense organs is untenable if the vital breath (prāṇa) is the self: He says: [the following].

Because the ear and other senses are subordinate members, they always remain awake when that [prāṇa] is awake, and they sleep when it sleeps, being under its control. The senses would not possess their own independent power if they were not recipients of the gift of life from prāṇa; for when the ministers lie down, the king suffers distress within himself.
"[They] wake up" (p.
Now, [one might object]: since these are names not well-known as names for the vital breath (*prāṇa*), how can they be used?
Because they have been awakened, there is no further arousal [of the senses], since they are not of a manifold nature; thus he says:

"If it is argued that there is no awakening because of the mention of names whose self-designations are unestablished," he states the purpose of addressing [the senses] by the names of deities: because it is for the sake of negating the [independent] selfhood of the deities.

"The grasping of that [name] is meaningful"—this he elaborates: "The non-enjoyership of the vital breath (prāṇa) is established even from the non-grasping of its own name; it is understood that [the names] are for the purpose of excluding the deities, by means of the names of the moon. The meaning is this: the principal vital breath, which possesses fivefold functions, is not [the enjoyer].
Thus, although he was addressed by his own name in this manner and so forth, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) did not rise up.

Therefore, the addressing by means of the names of the deities is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that the lunar deity (*candradevatā*) is the agent and the enjoyer in this body. Such is the case with the vital breath.
Having refuted the selfhood of the soul and having refuted the selfhood of the senses,

he refutes the selfhood of the senses by means of the reasons— namely, the impossibility of the connection between memory, cognition, desire, and so forth, and [the senses]— and [establishes their] non-experiencer-status.

"It is not accepted here [that the self consists of] parts, as in the case of the [parts of a] whole. Since memory, desire, recognition, fatigue, and so forth would be impossible if the eleven sense organs were each a separate self, the sense organs do not constitute the self.

Furthermore, because the collection of instruments is insentient, it lacks the nature of a self; thus he says: "Since that which has been so described is non-conscious, how could there be the possibility of its being an enjoyer? He demonstrates its insentience as follows:

Because that which is other than consciousness (cit) is an object of enjoyment, there is no state of being an enjoyer for anything else; or rather, he says "that which is other than consciousness" because it is also invisible, and thus not an enjoyer—
this is for the purpose of refuting the life-force (prāṇa) as the Self, and because [the life-force] is swallowed by the deity.
He states that the selfhood of the instruments has been refuted:

"By the logic of the 'stick and cake' (daṇḍāpūpika), the instruments are indeed non-enjoyers. Now, even though the moon-deity, who is the cause of the vital breath, is a non-enjoyer, [what of] another deity?

Anticipating the objection that there is a "consumer" (bhoktṛ) in this body, he states that no deity exists apart from the vital breath (*prāṇa*): "And no other deity is possible apart from the *prāṇa*. Now, one might object: "But was it not stated previously that there is a distinction regarding deities, such as 'the *prāṇa* and so forth'? [The answer follows: That...
How it is warded off is easily understood.

He says that it is not so because that [breath] is merely the vital force (*prāṇa*), for there is no single vital force for all of them due to their unity; this is established through such analogies as the spokes and the hub, and likewise by the predominance of air (*vāyu*).

Having refuted the selfhood of the vital breaths, the senses, and the deities, [the author] now presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) in order to refute the selfhood of the gross body as well (p.

"Let the aggregate alone be the enjoyer, because it is connected with direct perception; however, there can be no eternal enjoyer distinct from that [aggregate], because such a thing is impossible. [The opponent argues: "The body, which is a collection of the four elements, is indeed the enjoyer, because it is perceived through direct perception in such ways as 'I am fair,' 'I see,' and 'I hear.'"
He establishes the final conclusion— that there is no lack of knowerhood for that which is distinct from [the body], because there is perception of the knowerhood of objects such as sound—
by stating: "The state of being an enjoyer (bhoktṛtva) cannot in any way be conceived for that which is insentient."
If it is argued that its lack of consciousness is unproven, he says in response: "Because that which is other than consciousness is an object of enjoyment, like a blanket, rice, or water.
The meaning is that the body cannot be the Self because it is visible and therefore lacks consciousness. Furthermore, the body is not the Self even when qualified by consciousness.
The admission that [the self] is the enjoyer is precisely that. In this regard, there must be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);

if it is argued that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is such a means, he says "no," for the state of being qualified by consciousness (*cidviśiṣṭatva*) cannot be established through perception. He states that this is because consciousness is unfit for perception—let it be so.

If it is argued that the body itself is the perceiver of that excellence in speech which is perceptible, or perhaps something other than the body— [we reply] no, because it is impossible for a single entity to be both the object perceived and the perceiver; therefore, [the opponent] asserts that there is no knower.

Furthermore, he states that because consciousness is not self-luminous when apart from [the self], the body and so forth cannot be the Self: "Moreover, for the sake of perceiving the connection with consciousness, one must postulate a knower of that [consciousness].
220) Thus, since consciousness is not self-manifesting when it is other than [the Self], the body and so forth do not possess the nature of the Self.

Here, nothing whatsoever is accepted as having its own independent object apart from consciousness (cit), nor does anything become the recipient of the fruit of a means of knowledge apart from its own object; moreover, when the connection with consciousness is known, then consciousness itself must also be known— therefore, [the fruit arises] from the knower of consciousness.
Let it be said: there is no difference between consciousnesses (*cid*), because a distinction between consciousnesses is unestablished.
If it is argued that there is non-consciousness (*acit*) therein, [we reply] that no object of knowledge (*prameya*) consisting of non-consciousness is ever perceived;
this means that such a thing is never observed. Furthermore, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is consciousness, and the grasper is consciousness.

At the time of grasping the relationship [between word and object], it must be stated whether that [object] is insentient or non-insentient. It cannot first be non-insentient, because one non-insentient thing cannot be established by another non-insentient thing, as they are equal [in this regard], like two lamps. If it is insentient, he says: "Nor is it experience..."

[The opponent argues: "Perception depends on something else because it is insentient (*jaḍa*). Indeed, nothing other than [the object] such as a jar is observed or logically possible as the establisher of that which is insentient; for it is insentient.
Furthermore, according to your view, perception has the body as its agent; in that case as well, a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) must be stated.

First of all, perception is not a means of valid cognition because its object consists of things possessing form and so forth; nor is it established by inference that "perception is my means of valid cognition," for he says: "And perception is not admitted [to exist] when perception arises from the body."
Furthermore, since the inferential mark (*liṅga*) lacks validity, how could there be anything established by direct perception? Moreover,
for the Cārvāka, a retrospective reflection such as "this was known by me" cannot be established.

He says, "due to the absence of a prover," meaning that when there is a connection with another object, perception is restricted to the body; thus, no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is accepted for the establishment of a unifying consciousness (*anusandhāna*). The meaning is: just as perception is not a means of knowledge [for such a consciousness] because the body is its agent, so it is here.

"Another object" refers to the objects such as sound and so forth; that perception which has a connection with those is "connected with another object. And that [perception] is "situated in the body," meaning it is dependent upon the body.
This is what is meant: perception, being dependent upon the body, [operates] with respect to objects such as sound and so forth.

This [self] is your authority. This being so, the synthesis "this has been known by me" is not established by that perception, because its objects are sound and the like; nor is any other means of knowledge possible whose object would be that [synthesis]. Alternatively, the synthesis is "I am he."

That unity which is to be grasped by recognition is not established; for if perception residing in the body has sound and so forth as its objects, and thus possesses authority only with respect to sound and so forth, then—surely, just as that perception is authoritative regarding its own object, it must likewise be authoritative regarding its own substratum, like a lamp. Therefore:

The subsequent perception, accompanied by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the initial perception, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the identity [expressed as] "that is I" (p.
If it is true that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*)—

since they are not perceptible due to being devoid of form and the like, nor are they established by inference and other means— then the synthesis "I am he" is not established because there is a lack of evidence for the impression; and likewise, the synthesis of objects is not [established].
To establish that inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) against the Cārvāka, he argues as follows:

This utterance of speech by one who denies the validity of inference would be purposeless—whether it be the construction of a subsequent [meaning] based on what is not perceived, or like the utterance of the sentence "Bring the cow"—if it were not connected to a [logical] postulation (*parakalpanā*). At the conclusion of such an utterance, [the meaning is understood].

For what purpose [is it]? First, it is not for the sake of one's own conviction, for no one acquires anything previously unknown from the meaning of a statement composed by oneself. Nor is it for the sake of another’s conviction, in the sense that another’s conviction regarding the meaning of this statement arises; this is not established by direct perception.
If [the opponent argues] that "from this inference, my knowledge has indeed arisen from a sentence uttered by another, and likewise, knowledge will arise for others from my sentence," then,
if that is so, the utterance of the sentence would be useless. Furthermore:
He states that while this treatise is composed for the benefit of living beings, the composition of other logicians' treatises is for the detriment of living beings:
"Even if one conforms to the view of one's own self, only delusion results."
Because of his reputation among virtuous people, no one would wish to give anything to him; thus,
due to the absence of fear regarding unrighteousness and other such things, they would seize him without hesitation out of anger.
"Forcefully, he says that the fruit belongs to this [body]"; this states another reason for the fact that the previously mentioned body of the manifest world is not the Self:
"Because a distinction is observed upon inspection, the aggregate of the body is not the enjoyer."
If it were imagined here that the mere aggregate is the experiencer of the fruits of pleasure and pain,
then because the aggregate remains unchanged, there would never be even a slight alleviation of suffering.

Regarding the observation of the fruit immediately upon contact, as well as [the observation] in that same manner—this half-verse of the *Vārttika* addresses the following doubt: even if the self is distinct from the body, this specific [phenomenon] would not be possible; having raised this objection, he provides the answer.

For that proponent for whom the enjoyer is of a different class from the objects of enjoyment and so forth, it would be consistent because of the multiplicity of connections with causes such as merit (*dharma*) and the like; what is that [proponent]? To this he says: "The distinction would arise from the sensation produced by grinding or not grinding. This is the meaning.

Due to the causes that are the latencies (vāsanā) of merit and demerit, there is a manifold connection for the self, as well as its connection with the body produced thereby; therefore, arising caused by those [latencies] is entirely logical.
Furthermore, because the visible causes for arising are manifold, there is arising.
He says that a distinction is possible: "When there are causes for pleasure, sound, and so forth,
it is entirely logical that there should then be this specific awakening of them as superior, inferior, or middling."

[Objection: Surely every person rises from mere slight contact with the state of being "all" (the universal); therefore, the existence of a self distinct from the body is not established. To this, he says: There is indeed this distinction here, that while one is merely touched [by the breath], yet remaining unconscious, one has fallen asleep and will continue to sleep.
Regarding the phrase "awakened" (*bodhita*): he who has arisen from the state of being enveloped (*āveṣa*) is the Self (*ātman*.

This is because it is understood that he who has emerged from the envelopment along with the instruments (*karaṇas*)—like a king together with his ministers—is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). The subsequent [portion] is an elaboration of this.
The two Vārtikas state:
"He who remains liberated as if placing this corpse-like body within his own consciousness,
yet distinguishes it by means of knowledge and virtues— such as anger, greed, fear, and agitation— he should be understood as the enjoyer."

"Let it be determined that he who possesses the body is the liberated one, and he is the enjoyer. Having thus established that the body and so forth are not the Self, [the author] further proves that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not the Self by means of the reason of being for the sake of another: "Moreover, the vital breath is for the sake of another because it is a composite."
Therefore, like a house or similar objects, it is not logical for that which has the nature of being an object of enjoyment to possess the status of an enjoyer;
thus, "being composed of parts" (*saṃhatatva*) has been stated as the reason for its being for the sake of another (*parārthatva*).
To the objection that this is unproven, he says:
"The vital breath (prāṇa) residing within the body always supports the body like a pillar;
it is conjoined with the body just as air is. For it is thus conjoined.
Therefore, he says that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) exists for the sake of another, just like a house and so forth:

"Since this is so, the vital breath is accepted here as being like a house and so forth. He further states that the Self, for whose sake the vital breath and the aggregate are primary, is distinct from them: "And the bodies..."
Fearing that the self whose nature is *dharma* might be experienced as something belonging to the body's attributes— just like bedding, seating, and so forth—

and thus that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) would be for the sake of another through its being a composite, he says: "Because it is a composite, like a house [which has a distinct fruit] from its own parts, its constituents, and things of the same class."

Just as a wise man, acting for the sake of his own enjoyment, moves from one house to another—from a part of a house to another house—so too the vital breath (prāṇa), because it is composite, is the means of enjoyment for that which is non-composite; its "house" is the fruit, the object of experience. Now, even if this is so...

A house is a means of enjoyment for one who is not a composite being; nevertheless, Devadatta is indeed a composite being because he possesses a head, hands, and so forth. Likewise, that for whose sake this aggregate of the body and the subtle body exists must also be a composite being composed of something else.
If it be argued that this is not so, we say no; for [that view] is inconsistent and contradicts scriptural texts such as those concerning the "gross" (sthūla).
Therefore, one must grasp the intended portion by means of an illustration. Thus, he elaborates upon the illustration of the house (sadma):

The meaning is as follows: having observed that which is characterized by birth, increase, decline, and destruction—namely, the phenomena of birth and so forth—and having understood the object of knowledge as being perceived solely within its own sphere, [the author] says "hī" (indeed), signifying its nature as the self-interest (*svārtha*) consisting of *sattva* and the other [guṇas], which is attained independently of [external] factors such as the direction of birth. Here, "one's own birth" (*svajanma*) refers to "one's own people" (*svajana*), by means of the word "own" (*sva*).

The "house" (gṛha) is so called. By the words "birth" (janman) and so forth, its properties (dharmas) are expressed: namely, its own birth (svajanma), growth (upacaya), decay (glāni), destruction (nāśa), name (ākhyā), and form (ākṛti). Birth and the others—growth, decay, destruction, name, and form—are indeed the properties; [thus] its own birth, growth, decay, destruction, name, and form, starting from birth.

Phenomena (dharmas) have acquired their own nature as "sentient beings" and so forth entirely without depending on them; by which [nature], being independent of phenomena, he has acquired that form of his own nature as "sentient beings" and so forth.
Furthermore, what is the characteristic of that [nature]? It is the cognizer who perceives only its object, and it is designated by that term.

By the word "range" (*gocara*), the house and its properties are meant; their sole observer is the "sole observer of that range," and he alone is the knower. Thus, one perceives that the nature of being an object for Devadatta and others belongs precisely to the house and so forth. Now, the application of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*):
He demonstrates this: "of the vital breath" (prāṇasya),
meaning that the reality of the vital breath and its qualities should be understood in that manner.
Let it be understood that the same [nature] applies to the vital breath and the body, as well as to their respective attributes.
The meaning is that the same state [of non-existence] is determined for the vital breath and the body, as well as for their respective attributes.

Thus, through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and other means, the distinctness of the Self from the body and so forth has been established; regarding this, an objection is raised: "But surely, according to the Vedānta doctrine, another entity is accepted?"
The proponent of the previous view establishes the non-existence of any other entity, stating: "Just as the self of the Sāṅkhya is internal, there is only the single reality of the inner self;
thus, by the injunction of the unity of the self, everything imagined by opponents [is sublated]."

Whatever is born of the non-self, such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth—whether it be form, name, or action, and whether imagined or unimagined—all this is accepted as being the Self alone. Therefore, the statement regarding positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is not applicable here, because of their identity. [Objection: But surely, positive and negative concomitance are not possible?

If it is argued that positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) belong to the imagined (kalpita) [nature] rather than the unimagined (akalpita), he says "no": there is neither positive nor negative concomitance for the imagined, because it is unreal (anṛta). If it is then argued that positive and negative concomitance belong to the unimagined through its relation to the imagined, he says "no": there is neither positive nor negative concomitance.
If it is argued that this is not so, [the author] says:
"Because the non-conceptualized is one, it is not established as something other than that"; this refers to the phrase "because of oneness."

The meaning of this is as follows: because of non-duality (*advayatva*), if one were to accept duality, then difference (*bheda*) would have to be accepted as ultimate (*pāramārthika*). Now, he establishes his own position (*siddhānta*):

"Because the primary aim is the instruction of persons (*puṃvyutpatti*), there is no fault in [the use of] positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth. This is the meaning: it is not [the case that...].

The connection [of the Self] is stated by the Śruti by accepting a difference in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), but it is stated by the Śruti as a connection for the sake of self-knowledge by relying on an imagined difference (*kalpitabheda*).
Now, one might object: why state the connection and so forth for the sake of self-knowledge, since the Self is established by that very [connection]?

To the question, "What is the purpose of the statement beginning with 'What is that reality? he replies: "But here, the establishment of the reality of the thing does not occur through positive concomitance (anvaya) and so forth. If it is argued that the self is established by relying on the sentence [itself], then since the self is not established prior to hearing that sentence, how could one perform positive concomitance and the like? For [such operations] can only be performed by means of something already established.

Anticipating the objection that positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) exist for an established entity, just as they do between smoke and fire, he states: "Even though this [world] is imagined through ignorance, it is understood by the world that the enjoyer is one who possesses the means of knowledge in the form of the notion of 'Self'."
Now, one might object: "The Self is not self-luminous; rather, it is established through the establishment of its objects. To this he says, "But not in the non-Self," etc. (p. 229).

Since the term "delusion" refers precisely to the purification of the meaning of the word *tat* through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and other means, he says that the Śruti teaches its identity with Brahman by restating that self which has been established [by that purification]:
"Therefore, having restated [the self] as it is established through the distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)."
"How is it that non-duality and so forth are awakened to through the scripture? To this he says:

"For the persistence of consciousness is observed everywhere within its effects; even its absence [from them] is established here through the negation of the effect—namely, ignorance and its effects."
The pervasion by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) is called the "concomitance" (*anvaya*) of consciousness;

and the persistence of consciousness even when each of the states such as waking and so forth is absent is called its "absence" (*vyatireka*). The meaning here is that these two are not established in the world [in the same way]. Moreover, in the view of monism (*ekātmya*), concomitance and so forth do not exist.
It has been stated that [cognition] arises; regarding this, it is now analyzed: Is the measure (*māna*) the act of measuring (*miti*), or is it the object measured (*meya*)?
In both cases, its impossibility follows. Or, if it is neither measured nor being measured, there is the fault of the impossibility of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth.
Therefore, he says: "In the proof of non-duality (*aikātmya*), there would be a fault. But surely, non-duality is always already measured!
Because it is self-luminous, there would consequently be an absence of constant conjunction (*anvaya*) and so forth; to this he replies:
"And its establishment is not real," meaning that cognition, being of the nature of one's own essence (*svarūpa*), [is not established as such].
The meaning is that it is contradictory to positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth. What, then, is the proof that is contradictory to positive concomitance and the rest?

He says "authoritative" (*prāmāṇikī*), meaning it is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, he concludes that the establishment of its own nature (*svarūpasiddhi*) is not contradictory to that:
"Hence, this is not contradicted. Alternatively, or rather...
It has been stated that the establishment of this [momentary destruction] through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth contradicts our own view;
however, it is now raised as an objection:
"Let there be no further dependence on an already established entity such as a jar; for even by mere perception, this [destruction] is indeed observed."

Regarding the point that validity is not incompatible with the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he says therein: "Nor is there dependence on the operation of a means of knowledge (*māna*) for the ascertainment of identity, because its result is already complete;
therefore, such dependence is fruitless," since the Self is self-luminous and of a single, uniform nature.

The meaning is that because all ignorance residing therein is removed by knowledge arising once and for all, there is no further dependence on a means of valid cognition (*māna*). Now, one might object: since qualities such as self-luminosity (*svayaṃprabhātvatva*) are equally present even prior to the arising of awakening, there should likewise be no dependence on a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) beforehand; to this he replies:

As long as one does not know the non-dual Self directly from scripture, who can prevent that [practice] for the sake of attaining self-knowledge through means such as *anvaya*? Indeed, [it is not prevented],
because [such practice] is a means for the knowledge of the Self.
He says that there is no loss of non-duality:
"Having meditated upon both the Self and that which arises from it, precisely because their true nature was previously unknown. (p. 231)

The meaning is that the world is merely the unknown aspect [of the Self]. Now, if everything is merely the Self, how can its cessation occur through the knowledge of it? To this he says: "Through the awakening to that reality, there is its sublation, like the awakening regarding the snake and the rope. Furthermore, even your permission [to speak] is imagined; how [could it be real]?
"Therefore, there is sublation by the other. To this he replies:
"Just as even among established things, such as a rope, there may be the removal of one established thing through recourse to another imagined thing, so it is here in the case of the Self."
He concludes the result of the investigation:

"Since the internal self is the sole measure and the object of measurement, the enjoyer is distinct from that which is enjoyed; even though the objects of enjoyment vary, the enjoyer alone is not subject to variation. This is the meaning [established] by himself.
The Self is indeed the luminous element of consciousness, whereas the vital breaths and so forth are non-Self because they are objects of perception.
And that [non-Self] is deceptive, like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; the Self, however, is immutable. Having thus concluded this inquiry, he returns to the explanation of the scripture at hand.

Although the vital breath (*prāṇa*) was being diligently awakened by [the mantras] beginning with *bṛhan*, it did not wake up at all; when [the King] then employed another effort, Kāśya, having repeatedly entered the lifeless body, awakened the one who was asleep. Consequently, due to the agitation arising from that entry, he regained consciousness.
232) These two verses are easily understood. Now, one might object: "The self is the agent of rising;
it rises by itself, so what is the need for invocation and the like? To this, he says:
This is the nature of causes: that the production of their own effect occurs by depending on another efficient cause, just as threads [produce] a cloth from the sky.

The meaning is this: although space is not a material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), it nevertheless depends on instrumental causes such as the east wind; likewise, the Self also depends on karma and so forth.
Now, one might object: "Arising" (*utpatti*) refers to the soul's emergence from the state of deep sleep (*supti-sthāna*).

And thus, [there is] equality with a jar; regarding this, he says: "In the production of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, which are dependent [on causes], there is no production of the Supreme Self (*parātman*) in the same way as the space within a jar, because the Seer (*dṛśi*) is eternally [present]. This is an incidental [remark].

Having resolved that objection, he says: he summarizes the relevant meaning of the passage beginning with "a man who has fallen asleep," stating that therefore, due to a lack of awakening, one may generally be called an "enjoyer" (bhoktṛ), whereas through the awakening of that person, his status as an enjoyer is indeed determined. Now, [an objection]: ... [text continues] ... nanu (but surely...)
The status of the vital deity (prāṇadevatā) as an enjoyer is also well-known; how is that so?
To this, he says:
"Just as things that are not themselves burning possess the quality of being burners through the proximity of that which burns."
"The state of being an enjoyer belongs to the divine self (devatātman) by virtue of its conjunction with the enjoyer, just as [fire] possesses [the quality of heat] through conjunction. Thus,
[the text] introduces the interrogative statement "He said" (sa hovāca), preceded by a recapitulation of what has occurred.

Having distinguished the Self as the solitary enjoyer from the body, the senses, the mind, and the intellect, the King then questioned Gārgya; regarding this, it is said: "By means of inquiry, he realized that which is distinct from the vital breaths and the rest; where was this [Self] before awakening?"

And the person has come as a being. Regarding the term "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*), some hold that "consciousness" here refers to the Supreme Brahman and that the living self (*jīva*) is its modification; therefore, they maintain that the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of a modification.
To refute this, he says:

In the case of the connection with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the term *vijñāna* would be a suffix denoting the agent (*kartṛ*) [meaning "that which knows"]; it would have the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).

It would be a derivation denoting the action (*bhāva-sādhana*) when referring to the act itself; it would be a derivation denoting the object (*karman-sādhana*) when there is an intention to express the object of cognition (*prameya-artha*). Since the aforementioned [other senses] do not possess those states, [the term *vijñāna*] is used for the sake of the majority [of cases].

Regarding the phrase "in the inner self" (*pratyagātmani*), this is the meaning: when the word *vijñāna* ending in the *luṭ* suffix is intended to be connected with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and the internal organ is intended to be expressed [as the agent], the suffix would denote the agent because that [internal organ] is the agent of cognition; and consequently—

"It cognizes" (*vijānāti*): consciousness (*vijñāna*) would be the internal organ (*antahkaraṇa*). When the denotative function of the word is intended to refer to the eye and so forth, then that suffix would have the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*). At that time...

That by which one cognizes is "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); it would be the eye and so forth when there is a connection with the activity of cognition. When the activity itself is consciousness, then it is "representation" (*vijñapti*). Thus, consciousness would be the activity.
If it is intended that the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) denotes objects such as a jar, then that which is cognized—
namely, the jar and so forth— would be consciousness; for the word "consciousness" applies to those objects and not elsewhere, except by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as has been stated.

Since [agency] is impossible in Brahman, how can there be such impossibility? Just as [there is no agency] in the case of being the agent of knowledge, Brahman is immutable (*kūṭastha*); for this very reason, it is neither the instrument of action nor the cause of action, and because of the contradiction with scripture stating that it is "immeasurable" (*aprameya*), Brahman is not [measured] through action; nor is it [denoted] here by the word "knowledge."

Therefore, since it is that which is grasped, it is impossible to maintain that the suffix *mayaṭ* here has the sense of a "modification" (*vikāra*). Consequently, "vijñāna" is that by which one discerns— the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)— and "consisting of that" (*tanmaya*) means having that as its primary constituent (*tatprāya*).

Because the inner self (pratyagātman) is accepted as being a modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), the subsequent Vārtikas— which establish that the suffix *mayaṭ* has the sense of "consisting of"— are easy to understand:
"Due to the delusion of pervasion by the intellect and so forth, which arise from ignorance and possess its own reflection..."
Because of the conceit of identifying with that [intellect], the self is characterized as consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*);
because it is perceived as a witness, and because it serves as the substratum for the intellect and other objects of witnessing.
Because it is the fruit of being a non-agent, it is therefore primarily desired;
for, being composed of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), one understands every object through that consciousness.
Therefore, because this [Self] proceeds from the inner witness as the cause of awakening, or because it does not attain anything other than what is distinguished by consciousness.
Therefore, because of the perception of identity with that [Self], the term "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) must be understood in its primary sense;
for after stating "consisting of consciousness," there is the mention of "consisting of earth" and so forth, as well as the negation of the six modifications.
Thus, the primary sense is appropriate. He now explains the meaning of the word *puruṣa*:

Since he is non-conceptual because he completely fulfills all that is non-self through its very state of being conceptualized— just as a rope [fulfills] the snake and so forth perceived within it— is it not the case that he is called "Puruṣa" because he dwells in the city (puri-śayana)? To this, he says:
This very etymological derivation is established here by examining them through the process of exclusion, beginning with "Is it that?
and concluding with the determination "Not this," and so forth.
Thus far, the meaning of the term *vijñāna* (consciousness) and the others has been stated; now, [the meaning of the subsequent terms will be explained].

He says that the connection between the preceding text and the subsequent text is stated by means of the preceding text: "This, first of all, is the statement of the subject matter; now follows the statement of the connection. But why this inversion of the sequence? Because the connection must be explained first.
Because there is no fixed rule for the statement of the meanings of the words and because of the prohibition [of such a rule], he raises a question in order to state the relationship:
236) [He] raises the question for the purpose of stating the relationship—because there is no fixed rule for the explanation of the meaning of the words and because of the prohibition.

Regarding the passage beginning with "praśnasyatvaiṣa," [the author] explains that the purpose of this inquiry—"Where is this? and so forth—is for the sake of attaining the true nature of the Self as distinct from both bodies. Thus he states that the commencement of the discussion with "kvaiṣa" and so on is intended for that purpose.

Some explain the statement of the question as having its sole root in an objection preceded by the presentation of Bhartṛprapañca’s views; others declare it to have arisen for the purpose of attaining the true meaning.
Thus, according to Bhartṛprapañca, both the question and the answer are as follows:

He demonstrates how it has been explained by showing the manner in which it was explained there. First, he shows the statement of the question as it was explained by them: "Insofar as the self is of the nature of consciousness and the instruments exist as the means for knowledge, this being so prior to liberation..."

How is this [knowledge] occasional? Is this knowledge of the self and non-self due to having gone elsewhere upon abandoning the limitation of the body, or is it because it has perished during the time of sleep? If it is the position that it has gone elsewhere, then the cause for its return must also be stated.

"But surely all of this should have been asked by Gārgya himself, since he had accepted the status of being a disciple; why did he not ask? [The author] replies: "It is true that this ought to have been asked by Gārgya because of his status as a disciple, yet he did not urge it. But surely...
Because he did not understand how the question was formulated, [the opponent] said:
"The King asked why the questioning had ceased"; to that, [the author] replies: "Neither of these two is so for us."
The meaning is that because he has personally accepted [the goal] through his awakening, he has effectively promised it as "his own.

Now, one might ask: even if it was promised, let it be abandoned; what is the fault? To this he replies: "A man who, having promised wealth to a seeker, does not fulfill it, is not truly a man"—this is the truth.

Having thus explained the king’s intention in asking his own question instead of Gārgya’s— namely, that it was the "vow of the person" (puruṣavrata)— he resumes the explanation of the very question at hand according to the view of Bhartṛprapañca: "His consciousness is immutable."

If you argue that this meaning is as follows—that the Self is the immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-bodha*) and not an occasional cognition, and therefore it neither goes nor perishes—then [the author] says that this contradicts experience: "How could it be occasional? You are asserting something that contradicts such experiences as "I was unaware of anything."

This is the meaning. He states that this fault does not apply if consciousness is impermanent: "If consciousness were impermanent, how could it be occasional? How then would it be meaningful? This is the meaning of that [verse]:
it is not tenable that occasional knowledge belongs to the Self.
Thus it was said [regarding] this person (p.
"In this very way, he then became such," and so forth, is the interrogative statement.
He demonstrates how Bhartṛprapañca explained [the text] by way of objections,
and how he explained the words of the response as having a specific intention, serving as the answer to those objections: [The following passage continues...]

"His identification with the body and so forth is occasional and has a cause; his state of being the witness is eternal and without cause. This is the meaning: the Self is indeed eternally unchanging because it is the witness of the intellect and other faculties; nevertheless, for one situated in the body, cognition occurs only occasionally.
The characteristic of identifying with the body and so forth is thus established. [Ignorance] becomes awakened in order to yield the fruits of merit (*dharma*) and the like;

consequently, there arises the identification of the Self with the body and so forth. When it is not awakened, why is it that the eternally conscious nature of the Self and its occasional consciousness are both possible?
[Objection: "But even if it is produced by causes, why does the identification with the body not occur constantly, since the cause is always present? To this, he says:
"Because this very thing—namely, the coming into being after having not existed—occurs for those things that depend upon causes."
Therefore, the argument that "occasional occurrence is not a fault" is now refuted by the two subsequent verses of the Vārttika.
Since [the answer] arose from and returned to the inner self (pratyagātman), just as it was directed toward the west,
there is no redundancy in the response because it is contrary to the meaning of the question.

The meaning is that your explanation— that since the means for movement and so forth reside only in the body, how could there be movement to another body for the person, and yet its destruction is not logical— is not consistent with the wording of the question. This begins from the words "the conceit regarding the body and so forth."
Some maintain that this is precisely the refutation of Bhartṛprapañca’s commentary;

having thus dispelled Bhartṛprapañca’s commentary, he elaborates upon the doctrine of the Blessed One (the Vedāntin), which was briefly indicated by the phrase "for the sake of attaining the true nature," through four Vārtikas.
It is explained in due order.

Because the direct realization of Brahman has been promised as the goal, it is therefore appropriate to explain immediately the true nature of the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment. This is easily understood;
what, then, is the essential nature of the enjoyer, and what is that of the object of enjoyment? Having thus distinguished both of these—

He demonstrates that form (*rūpa*) arises from causes such as karma and is not the ultimate reality (*atatva*); because it follows upon that [cause], it is non-causal (*animitta*) in itself, since it is always subject to deviation. Thus, form is an effect of an action performed by a non-agent.
Everything up to ignorance (*avidyā*) is an object of experience (*bhogya*), because it does not persist during deep sleep; whereas consciousness (*caitanya*) is non-deviating.
The meaning is that the nature of the Self is distinct from action, its factors, and their results.
Such a nature [is present] in the state of deep sleep.

He says that it is intended to be awakened: "Prior to awakening, [the Self] is to be easily awakened for the enjoyer who exists within this sphere of experience. If it is argued that there is no logical connection (*ananvaya*) and that [the premise] is unestablished (*asiddha*), he says "no," because prior to awakening, not even the slightest effect such as action (*karman*) is perceived in the inner witness (*pratīc*).

Regarding the phrase "from pride": since this is so, he concludes that the immutable one, whose very nature is non-dual consciousness, is indeed the Self; thus he says, "Therefore, this [Self] is by its own nature that."
Having thus described the meaning intended by the venerable Bhagavatpāda regarding the subsequent portion of the text, he begins the word-by-word commentary:
"Where was this [self] prior to awakening, and from where has it come? Explain these two."
"O Gārgya, [is it] established in speech, or [is there] a limit? Thus he reveals the intention of the questioner:
"If this [Self] were other than the inward one, or if it had come from this [world], then it would possess the nature of an agent."

It might be argued: "This cannot be an illusion, because [the self] remains in its own true nature during sleep and returns from there. If that were so, then he states the proof for the illusory nature of the conventional usage of action, agent, and result, as opposed to the non-illusory nature of the other, in the passage beginning with "yatra vā" (or where).
"Whereas [the state] is otherwise, there is another [state expressed by] 'But when for him'"; such is the effect of ignorance and knowledge, and thus the Śruti has declared.
Since the child was unable to speak or ask, the King of Kāśī himself proceeded to explain the meaning of the two questions; for even though he had been asked, [the child] did not...
"This which has been understood by you, I shall now declare; you ought to hear it correctly according to reality.
Regarding that wherein he was asleep and did not hear the sound of his own name being called—listen to this cause for the sake of knowing that cause."

These three *vārtikas* are easy to understand. The meaning of the phrase "the cause of which" (*yannimittam*) is as follows: the cause for the absence of specific cognition is the abiding in Brahman through the withdrawal of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
He states the intended meaning of the use of the genitive case in the word "of these" (*eṣām*):

Since a variety [of forms] is observed within the domains of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), this genitive case is employed by the scripture in the form "this belongs to them" (*tad eṣām*).

Furthermore, there is another [characteristic]: the conformity with their cause, which is the manifestation of internal consciousness; thus, those whose nature is the instruments (the senses) have conquered the external objects.
Among the categories of objects beginning with intellect (*buddhi*) and ending with vital breath (*prāṇa*), three categories are understood.

The meaning is that the use of the genitive case is intended by way of specific intention; that is, the three categories perceived among the objects such as intellect and so forth are [indicated] by means of the genitive of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*).

The phrase "it is being pointed out for these" refers to the application (*viniyoga*) of the aforementioned categories; beginning with the words "the exhaustion of karma while waking," the author will now demonstrate this [on page 242].
By means of the previous commentaries, he shows that this transmigratory existence has karma and other factors as its cause.
In order to establish that upon the exhaustion of karma and the rest, it abides in its own essential nature during deep sleep, he first demonstrates that it is caused by karma:
Since the entire range of effects beginning with the intellect arises from the manifestation of the person's karma,

the projection and withdrawal of the intellect and so forth are therefore dependent upon karma; thus, his transmigratory existence is caused not only by karma, but also by the practice of the semblance of knowledge.
He says that it must be cultivated:

"The supreme subject and agent, which illuminates its own self and is caused by the knowledge of the Self, is indeed called the 'supreme enjoyer' and 'agent' because it is not distinguished from duality. Thus it has been stated that through the destruction of karma comes the destruction of saṃsāra.
He elaborates on that:
when the karma of one who employs [it] for the sake of the fruit of waking is abandoned due to the absence of the state of emergence, then the agent is said to be "desirous of deep sleep."
He demonstrates that the states of being an enjoyer and so forth are mutually causal:
"Prior to knowledge, in order to establish the non-interruption of saṃsāra, agency is prompted by the enjoyer;
action is prompted by the agent; and from that, enjoyment is prompted by action."

This person, conditioned by the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) such as pleasure and pain arising from those [past] formative forces, and impelled by attachment, aversion, and so forth, proceeds further from that state. (p.
He states the result— the mutual relationship of cause and effect among the enjoyer and so forth— following that restatement:
"And this mutual state of being an effect, as well as the state of being a cause, belongs to these [very same factors]."
"Therefore, prior to awakening, this self possesses unextinguished latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
To what does this state of having unextinguished latent impressions lead? He says:
"Established within the wheel of false cognition, this yogi remains connected with ignorance from the level of Brahmā down to a post."
"The Supreme wanders incessantly. Thus has saṃsāra been described.
Now, he shows the distinct application of the entities indicated by the sixth case:
"Upon the exhaustion of karma while waking, this [self], having taken up all latent impressions (bhāvanā), being of unawakened nature..."
The "being" (*bhūta*), consisting of the mind (*manas*) and so forth, which arises from the nature of the substrate (*ādhi*), is called the "agent of giving.
By the word "having taken" (*ādāya*), the agent of the gift is designated; this is how it connects.
That it is indicated as the instrument by the term "by means of consciousness" (*vijñānena*) refers to its status as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Consciousness (*vijñāna*), having arisen from that which is of the nature of the unawakened self (*asaṃbuddhātman*) in the form of the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and so forth, and being born from the nature of desire (*āśā*), is designated as "the instrument of the appearance of grasping" (*ādānasyābhāsaṃ karaṇam*); this is the meaning.
Some say it is the agent (*kartṛ*). Having analyzed the statement using the suffix *-lyap*, he shows the agent: "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*).

"The one who brings about the end of existence is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña)"—this means that the instrument is a reflection, and thus it is the "reflective agent"; [it is] the consciousness which has become the object of appropriation.

Regarding the statement "designated by the word *rañjana*," he says that it is the capacity of the senses to grasp their respective objects; here, the capacity of speech and the other [organs] directed toward their objects is to be understood as consciousness (*vijñāna*), as well as that of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "the acquisition of objects": by the word *bhāvanā* as well, that very thing is expressed— the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), having taken up the capacity of the senses to grasp objects,
effects the manifestation of consciousness (*caitanyābhāsa*) and thus follows the causal process within the space of the unknown Brahman.
One meaning has been stated for this [word] as "it lies within that which is denoted by sound";
now he states another meaning: "the powers (śaktayaḥ) are understood here as the instruments (karaṇāni)."

But when grasped as the ultimate reality through its causal nature, it has a form non-different from its own manifestation; this is one meaning. It is said that the objects and the instruments are grasped by the self in the form of knowledge accompanied by manifestation, and thus the Supreme itself appears as grasped. Regarding this, he states the proof:

How does the Śruti, in the Saṃvarga-vidyā, state the withdrawal of speech, fire, and the other elements into the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa-vāyu), and not by any other means? Furthermore, on account of what commonality is it said that "everything is established in prāṇa"?
And from the statement regarding the binding of the vital breath (*prāṇabandhana*), it is said that "this sūtra is as previously described"; thus he explains the meaning of the word *ādāna*:
"The conjunction of the manifested effect with its causal self."

"Here, the taking up of speech and so forth occurs, just as [the taking up] of bubbles by water"— thus the third case ending was explained as denoting the instrument (*karaṇa*). Now, he states another meaning:
Or, this instrumental case in "by consciousness" (*vijñānena*) expresses accompaniment;

that is to say, the withdrawal of speech and the other organs occurs together with the knowing subject (*pramātṛ*). Thus, the meaning is that there is a withdrawal of the instruments (*karaṇa*) along with the subject. Alternatively, it means [withdrawal] together with the cognition of objects (*viṣaya-jñāna*).
Furthermore, he states another meaning for the third [instrument]:

"Or rather, let the third [instrument] be thus; that is, when it expresses the sense of 'being in such a state,' it is the synthesis of cause and effect by means of the nature of direct cognition, which is the very form of experience."
The meaning is the dissolution of the world together with its causes. He explains the meaning of the word [“this”]:
“He who is called ‘this’ is perceived as having no other form. Being self-luminous...
The meaning is that this object denoted by the word (*padārtha*) is being described as something directly perceived (*pratyak*). Some say it is the referent of the word "Thou" (*tvam-artha*).

For the purpose of attaining the identity of that referent of the word "That" (*tat-padārtha*) with the referent of the word "Thou," there is the mention of the interior of the heart; thus, for the sake of direct perception (*pratyak*), the heart is indeed designated as the limit of the location.
The meaning is that by stating "even of Brahman," oneness is established.
To facilitate the knowledge of this oneness, he demonstrates the discrimination of the referent of the term *tvaṃ* (the "thou").
"Having drawn your mind away with diligence even from the levels of objects of knowledge,

look directly at the Self with an inward-turned vision; thus, having discriminated the Self from the categories of the ego-identification with the body and so forth, perceive the Self as the witness of all cognitions and of that very cognition."
The meaning is that one should know [this] through the vision of discernment (*viveka*). He demonstrates the method for discerning the categories of reality (*padārtha*):
"This notion of a self in men..."
It will be stated that [the term] "in the non-self-cognitions" refers to the inner Self (*pratyagātman*) among those that are non-deviating.

Consciousness (*caitanya*) is the cognition of the Self; that is non-deviating and immutable (*kūṭastha*), whereas other cognitions of the non-self are deviating along with their objects—such is the definition.

The meaning is the purification of the categories of existence (*padārtha*). Now, an objection is raised: if the vision of one's own true nature (*svarūpa-dṛṣṭi*) is immutable (*kūṭastha*), how can there be the appearance of agency and so forth therein? To this he replies:
"Even though it is of the nature of the intellect (*buddhi*), it appears as such due to the delusion of knowing external objects."
"It appears as if being mixed up for those whose self is afflicted by darkness.
Here, "Buddhātman" refers to the Self that is awakened; its "light" (ābhā) is the vision that constitutes its very nature.
Although that vision is immutable (*kūṭasthā*), it is the cognition of external objects.

Due to delusion—specifically, the delusion that the body and so forth, which are not the self, are the self—the intellect appears as if it were being conflated with them, appearing as if it possessed attributes such as agency; thus he says:
"The intellect, though formless, [appears] as if possessing form."
p.
247) Others [hold this view]. He states the result of the fact that agency and so forth are produced by ignorance:

"When the effect has been entirely burnt away and the cause [likewise destroyed] by the knowledge of the Self, one perceives the Self as having the nature of the 'not-yet-arisen' (apūrva) and so forth."

"Let it be determined within the Self alone"—thus has the discrimination of the referent of the word *tvam* been shown for the sake of realizing oneness. Now, he says that by means of the words "taking up" (*ādāya*) and "space" (*ākāśa*), the state of identity (*aikātmya*) is being established. How so? By taking up [the Self] again and again.

The meaning of "taking" (*ādāya*) is stated as the "knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*), because ignorance is destroyed here through the direct revelation of the identity of the knower of the field and the Lord (*īśvara*).

The meaning of "space" (*ākāśa*) is the "Lord" (*tad-artha*); the meaning is that the identity of these two is expressed by the word "lies" (*śete*). He says that the "heart" (*hṛdaya*) is the internal organ (*antaḥ-karaṇa*).

If it is asked why the intellect (*buddhi*) is designated here by the word "heart" (*hṛdaya*) in its entirety, he says: "For the sake of realizing the identity of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
To establish what kind of identity is intended between the two, he provides an illustration.

Just as when "the space within a jar" and "the great space" are mentioned, there arises a single cognition, so it is here as well; it is stated thus so that there may be direct realization. Now, one might object: "Does not the word 'space' here refer to the elemental space (bhūtākāśa)? To this he says: no.
"Since no object other than the inner conscious Self (pratyak) can be conceived within the intellect (buddhi),
therefore the inner Self is denoted by the word 'ether' (ākāśa). In this regard, [the word] "ether"...
Having drawn back [the subject] by means of the word "Self" (ātman) as previously stated, and because the origin of the world is heard [to proceed] from that,
he says that the word "ether" (ākāśa) refers to the Supreme: "Since the birth of breath and the rest will be declared [from Him]."
Therefore, because of the inner self (pratyagātman), Brahman alone is denoted here by the word "ether" (ākāśa).
Furthermore, on the basis of another scriptural passage, he states that Brahman alone is expressed by the word "ether," citing the Śruti:
"For indeed, O Somya, that which is called 'ether' is Being. Thus, Brahman is beyond the ether.

"No other space is grasped here"—thus he explains the meaning of the word *śayana* (reclining): "In this immutable [Self], which is by nature the form of self-awareness, that which rests (*śete*)—meaning, that which lies down (*śete*)—is called the enjoyer who has completely ceased [from activity] as an agent. Thus.
He states that the example of the prince and others also fits if the word "lying down" has this meaning:
"And the example of the prince and so forth likewise fits directly and clearly."

"Because it consists of pure consciousness alone. Now, [an objection is raised]: "But sleep is slumber; is it not so? He replies: "But sleep is not appropriate here," meaning this is due to the force of the reasons already stated.
He introduces the passage beginning with "tārkikāṇām" (of the logicians) preceded by a doubt.
When this [self] exists having abandoned its presiding over the body and so forth, then it abides in itself alone; why is this? Because [the scripture says] "he sleeps."
p.

249) Thus [it is said]. And he states that this sentence is for the purpose of accumulating reasons: "For this reason as well, this person, abiding in the inner self and not elsewhere, sleeps while in deep sleep (suṣupta), because of the scriptural statement 'he sleeps'."

"This is what is being stated": the meaning is that Brahman is grasped by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) and because of the word "sleeps. Having thus demonstrated the defects in his own commentary on the passage beginning with "tandoṣām," he shows the interpretation of Bhartṛprapañca.
In order to refute this, they explain it thus:

having taken up the knowledge of speech and the other organs which has spread out as the cognition of the intellect (*buddhi-vijñāna*), that which lies within the heart when [the body] has arisen is [the self];
or rather, having taken up the knowledge of the instruments such as speech through the intellect, [it resides] in the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) delimited by the lotus-heart.
They explain [it thus]: the meaning is that, being amazed by their own commentary, they consider our commentary to be flawed. He shows the sequence of the summary:
"In deep sleep, the Self, by means of the mind alone, withdraws the vital breaths along with its own powers into the mind itself."

The meaning is that even the mind dissolves into the Self; thus, at the time of sleep, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) withdraws the senses into the form of the mind, and the mind, in turn, withdraws itself into the Self alone.
To the question, "How does one whose instruments [the senses] have been thus withdrawn perceive dreams?", he says:
When the collection of sense organs has dissolved and the self is endowed with the cultivation of the intellect,
it issues forth from the space within the heart through the channels and experiences the dream state.
"The consciousness of mind, speech, and so forth constitutes the body, which is designated as the instrument. This is the meaning:
during the waking state, the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) possesses a body composed of the consciousness of mind, speech, and so forth;
at the time of sleep, there is a withdrawal of the activity of all the senses, yet it remains joined with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the waking state.

Having emerged from the space of the heart through the gateway of the channels, one experiences dreams by means of the intellect (buddhi) known as the instrument (karaṇa), that is, by means of consciousness (vijñāna). When the word "consciousness" (vijñāna) is intended to denote the agent, it refers to the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
When the absence [of an object] is intended to be expressed, then it would be "other" (apara); this is what he states by saying "he cognizes.
[The rule] "when the action resides in the agent and is other [than the agent], it is derived from the root in the sense of an abstract state" applies here. Now, one might object:
at the time of sleep, the reclining of the self is necessarily within the very space delimited by the region of the heart.
To the question, "Why does the Śruti say that one should leave the space delimited by the interior of the body? he states the intended meaning there:
"The manifestation of light which belongs to the ignorant person, being followed by its attributes, rises up."

Therefore, they know [it] as the dissolution of the specific modifications (vṛtti-viśeṣa). The meaning is that since the consciousness of the Self (ātman-caitanya) becomes directed toward objects such as sound by means of the heart, the dharmas, and the channels (nāḍī), its "lying" is said to be within the space delimited by those [modifications]. This refers to the phrase "by means of the knowledge of speech and so forth."

"Having completely withdrawn from the heart-space (hṛdayāmbare) all conceptual proliferation (prapañca)— that is, the knowledge directed toward its own objects such as speech and so forth— the ignorant one sleeps with the notion that nothing exists. This is [the meaning].

He explains the meaning of the word "lying" (*śayana*): when consciousness, taking the form of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), becomes manifest in the heart and shines forth as an object for the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), one says "he lies in the heart.
Thus, at the time of the heart's [contraction], consciousness, which takes the form of the impressions (*vāsanā*) of the waking state, [is said to lie there].

The meaning is that because [the mind] appears as having the form of objects such as sound and so forth—which are manifested through the power of karma—it is said to "lie in the space of the heart" (*hṛdayākāśe śete*). He concludes this explanation with the words:
"Thus, this Śruti has been explained by some with great effort. Regarding this:
Anticipating this objection,
he says: "Having examined these two, they should be accepted by the investigators themselves"—
the meaning is that the commentary of Bhartṛprapañca has been observed [to contain this view], and thus he points out the fault.

Because the mind has been withdrawn by means of the intellect through extensive cultivation based on what was heard, there could be no further withdrawal of it by that [intellect]; therefore, this conception that "the mind is grasped" is false,
since the withdrawal of the intellect as well is heard [in scripture].
The meaning is that the conceptualization of [the Self] as being withdrawn by the intellect is a false interpretation;
thus, having set aside the interpretation of Bhartṛprapañca, he continues with the interpretation of the Śruti itself.
"When it itself takes up speech and the other organs that have been released from their respective domains,
then they say of it, 'It sleeps' (svapiti). Thus, by the force of the very name "sleeps," he concludes that its abiding in its own nature during the time of sleep is established.

Therefore, because it depends upon conventional designation (*samākhyā*), that [name] did not previously exist in the inner self (*pratyagātman*); even the ear and so forth do not possess a name. Consequently, how can it be said that "by virtue of possessing a name, it has its locus in its own nature"? To this he says: "And if there is deviation even with respect to the name. If that is so—

He states that the reasoning for abiding in one's own true nature (*svarūpa*) is expressed by the subsequent sentence: "Therefore, the reasoning is also set forth. He explains that by the word *prāṇa*, the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) is meant, and not the primary vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), because the word *prāṇa* refers to the source (*prakṛti*) of speech and the other senses.
The nose is understood [as the primary sense] because there is no withdrawal of the principal [sense]; thus, it is not desired that [the term] denotes that [specific sense].

In this way, both from the perspective of conventional renown and from the standpoint of reasoning, it has been stated that when all the instruments [of perception] are withdrawn, the inner self (pratyagātman) becomes entirely free from the cycle of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra).

In this regard, the following objection is raised: since the world is perceived even during the state of dreaming, despite the absence of the operation of the instruments of action, this transmigratory existence must be non-natural to the Self. To this, he replies:
"And in a dream, that which rests upon the organs of action has as its cause nothing but latent impressions (vāsanā)."
Because all the senses have dissolved, there is no activity as there is in the state of awakening; thus,
when associated with limiting adjuncts such as speech and so forth, the state of being a transmigrating soul (saṃsāritva) is observed, yet those [adjuncts] have been withdrawn.

"Thus, all [states] are the state of transmigratory existence for the Seer"—this [statement] shows the elaboration of the preceding passage, "In whatever place... and so forth; it demonstrates the doubt [raised by the opponent]: "But even in a dream, the waking perception is experienced."

"Even when there is a separation from all the sense organs, the self possesses states of pleasure and pain. Indeed, having raised this objection, it was already resolved in the passage stating that [the experience] has only latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as its cause; yet, the author of the *Vārttika* himself now raises this same objection in order to introduce the sentence beginning with "sa yatra... (where he...).

To this objection, he introduces the passage beginning with "When [he dreams]" (*sa yatra*) as the answer; the Śruti states that this is not so, because the transmigratory existence characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth, described in dreams, is false.

Regarding the state of being false: even though the waking and deep-sleep states are considered to be the ultimate reality, they do not pertain to the Self; for what reason? He says: "For this [Self], there is neither sleep nor waking; how, then, could a dream be possible?"

Therefore, he says that the three states are merely the Self: "Waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are its very own nature. Alternatively, by the phrase "not of this [Self]," the falsity of the three states is indicated.

Therefore, it has been stated that this is merely ignorance (*avidyāmātra*); this is expressed by the word "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), because ignorance is grasped by that term, according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) that "it is intrinsic nature that proceeds."
If that is so, how does activity occur in that state? To this he says:

"He who thinks 'I am asleep' or 'I am awake,' or likewise 'I am seeing a dream'—this is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of beings who lie within the enemy of ignorance. This [verse] refers to the former [state] in the second alternative.

What more need be said? Elaboration (*prapañca*) is merely the illusion (*māyā*) of the world, and its essence (*ātman*) is the reality (*tattva*). Thus it is said: "All this world, both moving and unmoving, is mere illusion; like the rope [mistaken for] a snake and so forth, its supreme state is the Reality. Even though this is so...

Nevertheless, because of the failure to fully understand the reality of the Self, this world remains submerged in saṃsāra, characterized primarily by agency; thus it is said: "In this mere delusion of the mind, the world suffers, its consciousness agitated by confusion regarding the directions, like a traveler who has lost his way"—so it is taught from the perspective of the inward-turning [knowledge].
It has been stated that this is *saṃsāra*, and by implication, it has been declared that liberation (*mokṣa*) results from the knowledge of that;
regarding this matter, he states that the word of the Blessed One is the authoritative proof:
"In this regard, the ancient and eternal one who upholds the Yadu clan spoke these two verses."
"Viṣṇu [protects] the one who has sought refuge," [he says]. He recites two verses (p.
"The foolish, the lowest of men, who have committed offenses, do not seek refuge in me."

"Those whose wisdom has been carried away by illusion (māyā) have resorted to a demonic nature; for this divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the gunas, is indeed difficult to overcome.
