But those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion"—the meaning of the passage beginning with "Me alone" is stated as follows:

"Whoever knows through the [great] sentence that this entire world is indeed the Self, characterized by reality, existence, and so forth—for him alone here is the fulfillment of life's purpose. Now, if liberation is knowledge, why must it be knowledge born from the sentence? Could it not also be produced by sensory perception and other means of knowledge? To this, he says:
The meaning is that the notion that "worldly cognition has completely dispelled direct perception" is an error.

Now, [the author] says "ignorance regarding the inner self" (pratyagātmanyavidyā) to show that the connection with ignorance is not ultimately real. Furthermore, [he asks] "where is there the postulation of ignorance? because [ignorance] is dependent on something else.

He states that dreams and the like are false: "The conceptualization of existence, non-existence, and so forth is to be understood only with respect to one's own object; for both waking and dreaming are established only with respect to one's own object, not by themselves. Alternatively, [one might argue] that because the world is self-established like the Self...

Regarding that, he says "in the ultimate sense" (paramārtham), meaning "only with respect to its own object. Now, [an objection is raised]: since it is perceived just like the waking state, the dream must be real. To this he replies:
"If the dream were equal to waking consciousness regarding what is perceived through speech and other means. Here:
He states the objection: "How is the establishment of these three states to be understood?
Let it be investigated. If the dream were real, then that [establishment] would be established from the very beginning.
The meaning is "it might be so. And on the strength of the statement ending in the suffix *ktvā*, he says that the dream is false;

for by the statement ending in *ktvā* in the word "having taken" (*ādāya*), [it is shown that] the accomplishment of the single action occurring at a prior time belongs to the dream alone, because it is impossible [for such an action] at the beginning or at the end. By the word "having taken," [he refers to] the vital breaths (*prāṇān*).

The word "having taken" (*gṛhītvā*) is intended here; for "taking" (*grahaṇa*) and "bringing" (*ādāna*) are one and the same. Now, why is it explained in this way? It is said: in the word "having brought" (*ādāya*), the transition from the waking state to deep sleep (*suṣupta*) is expressed, not the transition to dreaming; therefore, it is explained in this manner. Or else:
This is stated by relying on the position of Bhartṛprapañca;
for their other statement, "having taken them," has dreaming as its subject matter. What is meant is this:
by the force of the expression ending in the suffix *ktvā*, the absence of dreaming in the waking state is understood, and likewise its absence in deep sleep.

Since a dream is of the nature of a mental intuition (*pratibhā*), it is indeed established [as such]; therefore, its falsity is established only from the perspective of the intermediate state (*madhyama*).
Thus, regarding the realization of the falsity of objects seen in a dream, does it occur during the dream itself, or for one who has awakened from it? He says: "for one who has awakened."
Thus, for those whose eyes are opened by the knowledge that awakens to the true nature of reality, there is no disease, no old age, no death, no further succession [of rebirth],
no illness, no suffering, and no inundation by desire and the like.
There would be no joy, fear, or agitation; no loss, increase, or death; no sorrow, nor any discontent;
no agency, nor any state of being an object. Yet, even the absence of these is not admitted [as a reality].

This is the meaning: the waking world is the reality; knowledge is indeed the contact with that [reality]. Therefore, for those whose eyes have been opened by it and who have understood the objects of the waking state through it, the objects seen in dreams are false. It is the same for the knower of Brahman as well.

He says that the world is sublatable (*bādhya*): "In this knowledge of the connection between the meanings of the imperishable (*akṣara*) and the perishable (*kṣara*), by the fire of perfect awakening—which is established in the direct reality of the Self and by which the ignorance that is the cause of conceptual construction has been destroyed—no conceptual construction remains. This is the meaning.
The world, which is the manifold of duality consisting of the perishable, and the collection of sense organs such as the eyes, function through the doors of the ears and other senses;
when knowledge of the objects of the eyes and so forth arises, the knowledge "I am Brahman" arises in the qualified seeker. Immediately thereafter, ignorance ceases along with it.
"By means of the effect" (kāryeṇa): alternatively, the ultimate reality is the non-dual inner self; knowledge is precisely the awakening to that.

For those whose eyes have been opened by that [knowledge]—that is, for those who know the identity of Brahman and the self—the world does not exist; this is the meaning. He states the cause of such knowledge as follows:
In this context— "in this [knowledge] which is the eye of the world for understanding the connection between words and their meanings"—
this commentary (*vārttika*) on the phrase "of ignorance, which is the cause of conceptual construction" serves as a summary of the aforementioned position. Thus,
[it concludes] that "it does not exist," and so forth.
Having begun with "it does not exist" and having established the falsity of dreams through reasoning,
the king then introduces this statement in order to make this matter known to Gārgya.
Regarding the phrase "where," and so forth, he says: "that supreme succession of liberations."

He states the meaning of the Mādhyandina recension: "Because it occurs in sleep, it is called *svāpti*"; thus, for the sake of clearly establishing the falsity [of the world], a distinction is made between waking and sleep by means of the explanation of dream. [Now follows] the manner of going from the waking state to the dream state for the purpose of explaining dreams.
He demonstrates this with two and a half *vārtikas*: when night has fully set in,

for one whose senses have been withdrawn by sleep, once the waking activity has ceased and the experience of dreaming has presented itself, the state of waking is concealed, [revealing] that which is characterized as the substratum of waking and so forth.

With mental impressions manifested by karma, he went there through the desire for amorous play in a dream; as one skilled in illusion proceeds by means of his own magic, so did he go into that dream. As to what he did having gone there, it is said: "He created many objects, both high and low."

[The opponent objects: "But surely, if dreams are produced by means such as ignorance, desire, and karma, then because they are accomplished by desire, karma, and so forth, they must be real. [The author replies: No; for he says: "That which is common to one's waking state is what is seen in one's dream."
The meaning is that the state of being seen by no one else indicates falsity. He states, "The word 'worlds' (loka) refers to the fruits of action," because the fruit of action [is what is meant].

He states that falsity (*mithyātva*) is expressed by the word [“unreal”]—namely, “their falsity is stated,” beginning with the words “by them,” and so forth. It is clear that these are cognitions of oneness (*aikātmya*). Now, one might object:
since even a dream does not deviate from its own time, it must be as real as the waking state; to this he replies:

Is it not said that, just as people in the waking state are non-deviant from their respective times, so too those situated in the time of a dream should be understood to exist [in that state] like a dream? But how can the falsity of the waking state be established by the two statements regarding the hand and the dress?

He challenges the proponent of the objection who argues that the reality of the dream is established by means of that analogy: "But has not the falsity of the people in the waking state already been explained at length, and its being caused solely by ignorance [demonstrated] through the awakening from the hand-dress? And this being so..."
"The example provided by you is not tenable because everything is illusory in nature.
To this he replies: "The example of the waking state is applicable; therefore, by taking the example of what is produced, one [realizes] the Self directly."

"The purification of internal and other defilements is what is taught here. Having raised the doubt that a dream might possess reality just like the waking state, [the text] proceeds with its refutation on page 260.

The meaning is that, having established the falsity of the dream state, it is now being proven that the waking state as well is false. But surely you yourself have stated that the falsity of the waking state was established by implication in the passage concerning the clapping of hands; that very point applies here as well.

If it is argued that this results in redundancy, then the logical principle (*nyāya*) of avoiding repetition (*jāmitva*) applies there by relying on some degree of commonality; therefore, what has been urged is not correct. The subsequent *vārttikas* concern the waking and dreaming states.

The proofs for [the existence of] falsity are easy to understand; they are written here: it should be known that the Great King and so forth are not the objects of one's own dream-experience, because they are perceived as distinct from that [dreamer], just like a king lying on his bed.

Based on means of valid cognition such as direct perception, it is observed that a king who has gone to the forest in a dream is seen by those seeing the dream; yet, in accordance with his own experience, for the king who is awake,
the grasping at the forest in the dream would be false.

What is seen while awake is false in the dream state, and what is seen in the dream is false upon waking; because the objects of the dream and waking states mutually deviate from one another, how could there be seeing for me at night when my senses are withdrawn? Likewise, the living of the dead is similarly [unreal].

Whence comes youth for the elderly? How can there be the perception of the eyes and other senses within the body? And how could there be the internal presence of the Himalayas and such mountains within the heart?

Nor does he, having emerged from the body, behold the mountains; for how could he go without the body, being devoid of the means of locomotion? These are his [objections]. Now, one might ask: "Does he perform an action without a body? To this, he says:

"If he performs his work even without a body and so forth, then the assumption of a body and such by him would undoubtedly be useless. Thus, in order to introduce the passage beginning with "Just as," [the author] raises an objection: "Surely, those seated on a couch go..."

He says that these [objections] are not to be raised, [thinking]: "He will see the Self outside the house by means of a palanquin in the forest. The meaning is that this is not so, because it is like a dream within another body.
He applies the scriptural passage to this point: "Just as he takes his ministers and so forth..."

"Just as a king, situated in the midst of his own country, moves about as he pleases for the sake of accomplishing his own enjoyment; so too the Self, residing within its own body-kingdom, having taken up the waking vital breaths (prāṇas) which consist of mental impressions (bhāvanā), perceives dreams according to its will. Thus.
The meaning is that because the self lacks stability, even the waking state is merely superimposed upon the self, just like a dream.
Now, one might object: "If everything is false, how can it possess the status of a means of proof, like false smoke?
To this, he says:

By means of knowledge (*vidyā*), this very Self— which is immutable, devoid of contact, and whose impurity has been superimposed by ignorance (*avidyā*) through unreal limiting adjuncts (*asatyopādhi*)— is purified; thus it is said that [the Self is purified] by means of the limiting adjuncts of ignorance.

Through the knowledge produced by the Vedas, the teacher, and so forth, the Self becomes free from all ignorance and its effects. The meaning is that one should remember that even that which is imagined (kalpita) can serve as a means to knowledge. This establishes the absence of impurity, which is superimposed by ignorance, upon that which is unattached.

A real conjunction of the immutable Self with the perishable non-Self, which is possessed of attachment, is not possible. Now, one might object: "Even for one devoid of ignorance, agency and so forth exist, as they are observed even in the case of the enlightened person"; to this he replies: "Being [the Self] is denied along with its association, even when accompanied by the permission of the immutable."

Because of delusion regarding other things such as the agent (*kāraka*), one does not direct oneself toward the Self. This refutes the explanation of the phrase "having been granted permission by the Immutable" (*kūṭasthā dattānujñam*);
for the reason that [the Self] is "together with itself" (*saha svayam*), the knowledge of being an agent and so forth, once sublated, does not touch the Self.

"But the appearance [continues] due to the persistence of what has been sublated, because of the affliction of delusion. Now, he shows a doubt for the purpose of introducing the sentence, "When one is in deep sleep," as follows:
"But surely, you have stated that his transformation and the state of being the seer and the seen occur through the power of desire."

How is it that [the self] is pure while being thus? He says that there is no connection of the self with desire and so forth: "Not so, because of its inherent Buddhahood; how could there be a conjunction with cognition?
"Except by abandoning the accumulation of ignorance, there can be no union with that Knower"—

the meaning is that because of the absence of a connection with ignorance, there is no association with its effects, such as desire and so forth. To the question, "What does this absence of a connection between ignorance and its effects result for the Self?", he says:
Thus, because this Self is pure by its own nature due to the non-association with a second, it is therefore liberated by its own nature as mere immutable consciousness; in this way,
he establishes the absence of connection with desire and so forth by means of an illustration, just as [in the following].

"Just as there is a meeting of auditory consciousness with form, so too is there a conjunction of the self with transmigratory existence until the limit of immutability. To demonstrate this kind of meaning, he states the subsequent sentence: "for the purpose of understanding this meaning."

"The subsequent section is introduced. He states another meaning of this very point: "Having explained the purity and the distinction between the states of dream and waking, and having stated the non-duality of the Self, it is now being discussed in relation to deep sleep. Having thus stated the connection (*saṃgati*), he explains the meaning of the words (*padārtha*).
By the scriptural statement "not knowing," the agency of the Self is negated; for even though it sees, because of its immutability (*kauṭasthya*), it does not see [in the sense of being an agent].
Thus, the Self is the witness of the knower and the agent, and not itself the agent of knowledge. This is also stated in another scriptural passage.
He says that this has been shown by the words "Now, he who knows," thus demonstrating that the inner Self (pratyañc), as the witness of the knower, is not an agent.

"It is established everywhere. If that is so, then the Self is only the witness of the knower (*pramātṛ-sākṣin*), and not [the witness] of cognition and so forth. He says "no": in some cases the Self is the witness even of the knower; in some cases it is the knower of cognition;
and in some cases it is the knower of external objects. Such is its nature as a knower.
"It is negated" means that its state of being the knower is negated; the meaning of this is that its agency in the cognition of objects such as the subject (pramātṛ) and so forth is negated.
He supplies the word "its" (*tasya*) [to clarify the referent]:
The agency of knowing belonging to another inner self (pratyagātman) is said to be "his" [the self's] because it arises from a relation;
thus, the genitive case is used here because the self's status as the agent of knowledge is produced by its connection with an object.

The meaning is that it is being pointed out. And thus he says, "the genitive [case] is used for the object" (*ṣaṣṭhī karmaṇi*): because the agent and so forth have already been expressed, and because when that [object] ceases, they cease;
therefore, this genitive is rightly applied to the object with the intention of expressing the absence of duality. There is no agent or anything else whatsoever.

The meaning is that he does not experience [the world]. It is not the case that he does not experience it simply because the agent and so forth remain present; rather, since the world is the object (*karman*) of the agent and so forth, in deep sleep there is an absence of the object, and consequently, due to the very absence of the world, he does not experience the world. Thus, he states that the word "ca" (and) is not redundant.

And since this word "api" (even/also) has the sense of "and," what is established by that? It is established that it is not only the existence of the world that is negated during deep sleep, but its non-existence as well.

He says that it exists because even non-existence (abhāva) is a sublater [of duality]. Why, then, is non-existence negated? To this he replies: "The remainder and the remnant" (śeṣa-śeṣī); in the state of concealment (tirobhāva), it is called deep sleep (suṣupti). The absence of the subject and so forth is the remnant, and its existence is the remainder.

He states that the meaning of the sentence beginning with "unobstructed by the *hitā*s" is as follows: now, in order to prescribe the sequence by which this [self] attains deep sleep (*suṣupta*), the phrase "the *hitā*s" is spoken for the purpose of establishing that sequence. In this regard, there are the following *vārtikas* intended to describe the nature of the channels (*nāḍī*):
Easy-to-understand [descriptions] are written: from the navel up to the throat, the heart is situated in the middle;
it has a stalk, resembles the sheath of Brahmā, possesses five apertures, and is downward-facing.
Within the center of the heart are the locations for the support of dreams for embodied beings, appearing with blue and other hues.
Furthermore, his [the body's] limbs and even its cavities are inhabited by gods such as Śakra and others;
these openings arise as perceptions just like those in the waking state. From these, one hundred and one channels extend outwards, ten from each, emerging toward their respective sense objects.

The channels arise from causes such as karma for the sake of experiencing results such as dreams; just as rivers carry water, so do the channels carry the fruit of karma. There is one channel that goes upward to infinity; by traveling through it, one is liberated. Furthermore, within each individual channel, there are subtle subdivisions.
Proclaimed by those who contemplate yoga as seventy-two thousand, those channels (nāḍīs) extend from the heart in every direction like the filaments produced within a *kadamba* flower. (p. 266)

"By which the little body is pervaded"—thus [ends the verse]. Regarding how that is the nature of the channels (*nāḍī*), he says: "Because they bestow beneficial fruit (*hita*), they are called 'beneficial' (*hitā*);
they have issued forth from the heart and are like the rays of the sun and so forth."

The word *tat* denotes a piece of flesh that encircles the heart; nevertheless, here it refers to the body. He says this for the purpose of establishing that the channels (*nāḍīs*) pervade the entire body: by the name *purī*, what is meant here is the encircling of the heart, which serves as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*).

"One should know [this] with the intention of explaining the pervasion of the body. Thus, for the purpose of demonstrating the downward descent (*pratyavasarpaṇa*), he first shows the expansion by means of the channels (*nāḍī*):
"The latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by the karma of dreams, which reside in the heart, [flow] through those channels..."

Having expanded itself, the Self perceives dreams according to its desire; now he describes the manner of withdrawal: having enjoyed the objects of experience in the form of dreams without remainder, when the activity of dreaming ceases, the wise one departs, having withdrawn [the self] by means of those very same [limbs].
Regarding the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptatā*): this has been elaborated upon in two subsequent sections of the Vārttika.

Having withdrawn the senses from the manifold enjoyments produced by the activities of waking and dreaming that have been experienced many times over, one sleeps within the Self through the channels (*nāḍī*) by means of ordinary consciousness (*sāmānyaprajñā*).
Having pervaded the body internally and externally in succession,
one reaches the supreme station like a hawk and thus attains the state of deep sleep.
It is stated here that the exit from and entry into the place of sleep occurs solely through the *nāḍīs*.

Therefore, having raised the doubt that the Self is delimited by itself, he says that this doubt does not apply because what is intended here is entry and exit by means of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
"The locus of the intellect—that is, the internal organ—is held here to be the heart; therein [reside] the senses."

Since all the mental faculties (*buddhitantūni*) are always thus, it therefore extends them through the channels (*nāḍībhiḥ*) by the power of karma, like a fisherman spreading out his net; having spread them outward,
it presides over those faculties situated in their respective seats during the waking state.

Likewise, this unchanging [Self], though inactive, pervades everything—just as the sun pervades the ten directions—when it withdraws those two very functions of the senses, which are themselves inlaid with its own consciousness, through its inward-turning nature;
at that time, it is said that "the Self sleeps. These...
Beginning with the statement "The intellects [are] easily understood by the internal organ," he briefly states the meaning of the aforementioned Vārttikas:

"In accordance with the limiting adjunct of the intellect (buddhyupādhi), there is neither origination nor dissolution for the individual self; however, it is devoid of both distraction and absorption."
"Like a potter, the other [agent] acts from himself" (p.
Having supplied the required meaning, [he returns to] the subject at hand.
He follows up with an explanation of the Vedic text:
"Having descended through those channels, the Self brings the functions [of the senses] back;
having pervaded its own body like heated iron, it rests in its own self"—this refers to the sense organs as well.
He states that those [faculties] are pervaded by way of their causal nature, but not by way of their effect-nature:
"The abiding of the sense-faculties is due solely to their own causes, not because they are effects;
therefore, the pervasion must occur only through the reflection of consciousness by way of their causal nature."
It has been stated that there is a general pervasion regarding the body and the senses, but there is no specific pervasion; thus he says:
"In deep sleep, there is no connection of the inner self with the body, nor..."

Through the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other faculties, there arises a direct connection for those residing therein. This results in the conceit of grossness and so forth regarding the body due to its pervasion by objects, and the conceit of being a knower and so forth regarding the intellect and the other faculties. In deep sleep (*suṣupti*), however, there is an absence of such specific connections.
He states the proof: "For he has crossed over," and this will be explained further on.

"In deep sleep, even the father [is not perceived]"—this indicates the cessation of all relations. Thus it is stated that in deep sleep, the Self becomes entirely liberated from the cycle of transmigratory existence.
Just as an infant at the breast is free from attachment and aversion, so too, objects do not always produce mental transformations through their mere appearance; this is "childishness. (p. 269)

The cause for the non-occurrence of passion and so forth has been stated; now, he states that the lack of firmness in the sense faculties is the cause therein: "Or, due to the undeveloped state of the sense faculties, there is no concealment of passion, hatred, and so on;
like a soft thorn, their cognition is not capable of piercing its own objects. Thus says the Great King.

He states the meaning of the verse beginning with "vetti": "And everywhere his command is unimpeded because he is of a compliant nature; thus, whether he be a king who is exceedingly happy in this world despite having fully developed sense faculties, or a Brahmin who has realized all principles."
Having reached the supreme limit of bliss, one who has accomplished all that was to be done becomes tranquil;

intending to show that the Brāhmaṇa alone is the illustrative example, he says: "Even this triad beginning with the child is accepted as a single illustrative example. He clarifies this very point: The child, the young man, and the aged man—these three stages of life are considered a single illustration for the sake of demonstrating the attainment of the state of Brahman. Just as a Brāhmaṇa, having performed his duties, reaches the highest peak of bliss and becomes liberated, so too are these three states intended to illustrate the same realization. Thus, the entire sequence from childhood to old age is presented as one unified example.

"Now, it is said for the purpose of removing the blindness caused by the intoxication of childishness and delusion. This means that a king who is childish, deluded, and blinded by pride speaks thus in order to eliminate those two faults; the sense is that he refers to the acceptance [of gifts] from Brahmins.
Furthermore, the great Brahmin himself serves as the illustration here; such is the sequence.
He demonstrates this:
because the fool lacks discernment, the discerning lord of the earth is called a "great brahmin" for the purpose of negating his blindness to pride.
Thus, having previously perceived a fault in the case of a king, and perceiving a fault even there, the Great Brāhmaṇa was chosen; therefore, only the Great Brāhmaṇas [are suitable].

Regarding the example: there is a great Brāhmaṇa who is not a knower of Brahman, but rather a learned Śrotriya established in the world, free from pride and wise, who explains the meaning of the word *ghnī*. He strikes away (*atītya*) the causes of suffering and destroys suffering and the rest entirely.

"The supreme culmination of bliss is therefore called 'exceedingly intense'. Now, taking up a variety of examples, he says: "Because an exceeding joy arises within their own selves even for children and others who are changeless, that is the illustration."
The intended meaning is that there is no deep sleep for them. In this very way, he explains the meaning of the word "lying down" (*śayana*) in the passage "he moves about here" (*eṣa etacchete*):
the Self, having attained a supreme connection with those whose forms are causal, [attains] the state characterized by oneness (*aikātmya*).
"It is directly designated as 'white'"; some say "by those very [qualities]".
Now, if one has attained oneness with Brahman, why does he not realize "I am Brahman"? To this, he says:
"Even for those who are extremely close, they are perceived as having distinct natures."
Collyrium and other substances applied to the eyes are not intended to be seen by the path of vision.

How much more so, then, in the case of the Self, in whom all causes of differentiation have been utterly destroyed? For the relationship between the grasped and the grasper is that which removes all distinctions; it is an extraordinary proximity (*atiśayasannikarṣa*).

The meaning is that it is not a cause of knowledge, but rather something opposed to knowledge. This is an elaboration of the phrase "of those whose selves are changeless": the world is perceived by them as being in its very state of natural composure.

This means that sleep itself is intended to be directly expressed as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). He states the reason for this: "by virtue of being the thing illustrated" (*dārṣṭāntikatvena*), because it is deep sleep (*suṣupta*) that is intended here.
[Objection: But is not sleep the case for children and others, while for others it is merely an illustration of sleep?
In that regard, no distinction whatsoever is observed even in the sleep of infants and others. [Objection:

But surely there is no happiness for an infant and so forth during the state of health? [Reply: No; he says "him"—that infant—who has reached the supreme, unsurpassed culmination of bliss, which is free from all excelling states.
Regarding the phrase "he practices": the so-called "changelessness" of the infant consists in being free from passion (*rāga*) and the like;

the establishment of his bliss has thus been stated. Now, he shows that as passion and the like become more intense, pleasure diminishes, to the extent that the growth of passion and the like arises in the child.

"To that same extent, the growth of suffering also arises"—this means that it is well known that when there is an abundance of suffering, there is a paucity of happiness. And when passion and the like are diminished, suffering and the like are likewise diminished; and from that...
Intending to state that this constitutes a happy way of life, he says:
"In this manner, to whatever extent there is a diminution of those various [afflictions] for the self in this world, to that same extent there is also a diminution of suffering."

It would be so, up to that extent, for one whose nature is happiness. For this very reason, it is stated in the Śruti that the increase of happiness occurs through the destruction and growth of desire; thus he says:
"Therefore, through successive increase, due to the destruction of the causes of suffering, [happiness increases] by a ten-thousandth part in the Śruti."

"its culmination is said to be [bliss]. Thus, where bliss culminates, that is supreme happiness; the scriptural passage "And this very one... is the authority for this. Regarding this, he states that the sentence beginning with "Wherein indeed is the Bhūman," etc., is also an authority: "unexcluded and unaccompanied."
"Because [the state of] 'mere' [bliss] is completed in the opposite direction;

for the scriptural statement says, 'The supreme consummation of bliss is in the Infinite (bhūman) alone. Thus, because the locative case "in the Infinite alone" indicates the locus for what is to be performed, there is a distinction between bliss and the Self.
He says that it would not be so:

"Bliss itself is the Self, devoid of differentiation and conjunction; being liberated from the causes of suffering, it attains by its own nature that which destroys the cycle of existence"—thus he restates what has been taught.

The meaning is that the answer to the question "Where was he? has been stated in its entirety, along with all its details and exactly as it is, in the passage where Kāśya questioned Gārgya for the purpose of establishing the connection [between the two texts]: "Where was this one when he went to sleep? and so forth.
(p. 273) He states the determination of the results of the first question:
"And by this aforementioned [method], for one who has arisen from the planetary configuration (*pāṇiveṣa*), [one determines] the purpose of delusion from all remaining activities."

"Śruti has declared purity"—this means that the purification of the referents of the terms "Thou" and "That" has been accomplished. Now, he states the connection [of the next section] with the words "whence did it come? (kuta āgāt), intending to resolve the meaning of this question; namely, when the transition from deep sleep to the waking state occurs, that is now being explained.

Thus [it is said]. One objects that the resolution of the subsequent question need not be stated, since it has already been accomplished by the resolution of the first question: "Surely, he who departs from here—whether from his house or from his name—must certainly depart from that very place; therefore, this follows by implication."

The determination of the answer to the question is established. An undertaking for the sake of that determination should not be made because of the fault of [logical] genus (*jāti*). Now, why is this so? If the ablative case (*pañcamī*) were used in the sense of the point of departure (*apādāna*), there would be the consequence of redundancy. However, this ablative case—

Regarding the claim that "he has come here for the sake of the cause (nimitta) of that [ignorance] of the one who is to be liberated," the author replies: even the sense of being a cause or the like is not tenable for the ablative case (pañcamī).
As for the argument that a cause and so forth are understood through the analogies of the spider and fire, [the response follows].

By the inclusion of the word "ādi" (and so forth), "implication" (*ākṣepa*) is understood here, not the sense of "implication" itself; the meaning is: "Why is this so? If the causal factors (*nimitta*) and so forth are not perceived, then [it would apply] to the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*).
He states this [point] regarding the fifth case:

"If, in the case of a response (*pratyukti*), the cause (*nimitta*) and so forth are not directly perceived, let there be only the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*); for a fault is seen elsewhere. But is it not the case here as well?
To the objection that the fault of tautology has been raised, he says: "But is not the same fault present here, namely the tautology of the sentence? He replies:
"Not so; for what is intended to be expressed is the destruction of the effect by means of the destruction of its cause."

"Since the Brahman intended to be expressed previously is neither excluded nor followed [by anything else], but has as its sole reality the nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), there is no fault of redundancy (*jāmitā*) from that. Thus, Brahman is non-dual, free from all ignorance and its effects, and is the inner self.

The meaning is that, since [the author] intends to establish [his point] by means of two questions, there is no fault such as redundancy. If it is asked how these two questions have this purpose, [the author], in order to demonstrate that, restates the subject matter of the third chapter: "the two objects."

Two subjects have been presented here: that which pertains to the nature of knowledge (*vidyā*) and that which pertains to the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*). The object of knowledge was previously cited as "the Self alone" (*ātmaiveti*); likewise, the object of ignorance has been described as the misfortune of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), consisting of name, form, and action, characterized by the distinction between actions and their agents. Among these, the effect arising from ignorance is as follows:
Whatever one intends to say, all of that must first be heard with effort by the opponent alone.

This is the meaning: "‘The Self alone’" thus summarizes the knowledge that has liberation as its fruit; then, "‘Now, [he who worships] another [deity]... summarizes the effect of ignorance, and that aphorism is explained up to the end of the third chapter, while the other aphorism—
Since "Nami" has already been explained, he states that two questions are raised in order to explain it:
"Now the object of that knowledge which is to be attained through ignorance must be declared; therefore, two questions suitable for that purpose have been set forth."
Regarding how knowledge (*vidyā*) serves as the antidote to ignorance (*avidyā*), he says in this regard:
"Because the causes, natures, and effects of ignorance and knowledge are mutually contradictory, the question is therefore appropriate. If it is asked, "What is the effect of ignorance?"

It is stated that the status of being an agent or an object, the status of being the subject matter to be treated, and all other relations between action, its factors, and their results—all these are the objects of ignorance; they are the domain of knowledge.
Thus he says: "This conventional usage of the factors of action always belongs to the realm of ignorance, like [the perception of] the support and the supported upon a wall."

The status of being an agent (kāraka) is attributed to those two. Just as one who goes from something does so only when there is a distinction [between them], such is the established nature of ignorance (avidyā); knowledge (vidyā) is its opposite.
It has been stated that the object of knowledge is the reality devoid of the distinctions of action and agent; the other is ignorance.
And [it is said], "the effect.
For that very reason, he states this: that ignorance, together with its effect, is sublated by knowledge.
The notion arising from the distinction between action and its factors (kriyākāraka) is worldly;
it is sublated by the correct knowledge of the true nature of the self as it actually exists. He states that this manner of sublation is expressed by the answer to the two questions as follows:
"This self was not other than that, nor shall it be other than that"— by these two [statements],
the destruction of all effects of delusion is intended; thus, through these,
the scripture directly negates any difference between the cloth and the self.

"Because of the negation of the cause of difference"—this is an elaboration of what preceded; therefore, the Self is without difference. Now, one might ask: "How can there be non-difference of the Self from the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, given that these exist? To this, he says: "How so? [It is] by way of an illustration."

"It is said that [the spider] and so forth are examples. Now, if it is argued that a creation in the ultimate sense is being described here, he says "no": "This creation of the Self is not real, but depends upon a figurative application (vṛtti).
If one asks how this is so, he says thereupon:

There is no connection between the non-existent and birth, nor is it accepted that the existent possesses existence; there is no modification in that which is immutable, therefore birth arises from ignorance. Furthermore, because the creation exists for the purpose of knowing the Self, he says that it is not ultimately real:
277) This creation is spoken of under the guise of a pretext for the purpose of awakening men;
for it is in no way possible for creation to arise from the Self, which is immutable.
He states that even those who uphold the established tenets of the Vedas have declared that the purpose of creation is for the sake of self-knowledge:
"This has been stated by the Gauḍācāryas, who were learned in the entirety of the Vedic tenets."
He shows the statement, "The reality is as we have explained," with the verse:
"The creation described otherwise by means of clay, iron, and sparks is a pedagogical device for the sake of instruction;
there is no contradiction whatsoever. Since the purpose of the creation [accounts] is something else...

He states that even the objections (codya) which are about to be mentioned do not apply: "In the case of the creation by the Supreme (Parā), there is no possibility of an objection. He then demonstrates these objections.

"How can there be origination from that which is immutable? How can there be activity from that which is conscious? And how could effects be produced without instruments? How could the emergence of the manifold forms of the universe occur from that which is of a single form?"—even though such a collection of objections exists.

Although [the passage concerning] creation does not apply because it has another purpose, nevertheless, in order to provide a rebuttal to that series of objections regarding manifestation according to human understanding,
he says: "As it is," and so forth.

"Thus, regarding such objections as these, the scriptural response is given in accordance with the nature of the person [who raises them], but not in accordance with the actual reality. Having thus stated the intended meaning (*tātparya*), [the author proceeds].

He applies the illustrative statement: "The spider, as its own agent, employs [its threads] as its action by itself" (*ūrṇanābhiḥ svayaṃ kartā prayuṅkte karma cātmanā*). This is an explanation of the phrase "employs action by itself" (*tanūnityetadātmanā*), meaning that it acts as its own instrument.

Just as one accomplishes the act of weaving cloth by means of an instrument that is self-established, so too does the One accomplish the creation of the world— including space and other elements— within Himself, even though He is Himself insentient, by virtue of His sentience; just as sparks [proceed] from a fire.

"And just as [creatures] are born from fire, O Agni, being devoid of intrinsic nature (*nisvabhāvaka*), so too is the emergence of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the rest from the Self in deep sleep. These [verses] are easy to understand. Now, one might object:
since it was stated "from the Self in deep sleep," does this not imply that the state of deep sleep itself is the cause?

"No," he says; "by this illustration of deep sleep, it is indicated that prior to the manifestation of duality, Brahman alone exists, devoid of name and form. This being so, he says that other scriptural passages as well are consistent in this way throughout all the Upaniṣads.
No other cause for the self is heard of; therefore, the Supreme Self alone is the ultimate cause of the world. (p.
Thus his own position has been shown; now he states the fault in the position that the Supreme Self is the creator:
"In this world, when [the world] has entirely set within Brahman, who is there for the production of the world? (Brahmaṇyastamite 'rtham asmiñjagaty aśeṣataḥ jagatprasūteḥ kaḥ).

"Is the cause other than that [world] because of its exclusion? Indeed, this fault would apply to those who follow their own [sectarian] scriptures, but not to the logicians (tārkika), since they accept a Lord as the presiding deity distinct from the material cause of the world. To this he says: "There is a Lord."

Regarding the phrase "if [the Lord] were distinct," he states the refutation here: "Would He not also set the world in motion? Or would He destroy it? If this [activity] were due to Himself, why does it not occur at all times? If it is argued that this fault does not apply because the Lord depends upon factors such as *dharma*, we reply: there can be no dependence on anything else for the Lord.

He says, "Because of the loss of the status of a [rational] Lord," and "Nor can independence from sovereignty be conceived, because of the lack of proof. Now, one might object: "The effect itself, when dissolved, exerts activity toward its own production and does not depend on a cause"; to this he replies: "Nor is the effect [the agent], because it is dissolved."
"It proceeds toward its own production"—the meaning is that this would entail the consequence of [the effect] being produced at all times.
Furthermore, regarding the cause and effect, are they different or non-different? He states the refutation in both cases:
"If the effect were different from the cause, then since the two are established as separate entities, what would this relationship of cause and effect be?"
"Like the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains, if they were non-different due to their oneness, how could there be the relation of cause and effect?

Furthermore, whether the cause acts or does not act, if it acts, there would be an infinite regress and the consequence that the effect itself becomes a cause. Now, if it is argued that it does not act, [the author] says: "Nor can causality be established for that which is inactive. The meaning is that, if it were so, there would be the consequence of the effect being produced at all times.
Furthermore, he states that there would be a contradiction with your own accepted position regarding the side of the non-agent: "And whatever entity is devoid of activity is held to be a non-agent.
Therefore, if that which does not act were a cause, the production of the effect would necessarily occur at all times. Now, [one might object]:

If it is argued that this objection does not apply because time and other such causes determine the production of effects, we say no; for even those have dissolved away. Since they are themselves effects, they do not exert any activity toward their own production; how then could they produce anything else? For they have reached their end through dissolution alone.

"Time, karma, and other such causes are incapable of producing their own selves; that manifest world exists by virtue of possessing causal capacity. Having thus refuted the two positions—that a cause acts [to produce itself] and that a cause does not act—[the author] now refutes the position that "a cause is that which possesses causal capacity."

In this regard, is the power eternal or non-eternal? He states the refutation regarding the position of its eternity: "Even on the view that power is eternal, the simultaneous production and so forth of all effects would follow, yet it is not the case that they occur in such a manner. He then states the refutation regarding the position of its non-eternity:
And if one accepts that power (śakti) arises [from something], then the cause would be devoid of power;
furthermore, if power [arises] from another power, an infinite regress (anavasthā) results. Thus, [the cause] exists in the preceding moment.

All proponents of the theory of cause and effect (kāryakāraṇavādins) must necessarily accept that the cause is the effect existing in the subsequent moment; [the opponent asks] what is the basis for the distinction between past, future, and so forth? This is an elaboration upon the previous point. [The author replies: "Is time not a substance (dravya), but rather an action (kriyā)? he says.
If it is argued that time is the movement of the sun and so forth, the author states the refutation here:

"arising from the unmanifest" (*avyaktasamutthitau*). The meaning is this: when the sun and other such phenomena arise for one who does not know Brahman, there would be a time consisting of the movement of the sun and so forth. And therefore—
He says that it follows that there is an absence of time prior to its production:
because the sun and so forth have dissolved, their activity is not admitted at that time; therefore, the designation "prior to production" is not established. And as for the effect-substance...

The Vaiśeṣikas maintain that the causal substances are the parts (*avayava*) and that the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*) subsists in them; in order to refute this, he says: "And there is no subsistence of the whole (*avayavin*) [in its parts], because [the whole] possesses the nature of being a single undivided cause. This refers to the effect-substance.

The meaning is that because there is no separate constituent part within the constituent parts that compose its own self, and because it is a single unity, it lacks the capacity for simultaneous existence in multiple locations; thus, both partlessness (*niraṃśatva*) and oneness (*ekatva*) have been stated as the two reasons. Now, [the author proceeds]:
282) By restating that [point], the reason "because of being partless, unitary, and devoid of universals" is stated; for indeed, among those constituent substances which are without parts...

If it is argued that a subsistence (vṛtti) is indeed possible because it is observed, he replies to that: "If the substratum is partless and the superstratum is likewise [partless], how can there be a single composite (avayavī) existing in those [substrata] which occupy different locations? Therefore, by the manner previously stated...

Since distinctions of time and distinctions of space have been refuted, and because distinctions of substance are likewise refuted, he states that the entire manifold of differentiated phenomena—just like the distinction of directions in space—is superimposed upon the inner Self (pratyagātman): [He says: "Because there is no difference of time, and because differences of place and so forth are also excluded, and since even the difference of entities has been refuted, the entire manifold (prapañca) along with its divisions is imagined in the inner Self, just as the division of directions is imagined in space."
Therefore, no distinction such as space or time can be attributed to the cloth;

rather, this distinction belongs to the Self just as the distinction of directions is attributed to the sky. He says that the distinctions such as the origination of the world are merely conceptualized, just like the world itself.

"The creation and destruction of the world are likewise imagined in the Self; the occurrence of creation and so forth is brought about only upon examining the nature of reality. Starting from the passage "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," it is stated that the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), consisting of action, instruments, and results, is of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Thus he said:
"I have previously explained that the agent and so forth are just like an illusion.

Thus, since everything is illusory, he states that even sentences such as "the gross [body] and so forth" are meaningful: "The whole is the Self," and "not this, not this"; for it is only thus that they become logically consistent. Since, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the origination and other states of the world are impossible, therefore, by means of ignorance (*avidyā*) alone, moment by moment—

He says that they would be seen as such: "Therefore, the arising, persistence, and destruction of the world occur at every moment, because their cause is mere ignorance. For this very reason, he states that even the sequence of origination and so forth is not intended [to be real]: "No sequence exists among these. Thus...
Having concluded the incidental discussion, he returns to the explanation of the *śruti* itself:

"The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) here should be those considered to be seventeen. Now, how can they be seventeen, given that they exist in the forms of the internal self (*adhyātma*), the elements (*adhibhūta*), and the divine powers (*adhidaivata*)?
"Many are the vital breaths (*prāṇas*). To this he says:
"The distinction among these, characterized as 'pertaining to the self' (*ādhyātmika*) and so forth, is delimited by the world (*loka*).
By the word "world," the body is understood. He states the meaning of the phrase "all worlds":
"The worlds are of various kinds, distinguished by the divisions such as those born from a womb (*jarāyuja*) and so forth. He states the meaning of the phrase "all the gods" as follows:
"Likewise, the deities who are the selves of the presiding divinities (*adhidaivata*) exist in many different forms."

Therefore, he says that although the gods, such as Āditya and others, are specific to the individual body through their distinctions as the eye and so forth, they are common in their cosmic (ādhidaivika) form: p. 284) ata ādityādayo devā adhyātmadehe cakṣurādibhedena asādhāraṇā apyādhidaivikarūpeṇa sādhāraṇa ityāha—

"These vital breaths (prāṇas) are common; they are common within the body. And he says that these vital breaths, as well as the worlds and the gods, are elemental (bhautika), for "this is the transformation of the elements according to karma and according to sacred learning"; thus, all these are the Self (ātman).

This is the Mādhyandina recension. He explains its meaning: "He was born from the birth of the vital breaths and so forth, just as space [is manifested] through the births of jars and the like. Now, one might object: "Does not the Self arise by itself, just like a jar and such? To this he says: "No."

The arising of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is not held to be anything other than the arising of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth; for how could those [breaths] exist apart from Him? Thus, a clear statement has been heard in scripture: "It is the Supreme Self alone who, through ignorance, exists in the form of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the vital breaths, and in the form of the Knower of the Field."
Having thus stated the reality, he says this further to address the question "What is the fruit?":

because the Self, by means of ignorance alone, assumes the forms of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), whereas in its own nature it is the Supreme Brahman; therefore, he speaks of the Upanishad of that [Self], which consists of the meaning of the sentence and will be described hereafter.
"Its secret doctrine (upaniṣad) is being stated"—and this secret doctrine is established for the purpose of realizing the true nature of reality. He states another purpose for it:

"That secret name which is called an *upaniṣad* for the purpose of worship—that is his supreme secret; one should worship him with that according to reality. Thus, this [name] results in the arising of the knowledge of Brahman, because it is recited in the section concerning the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) for those with difficult latent impressions (*durvāsanā*).

Intending to show that any other meditation (*upāsana*) read within the section on knowledge (*vidyā-prakaraṇa*) has only the origination of that knowledge as its fruit, he says: "In this context of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), whatever meditation whatsoever exists, it belongs to the knowledge of Brahman."

"One should point out that all that is the fruit. He establishes the stated point by means of an illustration: "In the same way as the *godohana* vessel and so forth, every form of meditation (*upāsana*) should be understood thus; because it exists within the scope of knowledge (*vidyā*), it cannot have an independent fruit."
Because it subsists upon the manifested world for the sake of knowledge,
it is like the *godohana* vessel which subsists upon the carrying forward of the water (*praṇayana*) for the sake of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
Just as the *godohana* [subsists] upon the injunction of the New and Full Moon sacrifices by way of the carrying forward of the water...
Having accomplished heaven by means of that [sacrifice], one should accomplish the animal [offering] only after having accomplished it; likewise,

because one subsists upon the manifested world (prapañca) for the sake of knowledge, one should accomplish knowledge by means of the world only after having accomplished it, and thereby accomplish another fruit— this is what is meant.

Since action becomes a means to knowledge by way of purification, [the author] states the meaning of the passage beginning with "The vital breaths (prāṇāḥ) are indeed truth" as follows: "That which is called the Upaniṣad of Brahman is the 'truth of truth'."

The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) indeed constitute the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of the Real (*satya*). Having pervaded all things, these vital breaths—which consist of name and form—are called "the Real" because they are in intimate union with the Supreme Reality. Regarding them, it is said: "The Real is their supreme state. This refers to the two subsequent Brāhmaṇas.
He describes his meeting with the Brahmin Ajātaśatru:

"He who is the perfect expounder of the meaning of the Upaniṣads that was spoken—'I am indeed the Child,' and so forth—will become two Brahmins. Let there be [an explanation] of that which is the answer to the Upaniṣadic statements.
It is not known to whom this Upanishad of the two Brāhmaṇas belongs—is it of the individual soul (jīva) or of the Supreme (para)? Please speak; let there be an explanation of this Upanishad.
"Whose name indeed is this of the two Brāhmaṇas concerning the transmigrating Brahman? Let it be told."

If that [result] bears fruit for one who is a transmigrating being (saṃsārin), he says: "If that belongs to one who is not a transmigrating being when [the mantra] is employed by the clapping of hands, then he alone is to be known; liberation comes from the knowledge of him alone, and he would then be the very one designated by the word 'Brahman,' even though he is a transmigrating being."

287) We understand that "the knowledge of that" (tadvidyā) means "the knowledge of Brahman" (brahmavidyā). Regarding the word "that" (tat), if it refers to Brahman, then he says that everything as previously described goes to Brahman.

Now, if it is determined by logic that there exists one who does not transmigrate, then whatever has been said regarding the transmigrating being will apply to him; therefore, the meaning is that an investigation must be undertaken.

Furthermore, he states another reason why further investigation must be undertaken: "If those two were of different natures, the defects [of duality] would contradict the scriptures that establish Brahman-hood, for nothing can become something else. This is because it is impossible for two distinct things to become non-different through any means whatsoever.
Therefore, this investigation must be carried out;

it cannot be established by the authority of the Upaniṣads alone. The meaning is that there is a contradiction with those scriptural passages which establish the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para). Now, regarding the claim that the individual soul is non-different from Brahman, he says:
"And since [the soul] is not distinct from Brahman, and being thus non-existent [as a separate entity], there would be no sufferer for whom the knowledge of Brahman could be taught."
[Otherwise] futility would follow. Furthermore, the cause of doubt is the motive for inquiry;
therefore, inquiry must be undertaken because it effects the removal of the aforementioned doubt.

[If there were no difference], when the individual soul (*jīva*) is non-different from Brahman, to whom would the state of being Brahman be taught in the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*)? Nor is it the case that...
Since that Brahman alone is eternally liberated and thus has no need for instruction,
and since there is no other who is bound, and because the position of both difference and non-difference is defective, such being the case—
And since this is the cause of doubt that motivates inquiry, the meaning is that inquiry must therefore be undertaken.
Having thus stated the motive for inquiry, he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
"There is no other supreme being who is not subject to transmigratory existence. If there exists a Brahman who is not subject to transmigratory existence, then this [world] belongs to Him...
The doubt arises that [the Self] is as poisonous as the Upaniṣads; the meaning is that this very [doubt] does not exist.

Here he states the reason: because its origination from the state of the *prājña* (deep sleep) Self is heard in the Śruti when [Brahmā says], "I shall tell you Brahman," starting with the words, "[You were] awakened by the clapping of hands."
Having made this promise, the King approached a sleeping man and awakened him with his hand;
having himself led him through the various stages [of consciousness] by way of the path of dreaming,
he then declared from that state of deep sleep (suṣupti) the origin of the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth— this is the meaning of the Vedic passage.

"The pair [of questions] is an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the former [subject], and because the context concerns the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*), this Upaniṣad belongs to that alone and not to another; thus he says: 'And because the context here begins with the transmigrating soul, nothing else is possible therein. Starting from 'Those two' (*tau ha*) up to the end, [the text] subsequently concerns the individual soul (*jīva*)."
And because that very [self] is designated as the object to be seen through debate, he says that it is precisely that which is being established:
And having referred to the beloved self, it is stated that "He is to be seen. He says that in other Vedāntas as well, it is heard that the individual soul (jīva) alone is the object of knowledge:
"In all the Vedāntas, it is the inner self (pratyagātman) alone that is enjoined as the object of knowledge, and not [the Supreme Self]."

"It is enjoined that one should see [the Self] as distinct from that. Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not the case that the transmigrating soul itself, having entered another state called deep sleep, becomes the Supreme? Therefore, it is said that the origin of the world proceeds from the Supreme itself? To this, he says:

"If it is argued that even this transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*) will become non-transmigrating by its very nature through connection with another state, this is not possible," he says: "Because such a vision is impossible. He elaborates upon this in two verses: The transmigrating soul, though naturally subject to transmigration, will become non-transmigrating through connection with another state. This is not possible, because such a vision is impossible.
