In this world, no object distinguished by one genus ever attains another genus from itself,
except through the cause that is the Lord; for if fire were to abandon its own nature,
it would certainly become cold, which would contradict all means of valid cognition.

The phrase "it might be upside down" means that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the state of being a transmigrating soul (*saṃsāritva*) is not tenable for the transmigrator. Since the Sāṃkhyas and others have established through many arguments and with great effort that he is not a part of that [transmigratory state], who could be wiser than them?

290) This is indeed easily understood; however, intending to show that the transmigrating soul must be distinct from the Supreme because it lacks the capacity for the creation and so forth of the world, he says:

He says that because even a transmigrating being lacks the capacity for the acts of creating the world and so forth, it is unreasonable—and contrary to scripture—to claim that such a being is the cause of the world; thus he states:
"Not by the force of scripture," and elaborates on this point: "Whatever is beyond the range of the senses and so forth..."

"It is also determined from the scripture that, in the same way, the world's being acted upon by one who is not subject to transmigration is to be understood from the Śruti. This means "like dharma and so forth. He establishes that there exists a Brahman who is not subject to transmigration:

Thus, this position has first been established through reasoning according to the principles of the treatise; now, another position is also set forth, beginning with "He who is all-knowing, all-wise, free from [defects] such as Uśanas," and "He who on earth... and so forth, and likewise "not so."
There is scriptural authority stating "not this," as well as the description of the Imperishable (Akṣara) as "not gross" and so forth, and likewise from previous passages;
thus, there exists a supreme Lord who is beyond transmigratory existence and under whose control all this is. Now, he states that He alone is the creator of the world:

And that very creator of the world, characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth, [is the cause] because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "from that" and "of the Self. Here, an objection is raised: "Surely, for one who is subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*), there is birth...

"It is proclaimed as 'just so'"; this is not the essence, for he says: "It is not thus, because Maheśvara alone is the locus of that which is called space. This is the meaning: what you have said would indeed be true if the word "space" (ākāśa) were not supreme; however, in the passage "He who is this," it is precisely the Supreme [who is meant].

Regarding this, he states the proof by means of four *vārtikas*: "If one were to say 'I am Brahman,' [it would follow that] the teaching of Brahman is directed toward the *prakṛti*; how could one who is not Brahman speak of that which is not the *prakṛti*, especially when the King is so highly concentrated? Furthermore, there is a contradiction with other *śrutis* if it is said here that the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*) is [identical] with Being (*sat*)."

By the name "Somya," Brahman is intended there; and by the phrase "Ākāśa indeed is the name," it is Brahman itself that is devoid of name and form, as heard directly in another Śruti as being like the supreme Ākāśa; and thus the secret scripture speaks of the Supreme.

And as for the phrase "in the self," there is no room for a sufferer other than Brahman in deep sleep. Furthermore, here the origin of the individual souls (jīvas) from that which is denoted by the word "ether" is heard in exactly this same way; therefore, there is no doubt on this point.
Because of the reference to the subject at hand, and because space is the primary subject here,
if one were to take "space" as the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), then the origination of living beings (*jīva*) from that [ether] would also follow; since that is not tenable, he says:

Since Brahman is not subject to modification and the dissolution of the self is likewise [unmodified], how is it that the application of the elemental ether as the object here is not appropriate? (p. 292)
Since a transmigrating being lacks the capacity to produce the world and so forth, it is the Supreme Being alone who must be understood here;
thus he says:
"The capacity for the creation of the world and other such powers do not belong to a suffering transmigrating being."

"Having considered [the case] of ourselves and others, it is thus. Now, it was argued that by the power of the scripture, the creation of the world and so forth must belong to the transmigrating soul; to this he replies:
"The scripture does not effect the bestowal of power upon it, because it is merely its manifestor," referring to the individual soul (*jīva*).

Furthermore, because the absence of capacity for producing the world and so forth is directly perceived, it cannot be based on scripture alone due to contradiction with that perception; thus he says: "For a means of knowledge does not operate when there is contradiction by another means of knowledge. This is precisely what has been established through such great effort: that [the object] is Brahman itself.
The established conclusion will be that this Upaniṣad concerns that which has become the inner self (*pratyagbhūta*).
To refute that [view], he negates the non-difference between those two [the individual soul and the Lord]:
"If the transmigrating soul and the Lord existed by themselves, independent of each other, there would be no identity (*aikātmya*)."

Since the distinction between these two is like that between light and darkness, the knowledge of their identity is impossible; thus he says: "Therefore, it is not logical that 'I am Brahman'; for if Brahman were directly grasped as being identical with the inner self (pratyak), then because the sufferer is other [than Brahman], [Brahman] would incur the taint [of suffering]; hence it must be otherwise."

If it is asked, "In that case, how is liberation attained?", he says in response: "But by worshipping with virtuous deeds that God, the supreme cause of the world, one attains that most excellent state through His grace."

Thus, if that were the case, even those scriptural passages proclaiming the identity of Brahman and the Self would become mere *arthavādas* (eulogies); otherwise, there would be contradiction. Therefore, it is established that there is no conflict with the treatises on logic (*tarka-śāstra*) nor with worldly maxims, provided that [the view] is maintained in this manner.

The two *vārtika*s beginning with "it is replied" (*pratividhīyate*) are easy to understand. Thus, when the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been reached, he establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*):
"This is not so, because its very entry [into the Veda] is heard to be by means of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas."

"Directly from the Supreme Lord, everywhere. In this regard, he cites Vedic passages: "He made the cities for the two-footed and the cities for the many-footed"; and "The Supreme Brahman itself, having entered the cave of the intellect, is the individual soul (jīva)."

From this hearing, there is no difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman; therefore, this Upaniṣad belongs to that very [Brahman] and not to a separate Brahman, nor to the individual soul alone.
This is also illustrated by the words of the Mantra and Brāhmaṇa: "He made bodies with two feet... and so forth.
The Puruṣa entered;
you are every form, you are both woman and man.
Thus the collection of mantras, as well as the Brāhmaṇas, have entered here;
such was the statement previously declared by the Brāhmaṇas, namely that they were created from him. Likewise, the sentence "seyaṃ" and so forth is heard in the Taittirīya Śruti.
Also in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, it is stated: "The Self is Brahman," and so forth.
Because of this grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), he says that there is non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*):
"In the same way, because of the scriptural hearing of the single imitation [of the word] by both the words 'Brahman' and 'Self,' one should determine: 'I am Brahman.'"
Therefore, this would indeed be logical. To this position, an objection is raised:

"If the position is established in this way, then this defect follows—that the Supreme Being possesses transmigratory existence (saṃsāritva)—because of the cause of non-difference from it. Or, if He were non-transmigratory...
"If it is somehow established [that they are non-different], then instruction is purposeless; for even in that view, he [the Lord] would be liberated.

This is the meaning: if Brahman is non-different from transmigrating beings, then Brahman itself would possess the state of being a transmigrator; or, if Brahman were non-transmigratory despite this non-difference, then instruction would be purposeless.

How can it be said that even for one who is non-different from the transmigrating being (*saṃsārin*), there is a state of non-transmigration? If at that time there is transmigration, then even from that [non-difference], he is not a non-transmigrator. Therefore, the teaching is indeed useless.
To this, [the author] first shows the rebuttal of those who hold a partial view of the established doctrine (*siddhāntaikadeśin*).
When it has been urged in this way for the sake of refutation, some offer a rebuttal— how so?
To this he says:
"In the created [beings], she did not enter the Supreme Lord directly; rather, having assumed a modified form, she entered him whose characteristic is the purpose of consciousness."
"The Supreme entered into all beings from Brahmā down to the level of stationary objects. The meaning of this is as follows:

that which is called the *jīva* is a modification (*vikāra*) of Brahman; it has entered into the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) in that form [of Brahman]. It is not [Brahman] itself that has entered; therefore, the aforementioned defect does not apply. But [an objection may be raised]: "However..."

If it is argued that even though the individual soul (*jīva*) is a modification (*vikāra*) of Brahman, the aforementioned defect would still apply because of the non-difference between the modification and Brahman, he says "no": "And the conscious self (*vijñānātman*) is to be known as both different and non-different from the Great Self, whose nature is the Supreme Self, due to its own inherent character."

Regarding all things: by that [distinction] through which another is held to be a transmigrator subject to karma, in the case where there is no distinction, when it is said "I am Brahman," one will attain Brahman;
thus, the connection with the aforementioned defects will not occur. This is absolute non-difference (*atyantābheda*).

He states that the aforementioned fault would indeed apply to this position as well: "Because in a conception other than this, there is a connection with a fault. He now refutes [the opponent's view]:
"Having restated the established connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the body, which arises from internal dependence, [one might claim] the state of being Brahman [for the Self]."
"What you have stated— that they do not enter from the sentence because it is not heard [in the scripture] (p. 296)— is true, provided that entering and so forth are not what is being propounded."
If it is argued that the individual soul (*jīva*) cannot be the subject to be explained because it is not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), then what is it that is to be explained?

It is said: having referred (*anūdya*) to the world-established individual soul as qualified by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body, Brahman-hood is explained with respect to that [soul]; for there is no purpose [in explaining it] otherwise, as indicated by scriptural passages such as "fearless" (*abhaya*). Thus, it is the *jīva*.
In order to state the refutation of the position that [the world] is a modification of Brahman, he analyzes the alternatives:

these various courses of the individual self (vijñānātman) would constitute a transformation; or there might be a supreme being consisting of a collection of diverse substances, like the earth. Of that [being], which possesses parts...

It might be argued that there is a transformation of a single part. This is one alternative, and its meaning is as follows: either a collection of many substances transforms into something else, like a heap of sesame seeds; or rather, those very many substances, in dependence upon one another, transform into a single part consisting of the nature of consciousness (*vijñānātman*).

"That which they call the conscious self (vijñānātman) is a transformation (pariṇāma) of the Self; for it is a modification of a single part of this [Self], like a jar or other objects of the earth. This is an elaboration of the preceding point. Now, he presents another alternative view:
Either it would transform into the other without its own configuration being destroyed— like hair, saline soil, and so forth— or else it would transform entirely, like the substance of milk.

297) [Thus it is said. Now, one might object that there are other alternative positions as well; to this he says "no"—"there can be only these many positions regarding the modification of the Supreme Self. He states the refutation of the first alternative:
"It is not logical for a collection of distinct substances to possess primary unity;
rather, unity arises from the quality [of being] due to the connection with a single genus. And if that were the case, your own established doctrine would be undermined. This is the meaning.
If it is held that the transformation of a single part of Brahman— which is a collection of various constituent substances— is for the sake of cognition,

or if this refers to the second alternative [of the soul being a part], then the oneness of the cognizing self with the Supreme would be merely figurative, because it is a transformation of a substance belonging to the same genus; or else, [the oneness would be figurative] for some other reason.

If the "other" (the whole) is a collection of various substances, or if it is those very various substances themselves in mutual dependence, then there would be no single "other," because even among substances of a single class that are mutually related, there is an absence of unity, as is the case with a collection.

He restates the second position for the sake of refuting it— arguing that because [the whole] would be subordinate by virtue of being imagined (*kalpitatva*), your own established doctrine (*siddhānta*) would be abandoned: "If the whole (*avayavin*) is eternal and follows along with its inseparably established parts (*ayutasiddhāṃśa*), then [if] a part of it belongs to it while it remains in that state..."

"He entered into the state of transmigratory existence. This is the meaning: it is not a mere collection of various substances, nor are the substances themselves merely bound together; rather, it is a single [entity] within those substances that are bound to one another.

Having abandoned the understanding that [the self] is interwoven with the substance of the whole (avayavidravya), it attains the royal consecration of its own nature as non-existence (abhāvatva). Having attained this—

The Lord does not undergo consecration upon attaining the lion-throne because he has already attained the status of a prince; for one whose self is distracted by delusion, there is an excess of that delusion until it is destroyed through meditation.
Upon the attainment of the status of a prince, he requires nothing else—just as these [examples] show.

Now he shows the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*): "In the same way, this very Brahman, through the mere awakening to Brahman, has attained the state of selfhood (*ātmatva*) with respect to the intellect, the senses, the body, and so forth.
He states the result of the conceit of self in what is not-self (*anātmanyātmābhimāna*): "This is that..."

"Due to the failure to awaken to the reality of the inner Self (pratyaktattva), one divides one's own Self from worldly objects by means of non-self entities that are contrary to it. Regarding such a person,
one who desires liberation from saṃsāra [proceeds] through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
The Teacher explains the meaning of the sentence by means of purifying the two categories [of the Self and the non-Self], saying:

"He who sits upon the plane of transmigratory existence, established in the thought 'I am a transmigrant,' is the seeker of liberation; whereas the knower of reality has truly risen above the desire for transmigratory existence and the like."

Through sentences such as "the Self" (ātman) and so forth, and by means of positive and negative concomitance, the Guru should awaken the person by means of the sentence "That thou art" (tat tvam asi).
The meaning is that the teacher has performed his duty toward the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) regarding the transmigratory existence superimposed upon the Self.
Having stated that "the Guru should awaken [the disciple]," he now states the fruit of that awakening:
"Having abandoned the great darkness by means of the contact with the fire of perfect knowledge of the reality of the Inner Self (pratyaktattva)."

Some maintain that even for one who knows Brahman, there remains something else to be practiced—such as repeated meditation—beyond the knowledge of Brahman, thinking, "I am indeed Brahman alone, arising from [the removal of] all defects; I shall go to Brahman.
That too has been refuted, because exclusive knowledge alone is the means to liberation.
He states [the reason] by way of justification:
since there is not even the slightest other means for liberation apart from the destruction of the darkness regarding the inner Self (pratyaktattva)—
because [such a means] is impossible at birth and so forth— therefore [this alone is required].

Because there is nothing beyond the realization of Brahman, no other task is possible. Furthermore, if there were still something to be done even for the knower, then the scriptural teaching that liberation comes from knowledge would be rendered useless; thus he says:
"And the word [of scripture] would also be in vain. In this way, the application of the analogy has been shown.

Beginning with the word "Stay," the mention of the prince’s madness and so forth in that illustration would not be for the sake of making the prince know, "I am the king's son"; likewise, the mention of creation and so forth is merely subordinate.

It has been stated that [the scripture] is intended for the purpose of knowing the oneness of Brahman and the Self, and not for the sake of one's own [individual] interest; therefore, it was said that "part and whole-ness" is not what is intended. Now, [this is further explained]:

Furthermore, because it would contradict passages such as "Brahman is gross," etc., the relationship of part and whole is not intended; thus he says: "If the relationship of part and whole were directly intended in the knowledge of Brahman, then the Śruti would have declared it with emphasis, just as it does for the ocean and so forth, that which has not arisen."

That which is understood through speech and the mind, such as the "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) and so forth, as well as the statement regarding the rock-salt fragment (*saindhavakhilya*), the censure of the perception of multiplicity, and likewise the words of Death (*mṛtyu*):
if [the author] had intended to express a relationship of part and whole (*aṃśāṃśitva*), he would not have employed such expressions. Therefore...
He states that the accounts of creation and so forth serve solely for the purpose of knowing oneness:

"Therefore, the scriptural texts concerning creation and so forth are for the sake of establishing the firm conviction of the intellect regarding the reality of the single, uniform, and unitary Self; they do not, however, intend to convey that [creation] as a literal fact. Now, one might object:
If it is argued that the conceptualization of part and whole and so forth is not by the force of scripture, but rather by the force of logic, then we ask:

is this the imputation of a transmigrating part upon that which is partless and non-transmigrating, or is it the imputation of such parts upon that which already possesses parts and is transmigrating? If you say it is the former—that a part is imputed upon the partless and non-transmigrating—then the author says in response:

Furthermore, it is not logically tenable that a partless Self, as a transmigrating being, could inherently possess the state of being a transmigrating part. Now, [one might argue] that the individual soul (jīva) is a part of the Supreme and is subject to modification...

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because transmigratoriness is merely adventitious (*upādhika*), [the author] replies: "Let it be so; for since the adventitious is false, this notion of a transmigrating self is a mere conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) based on imagined limiting adjuncts (*kalpitopādhi*)."
Granted that, among such [beings], the intellect of the wise should not be otherwise than fixed on the Truth;
therefore, it is established that the scripture has unity as its ultimate purport. In this regard, he raises an objection: "If the identity of the Self were intended by all the Upanishads—"
"Regarding the statement 'the merging of consciousness, the self, and so forth,' some declare thus:

[If it is argued] that even in the case of pure unity, the authority of the *karmakāṇḍa* (the ritual section) is established, [the author] says 'no'— because [the self] is liberated by its very own nature, and likewise because of the Vedāntas."
"Likewise, it follows that the undertaking [of action] would be partless. If it is argued:

"Is it not the case that, starting from the section on the connection with the *bhāvya* (the goal to be accomplished), this objection has already been refuted; why then is it raised again and again?"—it is true that the objection is being raised again even though its answer has already been stated.
Intending to provide an alternative resolution, he says: "Thus, such objections and their refutations have been described; indeed, the relationship itself has been celebrated in many investigations.
[The opponent asks: "Does the proponent of non-duality (aikātmyavādin) accept the authority of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa)?"
And because of that contradiction, the authority of the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa) is not established;
with this intention, he says:

"Furthermore, due to their mutual contradiction—like light and darkness—neither of the two, the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) nor the Upaniṣads, possesses authority. [Objection: "If authority is not possible, then let the authority belong to the knowledge section (jñānakāṇḍa) alone. [Reply: No; he says: "In the case of that which exists... [The rest of the verse follows].
If both were authoritative, then validity would belong to both; however, let it be determined that authority belongs to that very *karmakāṇḍa* alone.
But surely, if you accept the authority of the *jñānakāṇḍa*, then [the same must apply].

He says that since the authority of the *karmakāṇḍa* has been refuted, that which is intended by us is established: "If both [the *jñānakāṇḍa* and the *karmakāṇḍa*] possess authority because the *karmakāṇḍa* is authoritative, then that identity of all things (*sarvagrāhyaikātmya*) has been declared here by force. If this is so, then...

He states that the Upaniṣads lack authority: "If this is so, let there be non-authoritativeness for the Upaniṣads at all times. Furthermore, he states that the Upaniṣads do not possess authority because they contradict perception and other means of knowledge: "And because of contradiction with other means of knowledge, their status as valid authorities is not accepted."
Thus, because they also obstruct their own purpose, the Upaniṣads do not possess authority; so he says:
"And since the Upaniṣad also effects the obstruction of its own purpose, it lacks authority; therefore, the authority belongs to the Karmakāṇḍa."
If it is asked how [this view] obstructs its own purpose, it is replied:
because non-duality is incompatible with distinctions such as those between disciple and teacher; therefore, when that distinction exists, [non-duality is undermined].
"How is the establishment of non-duality [achieved]?"—to this, he now states the final conclusion: "This objection raised by you is not correct, because it has already been answered;
if you say that it is useless here because its purpose has already been explained previously, we reply that the scripture of knowledge is not devoid of purpose."

The meaning of the statement "it is not subsidiary to anything else" is that it reveals its own purpose: "Since liberation is directly experienced at the very moment the realization 'I am Brahman' arises, there can be no pointlessness [to this knowledge]. To the question, "Where was its non-subordinacy stated?", he replies:
Since the determination of the mere thing was already established regarding the relationship [of words],
the Upaniṣads cannot possibly have any other purpose; thus,
the Upaniṣad establishes the definition of what is authoritative and what is not.

In order to establish the nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is established that validity and invalidity are otherwise [distinguished] by the single cause of the impossibility of producing a cognition of its own object; listen with an attentive mind to all of this as it is relevant to the subject at hand. Furthermore, what follows from this? If indeed it is so... [listen with one-pointed mind to everything].

When this is the case, if that entity directly realizes valid cognition regarding its own object of cognition— that is, if it brings about valid cognition regarding its own object of cognition— it would follow that [the scripture] lacks authority.

How could there be validity for that [scripture] from this source? Otherwise, it would not be stated that "the Upaniṣad produces valid knowledge. Your statement would contradict perception, like saying, "Fire does not burn wood" or "The sun does not heat."
Just as that statement [of yours] contradicts direct perception—these points are easily understood.

It might be argued that, since non-arising is the defining characteristic [of Brahman], it cannot serve as a means of valid cognition in the manner described; however, let it not be thought that it lacks authority due to a lack of purpose. To this he says:
"Like the burning by fire and so forth, the fruit born of the knowledge of the Vedānta is immediate."

"The destruction of the miseries of saṃsāra is experienced through direct perception. As for what was said—that [obstacles] "obstruct one's own welfare"—that is extremely trivial; you ought to hear it as it is being stated exactly as it is. This is easily understood.
If it is argued that [the Vedas] do not possess authority because they teach their own nature (*svarūpa*) in the manner previously described, he says:
"For the awakening of one's own object of measurement (*prameya*) is said to be the 'own purpose' (*svārtha*) of means of knowledge; if they perform that..."
"Whence then [the status of] the Vedantas? Is it not the case that they lack authority because they are sublated? To this he says:
"And there is no sublation here of the knowledge arising from the Vedanta texts.
Thus [it is said]. Here he states the reason:
"Because even those things considered sublaters exist in the form of the true nature of the inner self (pratyag-yāthātmya).
This means that even perception and the other means of knowledge, which are regarded as sublaters, [are themselves of the nature of the Self].

The meaning is "because it is its very nature. Now, if it is argued that such a self is impossible, he says "no"— it is producing valid cognition, invalid cognition, and likewise the semblance of valid cognition, while indeed performing the act of cognizing.

Regarding the claim that [the scripture] lacks authority because it contradicts perception and other means of knowledge— due to the impossibility of that [which it teaches]— he offers the following analysis in order to refute it:

"Whether the contradiction between means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arises from having the same object or from a difference of objects—let this be explained. With these words, he raises the first alternative: "If there were sublation (*saṃvādha*) by another means of valid cognition... [The term *saṃvādha* refers to sublation.]

By the word "one," a single object of reference is intended. Regarding that, he states the refutation: "There is the fault of being a mere restatement (anuvāda), but there is no contradiction among means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) when they converge upon a single object. In this view, the meaning is that the fault lies in being a restatement, not in contradiction.
And when the objects of cognition are distinct, since the auditory and other organs are,
in whatever way, mutually independent, they are all the more not in conflict; this is indeed easily understood, for one means of valid cognition does not contradict another.
"But the sentence 'That thou art' (tat tvam asi), etc., declares itself to be contradictory to its own meaning.
To this he replies: "And a single valid sentence cannot both establish and negate [the same thing]."

"And while performing the negation of that [negation] of validity, he is seen in some place. This is the meaning: neither Vedic nor worldly speech produces valid cognition; thus, while performing both the production of valid cognition and its negation, he is not seen anywhere. But surely, in the world...

Thus, he states that [the cognition] is observed to be one that conveys a meaning not contradicted by the sentence: "Fire is cold and likewise hot," and so forth. [Objection: But surely this is seen to be an apprehension of a contradictory meaning as it arises; [Response: No.

He states that it conveys a meaning contrary to that [of the preceding sentence]: "A contradictory meaning is not determined by one [word], nor even by two; rather, by restating [the subject] with a portion of what was said, it is understood that 'fire is cold.
Is the sentence cited by you a single sentence or two sentences?

In every respect, that which conveys a contradictory meaning is not [valid]; thus, when there is one [sentence], the meaning is that "cold fire" is understood by way of restating the "hot fire. Now, [one might object]:
"Cold fire is impossible; how can 'cold fire' be understood by way of restating the 'hot fire'?"
Regarding that, he states the procedure for cold fire:
"A cold fire is indeed possible, being within the scope of other means of valid cognition; and even the awakening by another song is accepted as such. When it is hot...
Thus, even then there is no contradiction; so he says:
"Or, it may be cold like [the sensation of] cold, because the quality of coldness has not been removed; even so, there is no contradiction. (p. 307)
"It may also be [known] by other means of knowledge. It has indeed been stated that "cold fire is possible";

as to what that is, he shows it: since the absence of contradiction was stated when there is oneness of sentence, it is the same even when there is duality; thus he says this for the sake of such a meaning: "Cold fire might be frosty."

Likewise, "the earth is hot" [is not contradictory] because it is understood as having distinct fires; thus there is no contradiction between the two statements. Having restated that there is no contradiction due to the lack of conflict when "fire is hot" and so forth constitute a single sentence with a single meaning, [it is now shown that] even when there are multiple meanings within a single sentence...
He states the absence of contradiction: "There is no contradiction because of the single purpose, even when there is a twofold meaning, due to their common substratum.
This is the meaning: when a single sentence, such as "fire is hot and cold," conveys only one meaning according to the method previously described, then there is indeed no contradiction.
When this very sentence makes known both the heat of fire and its coldness—

whether as distinct properties of different fires or as properties of a single fire— there is still no contradiction, because it is established by its own authority through its respective substrata according to its own meaning; [this is so] even when [contradicted] by another means of knowledge (*mānāntareṇa*).
If it is argued that there is a contradiction, he says "no": because [the Self] is not an object of another means of knowledge, there is no contradiction with another means of knowledge.
The meaning here is this: you assert that there is a contradiction because of a single object of reference (*ekaviṣayatva*).

[But we say] it is through different objects of reference. First of all, there is no contradiction through a single object of reference, as in the case of the two meanings of the sentence "Fire is hot and cold," which exists apart from that [single] statement.

He states that this is a doctrine of acceptance (*abhyupagama-vāda*)— even though [the opponent] claims that the suffix *mā* has the sense of "prohibition" because the intermediate [meaning] is not its object:
"This was said having accepted [this objection], but it is not the method of those who know the rules of sentences, namely, that [a word] conveys multiple meanings."

And he demonstrates the logical principle of those who know the nature of sentences: "of that which is indeed one. Furthermore, the definition of a sentence is stated as follows: "If it were to convey multiple meanings, the speech would not possess the characteristics [of a sentence]. Moreover:
He states that there is no contradiction whether this statement is considered a single Vedic scripture or two statements:
"When the entire Veda is accepted as being but a single statement..."

Since no other sentence is possible, how could there be contradiction? If it is argued that there are two sentences, or that there is a difference between the established and the probandum meanings, even then there is no contradiction here, as they convey distinct meanings. Thus, the contradiction with perception and so forth has been raised.
Having set aside the objection that [the opponent's position] causes the destruction of both one's own purpose and the purpose of others, he now addresses the point that has been raised.

If it is argued that the purpose [of this work] is that the Upaniṣad never destroys either one's own interest or the interest of others— [a claim] which is the speech of the shameless— he says [the following] regarding that:

"If the attainment of all human goals and the perpetual cessation of all misfortunes were to occur through the knowledge of Vedānta, what other self-interest could be desired? Thus, he refutes the objection that [the teaching] obstructs the welfare of others. He neither prohibits nor enjoins anything.
"And the Upaniṣad [is exhausted] with respect to ritual action, because its sentences are exhausted upon the direct realization of the one [Self]. Now,
if the Brahman-texts are exhausted in establishing non-dual Brahman, then what of the ritual texts?
If it is argued that [the Veda] does not produce valid cognition regarding its own subject matter, he says "no":

"Nor does the statement of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) produce valid cognition regarding its own subject matter; how can that which produces no cognition be called authoritative? Furthermore, for one who maintains that valid cognition does not arise from the sentences concerning ritual action...

And he states that there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*). He says: "The production of valid knowledge is for the sake of direct perception. Because the production of valid knowledge arises from sentences such as those concerning the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, it is impossible to say that no valid knowledge is produced [from them]. Now, [one might object] regarding the duality that is the subject matter of the ritual injunctions (*karmavākya*):
He says: "If it is argued that because [the object] has been taken away by the word of Brahman, how can valid knowledge arise from a ritual statement—[the answer is]:
'If not, then there would be no production of valid knowledge regarding liberation through the statements of the Vedānta. Now, one might object:
"But you are stating an inference, and that is contradicted by perception"; to this he says:

(310) First of all, there is no [contradiction] with the two types of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because [the latter] is awakened by inference (*anumāna*). Now, if even the scripture on ritual action (*karma-śāstra*) is a means of valid cognition (*māna*) regarding its own object, then the differentiation of ritual actions must also be ultimately real (*paramārtha*).

To the objection that this would result in the abandonment of non-duality (advaita), he replies: "Just as one who follows the sway of desire and aversion, having accepted what is established [as real], always thinks, 'May only what is desired be mine, and may even the undesired never come to pass.'"
"The Śruti, teaching for the sake of attaining what is desired and for the removal of what is undesired, does not state anything for any other purpose. Thus,
[the Veda] is exhausted in merely stating, "This is a means to the desired" and "This is a means to the undesired."

The meaning is that the treatise on ritual action (*karmaśāstra*) does not operate with respect to the essential nature of action, nor with respect to its distinctions, whether imagined or unimagined. Regarding this, he provides an illustration:
"Just as in the case of the optional *agnihotra* and other rites, there is a connection between the goal to be accomplished and the means."

"Establishing their falsity and so forth, [the scripture] speaks of desires in certain places. Now, one might ask: "If the reality of desires is not asserted, how is it that persons engage in them? To this he replies:
"And yet, persons do not fail to engage in actions prompted by desire, because desire exists even for those who know the truth."

"It never turns back"— this is the meaning: although the injunctive statement such as "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*) does not operate with respect to whether a result is imagined (*kalpita*) or unimagined (*akalpita*), [the action] nevertheless never ceases.
Nevertheless, when it is said that "this result arises from this," those who desire [the result] do indeed engage [in the action].

The phrase "nevertheless" (tathāpi) implies even in the case of non-action. Now, one might object: since there is no desire for results in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), such engagement driven by desire does not apply there.
To this, he states the authoritative proof that desire exists even in that context:
"No action whatsoever is seen to be performed by anyone without desire; for whatever a living being does, that is the movement of desire.
He states this so that this meaning may be preserved even by the Śruti, saying "That which is desire," and so forth;
and this meaning will be explained in detail [in the section] beginning with "free from desire."
The scripture itself demonstrates his absence of inherent nature (prakṛti), stating:

"And acting thus while being free from desire, one is liberated. Now, it may be objected: even in one who is devoid of desire, activity and cessation are observed; how then can he be said to be "free from desiring"?
Regarding the statement "one is liberated by acting," it is said in this regard:

for one who has not destroyed all offices of authority and has not attained complete self-awakening, whether in engagement or in withdrawal, the status of being subordinate [to the gunas] is considered equal. This is because [the same applies] to one who is undiscouraged and lacks dispassion.
It is not possible to deny engagement in action, nor can the arising of valid cognition be denied;
therefore, objections such as the lack of authority of ritual injunctions (*karmavākya*) due to the non-duality of Brahman and the consequent absence of an object of knowledge are refuted.

Thus he says: "Therefore, because Brahman is one, all that has been asserted—such as the absence of an object and so forth—is to be understood as refuted by the very path already described. Now, [one might object]: "But surely, on the basis of the scriptures..."
If it is argued that engagement and withdrawal do not occur by the power of passion (*rāga*), [the author] says "no":

for one whose mind is drawn away by passion and the like, it is impossible to turn them back; and because their minds are detached, the scripture is not capable of inciting them. Thus, [actions] have desirable and undesirable fruits.

"By revealing the means of accomplishment, the treatise does not effect the engagement or withdrawal of the person. For this reason as well, activity does not arise from the power of the treatise, but rather solely from the power of passion; thus he says:

Even today, persons who act by transgressing the scripture due to the strength of passion and other afflictions are seen; how can this be so? If that is the case, one might ask: "If the scripture does not cause [such] activity, then what does it do? To this, he says:

Because the relationship between the goal and its means, as well as the arising of desired and undesired fruits, are always directly illuminated by the scripture like the sun, one engages with those means out of attachment; thus he says: "In those [means], which have the scripture alone as their lamp."
"Men proceed along the paths of the goal and its means according to their own inclination, and not according to the scripture. Now he concludes the present topic.
Therefore, the Vedāntas do not sublate the scriptures of injunction (*vidhiśāstra*); nor would they be devoid of an object,
because— like the sense of touch and so forth— their objects are distinct, consisting of imagined karma and the like.
Because the statement regarding ritual action has as its object the ultimate non-duality, the meaning is that it refers to the statement regarding Brahman;

thus, within the perspective of the oneness of Brahman, contradiction has been refuted in every respect. Nevertheless, some here raise an objection. To this he says: "But some who consider themselves wise [assert] contradictions..."
The meaning of the first [verse] is that all means of knowledge (*māna*) mutually corroborate one another because they have a single object; thus,

when the unity of Brahman is accepted as the meaning of the scripture, it is possible for both the scriptural treatise on Brahman and perception and so forth to have mutually non-contradictory objects.
He demonstrates the contradiction with the scripture on Brahman (*brahmaśāstra*) by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*):

"Since sound and the other objects, being distinct from the ear and the other senses, are perceived as mutually different, the [claim] that 'everything is the Self' contradicts direct perception. Now, [he shows] the contradiction with inference (*anumāna*).

He demonstrates that there is a contradiction with the logical mark (*liṅga*) because the perceivers and agents of objects such as sound are inferred individually and separately; therefore, there is opposition to the logical mark. He states the contradiction with scripture (*āgama*):

Furthermore, those who revile the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman, being filled with joy, point out contradictions with scripture based on distinctions such as the desire for villages and so forth.
Thus [it was argued]. Now, having stated that the oneness of Brahman is not possible due to these contradictions, he resolves the contradiction:
"How can there be a contradiction to the oneness of Brahman for you, who possess cognitions of diverse objects?"

"Those who propound difference must be questioned by the knowers of Brahman after they have passed away. [The opponent asks: "Does the oneness of Brahman contradict anything? [The author replies: The non-duality of Brahman—that is, its oneness—is not contradicted by perception or other means of valid knowledge. Regarding this, he provides an illustration:
"O sir, does the oneness of space contradict [itself] through the distinctions of sound and so forth?
If it does not contradict it, then why is such a contradiction loudly proclaimed?
To this, he says that there is no contradiction with its non-duality:

Nor can there be a grasp [of reality] by means of perception and the like, which are limited to thorough differentiation, because the mere existence of an entity as distinct from others is not apprehended by anything anywhere. Just as there exists no means of valid cognition whatsoever that grasps duality, so we shall explain further on; therefore, [our position] is not contradicted by any means of valid cognition.

Having repeatedly stated that this exclusion of one thing from another— which is of the nature of non-existence— is not graspable by perception, and as will be further explained in the investigation of views (*dṛṣṭi*), it follows that non-duality is not contradicted by perception. As for the contradiction with inference (*anumāna*) that was mentioned:
He restates [the opponent's position] in order to refute it: "As for what was said—that [souls] are inferred to be distinct and diverse in each body" (p.

The proponent, stating that "those who perceive objects such as sound and those who are the agents of actions" constitute the inference for the plurality of selves (*ātman*), is to be questioned; thus he says: "By what means are they inferred to be distinct? To this, [the opponent] replies: "If, being thus questioned, he should say..."
Regarding the phrase "by those skilled in small liṅgas," he states that this is untenable: "And this is not logical.

He demonstrates its lack of logic: "In the case of an object that is not distinct from the means of knowledge, there can be no differentiation within the inner self (pratyagātman). Furthermore, the outer self (parātmā) and other objects of knowledge (prameya) are not the self; they do not exist [as such], like a pillar and a jar."
Thus [ends the quotation]. This is the meaning: the Self (*ātman*) is, first of all, self-luminous; in that regard, there is no differentiation.

Since there is a lack of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), if it were to be apprehended through inference, its nature as a sacrifice would be like that of a pillar or similar objects. To the question, "Who are you who have spoken thus by means of your skill in logical marks (*liṅga*? he replies:

"You are skilled in inference; explain who that [self] is"—thus the proponent states our position. "The body, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) exist as objects within all beings. This is the inference regarding the plurality of selves.

And he says that it is contradicted by perception: "And likewise from the perception of the self. He elaborates on this: the very cognition of the self is the self; in all bodies and at all times, no one perceives multiplicity in the self as they do in non-selves, nor does anyone perceive multiplicity in the self through inference.
For those who assert [the existence] of a self,
there would be a sublation of their inferential cognition by means of direct perception.

The oneness of the self is understood through the perception of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), which occurs as "I am one in all bodies. Multiplicity is not [perceived], for that would be contrary to it; thus, your inference regarding the difference between selves is invalid.
[Objection: But is there not also the appearance that "I am one, while in another body I am another"? [Response: That is an illusion.
Therefore, your inference is contradicted by direct perception. Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa of the fourth [Adhyāya].

Śrī [the author] restates the subject matter (*vṛtta*) in order to establish the connection (*saṃgati*): having previously promised that "the Supreme Brahman is that from which the birth, maintenance, and destruction of the world are accomplished."

"Shown as it truly is": having made the promise, "I shall tell you of Brahman," that from which the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of the world proceed is Brahman; this is what has been stated as it truly is.
He says this because it has also been stated [in the Upanishads] that "it is the Truth of truth," and that it belongs to that very Brahman.

It has been stated that "its secret doctrine (upaniṣad) is such-and-such. To explain that secret doctrine, he says that the subsequent two Brāhmaṇas [are provided]. Now, their explanation is being given: for the sake of Maitreyī’s realization of the Supreme Brahman, which is Truth. Thus it is with both Brāhmaṇas as well.
Having explained the connection through the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), he states the unique relationship of the child Brahmin (*śiśubrahmaṇa*).

Since the birth of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth was aphoristically indicated in this context of the creation, the detailed explanation concerning the connection with the vital breaths is now elaborated first. This is because the connection with the vital breaths arises from the initial mention of the birth of "all the vital breaths."

The meaning is that "thought" (*cintā*) is stated first; he says that by the subsequent Brāhmaṇa, the true nature of the worlds and so forth is explained—namely, that "thereafter, the true nature of the worlds and so forth is also explained.
What is that true nature of the worlds, the vital breaths, and so forth? To this, he says:

Regarding the internal (adhyātma) and the divine (adhideva), everything here— including the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth— is based on the deities as instruments and consists of the reality of the five elements; the reason for this is that nothing whatsoever is admitted to belong to the inner self (pratyañc) apart from the elements, due to its connection with the vital breaths.
It was stated, "The previous explanation is being told"; as to what that explanation is, he says:

"It has been said that 'the vital breaths (prāṇās) are indeed truth'; now, those vital breaths and also those Upaniṣads [which concern them] are explained with effort. Thus, by means of the vital breath...
How one performs the satiation with food, water, or speech and so forth by means of the middle [channel], that should be explained, as well as those [teachings] from the Prāṇopaniṣad.

This is an elaboration of what preceded. Having thus shown the connection, he begins the explanation of the Śruti text: from "yo ha vai" (he who indeed), which states the question, up to "sadāmaṃ veda" (he knows the eternal food), which is the conclusion of that [question].

The meaning of this response, beginning with the question "Is it a child? and ending with "This is its resting place," explains that the vital breath (prāṇa), having been deposited within the bodies, is likewise drawn back into the head; thus, it describes the childhood state of the prāṇa.
Because it does not cling to sense objects, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is called "infant" (*śiśu*), just as speech and the other [senses] are;

for there is no lack of attachment in the case of the vital breath. Regarding the phrase "the hateful rivals," he explains the meaning of the word *bhrātṛvya*: those who are established in the vital breaths of the head.

Those enemies characterized by attachment to sound and the other sense-objects are [overcome] from the very moment of birth through the removal of the inward-looking vision; this is an elaboration of the statement "for they are placed within the body.
The term "body" refers to the locus of placement, because [the senses] reside in the body by way of their general function.
Therefore, this *prāṇa* is called the "foundation. He states another reason for its being the foundation of the body:
"Since speech and the other [senses] rest upon the *prāṇa* which has taken refuge in the body, it is sufficient [to say that the body rests on *prāṇa*]."

"However, for the accomplishment of its own function, it does not depend solely on the vital breath (prāṇa)"; thus, [the senses] whose functions have been swallowed by the prāṇa in the head and other locations are not capable of performing their tasks.

The establishment of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—which, when supported by the body and supported by the vital breaths, is capable of performing its functions—is thus deposited in the head; this he elaborates as follows:
"And because it is established through comprehension, they know the head to be the secondary receptacle (*pratyādhāna*)."
"Concentrated upon each specific region of the head"—thus he explains the meaning of the word *prāṇa*:
"The power arising from food and drink is *prāṇa*, as well as strength. This refers to its [the breath's] nature.
He states that its nature as a pillar is logical: "Upon this support of strength, the vital breath (prāṇa) remains in the body.
Regarding the statement that the vital breath is the support of strength, he provides the scriptural authority: "It becomes weak... and so forth.

Regarding the statement, "In this way, he will explain the departure of the vital breath (prāṇotkrānti)," some describe that by the phrase "the vital breath is the pillar" (prāṇaḥ sthūṇā), the function of inhalation and exhalation is being expressed; thus [the author] says:
"Some declare the wind, characterized by the activity of inhalation and so forth, to be the pillar and the food."

In order to explain the meaning of the word *dāma*, he describes the transformation of food: "Food, having been consumed by contact with the digestive fire, undergoes a threefold transformation in succession; this [food] becomes both gross and subtle, and its gross portion goes to the earth."
Feces and urine are proclaimed as the middle portion, for the purpose of nourishing the gross body.
That subtle essence of food which is called "immortality" (amṛta),

having reached the region of the heart and taken its seat within the channels, nourishes and gratifies the deities of the subtle body (liṅgadevatā) through the channels radiating from the heart, [serving] as the sacrificial offering.
It is said that these [points] are easy to understand. To the question, "How does another become a tether?
he says in response:
"Having bound the body with [the elements such as] rasa and so forth, the child likewise [binds it] with a subtle portion."

"Because it is connected to the two nooses and so forth, food is called a 'rope' (dāman). He shows the reason for food being a rope through a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "When the rope becomes extended, then, upon the exhaustion of karma, the vital breaths depart from the body according to their own nature, severed."

Regarding the phrase "the bonds," he states the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "these [are] for him" as follows: since certain secret doctrines (*upaniṣad*) concerning the eyes are to be taught to that very child who is ignorant of the supporting substratum (*pratyādhāna*),
the Śruti [proceeds] from this point to describe the method of meditation and the manner of the fruit.
And he demonstrates the fruit [of this knowledge]:

"Having known that the seven deities, beginning with Rudra—the Upāsaka and the Īkṣiṇī, and Prāṇa—are imperishable, one does not experience the exhaustion of food. By the words "Rudra" and so forth, those [deities] well-known [in tradition] are meant.
The deities have been mentioned previously; now [the author] states that the vital breaths (prāṇas) are denoted by such words as "Rudra" and so forth: [p. 321]...

The verse, "The sages known as the Prāṇas— the Rudras and others— constantly and with effort worship the Prāṇa established in the head," also refers exclusively to the host of deities denoted by the term 'senses,' such as the ear and so forth, and not [to the vital breath].
He states that [this] concerns well-known deities:
"Since the preceding groups of deities have already been explained as being the eyes themselves,
this first half of the verse has been cited for the purpose of explaining the sense organs, such as the ear."
The eye is indeed the sense organ, since the group beginning with Rudra has already been explained in that very context;
by the word "Rudra" and so forth, the collection of instruments (the senses) is to be understood, meaning that the ear itself is the verse.
He explains the meaning of the words "Viśvarūpa" and "Yaśas": Viśvarūpa is to be known as fame.
"The light that manifests objects such as sound is also manifold in nature because it manifests distinct objects. This is the meaning:
the light that manifests objects such as sound is the collection of instruments beginning with the ear, and that...
The fire that constitutes the causal instrument is manifold in its objects and manifold in its forms;

because it makes known various distinct objects such as sound and the rest, it is therefore "universal in form" (*viśvarūpa*). This very collection of instruments is what is denoted by the word "seer" (*ṛṣi*).
And on the shore of that lake (Cetyā),
there dwell seven winds which are the supports of the senses, as well as the sages and glory.
Regarding the statement "by the reason already mentioned," if it is asked how the seventh [speech] can be established as the eighth, he says in response:
"By the distinction between being a speaker and not being a speaker, speech—which is in fact one—is divided; thus, the seventh is [the eighth]."
"And the eighth [tattva] as well—thus that one alone is so called. He explains this:

"The production of phonemes occurs through speech, and likewise the perception of the primary rasa (flavor) arises from the conjunction of the two functions; thus the seventh and the eighth are both 'speech' (vāk), being subtle."
There is no fault here in the statement that the function of the tongue-faculty (*rasanendriya*) is likewise the function of speech;

for by the term "tasting of flavor" (*rasavedana*), the act of chewing (*carvaṇakriyā*) is intended, and thus there is no fault. He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "these two alone" as follows: for the sake of establishing a specific invocation (*viśiṣṭāhvāna*).

The subsequent scriptural passage of the sages begins with "These two alone," and likewise [the principle] that "the acquisition [of knowledge] should be fruitful" is stated through the result of the meditation on the prāṇa mentioned previously,
starting with "of everything," etc.; thus he says:

"The statement 'of all' would be a declaration of the fruit of the aforementioned meditation and action. He states the intended meaning of the phrase "all food becomes his" as follows: "It is said that 'all belongs to him' for the purpose of negating [his] status as an eater of food. That which has become an object of enjoyment for this meditator—
The meaning is that it becomes its enjoyer.
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa of the fourth [Adhyāya].
Having restated what has been previously discussed, he explains the connection to the subsequent Brāhmaṇa with the following verse:

"The secret doctrines (upaniṣads) of the vital breaths have been declared, and the vital breaths themselves have also been explained in brief; that which is their ultimate reality is now being determined," as expressed by the subsequent commentary beginning with "yat tu" (but that which...).
It is elaborated upon as follows:

the meaning is that one must state such things as, "Of what nature are these vital breaths (prāṇas), and how is their reality maintained? This is the subsequent scripture concerning the five elements and the eternal principles (tattvas).

In order to determine the true nature of the body, the instruments [of action], and the self, this supreme Brāhmaṇa has been commenced; now that very reality which was intended to be clearly revealed through the negation of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) in the "Not so, not so" (*neti neti*) Brāhmaṇa is being stated here. Regarding the phrase "of the real" (*satyasya*):

The meaning is that the commencement of the Brāhmaṇa is for the purpose of explaining the essential nature of these two: that which is denoted by the word "truth" in the genitive case (the object to be abandoned) and that which is denoted by the word "truth" in the nominative case (the object to be accepted).
Having thus stated the connection, he begins the exposition of the Śruti.

The supreme Brahman, which by its own nature is formless, is designated as having two forms due to causes such as ignorance (avidyā), just as the ether (viyat) appears dual when it is contained within a jar.

The meaning is that Brahman is thus twofold by way of the forms of what is to be abandoned (*heya*) and what is not to be abandoned (*aheya*). Alternatively, he says that the two forms born of Brahman are said to be only what is to be abandoned: "Or one should know the two forms of Brahman—the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*)—along with their latent impressions (*savāsana*). If it is asked how these two possess the nature of being forms of Brahman:
By these two, Brahman is "rūpyate," meaning it is known; however, it is not like white or other such qualities. Thus he says:
"Brahman itself is made manifest (rūpyate) by those two, for its nature as Brahman is not possessed of form.
It has been stated that Brahman is of two forms by way of its aspects as the rejectable and the non-rejectable. In that regard, the causal form—
It is elaborated through four Vārttikas; they are written here for easy understanding:

That Brahman, when limited by the adjunct of mere ignorance (*avidyā-mātra-upādhi*), is called the cause. That very same [Brahman], by taking recourse to the adjunct of the intellect (*buddhi-upādhi*), attains the state of being the knower. Abiding within the adjunct of its own mental modification (*vṛtti-upādhi*), it is that which is called "knowledge."
It is said that whatever is connected with a deity or a sense organ is designated by that very name;

likewise, that which is connected with the body and so forth becomes characterized by suffering, birth, and the like. One who identifies with cattle, wealth, and so on is called "wealthy" or "possessor of cows"; similarly, the inner controller is called the "Witness."

And thus, through ignorance (*avidyā*) and the false superimpositions (*mithyādhyāsa*) that are its effects, the immeasurable (*aprameya*) is measured as "the omniscient one. He summarizes this unreal form:
"In this way, first of all, this form of Brahman is born from the cause of delusion (*moha*). Now he shows the form that is to be abandoned:
The true nature of the Self is cognizable solely through the intuition of its own essence;
it is neither excluded from nor followed by anything else, being unborn due to the impossibility of a second entity, and it is not the referent of either a sentence or a word.

Because it exists as both particularity and generality, it is not to be known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); however, in the case of the "Other" (*parākhya*), there is no such coordination (*asamanvaya*). That which is independent of the *mātrās* and so forth arises from the coordination of ignorance (*avidyā*). These two and a half verses of the *Vārttika* are easy to understand. Now, if [it is argued that] it is indeed independent of the *mātrās* and so forth...

How is its establishment [attained]? To this he says: "The oneness of meaning between the two words of the sentence does not arise from the self; rather, it is self-luminous. This means that it is self-manifesting. If so, why is it not self-dependent? To this he says: "But the second would belong to the self."

"Non-self as its cause" means that the world, being accompanied by ignorance, is established as dependent on another; therefore, it is self-luminous [in appearance] yet imagined like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—this is the meaning. He states the result of the world’s being imagined: "By myself I am, by myself I am one, I am alone. By myself...

The meaning is that the Self is thus non-dual; or rather, explaining the statement "one should know the two forms of Brahman" by way of negation, it is said "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), taking ignorance as the limit, which expresses the meaning of the word "evil" regarding these two forms of Brahman.
He brings about the restriction that "there are only two" by means of the term "determined.
He says that the two, the formed and the formless, which are characterized by specific attributes such as mortality and so forth, are to be restricted [as the objects of knowledge]. (p. 326)

"By those subsequent qualifiers of the same class when they are combined. Regarding the phrase "and it is formless," there is no restrictive particle (*eva*) here; thus, it has been stated by the authors of the *Vibhāṣā* that "it is indeed with form.
He states the reason for this: the word "or" (*vā*) is employed by drawing back [the previous term] through the word "and" (*ca*).
And that form of Brahman is indeed corporeal, and [Brahman] is indeed corporeal;
the meaning is that the word "eva" (indeed) has been applied there in the sense of restriction (*evakāśe*), and thus it was stated.
By means of the two instances of "eva," the mutual exclusion between the corporeal and the incorporeal is not expressed; rather—

If there were anything else [other than these two] at other times, that would be excluded. Alternatively, the meaning of the particle *eva* (only) in both cases is the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). This is precisely the meaning of the reading "the word *pāpa* [is used].
Anticipating the objection that the two attributes of the formed and the formless are distinguished from other attributes, he says:

"Or rather, ignorance (avidyā) is qualified as the Supreme Brahman by means of characteristics such as 'formed' (mūrta) and 'formless' (amūrta); a mutual conjunction of attributes is not intended. Thus, there is a single referent for the qualified object because the attributes belong to that [single] entity; they do not [belong] to one another.
Likewise, the statement that their conjunction could never occur independently is an elaboration of what preceded.

Anticipating the objection that the form of Brahman— both manifest and unmanifest— is not directly perceptible for one who stands as a detached observer, he says: "Of Brahman, the Supreme Self, who is the goal of the person of realized knowledge, and of the one enveloped in darkness, there are two [forms]."

Regarding the phrase "in form" (*rūpe*), he states the reason for this as "because it is not distinct from that" (*tadanyāvyatirekataḥ*). The meaning is that the Self is non-distinct from Brahman, which is intended to be other than the Self. [Objection: But surely, because of the existence of both the possessor of form and form itself, there is a distinction; thus, the doctrine of non-duality (*advaita*) is lost. [Reply: This is not so; the point is as follows: *The commentary on the *Brahmasiddhi* by Śaṅkhapāṇi, p. 120, ll. 1–3:* "Regarding 'in form,' he states the reason: 'because it is not distinct from that. The meaning is that the Self is non-distinct from Brahman, which is considered other than the Self. [Objection: But surely, due to the state of being the possessor of form and form, there is a distinction, and thus the loss of non-duality. [Reply: This is not so. *The *Brahmasiddhivyākhyā* by Ānandapūrṇa Vidyāsāgara, p. 245, l. 17–p. 246, l. 1:* "In the word 'form' (*rūpe*), he states the reason: 'because it is not distinct from that. The meaning is that the Self is non-distinct from Brahman, which is intended to be other than the Self. [Objection: But surely, because of the existence of the possessor of form and form, there is a distinction, and thus the non-duality is destroyed. [Reply: This is not so. *The *Brahmasiddhivyākhyā* by Citsukha, p. 198, l. 1–p. 199, l. 1:* "In the word 'form,' he states the reason: 'because it is not distinct from that.
