He establishes this through two verses (*vārtika*) preceded by an illustration:

"Just as an unknown garland is always [perceived] as a snake or the like that has been imagined—whether that [snake] be real or unreal—there is neither a difference [between them] nor a non-difference. Indeed, this [world] is not so [different] from that [garland] by way of difference."
The two Brahmans always exist by themselves and are not distinct from it; indeed, they are non-dual Brahman alone—
[like] a form composed of parts such as water, which is plump, possessed of structure, and firm.
That which is contrary to this would be formless (*amūrta*), partless, and not like space (*deśavat*);

it would be subject to movement, subject to death, and characterized by perishability. That which is contrary to this would be immortal (*amṛta*) and eternal (*dhruva*), yet it would perish; it would be dependent, situated here, having moved, and all-pervading.
It does not remain as that which is contrary to it, nor does it remain as "existent" in its manifest form, characterized by the specific qualities being perceived.

"That which is perceived is contrary to that; thus, that which is not perceived is so described"—these are the *vārttikas* explaining the meaning of the terms, intended for easy understanding. Previously, it was stated that Brahman is the substantive (*viśeṣya*) qualified by attributes such as having a form (*mūrta*) and so forth; now, [the nature of] the elements (*bhūta*) is addressed.
And he says that there are two elements:

earth, water, and fire—these are called the "formed" (mūrta) two elements; and the "formless" (amūrta) are air and space alone. That which is formed is mortal and stable, and likewise, it is characterized by earthiness.

They know the three fires to be the formless and immortal; that which is the pair of wind and space is traditionally taught—this is an elaboration of what preceded. Now, [the text describes] the mutual relationship of the specific forms, beginning from the start up to the end, and finally beginning from the end.
By means of two explanatory verses (*vārtika*), he demonstrates the relationship of cause and effect from beginning to end:

"Because it is corporeal, it will be imagined as mortal; because it is mortal, it remains [in that state]; because it remains, it is graspable by the senses; having determined it as distinct through the 'this-ness' [of perception]."
"Because it possesses a specific designation (sopākhyatva), it is not all-pervasive; because it exists in only one part, it is situated [in that place];

and because it is situated, it is mortal; and because it is mortal, it is indeed corporeal (mūrta). This stated principle is shown to apply to the incorporeal (amūrta) and so forth as well: "Due to being incorporeal, there is immortality; that which is all-pervasive is beyond the senses."
Because it transcends the senses, it is all-pervasive; because it is all-pervasive, it is therefore immortal;
and because it does not abide, it is formless and devoid of the manifestation of any shape—this is the meaning of "because it does not abide."
He summarizes the meaning already stated: "The mutual connection of the embodied and so forth, by way of cause and its fruit, is like a rosary because their respective capacities are not lost.
Thus, the thorough connection of the embodied and so forth is to be understood through the relationship of cause and that which possesses the cause.
"Since, when even one [of these] is possible, all are possible"— this is an elaboration of what was stated previously. Because, in the manner described,
there is a mutual inclusion of the qualifiers, for that very reason, having mentioned merely the corporeal (mūrta), [the text proceeds].

The restriction "only the formed" (*mūrta eva*) has been made; however, having spoken only of the formless (*amūrta*), it must likewise be restricted. Therefore, he says that the mention [of the formless] right there is for the sake of such a restriction.
He then states the meaning of the passage beginning with "this is the formed" (*tad etan mūrtam*):
Of those two [categories] mentioned, the first, the corporeal (mūrta), is now described:
"The other [category] consists of air, the intermediate space, and so forth; these three elements are accepted here. He demonstrates the presence of the four attributes within these three elements:
This is embodied, possessing configuration; likewise, it is mortal, subject to destruction; it is situated, delimited; and this is the qualification of "existent" (sat).

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "of this embodied one" (*tasyaitasya mūrtasya*) as follows: the repetition is made for the sake of [establishing] the fourfold essence of this fourfold particularity consisting of earth, water, fire, and air; thus, it refers to that which is characterized by the qualification of being fourfold.

The meaning is that the repetition [of the mantra] is for the purpose of demonstrating that the mandala of the three elements should be constructed as qualified by all the attributes taken together, and not by each attribute individually; this indicates another purpose according to the maxim: "A further utterance [or additional statement] suggests a different meaning."

For he is the supreme of everything, consisting of the fourfold [powers] even in the moon and the fire; he is remembered as the essence of the three elements within his own domain. In this context, where it is said "he who shines," the *maṇḍala* (orb) is intended;
for the fourfold group, beginning with the formal [mūrtādi], is grasped within the *maṇḍala*. This is because of that.
The two *vārtikas* are easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "for this is the taste of the existent" (*sato hy eṣa rasaḥ*), the word "for" (*hi*) has the sense of a reason;
and the term "of the existent" (*sataḥ*) is intended as an indicator for the qualifiers of the other [elements]. This is what he states:
"For the connection of the four is indeed [the reason]," by which the reason is here made clear. And there is the mention of "the existent."

One should understand that this is an illustration of the four; just as the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇasāra*) is the locus for the eye whose nature is the instrument, so too is the orb (*maṇḍala*) the locus for Hiraṇyagarbha whose nature is the instrument—
this is easily understood— and yet, within that orb, there arises the cognition of something else.
The meaning is that [the maṇḍala] is not to be performed; it has been stated that the maṇḍala is the effect of the three elements.
In this regard, the following objection is raised: the word *rasa* denotes fire (*tejas*), according to the Vedic scripture, "Fire is *rasa*."

In that context, why is the word *rasa* (taste) alone employed in the mandala? [One might argue] that the word *ap* (water) and so forth could be used, since there is no difference in their being effects of the three elements. To this, he replies: "Because fire (*tejas*) holds predominance in the manifestation of form (*rūpa-nirvāṇa*) by way of general rule (*utsarga*), therefore the designation of *rasatva* (the state of being taste) is made."
Within the nature of the maṇḍala, the moistened earthly element is cooked by heat;
for such is the primary function of heat in the manifestation of the [vowels] beginning with *a*. This is an elaboration of what preceded.
There is an alternative reading, *apsvantar* (within the waters), and because of its usage by learned scholars, it refers to the maṇḍala.
He states that this is the essence: "The essence of the three elements is called the *maṇḍala* (orb);

indeed, the wise say that these three elements have this as their essence. He explains the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "That which... as follows: "The instrument [of perception] which resides in the abode of the orb..."
"That which is resorted to by the Lord Virāj, the God of gods, is now described here":

thus, that which is within the Sun is designated as the "instrumental self" (karaṇātmā), because therein is the connection with the formless through its nature as the essence of air and space; this refers to what was previously [stated].
The proliferation (*prapañca*). Because it acts as the essence of air and space, it is the internal self of the instruments (*karaṇa*); thus he says (p.
"The emergence of air and space from Īśvara is for the sake of accomplishing the commencement of the *kaliṅga*."

Because the *liṅga* arises from its cause, therefore the *rasa* belongs to those two; for this is the *rasa* of that—this statement is as before. But when it is said, "This is the *rasa* of wind and space," the reason is shown: "for this is the *rasa* of that," as previously stated regarding the nature of the *maṇḍala*.

Having thus presented the view of the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), he presents the view of Bhartṛprapañca for the sake of refuting it, stating: "Some declare Hiraṇyagarbha to be the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) and the Essence (rasa). He states the reason for this here:
Since the cause is denoted here by the word "rasa," this is the meaning: here, the word "rasa" refers to the cause of air and ether, or the cause of the remaining three elements— that is,
its nature as the cause of the five elements.
This [agency] is possible only for the *kṣetrajña* Hiraṇyagarbha and not for anyone else;

therefore, he alone is said [to be the agent]. He establishes his causality by showing that the actions of Hiraṇyagarbha are the manifesting agents (*prayoktr-vyaktyoḥ*) of wind and the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).

Because he is called the "knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*), this very essence—namely, his being the cause of the two elements—establishes Hiraṇyagarbha’s nature; thus it is said: "The essence of the two elements is to be known as the insentient Person within the mandala."

If it is argued that since the scripture has already stated two causes for the establishment of "this indeed is the essence" by naming the cause, what is the purpose of stating the reason? To this he replies:
"The instrument of the knower of the field [is established] because the matter proposed is fully accomplished through the statement of the logical principle."

Therefore, the reasoning is stated here. He elaborates upon its causality by means of action (*karman*): within this orb (*maṇḍala*), that which has attained the state of the inner cognitive self (*vijñānātmatva*)—due to the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*), mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and action (*karman*), arising from a mutual causal relationship—possesses a form consisting of action (*karmarūpa*).

That [space] is the cause of wind; sound is the activity of that wind, which consists of vibration. Through the channel of air and space, fire arises from that; once fire is understood as being included therein, so too are water and earth.

"So be it"—this is the meaning. That which, by the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), karma, and so forth, has attained the state of being the self of consciousness (*vijñānātmatva*), produces the space of karma (*karmākāśa*); immediately thereafter, it becomes the space of karma. For that karma in such a state, the wind is the effect; from that...
The meaning is that wind arises; from the action that has entered into the state of wind, fire arises;

from that, water arises; and from the action that has entered into the state of water, earth arises. Thus, by the power of its own action, because of its being the cause of wind and space, [the world arises] from Hiraṇyagarbha.
Regarding this state of being *rasa*, he says:
"Arising occurs through human action itself, which has become *rasa*. (p. 334)

"Because of their state of being *rasa*, the male [Puruṣa] exists within those two, namely air (*vāyu*) and the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). He states the authoritative proof for this stated meaning in the passage beginning with "by means of intelligence and austerity" (*medhayā tapasā*). And thus it was previously cited.
Having taken all of this to heart, he declares that Hiraṇyagarbha possesses the nature of *rasa* by means of this principle.

"The Person (puruṣa) is denoted by the word 'rasa'. He states that the reasoning by which Hiraṇyagarbha is the referent of the word "rasa" has been set forth in the aphorism: "For this is his essence" (asya hy eṣa rasaḥ).
For it is said, "This belongs to him," and by this statement based on logic and scripture, he is so described.
He restates this view:
"This cannot be so, because its form is dissimilar to that of the liquid (rasa)"; that is to say, there is a dissimilarity in their substantiality (*bhūtatva*).
He said, "No":
you have declared that the *maṇḍala* is the essence (*rasa*) of the three material elements;
yet it is endowed with the four attributes beginning with form (*mūrta*), just like those three elements, even though [the other two] are immaterial (*amūrta*).

"Let the *rasa* be understood as having the nature of the *liṅga*; for since the application of the scriptural statement is the same, it is not proper here to accept it otherwise, as that would entail the defect of being of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). This is the meaning: the orb [of the sun] is insentient by virtue of being the *rasa* of the material form (*mūrtarasa*)."

Even though it is grasped as having the nature of formless essence (*amūrtarasa*), the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) must be understood as being merely an instrument (*karaṇa*); otherwise, there would be a discordance in the sentence due to the apprehension of something insentient in one instance [and not in another].
He states that even by the term "solidified essence" (*mūrtarasa*), the conscious Brahman entered into the orb is not meant;
thus he says: "Now, if it is argued that although the 'solidified essence' was mentioned, the 'grasping' (*graha*) refers only to the conscious [Brahman]," he here provides the refutation:

"What you have said is far too little, because [Brahman] is for us always like the Self. By speaking thus, the meaning is that even by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*), Brahman may be grasped; who is there to prevent it?
The point is that there would be an abandonment of the literal meaning of the scripture. Moreover, of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*)...
The status of being a cause is untenable for anything other than Brahman, since Brahman alone is the cause of all; this he states:

"For no cause whatsoever is accepted apart from the Akṣa (the Self); rather, it is the inner self alone that is the cause in its various respective forms. Thus, by virtue of being the support of the [solar] orb, the Person (puruṣa) [is the cause].

And because it is so heard [in scripture], he says that the *liṅga* is the *puruṣa*. Furthermore, within the support (*ādhāra*) which is the *maṇḍala*, let it be understood as the *liṅga*-self itself, since the instrument (*karaṇa*) resides therein;
thus, the conscious self (*vijñānātman*) is the *liṅga*. It has been stated that Brahman alone is the cause.

In this regard, it is asked: "Since Brahman is immutable (*kūṭastha*), how can it be the cause? To that, he says: "Because the Person (*puruṣa*), when unknown, is designated by the terms 'effect' and 'cause'; [it is so] because its nature is falsely perceived as unknown, but not [because it actually changes]."
In reality.
(Thus it is said on p. 336.
Now, one might object: since the word "puruṣa" (person) is applied to the support of the maṇḍala, it must refer to the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) alone; to this he says:

If it is argued that "in this world, the designation 'puruṣa' is not seen applied to insentient things," he replies: "It is not so, because [the term] is seen even in the case of insentient things. To the question "Where is this seen? he says: "They [made] these seven puruṣas," and so forth.

From Vedic statements such as "The Person is eternal," etc., the designation "Person" (puruṣa) is seen to apply even to that which lacks consciousness, such as in the case of intention (*vivakṣā*) and so forth. Having concluded the investigation,
he resumes the explanation of the Śruti itself, by making known the limits of the discourse concerning the Adhyātma through the mention of the Adhidaivata.

"The glorification [of the Self] is this division between the formed and the formless; now the spiritual (adhyātma) is being described. He says that whatever is other than the space of the heart and the vital breath—the triad of elements beginning with earth, namely the body—is indeed what is denoted by the word "formed" (mūrta): He says: "Now the spiritual (adhyātma) is being described. He states that whatever is other than the space of the heart and the vital breath—the triad of elements beginning with earth, namely the body—is indeed what is denoted by the word "formed" (mūrta).

The triad of elements beginning with earth is also included within the body by the term "material" (*mūrta*), as it is said: "that which is from breath, that which is in the heart, the mind, and what is other. Here, he states that the eyeball, which occupies the place of the *maṇḍa*, is the substratum of the instruments: "it would be for the three [organs] beginning with sight and taste."
To the question, "How can the eye be designated by the term 'taste'? he replies: "In this case, light is specifically established [as its essence] for the entire body.

Regarding the phrase "because of being the creator, there is no doubt," he states the proof here: "The first refinement"—for a mantra-text is also seen stating "ever devoid of semen"—and thus it is established by scripture; in this way, the five elements along with their effects [are explained].

These have been explained according to the scripture as being both manifest (mūrta) and unmanifest (amūrta). In that regard, since the definition of the manifest as "the state of being an agent" does not terminate at this point, he says that this division into manifest and unmanifest is intended here for the purpose of including the root cause by means of the word "manifest."
It is said that even so, this much is not grasped as the *adhidaiva*;

here he states the reason: "Since the two forms of the entire Brahman—the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*)—are intended [to be expressed], therefore this totality would not belong to the *devatā* and the *adhyātma*. This is the meaning.

For the purpose of establishing the non-duality of Brahman, the Śruti postulates that the embodied form and so forth are the forms of Brahman; and that non-duality is established through the characteristics of the embodied and so forth as described for both the internal self (adhyātma) and the divine principle (adhidaivata).

"Because the primary cause has not been grasped. By the word "deity," the presiding divinity (adhidaivata) is understood; and since the characteristics as previously described are impossible in the case of ether and the other elements, he states that the undifferentiated (avyākṛta) must be understood here, for those [elements] whose effects have already begun are not what is grasped.
And there is the possibility [of this] on the aforementioned stages (*bhūmi*) in their primary sense, according to the characteristics described here. Now, even if...
The characteristics of the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*) do not apply to the five elements in their primary sense;

nevertheless, that very [definition] must be accepted, because there is no reason to abandon what has been heard in scripture. To this, he says: "An explanation alone is a proper definition; otherwise, it would not be a definition of them."

"But the detailed exposition is stated here concerning objects that are delimited. To the question "What, then, is cognized?", he says in response: "This being so, wherever the fourfold definition beginning with 'having form' (mūrta) is present, there it is complete."
Regarding the phrase "of the mortal, the causeless, and the effect": this is elaborated in the subsequent half-verse and the commentary (*vārttika*).
That which is denoted by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*), being the primary cause of all causes, is capable [in that sense] alone to possess the characteristic of being formless (*amūrta*). On earth...

Furthermore, regarding that which was stated as the primary definition of the "material" (*mūrta*)— namely, that among intermediate entities, the material is the definition of the material— he says: "The definition [of these] consists of objects situated between the two [extremes], whose characteristics are mutually intermingled."

"It would be merely figurative for the last two and the middle two among these. Now, one might object: "Since the conventional usage of 'formed' (mūrta) and 'formless' (amūrta) does not exist regarding entities that occupy a middle position, how can there be a figurative application of the definition there? To this, he says: "In that case as well, the conventional usage of 'formed' and 'formless' is observed."
Thus, he concludes from his own perspective:
"In order to grasp the primary sense [of the term] and to establish the definition of pervasion, [the argument extends] from the earth up to space."

It may be asked: "What is the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of the formed and the formless? Thus, the characteristic of the formed is fully present in earth, and the characteristic of the formless is present in unmanifested matter and in intermediate entities;
however, the characteristics of the formed and the formless are not entirely present everywhere, but only in certain places.

Something exists. Therefore, since the possession of qualities such as material form has been explained in relation to earth—which itself possesses qualities such as material form—the doctrine of Bhartṛprapañca is established as faultless; now, he proceeds to follow the interpretation of the Śruti itself:

Because it is observed in scripture that "this one sees with the right eye," some specific distinction of the *liṅga* is intended for the right eye; and he states that the non-measurement of the *liṅga* is an indicator for its placement in the right eye, for [it is said] "in the world, the right [side] is powerful."

"Since that limb was seen there, it is desired here with effort based on the scriptural statement 'the right eye'. He recounts the preceding context in order to establish the connection for the passage beginning with "Of him, indeed... [by means of] the division between the body and the vital breath (piṇḍa-prāṇa).

Thus, the distinction between the embodied and the unembodied forms of Brahman, both with respect to the internal self (*adhyātma*) and the divine (*adhidaivata*), has been explained. Now, he states the connection [between the sections] as follows: "Now, at this point...

The meaning of this statement is as follows: "We shall describe the nature of that very subtle body (*liṅga*), which consists of the instruments [of action], as well as the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the non-self. This sentence is intended to establish that the latent impressions—namely, the impressions of passion and so forth—belong specifically to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is the essence of the formless [subtle body].
He states the reason for attachment (*rāga*) and so forth residing in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) with the words:
"Because of its connection with the corporeal and incorporeal, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) rests upon the subtle body (*liṅga*). This is the meaning:
therefore, the entire connection with the head and other parts belongs to the internal organ alone; hence, it [the attachment] belongs to that alone.

"Passion and so forth are produced by that [mind]. Now, an objection is raised: "Is this not a fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya)? He replies: "It appears as such through delusion; indeed, it is said that the Puruṣa perceives it in the form of the delusion of its own reflection.
Therefore, he states that the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) alone consists of the three types of latent impressions (vāsanā): "accumulated with manifold latent impressions."
"The *talliṅga* (that which bears its own characteristic) is like a painted cloth, similar to an illusory conjuration (*māyendrajāla*),

and is the locus of the self's delusion. Here, for the sake of purifying his own doctrine, he establishes the division of the quarters [of the verse], stating that it is "only this much," wherein there is no resort to error.

The Vijñānavādins, as well as the Naiyāyikas and others, [hold that] this form consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which is a quality (*guṇa*) of the self (*ātman*) as a substantial entity (*dravya*), is its transmigratory state.
The Vaiśeṣikas and others [ask]: "What quality, existing in the *pradhāna*, is [perceived] for the sake of the *puruṣa*?"
"The followers of Kapila [hold that] this [Prakṛti], being independent (svatantra), proceeds by means of a cause, thinking 'this is for me'. This is the meaning of these three Vārtikas.

The Buddhists maintain that this very internal organ— characterized by its mental modifications, naturally transitory, and the substratum of attachment and other passions— is the self, and nothing else;
they hold that this internal organ alone is what is grasped by the notion of "I."
The Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that the Self is not something other than the various qualities such as passion (rāga) and so forth.

[They hold] that the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) alone is not the Self, but rather that the Self is distinct from it—immutable (kūṭastha), all-pervading (sarvagata), and self-luminous (svayaṃprakāśa). This internal organ exists for the sake of its experience (bhoga) and liberation (apavarga).

"It proceeds"—thus says the follower of Kapila. That wherein such a variety shines is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); it is this that is called the cause here, and not the Self. Now, regarding the statement beginning with "the cause" (*hetu*) from the *Bhartṛprapañca* [text]:

He demonstrates that the meaning has been stated by himself: "Even for the purpose of refutation, some who consider themselves followers of the Upaniṣads, being internally purified, having composed a system, speak [thus], O scholars at the end of the Vedānta. When that...
In order to demonstrate the connection of the sentence beginning with "the cause" (*hetu*), he provides a summary of what has preceded,
showing it thus:
"Whatever scope of the discourse there was, which concerned the envelopment of the *kṣetrajña*."
Whether with respect to the internal (adhyātma) or the divine (adhidaiva), that which is undifferentiated (avyākṛta) becomes differentiated (vyākṛta) through the division of name and form;
it is only this much [that exists] here, whether it be embodied (mūrta) or indeed unembodied (amūrta).

"It is called *sat* and *tyat*. This is the meaning: whatever collection of effects is intended as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), which has arisen from the Undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*), all that is designated by the word *satya*;
it has been explained in the form of the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*). Now, [as for] the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*)...

Since it was stated that "it is indeed the truth" refers to the truthfulness of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), one might ask: how is the truthfulness of the elements (*bhūtas*) explained? To this, he says:
"The truthfulness of the vital breaths also [arises] from their connection with the truth of the elements and so forth."

The meaning is that the vital breaths (prāṇas) possess reality because they are effects of that which is denoted by the word "truth" (satya). He establishes this in order to explain that even other categories of worldly activity bound up with the vital breaths exist solely through their connection with the elements (bhūtas): He says: [the following].
Tell us: how is it that all these vital breaths (*prāṇas*), which are characterized by the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*),

being devoid of name and form, yet existing through the cause of their connection with Reality, have become embodied beings manifest like the vital breaths themselves— though they remain formless— and are thus rendered fit for designation?
The meaning of "the vital breaths indeed, and not otherwise" is as follows: the eleven vital breaths,
like the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), are characterized by the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) and serve as its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),
because they are effects produced through the conjunction with the five elements which are designated as real.

Some explain the meaning of this passage as follows: "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*), which were originally devoid of name and form (*nāmarūpa*), have become possessed of name and form (*nāmarūpin*)," based on the preceding scriptural statement beginning with "Of that... (*tasya ha*).
He says that everything denoted by the word "truth" has been shown:
"All this truth here has been clearly purified by the Śruti. Thus, [he describes] the nature of the *kṣetrajña* who is distinct from the mass of truth.
That which remains to be stated is the sentence beginning with "the reason" (*hetu*), etc., for the purpose of that [remaining point]; thus he says:

"But that which is the true nature of the very Self consisting of consciousness, which is distinct from the aggregate of reality—that alone remains to be stated now. When this Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*)...
He says that when one has turned away from the mass of reality, the well-known status of the embodied self (*kṣetrajña*) as an enjoyer, along with the body, senses, and so forth, ceases to exist:
"In this state, the distinction [between them] ceases; this is the enjoyer."

"The conscious self [is one thing], while the deities are of the nature of the unconscious self"— thus he reveals the cause of differentiation by means of the cessation of that very cause of differentiation:
"For this particularity, characterized by name, form, and so forth, belongs to the substratum (the body), and not [to the Self]."
"And that [reality] is purified of name, form, and so forth by its own nature" (p.
for all distinctions such as name and form have the five elements as their limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Regarding that...

The meaning is that because [the Self] has been separated from the self, this division ceases. This refers to the fact that, having purified the expansion of the all-pervading, established mass of reality (*satyarāśi*), that which is the Self of all-cognition is demonstrated; this is what is meant here by "of the mass of reality."
He states that the nature of that which is distinct [from the material] is common to all knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*):
"Therefore, this characteristic would be the same for all knowers of the field."

"Because no distinction whatsoever is possible here. He says, "That which is the common form is called its cause, and so forth," thereby indicating that the "form" (rūpa) of that person is what is being described now.
[An objection: But does this not also refer to the corporeal and other such qualities? [The author] replies, "No," regarding the person (puṃsaḥ).

The meaning is that what was stated in the passage beginning with "Form has been exhausted; the two forms of the Brahman of evil consist of the formed and the formless" refers to this. If one asks, "What kind of form is here said to belong to living beings?
he replies, "Non-material," by which [he means] for him...

The nature of the qualified [self] is held to be consciousness, as it exists as something differentiated from the supreme non-dual Self. And here, the physical form of water is intended to be illustrated by the phrase "as [the cloth] dyed with safflower," which consists of the accumulation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Of that—
345) He summarizes the relationship of the sentence beginning with "the reason" (*hetu*) as stated by Bhartṛprapañca:
"Some have thus elaborated its very relationship. Now, this...
He refutes the [alleged] connection, stating: "That is incorrect; it is explained according to the proper principle as follows.

Since it was stated that its nature consists of the accumulation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he says that a connection with latent impressions is not possible for the inner self (*pratīc*): [The text continues: "It has been said that its form consists of the accumulation of latent impressions (*vāsanopacayātmakaṃ tadrūpam*).
He states that a connection with latent impressions is not possible for the inner self (*pratīco na saṃbhavati*)."

For it is observed that the perfuming of flowers and the like occurs only in relation to substances of the same class, such as cloth and the like, and not in substances of a different class; indeed, no perfuming is admitted in the case of space (*vyoman*). And how could there be perfuming in consciousness (*caitanya*), which is neither a substance nor of the same class? Furthermore:

Is the form called *vāsanā* (latent impression) distinct from the Self or non-distinct? If it were non-distinct, then Brahman would not be the Self, and because there would be a difference within the Self, [the Self] would be insentient;
therefore, [this position] is futile. Thus he says: "If *vāsanā* is a constituent part of the agent, and consciousness is like a potsherd..."
"Latent impressions (vāsanās) would be fruitless because they do not exist apart from consciousness.

He states that there is no connection with latent impressions because [the Self] is unattached, immutable, and not an object: [The verse continues: Since it is unattached, immutable, and not an object, there is no connection with latent impressions.
Thus he says:

For consciousness residing in the ear is not employed for the perception of form; even though there is no difference in their being objects [of cognition], how could there be a determination of sameness? Furthermore, the negation of the six modifications applies to the conscious self.
Furthermore, it is repeatedly heard in the Śruti that he is called "the Unattached" (asaṅga). One who says, "He has attained [this state] through the conjunction of the elements,
yet he is not composed of the five elements," will be laughed at in this world.

This is easily understood even by children; furthermore, you yourself have stated that when the distinction between the embodied and the unembodied ceases, the division between the individual soul as the enjoyer and the deities as the conscious selves also ceases. Therefore, upon the cessation of that division—

The differentiation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) also ceases; for in the absence of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), there is an absence of effects. Therefore, if you maintain that there is no forgetting of that [nature], or if you do not admit a plurality of latent impressions, then you cannot possibly assert a distinction between those who possess latent impressions and the self that knows them. Thus he says:

Without forgetting his own statement that "the distinction between this [Self] as having form and being formless ceases," how can there be talk of a distinction in latent impressions (*vāsanā*)? Once again, he presents another conceptualization of the followers of Bhartṛprapañca for the sake of refuting it.
In that way, they compose a virtuous system devoid of logic:
"The aggregate of manifest and unmanifest objects is indeed considered one external [category];
the supreme aggregate called the Supreme Self (paramātman) is designated here as the middle one; and this third one is..."
By those two, this agent who is the instigator of the heap [of karma], having arisen from the clapping of hands, [is joined] with the self as the enjoyer.

The collection of cultivation, knowledge, action, and so forth is the motivator (*prayojaka*), while the aggregate of the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*) is the motivated (*prayojya*); such is the means (*sādhana*). This is the meaning: one external aggregate, consisting of the formed and the formless, is indeed intended; the supreme aggregate of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), together with the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), is the other.
The aggregate mass of karma consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is the intermediate one, and it is the motivator of the mass of the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*).

It is not something to be spoken of as either the motivator or the motivated, nor is it something to be accomplished. Having thus established the conceptualization of these three masses, other conceptualizations [are also] presented by the logicians.
He says that they bring about what is called a "false agreement," adding:
"They desire to make peace with the logicians according to their strength. To explain how this is so, he says:

Having stated, "This causal aggregate (prayojaka-rāśi) indeed rests upon the subtle body (liṅga)," they then postulate it otherwise out of fear of being identified as Sāṃkhyas. The meaning is this: first, they assert that the causal aggregate rests upon the subtle body; however, [they then say]: "In that case..."
"Because this [view] belongs to the Sāṃkhya school, they postulate it otherwise out of fear of that. He demonstrates this alternative postulation:
"Just as fragrance, though residing in a flower, remains by resorting to a folded leaf."

Just as in the case of the gathering of flowers, so too, by virtue of being situated in the *liṅga*, [the impressions] exist in the form of latent dispositions (*vāsanā*); thus, the latent dispositions, desires, and karmas reside only in the *liṅga*, not in the Self.

"The self emerges from the *liṅga* just as fragrance emerges from a fragrant casket"—this is an elaboration of what was stated previously. Thus, he explains how the individual soul (*jīva*), though devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) as a supreme portion [of the Self], nevertheless possesses qualities: "Though devoid of qualities, that supreme single portion [becomes qualified] by that which has arrived externally."
"It is declared that through action, the one endowed with qualities becomes manifest. By those such as the Vaiśeṣikas who speak thus, the mind has been followed; so he says:
"And therefore, the agent and the enjoyer, as well as the bound and the liberated, is the *vijñānātman* (the conscious self)."
"Kaṇabhuj [the Vaiśeṣika] thus relies upon the mind alone. By what sequence does the aggregate of the motivators reach the self? To this he says:
"From the aggregate of the elements comes the subtle body (liṅga), and from the aggregate of karma..."

"From the *liṅga* he went to the Self; from the cause of association with the *liṅga*. This means that the causal aggregate (*prayojakarāśi*) went from the aggregate of elements (*bhūtarāśi*) to the *liṅga*, and from the *liṅga* he went to the Self—that is, due to the connection between the Self and the *liṅga*. There is another [explanation] as well:

His process is now stated: for the sake of following the views of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, it is said that even *avidyā*, which is the power (*śakti*) of Kṛṣṇa, arises from the Supreme Being alone; having undergone transformation, it abides within the Supreme Self as the individual self (*vijñānātman*), such that the living being is called "the knower" (*jñānin*).
The Vaiśeṣikas and others [hold that] that mind is followed by ignorance (avidyā), meaning it is stated to have the individual soul (jīva) as its locus. This refers to ignorance arising from another.
He establishes that [the defect] has the living being as its locus by means of an illustration:
"Just as the defect consisting of barrenness was born from the earth itself... having corrupted a single portion of the earth, it is like a heap of barren soil"—thus says the Sāṃkhya.
To refute the claim that they follow the established doctrine out of delusion, he says:

"It is not proper to imagine this, because it would contradict the established doctrine of the Veda; for [if one were to do so], it would entail that the Supreme is subject to modification and possesses parts, and that the individual soul (jīva) is a part or a modification."

The meaning is that there is a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning [the Lord] being gross and so forth. He states that this was also said during the investigation of the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*:
"This has been stated previously as well, namely, how there would be a sublation of the Vedānta. He clarifies this very point:
all the defects characterized by transmigratory existence and so forth, which were attributed to the Supreme when He is described as possessing parts (*sakala*), [would likewise follow].

"...they come to realize the inner self as one. Now, if it is argued that the individual soul (jīva) is neither a part of the Supreme nor a transformation, but rather something entirely different from Him, to that he says:
"In the consciousness of the Knower of the Field, there is absolutely no possibility of oneness with the Supreme Self by its own nature."

The meaning is that, in that case, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning the identity (*tādātmya*) of the individual knower (*kṣetrajña*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*).
[Objection:
Is it not the case that the Self, characterized by the marks [of the body], is intended as a supreme part through conceptual construction, and not [as something else]?

To the objection, "In that case, what is the fault [of the body being the self], just as the hand and other limbs are? he says: "Furthermore, the region of the metaphorical designation (upacāraka) is considered the very mark (liṅga) of the self. The meaning is that the self has the mark as its limiting adjunct (liṅgopādhi), for it is that which is marked (liṅgyate) [by it]. Here he states the refutation: "It is not so; when the mark is destroyed, [the notion of the self] residing in the latent impressions (vāsanā) is not tenable."

If one were to speak thus, there would be a contradiction with one's own system; for it is your doctrine that even upon the separation from the *liṅga* (subtle body), the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) residing in the *liṅga* remain in the individual soul (*jīva*). That [doctrine] would not be established if one were to say that the Self has the *liṅga* as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), [only] in the absence of the *liṅga*. This refers to the nature of the reflected self (*bimbātman*).
He states that the principle already set forth here regarding the substratum of latent impressions (vāsanā) should be applied to the refutation of the substrata of perfumes and so forth:
"The principle previously explained here concerning the latent impression with respect to its substratum..."
"Everything here should be investigated for the sake of refuting the prima facie view"—

this means that the arising of ignorance from the supreme Self, whether by itself or like saline soil and so forth, is not tenable; this is easily understood, and [the author] now demonstrates the untenability.
The persistence of non-despair would be ignorance regarding the Supreme Self, as would the attachment to the doctrine of no-self;
[therefore] the destruction of delusion would occur here.

Thus [it is said]. This is the meaning: if ignorance (*avidyā*) were a modification of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), then transmigration (*saṃsāra*) would belong to the Supreme itself, since it is admitted that ignorance is what constitutes the transmigrating being; and consequently, as long as ignorance persists, liberation (*mokṣa*) could not be established. On the other hand, if ignorance perishes, then...
It would result in non-existence; for it is impossible for an effect to undergo absolute destruction while its cause remains.
Furthermore, according to your view, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) must be described as being [composed of] impressions (*vāsanā*) such as form and so forth.
Therefore, because it is impossible for those impressions to go elsewhere upon abandoning that [organ], [the effect cannot cease].

He states that the self is the substratum of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), for it is not accepted that a latent impression moves to another location apart from its own locus, because it lacks the nature of a substance possessing qualities; furthermore, the postulation of latent impressions as a substance is untenable due to its contradiction with scripture. Therefore, he says:

It proceeds with consistency; for in the aforementioned conceptualization, even the meanings of the scriptures are not appropriate, and thus the scripture provides an illustration to show that such a conceptualization is incorrect. Desires, volitions, and so forth are heard in scripture as attributes of the mind (*manas*), not of the Self (*ātman*).

In the Śāstra, [it is said] "because of the prohibition against attachment to others," and "for such forms indeed [appear] in the heart," and furthermore, "for his desires in the heart," and so forth, ending with "he has crossed over. Likewise, it says "speech. But surely, as for what you have cited...
If it is argued that by the words "mind" (*manas*) and so forth occurring in the passage, the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is being denoted,
he says "no," because there is no meaning other than that which is heard [from the scripture] for those words as they have been explained.
"It is impossible to conceive [it], therefore such a conception is not tenable.
This means that the conception of the self as the substratum of desire and so forth is therefore not tenable.
Furthermore, because all the Upaniṣads are intent upon establishing the identity of the self with Brahman, [desire and so forth do not belong to the self].
He states that its purpose is for the sake of another:
"In order to establish the realization of Brahman within oneself, every Upaniṣad is such;
for the Vedāntas are exhausted by having that alone as their purport. Thus.
Having now refuted the view that [the channels] are the substratum for the latent impressions of the agent and so forth, he refutes the conceptualization of them as three groups:
"And in the case of the position of the three groups, the purpose of the channels is not rendered consistent by such a conceptualization."

The meaning of the Śruti—that [the three aggregates] would contradict all principles—is not established as consistent under the position of the three groups; this is the sense. If it is argued that this is the same even in your own position, he says "no":
However, when there are only two forms— the formed and the formless along with their latent impressions— and the third is the form of Brahman,
then it is logical that [the self] is "sinful" (pāpa); thus, in your own conception, the conscious self (vijñānātman) would be included among those possessing form.

(If it were argued that) these two forms belong to the individual self (*vijñānātman*) which is a part of Brahman— just as one might say that these two forms belong to the person within a form, or to the person within a corporeal being— then he says: that is not tenable.
If the statement conforms to one's own imagination— whether regarding the individual self (*vijñānātman*) or the supreme self (*paramātman*)—
then one will say that the conception is based on scripture (*śrautī*), even though there is no scriptural statement to the effect that "the individual self has two forms," or otherwise.

Even though there is a scriptural statement that there are two forms of the Supreme Self by way of the conscious self (vijñānātman), nevertheless, the inclusion of the conscious self within the aggregate of forms would still result in the dual number "two forms" and the concluding statement of the passage being untenable; thus he says:

"And therefore, a twofold statement is appropriate because its threefold nature is not possible; for there are two forms, the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*), and the third is latent impression (*vāsanā*). [Objection: But why is it untenable that the two forms of Brahman called the formed and the formless, as well as the one called latent impression or consciousness (*vijñāna*), [are distinct]?

Regarding this, he states the following view: "For it is held that the two forms of Brahman—namely, the embodied and the other—are eternal; however, for the *kṣetrajña*, these two do not exist at all, being manifested merely as latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Here, he states the refutation:
"Even then, when the omnipresent Lord undergoes modification through the medium of the individual soul (*jīva*..."
(The statement) "the connection with latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth" is a meaningless utterance; this is the meaning.
Thus, when you speak of those two states, you do so by way of the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

It should not be said that the form of that which is being transformed consists of the manifest and the unmanifest, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of even latent impressions (*vāsanā*) having a connection with Brahman; since there is not even the slightest distinction among latent impressions regarding their status as being mediated by the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).

"Therefore, that which is conceptualized is non-existent"—this is an elaboration of what preceded. The meaning is that "conceptualized" refers to that which is modified through the medium of consciousness during the process of establishing distinctions; thus, even transformation of the Supreme [Self] through the medium of the individual soul (jīva) is not possible.
Thus he says:

"In this world, no entity can truly be said to undergo transformation into another entity through primary growth. This refers to the case where the individual soul (*jīva*) would be a separate entity.

It has been stated that such a transformation of form is not possible. Now, you do not accept that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a distinct entity; if that were so, it would entail the abandonment of your own established doctrine (*siddhānta*). Thus he says:
Furthermore, it is not accepted by the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) that there is any other entity distinct from the Supreme Self;
for such a conceptualization would certainly result in the abandonment of one's own established doctrine (*siddhānta*). Therefore, by those who wish to explain the meaning of the Vedānta:
Furthermore, he states that it is improper to postulate the three types of latent impressions (vāsanās), such as desire and so forth, for the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña):
"Therefore, by the great-souled ones who wish to reveal the meaning of the Vedānta, such [a view]... (p. 355).

"It is appropriate for those seeking the welfare of others to speak [of this] through conceptualization. Therefore, he says that only the *liṅga* (the subtle body) is grasped by the words "of that" and "of this," and not the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field):
"The person in the right eye"—thus, the *liṅgātman* (the self consisting of the subtle body) is what is grasped.

"Whether with respect to the internal (adhyātma) or the divine (adaiva), that very [Self] is the subject under discussion. Now, one might object: "If it is because of being the subject under discussion, then since the term 'liṅga' is also employed to denote that [Self], only the *liṅga* (the subtle body) would be understood, and not the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field). To this he replies: "The person in the right eye is the *liṅgātman* (the self consisting of the subtle body)."

It is grasped both internally and divinely, because it is that very [Self] which is the subject under discussion. Now, if it is argued that because of being the subject under discussion, the individual soul (jīva) is also included since its gender is mentioned, and therefore the word "his" (*tasya*) should refer to the soul—why is this not so? To this he says: "Let there be the inclusion of the soul here; indeed, let it be."
Since there is no distinction in their being the subject under discussion, these forms belong to that [Self] alone;

therefore, let it be stated that "it is not so. He says this because it is improper to take the individual soul (jīva) as the referent in the passage concerning the "pressing with the hand," despite its being the subject under discussion.
For it is not as something possessing form that the *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field) is intended here by this scripture;
rather, the *kṣetrajña* [is intended] as Brahman, whose nature consists of both the formed and the formless.
The meaning is that because it is intended [to be the agent], it does not have the nature of being colored by latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Therefore, he states that it is precisely the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that is colored by latent impressions: "Therefore, in this context, it is intended as having the nature of an instrument (*karaṇātman*). This is because the subtle body (*liṅga*) is the substratum for all latent impressions, such as agency and the like.
And because it is perceived by the witness (*sākṣin*), it is the subtle body (*liṅga*) alone—consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—and not the Self; thus he says:

"Therefore, it is the subtle body itself that is intended here. For the subtle body alone is perceived by the witness as the substratum of all latent impressions, such as agency and so forth. Thus, it is the subtle body alone [that is meant].

He says that the self is not of the nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*): "The subtle body (*liṅga*), which follows latent impressions, is perceived by the witness (*sākṣin*) as being soft or hard according to its modifications; therefore, it does not possess the form of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). Furthermore, if agency and so forth belonged to the individual soul (*jīva*), [it would follow...]

If the ultimate form of the Self were [described] as "saffron-colored" and so forth, then the teaching of the individual soul (*jīva*) through the negation of all specific attributes—namely, "not this, not this" (*neti neti*)—would be untenable; this is what [the author] expresses in the passage beginning with "if the form of the witness were... and concluding with "...then he would not have taught 'not this' regarding the Self."
An objection is raised: "Is this not an instruction concerning the individual soul (jīva), rather than Brahman? Anticipating this, he says:
"This is not an instruction concerning another [than Brahman], for it cannot be stated [so] on the basis of valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).

"Not this, not this"—this is the illustrative example for that very [instruction] at the conclusion. In the passage "This Self is 'not this, not this,'" because the word *ātman* (Self) is heard, the meaning is that this instruction refers to the Self itself, and not to a Brahman standing apart from it. Furthermore, if it were the Self alone...
In order to establish [the Self] as Brahman by means of the negation of all distinctions,
the intended [teaching] is "Now, therefore, the instruction is 'not this, not this'";
thus he says that the proposition "it is indeed so" becomes meaningful, and only then would that proposition possess the quality of being imperishable (*akṣaratva*).

If this instruction were intended for one who has merely arisen from the pressing of the hand, then how could there be the teaching of the individual soul (*jīva*) as being Brahman? For there is a difference between the *jīva* and Brahman. To this, he says:

"If [the soul] had arisen from the pressing of the hand as something other [than Brahman], then [the teacher would have said] 'no, it is not so'; and therefore [the soul is] not other than that. The notion that it is 'other' is false."

"Then that wisdom would arise from a cause of delusion"; thus, he states that there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as "then he knew himself alone" regarding the distinction between the individual self (jīva) and the supreme self (para), saying: "The realization 'I am Brahman' would not arise from a means of valid cognition."
"Righteous wisdom destroys all darkness and bestows liberation.

Therefore, he says that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) itself consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); thus, the grasping of its cause must pertain to that which is of the nature of an instrument (*karaṇa*), but it is not appropriate for its witness (*sākṣin*), because the form of that witness is denied.
Now, if all latent impressions (vāsanās) such as agency and so forth reside in the subtle body (liṅga), how is it that agency and the like appear to the Witness (sākṣin)? To this, he says:

"Those [powers], whose nature is the manifestation of latent impressions (vāsanā), residing in the subtle body (liṅga) and witnessing that which is beyond the subtle body (aliṅga), produce manifold forms, just as a covering produces various colors in a gem. This triad of subsequent verses, which provides an explanation of the categories of meaning, is easy to understand; it is written here as follows: [The verses follow.]

In the phrase "mahārajanam," the color turmeric is intended, since the safflower (kausumbha) has already been accounted for by the comparison to the *indragopa* insect. Just as a yellow garment appears slightly to the witness (*sākṣin*), so too does the subtle body (*liṅga*) appear to the vision when it is permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) arising from objects such as women.

Just as a pale substance such as wool appears [white], so too does the *liṅga* (the subtle body) appear; and just as the *indragopa* insect and others are red, so too is the mind intensely red. Thus, he states through two *vārtikas* that the cause for the variety of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the variety of qualities such as *sattva* is the power of knowledge and action; this is transcribed here: "Just as a pale substance such as wool appears, so does the *liṅga* appear. And just as the *indragopa* insect and others are red, so too is the mind intensely red. "Furthermore, the variety of latent impressions arises from the power of knowledge and action, while the variety of qualities such as *sattva* is the instrumental cause. This is stated in the two *vārtikas*, which are now recorded.
In some cases, an excess of *rajas* is observed; in others, an excess of *tamas*; likewise, an intensification of *sattva* arises from some cause.
In one instance, one of the three predominates over a particular object; in another, two do so;
and elsewhere, all three act together through the diversity of knowledge, action, and the like.
359) Thus it is said. Furthermore, he again follows the explanation of the meaning of the words with two *vārttikas*.
They are written as follows: "Just as the flame of fire is radiant due to the excellence of its *sattva*, so too is the mind."
Just as a white lotus is gentle and refreshing,
just as a sudden flash of lightning utterly dispels thick darkness,
so too has this final latent impression (vāsanā) arisen once within us with extreme brilliance, like a flash of light before our eyes.

He says that this occurs for Hiraṇyagarbha as he is being born from the Supreme Lord, because that [birth] is intended to be enjoined as an object of meditation for the purpose of praise: "Indeed, when the reality of Hiraṇyagarbha is being born, his form shines forth like lightning."

Regarding the phrase "of the Great-Souled One": he now describes the undesirable fruit for one who worships Hiraṇyagarbha as characterized by such latent impressions (vāsanā). Therefore, he who worships in this very form day and night [obtains a result] like that of lightning which destroys all darkness.

"May Śrī always take refuge [in him]"— since six examples have been presented beginning with "like saffron," a doubt arises there that the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are likewise only of six kinds. To dispel that, he says:

"Since there is no beginning, no middle, and no end, and because there is no measurable limit to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) accumulated over infinite eons, [the examples given] are merely illustrative. Thus he says: "The illustration...

The passage beginning with "māhārajanam" (dyed saffron) is not intended to specify a fixed quantity; rather, it is cited as an illustration merely to show the variety [of such things]. The word "satyasya," ending in the genitive case, has been explained as "the True.
The passage beginning with "yo ha vai śiśum" and ending with "athāta ādeśaḥ" [is to be understood accordingly].
Now, since the truth (satya) ending in the nominative case remains to be explained,

he states the passage beginning with "atha ataḥ" for that purpose: "Having thus explained the nature of truth in its entirety, an effort is now made to point out the true essence of the supreme Self and of truth."
Thus [it is said]. He explains the meaning of the word "atha" (now/then) with the following three verses:

"Since the entire reality consisting of the formed and the formless has been explained, therefore the instruction regarding that [reality]—which is of the nature of the formed and the formless—is given next to one who no longer possesses the conceit of 'otherness'."

"Furthermore, because there is no other reality remaining apart from Brahman due to the manifestation of Truth, this instruction regarding Brahman— which is beyond all instruction— is said to be for that which is beyond instruction, which is designated as 'the Supreme,' and whose nature is the non-dual Self consisting of pure inwardness. Now, [regarding] this...
He explains the threefold derivation of the word *ādeśa*:

"This word *ādeśa* may refer to the object (*karman*), or it may refer to the cause (*kāraṇa*), or else *ādeśa* is the instruction (*ādiṣṭi*): 'Not this, not this' regarding the non-dual Self. Here, the object (*karman*) is Brahman.
The instrument is sound; the state is "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).
361) If the two words were on the side of the instrument, they would be an instruction; and by that [instruction], how could Brahman [be known]?
It can be pointed out because it does not denote that [which is other than itself]; thus he says: "Not this, not this" (neti neti).
How could the true Brahman, which transcends the scope of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), be intended to be pointed out?
Even though this [expression] is not its denoter, nevertheless—
He states that ignorance (avidyā) residing in the self is the cause for the realization of Brahman by means of the removal of its effects:
"Listen to all that [concerning] the negation of the origin of that ignorance. Thus, it is by way of negation.

He says that there is no second [reality]: "Because that non-cognition is devoid of form, being of the single nature of pure inwardness; and because its effect is also devoid of form. It has been stated that this is a negation of that which arises from the ignorance of That; now he shows what that ignorance is and what arises from it: [The text continues: "The world-appearance, consisting of the aggregate of causes and effects, is the product of the ignorance of That. Its negation is established by the cognition of That alone, which is of the nature of pure inwardness. This is the meaning. How is this so? Because the cause of the world-appearance is the ignorance of That, and its effect is the world-appearance itself. Since both the cause and the effect are devoid of form (*nirākṛti*), they are negated by the realization of That, which is of the nature of pure inwardness. Thus, the world-appearance, which is the effect of the ignorance of That, is negated by the cognition of That alone. Therefore, the world-appearance is not real. This is the sense. What is the proof for this? He states the proof: "Because it is sublated by the cognition of That.
