The supreme limit of the formless was previously described as the causal self; likewise, that of the formed is proclaimed to be within the earth. The meaning is that the ultimate cause of those two, their final effect, and everything contained between them must be negated. Now, one might object:
To the objection that there exists something distinct from the inner self even beyond the three aforementioned [states], he says "no":
whatever object whatsoever is admitted for the mind and for designation, that lies precisely between the two already mentioned, being of the nature of cause and effect.
Thus, having joined the middle [verses], he shows:
"The Scripture did not proclaim that even for one who is established [in Brahman] there is inexhaustibility; therefore, there is no inexhaustibility because of the attainment of the whole."

It is said that [the world] does not exist because of the impossibility of establishing the validity of desire and action; therefore, it is called "improper. Now, one might object: "The destruction of the world by enjoyment is not total; rather, it is merely the cessation of the world's manifestation. To this, he says: "As for that which is destruction in manifestation..."
The meaning is that since such a destruction—heard [in scripture] as being of the nature of the cause—is not at all prevented by us even in deep sleep, the performance of spiritual means is futile.
For this reason, he says that the destruction of the world proceeds from ignorance alone: *ata evājñānādeva jagatkṣayaḥ* (Therefore, the destruction of the world is indeed from ignorance alone).

"The very birth of the thorough knowledge of reality (*pratyakṣatvaparijñāna*) is the cause for the destruction of duality; thus, no human goal other than this is desired. [Objection: "But why is the last one not desired? Karma is indeed desired for the sake of liberation (*kaivalya*). [Reply: True, but it is so by way of an indirect succession (*praṇāḍyā*), not directly.
He states the direct authority for that with the words "tam etam" (this very [Self]), and likewise shows that all ritual actions are employed for the arising of immediate knowledge; furthermore,
because of the scriptural hearing that the destruction of karma results from knowledge, he says "bhidyate" (it is split) to indicate that there is no direct assistance [from action].
The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are destroyed, and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both supreme and non-supreme is seen.
p.

363) Thus it is said. If that is so, then does it follow that there is no destruction even of *prārabdha* (commenced) karma? To this he replies: through the exhaustion of experience (*bhoga*), there is the destruction of desires and of prohibited actions, but not of those [actions] whose effects have already commenced (*ārabdhakārya*).
"Even the knower does not awaken. If that is so, then the other [karmas] would be the same; to this he says:

"But due to the absence of all acquired karmas, there is destruction of all [karmas], except for those whose effects have already begun, through the arising of perfect knowledge. Now, [an objection]: [The text continues: "But..."
If it is argued that the scripture itself is the authority for the exhaustion of karmas along with their experience, [the author] says "no":
"Just as there is an authority for the exhaustion of karmas at the arising of knowledge through their complete attainment, no such authority is accepted in any other way."

It has been stated there that [the Self] is the delimitator of ignorance; what then is this ignorance? Is it non-apprehension or apprehension otherwise? If it is non-apprehension, he says in response:
Ignorance is not a delimiting agent, because it is of the nature of darkness (tamas), since it is an obscuring factor.
"Endowed with all [aspects] in the form of the individual. If it is argued that even false cognition is likewise [endowed], he says:
"And false cognition is not accepted as a determiner; what does it determine?"
If it is argued that there is at least some cognition of the blue sky, then knowledge must possess the capacity to delimit its object;
to this he says: "Knowledge is the manifestor of what exists. But is not knowledge an agent?

If it is argued that [the cognition] is not a revealer, he says in response to that: "But it is not like a potter, insofar as [the potter] conforms to the object. Furthermore, what is called the "delimiting nature" (*paricchedakatva*) of cognition—

He states that there is no disagreement regarding the fact that [cognition] makes known its object as it truly is: "The intellect's conformity to the object of knowledge consists in its being a determinative cognition. Furthermore, he asks, "What follows if this is so? and answers therein:
If it is held that even ignorance conforms to the nature of the object, then liberation would always occur when the object has been stated; conversely, bondage arises from its opposite.
For if both non-apprehension and other-apprehension were to convey the object as it truly is, then that object to be known would always [be present].

Whether [the world] is liberated or bound, in both cases, because both states exist eternally, the commencement of the treatise would be purposeless. Furthermore, your view that the insentient phenomenal world has the sentient Brahman as its material cause is also untenable; thus he says:

"By itself, the self cannot be the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) of its own effects, because it lacks identity [with them]; for here on earth, threads do not produce a jar. If it is argued that ignorance alone is the material cause of the entire world, he says that this too contradicts their own accepted position: "Knowledge belongs to the supreme self by its very nature."
Desire and action come from the outside, but it is not ignorance that arises [from them]; this very point has been stated by you yourself. Ignorance does not arise from the Supreme Self.

You yourself have stated that desire and action are the effects of ignorance; therefore, the claim that ignorance alone is the material cause of the world contradicts your own admission. Furthermore, the idea that desire and action produce the world even when ignorance has been destroyed is also illogical.
He states that this is contradictory:

"Nor can desire and action produce non-existence as their cause, because that which is non-existent cannot arise, just as one cannot produce the desire for a son and so forth [from nothing]. This is because the birth of what is non-existent is impossible.

The meaning is that there is no birth because of the absence of a cause; or, even if a cause were to exist, if ignorance (avidyā) already exists, it cannot be produced anew. Thus he says: "Nor would a cause produce the birth of that which is absolutely non-existent, for even in the world, a cause does not [produce] its own self despite abundant rain."
"Arising from space" means that space [is the cause] because of the absence of flowers;

it was stated that ignorance arises from itself by its own nature through the Supreme Self. In that regard, he states another objection: "If Brahman alone is considered the cause of the birth of ignorance, while that [Brahman] exists..."

Even total destruction is my form; likewise are action, the vital breaths, the worlds, and so forth—whether it be the agent, the action, another thing, the cause, or the effect itself; birth, quality, action, substance, relation, and even existence.
p.

366) "Existent, non-existent, and both existent and non-existent," as well as "in aggregate and individually," namely: the knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the fruit of action—the negation of all this is expressed by the negative particle *na*. By that [negation]...
He says that by means of the syllable "na," which has as its object the pure inner self (pratyag-mātra), the true nature of Brahman is understood:
"by this negation, [Brahman] is supported in the pure inner self."
"How can there be a negation in the absence of anything to be negated? To this he says:
"In the case of names and so forth, it is accepted that they are merely indicators; therefore, negation is possible. He states:
"Then, negation is performed of that which has been indicated, not [of the indicator itself]. Now, as for Brahman...
Since the world is denied [as real], its existence elsewhere would result in the loss of non-duality; to this he says:
"The form of that which possesses form is drawn away and does not remain separate."
Regarding the phrase "unconceived in the world": if it is argued that what is prohibited in one place must exist elsewhere, [the author replies:
True, where an independent entity is prohibited within another independent entity, it is conceived as existing elsewhere; however, this is not the case here, as he says:
Even though a cloth is negated in a jar, it remains elsewhere than the jar; for even where it is not negated, there exists that subject which, while ultimately negated,
appears as a real entity arising from delusion regarding it.

"How can there be the persistence of that [pot] by way of its ultimate nature?"— this is the meaning: [the question concerns] whether the property of a cloth, which has been negated in relation to a pot, might nonetheless persist elsewhere in its own essential form without being negated.
It is understood that stability exists because of [the reality of] existence, but not so for that which is imagined; thus, there is no loss of non-duality (*advaita*).
Now, if it were as you say, the world consisting of space and so forth would be imagined, for what is imagined does not truly exist.
If this is argued, we say no, because of the lack of pervasion (*vyabhicāra*); he states that it is indeed imagined: "Of all things to be negated without exception..."

"Because of mutual deviation and because of the deviation of the inner self (pratyak), that which is superimposed upon it is negated. Now, one might object: "Granted that what is superimposed on the inner self may be negated, the establishment of Brahman does not follow from this alone; rather, this effort at negation is for the purpose of establishing Brahman."

Regarding this, it is said: "The negation of those things residing in words occurs within the nature of experience. In the verse, "O Infinite One, let that [negation] be determined as Brahman there," Brahman is not presented as the object of negation, because it is already established as such through the negation conveyed by the word.

[The opponent argues: "Because it is possible for Brahman to be the object of words such as 'is'. [The author] says, "No"—existence and perception of form and so forth arise from their own objects through the internal witness (pratyak), whereas because it is indefinable and so on, the notion [of these attributes] turns away from the Self; thus, the Self is self-evident.
Because of its sovereignty, it is not [negated] as being internal;
therefore, it is not denied. Since this is so, for that conscious self—

This negation, by its very force, negates everything. That conscious Self, through the cognition of its own form—that is, through the meaning of the sentence—having completely sublated everything else, remains as itself alone; thus he says:

"It negates the object to be negated by its own power; having destroyed the other through its own consciousness alone, the Cit (consciousness) reaches fullness by itself. To the question "What is that other?", he says:
"For in this [consciousness], which perceives only the inward-facing Self, throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep..."
"Other than that, each respective appearance is incessantly negated. He demonstrates the fruit of this negation:
"With eyes ever wide open, [he remains] for the destruction of the delusion regarding the inner self, which is established without inquiry."
"The one whose intellect is turned inward attains extinction in the Self. Furthermore, he establishes the falsity of that which is to be negated by means of an illustration:
"Therefore, the entity consisting of cause and effect, which arises from the causal condition of relative cognition, when subjected to inquiry..."

"There is no blackness in the sky, as there is none in the Self. Alternatively, let ignorance indeed cease; however, the world does not [cease] because it exists as the ultimate reality, since it is not its effect. To this, he replies:
"Because the grounds for the application of words are impossible in the inner Self."

(369) "And because it is not within the scope of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To this, he replies: "Because it is established by itself (*svataḥ-siddha*), there can be no denial. Here, the two negations are used distributively (*vīpsā*). In this regard:
He states the reason:
as long as this inner self (pratyagātman), which is the object of the designation "I," does not attain itself by itself,
so long does the negative particle [denying its reality] not cease during the state of ignorance.
As long as the inner self (pratyagātman), existing as the object of means of knowledge other than verbal testimony,

does not attain its state of abiding in its own nature through the exclusion of all particularities, so long does negation not cease; therefore, a distributive repetition (vīpsā) must be resorted to regarding negation.

Some say it is the object of the designation "pride" (māna), while others say it is merely phenomenal proliferation (prapañca). Now, one might object: since there is no negator for the negation, the persistence of that negation would result in the loss of non-duality (advaita). To this he replies:
"When ignorance and its effects have been dispelled, and the Self has been attained as the Self, then [the negation persists] because the cause of what is to be negated [no longer exists]."

"When [the world] has been destroyed, even negation ceases. Furthermore, he demonstrates by distinguishing the objects of negation: "Whatever has been manifested here, such as the state of being a knower (pramātṛtva) and so forth, and the absence of that—everything that is 'not this' is negated."
Now, [an objection is raised]: "Since negation culminates in non-existence (abhāva), existence would therefore not persist; thus, there is a loss of non-duality (advaita-hāni). To this, he says:

Since everything is to be negated, that which is not to be negated must be the essential nature of reality; therefore, it cannot be established as non-existence, because even non-existence would be denied.
Since existence is what is to be negated, he states this repetition: "Not this, not this" (*neti neti*); thus, one should grasp it through this repetition.

If it is argued that for one who is hungry, the negation applies to the whole [object], and therefore the negation must be distributive (vīpsā), and that even by resorting to distributiveness the cessation of expectancy is not achieved—[the author] says "no":
this expectancy ceases because [the object] is understood as being pervaded by both cognition and action; thus, there is no desire to know it further.

"In one [knowledge], there is the desire to perform the final act. This means that by means of knowledge, the expectation "this must be accomplished by me" is removed through the performance of the action.

The action based on repetition (vīpsā) is that which leads the knower to steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*) and identity with Brahman—which is beyond the scope of the two types of knowledge; therefore, even because of this, one resorts to repetition.
Some say that when the knower exists, one attains steadfastness through either negation or the knowledge of the absence of the gross and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that [ignorance] must have a sublater, he provides an illustration to show that the knowledge of the true nature of Brahman alone is the sublater: "The negation of the snake and its cause is possible through the knowledge of the rope's true nature;
it cannot be accomplished by anything else, even in hundreds of years. Furthermore:
Regarding the alternative of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), he states the merit:
"Whatever is obtained in this world— all that is indeed negated," and thus it is.

"Even the doubt regarding what has been pointed out as true is removed. Regarding the position that there is no repetition (*avīpsā*), he states the refutation: "If there is no repetition, then two sentences are intended therein;
since that [repetition] is exhausted by the negation of the two stated [cases], there would be a suspicion regarding an unstated subject."

If [it is argued that] for one who negates everything, [the statement] would have non-existence as its object— since non-existence itself is not being negated— or else it would be a speech established in emptiness; by the phrase "or else it has existence as its object," he establishes that very point regarding things established through direct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

"The apprehension of what is other than the prohibited" means that when things such as jars, which have been previously cognized, are negated in relation to a locus such as the ground that has also been cognized, then, upon that negation, there arises the apprehension of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) regarding those things that were previously established. This is the meaning.

When [an object] is negated in a place like the ground that has been measured (cognized) by a means of valid cognition, and the jar and so forth—which were themselves measured by a means of valid cognition—are negated, then [emptiness is apprehended].

In those two cases, the apprehension of both remains non-empty. However, when the world established by cognition is negated within Brahman, which is established by [its own] cognition, then the speech necessarily results in a state of nihilism (śūnyaniṣṭhatva),
because there is no means of valid knowledge for Brahman [in that context] and because [the world] was established by cognition.

Because any [entity] other than Brahman is prohibited. If it is argued that let there be a state of resting in the void (śūnya), he says "no": this negation is stated beginning with the word "instruction" (ādeśa).

"That by which something is directly pointed out is called an 'instruction' (ādeśa). This is the meaning, because after stating "this is the instruction regarding Brahman," a negation is then being expressed; or as, for example:

This instruction known as "negation" is solely intent upon answering the question regarding Brahman. Therefore, he says that by means of this negation-instruction, the wise person, having discarded the world of cause and effect along with the state of being a witness through the form of Brahman, abides in his own true nature: He who knows thus becomes Brahman indeed; Of death he dies not again; Of death he dies not again. (BĀU 4.4.6) The meaning is as follows: "He who knows thus"—that is, one who knows the Self as described above—becomes Brahman indeed. Because he has become Brahman, which is devoid of birth, he does not die again after death; he does not undergo further transmigration. The repetition, "he does not die again," is intended to indicate the finality of this state. (BĀUBh 4.4.6) Furthermore, since this instruction is for the purpose of removing the notion of agency from the Self—which is the witness of all actions—by means of the negation of the world of cause and effect, he says: When all desires dwelling within the heart are cast away, then the mortal becomes immortal; then he attains Brahman in this very world. (BĀU 4.4.7) The meaning is as follows: "When all desires"—desires are mental modifications (*vṛtti*) characterized by longing for objects such as sound, and they are called "desires" because they consist of desire—"dwelling within the heart," that is, residing in the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the seat of the mind—are "cast away," that is, completely destroyed. Then, at that time, the "mortal"—one who was previously mortal due to identifying with the body—becomes "immortal," that is, free from death. "Then he attains Brahman in this very world. Since he has become Brahman, which is devoid of birth, he does not die again after death; he does not undergo further transmigration. The repetition, "he does not die again," is intended to indicate the finality of this state. (BĀUBh 4.4.7) Moreover, since the instruction regarding the Self is for the purpose of removing the notion of agency from the Self—which is the witness of all actions—by means of the negation of the world of cause and effect, he says: When he finds freedom from fear, and becomes established in the All, then he attains Brahman in this very world. (BĀU 4.4.25) The meaning is as follows: "When he finds freedom from fear"—fear arises from the perception of duality, and its absence is "freedom from fear"; when he attains that state—"and becomes established in the All," that is, when he becomes the Self of all—"then he attains Brahman in this very world. Since he has become Brahman, which is devoid of birth, he does not die again after death; he does not undergo further transmigration. The repetition, "he does not die again," is intended to indicate the finality of this state. (BĀUBh 4.4.25) Furthermore, since the instruction regarding the Self is for the purpose of removing the notion of agency from the Self—which is the witness of all actions—by means of the negation of the world of cause and effect, he says: When he sees the Seer who is beyond seeing, the Hearer who is beyond hearing, the Thinker who is beyond thinking, and the Knower who is beyond knowing, he becomes the Infinite, my dear; there is no more beyond this. (BĀU 4.5.15) The meaning is as follows: "When he sees the Seer who is beyond seeing"—the Seer is the Self, and He is "beyond seeing" because He is not an object of the sense of sight; when he perceives Him—"the Hearer who is beyond hearing," the Hearer is the Self, and He is "beyond hearing" because He is not an object of the sense of hearing—"the Thinker who is beyond thinking," the Thinker is the Self, and He is "beyond thinking" because He is not an object of the internal organ—"and the Knower who is beyond knowing," the Knower is the Self, and He is "beyond knowing" because He is not an object of the intellect—"he becomes the Infinite, my dear. The Infinite is Brahman, which is devoid of birth; he becomes that. "There is no more beyond this"—there is nothing else to be attained other than becoming Brahman, which is devoid of birth. (BĀUBh 4.5.15) Furthermore, since the instruction regarding the Self is for the purpose of removing the notion of agency from the Self—which is the witness of all actions—by means of the negation of the world of cause and effect, he says: When he finds freedom from fear, and becomes established in the All, then he attains Brahman in this very world. (BĀU 4.4.25) The meaning is as follows: "When he finds freedom from fear"—fear arises from the perception of duality, and its absence is "freedom from fear"; when he attains that state—"and becomes established in the All," that is, when he becomes the Self of all—"then he attains Brahman in this very world. Since he has become Brahman, which is devoid of birth, he does not die again after death; he does not undergo further transmigration. The repetition, "he does not die again," is intended to indicate the finality of this state. (BĀUBh 4.4.25) Furthermore, since the instruction regarding the Self is for the purpose of removing the notion of agency from the Self—which is the witness of all actions—by means of the negation of the world of cause and effect, he says: When he sees the Seer who is beyond seeing, the Hearer who is beyond hearing, the Thinker who is beyond thinking, and the Knower who is beyond knowing, he becomes the Infinite, my dear; there is no more beyond this. (BĀU 4.5.15) The meaning is as follows: "When he sees the Seer who is beyond seeing"—the Seer is the Self, and He is "beyond seeing" because He is not an object of the sense of sight; when he perceives Him—"the Hearer who is beyond hearing," the Hearer is the Self, and He is "beyond hearing" because He is not an object of the sense of hearing—"the Thinker who is beyond thinking," the Thinker is the Self, and He is "beyond thinking" because He is not an object of the internal organ—"and the Knower who is beyond knowing," the Knower is the Self, and He is "beyond knowing" because He is not an object of the intellect—"he becomes the Infinite, my dear. The Infinite is Brahman, which is devoid of birth; he becomes that. "There is no more beyond this"—there is nothing else to be attained other than becoming Brahman, which is devoid of birth. (BĀUBh 4.5.15) Furthermore, since the instruction regarding the Self is for the purpose of removing the notion of agency from the Self—which is the witness of all actions—by means of the negation of the world of cause and effect, he says: When he finds freedom from fear, and becomes established in the All, then he attains Brahman in this very world. (BĀU 4.4.25) The meaning is as follows: "When he finds freedom from fear"—fear arises from the perception of duality, and its absence is "freedom from fear"; when he attains that state—"and becomes established in the All," that is, when he becomes the Self of all—"then he attains Brahman in this very world. The repetition, "he does not die again," is intended to indicate the finality of this state. (BĀU 4.5.15) The meaning is as follows: "When he sees the Seer who is beyond seeing"—the Seer is the Self, and He is "beyond seeing" because He is not an object of the sense of sight; when he perceives Him—"the Hearer who is beyond hearing," the Hearer is the Self, and He is "beyond hearing" because He is not an object of the sense of hearing—"the Thinker who is beyond thinking," the Thinker is the Self, and He is "b

Therefore, by way of negation, that which is to be negated— whether known or unknown— is always established within the witness of the Self (ātma-sākṣin), who is himself not subject to negation. Anticipating the objection that "even what has been once negated may arise again, like a snake [mistakenly perceived in a rope]," he says:

He establishes this—that [the self] does not arise—by means of an illustration: just as form is not grasped by the auditory cognition because it lacks the causal connection with form, nor does it grasp it, nor will it grasp it, like sound; for it is definitively known that, despite being perceptible, it is "not this, not this."

Just as from the statement "the Self has no cause, nor was it, nor is it, nor will it be," there follows the cessation of the world along with its cause, he says that this cessation is not something other than ignorance:
"The existence of a second Self is not other than ignorance, just as [the existence of a second moon is not other than a visual defect]."
In the same way, its cessation occurs through the realization of the Self and not through anything else;
thus, even when resorting to the repetition [of the word], the sense is established by the phrase "by this very means" (*evaitveti*).
He says:

"When its absolute identity, which is not dependent on anything else, is established directly even amidst diversity, then this [identity] should be accepted as having arisen simultaneously"; therefore, he concludes.
"Not this, not this" (neti neti) is a repetition because of the possibility [of further attributes] in the entity already described;
that is to say, by resorting to the repetition, the intended entity is established, and thus the person achieves their purpose. He states this as follows:

"The state of being the ultimate reality is thus; otherwise, it would not be possible. Now he concludes with the fruit of this negation: "The intellect, which was attached to external objects (parāgartha), by becoming colored by the internal self (pratyagartha), having turned away from external objects, attains the inward-facing [reality]."

Having thus established the validity of the commentator’s position regarding the meaning of "sthitim," he states another interpretation— that the sentence "not this" conveys its meaning through a positive approach— by means of the passage beginning with "vyatirekasya... [negation] of the negations imagined by other disputants."

By the prohibition of repetition (*vīpsā*), [the rule] ends with *aṣīti*. Thus the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) has been stated; now, the commentary (*vārtika*) is explained word by word. He says that this is not an injunction of negation for the purpose of establishing the difference of Brahman from the formed (*mūrta*) and so forth.

(374) Since the distinction [between the individual self and Brahman] has already been established by the instructions previously stated, for what purpose is this instruction [given] with the word "verily" (*hi*)? He says: it is for the sake of awakening the realization that the self is Brahman.
"This instruction is now stated for the purpose of directly establishing Brahman-hood. Now, one might object:
"This instruction does not have the sense of differentiation (*vyatireka*), nor is it for the purpose of establishing Brahman-hood;
rather, it is for the purpose of negating the forms [of Brahman] such as the embodied (*mūrta*) and so forth. Anticipating this, he says:

"The negation is not for the sake of negation, because it is intent upon providing a definition"—this means that it is intent upon establishing the meaning of "Thou" (*tvam-artha*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). He states the refutation [of the view] that it is intent upon negation: "Since Brahman is not established by any other means of knowledge, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) would consequently follow"; this refers to the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Regarding the argument that [the distinction] is established [by other means], he says there: "The form and so forth are already fully established as being distinct from Brahman simply by the use of the genitive case; therefore, [your claim of] repetition and attachment is refuted. Consequently, he states: "Therefore, the doctrine of *pāriśeṣya* (residual inference) cannot hold."
This is the meaning: as for your intended position— that by the statement "not this, not this" (neti neti), there is the negation of the formal and other attributes in their identity with Brahman,
and that Brahman is established as the remainder, distinct from the formal and so forth— that is not established, precisely because of the use of the genitive case.
"Because it is established by the logic of elimination (pāriśeṣya).
On page 375,
he states another objection regarding the view that [the text] is intended to negate corporeality and so forth:
"And it cannot be negated because it is based on perception and other means of valid cognition"— the meaning is that the negation of what is established by a means of valid cognition is impossible.
He states that even the human goal is not accomplished through mere negation:

"Due to [mere] negation, not even any desired human goal would be accomplished. Furthermore, if the sentence were restricted to the negation of enumerated forms such as "mūrta" (the formed) and so on, there would be no instruction regarding the Supreme Brahman; thus he says: "If it were restricted to mere negation, there would be no teaching of the Lord."
Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, he states that if the negation were restricted to the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), the non-dual Brahman would not be established:
"If it is stated that 'Brahman is not form and so forth,' there is no negation of form and so forth [in general]; and consequently..."

"Brahman-hood is established when there is a second entity. Furthermore, the explanatory expansion of the statement "not this, not this" would not be possible [if there were no second]. Therefore, he says that even though there is exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), the intended meaning of the proposition—that Brahman and so forth are established—is not [lost] through the negation of what has been enumerated.
"And since it would not be manifested [otherwise], by the principle of elimination (pāriśeṣya), the establishment of the intended object would follow.
Therefore, the intended Brahman is established in this manner.

He states that the sentence "not this" (neti) must be explained: "The explanation should be made in such a way that [the goal] is accomplished, because the teaching is direct. Thus, the negation of duality and the distinction [between the Self and the world] are already established prior to the words "therefore, hence" (athātaḥ); therefore, neither of those two is what is to be propounded by this [sentence].
To this he says:
The negation of every object that is not the Self is already established prior to the knowledge of the true nature of the inner Self, because [all such objects] are mutually inconsistent with it.
"Mutual deviation is observed in this non-self object,
and even the deviation from its own nature [is seen] in deep sleep and so forth, as witnessed by one's own self-evident consciousness. Now,
he explains the relationship between the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) and that which is characterized as being witnessed by one's own self-evident consciousness.
By means of the example, for the purpose of establishing that the inner self (pratyak) is the object indicated by the meaning of the negative particle, it is said:

"Just as this designation 'mother' and so forth is established through the realization of the inner self, so too is the non-existence of the knower and so forth [established] because they have their locus in the realization of the inner self. This is not [the case].

If it is argued that the non-self (anātman) is established by the power of the knowledge of one's own self (svātmabodha), [the author] says "no," because the self would then be subject to modification:

"The entire non-self, whose establishment is unexamined, becomes established solely through the form of the ignorance of the Self (ātmāvidyā), by depending on the Self which is established by itself. Alternatively:
Having raised the objection that, since it is established by experience, it must be as real as the experience itself, he refutes this with the following [verse].
Having stated, "Because it relies upon a self that is established by itself," he now explains its essential nature.

"Even though his consciousness is not obscured, he is free from all modifications, and for him there is no other subject or object of knowledge, because his nature consists solely of pure vision. Thus, he says that through the grace of such a Self, everything is accomplished: *atirohitasaṃvitkopyapāstāśeṣavikriyaḥ ananyamātṛmānādiḥ dṛṣṭimātrātmakatvataḥ iti | evaṃvidhātmaprasādāt sarvasya siddhirityāha-* [The text continues: "Even though his consciousness is not obscured, he is free from all modifications, and for him there is no other subject or object of knowledge, because his nature consists solely of pure vision. Thus, he says that through the grace of such a Self, everything is accomplished:"

"Thus, every accomplishment consisting of existence and non-existence belongs to the non-Self; since it is of a nature opposed to that [Self], it is accomplished in Me alone. Therefore, let the accomplishment of everything come about through My grace. By whom is He accomplished? To this he says: "By Himself alone."

"By means of no other experience, one remains as the self, which is directly present and immutable within the planes of the nature of entities, seeing the self as the very essence of the fruit. Therefore, he says that for the establishment of the Self, there is no dependence on the knower and so forth: "Hence, wherever the association with the knower and the rest ceases..."

In each instance, that which is directly present is established by its own majesty alone; therefore, since [the absence] is not established through experience at this time, he says that experience is defined by the absence [of the knower and so forth]:
"Therefore, the absence of the knower and the rest, which is established through self-awareness—that is the function of the negative particle (*nañ*)."

"One always perceives the Buddha as immeasurable and beyond measure. This refers to that in which there is the occurrence of the negative particle (*nañ*). The occurrence of the negative particle is non-existence (*abhāva*).
Established through experience, it indicates its own witness (sākṣin), just as the word "platform" indicates the person [upon it].

Therefore, in the phrase "not this," the negative particle (*nañ*) is the referent of the term *tvaṃ*; there is an alternative reading here stating that the negative particle itself is the function (*vṛtti*), whereas in the former case, it was the meaning of that [particle] which possessed the character of indication (*lakṣaṇatva*).

In both cases, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is the inner self (*pratyagātman*). Now, one might ask: why does the word not convey this directly? To this he replies: "Because of its distinctness, and because [the means of knowledge] and so forth have no application in the self, which is the experience of that which is non-different from them, even when accompanied by a cause."
The phrase "the realization of eternal consciousness" (nityabodhāvabodhana) indicates the nature of the self as the object of perception:

"Apart from ignorance and the like, the various categories such as cause and so forth are found to be of a nature already attained [by the self], because they are not distinct from the inner witness. Alternatively, it means "due to their distinctness."

Anticipating the objection that the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), he refutes it with this [verse]. Anticipating the objection that "the state of not being established by any other means of knowledge" (*ananyamānatva*) is unestablished, he says: "This reality is self-established, independent of the knower and so forth; therefore, for everyone..."

"How could that which is already established be established by something else? Thus, it has been established that the meaning of "thou" (*tvam*), the inner self (*pratyagātman*), is self-established and is the referent of the negative particle (*na*). This much has been demonstrated;
as for the meaning of the word, its external referent, the oneness of these two is expressed by the phrase "not this" (*neti*) in the statement "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).
To this he says:
379) "The establishment of the aforementioned objects of knowledge occurs through its own power alone, not from scripture."

"For the sake of realizing Brahman-hood, it is said, 'Not this, not this' (neti brahma). This means that for the purpose of knowing the Brahman-hood of that Witness who is not a material form, it is said, "Not this, not this. The meaning is that the sentence "not this" is the authority for their identity. Some read the text as "socyate" instead of "mocyate," in which case it would mean "it is taught."

Their intention is that the establishment of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) is what is being considered. Now, an objection is raised: since the individual soul (*jīva*) is limited, how can its identity with Brahman be made known? To this, he says:
"That which is directly indicated by the negative particle as the object of knowledge through the cognition of the Self..."

"Because ignorance and the rest have that as their essence, it is understood as Brahman"—this means that because the delusion regarding the inner self (*pratyag-moha*) and what arises from it are subordinate to the cognition [of the Self], he spoke thus: "It is Brahman, the dispeller of delusion. This is an elaboration of what preceded; for [the passage] beginning with "not from this" and so forth [is explained].
He raises an objection in order to introduce the statement:

"The instruction [is] 'atha' (now) after 'mahat' (great); this is a confusion; therefore, an instruction that is dissimilar is being uttered, which is indeed improper. He replies: "It is indeed similar."

This instruction alone is appropriate, since no further instruction is seen beyond it; for what other instruction could be intended here regarding Brahman? But is it not the case that there is also instruction by way of affirmation? True, that exists here as well.
In order to demonstrate that [it] is not possible, he says:
"The reality of this [world], which is beyond Brahman, as far as it extends therein... (p. 380).

"All those intended meanings are to be explained"— this means that because all qualifiers have been negated by the "not so, not so" (neti), there is no instruction by means of written words. He says "no" to the claim that their cessation is something else.
And their cessation, as previously described, is characterized by their having a single object;
therefore, a real existence in different locations is not possible there. It has been stated that "existence in different locations is not tenable," and here he states the reason for this:

"The primary meaning of the word *brahman* is held to be that which is neither excluded nor followed; for when something else exists, [the word] is determined by its meaning as *brahman*. He says that this is the instruction because genus and so forth are nothing but *brahman*: "Then, because the grounds for the application of words reach their culmination in a single object."

"This is the further instruction regarding those things denoted by that [instruction]"—with this, he concludes that "this alone is the further instruction," having accepted the relationship between the designation and the designated. For, since no word whatsoever can directly negate Brahman here in the Imperishable (akṣara), the instruction is thus: "not this, not this" (neti neti).
Therefore, it follows directly that [the scripture] negates the desires arising from the ignorance of that [reality].
Now he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "Then, as for the name": "For the vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed real as both formed and formless; therefore, they are the Self of truth."

"Because it has that as its limiting adjunct (upādhi), the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is designated as 'Real' (satya). Now, one might object: "Is this name 'Real' applied to the Supreme [Self] merely figuratively? To this he says: "Those distinctions characterized by effects, which are otherwise indefinable, are defined [only] in relation to them. In these [distinctions],...

"That which has obtained a footing is called 'the other' [in the sense that it is diminished]. Thus, the meaning of the word *satya* ending in the genitive case has been stated; now, by way of restating that, he explains the meaning of the word *satya* ending in the nominative case:

"The Truth consists of the formed and the formless; yet even for that which has the nature of an effect, such as the vital breaths and so forth, this is the supreme truth—that which is determined as 'not this, not this'. Now, he says that it is not true even in the form of the formed and so forth:

"Since these [phenomena] possess no reality apart from the reality already described, nor do they lack reality—therefore, their true state is the supreme reality. Thus he establishes the stated point by means of an illustration: "Just as those who possess self-awareness [perceive] a rope as a rope..."

So too are serpents and the like. Those possessing a self and those devoid of a self—such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth—are [unified] by means of the inner self (*pratyagātman*). Since everything possesses a self by means of the inner self alone, what is the resulting fruit?
He states that this very point results: "One should see that alone and nothing else," because it is so; therefore, having observed this...
By way of the manifest and the unmanifest, and so forth.
The supreme state, designated as the non-dual self of reality (satya), is the oneness that is indicated by means of the object denoted by the word "reality."

"One should see this by oneself alone; one should see the truth as it has been described. For this very reason—that the true nature (*yāthātmya*) of both the manifest (*vyākṛta*) and the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) belongs to that [Self]—the application of those names occurs there [in the Self] and not otherwise. Thus he says: "Therefore, the true nature of the manifest..."
It is taught by means of a designation that "this is the truth of truths," and not otherwise; for it does not partake of any other designation.
Therefore, he says that this name exists for the sake of designation: "This is a name for the purpose of designation;
no name of its own is known for it. Now, is there not here the designation "Brahman is the Imperishable"?

Regarding the phrase "by means of names," this fault does not apply, because the pronoun refers to Brahman as qualified by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of cause and effect; thus he says: "Since the name finds its footing in that reality which consists of cause and effect.
[An objection: But surely there is usage of words for things that are distinct from both [cause and effect]. [Reply: True.
He says [it is] by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*):
"The word, which is formless and imperishable, being connected to the form that is its denotation, indicates [the Absolute];
it does not directly express the Supreme Brahman in any way whatsoever, because [the latter] is not directly [accessible] through the causes for the application of words."
The third Brāhmaṇa of the fourth [Adhyāya], ending with the words "because of the impossibility in Brahman" (brahmaṇyasaṃbhavāt).
The venerable [author] provides a recitation of the preceding section in order to establish the connection: "‘The Self alone...
Thus, the commentary on the Sūtra is clearly introduced with the words, "I shall speak of Brahman."

The meaning is that, as stated at the beginning of the fourth chapter, the entire text from the point where it begins with "because the sentence is incomplete" up to the end of the complete sentence constitutes the commentary on the aphorisms concerning the knowledge that has liberation as its fruit.

In this regard, he demonstrates the sequence by which isolation (*kaivalya*) is accomplished through four *vārtikas*, in order to establish that this Brāhmaṇa section is intended for the injunction of renouncing all actions as a means to knowledge.
A person whose intellect has been purified by the performance of daily obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) and other duties,
having become detached from the faults inherent in the fruits arising from all residual karma,
turns away from the first [state] due to that perception of its defects, through the impressions and memories of the sufferings of *saṃsāra*.

With his intellect impelled and his tongue [of desire] uprooted, he alone becomes one who desires the means [to liberation]; having abandoned all cravings, he then attains certainty regarding the inner Self. Through the awakening to the true nature of reality, he casts off the cause of saṃsāra.
"With all saṃsāra turned away, he is liberated, yet he is not being liberated. Now,
if it is argued that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is a means to knowledge and that this too is to be understood from the scriptures, [the author] says "no"—
whatever is the effect of ignorance that serves as a cause for dispassion (vairāgya), [that is what is meant here].
384) His renunciation occurs spontaneously due to dispassion, not from the authority of scripture;
likewise, if its status as a means is already established through other sources, it does not derive from this [scripture].
He says that the Brāhmaṇa begins for the purpose of explaining that [sannyāsa] is a means to knowledge:
"The fact that sannyāsa is a means to realizing the true nature of Brahman was not known from the Āgama;
therefore, it is made known here by this Śāstra. This is another meaning of the word *brāhmaṇa*.
To explain the meaning of the previous section concerning the Brāhmaṇa, he proceeds:

Having led [the seeker] beyond the characteristics of cause and effect arising from the ignorance of Brahman by means of the teaching "not this, not this," the Supreme Brahman was revealed; now, regarding that...
He raises an objection:

"In this regard, the following objection is raised: does the fault consisting in the non-establishment of Brahmanhood apply, or not? Is that which is negated by 'not this, not this'—namely, whatever entity such as the formed and the formless—is it everything, or is it something that pervades all?"
"Therefore it is negated" means that [the world] is either non-different, different, or grounded in non-existence. He states the refutation regarding the position of non-difference:
"If Brahman were inherent in the world, then that [world] would consist of what is not the ultimate good (anartha)."
He states the refutation of the third position:

Thus, it has been stated that knowledge of a supersensuous object is not something to be enjoined; now, he says that even the knowledge of the worldly self is not to be enjoined:

Nor does anyone whose mind has arisen perceive anything other than the inward-facing [Self]; even one whose self has emerged, while perceiving the Self, beholds nothing other than within the Self. This is the meaning: "one whose mind has not arisen" (anutthitamanāḥ) refers to one whose mind has not been produced [from its latent state].

At the beginning of sleep and so forth, one does not perceive anything other than the inner self (*pratyagātman*) by which an injunction could exist; for even one who has awakened from sleep, or whose mind is manifest, perceives nothing other than his own self.

Because one perceives something else [than that], and because even the knowledge of worldly objects is established without a formal injunction (*vidhi*), there is no injunction [regarding it]. If it is asked, "In the case where the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence is not subject to an injunction, then what is the object of the injunction for the knowledge of objects well-known in the world? [the answer is: by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [one knows] the Self and the non-Self.
He states [the purpose] of this discernment: "The agent is enjoined to that wherein he possesses autonomy;
through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is the discernment of the Self from the non-Self. He states the reason for this:

Since the very ignorance of the meanings of words is the obstacle to the awakening to the meaning of the sentence, one is enjoined to that [study of grammar] for the sake of its removal. He explains that the knowledge of word-meanings is the means to the knowledge of sentence-meaning: "Thus, he whose word-meanings are known..."

Just as previously stated in the passage "Brahman indeed is this," one understands the meaning of the sentence from the sentence itself through a reasoning that follows the unity of purpose; for, by means of the contemplation of the inner self (pratyaktattva) which is neither excluded nor followed by anything else, the meaning of the sentence is apprehended without obstruction.

The meaning is "after the knowledge of the referent of the word *tvam*. Regarding the fact that the knowledge of the referent of a word is the means for the knowledge of the referent of a sentence, there is the statement of the Guru (p.
He cites [the following] as an illustration of its being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa):
"The cognition of the meaning of a sentence would arise directly from the sentence alone;
and the cognition of the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the recollection of the meanings of the individual words, [as established] through positive and negative concomitance."

"The meaning of the word is certainly remembered; thus one realizes the Self as being free from suffering and inactive. Thus it has been stated that the knowledge of the meaning of the words is the means for the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence. In this regard, the following objection is raised: "Let it be so..."

It has been stated that the knowledge of word-meanings (*padārtha*) is the means for the knowledge of sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), and that such knowledge of word-meanings depends upon syntactic connection (*anvaya*) and so forth; however, that [objection] does not hold, because it is not established by itself.
To this, he says: "Because of the delusion regarding each [word], [the meaning] exists through the predominance of its own nature."
Due to the persistence of ignorance, the Self previously did not know itself; therefore, through the arising of knowledge of the meaning of the [great] statement,
and by means of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), one extracts the Self from what is non-self and perceives the Self as "all is the Self."
In the operation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), injunction (*vidhi*) is simply the making known of what was previously unknown, and not that which you intend;
thus he says:
"And therefore, the making known of the unknown is here designated as injunction, whereas the non-engagement of one who has not yet engaged [is not]."

"Because there is no logical justification, it is not accepted"—or rather, by this [statement], it is expressed that the "injunction" intended by you is [untenable] because of the knowledge of the sentence-meaning in the manner already described.

Anticipating the objection that if knowledge alone is to be enjoined, then the object of that knowledge must also be enjoined, he says: That which is eternal does not come into being, nor does that which is eternally existent undergo production; therefore, it cannot be something to be performed, just like a sky-flower or space.

That which has origination and so forth by itself, and for which there is absolutely no action at all—because it is established independently of action—it is said to be "established by itself. This is an elaboration of the preceding point. To whom, then, does establishment depend upon action? To this he says: "But that which is capable regarding origination and so forth..."
One observes that the fruitfulness of an action depends on that [self], for it is that which manifests it.

Furthermore, he states another reason for the fact that neither the self nor the knowledge of it can be made subject to volition: "The effect would be dependent upon the cause, because its acquisition [of existence] occurs through that; otherwise, the effect of another would not be an effect."

"And no other cause is observed. This is the meaning: first, an effect such as a jar is dependent upon its own cause; furthermore, valid cognition is an entity that is dependent upon another effect—this is the meaning of "dependent"—and it does not observe any other cause.
It depends upon a means; even that self-substance which is not an effect depends upon a means.
Thus, he establishes that the knowledge of the Self is dependent upon its means of valid cognition: "The cognition that 'all is the Self' would arise from the power of the object of cognition."
"If that [knowledge] were dependent on the knower, it would follow [the object], like the cognition of fire upon seeing light.
The meaning is "by force. Therefore, he concludes: "Therefore, because it is dependent on the person (puruṣa), self-knowledge [is not dependent on the object]."
If it is asked, "In that case, what would be the injunction? he says in response:

"Because the nature of action depends upon [the agent's] engagement (*anvaya*) and so forth, hearing, reflection, and likewise the study of the scriptures (*āgama*) and so on are enjoined; for a person is able to perform that which has been thus enjoined."

"Therefore, this is enjoined. Furthermore, because the Self is the very nature of experience and is the fruit of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the Self cannot be an object of injunction; thus he says: "Since specific experience is the fruit of all means of knowledge, and that which is a fruit cannot be enjoined."

Therefore, it is enjoined as follows: "It is distinguished," meaning it is characterized by truth and so forth. Furthermore, he establishes that the knowledge of the worldly self is not something to be enjoined:
"Whatever may be a means of valid cognition, a non-means of valid cognition, or a semblance of a means of valid cognition..."

The meaning is as follows: since everything manifests as having the very form of consciousness—that is, because all cognitions are established through the self-luminosity of the Self—the Self is established; therefore, that knowledge [of the Self] is not something to be enjoined.
It does not assume various forms, but remains as the very form of consciousness;
it is the one non-deviating inward-facing [consciousness], while all others are deviating. This is an elaboration of what was stated previously.
Now, [one might object]: "In deep sleep and so forth..."
Since even self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvit*) is subject to deviation, how can it be said that cognition is one with the inward-facing [subject]?
To this, he replies: "Even though cognition has arisen, [it is so called] because of its apprehension of the state of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) and so forth."

"Because prior to its arising, it appears to people as if it were unarisen. Even though there is deviation regarding the mother and so forth, consciousness (*saṃvit*) is non-deviant; for even throughout the entire world, there is mutual deviation regarding everything other than that [consciousness]. Now, if the Self is of the nature of consciousness...
"Why is it that knowledge arises only when the defects have ceased? For what purpose, then, is there the injunction for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth?

To this he replies: "Even though knowledge has arisen, because of the persistence of the state of being a knower and so forth, it appears to men as if it had not arisen prior to its [actual] production. When [this occurs]...
By means of the practice of hearing and so forth, one dispels the delimitation [of Brahman] caused by the grasping of motherhood and other such attributes;

at that time, one considers that the knowledge of the partless, non-dual Brahman has indeed already arisen even previously. Thus he says: "When [Brahman] is directly established through the path of the aforementioned reasoning, it is indeed already arisen."
The statement "then consciousness is considered to exist even before" is an elaboration of the point that [consciousness] remains even when there is deviation regarding the mother and so forth.
Since everything would be Brahman, which is of the nature of its own self and is consciousness, it is non-deviating;
this is established by the inherent power of the scriptural injunction "the Self is to be seen."

He shows the implied meaning: for the purpose of refutation, the word "self" (ātman) refers here to those two [the seer and the seen] within memory, by means of the activity of the subject (*pramātṛ*). (p. 408)

It is said that "pervasion (vyāpti) is to be seen"; first, from the understanding of another word, such a [cognition] arises here. Now, he refutes [the claim] that there is direct experience (anubhava) from the Veda, or rather, it is to be investigated whether or not such experience exists as a real entity.

"Like the experience of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. The meaning is that the knowledge of the distinctions between the knower and so forth within the Brahman-Self, which is perceived through the power of the words [of scripture], is false, just like the knowledge of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like. How is it false? To this he says:
Whether it be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or an invalid one, [it is so] due to its connection or lack of connection with the object of cognition (*meyasaṃgati*).
"In this context, the distinction between the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*meyabheda*) is not first apprehended through valid cognition (*miti*). This is the meaning:

"Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which makes known an object as it truly is; that which makes it known otherwise is invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*). Such is the established position of those who know valid cognition.

Because Brahman and the Self are non-dual, no such distinction as that of the knower and so forth can exist therein; therefore, the knowledge of them [as distinct] arising from the mere appearance of words is false. Furthermore, because the Self is self-luminous, the cognition of it [as an object] is illusory; thus he says:

Since it is certain that the Self is the object accessible only to the inward-turned intellect (*pratyagdhi*), the word "intellect" (*dhi*) here refers to the cognition of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

He states that there is no attachment to its being the self because it is not self-luminous: "If it were not the object of the inward-directed intellect, it would be non-self, like a jar or similar objects. For that very reason, he says it is imagined:
"Consequently, its inclusion within the cycle beginning with Brahmā follows for it. Therefore, it is not [the Self].
He states that the Self is accessible through the transformation of the knower’s cognition, just like a jar or other objects:

"The Self is not reached by a distinct vision, as is the case with a jar. Although it is not accessible to another cognition, it is nevertheless not the case that it is not known by itself through itself; thus he says "no."

And there is no pervasion in the case of non-difference for the very same reason as before. If it is argued that [the self] must then be cognizable by another self, he says "no": "There is no seer other than the self of the seer," because of the negation of any other seer; thus, even though there is no other self, it is not [perceived] by that [other].
He says that it is "to be known," and that in the world, the relationship between seer and seen is not observed in two [identical] things; the meaning is that they are equal, like a lamp.
He states another refutation regarding the case where [the self] is known by itself:

"There would follow a contradiction with [the necessity of] action for one who perceives the Self as the Seer. Furthermore, if it were to be realized by itself through itself, then because its own realization would be eternally established, the purpose of spiritual practice would be rendered futile; thus he says: "Since that vision is eternally attained..."
Regarding the phrase "the connection with the futility of injunction" (p.
he states another objection to the view that the knowledge of the identity of the self with transmigratory existence is something to be enjoined.

Even if the transmigrating self were perceived, there would be no purpose [in such perception]; indeed, the very perception of the transmigrating object is itself a disadvantage. If it is argued that "therefore, the knowledge of the non-transmigrating self must be enjoined," he says "no," because since that which is other than it is not established, how could there be its observation?
Now, if it is argued that this self is already well-known, why then is the vision of it not enjoined?

The meaning is that whether such a self is seen or unseen, there can be no injunction for knowledge regarding it; furthermore, because the transmigrating self is established by common worldly experience, its knowledge cannot be enjoined by scripture.
He states the reason for this being knowable:
"Because the seer, the act of seeing, and the object seen are perceptible, there is no dependence on scripture.
Now, if the Self were distinct from the seer, he states the objection to that: "If the Self were separate from the seer..."

"It would be difficult to say that there is a separate self" means that what is divided, like a pot or other objects, lacks the nature of a self. Now, one might object: "The transmigrating self is not established by worldly experience; therefore, the knowledge of it must be something to be enjoined. To this, he replies: "And [knowledge] cannot exist if the self is not already established."
For the well-known nature of *saṃsāra* [is established] because a relation whose relata are not well-known is never accepted anywhere; here, by the word "relation," *saṃsāra* is meant.

Because it is dependent, that [transmigration] is established; its establishment does not occur apart from the establishment of the self, since transmigration is dependent upon it. Therefore, the establishment of the self must be accepted. Now, one might object:
"Transmigration does not reside in the self; what then is its instrument? To this, he says: "No."

"If this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is observed as being connected to the self and so forth, then from what cause does the desire for liberation (mumukṣutva) arise?— thus one should investigate. Furthermore, he states that there can be no injunction regarding the knowledge of the transmigrating soul because such knowledge is not dependent on human will:
"A threefold injunction is not accepted as false, just as [the injunction] regarding the birth of a barren woman's son;

likewise, this injunction for the perception of the inner self is not [false]. If it is asked, "How can there be a dependence of the knowledge of transmigrating beings upon persons? [the answer follows].

He establishes this by means of an analogy: "Just as the all-pervasiveness of space remains eternal within a jar despite its conjunction with or separation from various substances— since the presence of space cannot be avoided—
so too, the direct perception of the intellect remains [unchanged] during its connection with external objects such as sound or during their division."
"The connection with consciousness is eternal, witnessed by the eternal Self.

By stating that the knowledge of the transmigrating self is eternally attained, any restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) regarding that knowledge is refuted; nevertheless, an exclusive injunction (*parisaṃkhyāvidhi*) remains possible.

But when the knowledge of the unity of the Self has arisen, since that very knowledge is eternally attained, there is neither a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) nor an exclusive injunction (*parisaṃkhyāvidhi*); thus he says: "Therefore, it is [like] a side-view. (p. 412)

"There is no attainment here; neither a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) nor an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) is possible in the realization of the unity of the Self; therefore, this [statement] expresses the result of the former. Thus, some [hold that] because a sentence whose purport is an already established entity would entail the consequence of being dependent [on something else], its...
He says that because there is a connection with other means of knowledge regarding the meaning of an injunction, and because such [other means] are absent here, an injunction must be accepted;

for just as there is an authoritative means of knowledge in the *Karmakāṇḍa*, so too in the *Upaniṣads* there is only an injunction, since it is independent, whereas a declarative statement (*abhidhā-śruti*) is dependent.
Even though the oneness of Brahman is already established, because it lacks form and other qualities, it is not an object of other means of knowledge;

therefore, the validity of the scriptural statement of designation is justified. Thus he says: "Not so, because the scripture of designation brings about the correct realization of identity, which has not been attained by any other means of knowledge."

"Validity [of knowledge] is like a statement that awakens one from sleep. Now, an objection is raised: "How can the oneness of the Self (aikātmya) be an object of knowledge (meyatva), given the existence of the knower and so forth? To this he replies: "Since the object of knowledge is held to be the reality consisting solely of the non-agentive oneness of the Self, there is no distinction [of that object] from the means of knowledge (māna) other than that [Self]."

It is obtained. This means that since the distinction between the knower (*pramātṛ*) and so forth is not established by any means of knowledge (*māna*), it is logical that the immutable non-dual [Self] is the object of knowledge (*meyatva*). Now, [one might ask]: regarding Brahman and the Self...

If it is argued that there is an obstruction other than ignorance and that its removal results from the prescribed knowledge—therefore, that [knowledge] must be enjoined—the author replies: "Because for the primary identity, there is no other obstruction than ignorance.
Thus, let ignorance itself be the obstruction.
He says "no" to the claim that [ignorance] ceases through knowledge produced by injunction, stating:

"Because that which depends on injunction is something to be accomplished (*kārya*), it has no power over what is already known. The meaning of "because it is something to be accomplished" is "because it lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇatvāt*). Therefore, [the cessation of ignorance occurs] only through knowledge that is a valid means of cognition.
Nothing else has the power to remove ignorance. This is what [the author] says:

having stated that knowledge arising from the reality of the self as it truly exists is the cause for the destruction of darkness, there is no other cause than that; therefore, injunctions are not accepted as a means of valid knowledge, for indeed, even if something is enjoined... (Note: The final portion of the Sanskrit fragment appears to be a rhetorical objection or a transition leading into a discussion on the nature of injunctions (*vidhi*) and their status as a source of valid cognition.)

Although the validity of words such as "sacrifice" (*yāga*) is already established, it is nevertheless the case that the validity of the knowledge enjoined by a person is being produced. To this, he says:
"And the sovereignty of the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*) consists in the correctness of his cognition."

He says that [the objection]—namely, that because the object of knowledge (*meyam*) is the sole cause, there can be no dependence on the knower (*mātṛtantratā*), and thus if it were established as a finality, its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇyam*) due to such dependence would be untenable—is not valid:
"Just as there is independence in the case of an injunction (*vidhi*), so too in the Vedāntas there is the expression of the Śruti; however, in this case, [the opposite] is false."
Because it is universal and because it brings about the cognition of that which is beyond the senses,
[the word]—
being itself established independently as something not an object of the senses and so forth— is not a means of proof; yet, through its denotation, it makes [the object] known.

"That nothing else whatsoever is required" is an elaboration of what was stated previously. Because it is devoid of form and so forth, it is unfit for direct perception; therefore, it does not require an injunction.
The meaning is that the scriptural word is a denotative one (*abhidhā-śruti*). An injunction does not apply to an already established entity.

Thus, even though it was proposed that the status of the Veda as a means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) exists in the case of an injunction (*niyoga*), that status was refuted in the *Asambandhagrantha* on the grounds that an injunction is impossible. Therefore, he says: "By way of a digression, therefore, the authority of the injunction [resides] only in that which is the means to the desired end. Thus ends the section on the authority of the injunction.
"In the cognition of the probandum and the probans regarding that which is beyond the senses, it cannot be known by any other means; therefore,
he once again establishes the non-authoritativeness of injunction (*vidhi*) with respect to perceptible objects according to his own tenet."

"Just as the relationship between the goal and the means cannot be understood through denotation (*abhidhā*) on its own, so too it cannot be established by an injunctive word (*vidhi-girā*) when [the goal] is self-evident. Furthermore, because there is no productive activity (*bhāvanā*) here, there is no injunction; for since the identity of the Self (*aikātmya*) is self-evident, no action is required."
Consequently, there is an absence of cultivation (bhāvanā), because cultivation depends upon action; and in the absence of cultivation, there is no authority for an injunction (*vidhi*) therein.
This is the meaning: where there is action, there is the performance of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*);
where there is performance, there is an injunction (*vidhi*). Therefore, an injunction has no authority regarding an already established entity.
Consequently, he says "by itself" (*svataḥ*), meaning that only a sentence devoid of an injunction has authority regarding an established entity.

"Let it be that denotation (*abhidhā*) possesses authority because it awakens [the meaning] whose purpose is already established. Furthermore, with two verses of the *Vārttika*, he raises an objection in order to introduce the [concept of] injunction (*vidhi*). That is transcribed as follows:

"If it is argued that denotation is not authoritative because it is dependent [on something else], then [we reply] that denotation is considered to be like the world; its nature as denotation is [established] by others, etc."

And just as in the expression "fruits on the riverbank," the combination of words is not possible [if taken individually]; furthermore, since the denotation of words in a Vedic revelation depends upon the verbal form (ākhyāta-pada), and because there is a combination of words everywhere,
he states that a verb must exist even here:

It cannot be argued that there must necessarily be a collection of words because of the existence of a verb; for this [sentence] has already been explained, as it contains multiple designations in the scripture. Thus, it is appropriate that the sentence "the river's milk" is dependent [on something else], since its meaning is established by direct perception and not from that sentence alone.
He states that this is established by means of two *vārtikas*, which are cited as follows: "The fruits on the riverbank...
It is logical that the Vedic statement expresses a requirement, because the connection between the fruit and the riverbank is apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

(416) "This object is graspable by direct perception (pratyakṣa), and not otherwise according to the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); therefore, there is no certainty regarding such an object based on scripture (āgama) alone. [Objection: But surely it is established by another means of valid cognition?

This is the meaning that results: the sense [of the text] is not something to be understood from the mere sentence through a literal connection, for the establishment of the identity of the Self (*aikātmya*) arises solely from scripture (*āgama*). This is because its nature is here [in this context] beyond the scope of perception and other means of knowledge, as it is not an object of sight and so forth; thus he says: "But regarding the meaning of words such as 'unprecedented' (*apūrva*), etc."

"It depends upon perception and the other means of knowledge because the reality called 'the one self' is not an object of perception and the other means. Although there is a distinction between the sentences concerning ritual action and those concerning knowledge, insofar as they have mutually contradictory objects to be accomplished, nevertheless—

Since the cause of validity is equal in both cases, who could prevent the validity of sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) with respect to Brahman? This is stated in two *vārtikas*, which are cited here: "The quality of being a non-human (authorless) sentence is common to the Veda and [the Upanishadic] declaration."
The capacity to cognize objects beyond the senses is equal for both [the Veda and the Buddha] through their respective scriptural injunctions;

if there is any difference between them, it lies merely in the distinction between what is already established and what is yet to be proven as an object of knowledge. However, regarding their validity (*prāmāṇya*), not even the slightest degree of self-reliance (*svatastva*) is observed. Now, is it not the case that here [in the case of the Buddha], it is indeed valid cognition (*pramā*) itself?

To the question of how it is that no [new] arising occurs, he says in response that there is an absence of such doubt: first, the realization "I am Brahman" arises regarding that which is beyond the world.
Immediately following the hearing of such statements as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi),
since even an injunctive sentence possesses validity by virtue of producing valid knowledge, if that same validity exists here as well, why should it be invalid? To this, he says:

If this is so, why is the authority of the Veda not mentioned here? Why has the validity of the injunction (*vidhi*) also not been stated here, given its superior logic? Furthermore, since perception and the other means of knowledge possess the capacity to cognize their own objects, they too have validity; therefore, that [validity] exists for them as well.

To the question "In what way is it authoritative?", he says: The inherent capacity (*svaśakti*) of all means of knowledge exists for the purpose of cognizing an object as it is; and that [capacity] certainly exists in verbal expression (*abhidhā*) as well. Why, then, should it be considered non-authoritative? Indeed, if [it were argued that it is non-authoritative] because it is devoid of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth...
"Brahman is not amenable to perception; nevertheless, it is amenable to inference and other means of knowledge, therefore verbal testimony depends upon inference and the like. To this he says:
"Nor does a means of knowledge depend upon signs (liṅga) and so forth when its object is established as beyond the senses. But [an objection is raised]: "But..."

One might argue that although this Brahman is not an object of ordinary perception, it is accessible through the perception of yogis, and therefore statements such as "That [is] Truth" (*tattvamasi*) depend upon that; to this he says "no," because neither of those two is its object.

He states the reason for its not being an object: from such scriptural passages as "Not this, not this" (*neti neti*) and "It is neither coarse nor fine" (*asthūlam anaṇu*), the meaning is as follows:
This [Self] is approached as being accessible through the direct perception of yogins,
and not because it is the cause of that cognition; [this is established] through scripture, inference from the meaning [of scripture], and so forth, regarding the Self.
The meaning is that because it is his very nature (*svarūpa*), the Self is not capable of being [perceived] by that [means].
Because it is incapable of being perceived by either of the two types of perception, he says that it is not apprehended by inference:
"And because perception does not apply, it is not measured by inference regarding the connection between the property and the possessor of the property."

"Not when it has not been grasped through inference. Now, an objection is raised: although Brahman is not perceptible to those of the present age, it was nevertheless perceptible to those living in other ages, because of the possibility of such extraordinary excellence in their perception. To this, he says:
