"From the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and other such sources here, [the existence of] that other [cause] is established through its effects. Thus, he establishes the causality of the Supreme alone: "That whose causality is directly ascertained by valid means (pramāṇa) must be accepted as the very agent of those effects"—this refers to Brahman.

Since its status as the cause of all things is firmly established in the Śruti, although there are various traditional recollections (smṛti) here and there—such as that which was proclaimed by Vāyu or that which was proclaimed by Parāśara—nevertheless, the meaning remains that Brahman alone is the cause even in those cases. Now, [one might object]: the Veda, simply by virtue of being the Veda...
[The opponent might argue: "Let it be that the Brāhmaṇas and even the Itihāsas and so forth are thus [authoritative]; what is the use of their being rooted in the Veda? To this he replies:

"Nor is the Veda intended here as a mere collection of texts because it is stated in the Veda; rather, it is because the grounds for non-authoritativeness are impossible in the case of Vedic sentences. Nor is the Veda...

The meaning is that the Veda is authoritative precisely because it is the Veda, since causes for its lack of authority—such as the impossibility of its production and so forth—are absent. Nor is the Veda non-authoritative due to dependence on other sources like the *itihāsas* and the like; he states this because the Veda is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).
The authority of Vedic statements does not depend upon other means of knowledge;
for perception and the like lack the causes of authority, such as the non-arising [of error].
And he says,
"Because of independence," meaning that even the validity of the senses and so forth arises from the very reason already stated.
He [now] establishes the connection of the passage beginning with "Just as he [is the cause] of all these," preceded by a recitation of what has occurred.

He says: "Just as no other entity apart from consciousness (prajñāna) can be conceived in the case of maintenance and creation, so it is stated even regarding sovereignty. Having thus stated the connection, he applies the sentence [to the example] of rivers with diverse names and forms.
Just as the ocean is one in its undifferentiated form, name, and dissolution, [the author] now states the application of the illustration:
"The skin and other [senses] are the single locus for the various cognitions of touch and so forth; therefore, they [are one]."
The skin and the other [senses] dissolve in that same manner into the intellect (*buddhi*), and likewise the intellect dissolves into the mind (*manas*) through the exhaustion of karma;
thus the intellect remains as the cause. This process is common to all, being preceded by the internal cognition (*pratyag-buddhi*);
such is the dissolution of the cognitions of objects into the sense organs, of the sense organs into the mind, and of the mind into...
When the intellect [returns] to the Intellect through the exhaustion of karma, it assumes its causal form;
this is the dissolution common to all living beings, such as that occurring in deep sleep and so forth, known as *iḍa*. If so, what then is the uncommon dissolution?
Regarding this, he says:
"From the knowledge of the true nature of the inner self, in accordance with the actual state of things..."

"Dissolution [occurs] from the destruction of ignorance; that which is preceded by consciousness," thus he elaborates upon natural dissolution by means of an illustration: "Just as the ocean is the single point of convergence for all tactile sensations pertaining to the skin of worldly existence."

He elaborates on the illustrative example that "the skin alone is the supreme resort" by means of the term *sparśa* (touch), wherein the object perceivable by the skin is denoted. Likewise, by the term *gandha* (odor) and so forth, the objects of the nose and other senses are intended. Thus, by the term *sparśādi* (touch and the rest) [the respective sense-objects are indicated].

In this context, the knowledge of the sense organs and their objects is understood as being included within the objects themselves; their dissolution occurs into the respective sense organs that perceive them. The dissolution of the sense organs into the mind, the mind into the intellect (*buddhi*), and the intellect into its cause, should be understood as previously described. Now, [the following is stated]:

He shows [the views] found in the commentary of Bhartṛprapañca regarding the state prior to dissolution, specifically for the purpose of demonstrating dissolution: "The earth is a collection of smell and the rest up to taste;
likewise water [is a collection] of three [qualities]; fire [of two]; wind [of one]; and space has a single object."

Thus, one should describe these five elements according to their characteristics. Now, is it not the case that the pentad of elements, beginning with earth, is defined as the collection of qualities such as odor when they are established in states of increase and decrease? By this analogy, this [point] is...
He establishes [the point]: Just as the seed alone is accepted as the cause of the sprout and so forth, in that same way,
the seed alone is the cause of that which has the nature of the sprout and so forth.

Since the seed is determined as the inner self (pratyaktva) at both the beginning and the end, therefore, let that very seed be the cause of the effects in the interval between them; this is the meaning: Brahman alone is the cause.
If it is asked how this is explained, he says:
"The manifestation of the formed and the formless is intended as the manifestation of the qualities (*guṇas*). This is the meaning:

because it is the cause for the manifestation of the qualities, that very [manifestation] is the manifestation of the elements denoted by the terms "formed" and "formless"; likewise, their dissolution is simply the dissolution of those [qualities].

Some say this is stated for the purpose of demonstrating that there is a dissolution of the qualities (guṇas) and likewise an origination of the two elements; they hold that the word "quality" (guṇa) here refers to the subtle elements (tanmātras). Having thus grouped them together, he explains what kind of dissolution occurs for the specific elements already mentioned:

The phrase "the causal nature of the elements whose specific qualities have been withdrawn" is to be supplied here, as in the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others; the meaning is that dissolution occurs here [in the qualities]. Now, one might object: "But the dissolution of the elements is not heard of here; rather, it is thus for the qualities alone."

Therefore, in this context, the tangibles and so forth mentioned in the scripture (p. 463) are intended as indicators for their own substrata, such as air and the rest; otherwise, [the argument would fail].

Intending to show that all [elements] are not established as being entirely absent, he says: "In that case, by the very perception of touch, a portion of air is apprehended here; likewise, a third part of fire, a fourth of water, and a fifth of earth. This is based solely on the relative scarcity or abundance of their qualities.
He states that there is also a mutual distinction between earth and the other elements: "The distinction is not by means of my qualities.

Just as the classification of the elements arises from the classification of their qualities, so too each individual quality, such as touch and the rest, exists in manifold ways according to the relative paucity or abundance of the elements, such as earth.

He says that [the distinction] is caused by the multiplicity [of elements]: "In the same way, this should be accepted for touch; the same should be applied to smell and the others; this difference arises from the difference in qualities. The meaning is that it is caused by the scarcity or abundance of the elements; for the differentiation of qualities therein is produced by the increase or decrease of the elements.

First, he shows the fivefold division of touch: because of the predominance of the earth element, touch is considered to be rough; because of the predominance of water due to its viscidity, touch is considered to be cold;
and because of the abundance of fire, touch is hot, as well as soft.
It should be understood that [the world] consists predominantly of *marut* (wind) because it relies upon the qualities as previously described.
Now, if the world is thus multiform in nature, how can Brahman—which is eternally unchanging (*kūṭastha*) and of a single essence—be its cause? To this, he says:

For Brahman, whose every modification has been destroyed, that very transformation— beginning with fire, light, and so forth— would belong to the Self through ignorance; and because of contact with the Self, it would become absolutely supreme.

"It has become solid. If it is asked how this transformation is established, he says that the cognition produced by the sense organs and so forth is known through direct experience and is not inferable:
"Because of the contact of the skin with that [object], there arises the cognition of a manifested tactile sensation."
"The thorough knowledge of the distinctions among touches is therefore abandoned by the two eyes"— to which he replies that such knowledge is not self-luminous:
"The cognition of the distinctions among touch and so forth must indeed be insentient, just like touch itself."

"Because it is for the sake of another, that [knowledge] is not for its own sake, unlike the case of a witness. Thus, the state prior to dissolution has been described; now, he shows the process of withdrawal into the Inner Self (pratyagātman) by means of discernment (*viveka*) together with that knowledge. Exceedingly...

Through contact with the skin, there arises coarse knowledge; through its conjunction with the mind, from that, pure cognition (dhī) arises; and even beyond that, subtle discernment born of the union with the intellect (buddhi) occurs, as long as there is pervasion by blood within the body.
"But here, through the universal functioning of the intellect (buddhi), [the Self's] pervasion lasts until the dissolution of the body;
like the reflection of consciousness, the vital breath (prāṇa) remains pervading that intellect.
Being one whose own self is neither effect nor cause, [the Self] remains having set aside that [intellect]. This is the meaning.

When that [consciousness], which consists of the cognitions of the sense organs such as the skin and so forth, becomes gross and is connected with objects by means of the mind, it is then defined as "mere mind" (*manomātra*); at that time, that consciousness becomes clear. By abandoning its gross form, it becomes subtle. When...

It is connected with the intellect (*buddhi*) and is determined to be mere intellect; it becomes even more subtle than the mind (*manas*), because the intellect is subtler than the mind. And that intellect pervades the entire body;
the Self, which is the cause of the appearance [of consciousness], pervades that intellect. That is the intellect.

The mere cause is indeed the cause, yet it is the mere inward-facing reality (pratyag-mātra) distinct from both cause and effect. Now, by means of several verses (vārtikas), [the author describes] the nature of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra-prakāra) of the Self in its state prior to dissolution.

He demonstrates this: if even in natural dissolution that [suffering] does not exist, what need is there to mention intentional dissolution? To establish this, he shows that when the body undergoes transformation through contact with thorns and the like, then suffering arises from demerit (*adharma*) and so forth.

The statement "it is born from modification" is easy to understand. Furthermore, he explains how that suffering, having arisen as something pertaining to the body, becomes associated with the notion of the body:
"Suffering, which is a part of the body, qualifies the intellect residing in one's own body. He then explains the meaning of this.
"Because that place is painful, pain arises for the intellect. Thus [it is said regarding] that which is joined with thorns and the like.

The meaning is that suffering arises in the intellect (buddhi) due to a particular region of the body; for the purpose of delimiting—that is, specifying—that suffering, another mental modification (vṛtti) arises simultaneously with the birth of the suffering, as he says: "the modification [arises] for its delimitation."

"Through the very arising of suffering, there occurs the connection between the enjoyer and the enjoyed; this [suffering] of the self is caused by that."—[the question being] "What is this function?"—he states it: "This function of 'I' belongs to the intellect (buddhi), and it is that which cuts off suffering."
"Being (satī) distinguishes the knower by means of its own appearance as the object of knowledge.
This is its meaning: the mental modification (*vṛtti*) characterized by suffering qualifies the knower—the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which possesses that modification—as was previously stated.

By the word *dhī*, the universal function (*sāmānyavṛtti*) pervading the body is grasped; and that cognizer (*boddhā*), being characterized by suffering, qualifies its own internal reflection known as the individual soul (*jīva*) with its own inherent suffering. And that reflection [qualifies] its own inherent suffering in the Witness (*sākṣin*).

It attributes [the state] thus: "The self is a transmigrator. Now, one might object: "Since the emergence of the 'I'-modification (*ahaṃvṛtti*) occurs only at the very time of transformation into pleasure, pain, and so forth, how can it be said that it is possible at another time as well?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Not apart from external modification..."
"The occurrence of the notion of 'I' in the body does not appear as 'I' to one whose senses, mind, and intellect are at rest. This refers to one whose mind is concentrated (*samāhitacitta*).

The meaning is: "Because I do not perceive [them as] my own functions. Now, one might object: "Just as pain arising from contact with thorns and the like is connected to the limbs of the body, so too might pain arise from the connection of egoistic identification (*abhimānika-sambandha*) with sons and others.
Anticipating this, he says: "This egoistic identification is due to ignorance (*ajñāna*)."

In the case of knowledge, [the dissolution] occurs at the limit of the objects, but not in the detached, immutable Self (pratyak). As for the statement "I am dead," in the previous section it was stated—by way of a prima facie argument—that there is a dissolution of the cognitions of objects and the objects themselves into the sense organs. Now, he demonstrates the established conclusion (siddhānta): "No."
Regarding the term "effect" (*kārya*):
the dissolution of an effect is not observed apart from its cause;
therefore, in this context, the generality (*sāmānya*) that initiates the skin-egg is understood as being within the skin-egg itself.

He elaborates upon this point with two verses: "Because it is an effect, there can be no such dissolution of objects within the sense organs; for a jar does not dissolve into clay, nor does a bowl dissolve elsewhere [than its own material].
Therefore, words such as 'skin' and so forth refer either to the skin and other organs themselves, or to their constituent causes, and thus apply everywhere."
"It is to be understood that there is no dissolution elsewhere" means:
because they are effects, the sense organs have the objects as their material cause (*prakṛti*). Regarding the phrase "of all odors": [this refers to the fact that]...
Coarse earth is understood as being characterized by the five qualities beginning with sound; or else, [it is characterized] by odor.

Because it possesses manifold forms, the innate odor is perceived; thus he says that the word "odor" does not encompass the entirety of earth, or rather, that there is another aspect of this odor due to its many divisions—thereby demonstrating the manifold nature of odor. Odor is heavy, predominantly earthy, and refreshing.
Coldness predominates in water; heat, due to its abundance, predominates in fire; lightness predominates in air; odor is clear and pervasive, as is space, which predominates there.
Furthermore, due to the moistening by fire, the portions of earth and water become inferior, foul-smelling, and [heavy].

"An odor arises awakened by evil karma; however, when there is a transformation of equal proportions, a fragrant and auspicious odor arises for a living being engaged in meritorious karma, acting as a cause for non-attachment. Thus, in the preceding [section], touch was described in many ways.

Now, he states that this same principle applies to odor as well among the remaining [objects]: "In the same way, one should apply what has been said to those following taste and form; for the manifestation of the qualities occurs through their relationship as primary and subordinate."

In the statement "the generality that initiates the skin," it was asserted that the sense organs are composed of their respective objects. He establishes this: by means of inference from the fact that they grasp specific [qualities] such as odor, let there be no primacy [of the elements] over the object of perception.
"One should point this out regarding the nose and the other [senses] as well" (p.
He elaborates upon this Vārttika with three further Vārttikas, which are now transcribed:
The sense organ would be of the same class as its own apprehended object, like a lamp.
If it were not the case that form alone possesses the nature of appearing, then [the cognition] would not be like form, as the scripture states here.

If there were no grasping of all objects that is of the same nature as the object [itself], then the grasping of all objects by each individual sense organ would be like that of the mind and the intellect (*manobuddhi*). However, it should be understood that because they consist of the essence of all elements (*sarvabhūtātmakatva*), the grasping of all objects belongs to both the mind and the intellect; otherwise, such grasping would be impossible. Thus...

The material nature of the sense organs has been established; now, what is their common form and for what purpose do they exist? By what are they impelled, and how do they function? Furthermore, what is the distinction between the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*)—this is the subject matter [to be explained].

He explains this by means of three *vārttikas*, which are written as follows: "Intellect (*buddhi*) is said to be the generality (*sāmānya*) of the powers of cognition, such as the sense of touch; likewise, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone is said to be the generality of the power of action. Furthermore, for the sake of accomplishing the enjoyment of sound and other objects, there are the powers of cognition belonging to the ears and other senses."

In the same way, for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of karma, there are the powers of action such as speech and so forth; the projection of these aforementioned powers is preceded by the mind and the intellect, through the functions of volition (*saṃkalpa*) and determination (*adhyavasāya*). Furthermore, the distinction between those two is twofold. [Objection: But regarding the feet...

The activity of the hand-faculty is not seen being performed [by itself]; even by the hand, there is the activity of the foot-faculty, for all [faculties] have the eye as their ear (i.e., they perceive through it).

"And since it is heard [in scripture], there is therefore no fixed rule"—to this he says: "Or rather, that which belongs to a sense organ capable [of perceiving a certain object] is to be designated as such even when it functions elsewhere; there is no confusion of their intrinsic natures. Thus [ends the discussion of] the sense organs.
Having raised the doubt as to what purpose they serve, it was stated that sound and the other objects exist for the purpose of being perceived through their respective injunctions;

now, [the author asks] for what purpose is the creation of the body? To this, he says: "Thus, the projection of the powers of knowledge and action [belongs to] the World-Self (jagadātman) for the sake of providing a locus for the cause."
"The manifestation of the body of the Self" means that the connection is with the "Self of the world";
the meaning is that the creation of the body occurs as the locus of the instruments for the transmigrating self (*saṃsāry-ātman*).
Since it has been stated that the causes are the effects of the elements, he says that their dissolution also occurs in those very [elements].

This being the case, whatever effect has manifested from a particular cause, that very effect undergoes dissolution back into its own cause. [Objection: Since it was stated "from which [cause] whatever," one might suspect that a cause other than Brahman is being admitted; anticipating this, he says:
The dissolution of all these must occur in their very primary cause, because effects [dissolve] into their own causes, and not into another effect.

Thus [it is said]. Now, if the dissolution of all effects occurs in Brahman alone, how is it that the well-known dissolution of clay-pots and the like occurs in clay and so forth? He replies that this is an illusion: because of direct perception, there is the notion that "the dissolution of pots and the like occurs in the lumps [of clay] themselves," whereas in reality, this dissolution of prior effects occurs [only] in [Brahman].

Regarding the phrase "due to delusion" (mohataḥ): the meaning is this—since clay and other such materials are perceived by direct observation at the time when jars and other effects dissolve back into their causal material, Brahman, the dissolution of the jars and so forth occurs within those perceptible materials; thus, there arises the erroneous notion that the dissolution of the jar and so forth takes place in the clay itself.

Regarding the phrase "of whom it is born": this demonstrates the manner of dissolution of every effect into its root cause. Thus, just as the subtle elements (tanmātras) such as touch dissolve into their respective causes like the skin and so forth, so too do those [subtle elements] dissolve into the mind within the generality of objects.

The dissolution of that cognition also occurs within the single universal of its own object, just as rivers dissolve into the ocean; and even the universal consciousness of objects dissolves into the Supreme Self, which is free from modification, dissolution, and distraction— this is now [the case].

He shows the manner of dissolution of the organs of action and their respective objects into the Supreme: "In the same way, there is dissolution of all the organs of action into their own specific objects, and likewise into their five commonalities."

The meaning is this: the dissolution of the specific objects of the organs of action, such as speaking and so forth, into the general functions of those very organs of action, such as hearing and so forth; and of those [general functions] as well...

The dissolution of the general [elements] occurs in the vital breath (prāṇa), and the dissolution of the vital breath itself occurs in its cause. Now, in order to demonstrate that the dissolution of the sense organs of cognition and their objects also occurs in the vital breath, and that the dissolution of the vital breath occurs in the Supreme, the nature of the sense organs as being identical with the vital breath is established.
He establishes his own position:

"Vibration and luminosity exist in the powers of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), whereas vibration alone exists in the powers of action (*karmaśakti*) but is devoid of light; what follows from this? From that... [it follows].

To this he says: "All this movement (parispanda) should be known as having the intellect-faculties (buddhīndriya) as its support and being of the nature of vital breath (prāṇa). Since movement is of the nature of vital breath, and since the intellect-faculties consist of movement, they possess the nature of vital breath.
The meaning is that it is established. Regarding this, he states the proof: "And the scripture says, 'O slayer, you are indeed [the breath]'".
Furthermore, he provides the proof for the fact that the sense organs have the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as their self:
"On account of the illustration of the hundred and twenty-six, they are indeed the functions of the vital breath alone."
"When all the organs of action as well as the organs of perception have been withdrawn, and the person is established in his own self,
then the fires of the vital breaths remain awake in their purity"— such is the statement of the Śruti. Therefore:
Intending to show that the sense organs dissolve into the vital breath (prāṇa), and the vital breath likewise dissolves into this [Self], he says:
"Therefore, the power of knowledge dissolves together with the power of action.
And the Śruti speaks of it as being within the self of the vital breath, saying "in that" and so forth with reverence. And this is the dissolution.
He says that this is also stated at the end of the fifth [chapter]: "This dissolution is common;

it is prescribed at the end of the fifth [chapter], because through contact with its own cause alone, it is not absolute. He demonstrates how dissolution is taught at the end of the fifth [chapter] as follows:

"Because of the omnipresence of the powers of knowledge and action, the Supreme Imperishable, having projected itself into the reality of the universe, withdraws it back into its own self. Regarding this, he says:
"Having withdrawn," and thus by scripture the causal Self is designated as such; therefore, from the cause.
He states that the supreme reality is also taught in that very same place with the words "he transcended" (*atyakrāmat*);

by this, his state of being seedless (*nirbījāvasthā*) is described. Since the phrase "having cast off" (*nirūhya*) denotes the root cause, he says that the sequence of dissolution is also expressed here by the Śruti through the word "from which" (*yataḥ*).

Thus, because all powers of knowledge have dissolved into it, the single *prāṇa* remains as that which withdraws all functions; by the word *prāṇa*, the function of *prāṇa* is denoted, not the [subtle element] *prāṇa*.

The chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) indeed possesses the capacity to withdraw all functions; for as long as that *prāṇa* exists, all worldly activity proceeds. He states that this *prāṇa* dissolves into the *apāna*, and likewise, the *apāna* dissolves into the nature of the *vyāna*: "In the *apāna* [the *prāṇa* dissolves], and likewise the *apāna* dissolves into the self of the *vyāna*."
The vyāna indeed enters the udāna, and the adāna likewise enters the samāna; by the term "samāna," the fundamental cause is expressed.
Thus he says: "By the mention of 'samāna,' the very self that is the cause of the world is denoted. And he says that this dissolution is not preceded by conscious intent:

"This dissolution is considered to be the primordial (prākṛta) one, common to all. Now, let this indeed be the primordial dissolution; however, does the dissolution of everything occur therein or not? If it does occur, that is not tenable, because the root cause is a mass of pure consciousness (prajñānaghana).

It is stated in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad that "consciousness" (*prajñāna*) is a transformation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); therefore, the internal organ persists even at the time of dissolution.
To this, he replies: "Even its state as a mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*) is not expressed by the intellect or by consciousness."
"It is called *prājña* because of its connection with the appearance arising from inward-directed wisdom (*pratyak-prajñā*). Now, an objection is raised:

"If the instrument (the intellect) possesses the density of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*) due to its connection with the reflection of the Self (*ātmābhāsa*), then there would be a difference between the cause (the Self) and [its effect]. To this he says, "No."

The reason why the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) possess validity here is said to be this very fact that their true nature (yāthātmya) has not been fully understood; for [validity arises] from a single realization.
He says that even the statement asserting the unity of all consciousness is to be understood in this very way:

"When that is known, this entire world, both moving and unmoving, is known; and when it is unknown, it is likewise unknown—this alone is what is called that [Brahman]. But surely, here, by the scriptural teaching on dissolution (*pralaya*),...
Thus it is said regarding the object; however, the instrument has not been mentioned at all by the proponents of logic.

It is said that the Śruti considers the instrument to be of the same genus as its own domain (svagocara); therefore, by the statement of the dissolution of the object, the dissolution of the instrument is also stated. Thus should the Self be understood, because [of this].
As previously stated, by means of the logical method of the examples involving the drum and so forth,

and through the diligent reliance on the cause of the origin and dissolution of the universal Self, the meaning of the proposition— that "the Self alone is all"— has been established; this dissolution is natural.

Thus the experts in the Purāṇas have sung: "But dissolution preceded by consciousness is preceded solely by perfect knowledge. These [verses] are easy to understand. To explain what distinguishes natural dissolution from dissolution preceded by consciousness, he says: "Abiding in the form of mere potentiality (*śaktimātrātmanā*)."

"That which is the dissolution of effects into their own causes is the dissolution of the non-self, which provides the occasion for further birth"—thus has the natural dissolution been described; now, the absolute [dissolution]...
He states the scriptural passage beginning with "Just as a lump of salt... for the purpose of demonstrating dissolution:

"The destruction preceded by the cognition of the reality [of the Self], which is the cause of the birth, death, and so forth of the past, future, and present—that is the supreme Vedic revelation (parāśruti) regarding that which is immeasurable. [This concerns] cause and effect.

He provides this illustration to demonstrate how the dissolution of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) occurs through knowledge within the Self (*ātman*), which is of a different nature from that proliferation; for the sake of establishing the matter as stated, this illustration is here set forth. Now follows the explanation of the words of the verse.

He begins: "Just as a lump of rock-salt, having dissolved here in its own source, the ocean, becomes non-existent as a lump due to dissolution in hard water"—thus he explains the meaning of the verse beginning with *alīnahāsya* and so forth, by means of two and a half verses (*vārtikas*). That is transcribed as follows: The meaning of the verse beginning with *alīnahāsya* is explained by two and a half verses (*vārtikas*). It is written thus: "Just as a lump of rock-salt (*saindhava-khilya*), having dissolved here in its own source, the ocean, becomes non-existent as a lump due to dissolution in hard water; in that same way, O Goddess, this universe, though appearing as a solid mass, dissolves into You, who are the supreme consciousness, and becomes non-existent. In this context, "hard water" refers to the state of ignorance (*avidyā*) or the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of duality. Just as the lump of salt loses its distinct form upon contact with the ocean, so too does this universe, which appears as a solid entity, dissolve into the Supreme Consciousness, the Mother of all, and thereby ceases to exist as a separate lump. This illustrates the process of the withdrawal of the universe into its source. (Note: The term *kaṭhinodaka* is interpreted as water that is solidified, representing the density of ignorance or the persistence of dualistic tendencies.)

No man, however skillful, is able to extract that which has dissolved from the waters for the purpose of grasping it; no one is capable of seizing it in its former solid form, as it is no longer distinct from the nature of the ocean.
For wherever one might wish to grasp it, one would have to take up the water of the ocean itself.

"Therefore, therefore, one knows that salt exists as a residue nowhere else"— now, he elaborates upon this Vārtika, "Just as a lump of *saindhava* salt [dissolves]," by means of a group of six Vārtikas,
in their proper sequence.

477) It is explained as follows: first, having stated the cause for being a solid mass (*khilyatva*), he explains the meaning of the two terms *saindhava* and *khilya*. The ocean water [attains] the state of being a solid mass...
Because it goes from the ocean by the power of the sun and returns from whence it came, it is called *saindhava* (from the ocean).

Furthermore, because its parts are not distinct [when dissolved], it is called a *khilya* (a fragment). This very thing is called a *saindhavakhilya*; just as here in the great ocean, having encountered that which opposes its brilliance—

The meaning of the phrase "then it abandons its form" (*pratikṛtiṃ vijahāti*) is as follows: through contact with heat, water is transformed into a solid state; then, upon reaching the earth—which is opposed to water—it reaches the limit of the water and abandons that form. To this, he says: "From separation from heat, solidity [arises]."
"It becomes clear, that density [is dissolved]"—the meaning is that hardness is removed.
Having stated that hardness is removed, he now says that its substratum is also removed: "When the cause of hardness has been destroyed, the solid remnant here in the great ocean..."
"The solid water is destroyed and dissolves into a residue. What then remains? He says:
"Only that which is its uncreated nature remains."
Since that which arises from the connection of light-particles ceases, the particles of light are not the cause, nor are the particles of earth and water [the cause].
He states the reason: "Fire and so forth" is also connected [to the previous statement] as the cause;

for that which has the nature of a solid mass (khilya) exists when those [elements] exist, and it perishes when they perish. Now, he says this in order to explain the sentence concerning the subject of the illustration: "In this very way, O Āre..."

Thus, he explains the meaning of the two words *bhu* and *ta*: "The term *mahat* (great) would be used for the sake of realizing the nature of Brahman as non-excluded and all-pervasive, since the actual mode of being of the inner self (*pratyañc*), when viewed in terms of cause and effect, is described as contradictory."
And regarding the statement "the word 'being' [is used] for the sake of immutability," he states the purport of the passage beginning with "the Great" (mahat):

"Relying upon the actual state of affairs, prior to awakening, that which is self-established as the inner self (pratīc) is designated as 'the Great' and so forth by its very nature of consciousness."

The meaning is that the statement beginning with "the Great" (*mahat*) is intended to demonstrate that the form of the Self as the Great and so forth is eternally established. The expression "endless" (*ananta*) is a negation of its cause; the word "shoreless" (*apāra*) refers to the "shore" of the effect—that is, the cause of the effect—and [likewise] the shore of the cause.

Thus, because it is established as beginningless, the effect [is explained] by the two *vārtikas*— "consisting of the nature of the intellect as a mass of consciousness"— for the purpose of negating other types of birth; now follows this collection of explanations for the meaning of the words "the Great One" (*mahat*) and so forth, which are intended to clarify the meaning of the categories (*padārtha*).

479) He states the fruit of knowing the meaning of the passage beginning with "the Great" (mahat): "In this way, there is a connection between the field-knower and space as cause and effect; having attained their state of being like a single locus, it has been declared."

From such statements as "the Great One ceases," the connection of one who has attained the oneness of the Self— which is like a treasure-trove of knowledge arising from those words— and who abides in that very form, ceases; the meaning is that the world, consisting of cause and effect, ceases.
Some maintain that conjunction itself is the agent of attainment; he states the result of the destruction of cause and effect as follows:

"Upon the destruction of the cause within the effect, through the awakening to the identity with Brahman, there is the acquisition of the Self with its attributes, just as a fragment [attains its true nature] in the great ocean. This is like [the state after] dissolution.

To the objection that it is not stated [in the text] that she remained in her prior state before the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence "I am Brahman," he replies: "Just as [the water], having come into contact with fire, attained the state of being an internal residue."
"In the very same way, he who was beyond the ignorant beings attained the state of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
He explains the meaning of the word "beings" (bhūta):
"Wherein the self of effects, undergoing diminution, reaches its final consummation."

They say that those which have become non-manifest are "ignorance" (*avidyā*), characterized by being established in dissolution. That fundamental cause in which every effect dissolves is denoted by the word "become-ignorance" (*avidyā-bhūta*).
It is not merely the state of being the knower of the field (*kṣetrajñatva*) that constitutes the manifestation of the Supreme Being caused by ignorance;
rather, He states that its being the nature of the entire aggregate of causes and effects is caused by ignorance: "The Supreme is distinct from both cause and effect, because the Self is primordial."
It has entered into the state of cause and effect from these elements which are essentially ignorance.

He states the result of the fact that the cause and so forth are produced by ignorance: since ignorance alone is their cause, therefore, upon its cessation, this distinction between cause and effect does not exist; [one realizes] "I am Brahman."
"From awakening. He states the fruit of the cessation of duality:

"When that [ignorance] is destroyed, then through perfect awakening, because only the absolute unity remains, even the specific designation does not exist for him, since there is merely the designation of the Full One (Pūrṇaprajña). Again:

He elaborates on the meaning of the word "origination" (*samutthāna*): "Those things which I have described as 'ignorance' (*avidyā*) because they are established without being critically examined— from these elements (*bhūta*) acting as causes—
arises that which is called 'origination,' having the nature of cause and effect, or possessing the form of cause and effect."
Regarding the word *samutthāya* here, he elaborates that by this term the form of Brahman— which is both cause and effect— is described as possessing cause and effect:
"Through its association with ignorance, it arises as manifold in form, appearing as both sentient and insentient."
Regarding the phrase "characterized by selfhood and non-selfhood" (p.
if the nature of cause and effect belongs to the self only through something external, then to what does it belong intrinsically?
Regarding this, it is said:
"Darkness (tamas), which is based on mutual dependence in the form of cause and effect, has attained the state of causality;
the Self (ātman) likewise, by the power of darkness, [attains it] through manifestation (ābhāsa) even in its manifold forms."

He says, "It must be so": "O Mind, you become manifold through your own appearances by means of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect (manas), the faculty of understanding (buddhi), and so forth. Now he shows the sequence of its arising:
"Darkness" (tamas) is false knowledge (mithyājñāna) consisting of non-apprehension (agraha), which arises from a cause. It is the state of not knowing, [expressed as] "I do not know."
The meaning is this: while performing such an action, one performs that [subsequent action]; this sequence is knowledge.

However, performing a false cognition—such as the deluded cognition of a self—one acts by first producing a false cognition of the form "I do not know," and only then does one perform the other [action].
Just as the reflection of the inner self (pratyagābhāsa) residing in the intellect— which is the product of ignorance—

is designated by such terms as "the knower" and so forth, so too does the Supreme Self assume the forms of "the hearer," "the toucher," and likewise "the sufferer," "the fair-complexioned one," or "the twice-born" through the functions of the senses.
After arising from the body, whether one is wealthy, a possessor of cattle, or poor,

through the pursuit of wealth and other objects— and even though one does not possess them— one attains the aforementioned nature due to delusion; this [cycle] begins with Viriñca and arises from the delusion regarding the true nature of the inner self.
"Poison [is removed] by the distinction of the knower of the field; for the arising of the Seer is like that of a tree from its stump.
482) These statements clearly indicate the sequence and the causes of arising and are easy to understand.

He now states the meaning of the passage beginning with "those very [elements] as described in the prior state": "When, through the hearing of the Vedāntic declarations, there arises an awakening to reality as it is, then those elements from which one attained the state of being a knower of the field (kṣetrajña) perish as they are being practiced."

To the objection that "awakening does not remove ignorance," he says: "Because right awakening destroys all darkness by the mere acquisition of its own nature, it does not require the application of instruments. To this, he provides an illustration:
The manifestor does not destroy that darkness by repeatedly manifesting suggested meanings;

for it is the inherent nature of the manifestor that it does not depend upon repeated application. Now, if the cessation of ignorance results from the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self, then since the oneness of Brahman and the Self exists, [it follows that] for Brahman...
"How can there be both the state of being beyond perception (*parokṣatva*) and the state of being a transmigrating being (*saṃsāritva*) for the Self? To this, he says:

"Because that which is the nest of delusion and its effects is joined with ignorance, the inner Self (*pratyagātman*), though it is Brahman, has become 'beyond perception' (*parokṣa*) falsely; likewise, although it is essentially non-dual, it appears as such."
Due to the cause of not realizing that [identity], the Self undergoes the state of transmigratoriness, just as water acquires blackness [from a dye]. Thus,
although the mutual identity of the Self and Brahman is self-evident,
through ignorance (avidyā), Brahman remains remote and the Self remains a transmigrating being.
Thus it has been said; he states that its attainment results from mere consciousness itself, which is self-established:
"Since the state of Brahman belongs to the Self, and the state of the Self belongs to Brahman, [this is] by its own nature."
"Because it is obstructed by a mere trace of *tamas*, that [avidyā] is destroyed only when that [trace] is destroyed. Now, one might object:
although ignorance (*avidyā*) is indeed removed by the mere arising of knowledge, its effects do not cease except through repeated practice (*abhyāsa*); to this he replies:

"By the correct cognition that 'the Self is everything,' all darkness is destroyed by its very birth; consequently, no designation arising from ignorance remains. [Objection: But if the knowledge of the Self were an effect, then the Self would also be insentient, because it possesses adventitious knowledge. [Reply: This is not sound.

Intending to show that while knowledge arising from verbal testimony and the like is occasional, the knowledge of the essential nature [of the Self] is not, he says: "The cognition of the causeless, which has the form of the Self produced eternally, is the cognition of Brahman; therefore, the cognition of Brahman precedes the cognition of any other cause."

The meaning is that because the knowledge of the essential nature of the Brahman-Self exists eternally both prior to and subsequent to the knowledge of its causes, there is no consequence of insentience. [Objection: But if you say that the knowledge of the Self exists eternally while being produced by the knowledge of its causes and so forth, then a distinction [between them] is admitted.
"It is not the case that everything becomes known through the knowledge of the Self. To this, he says:
"That form which belongs to [the Self] as it exists within the differentiated world, yet from which all differentiation has been cast off—that is known precisely by the knowledge of that [Self]."
"It is known as such because of its lack of specific distinctions" means that for the inner self (*pratīc*), from which all residual differences have departed,
whatever form appears as distinct from space and so forth is known precisely by that knowledge—
namely, by the knowledge in which all specific cognitions have been eliminated— because it consists of nothing more than that.

If that is so, then the world too must be real; if you say it is not because it is subject to sublation (*bādhyatva*), we reply: sublation occurs only with respect to the nature of its manifestation. He says: "The manifestation exists in the form of cause and effect, while the world, being different from that, is consumed by [the logic of] cause and effect."
"One alone is distinguished; one alone remains"—thus it is said, establishing oneness.

By perceiving only the inward Self (*pratyag-ātman*), delusion regarding the Self and its products are dispelled, because a second [entity] is impossible, [realizing]: "I am that which was previously described as 'the Sweet' (*svādu-pūrva*)."

Alternatively, having raised the doubt that it is the number one (*ekatva-saṃkhyā*), this Vārttika is provided for the purpose of refuting it: "without leaving anything else remaining. Thus, since the selfhood of everything has been stated, the following objection is raised:
"But if everything consists of nothing but the Self, then in the cognition of a jar and so forth..."

If it is argued that Brahman would become known through the knowledge born of [the Vedas], what then is the use of the knowledge born of the sentence? To this he says: "The nature of the Self, which is the most subtle and subject to appearance and disappearance, is directly realized through knowledge that conforms to that [nature] alone."
The meaning is that one cognition grasps another form.
Since it has been stated that "one cognition grasps another form," there is a distinction. And therefore—
"It is not the case that everything becomes an object of knowledge simply because of that [universal] cognition. To this, he says:

"Because the reality of the nature of the causal substance consists merely in its being perceived, there is nothing anywhere that is unknown, nor is there anything from which darkness has not been dispelled. Not so.
He summarizes the meaning of the statement "there is no consciousness after death" in order to raise an objection:

"Since there is no longer any distinction between the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) and the Lord (īśvara), and since the darkness that is its cause has been destroyed, how could there be consciousness based on a causal basis? Thus, there is no consciousness for the self after death.

"Thus he urged [me], fearing for his own destruction out of respect; and because of the contradiction between what was understood through the dense statement and the words that were not clearly perceived, my mind became utterly bewildered. These two verses from the Vārtika have well-known meanings.

He resolves the objection: "I have spoken to you that which is non-contradictory and very clear; however, due to your own fault, you perceive my words as having a contradictory meaning. To the question, "In what way was it stated without contradiction? he says:

By stating that consciousness is one, you have taught me your doctrine of the identity of the whole; yet, when consciousness perishes, ignorance does not perish, for it is likewise a denial of what has arisen from a cause.
This is the elaboration of the latter half [of the verse]:

"The specific designations that belonged to this [self], characterized as the 'knower of consciousness' (vijñānātman) and so forth—all those cease completely for one whose delusion has been destroyed. Such is the meaning.
The elaboration of the first part:

as for the claim that the soul's real knowledge—which is unsurpassed, infinite, and immutable—is withdrawn from its own self-established state; why should that be so? This is the point [of the following].

"Yājñavalkya also spoke thus to his wife. This is easily understood. He explains the meaning of the word *alam*: "That reality which is self-established in the destruction of cause and effect, and which is non-different [from itself], is independent within the self-awareness of its own nature"—this is where [the meaning lies].

He states the meaning of the verse beginning with "hi" as follows: "Where that Self, whose nature is reality, is unknown, there the intellect is enveloped by ignorance; therein, seized by false grasping, one possesses the cognition of distinctions such as 'seer' and 'seen'. When...

The meaning is that when one does not know one's own true nature (*svasvarūpa*), then one becomes a seer of non-duality (*advaitadarśin*). "Where there is no knowledge of the reality of objects, there the eye is covered by darkness; therein the man, whose intellect arises from ignorance, perceives the self as consisting of the elements"—this is an elaboration of what preceded. Where... [text ends]
Regarding the word "hi" here, he explains its meaning:
"I have previously stated that the world has nothing remaining but ignorance.
Having bowed, [the author] states: "Therefore, this state is the cause of policy (nīti) because it is the effect of ignorance.
The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is for the purpose of establishing that duality is the effect of ignorance.
He proves this point by means of an illustration: "If, according to you, the means of knowledge is the very nature of the manifestor of the existent..."

This would be the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*): that which is traditionally held to be the cause of what is non-existent is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that makes known things as they truly are; likewise, ignorance is that which makes known things as they truly are—such is the established position. In that regard, the nature of ignorance is the manifold world of non-duality (*advaitaprapañca*).
The meaning is that the word *hi* is used for the purpose of providing a proof. Now, one might ask: how does the word *hi* illuminate such a meaning?
To this, he says: "The intellect illuminates the meaning of the stated reason; thus it is classified as a particle (*nipāta*)."
He explains the meaning of terms such as "duality" (*dvaita*): "Duality" (*dvaita*) refers to that which is accompanied by a second;
the state of being that is called "non-duality" (*advaita*). The word "as if" (*iva*) is for the purpose of comparison; "it becomes" (*bhavati*) is the verb.
Let there be no [confusion regarding] dream as non-duality and waking as duality—this is the meaning. Now, even for the wise person...

To the question, "How can there be equality with that [the real] based on the perception of duality? he says, "No; it is only in that very state of ignorance that this designation 'as if' (mṛṣā) is appropriate. Regarding the phrase "as if duality" (*dvaitam iva*), he raises an objection: "How can this comparison 'as if duality' be possible, since duality is a real entity (*vastu*)?"
"If there were not a single selfhood for everything" (p.
he says that this objection does not hold:

This is not a fault, because it is observed that even in a single object there can be the relation of both the subject of comparison (*upameya*) and the object of comparison (*upamāna*), as in the expression "the quarters are like the sky. This is the meaning: since there is no proof for the existence of the quarters apart from space, nevertheless, the usage [of the phrase] occurs: "space appears as if it were the quarters."

It is seen. Thus, although duality is not possible apart from the Self, nevertheless, the figurative usage "as if there were duality" is appropriate. To illustrate the relationship of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison for a single entity, he provides another example:

"The battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa is like that between Rāma and Rāvaṇa; just as it is well-known in the world, so too should it be understood here. Or rather, he says that this simile has been established by me from the perspective of non-duality (*advaita*) or ultimate reality (*paramārtha*): "Or else, let it be understood here in this very way, just as the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa is renowned in the world—between Rāma and Rāvaṇa themselves. Or else, this simile has been accomplished by me from the standpoint of non-duality or the supreme truth."

"One perceives non-duality as a delusion (māyā), because it is established through comparison with that. The meaning is this: by means of its own ignorance (avidyā), the Self becomes as if a duality were manifested by the Great Illusion (mahāmāyā), though no duality has actually been shown. Now, [one might object]: "Is it not the case that for one who has established a duality through illusion, that very duality is established by illusion?"

He states the illustration for that: "just as in the case of a dream and a magical illusion (*indrajāla*). That is to say, a dream is like a magical illusion, and a magical illusion is like a dream. Just as it will be so in the formal argument (*prayoga*) there as well, this is also by virtue of what is well-known in the world.

489) He states the established doctrine of the appearance of duality through illusion (*māyā*): "Even that which is real appears as if false; this is also said in the world. Yet, no one is able to say that the state of being false does not exist."

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the point that the passage beginning with "where" (*yatra hi*) is intended to refute the positions taken both collectively and individually concerning false statements and so forth, he says: "The form consisting of the collective and individual [is what] one speaks of here as the Self;
this is not a negation of that which is the primary purport of the Śruti, as is stated in the passage beginning with 'where' (*yatra hi*)," and so on. Thus.

Having stated the purport, he provides a word-by-word commentary: "In that state of ignorance, having entered the state of dream, just as one who has awakened smells a nearby fragrance with the nose"— in this sentence, there is first of all the smeller and the object smelled.
It is understood from the generality of the sound itself. In that regard, the olfactory faculty is observed to be the factor that brings about contact with its object;
therefore, he says that it is included because it serves a visible purpose as a causal factor.

"Because of the relationship between the olfactory organ and its objects of smell and so forth, the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa) and others is intended. Regarding the word "jighrati" (he smells), the cognition of odor appears directly from the verbal root itself;
therefore, he states that the experience of that result must also be understood there, saying: "The instruction 'jighrati' refers to the action."
"Of those two, there would be [the result]. Thus, this application should be understood as previously stated even for the subsequent statements.
This is easily understood. He concludes that "this [distinction] is produced by ignorance regarding the grāhaka (the grasper) and so forth."
It is stated that the mere ignorance regarding the inner self (pratyagajñāna) is what is here called the "grasper" (grāhaka) and so forth. This very point is clarified by the statement:
"This is declared to be the object of the designation 'action' and 'factors of action' (kriyākāraka)."
Since it is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), its cessation occurs through knowledge (*vidyā*); thus he says:

"Therefore, upon the complete destruction of ignorance, this notion ceases. This explains the statement, "Those who have arisen from these elements," beginning with the words "For where... and so forth.

Regarding the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), he says that this subject is stated by the passage beginning with "wherein all has become the Self alone for him," following the statement "a mass of consciousness" (*vijñānaghana*). [The phrase] "the wise one whose ignorance has been destroyed" expresses the intended purport (*tātparya*); having thus stated the purport, [he proceeds to] the word-meaning (*padārtha*).
He performs the primary task:
wherein, for that ignorant self, through the grace of the scriptures and the teacher, there arises the radiant light of the sun— the direct realization of the true nature of reality.
"Tell me, when all ignorance has been completely burnt away, who can smell what by what?

For, through the state of pure oneness alone, everything is nothing but the Self. Here, the genitive case in "of the ignorant Self" (*ātmano 'jñasya*) is used in the sense of the locative; [it means] "by the grace of the scripture and the teacher. Thus.
The word "arisen" (*utpanna*) from above should be supplied here; this is what is meant:
[wisdom] has arisen within each and every ignorant person, by the grace of the scriptures and the teacher, characterized as follows.

"By the rays of the sun that is the radiant light of the knowledge of the true nature of the inward Self, all ignorance has been utterly consumed. Now, one might object: "Even for the knower, duality exists because it appears;
how, then, can there be the state of being the Self alone? To this, he says:
Just as with the sixth object of perception, the entire world—consisting of cause and effect—is superimposed upon one's own Self;
for the wise person, the arising of perfect knowledge occurs once this is understood. If so, what remains?
To that he says: "That which is neither excluded nor inclusive, the single cause, the mass of pure consciousness."
Thus, the state of oneness is established as the face [of reality]. He describes the category of the "mass of consciousness" (vijñānaghana):
"In this [state], there is no division into subject and so forth, because the cause for such [division] is impossible; for pure consciousness is [self-established] by itself."

"Because [the Self] is described as a mass of consciousness, once [liberation] is accomplished. It has been stated that the division of causes and so forth does not exist in the inner self (pratyagātman) because the cause for such a division is impossible. If it is argued that the cause is the division of agents and so forth, he demonstrates this: "Without resorting to the ignorance of the Self, there can be no state of being an agent."

No agent is found without depending [on action], and here no action is established without [an agent]; likewise, without action, the fruit is not established at all. Thus, this very ignorance manifests itself through the nature of the agent and so forth.
Therefore, what arises from that? To this he says:
because it is thus, therefore, upon the complete cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), this world—both the manifest (*vyākṛta*) and the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*)—[ceases].

"Through awakening, it attains its state as the all-encompassing Self. Now, one might object: "In deep sleep and similar states, even though [the Self] is completed as the mere Self, one still awakens; likewise, through knowledge, even though [the Self] is completed as the mere Self, one would likewise awaken.
Anticipating this doubt, he says:

Furthermore, it regains its designation when dissolved within the causal self, just as this world [regains its name] when dissolved; likewise, there would be no such designation upon the dissolution of ignorance. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "by which this... as follows:
let it be for now that there is no designation even for the self here at the time of the arising of knowledge.
In the science of the true Self, there is no such notion as "Self" regarding the Self; he applies the statement to this meaning:
by which immutable witness all the world, beginning with the subject (grāhaka), is illumined.

"By what means would one say 'he cognizes' or 'let him know'? In this insentient world, there is only the Witness (sākṣin) and nothing else that is sentient; even the perceiver and so forth do not require the establishment of a Witness for their own proof. This is an elaboration of what was stated previously.

Since there is no conscious element other than the witness, the meaning is that even in the state of ignorance, there is no cognition of the division between the grasped and the grasper within the Self; he states the meaning of the passage, "By what, my dear, should one know the knower? as follows:

(493) Is this [not] the very name for the sun of perfect knowledge, which has arisen as the true nature of the oneness of the self, having utterly destroyed the cause of the misfortunes of saṃsāra? Furthermore:

He says that even in the case of the knower (*pramātṛ*), there is no division such as the grasped and the grasper, much less so for its witness: "Even with respect to the cognizer, there is no designation in the inner self (*pratyagātman*)."

"Since the knower is not grasped by the objects of that knowledge belonging to the knower," therefore he concludes that this very body of ignorance is such that no distinct designation or entity exists as a certainty: [he says].

The cognizer and so forth, whose establishment is unexamined and which possesses the nature of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), manifest through delusion as mere designations; however, they do not constitute a determination of reality, because at present the knower is not grasped by means of objects that have been set aside for the sake of the Brahmin. Thus it is said.

Therefore, he concludes that this specific designation, which is determined regarding an object, is indeed the very body of ignorance: "This designation, whose establishment is unexamined and which possesses the specific characteristics of the knower and so forth, appears through delusion; it is not, however, determined regarding a real object."
Now he concludes the section for the sake of the Brāhmaṇa:

Since this is so, it is established that the means for the realization of the inner self (pratyagātman) through scripture and other means has been declared as "all is the Self" directly; thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa of the fourth [Adhyāya].
This is the Vārtika-Ṭīkā of the venerable Paramātmasvarūpa-bhaṭṭāraka.
Page 494.
Śrī Hariḥ Om.

"Salutation to Viṣṇu, whose knowledge is Nārāyaṇa, who is the self-awareness of the knower and the known, and who has swallowed all great ignorance with his threatening gesture. [Objection: But surely, salutation is appropriate at the beginning and at the conclusion of a treatise; why is it placed out of place here?
If it is asked, "How so?", it is said: this Brāhmaṇa constitutes the conclusion of the Madhu-kāṇḍa;

therefore, the salutation is indeed praiseworthy. Alternatively, two components of the meaning have been explained by the word "Brāhmaṇa," and now the meaning of the sentence as a whole is being stated. Therefore—

That which is established in the meaning of the sentence, in faith, in tranquility, and in oneness, is declared to be the means for renunciation—the sole means for attaining immortality. There is no fault in [using] the salutation (*namaskāra*) for the purpose of making this known. Furthermore, even within the scripture itself—

The learned remember that an auspicious invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) is [required]; since a salutation (*namaskāra*) is also an auspicious invocation, it is understood that a salutation should also occur in the middle [of the work]. Thus, having performed a salutation, he recites the verse (*vṛtta*) in order to demonstrate the connection (*saṃgati*).

Knowledge established in the unity of the Self, which completely destroys the darkness of the inner self, is declared to be the means for renunciation and the sole means for attaining immortality. Furthermore, the causes for its attainment—beginning with hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth—are also stated here exactly as they are; this is what must be heard.
Based on the statements of the Vedas (p.
it should be reflected upon through subtle reasons illustrated by the aforementioned analogies.
"By those whose nature consists of the commonality of consciousness, the arising of consciousness, and the single dissolution into consciousness. Now he states the connection:
"Having raised the doubt regarding the non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhatva*), this Brāhmaṇa is spoken. This refers to the non-establishment of the reason.

If it is asked how so, it is replied: "If you ask, 'How is there non-establishment? then listen as I explain it. Because there is no generality or particularity [apart from itself], how could consciousness (cit) be a generality?
For opponents such as the Sāṃkhyas, the arising and dissolution of consciousness are unestablished. This is the meaning.
Since the nature of consciousness (*cidātmā*) is devoid of both universality and particularity, how could it be a universal?
Or how could the production of the world be explained? He states that the cause called dissolution is declared by the Madhu Brāhmaṇa, thereby concluding the initial proposition (*pratijñā*).

Having first asserted non-duality and stated the reasons for the sake of establishing that [assertion], the subsequent portion of the text is intended as the conclusion (nigama) of the initial proposition. Thus, after stating the various reasons for the sake of proving the meaning of the proposition, there follows the final withdrawal of those reasons.

"Now it is performed by means of subsequent statements"—this is an elaboration of what preceded. Some say that [the following] are concluded as if they were reasons (*hetu*). The three categories of hearing and so forth were mentioned below;
among them, hearing and reflection have already been explained here, and now meditation (*nididhyāsana*) is addressed.
It is being explained. Thus, having restated the opinion of Bhartṛprapañca— that the Madhu Brāhmaṇa begins because of the desire for that [knowledge]— he refutes it.
"Some explain this Madhu-brāhmaṇa as being for the sake of achieving *nididhyāsana* (contemplation), but that does not appear correct to us. He elaborates on its incorrectness:
"That object which has been heard from scripture (*āgama*) is also [to be] corroborated by reasoning (*tarka*)."

This very meaning, when thoroughly mastered, is called *nididhyāsana*. Thus, the meaning is that the result of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*)—which is the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence—is denoted by the term *nididhyāsana*, and not the meditation (*dhyāna*) intended by you; this is established here through scripture, the teacher, and experience.
When one is endowed with the [proper] causes, such a realization of oneness is called *nididhyāsana*.
Thus he says that the division of the text following the previous question is indeed purposeless:
"Therefore, this effort for the sake of accomplishing *nididhyāsana* is useless regarding the true nature of the inner self (*pratyag-yāthātmya*)."
"Because it is merely consciousness itself, for that reason"— having thus refuted the opposing position,
he applies the statement to his own position concerning the relationship [of the self]:
"The earth [is inhabited] by all living beings through their respective karmas for the purpose of experiencing the results of their actions."
The earth was asked for their honey; therefore, all living beings were created by the Great Earth for the sake of her own enjoyment.
The two *vārtikas*, "Since earth also is an effect, honey and other things likewise arise from it," have well-known meanings. He states another reason for earth being the creator of the elements:
"Because the bodies of all embodied beings are composed of earth, they [arise] from earth."

Since they were created from the earth, as seen from their shared nature with the earth, the relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed is established precisely because of the cause-and-effect relationship between the elements and the earth; thus he says: "And because of the mutual causality of the elements and the earth."
Therefore, the relationship of enjoyer and enjoyed is established between them.

The word "honey" (madhu) denotes both the effect and that which is to be enjoyed; by means of this [term], the causality, the state of being enjoyed, the agency, and the state of being an enjoyer of the earth and the other elements are explained here through their mutual dependence.

Since earth and the other elements are not specified as being in the nominative case in the word "kriyate," they themselves must be the cause that is the enjoyer; thus it is said: "The state of being enjoyed (bhogyatā) of earth and the others is expressed here by the nominative ending; let their state of being the enjoyer (bhoktṛtā) also be told."

"It is denoted by the word ending in the sixth case. In that context, because the insentient portion is predominant, it is said that "the state of being an enjoyer belongs to that [portion] alone"; thus he says:
"Because the insentient part is predominant, the relationship of cause and effect is predicated [of it]."
The relationship of enjoyer and enjoyed exists between the conscious and the unconscious; [likewise] there is a mutual relationship of effect and cause among earth and the other elements.

If it is asked what is established that is relevant to the present topic, he says: "Because of the connection between cause and effect for all beings, and because of the destruction [of duality] consisting of the nature of all beings, it is as it is for the Self of all. Just as [it is for the Self of all], so too...
The root cause is indeed of the nature of all; thus, everything is of the nature of all, and therefore there is no difference.

Consequently, the conclusion that "everything is merely the Self" is logical. The causal relationship of the gross aspect has been explained; now, for the purpose of stating the causal relationship of the subtle body (*liṅga*), [the following is said]:

He states the subsequent statement: "Having withdrawn the gross support of beings, namely the earth, and likewise having withdrawn that which is supported by it, [he reaches] that which is designated by the word 'Yam'.
Having thus stated the purport (*tātparya*), he provides the word-by-word commentary (*akṣaravyākhyāna*): "in this earth..."
And that which is the embodiment of radiant consciousness is indeed immortal and eternal; it is not subject to destruction like the gross body. It is the honey of all beings, and they are its honey;
all beings are the honey of that [Self], just as I have previously declared—that everything is the honey of everything.

The object of action, the object of enjoyment, the instrument, and the enjoyer have been thus described. He now elaborates upon that very point: indeed, this entire world, together with its internal and celestial aspects, exists as the object of enjoyment for every single individual self.
"Everything is the effect of everything, and everything is the enjoyer of everything. To this, he says: "If that were so, everything would be as it was before."

"Elaborated upon" means that [in the passage] "All this is what this Self is," the fact that the Self is everything was previously elaborated; thus, it becomes established. The meaning is that because the Self is the cause of everything, it is the Self of all. Furthermore, he continues the very same explanation of the Śruti.

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "this very [Self]"— namely, that which is internal and corporeal, resting upon the earthly element, and which is honey for all, while all beings are honey for it— by means of the distinction between cause and effect.
"The fourfold [elements] beginning with earth are declared to exist as the enjoyer and the enjoyed;
now their true nature (tattva) is stated. This means that the Self is said to be of the form of the fourfold.
If it is asked how the Self is the true nature of the fourfold, [the answer is: because that very [Self] exists in the form of the fourfold.
He states that it is because [the Self] is manifested through its own ignorance:

"By means of the fourfold division, the Self, though its own object, is divided; yet, because it exists for the sake of that [division], the Self is therefore grasped here as its transformation (*vivarta*). Thus, by virtue of being the Self's manifestation...

The meaning is that, because the fourfold [set] has no self as its purpose, "self" is understood here as the enjoyer and the reality (p. 500). Alternatively, this was introduced in response to the inquiry, "What is that reality? (kiṃ tattvam?).

That which is denoted by the word "this" (ayam) is described as that which manifests as the inner self (pratyaktayā), being distinct from the fourfold [categories]; because it is directly perceived, it is designated as the "inner witness" (pratyak-sākṣin) by means of the expression "this very one. This refers to the intended aspect [of the referent] through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
Having said, "This indeed is that," by means of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the true nature of the inner self alone is made known for that which was described in four ways.

"That which was previously explained as being both internal and external within the earth and other elements is to be known as the Self alone; such is the praise of that awakening. This is an elaboration of what preceded.
He states the remainder of the passage beginning with "That which is this... in order to explain the meaning of the word *ayam* ("this").

The remainder [of the sentence] beginning with "this" (*ayam*) would be that which begins with "he who is this" (*yo’yam*); the word "only" (*eva*) is used for restriction, serving to negate association [with anything else]. Thus, the reality of these four is the inner self alone (*pratyagātmaiva*), which is absolute, neither excluded from nor inclusive of anything else, and in which ignorance has been destroyed.
The explanation of the word *adudbhavaḥ*, including this very *Sārdhavārtika* commentary, is easy to understand.

Alternatively, the word "this" (ayam) refers to the fourfold [aggregate] that is present; the word "that" (sa) refers to the Self under discussion as the object to be seen in the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa. Thus he says:
"Or rather, this word 'that' may be a designation of the Self under discussion."
p.

501) "This is called direct [perception] because of the fourfold contact. Even in this view, he states that the meaning of the sentence is the same: "That which is to be known as 'this is that very one'..."

"Stated as that which is to be seen": the meaning is that this very self, consisting of the fourfold [sheaths], is the one spoken of in the passage, "Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen. Furthermore, that nature of the Self which has been described as immortality—namely, that which was stated as immortality, and that which follows as the instruction: "Not this, not this"—[is this same fourfold self].
That Brahman which is described as being free from all distinctions— that very reality of the Self, Brahman, which is stated to be the fruit of knowledge as "all this has become that"—
is precisely that much, once the absence of both positive and negative concomitance has been set aside.
One should understand this as follows:
that which was spoken by Yājñavalkya to his own wife as the immortal Brahman— devoid of all distinctions and previously described as "not this, not this"— all that has become entirely complete.

If, through the realization of the true nature of things, one should know the earth and its earthly portion, as well as the embodied self together with its presiding deity, as "All is the Self," characterized by the negation "not this, not this"— he who is thus indicated by words is indeed that very [Self].
That which was indicated as immortality and as the Self in the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa is indicated as the non-differentiated Brahman in the Mūrtāmūrta-brāhmaṇa (p.

Thus, the meaning is that the self alone is established as the fourfold [reality]. In the subsequent statements as well, one should understand that the author, while investigating, has explained this very meaning of the sentences by following the same path as previously described; this is easily understood. Now, for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the phrase "this is dharma":
He recites the verse: "The elements beginning with earth, their respective parts as described,

the portions of the Hiraṇyagarbha-liṅga, and likewise the forms previously mentioned"— the meaning of this is that the great elements beginning with earth have been stated, as well as their constituent parts.
The portions of the *sūtra* such as the body (*śarīra*) and so forth have the elements (*bhūta*) and the body as their substrata;
and their forms (*mūrti*), which constitute their very nature, are those same portions of the *sūtra*, and they have been described as such.
That by which these aforementioned categories, as if impelled, perform their respective functions through their own operations—that [Principle] is here [the subject].
He says that it is expressed by the word *dharma*:
"That by which all things, as described, when employed with their respective functions, benefit us in every way—that is designated as *dharma*. Now, [one might ask], what is *dharma*?

Anticipating the objection that since this [Self] is to be understood solely through the scriptures (*śāstra*), it is imperceptible (*parokṣa*) and therefore how it can be described, he says: "Its effect is stated here in two ways:
by way of its general nature and by way of its particularity. Here, earth and so forth are the general; the particular is..."
This [inference] is like perception because its object is perceived here as a mere aggregate, due to the metaphorical attribution of non-difference [between the whole and its parts].

"Therefore, it is called *dharma*. Regarding this, he explains that the *dharma* mentioned here in "this is *dharma*" is that which initiates [the formation of] earth and so forth, while the *dharma* mentioned here in "internal *dharma*" is that which initiates [the formation of] the body and so forth; thus, it is common to both.
