By the phrase "that which is this [element] consisting of earth and so forth," the property of being an agent is designated;

likewise, by the phrase "and that which is internal," there is a common designation. By the phrase "this which was made for the sake of the subject," both together refer to Hiraṇyagarbha, who previously was the originator of the entire world.
Regarding the statement "this is the Dharma," he says:
that which possesses the nature of both the common and the specific, which is unprecedented (*apūrva*), is called the *prājāpatyam apūrva*;
it is that which impels all beings and is the performance of the internal ritual injunctions. This is it.

Regarding the phrase "declared as Dharma": that very form of Dharma, existing in the form of conduct (*ācāra*), is established by worldly consensus as the cause for the regulation of boundaries; this is called "truth. Thus he says:
that which is perceived directly in the form of conduct is itself Dharma.

"It would be true if the state were the determinant. [The author replies: "Even though it is true, like *dharma*, it is twofold because it is a cause of non-determination due to its being both general and particular. He says:
"That too is twofold, like everything else, by virtue of its commonality and its particularity."
p.
504) "Because it is the cause for establishing common and specific meanings.
To explain the meaning of the phrase "this is human," he says: "This [person] is one who is devoted to dharma and truth."
"The *liṅga-piṇḍa* is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), as well as the *virāj* and the *hiraṇyagarbha*;

and that is endowed with genus (*jāti*). This means that the two bodies [the subtle and the gross] are endowed with the genus of humans and so forth. Now, regarding "humans and so forth"—how is this [to be understood]?
Because of the mention of "human" (*mānuṣa*), he says there:
"The mention of the human species is an indication for all species; let this [explanation] of 'this is human' be as before. Starting from "This earth," these are parts of the *Virāj* Sūtra.
[The preceding] has been explained. Now, regarding the statement "this is the Self," which is an indication of its constituent parts, he says:
"That which was previously described in parts as 'the earth is the body'—namely Virāj and Hiraṇyagarbha—that is not the Self; such is the teaching. But even here...
To show that it is not the case that only the parts thereof are called "honey," he says:

"Because the state of being honey has been stated separately for the various forms of Hiraṇyagarbha and for the elements, their functional capacity is now described. (This refers to the nominative case endings.)
The word "ātman" here denotes Virāj; it refers to that which is indicated by the word "ātman" in the locative case, within which [the subsequent elements] are contained.
Contained within that is the golden womb (*hiraṇyagarbha*), consisting of light, which is this very Self;
and that which is the reflection of consciousness is called the individual soul (*jīva*). This is what is stated [in the text]: "This is the Self.
This designation is considered to refer first to the Virāj; by means of the locative case ending (*saptamyanta*), the inner subtle-body self (*liṅgātman*) is thereby denoted.
"The self consisting of action and the self consisting of instruments always exist for his sake;
and he who is here called the 'Self' is known as the 'Self of Consciousness' (vijñānātman).
He states the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "Now, this Self" as follows:
In that Self, whose nature consists of both the determinate and the indeterminate, having been destroyed,
the conscious self (vijñānātman) was introduced by means of the analogy of the fragment; now, darkness having been dispelled by the knowledge of Brahman, one is established in that Brahman.

Therefore, because the effects arising from that [ignorance] are absolutely impossible, he who was previously the embodied soul and a transmigrator due to ignorance is now directly the Supreme Brahman through knowledge. This is the meaning:

He briefly states the meaning of the three Vārtikas, explaining that the one intended by the statement "That thou art" (sa vā eṣa) is the inner Self (pratyagātman), from which ignorance and its effects have been cast away, and who has become the non-dual Brahman of unsurpassed bliss.
This [world] has arisen from destroyed ignorance; here, through true consciousness, the Self alone—whose limit is infinite—is established in its own majesty.

Thus [he says]. He introduces the statement regarding the meaning already explained: "The passage beginning with 'That indeed' (sa vā eṣa) and so forth, together with its illustration, is set forth for the sake of knowing the true nature of the inner Self, which is neither prior nor posterior. Having thus introduced the statement, [he continues].
He provides an explanation of the terms: "I am Brahman" is because of the destruction of darkness through complete realization;
"King" is because of shining with royal splendor through unobstructed vision of the Self; likewise by the word "Lord" (adhipati).

"Independence is expressed [as follows]: 'Because it is self-referential (svāt), because it is inward-looking (pratyak), and because it is the cause of the world-soul'. He states the intended meaning of the illustrative sentence beginning with "tadyathā" as follows:
"Desiring to reveal that the world-soul is completed as mere inward consciousness,

the supreme Śruti [states] 'Just as...'"— this is said with the intention of expressing the completion of the phenomenal expansion of cause and effect within the mere Brahman that has been realized as the inward self.
This is the meaning of the example. Having thus stated the intended purport (*tātparya*), he provides an explanation of the words:
"Just as the Lord of the Wheel is situated [within], so too are the spokes on the outer rim of the wheel."
"The vital breaths and so forth are likewise woven like warp and woof in the Supreme Self"—
this illustrative statement has been explained according to our own position; now, [the author] presents the interpretation of Bhartṛprapañca for the purpose of refuting it.
The division of the section on *nididhyāsana* is also stated here; since it was mentioned previously with the intention of discussing *nididhyāsana*,
that position is presented here for the sake of refutation.

Some proponents of Brahman explain this illustration regarding the Self in a different way for the sake of establishing the meaning of the entire thesis and so forth. To show how this is so, he says: "Having unified one's own self with the imperishable Supreme Self..."

"A wise person should conceive of himself as the hub of a wheel; and having conceived this world—with its deities and so forth—as the spokes and the rim of the body, he should always meditate with a mind permeated by that [reality]. By these two verses, which have well-known meanings, [the author] states the fruit of meditation.

For one who meditates by means of the path of meditation, there arises at all times a state of oneness like heated iron, from which return is difficult to attain. Thus he states the fruit of oneness: "Having reached this state," etc.
One who has attained this state ceases to be a meditator.
It is said that he perceives the state of being an object of meditation for those blinded by the darkness of ignorance. If one asks "Who is this?", it is said here:
"Having reached that abode of yogis which is beyond thought and unthinkable, they do not return;
having attained supreme Nirvāṇa, through meditation upon that, they abide in its very form."
The meaning is that it becomes the object of meditation (*dhyeya*).
Furthermore, another method is stated [in the following], for this [process] occurs for each individual living being: (p. 508) "Indeed, for every single living being..."

"The Wheel of Brahma is situated. This means that this wheel called Brahma is established and exists within the hearts of all living beings. [Objection: If so, why is it not experienced by everyone? To this, he says:

He concludes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) by stating that because they are not fully awakened, this [bliss] is not experienced by all living beings; some explain it clearly as being from the *Vaiśvānarīya* [section]. Now, he refutes it:

That which lacks a connection with the literal words must be abandoned, even if it is such that it appears to be something to be established. If it is asked, "But how can there be a lack of connection with the literal words?"— since it is being stated by the force of the illustrative example—
the author says in response:

"Even if [a meaning] is obtained through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*), if it is not preceded by the literal word (*akṣara*), those who know the scriptures say that such a thing must indeed be meditated upon as it is. This is the meaning:
although the matter intended by you appears here by the force of the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta-sāmarthya*), nevertheless, in this case—

In the case of the *brāhmaṇa*, because there is an absence of words expressing that [totality], and because, on the contrary, it negates the phenomenal world of effects, instruments, and so forth, and because it contradicts other Vedic texts through its statements regarding the "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) and so on,
the illustration is not intended to mean the totality of Brahman; furthermore, this applies to anything else as well.
Because there is an absence of any conceptualizer (*kalpaka*) of the whole and so forth,
Brahman does not possess the form of a whole and so forth. Now, [if it is argued that this is] apart from the means of valid cognition (*pramā*) that conceptualizes...
"You postulate Brahman as having the form of the aggregate and so forth; that is not tenable," he says:

"Even if there were hundreds of unseen things, they should be postulated only if they possess a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavat*); not even a hundredth part of an unseen thing is to be postulated in the absence of a means of valid cognition. This is the meaning of the term *pramāṇavanti*.

Regarding the phrase "those who possess imagination": [the opponent objects]—but is it not heard from the syllables of the Veda that such a state of Brahmanhood is indeed not imagined? To this he says "no"—"The aforementioned arrangement of the wheel is not heard as being preceded by [mere] syllables."

It has been stated that "one should reflect" (*niddidhyāset*), but even that is untenable because the word "meditation" (*upāsana*) is not heard here; thus he says, "Furthermore, the word 'meditation' is not found in the entire Brāhmaṇa. [This applies] everything belonging to the illustrative example to the thing illustrated.

And because [the term] "hearing" is mentioned, it is not intended to refer to the totality [of the parts] and so forth; thus he says: "Since, in the statement of the illustrative instance (*dārṣṭāntika*), the Self alone is directly heard here as the example for the two positions of the hub and the rim. Again:
He demonstrates the very difference between the illustration and the thing illustrated:

"The entrustment of the vital breaths and so forth is heard [in scripture] with respect to the inner self; how can that which is not heard regarding the deities and so forth with respect to the elements be accepted?"
510) Furthermore, because it contradicts the principal statement beginning with "tadetad" (this very thing), he says [in the verse] "the nature of the whole and so forth":
"Its division into external and internal, as well as its state of cause and effect, is [described] by the sentence 'tadetad'."

"The opposite view is refuted right here. For this reason as well, he states that meditation on the aggregate and so forth is not intended: "Now, as for another [view]... Likewise, because the perception of difference has been discarded, it is my opinion that the injunction for the object of meditation and the act of meditating is not correct. But [an objection]: nanu...

If it is argued that since the identity of the self with Brahman cannot be established apart from meditation, meditation must be accepted; and if meditation is accepted, then the state of being the whole and so forth must also be accepted as belonging to Brahman, otherwise it would not be an object of meditation— then he says in response:

And because there is no means other than the knowledge of Brahman for attaining that [Brahman], which is the fruit of the injunction consisting solely of the removal of ignorance and the realization of identity with Brahman, and because the status of the object of meditation as Brahman has been refuted, he says that Brahman is not an object of meditation: "That which is expressed by speech... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4).
"Know that very Brahman which the mind does not think; do not know this which they worship.

Since being pervaded by the act of worship is the defining characteristic of non-Brahman—as indicated by the scripture—how can that which is thus worshipped be Brahman? [Objection: But surely there is the practice of worshipping Brahman.
If it is argued that a ritual procedure is also heard of in some places, [the author] says "no," because there is the statement: "But it is seen by the highest intellect, by the mind alone."

511) Therefore, it is for the purpose of enjoining the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*), not for enjoining meditation (*upāsana*). How is it for the purpose of enjoining the knowledge of the Self? To this he says: "Because Brahman [is not known] by that which is permeated by *rajas* and *tamas*..."
"Because it is understood by you that the pure consciousness [is Brahman], therefore one should know Brahman as the inner self"— he states another meaning of this:
"Or rather, prior to the connection with the self and so forth, there was no abiding in oneness."
"The meaning of the word would be the intellect (buddhi) of all living beings.
Thus [it is said]. "Established in the unity of self" means having the form of consciousness (cidākāra); he concludes the meaning of the preceding Vārttika as follows:

"This is the meaning of that statement: there can be no injunction for the desire for form; for when there is absolute unity in which all difference has been destroyed, there is no injunction for ritual worship. Therefore, he concludes that the commentary of Bhartṛprapañca is flawed:
"Therefore, the arrangement of the *cakras* is excellent according to the Śruti and other authorities; thus it is from the outside. [The opponent asks:
"In that case, what meaning is intended by the passage beginning with 'tadyathā'? To this, he says:
"Therefore, the meaning of the sentence 'tadetad' should be grasped as being possible and limited; thus, this is Brahman."
The meaning is that the sense of the word "previously" (*pūrvam*) is intended to be expressed by this sentence containing an illustrative example (*sadṛṣṭāntavākya*).
Alternatively, the fruit of knowledge has been stated as "therefore, he became everything"; [now] its worship...

By the statement beginning with "He said, 'It is dear,'" the purpose of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), which was previously introduced as being dependent [on other factors], has been determined;
thus, some hold that this is merely an elaboration of what was already stated earlier. This indeed...
He provides a recapitulation of the preceding context in order to introduce the statement beginning with "consisting of that" (*tanmayī*):

"The Śruti has correctly performed the exposition of the identity of the self through five Brāhmaṇas for those whose understanding of the entire meaning [is complete]," according to the sūtra *ātmaikye ca*.

This entire Brahma-vidyā for the attainment of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), which Yājñavalkya spoke at great length to his own wife, is now concluded. This [preceding section] was an elaboration of what went before.
Now, as a praise of the aforementioned Brahma-vidyā, there is this passage beginning with "vaitasam" and so forth.
He introduces the passage: "Beginning with 'of the aforementioned knowledge of Brahman' and so forth, it is said:
this narrative is for the purpose of praise, not for the sake of [actual] engagement through it."
If it is asked, "What is the meaning of the narrative (ākhyāyikā)? he says in response:
"The Veda, out of reverence, explains the meaning of the narrative through two mantras.
If it is further asked, "Why is its meaning stated by means of two mantras? he says in response: "Because it is praised by the Vedic mantras."
"For it attains acceptability through its hidden meaning. He demonstrates the manner of praise [as follows]:
"Even Śacīpati, though he has attained the goals of human existence, is free from pride toward her" (p.
"Thus, the knowledge of the Inner Self alone would be the means for attaining the noble fruit. He elaborates on this very manner of praise:
"Since in ancient times the knowledge of Brahman was brought forth by the Aśvins with great effort, therefore no other superior means need be mentioned for it. Furthermore...
He demonstrates the very manner of praise [with the words]: "Just as among all human goals (puruṣārtha) liberation (kaivalya) is the highest, so too among means (sādhana);
thus it has been stated that the knowledge of That (tad-vidyā) is not a [mere] means. This is by means of both the narrative (ākhyāyikā) and the mantra.

The elaboration (*prapañca*) regarding the meaning of the narrative is made manifest because it is the cause for attaining the knowledge of Brahman; that which was previously unrevealed is now directly manifested by means of the two mantras. This is the purpose of the narrative whose meaning is thus revealed by the two mantras.

He explains the meaning with five verses along with their commentary (*vārttika*). Since its meaning is not obscure, it is written here: "Requested by the two Aśvins, Indra [gave] this [knowledge] to them, Madhu and Paippalāda; or rather, he said: 'Indra might cut off my head as I speak this'; therefore, out of fear, [he gave] this..."

"I shall teach you the science of honey (madhuvidyā). They both said to him, "Long ago, we two cut off our heads from Indra's body; having joined them to the head of a horse, we shall hear it. Therefore, O Śyena, speak the science of honey with that horse-head."
For the sake of liberation.
When it was granted with the words "So be it," they then cut off his head and joined it to the horse's head;
by means of that, he spoke again, and then [the horse] cut off its own head.

Then Indra joined the two Aśvins [to him], and having restored his head with their own heads, he spoke the remainder of the knowledge to the two Aśvins, saying, "Do not tell this word of mine to anyone.
He states the intended meaning of the word *pratāyan* (stretching forth): "Since it is thus, therefore, truth."

"It must be guarded with effort. Having thus stated the meaning of the narrative, he begins the explanation of the words beginning with "This," etc.: "This indeed is that honey which was mentioned in another section; it is heard [in scripture] that Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa [taught it] to these two."
This is the Madhu Brāhmaṇa spoken by the Brāhmaṇa; that which was previously mentioned as Sundarīghya, the son of Atharvan, teaching the means [of liberation] to the Aśvins—
this very thing is called the Brāhmaṇa, because from it the awakening of the Self (ātman) arises.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "tadetad" (this very thing) is explained as follows: "This rite is mandatory for the Aśvins and the Atharvans, yet the Seer did not declare it for the sake of his own seer-vision; therefore, this is being stated [to you].
This is the sense: by means of his seer-vision (*ārṣadṛṣṭyā*), the Seer himself, beholding that rite, declared it by means of a *ṛc*.
"And that is designated as action. Now, he provides the commentary here:
515) The *Mantravivaraṇa*, consisting of six *vārtikas*, is easy to understand; it is written down as follows:

"O men, today I shall reveal that deed of yours which you two committed for gain and acquisition— a cruel act against the secret of the cow. Just as the arrival of rain awakens the thunder, so do I now disclose the secret of your deed."
When the Aśvins spoke to you with the horse's head, saying, "This sage Dadhyañc,
having had his own head cut off and removed, joined a horse's head to him; he, possessing a horse's head,
then declared the honey to you both"— he, acting according to the *ṛta*, truly revealed himself.
Desiring to do this, that seer fell into a life-threatening danger;
from this it is understood that truth must be protected with effort even at the cost of one's own death,
for he spoke of the honey of Tvaṣṭṛ, which was beyond the reach of fear, for the sake of the goal.
"Even the two *dasras* are that which is the direct vision of reality (*yāthātmya*).
He explains the meaning of the word *dasra*:
"The two *dasras* would be those who cause the destruction (*upakṣaya*) of disease; therefore, they are the Aśvins. Not only...

He spoke of one girdle pertaining to Tvaṣṭṛ; the word *maśvi* has the meaning already stated. He explains the intended meaning of the mantra beginning with *puraḥ*, etc., preceded by a recitation of what has occurred. Thus [ends the discussion] of the two chapters on the Pravargya.
Having performed the withdrawal of the knowledge of Tvaṣṭṛ by means of the two mantras (p. 516), one should then perform the withdrawal of the knowledge of Kakṣya.
"It is performed; the *madhukānta* of the two *nyāyas* is concluded. Why is the meaning of the two chapters, namely "the heat" (*uṣman*), summarized by means of these two mantras?
To this, he says:
"Because the meaning taught by the Vedic mantras is relied upon by men"—this is the sense of the word "ta" (them). Having thus stated the purport, he provides an explanation of the word-meanings:
"He created bodies in the beginning; bipeds, characterized as humans, and then quadrupeds."

"By his own power of illusion (*māyā*), he made the animals his preceders; then, after the body has been enjoyed, the *saṃpattiliṅga* is described: 'He entered the nine new bodies like the moon in water. These two verses from the *Vārttika* are easy to understand. If it is asked, "How can the Self possess the nature of a person (*puruṣatva*)? [the answer follows].

If it is argued that this is stated by the Śruti itself in the words "therefore, he is the Puruṣa," [the author] explains that the Śruti teaches the goal of man (puruṣārtha) through the passage beginning with "He indeed... for the sake of realizing the single Self of all. Having thus stated the purport, he proceeds to explain the meaning of the individual words: "This Puruṣa..."

"Since the Self rests within all persons (puruṣa), for that reason it is said in this world, 'This is a person' (puruṣaḥ). [Objection: But surely, because of the designation of a locus and its occupant, there must be a distinction.

To avoid that [objection], he states the following reply: "If it is argued that there would be the consequence of [the self] being limited, let it not be so; for this world is not anything whatsoever unenveloped by this [Self], since nothing is unpermeated by the Self, like a thread woven through a cloth, nor is anything unenclosed by the Self, like a thread strung upon a string."
And thus, he states that this is established:
"Because of its fullness, it is the Puruṣa; therefore, this one Brahman is the Puruṣa. Regarding this point, he cites a mantra as authoritative evidence:
Because it is stated that "there is nothing beyond him, nor anything smaller or greater than he;
like an immovable tree, he alone stands in heaven;
by this Puruṣa all this is filled," and so forth, [he is established] as the cause, like the warp-thread [of a cloth].

He says "no" to the claim that "manhood" (puruṣatva) is intended [as the subject], stating: "The entire world has been made one's own by mere consciousness (jñapti); it is encompassed (saṃvṛta), meaning it is negated as anything other than the Self, such that only the non-Self is perceived. There exists neither cause nor effect that has not been assimilated into the Self by this [consciousness].
"There is no cause or effect that this Self does not pervade"—this is an elaboration of the preceding [verse]. He explains the meaning of the second mantra:
"For she has become a counterpart to every form; having entered into every body..."
It assumed the form of that body.
If it is asked what the cause is, he says in response: "It is reached through *māyās*, that is, through the ignorance of the inner self, or else through false cognitions."

"Though one, he appears as many forms through the cognitions of those who know him, like the sun in water. Regarding the use of the plural number for what was previously described as singular, and the mention of his manifold forms, he says: "The form of the All-pervading Lord consists of *māyā*, for the purpose of awakening to the true nature of the inner Self (*pratyag-yāthātmya*)."

Thinking that a thing cannot be understood here [in this world] without the aid of scriptures, teachers, and so forth, the material cause was explained by means of "illusory powers" (māyā); now, the instrumental cause is being stated by the words beginning with "is appropriate" (yuktā). With this intention, he asks: "Whence does its manifoldness arise?"
The cause is stated here:
"For it is joined with this" (Brhadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.3), because false knowledge is the sole cause.
That connection of the senses which occurs prior to self-knowledge due to ignorance is [the cause].
The meaning is that, by means of the knowledge arising from itself, it is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) for manifold manifestation.
He establishes the connection with the senses due to ignorance through an illustration:
"Just as a rope and [other objects like] a staff are joined [to the mind] because of the non-recognition of their true nature."

Because of the lack of realization of the inward-facing reality of the self, "the monkeys [run] toward [objects]"—thus, the senses (*indriyāṇi*) alone are the "monkeys" (*harayaḥ*), so called because they carry one toward sense-objects.
"Ten thousand and one hundred according to the classification of living beings"—this is easy to understand.

He explains the meaning of "This indeed is *vaiharaya*" and so forth, preceded by a statement of the reason: there is no other cause for this [state] than the knowledge of the three [realities], because here, in the self, this alone is the *haraya* (the horses) of the senses and so forth.

The phrase "as many as are their substrates" means that because they have the unmanifested effect (ajñātakārya) as their substrate, the sense organs and so forth are merely the Self (ātmamātra). [Objection: But since they have the unmanifested effect as their substrate, the sense organs and so forth must be mere consciousness (jñānamātratva).

To the question, "In what way is it merely the Self? he says in response: "This very [Self] is imagined as the sense organs and as the body; likewise, through differences in number, it is [imagined] as hundreds of thousands, and through differences in name, form, and action, just as I have previously declared. This very [Self], though not of such a nature..."
The non-dual is imagined by means of ignorance; therefore, it is established that everything consists of nothing more than that.
He concludes: "All this imagined world, together with its causes and effects, is nothing but the Inner Self."

"Consisting of the essence of the mass of radiant wisdom"—this explains the passage beginning with "This indeed," etc. Now, he states the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "That which is this," etc.:
"The quintessence of all the Upaniṣads is 'That which is this'"; thus it is said at present. It is not modified by verbal expression.
"Like a solid mass placed directly before one's eyes"—
as for what that essence (*sāra*) is, he says:

"This world is unknown, known through doubt, or known falsely"—having thus restated this, [the author] says "this reality is being awakened to"; what then is that reality? To this he says: "Brahman indeed is your true nature; first, that which has occurred is being awakened for you. But surely [this applies] to everyone?

"Brahman-hood is the fruit of knowledge; therefore, how can it be that [the Self] possesses Brahman-hood [prior to that]? To this, he says: 'Even prior to knowledge, it is indeed Brahman; therefore, it cannot be the fruit of knowledge.
Even before the arising of knowledge, everything is indeed Brahman; therefore, the Brahman-hood of all things is not [something newly produced]."

The meaning is that it is the effect of knowledge; it is called "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) for the purpose of negating its being an effect, and likewise for the purpose of negating its being a cause. Thus, there is no further deliberation; by the word "immediately following" (*anantaram*), the exclusion of those two [cause and effect] is established.
The external or non-external nature of cause and effect is negated by the word "sattā" (existence);
the [notion of] Brahman is prohibited by the subsequent term; and the specific [quality] is negated by the word "bāhya" (external).
Thus, these three *vārtikas* are intended to explain the meanings of the individual words, culminating in the form of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
It is easy to understand. In this context, "aperture" refers to the distinction between cause and effect; "not external" means the non-existence of those two.
This is stated for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that such Brahman might be something other than the Self.
He states the subsequent statement:
"That which has been described as the unprecedented [apūrva] and so forth cannot be conceived apart from the Self; therefore, Brahman is indeed the Self."

"The scripture speaks for the sake of establishing identity" means that by the statement "The Self is Brahman," mutual identity is made known. Regarding that, he states the purpose of making this mutual identity known: "It is said that 'Brahman is indeed the Self' in order to negate its remoteness."

"Likewise, [the teaching] that 'Brahman alone is the Self' is for the purpose of removing transmigratoriness. Now, one might ask: "How can those two [transmigratoriness and its opposite] be removed, since they are ultimately real? To this he says:
"Transmigratoriness belongs to the Self in the same way that Brahman appears as distinct, due to lack of full knowledge."

Therefore, he says that upon the cessation of ignorance, the Self becomes devoid of distinctions: "When darkness is destroyed by the knowledge of reality, the Self remains as 'not this, not this' (neti neti). This is indeed the experience of all; therefore, because He is the experience of all, this Supreme One is the All, being complete in His entirety.
The realization of pure consciousness (*cinmātratva*) is the reflective awareness of what has been thus stated; this is the means prescribed by the Vedas, the commands, and the teachers:

"This knowledge must be realized. This is the instruction of the Vedas. There is a fault in its transgression, and for one who persists in it, there is the consequence of the miseries of saṃsāra; yet for the Self, there is great gain.

The two explanatory verses (*vārtika*) beginning with "the state of having accomplished what was to be done" (*kṛtakṛtyatā*) are easy to understand. Thus ends the fifth Brāhmaṇa of the fourth [Adhyāya].
In the *Vaṃśabrāhmaṇa*, three things— praise (*stuti*), recitation (*japa*), and the removal of doubts imagined by persons (*puruṣotprekṣitāśaṅkānivṛtti*)—
are stated for the purpose of praising the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
The lineage of the knowers of Brahman is being described. This recitation is said to be the knowledge of Brahman for the sake of its birth;

it is stated in the Śruti that this lineage of the knowledge of Brahman, which arises from the deliberation of men, is declared by the Śruti with effort for the purpose of removing the doubt as previously raised.
Furthermore, he states another point:

for the sake of understanding that Self-existent One whose instruction [is given], the text beginning with Pautimāṣya and others is set forth by means of the Śruti; this is the lineage starting from Āgrya.

Regarding the phrase "because the Vedas have Brahman as their root": the meaning is that this lineage serves as the means by which that Brahman—the self-existent Supreme Self whose teaching is the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self—is to be realized. It is for the sake of attaining that Supreme Self that this genealogy is presented.

He says, "By means of the word 'Brahman,' [it is called] 'self-existent' (svayaṃbhū) for the purpose of negating a different cause," in order to demonstrate that the knowledge of the Supreme Being is not produced by another— unlike the knowledge of those such as ourselves— but is rather innate.
The term "Brahmā" does not refer to Hiraṇyagarbha; rather, the qualification "Self-Existent" (Svayambhū) is used for the purpose of excluding him as a distinct teacher.
Thus, preceded by the performance of the act of salutation, [the word] "Namaḥ" [is employed].
He explains the meaning of the word:
because this self of the Veda, being independent of anything else, is called Brahman.
"Therefore, one should always bow with devotion to Him through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Sureśvaravārtikasambandhokti* composed by the venerable Viśvānubhava, a disciple of the holy Pratyagbodha.

It is finished. Om! Having restated what has been completed, he explains the connection: "The meaning of the Madhu-kāṇḍa, contained within the Yājñavalkya-kāṇḍa, is finished; hereafter, the Śruti [proceeds] with effort."

"It is explained clearly"—this refers to the meaning of the *Muni-kāṇḍa*. With the intention of considering what that [meaning] is, he says: "Now this *Yājñavalkya-kāṇḍa*, which follows the *Madhu-kāṇḍa* and abounds in inquiry, is begun as the supreme [section]."

By this [statement], the repetition has already been avoided because it consists primarily of investigation (*vicāra*); nevertheless, one objects due to a lack of full understanding: "But surely the very same meaning that was stated previously is being stated here as well; and repetition is not appropriate for two [passages] situated within a single discourse."

He states the very same resolution of the charge of tautology once more: "Even though they have the same meaning, there is no tautology here; for the section belonging to Yājñavalkya is primarily concerned with logical justification" (p.
[Objection: But are not arguments (yukti) also stated in the Madhu-kāṇḍa? To this he replies: "The predominance of scriptural statements (āgama) in the Madhu-kāṇḍa has been set aside;
here, argument will be set forth for the sake of purifying the meaning of scripture. [Objection: But...

[Objection: "The dependence of scripture (*āgama*) upon reasoning (*yukti*) contradicts its independence. [Reply: No, he says—scripture's independence is not negated by the statement of reasoning, because reasonings are distinct from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for that very reason.

Because the reasoning [employed here] is distinct from that of the [other] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it demonstrates that these reasonings are subordinate to all means of valid cognition; since this has been established even in other treatises, there is no refutation of their independence. Furthermore, he states that because the subject matter differs, there is no dependence [on others]: [He says: "Because the reasoning is different from the means of valid cognition, it reveals that reasonings are subordinate to all means of valid cognition; as this has been set forth even in other treatises, there is therefore no refutation of its independence. And because the objects differ, there is no dependence."

This reasoning concerning the meaning of individual words is called *tarka* (logical inquiry); however, the meaning of the sentence [as a whole] arises from scripture (*āgama*) alone, and thus [scriptural] speech is independent. Furthermore, regarding a statement composed by a person, such as "Heaven results from worshipping a shrine," one must ask: is this produced by a reliable authority (*āpta*)?

For reasoning (*tarka*) is possible because one can investigate whether a work composed by an unreliable person—or even one composed by oneself—is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding its subject matter or not; however, since the Veda results in the ascertainment of its intended meaning (*tātparya*), no logical reasoning need be relied upon concerning the meaning of the Veda. Therefore...
The Veda is an independent means of valid cognition regarding its own subject matter; thus it is said on page 525:
"In the case of human speech alone, it is logical that [reliance] is desired primarily upon the speaker's intention. This is the intended meaning.
"The meaning [is established] by reasoning, not by mere reasoning. Now, one might ask:

"Granted that reasonings such as *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth possess the capacity to determine the intended meaning (*tātparya*); but how can reasonings such as 'beginning with speech' (*vācārambhaṇa*) be the cause for that? Listen: from the leaf understood through *śruti* and the other means...

Because it contradicts perception and other means of knowledge, the misconception [of duality] is removed by means of reasoning such as "consisting of mere verbal modification" (*vācārambhaṇa*); thus, those [reasonings] also serve as causes for that [realization]. Furthermore, because the identity of Brahman and the Self is not accessible to other means of knowledge, just like [the nature of] *dharma* and so forth, [it cannot be established otherwise].

He says that it depends on reasoning (*yuktyapekṣā*); because it is excluded from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other [means of knowledge], there is no dependence on reasoning regarding the meaning of scripture (*āgama*). He says that even with respect to an object within the domain of reasoning, there is dependence on scripture for the sake of the category (*padārtha*):
"In this way, there may be an expectation of scripture by means of the object of reasoning. Here he states the reason:
The reasoning is set forth in the Veda in accordance with the absence [of agency] in the person (pums),

because the person is understood as having Brahman as its true object; thus, the specific qualities such as agency superimposed upon the two categories of meaning constitute the nature of the person, and it is for the purpose of refuting that [superimposition] [that the reasoning is given].

In that case, it is reasonings themselves—through the presentation of arguments and the like—that are of assistance; therefore, the purpose of the statement is not dependent upon scripture (*āgama*). [Objection: But does not even that which brings about the understanding of the meaning of a sentence [require such dependence]?

[If it is argued that] the Veda [is interpreted] according to human intellect, and therefore depends upon reasoning (*yukti*), he says "no": the operation of scripture (*āgama*) proceeds in dependence upon the nature of the object of cognition (*meyavṛtta*); thus, the object perceived by a person would not be established as it truly is, for [if it were so], the object would be unstable due to momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) and other such properties.
Therefore, the meaning is that the Veda teaches the identity of Brahman and the Self precisely as an object established by its own nature, just like perception and other means of knowledge.
It was stated that the Madhu-kāṇḍa is primarily based on scripture; regarding that, he says:
[Objection: But were not the attainments of Dundubhi and others also stated in the Madhu-kāṇḍa?
How then can it be said that this [section] has scripture (*āgama*) as its sole primary authority? [Reply: True;
both exist in both places. Nevertheless, it is by way of the distinction between subordinate and primary [status].
Intending to avoid the charge of tautology, he says:
"There is no fault at all, because in that [context] reasoning is not the primary authority; rather, in the *Yājñavalkīya*, the primacy of reasoning is asserted. Let it be so.
The avoidance of redundancy: For what purpose are the reasonings (yukti) stated? To this he says:
"Because reasoning and scripture, when combined, are capable of making known even that most subtle reality, just as an amalaka fruit is clearly seen in the palm of one's hand.
Therefore, he states that the explanation of the reasonings should be understood for this reason.

Therefore, the arguments based on the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and so forth are stated in this section belonging to Yājñavalkya; and these arguments are of two kinds: the argument of debate (*vādayukti*) and the argument for one who has attained wisdom (*labdhabuddhi*).
The method of debate (*vāda-yukti*) has the determination of the truth as its primary aim, while the method of contentious debate (*labdha-yukti*) has victory and defeat as its primary aim.
Regarding this, he says that the methods of contentious debate are not stated in the fifth chapter: "by way of the discourse on contentious debate," as taught in the *Udgītha Brāhmaṇa*.

He states that the first inquiry is for the purpose of establishing the meaning of the *udgītha* and other such terms: "The sacrifices beginning with the *udgītha*, which were previously declared in the *Madhu-kāṇḍa*,—it is now undertaken for the sake of their purification. Therefore, at the outset...
He states that the meditation taught by Brahmā is supplementary to the meditation on the *udgītha*:
"Because this [meditation] is seen [in the context], it is therefore accepted as forming a single syntactical unit with that.
This same unity of syntactical connection applies even to the topics set forth in the second Brāhmaṇa and those that follow.
He says that it is to be seen:
"In the same way, regarding the other categories of meaning, [this applies] to both sections (kāṇḍa)"— thus,
the reasoning set forth at the beginning of the second Brāhmaṇa is the same as that set forth in the Madhu-kāṇḍa.

The meaning is: "for the sake of determining the true nature of the categories beginning with 'That'. Having thus established the connection, he provides an explanation of the meaning of the words: "This which is the means for the complete accomplishment of action, yet is overwhelmed by death..."

(528) "The master’s mantra has been seized and brought under control by the officiating priests, Agni, and the others. He explains the meaning of the word *mṛtyu*: "That ignorance which consists of limitation (*pariccheda*) and is accompanied by attachment (*sāsaṅga*)."

Regarding the phrase "designated as death": the meaning is that death is the deluded cognition of the self, accompanied by passion and other afflictions, which causes the differentiation of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and so forth.
He states that the first question concerns the means for the destruction of such death:
"By what means, then, is this sacrificer released from the reach of death?

He states the reason why there must necessarily be a means for the destruction of death: "That which is a mortal means is itself mortal as its goal; it is born [perishable], being inferred by its means."
"Since liberation is the goal to be accomplished by that [knowledge], let it be stated.

He says: "By this, the means for the destruction of death is stated"—namely, the response to the question: "One is liberated from the attainment of death through the *hotṛ* priest, through fire, or through speech."
Yājñavalkya also said, "What? Now, it has been stated that the logic of debate (*jalpanyāya*) does not aim at the determination of the true nature of reality (*vastunirṇaya*).
If this is so, why are three [stages] mentioned here? To this he replies:
when Aśvala and the others are questioning Yājñavalkya, who is the proponent (*pravaktā*) in this instance.
One knows [him] through the divine self; such a person should become a *hotṛ*.
529) Both the *hotṛ* and the sacrificer’s words are meditated upon in the form of Agni.
The meaning is that it is the means for the destruction of death. That fire of infinite form is the Hotṛ priest;
[the text states] "so that there may be liberation for the sacrificer from death as previously described, and likewise transcendence (atimukti).
This is an elaboration of what preceded, explaining the two categories of liberation and transcendence.

"O God, the attainment of the divine from an asuric means is here called liberation; likewise, the attainment of a divine goal from an asuric goal is called supreme liberation. Asuric means is meritorious action devoid of knowledge; the divine [means] is [knowledge]."

Some maintain that the knowledge of meditations on Hiraṇyagarbha and others, when conjoined with merit, is an asuric means and constitutes sinful action. From such an asuric means, one attains such a divine means and liberation; indeed, [liberation] results from the fruit of the asuric means itself.

"The attainment of the fruit of the means" means liberation (*mukti*). Some say that absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) itself is directly denoted by the words "liberation" (*mukti*) and "supreme liberation" (*atimukti*). If, however, it is intended that the deity is indeed the aforementioned latent impression (*vāsanā*), then for what purpose is this knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*)? [Objection: But surely...
The statement, "It is not for the sake of another fruit; here there is no other fruit than liberation from that," explains the intended meaning of the subsequent sentence (vṛttā p. 530).

Following the recitation of the preceding verse: "The liberation from death through demonic action has been declared here; now, liberation from death by means of time, in addition to [the mastery of] action, is being stated. Thus, it establishes that time itself is death.

"The means of accomplishment, such as the substance and the agent, are indeed inherent in the performance [of the rite]. And at the conclusion of that performance, all of it is wiped away. Prior to the completion of the performance, during the time before its execution, every means for accomplishing that ritual action exists perpetually, undergoing consumption.
This is an elaboration of what preceded; therefore, he states that time (*kāla*) is also established as death (*mṛtyu*):
"Therefore, let time be understood as death, distinct from karma. Hence, from that...

He states that the subsequent statement is for the purpose of explaining liberation; since liberation must be explained even beyond that, he begins with the words "another. Time is twofold, and because both kinds of time are death, he says "and time" to indicate that the question concerns the means for its destruction.
"Two kinds have been declared: one characterized by day and night (*ahorātra*), and the other characterized by lunar days (*tithi*) and so forth;
the explanation regarding these two is stated here. Thus he states that the first question concerns the subject of day and night:
"Since they present [the fruits of] action and likewise exhaust them within a day and night, therefore death occurs within a day and night."
From those two, liberation would then arise.
Thus it is said. He states the proof:
"The eye within is the Adhvaryu priest; with respect to the sacrifice, the pair is the Sun."

"Meditating that 'this one is directly the infinite-bodied one,' he is liberated. This means that when both the patron (*yajamāna*) and the *adhvaryu* meditate upon both as having the form of Āditya, then the patron is liberated from death by day and night. [This concerns] a limb of the Self.

"This very sun, my eye, the radiant one—I am indeed the Adhvaryu priest. Having realized this directly, what is being said? This is an elaboration of the preceding [statement]. By the word "Self," the sacrificer is meant; [the meaning is: "I am the eye, which is a limb of the sacrificer, and I am the Adhvaryu."
"Aṃśumān is indeed Āditya. Likewise, when the Adhvaryu stands having directly perceived [the deity], then the sacrificer is liberated from time and death, as is the Adhvaryu;
because the meditation is bound to its constituent parts (aṅga), the agency belongs only to the performer of those parts—this is the meaning.

It is obtained. First, he explains that through the attainment of the moon—which is of the nature of action—there is liberation from time characterized by lunar days and so forth. He further explains that this [liberation] also occurs through the attainment of the wind.
Through the increase and decrease of the digits (*kalā*) during both fortnights, the Moon acts here;
by attaining that [state], one is liberated from the two fortnights.

Thus, in the *Kāṇḍaśākhā*, the lapse of time characterized by the lunar days and so forth due to the attainment of Vāyu is described; therein he states the reason: "Since Vāyu is the agent of both decrease and increase [of the lunar days] from the moon, therefore the withdrawal occurs through Vāyu alone."

"The out-breath was made the Udgātṛ. Therefore, the out-breath of the sacrificer and the Udgātṛ are meditated upon in the form of wind (*vāyu*). Regarding the means of liberation from the two sides, he says that while in the *Kāṇva* recension liberation from the two sides is attained simply through reaching the moon, this is stated by the *Mādhyandinas*: [The text continues: "He who knows thus becomes the self of all beings; he becomes the self of all beings. This is the reward for one who knows thus. Now, as for the objection: "If the Udgātṛ is the out-breath, then when the sacrificer breathes out, the Udgātṛ would die; and when he breathes in, the Udgātṛ would become blind. To this we reply: No, because they are different parts of the body. Just as the head is not destroyed when a hand is cut off, so too the Udgātṛ does not perish when the sacrificer breathes out, nor does he become blind when he breathes in. Furthermore, the Udgātṛ is the out-breath and the eye of the sacrificer. And since the out-breath and the eye are both forms of light, the Udgātṛ is indeed the light. Therefore, the Udgātṛ is the out-breath and the eye of the sacrificer. Thus, the Udgātṛ is meditated upon in the form of wind. "The mind is the internal self (adhyātmyam), and Brahmā is that which pertains to the sacrifice (adhiyajñaga);

its presiding deity (adhidevatā) is the Moon"—thus says the Mādhyandina Śruti. Therefore, the mind and Brahmā are to be meditated upon in the form of the Moon; this meditation, which is a means to liberation, is established according to the specific Vedic branches (śākhā-vyavasthayā).

It should be observed: having first followed up on what has transpired, he introduces the subsequent question: "This one, liberated from action, time, and death, goes to heaven; by what sequence will he proceed there?"—thus it is asked. What is the subject matter of this question?

If it is argued here that the question concerns the means for going to the heavenly world, and thus it is indeed a question regarding the means, the author states the reason for this: "Because the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is without support,
there is a negation of a cause for going"— this question, therefore, pertains to the subject of taking up a body.
[The author] refutes the view of Bhartṛprapañca (p.
who asks, "How can this one who has died take on a body?"— but [the author maintains that] it is indeed through the assumption of a body.

The question regarding the "seizer" (*graha*) is asked only when there is one who goes; furthermore, its body has been previously established as the vision of fire and so forth. This question—"by what?"—is possible only when there is indeed one who goes, for even that much singing and the state of being a goer do not arise without a body.

Therefore, by the force of that very [scriptural statement], a body capable of moving is established; hence, a question regarding such a body is not inappropriate. Since the body of the mover is presented by scripture in passages such as "He became that fire" and "He became that wind," a question concerning that [body] is likewise appropriate.

Therefore, it is not logical that the question concerns the taking up of a body. He says that the mind of the sacrificer—which is both the *adhyātma* (the internal self) and the *adhiyajña* (the sacrificial aspect), namely Brahman—is perceived in the form of the moon as the means for attaining the world of Brahman; thus, the mind as the *adhiyajña* is indeed Brahman, the Brahmā.

"The moon is the presiding deity; by means of the mind as the moon, one shall go to the world through support"— thus he says that the sacrificer's vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the Udgātṛ priest, perceived in the form of Vāyu,
constitute the means for attaining the world, as found in the Mādhyandina recension.

The inner vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone would be the Udgātṛ; as for that which pertains to the sacrifice, it is Vāyu—such would be the reading in this sentence according to the Mādhyandina recension. The meditation on the Udgītha does not belong to the sacrificer as its master.

In the Udgītha Brāhmaṇa, it is stated that the muttering of mantras performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) does not have the sacrificer as its owner, nor is it performed by him as its agent. In that very same [text]:
He states another reason:

"Because of the mention of the sacrificer here, and because it forms a single syntactical unit with the preceding *udgītha*, it should be determined that the muttering (*japa*) there belongs to the sacrificer, as does the knowledge."
It recalls the fact that the knowledge concerning the installation of one's own golden [image] is designated as the *audgātra* (the duty of the Udgātṛ).

This is intended to establish that it belongs to him alone and not to anyone else; for while it may be possible that the measurement of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) pertains to the Udgātṛ, it cannot be that what pertains to the sacrificer belongs to the Udgātṛ.

Thus he explains the meaning of the word *iti*. For the particle *iti* is said to refer back to what has been stated and serves the purpose of extension (*atideśa*). One should observe that elsewhere as well, for the sake of liberation, they are likewise [to be understood] in this way. The indeclinable (*nipāta*) *iti* functions in the sense of "thus" (*evam*). Just as the liberation of speech and the other [organs] has been described, so too [is it here].

It should be understood that there is also a liberation beyond (atimokṣa) for the skin and so forth, even though they were not explicitly mentioned. To show how this is so, he says: "The views regarding them as having the divine self (adhidevatman) would be liberations beyond, everywhere, for the very reason already stated."

Everything pertaining to the meditation on the *udgītha* has been determined; now, in the section beginning with "Now, as for the correlative meditations" (*atha saṃpadaḥ*), he explains the meaning of the term *saṃpat*: [it occurs] because of the perception of some commonality in certain instances between fruit-bearing ritual acts and other things.
The prosperity of the great is such that even a very small deed leads to their downfall; or rather,
it may result in the mere partial increase of that very fruit.

"In the rites such as the Agnihotra, it is [mere] identification (saṃpad). Now, one might object: "Since the fruit is indeed [attained through] identification, its definition need not be formulated. To this he says:
"And if the attainment of the fruit were [possible] through identification, then for all three [classes], there would be no performance of rites such as the Aśvamedha."
"By reciting that [text], one shall become possessed of the fruit [of those rites] for the various castes.
Now, one might object: "How can the fruit of great deeds such as the Aśvamedha sacrifice be obtained through a minor accomplishment?
To this, he says:

"The scripture is not too heavy a burden for our intellect, provided it is devoted to that [ultimate goal]; for the meditation of the wise, which is the bridge to the highest good, is never obstructed anywhere. Having thus stated the purport (*tātparya*), he proceeds with the explanation of the word-meanings (*padārtha*) by means of the three verses beginning with "tisṛbhiḥ" (by three). [The syllable *saṃ* indicates the number.]

He stated the determination of the questions thus: "The determination of the meaning is by means of the number [of verses] through the application of the *puro’nuvākyā* and so forth. He then explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "Whatever here breathes":
Because of the commonality of the number three, there is the victory over the hearts of all living beings.
The worlds are three, consisting of the threefold afflictions (*tāpa*): *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *suvar*.
Likewise, the *ṛc* verses are also three, in the form of the *puronuvākyā*, the *yājyā*, and the *śasyā*; thus, by this commonality of number—
Having effected the accomplishment of the three worlds through the *puronuvākyā* and other [mantras], the *prāṇabhṛt* [verse] conquers everything.
Now, one might ask: "If the conquest of the worlds comes from worshipping the worlds, how can the vital breaths (prāṇas) be conquered? To this he says:

"Because the manifestation of all living beings occurs within these three alone. This means that a great task is accomplished through small tasks, or rather, it is the fruit itself that is accomplished.

It was stated [in the previous verse] that these are "accomplishments" (*saṃpad*). Here, one might think they are accomplishments of action (*karma-saṃpad*); however, he says they are accomplishments of fruit (*phala-saṃpad*).

Because of the commonality of qualities such as brilliance (*ujjvalatva*) and so forth, these are indeed accomplishments of fruit—such as the worlds and so on—and action is not intended here. That which was stated as "because of the commonality of qualities such as brilliance" is as follows:
He elaborates upon the commonality:

"Radiance, sound, lying down below, clarified butter, meat, milk, and water, as well as the attainment of the world of the gods and so forth, may occur because of the possibility of possessing radiance and the rest; for the mind is indeed infinite."
He states the meaning of this and the following verses: "Because its own nature is infinite activity (*vṛtti*), [the Self] is infinite;

because sound and the other objects are infinite, the activity of the Viśvedevas-natured [Self] is to be accomplished, since it cannot be achieved by anything else. Therefore, by that knowledge which possesses an object, it is indeed infinite."
One who possesses the aforementioned view pays homage to the world, considering the sacrificer himself to be the fruit;

by such a term, only the *puronuvākyā* and other verses are meant, as he says: "The three *puronuvākyā*s and so forth previously mentioned—those alone are to be known as the *trayī* (the triple Veda)."
Even in the *stotriyās*, there are no others;
they exist in the form of "wonderful thoughts" (*tāścaryo dhiyaḥ*) and "the knower" (*jñānī*). In what form do they exist internally (*adhyātman*)?
"They exist as the internal self; they exist as the internal self. Regarding this, it is said:
"The songs (gītayas) are the culmination of the sacrifice; what are they called as the internal self?
They are declared to be the forms of prāṇa, apāna, and vyāna as the internal self."
He states the fruit of this meditation:
"Victory over the elements, worlds, and so forth, due to the similarity of number and other qualities.
The commonality of number has already been mentioned; by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi), [other similarities are intended].
"The states of being first, middle, and last are grasped"—thus Aśvala desisted because his own question had been resolved; this is easily understood.
Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa of the fifth [Adhyāya].
Prefaced by a summary of what has preceded, he states the meaning of the second Brāhmaṇa:
"In the previous Brāhmaṇa, liberation from death and transcendence beyond it were presented; now, the subsequent Brāhmaṇa is spoken for the purpose of determining the nature of death. Thus.

The meaning is that the Brāhmaṇa begins in order to state that even the fruit of worship is seized by death. If one asks what the characteristic of death is, he says it consists of the senses and their objects.
Thus, when it is asked by what characteristic this death seizes [the practitioner]:
"It is said that he is swallowed by means of the form of the *graha* (seizers) and *atigraha* (over-seizers). Furthermore,
he elucidates the meaning of the term "death" (*mṛtyu*) through the categories of *adhibhūta*, *adhiyajña*, and so forth.

"Death consists of the nature of limited discernment, is the locus of delusion and attachment, and is characterized by the seizing of the body. Now, it may be objected that the form of fire and so forth has been declared for one who is liberated from death in the *Udgītha-brāhmaṇa* and in the *Āśvala-praśna*. Therefore...

If it is argued that Hiraṇyagarbha—who consists of fire and other elements and is the fruit of knowledge and action—is not seized by death, and therefore the attainment of him alone is liberation, this is not so; for since he too is something to be accomplished (sādhya), he is impermanent. Thus, [the author] says "ito" (from this).

For I have previously stated in the Udgītha Brāhmaṇa and likewise in the Aśvala Brāhmaṇa that fire and the other elements are by nature liberated; and this result is intended for those whose actions are joined with knowledge. However, because of their connection with origination and so forth, they must therefore be non-eternal.

Unlike a jar or similar objects, the form of fire and so forth is not described as being completely liberated from death; rather, it is [liberated] only from a small portion characterized by sin and the like. Therefore, even Hiraṇyagarbha is indeed seized by death because of his impermanence; since liberation is the fruit of that which is "not-measured" (nam), one must attain liberation through knowledge.
He says that effort must be made: "Therefore, from this aforementioned [teaching] characterized by the goal and the means...

"Liberation from the bonds of *saṃsāra* must be achieved through the destruction of ignorance"— this being the case, the nature of Hiraṇyagarbha’s bondage has been explained by reference to his birth and other attributes; now,
[the author] states that what is considered "death" is in fact merely a form of connection, because [Hiraṇyagarbha] is still seized by the senses.

"Even if it is true that the divine fruit of knowledge and action was previously described, nevertheless, because of the bondage of the *grahas* and *atigrahas*, that [fruit] remains white (pure) only in name. To explain how this is so, he says:
"Because the three forms consisting of speech, mind, and breath do not originate from the Self."
"Because of these forms of the *grahas* and *atigrahas*, Prajāpati was not liberated.

Having thus stated the connection, he proceeds with an extensive explanation. Now, [one might object]: "In the preceding Brāhmaṇa, there were four *grahas*, speech and the others, and four *atigrahas* pertaining to them."

It has been stated thus; how then can there be a further mention here? To this he says: "Speech and the others are known as the *grahas* (seizers), and the four and five are not intended. He states the reason for their not being intended: "Because of the extension (*atideśa*) from what follows. This refers to the mention of qualities (*guṇābhidhāna*).

He says, "This is logical; now their specific distinctions are being stated. The sense organs, such as the nose and so forth, are to be known as the *grahas* (seizers), while odors and so forth are the objects seized by them (*atigrahas*).

It is easily understood that odors and the rest are seized by the *grahas*, and both the *grahas* and the self are seized by their respective objects (*gocaras*). This is their state of mutual bondage.
He establishes this by means of an illustration:
"Just as a fragrance brought in by inhalation comes under the control of the sniffer."
In the same way, the apprehensions of the eye and other senses occur here through their companions, such as the nose.

Just as an odor impelled by the *apāna* wind comes under the control of the olfactory organ, so too do form and the other objects, impelled by winds corresponding to each, come under the control of the visual organ and the rest. Thus it is.

The senses, such as sight and the rest, also fall under the power of form and the other objects along with the various vital airs, such as prāṇa and the others. He establishes the status of the objects as "seizers" (grahas): "Since they, being situated in the objects such as smell, impel the awakening of action..."
"Therefore, the nose and the other [senses] would be *atigrahas*. To this, the subsequent interrogative statement beginning with "All this" explains the intended meaning:
"Is there yet another death for that death which has been mentioned here, or is there not?"

"Speak truly, Yājñavalkya! If it exists, there would be an infinite regress and no liberation; if it does not exist, [what then]? [The opponent] asked this out of concern that he was questioning the Inner Self (pratīc) with too little effort, thinking, "Is there even a death of death? Thus, the word "death" is not used here for the sake of establishing that.
He says that it is not established in any [specific] way, like the *aśvakarṇa* tree and so forth: "No fixed entity whatsoever is taught as being death" (p.

Since death is the destroyer and that which is destroyed is called "pratibhaṇya," he therefore adopts the position that it exists, saying: "Even though death exists, I declare that there is indeed a death of death.
He grasps the characteristic of grasping through the syllable *sa* [in *asmi*], thinking: "I am Brahman, I am death."

The meaning is that knowledge of the sentence-meaning is death. To the objection that this would lead to an infinite regress, he says "no," for it does not incur an infinite regress because it serves as the cause for the death of all. Having thus resolved the objection, he provides an explanation of the word-meanings: [Agni is so called] because of his devouring of all food.
"That death is indeed this [water] as well; water is seen to be the food of fire, and here there is no contradiction. Thus he states another meaning for the word "fire" (*agni*) and so forth:
"For Agni is Hiraṇyagarbha, and water is considered the cause of those effects."
Death is the cause that brings about death;

he states that the knowledge of Brahman is the death of the cause— namely, the realization of the true nature of the inner self (pratyag-yāthātmya-vijñāna) is the death of that death which consists of ignorance and is the cause of saṃsāra.

"Nor would there be any infinite regress here"— this statement, whose meaning has already been explained, establishes the absence of infinite regress and refutes it with the following: "Just as that which produces birth also brings about its destruction,
so too the realization of the true nature of the Self does not lead to an infinite regress."
Because it brings about the cessation of its own cause, which is individual ignorance (*pratyagavidyā*), it effects its own destruction and birth, as well as its own self, by itself alone.

The knowledge of the Self (ātmavidyā) itself would remove [ignorance]; therefore, because there is no dependence on another remover, there is no infinite regress. Consequently, the knowledge of the Self alone is directly death; the status of being "death" attributed to the staff of Yama and so forth is merely figurative. Thus, he says:

"Other than this, deaths are secondary; through them, one may die only to be born again. Even previous births do not destroy our perfect knowledge"—this interpretation of the sentence, made by inserting the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*), is [an argument] against its own position.

The scriptural declaration of the fruit, namely "he conquers repeated death," is thus rendered appropriate; for otherwise, if one were to accept the literal words as they are heard, he says: "In the explanation exactly as stated, this declaration of the fruit would be logical. In this regard:
He states the reason:

"But not from the realization of the Self which utterly destroys all saṃsāra. The meaning is that when such a realization of the Self exists, there is an absence of death; or else, it is exactly as previously stated.

"In the case of [other] explanations, because knowledge has not been grasped, this declaration of the fruit would be improper; however, it is not so when the awakening to the Self—which utterly destroys the entire cycle of transmigratory existence—is grasped. Thus he states the intended meaning of the passage beginning with, "When this person dies, from this [body]... and so forth.
"Samasta" (entirety)—
because of the complete awakening to the Self through the darkness of total death.
Death is introduced as another section through the cognition of its results. Having thus stated the purport, he begins the word-by-word commentary:
"When this person, whose true nature is that of the Self known as Truth, dies..."
"Are the vital breaths (prāṇas) departing from here, or not? Please tell me.

If they were to depart, there would be no liberation, because death exists for the sake of rebirth. Yet, if they do not depart, how can there be death while the vital breaths remain? This question is indeed difficult to answer. Thus [he spoke].
Thinking thus, he questioned [the sage]; and that wise sage, having received his portion, said to him, "No.
These three *vārtikas* are easily understood. He establishes the position that it is "no" as follows:
"For one whose ignorance has been destroyed through the thorough knowledge of the Self as a non-agent, [from all sides...]"

Since there is no grasping of another body, the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is impossible; when this has been correctly understood through the knowledge of right realization according to the scriptural tradition,
then all the vital breaths along with their causes vanish without a trace— this refers to the preceding [statement].
This is the elaboration (*prapañca*). Now, if it is argued that the negation of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) occurs after the time of knowledge, then one might ask:
was there previously a positive concomitance [of the Self] with the vital breaths and so forth? To this he says "no":
"The Inner Self (*pratyak*) admits neither positive concomitance nor negative concomitance (*vyatirekatā*), because of its immutability (*kauṭasthya*) and oneness (*ekatva*)."
The commentary on the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad] concerning the reality known as the inner self (pratyagātman). (p. 544)

Thus, he states the meaning of "they are withdrawn right here" as follows: "Therefore, for one whose darkness has been destroyed through higher knowledge, there is a withdrawal of the directions [of space] by way of cause and effect, just as [the perception of] snakes and so forth is withdrawn in the case of a rope.
But surely, even here, destruction is merely the merging back into the cause; how then [can it be called withdrawal]?
Regarding the statement "it is said that [the soul] departs with the eyesight," he says:
"And there can be no conjunction with the causes [of rebirth], because that [conjunction] is negated by knowledge;
furthermore, knowledge would be fruitless if there were a conjunction with the causes, provided that the vital breaths do not depart."
"In that case, this [person] would not be dead"—this is easy to understand. To show that this is not a valid objection, he says:

"The living being (jīva) never dies, for it is only the body that dies. He provides the proof for this: "Because of the scriptural statement 'bereft of the living being' and because of the denial of birth and so forth."

He states the reasoning regarding life and death: "Since even insentient matter is called 'living' due to its connection with that [Self], how could death occur for the body of that living being here? Therefore, it breathes," and so forth.
He says that the death of the body alone is what is being discussed:

"Therefore, the death of the body is established through direct perception. He explains the meaning of the question "Does this not abandon him? as follows: do only the vital breaths (prāṇas) dissolve, or is something else also [dissolved]?
"Because the instigator and so forth are entirely absent from the wise man who is dying without remainder.
If it is argued that [the breath] alone exists there, he says:

"Upon the destruction of his mere vital breaths (prāṇa), which cause further birth... Thus he shows the advantage in the alternative view: "When that [breath] is destroyed along with its causal agent, liberation is established for him.
Intending to say that the vital breaths perish together with the causal karma and so forth, he asks: "Does this not [liberate him]?"

"He abandons" means: "It is seen as 'name'"; thus he spoke. They explain the meaning of "name" as "it does not abandon anything at all. This is stated because of common usage; he clarifies this common usage, for it is understood from what was said that [everything] is reduced to nothing but name.

"Something might remain"—this is how it is here as well. He states the meaning of the phrase "The Name is indeed infinite": because the meaning of the word is its skill (cāturī), the Name does not perish; thus, the infinity of this Name is its very eternity, not a multiplicity of individual manifestations.
Although the name of this knower of Brahman continues to exist, it nevertheless exists from the perspective of others;
for names such as "Vāmadeva is liberated" or "Śuka is liberated" are observed, and thus the permanence of the name is not established merely on the basis of such designations.
The meaning is "he speaks of Brahman. He states the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "yatrāsya" (wherein his...):
because death is the motivator of that which consists of the *grahas* and *atigrahas*, of what [is it the motivator]?
It has been shown that my own commentary on the passage beginning with "I am He" (p. 546) demonstrates that this subsequent scripture was commenced for the purpose of determining the nature of form.

Having stated the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) of the passage beginning with "yatrāsya," he now demonstrates the meaning of the passage beginning with "saṃbandhe 'rtham enam" exactly as it was explained by Bhartṛprapañca; this [explanation] is for the purpose of refutation.

Regarding this, some of great intelligence say that even when one has attained Vaiśvānara, the person has not yet been fully liberated; rather, remaining in the intermediate state, he exists as nothing more than a name,
severed from the Supreme Self by means of the supreme knowledge (*vidyā*), with his desires and karma utterly destroyed.

That [state] is "entire" because of the enjoyment of its fruit; it is "one in whom all [defects] such as the intellect have been eradicated" due to the complete exhaustion of their causes. This subsequent work is commenced for the sake of awakening the knowledge of Brahman, in order to remove the perception of duality from this [person] by means of the vision of non-duality.
Thus [it is said]. This is the meaning of the four Vārttikas:

although the simultaneous performance [of the two paths], as well as the two bodies known as gross and subtle, have perished, along with their motivators such as desire and karma, nevertheless, this person is not liberated.
Having attained Brahman and being completely liberated from saṃsāra, he remains with only knowledge as the intervening barrier, with nothing but his name remaining; of him— (p.
It must be stated that through this very vision which cuts off ignorance, the attainment of non-dual Brahman occurs;

thus, beginning with "Then Kahola said to him," etc., it is commenced. Therefore, in the passage "Hence [he is called] 'Thus-Name,'" the one qualified for the vision of non-duality is indicated—this being so even prior to Kahola's question.
The preceding section should be consulted. Because it pertains to the subject matter of saṃsāra, this section— namely, the portion occurring before Kahola’s question—
is stated here as having that purpose, since it introduces the qualification for the doctrine of non-duality (advaita) being expounded.

Some maintain that [the refutation] begins from the words "yatrāsya" (wherein his...). Thus, having briefly shown that opinion, he refutes it. That which was to be understood here has already been stated more than once previously;
I am greatly reluctant to speak again with redundant words. [He addresses] the Self alone...

Since this point has already been refuted in the section refuting the system of Bhartṛprapañca regarding passages such as "one should worship the world," no further effort is made here to refute it again.
Because this is so, we state that [the meaning] is what is contained in the Bhāṣya, and not something not contained therein in any way whatsoever.

"The refutation of the opponent's statement is entirely like grinding what has already been ground. This is what is meant: we do not, in any way, state a refutation that was already included in the Bhāṣya; rather, we state only that which was not included in the Bhāṣya.
548) We shall state the refutation by following the system of Bhartṛprapañca;
even though those [arguments] were employed by him for the purpose of refuting his own position, they were not recognized as such by him.

"We shall state the refutations. Some say that this was taken from the commentary of Bhartṛprapañca; however, in order to introduce the subsequent text, [the author] states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) shown by Bhartṛprapañca—this is recorded by means of three verses (vārtika), and it is presented solely from the perspective of dualism (dvaitadṛṣṭi).

Because all effects of duality have been completely exhausted, there is not even the slightest seed remaining for the further appropriation of the mere elements (*bhūtamātra*). Since the purpose of the person has been fulfilled, the means (the scriptures) cease once their task is done.
Therefore, there is no further purpose for the realization of non-duality (*advaita*) beyond the realization of non-duality itself.

"And for this very reason, the undertaking of the entire treatise—which culminates in the human goal—is not even possible. This is the meaning: because the cessation of the whole of saṃsāra is the purpose [of the work] as the primary fruit of the initial synthesis, it is for the sake of manifold knowledge.

The objection that Kahola’s question is purposeless because there is nothing further to be done is refuted by establishing its commencement: "Its commencement is justified because of the mutual distinctness of their respective tasks,
due to the difference between the dualistic and non-dualistic perspectives of the two selves, like those of the mortar and the pestle."
