Because the two forms of worship—dualistic and non-dualistic—have different effects, and because [the goal] is not accomplished by means of non-dualistic worship alone, the inquiry of Kahola is commenced for that purpose.

Regarding the word "strives" (*ghaṭate*): he shows what the fruit of that twofold worship is—namely, that the activity of attachment is severed because the Self is free from the perception of duality.

For in this world, attachment alone is held to be the material cause (*upādāna*) of all beings; thus, through the perception of duality, this very [attachment] constitutes the side of action (*karmapakṣa*).
Desire is discarded, as are all latent impressions (*vāsanās*) which are preceded by food.

This is the meaning: the extraction of the elements that constitute desire, karma, and latent impressions is intended; the sense is that these [elements] are the cause for the grasping of the elements that initiate the body.
If it is argued that the fruit of the practice of non-duality (*advaya-upāsana*) is the cessation of those [desires] along with their own effects, one might ask:
"If all desires and so forth have ceased without remainder, what is there left for the practice of non-duality to cease? To this he says: "If everything has indeed ceased, what else remains?"
He says that ignorance remains:
"The consciousness that delimits that [Self] is what remains as ignorance.
That is to say, the knowledge that delimits that Supreme Self, which is the nature of consciousness, remains.
The meaning is that the worship of those two is to be abandoned. He demonstrates the distinction in the effects of ritual action (*karman*) and so forth by analyzing them:
"Even at the commencement of an action, agency is desired [only] for the agent himself, residing in his own substrate."
p.

550) "The state of being a causal factor (*kāraka*) is merely knowledge delimited by its own extent. Thus, when an action begins to produce its own fruit, it is not the cause for the manifestation of its own substrate, the person (*puruṣa*).

By the word *yatta*, limitation (*pariccheda*) is expressed. Limitation refers to the state of the self—the Supreme Self—in the form of an agent and other factors; that is, the self’s abiding in the form of an agent and so forth. Ignorance is the cause of such limitation.
He explains the meaning of the term "knowledge" (jñāna):

it is that very [faculty] which delimits ignorance, by which this [self], being delimited from the state of being the transmigrating agent of the Supreme Self, attains the nature of the individual conscious self (vijñānātman). Now, even though...

"Even though non-discriminative ignorance persists, if this [Self] were already turned away from all duality by the power of the impressions (*vāsanā*) of the two [truths], what would be the use of the practice of non-duality? To this he says: "Even if this [Self] has ceased from the objects of duality, it nevertheless remains in the state of *saṃsāra*."

"Because of duality, due to the distinction from Brahman. Even though he has not yet turned away from saṃsāra, he remains in the state of saṃsāra, because as long as ignorance (avidyā) exists, he exists in a state of duality by virtue of being non-differentiated from Brahman. Therefore, the scriptural statement functions for the sake of the knowledge of non-duality (advaita).

Thus he says: "Since a sentence that remains incomplete proceeds as before because it has not reached the human goal, [the inquiry] continues for the sake of determining Brahman. But [an objection may be raised]: nanu...

"You have stated that the fruit of both dualistic and non-dualistic worship is liberation; how then can there be a difference in their effects? To this he replies: "Therefore, there is a single purport for these two sets of statements regarding duality and non-duality, because the state resulting from the fruit of dualistic worship [is itself non-dual]."
Regarding the phrase "the worship of both," he says, "it is performed. The meaning is that these two constitute a single sentence. Now, an objection is raised:

if the fruit of the impressions (vāsanā) of both is the severance of the entire cycle of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), how can one who is in such a state have eligibility for anything else, since his purpose has already been fulfilled? To this, he replies, "No."
"Because the destruction of delusion alone does not complete all human goals, [one might ask]:
'Since the attainment of all human goals follows from the destruction of delusion itself, what is the purpose of the dual worship?
To this he replies: 'For that very task which is to be accomplished—the limitation [of the self]—is indeed removed when the internal organ (svānta) is destroyed.'"
"The non-agency of action persists, and attachment likewise remains. Now, one might object:
"Since delusion has been destroyed, its effects—limited cognition and so forth—have ceased; this person has thus become Brahman.
Therefore, what is the use of the cessation of desire and the like? To this, he replies: "What are these two—attachment and action—that have not yet ceased?"

Since ignorance (*avidyā*) remains capable of producing [further error], it always functions in mutual dependence with [the other factors], even though it exists without parts. This is the meaning: *avidyā* is false cognition (*mithyājñāna*).

When one remains engaged in action driven by desire, because the three [guṇas] function inseparably, it becomes like a triple-staffed [ascetic's rod] due to their mutual connection; therefore, there must be a cessation of that [engagement].
This is because, as long as there is no cessation, there is attachment to action, and consequently, ignorance and its transformations persist.

He says that it must come about through the cessation of that [duality], stating: "And as long as one is not purified, it is impossible to perceive non-duality within the realm of difference. Regarding this, he introduces the possibility of an objection, saying: "In this regard, etc.," which will be stated in the refutations of the arguments of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The meaning is as follows: because of the fear of excessive length of the text, the entire matter of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) previously stated is not set forth here; rather, even though there are many refutations, only a very small portion of the refutation is stated out of fear of making the book too voluminous.

He demonstrates the refutations: here, the refutation is stated both by the Śruti itself and by the statement "Or the Person," because it is declared that "therefore it would be so. Thus the position is demonstrated by the sentences: "The Person is the imperishable" and "or from this [Person]."

Since these statements have been refuted even by Bhartṛprapañca, who explained them as teaching the non-destruction of duality, how then can there be the destruction of duality through the first synthesis? Starting from the cause, the Imperishable, with the words "eating food after eating,"...

553) The Vārttikas establishing the inexhaustibility of the world, ending with the statement "birth itself is the thorough knowledge of reality," are easy to understand; they are written down here as well. Regarding that also, whoever...

That manifest portion is explained by way of a reason: "From the imperishable cause, food is produced here by the Person through action; it is generated into the state of rice and so forth by way of the unmanifested state and the rest.
Food, which exists in the form of the unmanifested and so forth, is generated in the form of rice and other such grains.

The meaning is "by means of action. This being so, if this [consciousness] were not produced solely within that which is initially conditioned (upahita), it would then perish. But this is not produced here; rather, it is eternal, just as food is consumed by the self through speech, body, and intellect, while the series of karmas remains undiminished.

In the same way, he also causes beings to be born as they perish through their karma; here, they are generated by the Supreme Self through the person (puruṣa). Therefore, that person is the ground for the experience of the auspicious and inauspicious fruits of the prior karma of persons. Consequently, due to the distinction of non-attachment, it belongs to another.
Furthermore, the process therein being thus, since living beings for the most part [act] out of attachment,

they repeatedly consume food under the influence of the latent tendencies of desire; some elements of being are diminished by enjoyment, while others are accumulated by karma, just as the wicks of a lamp [are consumed].
Just as a flame [persists] through its continuity,
so too the state of being one who consumes and one who experiences [objects] is based upon the conditioning factors (*saṃskāra*).

The entire world wanders about, unbound by the conscious self; for whatever conscious self exists, through whatever action it performs, that becomes the cause of heaven for the world of the presiding deity. This has been stated by the Śruti itself: "Just as karma is exhausted..."
"The attainment of divine speech and so forth belongs likewise to one who perceives the Self as the three-fold.
The meaning is that the attainment of the fruits of the meditations on Hiraṇyagarbha and others is imperishable;
he has declared its permanence throughout the three worlds, saying "this is that" and "that is this."

"But for that which is eternal, there is merely modification"— this means that birth is merely manifestation. Furthermore, the Śruti declares the inexhaustibility of ignorance, desire, and action even for one established in Brahman, because of the attainment of the Whole.

There is no destruction of desire and action resulting from this, because of the impossibility of their cessation; therefore, it is said that [this view] is incorrect. But surely, the world is not destroyed in its entirety through enjoyment; rather, what is meant is merely the cessation of the world’s manifestation.
To this he replies: "As for that destruction of manifestation which is taught as being of the nature of the cause—that kind of destruction we do not deny even in the state of deep sleep. (p.
Thus, the meaning is that the practice of spiritual means (sādhana) would be futile. Since this is so, he states that the destruction of the world arises precisely from ignorance:
"The very birth of the thorough knowledge of the reality of the Inner Self (pratyaktattva) is the cause for the destruction of duality."

"And it is not accepted that there is anything other than this for the sake of the human goal. Now, one might ask: "How is it that nothing else is accepted? It is true that karma is indeed accepted for the sake of liberation (*kaivalya*), but only indirectly, not directly; regarding this, he states the authority [for this view] in the passage beginning with "That very [Self]" (*tam etam*) and likewise for all others.
The application of actions toward the arising of direct knowledge has been demonstrated;
however, because of the scriptural statement that "from knowledge comes the destruction of karma," there is no direct assistance [provided by action].
Thus he says: "The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut asunder, and his [karmic bonds] perish."

"Karmas [are destroyed] when That, both the higher and the lower, is seen. If that is so, then does it not follow that even *prārabdha* karma is destroyed? To this he says: "By the exhaustion of experience, [there is the end] of desirable and prohibited karmas; but of those whose effects have already begun, even the wise ones do not perceive [destruction], even though they possess knowledge. If that is so—
To the objection that even so [the karma] remains, he says:

"But because all unexhausted karmas have not yet begun their effects, there is no destruction [of them], due to the non-arising of perfect knowledge. Now, is it not the case that the scripture itself [says otherwise]?

If it is argued that there is still a need for authoritative knowledge (*māna*) even when enjoyment has been exhausted along with [past] karma, he says "no": Just as there is authoritative knowledge regarding the exhaustion [of karma] upon the arising of knowledge (*jñāna*).
"Through the attainment of totality, pride [is abandoned] at the stage of destruction; thus nothing else is taught.
In that context, it was stated that [ignorance] is the delimiting factor; regarding this, what is this "ignorance"? Is it grasping or non-grasping? To this, he says:

"Nor is ignorance the discerning [agent], because it is of the nature of darkness; therefore, it is not logical that it [should be the agent] of one who possesses both collective and individual forms, since it is merely an obscuring factor. He says that even if it were false cognition, it would be the same:
"Furthermore, false consciousness is not accepted as being a discerning agent."
"Even a cognition of blue does not delimit space even slightly. To the question, "Then whose is the delimitation?

he says: "The means of knowledge (*māna*) is the manifestor of that which exists. If it is objected that "the means of knowledge is a producer (*kāraka*), not a cognizer (*bodhaka*)," he replies: "But it is not that..."

"Like the potter's [wheel]," etc. Furthermore, regarding the fact that the intellect possesses the capacity for discernment (*paricchedakatva*), which is to say its capacity for cognizing things as they truly are (*yathārthabodhakatva*), there is no disagreement;
thus he says: "The intellect’s discernment consists in its conformity to the object. Moreover, [he asks] "If it were so," etc., and to that he replies:
Just as non-cognition also conforms to the nature of the object, so too liberation is always present in the object of knowledge;

for this [non-cognition], bondage is its opposite. Since both non-apprehension and misapprehension function as cognitions of reality, the object to be known by them is always liberated—or rather, it is like greed.
Furthermore, because both [the cause and the effect] exist eternally, the commencement of the treatise would be purposeless; moreover,
it is the perception of that [Brahman] as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the insentient phenomenal world, just as water is the material cause of waves.

That too is untenable; thus he says: "The self could not be the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of that which is not its own effect, for it does not have that as its purpose; indeed, threads here do not produce a jar. If it is argued that ignorance alone is the material cause of the entire world, that too—
He states that this contradicts your own accepted position: "Knowledge of the Supreme Self exists by itself, while desire and action are external;
yet, by you who have arrived [at this view], it is asserted that ignorance arises from the Supreme Self, and that desire and action are the effects of ignorance."

"You yourself have stated that ignorance alone is the material cause of the world; therefore, this [claim] contradicts your own accepted position. Furthermore, you say that even though ignorance has perished, desire and action produce [a new body], which is also stated in contradiction to reason," he says.

Nor can desire and action produce non-existent ignorance, because they lack the necessary cause, just as [they cannot produce] the vision of a hare's horn and the like. The meaning is that since there is no possibility of the birth of what is non-existent, and since such a birth would be devoid of a cause, there is no birth. Or, let it be so.
Even so, if ignorance were the cause, it could not produce that which is absolutely non-existent;
for even in the world, a cause does not bring about the birth of something utterly non-existent.

"Even with good rain, the lotus arises from the sky"—the meaning of this is that there is an absence of flowers in the sky; thus it is said that ignorance (avidyā) exists by itself, independent of the Supreme Self (parātman).
Regarding that very point, he states another objection: "If Brahman alone is the cause of the birth of ignorance..."

If that [cause] exists, how could there be the complete eradication of ignorance? Now, if the absolute destruction of the effect occurs while the cause still exists, then since saṃsāra would be destroyed by itself, the performance of practice for its production would be futile; thus he says:

"If there were an absolute eradication of delusion even while its cause remains, then tell me: why would this perishable [delusion] not vanish by itself? What need is there for means? For this reason as well, he says that once self-ignorance has been destroyed, desire and action will no longer be able to function:
These two—desire and action—are unable to protect ignorance;

however, they are able to cause that which exists [as ignorance] to perish. How so? If it is argued that ignorance perishes, then this objection would arise; but if it is argued that ignorance does not perish, then it is desire and action themselves that perish.
He states that this too contradicts one's own accepted position: "If even when desire, action, and so forth are abandoned,
ignorance remains, then the explanation of the statement 'Not this, not this' would be contradicted."

558) He demonstrates, by means of two *vārtikas*, how the statement "not this" (*neti*) has been explained [by others], in order to show the contradiction; he says that the first [explanation] is possible as follows:
"Desire and action are not able to protect knowledge;

how indeed could they cause that which exists to perish? [One might object: "If ignorance perishes, this objection would apply; but it does not perish. Rather, it is desire and action alone that perish."
If this is argued, [the author] says that even this contradicts their own accepted position:

"Even when desire, action, and so forth have been abandoned, if ignorance remains, then the explanation of the statement 'Not this, not this' (neti) would be contradicted. This refers to how the sentence "Not this" has been explained by them.

He shows this as follows: "Brahman has been known as it truly is; therefore, he has passed beyond that"—here, the first word "not" (na) negates the formed and the formless, while the second "not" (yaḥ saḥ atha) [negates] that which is [beyond].

"That which effects the cessation of meditation and abides in those states of peace characterized by the distinctions of meditation and so forth— that is the partless, supreme Brahman, taught as 'not this,
not this'. Now, he demonstrates the contradiction:

"Since Brahman has been known as it truly is, darkness has departed from me"—this would not be contradictory, provided it is by the grace of Jātavedas; for it is said in the Vākya that "Brahman is just as it was known. Furthermore, even so...
(On page 559:
"Ignorance persists"—this is a contradiction; and it has been stated that [ignorance] does not persist for the sake of the non-dual reality.
To this, he says: "And what kind of persistence of the non-dual reality is there in this case?"

"Is it intended that there is a non-connection with non-duality, or rather destruction, like the purification of impurity? Is it the destruction of duality, or its purification; or else, is it the non-connection of non-duality with duality? He says that a second [alternative] cannot be stated: [The text continues: "It is not possible to say that there is a non-connection of non-duality with duality."

He states that even the destruction of duality is not possible in your position, because when both the whole and its parts are perceived, non-duality arises from duality; thus, it is logical that these two possess a single nature. Therefore, he says: "Nor is the destruction of duality admitted. He provides the reason for this:
"When duality has entirely perished, there can be no perception of both the whole and the parts.

Thus he states that the doctrine of the whole-and-parts (samastavyastavāda) is indeed flawed: "How could there be a coexistence in one place of two things possessing the attributes of being both whole and parts, which are mutually contradictory like cold and heat?"

Because this contradicts the sacred scriptures (śruti), he says that this position is not tenable: "While the scriptural statements concerning the *apūrva* and so forth remain intact, it cannot be asserted even by Īśvara that the Self consists of both the aggregate and the individual. Furthermore, because the knowledge of the Self is opposed to duality, [this view is untenable].

He says "it is faulty" because there is no negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) [of the perception] with the self and so forth, as there is with a pot and the like. If there were negative concomitance here, he says: there would be the occurrence of the state of being non-self.
"By way of the distinction between the seer and the seen"—thus he again raises the contradiction with the Śruti.

If, in the view that [the whole and the parts] are both combined and separate, the perception of the separate is not completed by the perception of the combined alone, then the scriptural statement "in the Self" would result as the authoritative means of knowledge;
for by this, there would follow such words as "what was heard from the heard," "in what? and so forth.

"It would be contradictory. [Objection: "But surely inference and so forth constitute the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for Brahman as the object of meditation both collectively and individually. [Reply:
He says "no"—"And here there is no other [means of knowledge]. Therefore, he states that this argument is an error.

In the perception of the whole and the parts taken together, nothing at all is seen, because [the world] has its sole cause in perfect ignorance, just like the perception of a snake in a rope and so forth. Moreover, you yourself have stated that the meditation on the whole and the parts is for one who possesses that knowledge; and it is not...
He says that [the world] can be known individually and without remainder:
"He who knows all these various dualities without effort would grasp every single atom. This refers to the manifested portion (*vyaktabhāga*).

It has been stated that [the world] cannot be known in its entirety. Or, even if it were known, there would still be a fault; thus he says: "And even when all dualistic distinctions have been perceived by someone..."
p.

561) "In that case, its state of being Brahman would be difficult to establish because of its infinity. This means [it would be so] because it would be limited by a finite measure (*iyattā*). As for the phrase "if not," it refers precisely to the fact that everything is nothing but the Self (*ātman-mātratva*).

It has been stated that the statement "in the Self" constitutes a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa); regarding this, the following objection is raised: "But even if everything is not merely the Self, nevertheless, the knowability of everything through the knowledge of the Self is indeed established, just as the knowledge of the qualities of a substance follows from the knowledge of that substance."

"No," he says: "Just as phenomena such as blue and so forth are perceived through the view of a substance (*dravya-dṛṣṭi*), so too are they perceived through the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); yet they are not perceived as non-selves, because of the contradiction.
Due to the contradiction between the self and the non-self, the perception of the non-self does not occur through the view of a self.

This is the meaning. He states that the contradiction is declared by the Śruti: "And thus, the statement of the Bhāgavata, 'But the Supreme,' clearly demonstrated to us the contradiction between the vision of the Self and the vision of the non-Self. Now, [one might object]: "Is it not the case that meditation on the whole and the parts is taught in the passage, 'Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen'?"

In such passages, an injunction is prescribed. How could that [injunction] be impossible? To this he says: "In the statement 'The Self, indeed, my dear,' there is no injunction for the perception of the non-Self. The meaning is that this is not an injunction for the perception of the non-Self. If so, what is enjoined by this? To this he says:
"Just as the view of self (ātmadṛṣṭi) is enjoined by restating exactly what has been established [in worldly experience]," and furthermore,
"elsewhere also, wherever those [views] arise through the force of the injunction for action based on the knowledge of the self..."

It occurs to him that even in that case, it should be viewed in exactly the same way; thus he says: "Wherever an injunction (*vidhi*) is observed, there, by means of one's own action, the vision of the inner self (*pratyagdṛṣṭi*) is enjoined through a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the entire non-self. Now, [one might object]: what about ritual action (*karma*)?

If it is argued that the statement of Brahman is likewise intent upon the application of sentences, this is not sound, because a ritual injunction (karma-vākya) is intent upon making known the relationship between the means and the end to be accomplished. [Objection:
But since the relationship between the means and the end is established by other means of knowledge, it cannot be something to be made known by the Veda.
To this he replies:
"Since knowledge arises from the connection between the goal and the means, and not from anything else than scripture,
the vision of the inner self is enjoined"— if this is so, then an injunction has been accepted.

Anticipating this objection and in order to refute it, some say: "This [is stated] as follows"—namely, that the nature of sacrifice and so forth is indeed established by means of perception and other valid cognitions (pramāṇas). Thus he says:
"In the case of other objects, [it is known] through perception and other pramāṇas."

It has been stated that the realization of the Self occurs through the non-appropriation of the non-Self; however, this objection might be raised therein: "If it is something to be realized, then it must be non-Self, like a jar or other objects. To this, he replies: "But when the Self is apprehended as following from all means of knowledge, the Śruti is not merely one among many equal means of cognition. In deep sleep... [the text continues].
(As stated on p. 563:

"Like the statement regarding deep sleep. This is because [the scripture] produces knowledge in the form of Brahman, which is the inner self (*pratyag-bhūta*), and thereby removes the ignorance residing therein.
The meaning is that this is the authoritative proof (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the mantra beginning with "And knowledge" (*vidyāṃ ca*), it was stated that it teaches conjunction (*samuccaya*);

however, he says that this mantra does not actually teach conjunction. Furthermore, the traditional recitation of the mantra has been presented so that it may not be contradicted here; we shall explain all of this in detail later, for everything is auspicious.
"Therefore, let this be so. Although an extension (*atideśa*) was made stating that the meaning of the mantra will be explained later, he nevertheless demonstrates the meaning of the mantra in brief.
It was stated here [in verse 1.26] that "two sciences are proclaimed by the distinction of higher and lower: the higher and the lower."

"Knowledge and ignorance are spoken of here; therein, by the word 'ignorance,' karma is meant, because it culminates in darkness (tamas). By the word 'knowledge,' the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence is meant, because it culminates in the reality (vastu). Now, [the meaning] of the mantra containing the word "together" (saha) is as follows:

He explains the meaning of the latter portion by means of a statement from Manu: "Austerity and knowledge are the supreme means for a Brahmin to attain the highest good; through austerity he destroys impurity, and through knowledge he attains immortality. The meaning of the word "together" (*saha*) here is that [knowledge] is the cause of the highest good in both cases. [This is so] because of ignorance (*avidyayā*).

Regarding the phrase "having crossed over death" (*mṛtyuṃ tīrtvā*), its meaning is as follows: by the word "ignorance" (*avidyā*), your action (*karman*) is meant; through that [knowledge], one destroys death—that is, one destroys impurity—by means of knowledge (*vidyā*).

The meaning of this passage, beginning with "by knowledge one goes to liberation," is as follows: furthermore, there might be an intermediate state, yet you maintain that the qualification for the injunction is the vision of the Self. To show that even this is not tenable, he says: "There is no connection with the self and so forth; it partakes solely in the delusion regarding the innermost Self."

Regarding the objection, "How could an insentient thing proceed toward an injunction such as 'it should be seen'?", this collection of faults has already been stated in the passage, "One should worship the Self alone, which is the world. Thus he says:
"This aforementioned fault [applies] to those whose nature has been refuted," and so forth.
"In this very context [of the passage] 'the Self alone,' it is not stated again here"—
thus have the objections raised by them been shown in the refutation of the system of Bhartṛprapañca. Even though they do not recognize [this] as a fault, it is a fault.
He states that the refutations presented in the Bhāṣya are easy to understand:
"The Bhāṣya has such clearly manifest meaning that it does not depend on a commentary (ṭīkā) at all; therefore, let the remaining meaning here be understood from the very words of the Bhāṣya. Thus.

Having concluded his deliberation, he resumes the subject at hand: "By what is that bondage—which consists of the organs of perception (*graha*) and their objects (*atigraha*)—employed? For the sake of its maintenance, O Yājñavalkya, by whom is it impelled? He said this, even though he was previously a knower of Brahman.

Nevertheless, he states that although the term "person" (puruṣa) is used here, it refers to the ignorant person by virtue of the mark of being the locus of karma: "On account of the sign of being the substratum of action, the ignorant one is understood here."
"And because the current division [of the self] relies upon another division" (p. 565).
This refers to the case where, for this ignorant person who has died due to the exhaustion of his lifespan, his own source [of rebirth] speaks.
The statement that "upon completion [of the body], the vital breath (prāṇa) follows after speech" is easily understood.
Here, he explains that by the words "speech and so forth," the sense organs are not meant;
rather, they refer to those portions of deities such as Agni which were acquired through one's karma for the purpose of experience.

Those very [elements] are denoted by words such as "speech" (vāk) and so forth, yet they are not produced by a person; thus, upon the exhaustion of a person's karma, the deities of fire and the others withdraw their respective portions.
This is what is called "withdrawal" (upasaṃhāra). When the person again assumes a body, the deities [re-enter] the locations within that body.
"Each part deposits its own [nature] for the sake of accomplishing the experience of its respective karma"—

these two *vārtikas* are easily understood. In the phrase "space is the self," the word "self" (*ātman*) refers to the space within the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*), because of the scriptural mention of dissolution into the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*).
And because the dissolution of the Self— denoted by the word "Self"— into that [space] is impossible,

and because the body is the subject of the question as being the material cause of that [Self], he says "of the Self"; for the space within the heart may here be called the "Self" due to its imperishability like space, since it is the object of praise.

"And because of the application of consciousness. Now, one might object: since the soul has the seventeenfold aggregate as its substrate, the question regarding the substrate is not appropriate. This is not sound. (p. 566)

Although the individual soul (jīva) is dependent upon the subtle body (liṅga), nevertheless, because that [subtle body] is directed by its presiding deity and does not grant experience [independently], it is as good as non-existent despite being present; therefore,
the question concerning the locus and objects that serve as the cause of experience is appropriate— this he says:

"Indeed, the organs of speech and so forth, being devoid of a presiding agent, are like laid-down tools; they are not capable of accomplishing the purpose of the person. Where does this person exist when separated from the body and the deities?
Thus [Vasiṣṭha] questioned the best of sages regarding the person's substratum.

He shows the manner of the inquiry with two verses: "Does time attain the nature of a cause? Or does it remain with some essence of its own? Or is it dependent solely on karma? Or is it the lord of the qualities (guṇas)? Or is it likewise [dependent] on the quarters?"
"Let it be said whether [the mind] perceives a continuous stream, emptiness, or destruction.

Regarding the term "cause": the meaning of the phrase "inner ignorance (pratyag-avidyā) together with its appearance by means of some self" is as follows: it is that which is not specified by particular attributes such as "this" or "that."

A certain entity, or rather, that which is itself its own substratum: thus says the Mīmāṃsaka who maintains the doctrine of action (*karmavādī*), the Sāṃkhya who maintains the doctrine of qualities (*guṇavādī*), the Naiyāyika who maintains the doctrine of God (*īśānavādī*),
the astrologer who maintains the doctrine of time (*kālavādī*), and the fatalist who maintains that man and others are merely instruments of fate (*daiva*).
The Lokāyatikas who propound chance, the Yogācāras and others who propound a continuum, and the proponents of emptiness are indeed well known by the term "annihilationists."
The destruction of the soul (*jīva-pradhvaṃsa*) is being discussed, and its proponent would be dependent on both the higher and the lower;

thus, regarding this topic, the previous proponent [is addressed]. The following four verses of the *Vārttika* are easy to understand and are therefore transcribed here. Being moved by the question, he was satisfied.

The Rishi took his hand and, being amazed that he had asked a question not shared by others, said, "For the sake of an extraordinary accomplishment, let it be between us alone. Furthermore, the concealment of knowledge is frequently observed even in the Śruti, and in this case, it was to be between the two of them alone.

"Just as this consciousness existed previously, so shall we two know it hereafter, exactly as you have stated when this question was being addressed in the assembly. If what was spoken by you were not established, then the purpose stated by us would certainly not be accomplished. [This refers to] the knowledge of the prompter.
It was not for the sake of uniqueness that Yājñavalkya departed from the company of people, but rather out of fear;
to this he says "no"—
Yājñavalkya did not say this either out of intimidation by another's speech or in the course of a debate.
"Because no one else speaks [thus] except by way of exclusion (vyatireka)," he says again, providing another reason:
"the remaining ones" (p. 568).

"He answered even the remaining questions by skipping over them in the presence of the assembly; therefore, there can be no cause for fear of his speaking otherwise. Since he answered the question by skipping over it in the presence of the assembly, and since there is no other cause for fear, he [answered] the remaining questions as well in the presence of the assembly.

"He came and explained," so it is said. Alternatively, if he had departed from the assembly and explained even the remaining questions, then there might have been a cause for fear regarding what others would say;
but since that was not the case, considering this to be well-done, the two portions [of the sacrificial fees] departed from Yājñavalkya, having slipped away from the assembly.
Having departed from the person with the people, those two conversed; and whatever they said there to one another after departing, all that the Śruti has recorded out of a desire to do us a favor.
Because he is dependent on karma and other factors, he is not intended here as the self-reliant [Ātman].

"Because it exists within the realm of saṃsāra, the self is not the locus of causes; because it is insentient, the primary cause (pradhāna) and so forth are not accepted as the abode of the person"—this half-verse and the three *vārtikas* are easy to understand. He further states that [the self] is not the locus of karma either: "karma does not know its fruit."

Nor does it have Hiraṇyagarbha as its locus; thus he says: "And there is no connection with him," meaning that its existence does not reside in the Lord, because of the consequence that the scripture would not need to be commenced.

If that were so, one would incur the loss of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done; this is easily understood. Let this [world], presided over by destiny and subject to the power of time, simply proceed with its actions.

Regarding the phrase "if it were a person": its meaning is that [the opponent] maintains that [the self] is dependent upon Indra and other deities, primary karma, and time; this he refutes by stating, "it is not tenable in this way because of insentience," and [he adds] that the previously mentioned fault also applies here in the case of the deity.

Having stated the refutation by assuming [the world] to be insentient (*jaḍatva*), he now states the refutation even if it were non-born (*ajatva*). Having repeated what was already said: "If it is thought that the previously mentioned ritual action directed toward a deity is effective, [then consider this:
whether there is activity or non-activity, if it were always determined by the sovereignty of the deities..."

Because the cause does not exist, there would be no necessity; such is the established position. Furthermore, action alone cannot be the support for the person (*pums*), because it has already been stated by me that [action] is flawed by the defects of insentience and impermanence. This agent must be followed [as the support], just like the self (*ātman*).
"How can there be ritualists who destroy the knowledge of sacrifice along with time and other factors?"—
these two *vārtikas* constitute the form of the [objection] "Is it not action or its fruit?
Having thus stated the refutation for each individual position as well as for the combined position, [the author proceeds to show that] action is primary...
He states this— namely, that time and so forth are determined by those two [knowledge and action] as the motivators of the person:
"Therefore, since it is thus, all factors such as time, destiny, God, and so on, are subordinate to the person's karma."
"Thus, this may be the unsurpassed substratum. Having thus concluded his own position, he proceeds to refute the views of the Cārvākas and others who stand outside the Veda.

Fortuitous chance (*haṭha*), necessity (*yadṛcchā*), and destiny (*niyati*) are not accepted as causes; the terms "fortuitous chance" and "necessity" denote non-existence. It is not possible for intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) to be the initiator [of things], because that would entail the futility of employing specific, determined causes—this is the meaning. Furthermore, the Buddhist position is also not tenable.
He says, "It does not apply," because:
"Due to the non-abiding in a continuum, there is no status as a substratum according to valid cognition. Here, "continuum" refers to the possessor of the continuum (*santānin*);
that which possesses the continuum is consciousness (*vijñāna*), and by means of that, [consciousness] acts as the substratum.

The claim that it is the initiator of its own basis, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), is untenable because consciousness and the other aggregates are momentary and lack stability. He demonstrates this instability as follows: "Karma is not possible in the preceding aggregates because they have already perished."

[Objection: But surely, the preceding aggregate (skandha) transforms into the form of the succeeding aggregate and subsequently perishes; therefore, since the aggregates serve as the substratum, the relationship between action and its fruit is established even in the Vijñānavāda. To this, he replies: "And not here..."
"Because of the subsequent conjunction of the aggregates through transformation," (p.
571) [this is stated] because the theory of transformation is not accepted and because it would entail the consequence of permanence.

The meaning is "of consciousness and so forth. Having raised the objection that action (karma) bestows its fruit even without a substratum, he says: "An uncompleted action and so forth would never result in the fruit of attainment," having thus stated the refutation by accepting [the opponent's premise of] momentariness.

He states that momentariness itself is not tenable for consciousness and so forth: "And there can be no simultaneous existence in one place for birth and destruction due to contradiction. [The opponent objects:
"But even in our view, there exists a noble self distinct from consciousness; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply."
To this he says "no"—
nor is anyone at all accepted as existing apart from the aggregates.
Thinking that "this [treatise] proceeds on the basis of this connection with enjoyment, liberation, and so forth," he thus refutes the Vijñānavāda and introduces the Śūnyavāda:
"And even in the case of emptiness, since this [treatise] is established as not being commenced, there is no commencement of the treatise."

Because it would follow that there is no purpose to be served, because this phenomenal world is perceived in such a way [as having distinctions], and because there is no means of valid cognition for the perception of emptiness [in that manner], this position is untenable. Having thus refuted the view of the proponent of non-difference, he concludes his own position: "Since this is so, therefore it is illogical."
"Karma alone is the support for this person on the ground of saṃsāra, because time and the other factors are subordinate to it. (p. 572)

Therefore, the Śruti itself has declared the primacy of karma alone, [stating]: "From time, fate, the Lord, and so forth; from time and the rest, because they are impelled by that [karma]. This is an elaboration of what preceded. Now, one might object: "If karma does not even exist, how can it have primacy?"
Regarding this, he says:
"The diversity of beings is possible when there is action.
By the word "action," he states that the other two factors are also included; thus he says: "By the word 'action,' knowledge [is also meant]."
The reason for stating that "cultivation (bhāvanā) is called action" is as follows:
the potency of pure action is held to arise through the initiation of the body; therefore, all three of these are designated by the word "action. Having thus deliberated, those two [should act].
For one desiring to go to the next world, free from the flood of defects, they declared that action alone is the support;

and as for what they praised among the aforementioned causes—action alone they praised with reverence among all those mentioned, even though there was no difference in their status as causes. Why [is this so]?
"The term 'pradhāna' (primary) would be a praise of the object of the act of seeing, because its primacy is thus established"—these three *vārtikas* are easy to understand.
Two *vārtikas* establish that primacy; they are written here [as follows]: "Having brought under control Īśvara and the others..."

Since it is observed that the instrument and so forth act as if they were independent in the accomplishment of an action, therefore the primary factor is the action, and by that [action] the performance is carried out. (p. 573)

Since even the Lord and other [factors] do not succeed when they have become subordinate, karma is therefore said to be the primary among them; thus he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "merit" (puṇya):
"Because it is so, therefore, having fallen from this body due to the departure of the deities and so forth..."

"By relying on the predominance of action, one becomes virtuous through virtuous action and sinful through sinful action"— this Vedic statement is to be understood as having scripture alone as its authority.
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa of the fifth [Adhyāya].
The venerable [author] recites the meter in order to establish the connection: "For those being liberated from saṃsāra,
although the destruction of the body and so forth is the same here in saṃsāra, for them there is rebirth therein."

"The absolute destruction of the body and so forth—whatever cause, whether present or absent, would result in this [destruction] for others, that is declared to be the *prayojaka* (the instigating cause). This is the meaning.
Although the destruction of the body and so forth at the time of death is the same for both those liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and those not yet liberated,
nevertheless, the liberated do not undergo the assumption of another body, whereas the bound do. The cause for this, as well as the instrumental cause, must now be stated.
Having stated that the combination of knowledge, action, and prior cognition has been described, he summarizes the point already explained:

"It is certain that action belongs to death, which takes the form of the *graha* (seizers) and *atigraha* (over-seizers). This means that action has been declared to be the cause of *saṃsāra*. Now, he shows the connection [of the next section] by saying, "It is being stated how great the pervasiveness of that action may be. That which is Vedic...
The meaning is that the section concerning the Brāhmaṇas begins in order to explain the transformation of the fruit of that karma.

In that regard, the fruit of karma is twofold; there, the specific form which was pervasive internally has been described in the passage beginning with "He became that fire. Now, for the sake of establishing its external pervasion:

Regarding the commencement of the section on the Brahmins, he says: "The establishment of action is by way of both the general and the particular. The specific arrangement has been stated previously; now, however, the general one is being discussed.

He states that the *Brāhmaṇa* begins now in order to explain the pervasiveness of both [types of karma]: "How great is the pervasiveness in saṃsāra of manifest karma, both in its general and specific aspects? This is what is being described through experience. This is what is meant. He says:

"The extent of the effects of the delusion regarding the true nature of the inner self is here described. The meaning is that everything to be accomplished (sādhya) is said to be nothing but the effect of ignorance (ajñāna).
This is the meaning. He states the purpose of explaining the general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*):

"When this has been correctly stated, nothing remains unsaid. Now, among meritorious deeds, the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) is foremost; and among great sinful deeds, the killing of a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇavadha*).

Regarding the eternality of the Great [Self], he said: "There is nothing superior to the killing of an embryo or the horse-sacrifice among merits and sins. In this manner, there are also statements concerning all actions; how many such are there? To explain what follows from this—that "if this is so, then that occurs"—he says:

Since the effect of an evil deed is limited even elsewhere, it is not mentioned further here; nor is it treated with disregard because of its harmful nature. Furthermore, because the abandonment of that [evil] is established by itself, it is not described here. Thus ends the fruit of the evil deed in this Brāhmaṇa section.

It is not so stated; for since the fruit of that [killing] has been described in the Udgītha Brāhmaṇa and other texts, there is no regard for it there because it results in an undesirable outcome and is therefore something to be shunned.
Thus, the meaning is that among sinful deeds, the killing of a Brāhmaṇa is said to be the greatest, in order to explain this point.

It has been stated that among meritorious deeds, the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) is the greatest; he clarifies its underlying intention: it is because the fruit of the rite called the horse sacrifice is supremely noble.
"The Vedic scriptures and the Smṛtis likewise declare in many places that virtuous action is the means for attaining all human goals without exception. (p. 576)
Because liberation, like heaven and other such goals, shares the common characteristic of being a human purpose (*puruṣārtha*),
there arises a suspicion that it might also be a means for acquiring merit (*puṇya*). Therefore,
this subsequent scriptural passage is commenced in order to dispel that suspicion.
To the question of how doubt is removed in that regard, he says:

even for the king of rituals, the act of sacrifice, though augmented by knowledge, its sphere remains only saṃsāra; it does not extend even slightly toward liberation—thus, even when accompanied by knowledge, [it is so].
The meaning is that the *Brāhmaṇa* begins in order to demonstrate that action (*karman*) indeed has its fruit as its essence.
Now, one might object: "Since transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is the fruit of action, it must be an effect of ignorance (*avidyā*"; to this he replies):
"The union with the true nature of the inner self manifests itself in the form of action and its factors."
And [they claim] that the objects of action and the factors of action are entirely non-existent. Now, in order to purify his own doctrine, he begins a great investigation:
"That which is asserted here by certain people who do not know the true nature of reality..."

"Action devoid of attachment to its fruits should be known as leading to liberation. Now, one might ask: "But action has saṃsāra as its fruit; how can it lead to liberation? To this he says: "Just as poison, curd, and so forth, though causes of bondage, produce results called 'liberation,' such is the analogy accepted here. Just as...
Just as one who has ingested poison, curd, and so forth abandons the natural effect produced by them when combined with mantras and the like,
and undertakes another task; so too does karma that has arisen through its own nature.
The meaning is that, having abandoned the impermanent fruit, one who is engaged in meditation undertakes the eternal liberation; now he establishes the final conclusion:
in order to refute what was stated [by the opponent], it is declared that "this is not correct," for the statement regarding its being "not to be undertaken" [is invalid].
For the sake of practicing the means to that [liberation]: if it is accepted that liberation is something to be undertaken, then it would be as previously stated;

however, this liberation is not something to be undertaken, since its establishment arises from knowledge. Because of the statement "Brahman indeed is all this," even prior to the birth of knowledge, the world is established as having Brahman as its self; therefore, [liberation is not a new undertaking].

The term "jagat" (the world) refers to those in saṃsāra who are subject to the process of liberation. The three *vārtikas* establish that [liberation] arises from non-action (*akriyodbhava*); everything else is easily understood. "If it is maintained that the entity is liberated by itself and bound by another, then effort for the sake of liberation [would be futile]."

"Then it would be fruitful; otherwise, it would not. Now, since it was stated that "its accomplishment arises from the cause of knowledge," does this not mean that liberation is something to be accomplished through knowledge? No, he says:
"Apart from the manifestation of knowledge, there is no causality toward a reality that is already established by itself."
In this world, for whom would [the perception of] reality not be possible, when the obstruction consists merely of ignorance and is constructed by mental activity?
"The fruit arises from knowledge regarding the object to be attained, because [knowledge] is a manifestor, like a lamp. Now, one might object:
"Is it not the case that there is something other than ignorance which brings about liberation—namely, action accompanied by the knowledge that brings about its cessation?
To this, he says:

Furthermore, no Buddha is held to be anything other than liberation apart from the cessation of ignorance; for it is said that "no action is performed here by which [liberation] exists. And because the conventional designation of "liberation" occurs upon the cessation of the ignorance that obstructs liberation, he states that liberation is eternally established and not something to be produced:

"Since liberation for the self is held to be merely the destruction of ignorance, therefore liberation must certainly be eternal as something distinct from that [destruction]. To this, he says: "In that case, it is not the case that the cessation of ignorance results from the combination of knowledge and action."
"There is no concealment of the individual's ignorance (pratyaṅmoha) other than through the excellence of right knowledge;
therefore, there can be no combination of knowledge and action.
He states that liberation is not achievable by action alone through three *vārtikas*, which are transcribed as follows:

Furthermore, because the scope of the power of action is well-known, it is observed even in the world that the effect of action consists of the fourfold set beginning with origination. For origination, acquisition, modification, and refinement are the fruits of action; there is no effect of action other than these. Therefore, [action does not apply here].
Liberation is held to be [the state] among those;
yet, none of these [views] is logically tenable as liberation.
Because the modes such as origination and so forth are associated with impermanence,
it was stated in the passage "and there is nothing other than ignorance" that there is no obstacle to liberation other than ignorance; now, the proof for this is presented.

Regarding the statement "it does not exist," he says: since liberation is accepted as being separated [from bondage] by ignorance alone, no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established for a separation by anything other than that. Thus, he again elaborates upon the previously stated prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): "If [liberation] were perishable and possessed of a fruit, it would belong to the self alone."
"But for that very action, its fruit would have to be substantial;

therefore, through the removal of the previous capacity, another capacity arises due to conjunction with a different entity, as is observed in the case of poison and the like. He refutes this as follows:

"Because no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is possible, this is not so; for speech is like worldly objects. No means of cognition other than scripture (āgama) is accepted regarding what has been stated. Since [the effect] is like poison, curd, and so forth, the statement 'action conjoined with knowledge initiates eternal liberation' would therefore not be well-said. Regarding this point:
The meaning is that there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because even in the case of an example, such [a cause] is absent;
namely, as in the case of poison, curd, and so forth, which exist apart from the stated effects.

"Even for action, there is no [cessation] upon the arising of another effect"—this means even for that which is solitary. Furthermore, by what kind of knowledge do you assert this synthesis: by knowledge of the object, by knowledge of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), or by knowledge free from latent impressions? To this, he says:
The locus whose nature consists in the exclusion of the probandum is indeed non-substantial; however, in that case, knowledge alone would be the substantial basis,
and not that action which depends on causes— this action of yours is of such a kind that this which is a conjunction of actions is not [action at all].

"Regarding the phrase *dhī-hā-samuccayaḥ*: Now, one might object that although the Vedic statement does not teach that liberation is the means [attained] through action—whether combined or uncombined—there nevertheless exists another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this; anticipating this doubt, he says: *sādhyasādhanasaṃbandhaḥ*."

"Based solely on the authority of scripture (*āgama*). Now, one might object: "But there is indeed scripture such as, 'We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal' (RV 8.48.3), and so forth. To this he replies: "And because it is taught as a means to liberation, action is not at all [taught] as such in the Śruti. That passage is a praise of action; for action does not bring about the cessation of ignorance.

It has been stated that "means" (sādhana) refers to that which exists beyond knowledge; this very point is elaborated by means of an illustration: "Liberation for us is the destruction of ignorance; action is not its means, for action does not destroy darkness, just as darkness arising within darkness [cannot do so]."
(581) Objection: Just like action, knowledge also arises from ignorance; therefore, it does not remove ignorance.
To this, he says:

Although knowledge and action both arise from the emergence of ignorance and conform to the identity of the object of cognition, he says "no" [to the claim that they are equal], because there is a distinction: such conformity exists for knowledge, but it does not exist for action.
Karma alone does not transcend ignorance; it merely produces a state of darkness that conforms to the self.

Therefore, it does not destroy knowledge. Knowledge destroys all darkness by its very nature because it is the sole cause for the emergence of the objective reality established in itself, whereas karma does not.

"Because it follows from darkness"—this is the meaning of what has been stated. Now, one might object: "Granted that action does not remove ignorance because it lacks the power of a real entity (*vastubala*), yet ignorance and the rest [of the three] do have that power, since they assume the form of that [Self], just like knowledge. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The triad beginning with ignorance is the reflection of the Inner Self (*pratyagābhāsa*)."
Even if it is maintained that [ignorance] is like knowledge, it is not accepted as existing prior to the arising of knowledge.

This is the meaning: although false knowledge, erroneous knowledge, and doubtful knowledge possess the form of consciousness (*caitanya*) just like the knowledge of Brahman, nevertheless, prior to the arising of knowledge—

Furthermore, the destruction of saṃsāra along with its causes cannot be established through false knowledge and the like alone, because that [false knowledge] lacks objective reality (*vastubala*), whereas this [true knowledge] possesses it.
He concludes the subject under discussion (p.
"Because it does not possess that [causal] nature, it is in no way tenable as a direct cause."
He states that [knowledge] is the means for the removal of ignorance, which obstructs liberation, by way of purification:
"But it is appropriate through a traditional succession when ignorance has been destroyed.
Furthermore, regarding liberation as something to be accomplished by action, does each [action] individually grant liberation, or do all of them together?

Whether by performing [the rite] once, or through repeated application, or by lifelong practice, it destroys the cycle of rebirth; such an option is held to be equal even regarding sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) of one [cow] and so forth.
Whether by means of rites for specific desires (kāmya), or obligatory rites (nitya), or all of them, or by means of Śrauta rites, liberation is thus desired.
Whether by means of the Smṛti-injunctions or by both types of actions,
their threefold alternative should be understood according to the distinction between the primary and the subordinate, for the sake of attaining the fruit of liberation.
If each one individually were to effect liberation— like the oblation of barley, rice, and so forth— then [liberation would be achieved] by any one alone.

Because their purpose has been accomplished, they do not perform anything further; thus, this same ritual procedure applies equally to the offering of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Now, having come together, they all perform the rites for liberation; there is a single impulse for the ladle (*sruva*), as there is for all the rites beginning with the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*).

Because of the unity of the fruit, that [undesirable consequence] would follow; for a different fruit from the fruit of liberation is heard of in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), yet their having liberation as their fruit is neither heard in scripture nor established by any other means.

These [points] are easy to understand. Now, one might object: "Even though rites performed for specific desires have heaven and the like as their fruits, it is possible for them to have liberation as their fruit, just as in the case of the cow-sacrifice (godohana). To this, he says: "That is not logical."

"One is engaged in optional rites (kāmyakarman); for there is no evidence that these have liberation as their fruit. This is the meaning: when, for example, the *godohana* vessel used for the *āpaṇayana* rite—which has cattle as its fruit—is prescribed by relying on heaven as its fruit, it is not so with optional rites.

Regarding the proof that the fruits such as heaven constitute the fruit of liberation: furthermore, if all ritual actions combined were the cause of the fruit of liberation, then the *dharmamīmāṃsā* would have to provide the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the differentiation of those actions; thus he says:

Furthermore, everything stated as the definition of differentiation would become invalid if liberation were produced by all actions acting together. Our notion of the means and the end regarding the next world does not arise from such a statement; nor have I ever heard of action [leading to liberation] from a Vedic text.
The statement "the fruit of liberation is found in some [cases]" is a restatement of what was previously said for the purpose of demonstrating the absence of ritual sentences;
he explains this absence of sentences through three *vārtikas*: "No sacrificial fees go there;
that is attained by knowledge alone," and the mantra "I know."
Through knowledge, one abandons other paths; there is neither diminution nor increase of the inner self through action.
"Its greatness is eternal"—this very point will be declared later as well.

"The world acquired through karma is perishable, but that which is won by knowledge is eternal"—this is a clear statement of the Śruti; therefore, it is not respected by you. Thus, through this commentary on the connection [between verses], there is a synthesis [of the two paths].
Although this has already been refuted previously, he says that it is nevertheless refuted once again here:

"And the conjunction [of the senses] has already been refuted more than once; remembering that, we shall explain it here once more because of the context and for fear of excessive prolixity. Furthermore, cognition does not arise through their coming together.
It dispels the ignorance regarding karma precisely because of the relationship between the goal and the means;

since they do not abide simultaneously in time, and because of their relationship as the proven and the prover, there is no coexistence in a single location— just as in the case of a lion and a ram— and thus there is no conjunction of the two by virtue of their being the proven and the prover.

Granted that there may be a combination; yet, as between the fuel and the fire, provided there is no impairment of their respective capacities, ignorance—which is not in accordance with reality—would be the opposite of knowledge, and thus a combination of these two would be like that of the sun and the moon. This is the meaning of the four Vārtika verses.
He states that for this reason as well, the conjunction [of the two views] is not tenable, as was explained at the beginning of the *Saṃbandhagrantha*:
"The classification [of action] would depend on the object, and likewise, the action depends on the agent;
[the notion of] agency and so forth arises from delusion regarding the Self, for the Self is by its very nature devoid of being a causal factor (*kāraka*). Regarding the Self:
The meaning is that there is a combination [of knowledge and action] because agency and so forth are immutable, because they arise from ignorance, and because self-knowledge is possible.

Furthermore, he establishes the absence of any synthesis by means of an illustration: "Just as a Kṣatriya does not participate in the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice, nor does a Brāhmaṇa who considers himself unworthy;
or as a Videha, freed from doubt and awakened to the realization 'not this, not this,' [does not engage in ritual action]."

Just as one who perceives the body and so forth as the non-Self does not likewise perceive its activity [as the Self], so too, because the ignorant person lacks the qualification for ritual action (*karman*), there is no combination [of knowledge and action]. He says: "Just as a child, lacking discrimination, imagines the nature of an elephant in a clay elephant, so the fool superimposes the body and so forth upon the Self."
"It acts" (viceṣṭate). Again, by means of another illustration, he explains that very same point:
just as one who mistakes a post for a thief flees in fear, so too the Self, deluded, exerts itself by superimposing [attributes] upon itself through the intellect and other faculties.
Now, he establishes the absence of a combination [of knowledge and action] by showing that knowledge is not an auxiliary quality of action, using an illustration:
"Just as the true knowledge of a post is not an auxiliary to running away."
"Similarly, the realization of the true nature of the self is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the injunction for ritual action.
Furthermore, because knowledge of the self consumes karma, it does not possess the status of an auxiliary; thus he says:
"For that which follows its own nature in accordance with something else is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to that [other thing]."
It might be argued that "the quality does not arise from the primary cause"; the meaning of "from the primary cause" (*pradhānāt*) here is "because the primary cause exists."
(587) Now, it might be argued: "Knowledge removes ignorance; but it does not remove it, because even in one who possesses knowledge, its effects are observed. To this, he says:

Since knowledge itself cannot be established without first dispelling ignorance, it follows that when ignorance ceases, its effect— the aggregate of causal factors— also ceases. He states that for an action devoid of causal factors,
knowledge cannot be a subordinate quality (guṇa):
Knowledge and action belong to different classes; how could they be performed together?

Because their causes, natures, and effects are mutually contradictory like light and darkness, there is no conjunction of knowledge and action; thus, through simultaneous engagement, action is destroyed.

Ignorance, which bears the form of an agent, and scriptural knowledge are incompatible; therefore, the conjunction of knowledge and action is in no way possible, because darkness is destroyed by knowledge alone. Since action has no role in that which is not an effect, what fruit could it have? It is not authoritative [in this regard].

"In the case of the direct attainment of liberation through the combination of knowledge and action, [liberation] comes from knowledge alone because of the destruction of darkness"— these [statements] are easy to understand. He states the authoritative proof that even action alone is a means to liberation:
Apart from [the means of knowledge for] origination and so forth, no such means of knowledge is established for ritual action (*karman*) either, for the sake of the cessation of saṃsāra.

Thus [it is argued]. He states that the absence of proof (*mānābhāva*) is unestablished: "Since there is always a proof, for ritual action (*karman*) is enjoined everywhere; and nothing possessing an origin and so forth has its fruit directly heard therein, nor is external efficacy (*sāmarthya*) conceivable in that regard, as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice."

Liberation arises from the emergence of fruits such as birth and so forth; therefore, that fruit [liberation] exists. Since a human goal (puruṣārtha) is present as a fruit, an injunction for obligatory rites (nitya-karma) is not logically possible [if liberation were the sole goal]; rather, it is only when that [human goal] exists that the injunction for obligatory rites is appropriate.
For those who act with prior reflection toward these obligatory rites, which consist of the nature of suffering, [would not engage in them].

"The [injunctions] would not apply to men if there were no fruit resulting from them"—these *vārtikas* support the view that obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) lead to liberation and are easy to understand;
however, this [author] refutes them, stating: "It is not so, because no fruit whatsoever is obtained from the scriptural statement."
"Because there is no mention of their capacity [to produce] a fruit, there is nothing whatsoever named 'fruit' [in this case]. This is the meaning:

since even other fruits besides liberation are not conceivable for obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) based on the support of passages such as "as long as one lives," how much less could liberation be [the fruit], given that there is no mention of such a capacity for obligatory rites?
Because no words are heard that establish liberation as the fruit [of these rites],

and because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) indicating that liberation is the fruit of any other specific obligatory rite (*niyata-karman*), it follows by implication (*arthāpatti*) that liberation cannot be the fruit of obligatory rites, for otherwise their [transient] results would not perish.
p.

589) Now, if there is the insistence that liberation is the fruit of the two types of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) even in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says in response: "Even if it is obtained through the result of a means of valid cognition, an abundance [of merit] is not to be rejected."
"That which lacks a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not to be accepted as a real entity, even if it is merely a statement.

Furthermore, he says that this [claim] is not to be accepted because the idea that liberation is the fruit of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) is merely a product of imagination: "And this postulation of a fruit is stated by you solely on the basis of human intention (*puruṣāśaya*)."

If it is argued that, having considered my own conjecture, one may accept this very meaning by means of such scriptural statements as "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), [the author] says "no": "Valid cognition independent of anything else is the deliverer of the object to be known"; and the absence of sin (*pratyavāya*) and so forth is the fruit of the obligatory rite (*nitya*).

The arrangement of ritual action is conceived for that purpose; therefore, liberation results from obligatory (*nitya*) action because one’s aim is fulfilled by that alone. There is no evidence for a connection between the injunction of obligatory action and the fruit of liberation; rather, it follows from the principle of "otherwise inexplicability" (*anyathānupapatti*).
If a fruit were to be postulated for this [daily rite] as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice, why would the Viśvajit-nyāya not apply?

Furthermore, like the optional Agnihotra, it would follow that the obligatory rite would also become optional because of its connection with a fruit. If it is argued that the exit [from the householder's life] is considered to be the obligatory fruit of this [rite], [we reply: no.
If liberation is accepted as the fruit [of the path], it must be admitted to be eternal; otherwise, because the promised goal would be lost, this [position] is not tenable either.

The fact that [the inquiry] is being commenced is due to the very nature of reasoning as something directed inward; or rather, it is commenced by way of expression, for action is the means to that fruit which is liberation, and [liberation] is to be tasted.
"Let the distinction regarding its being an effect be stated by you, since liberation is distinct from heaven and the like due to its imperishability and so forth; for therein lies fulfillment.
These [points] are easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "therein lies no fulfillment for you in liberation," this is the meaning:
there is no fulfillment for you in liberation; that is, there is no happiness in liberations.
Alternatively, "it is accomplished" means that liberation itself is what you intend as happiness; it is not accomplished because of the absence of liberation.

Now, if it is argued that liberation is a product of the non-eternal activity [of knowledge] by way of metaphorical designation, just like the product of [ordinary] cognition, this is not accepted. Liberation is said to be the effect of knowledge because its function is the destruction of ignorance; it is called a "product" only figuratively.

Since that [obstruction] does not exist, there is no lack of recognition of an obstruction to action; nor is there a function of destroying ignorance regarding action. Therefore, liberation is not the effect of action even figuratively.
Furthermore, no other obstruction besides ignorance is accepted as that which must be removed for the sake of liberation.

This [ignorance] is turned back by action; for in the world, the destruction of opposing factors is seen through an opposing factor, as in the case of darkness and light. If it is argued that action is not opposed to ignorance, and that it is rather this very ignorance which destroys action—
(591) Action never destroys action because they are not contradictory; ignorance is the non-manifestation [of knowledge], while awakening is the manifestation of the Self.
This relationship of the proven and the prover is possible between those two due to their mutual opposition; however,
ignorance and karma do not possess mutually contradictory properties,
and therefore this relationship of the sublated and the sublator is not applicable to them— these are the points.

[These are] easy to understand. Now, it may be argued that the power of knowledge to remove karma is not established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), nor is it observed; to this he says:
"If [it is argued] that the capacity of karma is observed to consist in the removal of ignorance," and he refutes this as follows:
"Because ignorance is destroyed by knowledge through direct perception, that [scriptural] statement is untrue.
He establishes this point by means of an illustration: "For when the husk is removed from the grain of rice by threshing, [the result] is indeed directly perceived."

By implication, you consider that the accomplishment of rites such as the *agnihotra* is possible [for the ignorant]; likewise here, since [the Self] is directly perceived through awakening, the efficacy of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) lies in the destruction of ignorance regarding the Inner Self (*pratyagajñāna*). Therefore, it is not logical for you to forcibly assume that knowledge is destroyed by them.
Thus, the notion that obligatory ritual (*nityakarman*) is either liberation itself or the cause of it has been refuted.

Previously, regarding the combination of meditation and knowledge, if the inclusion of ritual action is desired, then the statement that there is indeed a combination of actions [is supported] by authoritative knowledge as well.
(592) Having understood that there is a combination of actions, one performs them; likewise, there might also be a combination of action with the knowledge of Brahman. To this, he says:

That knowledge which is not in conflict with ritual actions— that which leads to the understanding of the reality of the deities and their substances— should be combined [with action], but not that which is opposed to ritual action. Regarding the production of liberation through obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), and regarding the adoption of renunciation (*nivṛtti*) for the purpose of removing the self that acts as an obstacle to liberation:

It has been stated that it is impossible to postulate a capacity not observed in debate; now, regarding the capacity that must be postulated, he says: "If a capacity not observed [in other cases] were to be postulated for eternal rites, it would contradict your own position."

Or rather, what is the use of [postulating] actions, since that which is devoid of arising and so forth is neither a produced nor a producing entity? A fruit such as that—which is not a substance, quality, or action—is merely imagined for eternal action; let such a fruit be postulated here in such a way that it accords with reason.

If one must necessarily postulate a motive for human activity, it is logical to postulate that the fruit exists only in those things characterized by origination and so forth; for the justification of the injunctions regarding ritual action is also exhausted therein. Thus he says: "And because of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), [the result] is in that very [place]."
Since there is no capacity [for action] due to the exhaustion [of the self] through the conceptualization of liberation, therefore the conceptualization of liberation is not tenable.

In order to support the point that one infers liberation as the fruit of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) accompanied by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the proponent demonstrates the logic of elimination (*pāriśeṣyanyāya*) in two *vārtikas* regarding the function of obligatory rite: [The two vārtikas follow: "Obligatory rite has no other fruit; for it is not possible for it to have heaven as its fruit, since it is performed without desire for results. Nor can it have the destruction of sin as its fruit, because it is not connected with any specific purpose [for such destruction]. Therefore, by the method of elimination, liberation alone remains as its fruit. [And: "Since there is no other fruit for obligatory rite, and since it is impossible for it to have heaven as its fruit due to its being performed without desire for results, and since it cannot have the destruction of sin as its fruit because it lacks a connection to a specific purpose, therefore, by the method of elimination, liberation alone is established as its fruit."
By resorting to the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is logical to postulate liberation, since no other [result] is possible;
for the fruit of liberation is that which one draws into a circle while wandering through that region for thirty-two days and nights with ashes.
