The sun is indeed this vast body of the cosmic man (Vairāja), the cause of the divine forms; let it lead these living beings to the accomplishment of their enjoyments in this region. Furthermore, the pervasion of the deities beginning with Agni is considered to extend beyond the world.

Devoid of light and shunned by all living beings, it encircles the world twice the size of the earth as previously measured. The nature of the Lokāloka mountain is devoid of all living beings; the ocean is twice the size of the earth.

Beyond this, those wise ones learned in the Purāṇas say that there stands the Ghanoda ocean; beyond that, the shell of the cosmic egg extends on all sides. These [oceans] exist within the Egg of Brahmā, and therein the ocean is heard of; by that [author], this [opinion] has been refuted.
To this he says: "Immediately after the earth, the ocean is directly heard [mentioned] in the Veda."
594) Therefore, in the Purāṇa, when there is a contradiction, it is the Smṛti that is sublated.
[Objection: But is this not for the purpose of describing the path for exiting from the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) for those who have performed the Aśvamedha sacrifice?
An objection is raised: "How is it that this measurement of the universe's dimensions, which is irrelevant to the context, is described by the Śruti? To this, he replies:
"This [text] has proceeded for the purpose of explaining [the fruit]; the fruit of performing the Aśvamedha sacrifice is as follows:"

"It can be stated by means of the measurement of Lokāloka and so forth. The meaning is that since it is impossible to describe the path without describing the structure of the universe (*bhuvanakośa*), that description was provided; and he states that it was also done for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*).

The statement regarding the dimensions of the effects, such as the worlds and the non-worlds, follows from the desire to describe the activity of meditation according to the aforementioned measurements. He reiterates this very point with two *vārtikas* in order to explain the path:

Indeed, this world exists with the aforementioned dimensions, pervaded by the light of the sun; beyond that world, however, lies the Virāj in a state of forgetfulness, and emerging from that world, the earth stands double its size.
And the ocean, twice as large on all sides, stands surrounding the earth.
Thus [it is said]. Now he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "as far as that" (*tadyāvatī*): "Having crossed which ocean, what else is there beyond it?"

Now, an illustrative statement is made regarding that which is to be destroyed: by implication, the space situated within the junction of its skull-halves is [the object of comparison], insofar as it is limited in extent; such is the illustrative statement used here.
"By this [verse], the Śruti is made manifest"—this is an elaboration of what preceded.

The meaning of the phrase "by implication" (*sāmarthyāt*) is as follows: because it is impossible for anything else of such a dimension to exist apart from the opening in the shell of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍakapāla*). Therefore, having pervaded the interior, he leads the Pārikṣitas—who have attained the nature of consciousness (*cittya-ātmatva*)—through that very [opening].
Regarding this phrase "the totality and the individuality," which is easy to understand, he says that the Virāṭ and the Sūtrātman are here expressed by the word *suparṇa*.
He states: "In this context, the conscious Self (*cityātmā*) is the *suvarṇa*, or else the Solar Self (*ādityātmā*) is meant. He provides the reason for this:
Since they have reached this region not by the path described as beginning with the sun and so forth,

but rather having gone to the world of Brahmā by way of the path starting with light (arcis), they possess the capacity for guidance outside the cosmic egg for those who have reached this region in the vicinity of the egg.
The meaning is that it occurs only in those two.

Thus, having caused all the Pārikṣitas to emerge from the cosmic egg by way of the open sky, Agni-Indra bestowed them upon Vāyu, who exists in a subtle form; this is easily understood. He explains the meaning of the word "Agni" as follows: "Aśvamedha... [and so forth].
"Prior to the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), the deity Agni is spoken of here.
He explains the meaning of the word *apūrva*:
"And this which has been described here as the unprecedented (*apūrva*) is an envelopment by air.

The meaning is that the *apūrva* consists of the nature of air; for this very reason, he states that air itself is the *apūrva*: "Therefore, the *apūrva* is considered to be the manifestation of the body of air itself. To them...
He states that the fruit of the *apūrva* is being described by the passage beginning with "vāyuḥ" (the wind), saying: "Immediately thereafter, the effect of the *apūrva* is now pointed out;
having taken up those sons of Parikṣit and having made them equal in essence to Vāyu, he caused them to go there."

This narrative, which has proceeded by proclaiming the unprecedented fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, concerns those performers of the horse-sacrifice who existed in the past— those whose sole form was their vital breath (prāṇa) and who, having departed from here, abide there; it tells how the one whose self is wind (Vāyvātman) caused them to attain the state of both the collective and the individual.
"This [section] has been completed without remainder"—thus [the commentator] states that these [verses] are indeed easy to understand.
Now, the Śruti itself has uttered the remainder of the question regarding the meaning of "Thus you purify this very Vāyu," and so forth: "He [purified] Vāyu alone."
"The Gandharva praised him, being greatly amazed. Thus ends this narrative that was previously introduced by the introductory account; it is concluded here without remainder. (p. 597)

It has been stated merely that he caused those who had performed the horse sacrifice in former times to go to where they were; however, the specific detail as to where those performers of the ancient horse sacrifices resided was not known. This specific detail is now declared by the Śruti: "Vāyu is with distinction."

This is the meaning. Here he states the reason: "Because wind has gone outside, and no other deity is found outside; therefore, wind is the greatest here in this world. Since wind alone is the greatest, it is for this reason that wind alone is spoken of by the Śruti—this is the meaning.

Therefore, he says that air alone consists of both the collective (samaṣṭi) and the individual (vyaṣṭi): "Since this is so, therefore the ignorant one [thinks] that air alone—and nothing else—is the individual and the collective, thus [saying] 'it breathes within the cosmic egg'. This refers to its pervasion outside the cosmic egg.
It has been stated that there is the collective whole (*samaṣṭi*), internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*), and the individual (*vyaṣṭi*); now he states another point:
"Pervasion in a specific form is called the individual (*vyaṣṭi*), and as a generality it is the collective whole (*samaṣṭi*);
thus the wind itself exists in two ways. [Objection: But is there not something other than the wind [that constitutes these]?
If it is argued that [the self] consists of both the universal and the particular, he says "no":
"In this world of moving and unmoving things, nothing whatsoever is perceived as having the nature of either a universal or a particular; let that very wind be observed [as an example]."
Because of the restrictive emphasis "only air," this meaning is understood; thus he says:
"There is no connection of any other entity with both the universal and the particular, [for that entity] is only air."
"It is made [to have] a universal application. Now, one might object that the particle *eva* serves to exclude connection (*yogavyavaccheda*).

To this he says: "In the case of excluding connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), this would be a praise of the horse-sacrifice and the like; however, it is not the exclusion of non-difference (*abhedavyavaccheda*)—such excellence is what is intended. [This refers to] ritual action accompanied by knowledge, such as the horse-sacrifice and so forth.

He concludes by stating that this fruit was spoken of by the Brahmin: "This majesty, characterized by both the collective and the individual, of the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha) has been revealed by the Śruti through the power of knowledge. He then explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "beyond death again" (apa punarmṛtyu):
"He who has taken refuge in the Vāyu as the Self, which consists of both the collective and the individual, destroys death;
he attains the Self, which is beyond death. This concludes the third Brāhmaṇa of the fifth [Adhyāya].
Having first followed the narrative sequence, he explains the meaning of the subsequent Brāhmaṇa:
"The entire effect of the non-realization of the identity [of Brahman] has been stated; now, for the destruction of that root, the subsequent portion of the text is introduced. Now...
He explains the meaning of the Muṣastabrāhmaṇa with two Vārttikas on page 599, preceded by a recitation of the context [of the preceding section]: "Impelled by merit and demerit..."

Bound by the fetters of the senses and their objects, that one of deluded intellect who wanders incessantly from Brahma down to a stationary post— this very person is described as "liberated" when he is impelled toward the supreme excellence of merit; thus, the subsequent text concerning the seeker of liberation and the indestructible is introduced for the cognizer to understand.

If it be argued that the transmigrating being is described as being joined with primordial ignorance (*avidyā*), action (*karman*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), such that the cycle of transmigration consists precisely of the fruits of action, then [the answer is: now, the referent of the term *tvaṃ* (you)—who desires liberation and upon whom the entire cycle of transmigration has been superimposed by way of the witness (*sākṣin*) of the knower—is addressed; thus, "Then Uṣasta... and so forth.
In this context, the meaning is "it is distinguished. He states the reason for this distinction:

"Since its existence is established as being distinct from the body, senses, mind, intellect, and sensations, one strives for its liberation. Now, [one might ask: is it not for the sake of distinguishing the subject (*pramātṛ*) itself?

Regarding the objection that [the self] begins with the Brahmin caste, he says "no": for those whose [existence] is understood from scripture as connected to a future world, the undertaking of such a path (tātpadisa) is indeed already established for them. [This refers to one who is] distinct from the gross body.

The meaning is that in the *karmakāṇḍa*, the subject (*pramātṛ*) established as having the form of an agent and so forth is indeed [unreal]. Therefore, he states that the commencement of the *brāhmaṇa* (the *jñānakāṇḍa*) is precisely for the sake of determining its true purpose:
"Prior to the establishment of the self as an agent, because of its non-difference from the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties... (p. 600)

The meaning is this: whereas the witness-self (sākṣyātmā) was previously described here as the seer of the agent and so forth, it is now defined as the seer in its capacity as the qualified candidate for knowledge (vidyādhikāritva). It is being considered who is the fit subject (viṣaya) for the knowledge of Brahman; for once the subject is determined, the instruction becomes purposeful.

This is an elaboration of what was stated previously. Having raised the alternative— whether the instruction regarding Brahman is for one who is already Brahman or for one who is not Brahman— and having stated the refutation in both cases,
[the author] proceeds to establish that the instruction concerning the nature of Brahman is given to one who is already Brahman by innate nature, being the very Self.
Regarding the beginning of the Brahmana, this is what is stated; it is set forth by means of three Vārttikas, which are now transcribed.
Whether the instruction would be for one who is already a Brahman, or for one who is not a Brahman:

since the status of being a Brahman is established by its own nature, it would be useless in the case of a Brahman; for by even a hundred instructions, his status as a Brahman can never be produced, because he is a Brahman by virtue of his own inherent nature. Therefore, [the instruction] does not apply to a Brahman.
It is maintained that because the true nature of everything is oneness with the Self, Brahman is not found here;
rather, it is said [to be attained] for the purpose of eliminating the suspicion of any distinction between the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) and the Lord (īśvara).

By the phrase "in order to prevent the doubt regarding the distinction between the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) and the Lord (īśvara)," it is indicated that Brahman itself, as conditioned by ignorance (avidyā), is the fit object for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā). Having thus stated the connection (saṃgati), the explanation of the meaning of the words [follows].
p.
601) By the word "that" (*yat*), the specification (*viśeṣa*) is intended to be indicated;
for since the particular is not cognized through the cognition of the mere universal (*sāmānyamātra*), it is that [which is specified].
The meaning is that from that [word], there is the cognition of the general (sāmānya) and not the cognition of the particular (viśeṣa), which denotes the qualified (viśeṣya).

He states that everything beginning with "directly" (sākṣāt) and ending with "the innermost of all" (sarvāntara) is a qualifier of the referent of the pronoun (yacchabda): "everything beginning with 'directly'."
Its specific distinction is stated as follows: "Because it brings about the cognition of a qualified self, like a blue jewel or a blue lotus.
The meaning is that this applies because the words denoting it bring about the cognition of a qualified self. [The opponent objects:
"But [the quality of] being 'directly' and so forth is independent; it is not a qualifier of the word-meaning. [The author] says: "No."
Furthermore, through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words beginning with "that which" (*yat*),

the relationship of qualifier and qualified is determined here by the Vedic text itself. He states that a perceptible object is denoted directly by the word, using the expression "directly" (*sākṣāt*).

Anticipating the objection that "an object is said to be directly perceived" might imply mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), [the author] states: "because its apprehension by the mind is excluded by the phrase 'not from sight'. Regarding that which was stated by the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*)—namely, that the object denoted by the term is perceptible—the following objection is raised: that the mind is that [perceiving agent].

The meaning is that the term "immediate" (*aparokṣāt*) is stated in the Veda in order to exclude the mind from being [considered] a means of direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*). Alternatively, it means "directly" (*sākṣāt*).

Specifically, because the triad known as the seer, the seeing, and the seen is commonly encountered in the world— since the perceptibility of these three is well-established— he speaks in order to exclude that [ordinary state],
saying "from the seer and the seeing," and he explains the meaning of this term:

Alternatively, there is the following alternative [view] to be stated later: since the term "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is a qualification when [the suffix] *draṣṭṛ* is applied, the word "immediately perceived" (*aparokṣa*) is used in order to exclude that [possibility]. This is because of the traditional rule (Pāṇini 5.2.91): "The suffix *tṛc* is used after a verbal root meaning 'to see' when it refers to one's own self (*svātman*)."

The meaning is that from the word *sākṣāt*, the agent of seeing (*darśanakartā*) is obtained; to exclude that, the term *aparokṣāt* is stated. Alternatively, from *sākṣāt* [meaning] "from seeing," the triad consisting of the seer, the act of seeing, and the object seen is obtained, as these three exist in the world.

Since [the term] "perceptibility" (pratyakṣatva) is already well-established, he states the following in order to exclude that [meaning]: "In the attainment of the object by the seer, the seeing, and the seen, because of the specific qualification of the proponent, it is called 'immediate' (aparokṣa) and so forth for the purpose of negating [that common usage], as in the world."

For the purpose of ceasing the object consisting of the conflation of the seer, the seeing, and the seen, the words [of the scripture] are for the sake of grasping the non-differentiated reality; this was stated as the result of the previous negation of proliferation— that it is "for the sake of grasping the non-differentiated reality"— and that very point he now clarifies.
By negating the conflation of the seer, the seeing, and the object seen, mere vision (dṛṣṭimātra), established by itself, becomes the result of the qualification. (p. 603)

He demonstrates the pointlessness of the term "Brahman": if that which is characterized as previously described were indeed one, of a single nature, non-dual, and yet [also] with duality, then for the reason stated it would not be so; therefore, in order to establish duality, this [term] "Brahman" is qualified.
He explains the meaning of the term *brahman*:
"That which is a reality neither excluded nor followed by anything else is called *brahman*.
This refers to the qualification of the word-meaning (*padārtha*). He says "no," [refuting that], regarding the words beginning with "that which" (*yat*) and so forth.

"Through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the relationship of qualifier and qualified is determined here by the direct statement (*śruti*) itself. He says that the perceptible object is denoted directly by the word; as to why it is qualified by the word "Self" (*ātman*), he replies:

This [body] has attained what is not the goal of man, provided that it were not the Self itself; therefore, for the sake of the meaning of the nature of the Self, the term "Self" is thus specified as the qualified object. Now, one might object: since the Self is distinguished from other selves and from the insentient, then that which is delimited by the feet and so forth— [The text continues: ...is merely a portion of the Self. To this we reply: No, because the Self is not perceived as such. For the Self is not perceived as being limited by the feet and so forth, in the way that a cloth is perceived to be limited by its parts. Furthermore, the Self is not perceived as something distinct from the feet and so forth, in the manner that a pot is perceived as distinct from its parts. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. Moreover, the Self is not perceived as something separate from the feet and so forth, like a horse is perceived as separate from a cow. Consequently, the Self is not a part of the body. Furthermore, the Self is not perceived as something distinct from the feet and so forth, like a forest is perceived as distinct from its trees. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. Additionally, the Self is not perceived as something different from the feet and so forth, like a quality is perceived as different from its substance. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. Furthermore, the Self is not perceived as something distinct from the feet and so forth, like a universal is perceived as distinct from its particulars. Hence, the Self is not a part of the body. Moreover, the Self is not perceived as something separate from the feet and so forth, like a whole is perceived as separate from its components. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. Finally, the Self is not perceived as something distinct from the feet and so forth, like a cause is perceived as distinct from its effects. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. And yet, the Self is not perceived as something different from the feet and so forth, like a knower is perceived as different from the known. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. Furthermore, the Self is not perceived as something separate from the feet and so forth, like a seer is perceived as separate from the seen. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. Moreover, the Self is not perceived as something distinct from the feet and so forth, like a hearer is perceived as distinct from the heard. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. And yet, the Self is not perceived as something different from the feet and so forth, like a smeller is perceived as different from the smelled. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. Furthermore, the Self is not perceived as something separate from the feet and so forth, like a taster is perceived as separate from the tasted. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. Moreover, the Self is not perceived as something distinct from the feet and so forth, like a thinker is perceived as distinct from the thought. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. And yet, the Self is not perceived as something different from the feet and so forth, like an agent is perceived as different from the action. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. Furthermore, the Self is not perceived as something separate from the feet and so forth, like a knower of the field is perceived as separate from the field. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. Moreover, the Self is not perceived as something distinct from the feet and so forth, like a witness is perceived as distinct from the witnessed. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. And yet, the Self is not perceived as something different from the feet and so forth, like a liberated one is perceived as different from the bound. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. Furthermore, the Self is not perceived as something separate from the feet and so forth, like the supreme Self is perceived as separate from the individual self. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. Moreover, the Self is not perceived as something distinct from the feet and so forth, like Brahman is perceived as distinct from the world. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. And yet, the Self is not perceived as something different from the feet and so forth, like the absolute is perceived as different from the relative. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. Furthermore, the Self is not perceived as something separate from the feet and so forth, like the unconditioned is perceived as separate from the conditioned. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. Moreover, the Self is not perceived as something distinct from the feet and so forth, like the eternal is perceived as distinct from the transient. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. And yet, the Self is not perceived as something different from the feet and so forth, like the infinite is perceived as different from the finite. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. Furthermore, the Self is not perceived as something separate from the feet and so forth, like the unborn is perceived as separate from the born. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. Moreover, the Self is not perceived as something distinct from the feet and so forth, like the undecaying is perceived as distinct from the decaying. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. And yet, the Self is not perceived as something different from the feet and so forth, like the immortal is perceived as different from the mortal. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. Furthermore, the Self is not perceived as something separate from the feet and so forth, like the fearless is perceived as separate from the fearful. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. Moreover, the Self is not perceived as something distinct from the feet and so forth, like the sorrowless is perceived as distinct from the sorrowful. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. And yet, the Self is not perceived as something different from the feet and so forth, like the desireless is perceived as different from the desiring. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. Furthermore, the Self is not perceived as something separate from the feet and so forth, like the tranquil is perceived as separate from the agitated. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. Moreover, the Self is not perceived as something distinct from the feet and so forth, like the stainless is perceived as distinct from the stained. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. And yet, the Self is not perceived as something different from the feet and so forth, like the pure is perceived as different from the impure. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. Furthermore, the Self is not perceived as something separate from the feet and so forth, like the enlightened is perceived as separate from the ignorant. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. Moreover, the Self is not perceived as something distinct from the feet and so forth, like the awakened is perceived as distinct from the sleeping. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. And yet, the Self is not perceived as something different from the feet and so forth, like the liberated is perceived as different from the bound. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. Furthermore, the Self is not perceived as something separate from the feet and so forth, like the released is perceived as separate from the fettered. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. Moreover, the Self is not perceived as something distinct from the feet and so forth, like the emancipated is perceived as distinct from the imprisoned. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. And yet, the Self is not perceived as something different from the feet and so forth, like the free is perceived as different from the enslaved. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. Furthermore, the Self is not perceived as something separate from the feet and so forth, like the independent is perceived as separate from the dependent. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. Moreover, the Self is not perceived as something distinct from the feet and so forth, like the sovereign is perceived as distinct from the subject. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. And yet, the Self is not perceived as something different from the feet and so forth, like the master is perceived as different from the servant. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. Furthermore, the Self is not perceived as something separate from the feet and so forth, like the lord is perceived as separate from the subordinate. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. Moreover, the Self is not perceived as something distinct from the feet and so forth, like the ruler is perceived as distinct from the ruled. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. And yet, the Self is not perceived as something different from the feet and so forth, like the governor is perceived as different from the governed. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. Furthermore, the Self is not perceived as something separate from the feet and so forth, like the protector is perceived as separate from the protected. Thus, the Self is not a part of the body. Moreover, the Self is not perceived as something distinct from the feet and so forth, like the guardian is perceived as distinct from the guarded. Therefore, the Self is not a part of the body. And yet, the Self is not perceived as something different from the feet and so forth, like the s
He says it is "attained": not overwhelmed by a second object, whether of the same class or of a different class;
like the person (*puruṣa*) in the Sāṃkhya doctrine, that [consciousness] is attained because of the perception of multiplicity.

Thus [it is said]. To provide a refutation of this, he states the following response: "Therefore, for the purpose of negating that, there is the declaration 'the innermost of all'. If it is argued that even in being the innermost of all there is still limitation, he says "no": "How can that object which is the innermost of all be said to be manifold? In this regard:
He states the reason:
"Because those things fashioned from serpents and so forth, like a garland, have as their sole form the individual self (pratyagātman) alone.
He establishes its status as being within all with a half-verse and a commentary (*vārtika*), by way of restricting [the inquiry] to the innermost reality.

No further meaning remains for one who has realized the nature of the immediate [Self], because the Self is the innermost of all, being non-deviating with respect to all things—whether they consist of existence or non-existence.
He states another interpretation of the passage beginning with "That which... as follows:

"That Brahman which is distinguished here by being both immediate and non-mediated," "having grasped that which is within all, [it is] the connection with the inner self"— the latter two *vārtikas* are an elaboration of this, as is the word "immediately" (*sākṣāt*).
The two qualities—being non-remote (avyavahita) and being non-figurative (agauṇa)—are possible only in the Inner Self (pratyak);

nevertheless, Brahman is qualified by those two. Likewise, although being the innermost of all (sarvāntaratva) might seem impossible for Brahman because it is the cause of everything, nevertheless, [it is so] because of the Self (ātman).
"It is distinguished. Thus, by means of this inversion, he demonstrates the fruit of the qualification:
"Therefore, since there is a single sentence [comprising] the two entities known as Brahman and the Self..."

"By means of the cognition of duality and association, the full reality is perceived. Thus, he states another interpretation of the verse beginning with "kṣaya" (destruction), namely: "If there were a direct conjunction of [the words] beginning with 'sākṣāt' as qualifiers with a single substantive."
"Mutually independent of one another" means that the entire collection of objects, such as "directly" and so forth, is both the qualifier and the qualified of everything. Now,
[the author explains] the manner in which a sentence conveys its own meaning and its result.

He demonstrates this with four verses along with their commentary: "Because they terminate in a single object and because they conform to one another's meanings, all qualifiers— such as 'directly' and so forth— qualify [the object], just like the word 'lotus' and others, once they have taken up their own respective qualificands."
Indeed, because it excludes its own contradictory objects through mutual opposition,
and because it obstructs various associations by way of the path of the ocean-like absorption of its own object,
the wisdom regarding the true nature of the Inner Self— by its very birth— destroys the darkness that is the cause of duality and attains what is already attained by itself.

The word "meya" (the object of cognition) is heard [in the compound]; because of the statement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) based on their form, there exists the relationship of qualifier and qualified through the process of the indicated and the indicator; therefore, one arrives at the meaning as previously described.
Because it is by way of not abandoning one's own welfare, the three specific phrases mentioned above on page 606 should be understood as again constituting the threefold meaning of the sentence.

He says: "If it were for all purposes (sarvārtham), then [the word] 'directly' (sākṣāt) would be a qualification; or else, it would end with 'immediate perception' (aparokṣa), or it would end with 'Brahman' (brahma) for the subsequent [case]. This refers to the first position.
The word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is the qualifier itself, while everything else is the qualificand.

In the second alternative, the entire complex "Brahman, the Self, and the innermost of all" (*brahmātma-sarvāntara*) is the qualificand; in the final alternative, the two complexes "the Self and the innermost of all" (*ātma-sarvāntarau*) are the qualificands. Thus, the sentence has multiple meanings.
Having thus shown them, he now demonstrates the position to be accepted:
that which is both direct and indirect [knowledge] of Brahman through its qualifiers,
from the sentence, from the connection with Brahmā and others, and from the basis of anything other than those— surely these are the two positions.
To the question, "How can that which is separated by Brahman be described as 'directly' (sākṣāt)? he states the meaning of this qualification:
because Brahman has the nature of pure inwardness (pratyag-mātra-svabhāvatva), there is no separation whatsoever from it; thus, whatever is seen as unseparated [from the Self] is directly perceived.

He states that because the word "immediate" (*aparokṣāt*) is non-figurative and its meaning is possible only in reference to Brahman, Brahman alone is the substantive qualified by the term "immediate": "They declare Brahman, which is neither excluded nor inclusive, to be immediate and non-figurative."
"It would be of such a nature and not otherwise in any way.
607) Now, one might ask: since the manifold world of duality exists, how can Brahman be something that is neither excluded from nor included within it? To this, he says:
"By the negation of everything within the self, consciousness is non-dual in the self. Now, one might object:

"If the non-self entity established by perception and other means is to be negated, then the self too must likewise be negated. Anticipating this, he says the second half [of the verse]: "But negation is not intended without having reached that which is other [than the self]."
Since [it is argued that] Brahman is neither excluded from nor followed by anything else, one might ask: "By what concomitance [is it known]?
To this, he says:
"The effect-entity is characterized by the absence of both exclusion and concomitance. If that is so, then...
There is no consequence of duality; for by negating such a manifold of effects, one realizes the Self as Brahman—thus he says:
"By the negation of causality, one attains the Self as Brahman. But [one might object] again:

To the objection that non-duality is lost because of the distinction between the prohibited and the non-prohibited, he says "no": because the reality of the causal and effected entities consists of nothing more than this [Brahman], Brahman alone must therefore be the Self, being neither excluded nor inclusive; such is the meaning of the verse beginning with "tam" (Him).
He said:
"You ought to describe to me, exactly as it is, that which is the Self itself— immediate, the innermost of all, and characterized in such a manner."
(608) But surely, since the difference between Brahman and the self is perceived through direct perception, how can the question concern their identity?
To this he says:

Since the expression of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) occurs between those two terms denoting Brahman and the Self, it is logical that these two signify identity; for even when there is a difference in meaning—as seen in cases of coreferentiality such as "name-Brahman" (*nāma-brahma*)—such usage is observed. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says here:

In order to establish that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is based solely on non-difference, it was stated [in the previous verse] "because of the mutual determination of the meanings"; that very point is proven by the following two *vārtikas*:
"It is specifically qualified as being directly by way of the nature of the identity of Brahman and the Self."

"Because it is impossible for that [Brahman] to exist elsewhere, Brahman is therefore [identical with] that; and since the self (ātman) also cannot possibly exist apart from Brahman, the statement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two words 'Brahman' and 'self' occurs. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "This follows from that."

Therefore, since Brahman and the Self stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified to one another, through the negation of non-Brahman and non-Self, there arises the cognition of their identity as a single essence. Now, an objection may be raised: since it is well known from scripture that the Self is Brahman, and since it is also well known that Brahman is beyond perception (parokṣa), [how can they be identified?]
Regarding how there can be oneness: it is true that if both of those were ultimately real, [the author] says that non-Brahmanhood belongs to the Self, which is Brahman, due to delusion,
but not to the reality itself.

"Even the self is beyond perception, and even Brahman is characterized by darkness (*tamas*). Therefore, he states that this is established: "First, the various forms of darkness are ignorance, because they exclude the non-self nature of Brahman."
"Brahman, whose nature consists of the unprecedented (apūrva) and so forth, attains a state free from all association. He elaborates on this very point:
"Due to the realization of the true nature of the inner self (pratyag-yāthātmya), darkness does not obstruct the Self."
"Because only the inward measure remains, [one thinks] 'I am the one who possesses the beginningless and so forth.
Thus the interrogative statement has been explained; now he states the meaning of the responsive statement:
"Having directed his vision toward the Self, colored solely by inward consciousness, he replies."
Thus it was said by the noble-minded Yājñavalkya as well. Now, if this is so, then the knower and other factors, which denote objects that are both verbal and perceptual, would also be perceptual;
therefore, he says: "Distinguish the meaning of the word and speak."

Since there exist here many things—such as the self (*ātman*), the knower (*pramātṛ*), and the means of knowledge (*māna*)—we do not know which one among these is intended by the word "this" (*eṣa*) when referring to the object of perception. He says that this word is distinguished by the term "self," stating: "He spoke of 'self' precisely for the sake of making known the intended object."
He states that the mention of "the innermost of all" (*sarvāntara*) and so forth is for the purpose of indicating all specific attributes: "But the grasping of the innermost of all...

The inclusion of "all" (*sarva*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of what was previously stated. He explains the meaning of the two words "that" (*tat*) and "Self" (*ātman*): the earth is mentioned first, up to space, expressed by means of the genitive case; and the word "Self" refers to the subject (*pramātṛ*) and so forth.

It is also the witness to the coming and going [of phenomena]. The meaning is that because the world is said to have a cause, that [cause] is called the "witness-self" (sākṣyātman). Now, one might object: "Since there is a difference in the objects witnessed (sākṣya), there must be a difference in the witnesses;
therefore, how can it be the 'witness-self'? To this, he says:
"Even though there is a distinction in the measure of the mother [the body], the witness does not differ in each body;
because it is like an external object, it is therefore called the Self (ātman).
Now, one might object: "But the Self also undergoes appearance and disappearance; how then can it be the witness of that appearance and disappearance? To this, he says:

Just as there is mutual deviation among the knower and so forth due to their being witnessed by the Self, the Self does not have such [deviation] because it is the witness for the non-existence of all knowers and the like.
[Objection: But is there not a distinction such that the Self is non-deviating while the non-Self is deviating?

He states that [this] is true in the state of ignorance (*avidyāvasthā*) and not in the state of knowledge (*vidyāvasthā*) by means of the words beginning with "directly" (*sākṣāt*): "That which is perceived directly through inward vision as the inward reality—apart from that inward reality, there is no other Self; thus it perceived. This is the answer to this.
Proliferation (*prapañca*) consists of the self and the non-self, which arise from ignorance and its products, because their true nature is solely the inward-facing Self alone.
"Because correct awakening consists in determining only that much, these two [perception and inference] are [limited].

Since the cause and so forth have the self as their sole essence, he says that the qualification "directly" (*sākṣāt*) and so on is even more appropriate in the case of the self: "Indeed, [the self is known] not in its entirety..."

"Because it is connected with a different object, everything such as 'directly' and so forth would be a possible qualification. Now, since it was stated "because of the connection," [the opponent asks] whether this is not the doctrine of difference; [the author] replies: "In that which is determined as sheer subjectivity (pratyaktā), there is no exclusion of any other entity whose nature is exclusively distinct [from it]."

If it is argued that "negation (vyatireka) is not obtained," then [the author] says "no" because it would entail positive concomitance (anvaya). He says "no" because of contradiction—that there is no positive concomitance for this, just as there is no "cowness" in a fragment of earth and so forth. If that is the case, then [there must be] negation.
"No," he says—
"even difference is not possible on account of the true nature of non-duality.
Therefore, having set aside the absence of both positive and negative concomitance, he states that the world is nothing but the Self:
"Therefore, because [the Self] is merely the inward-facing witness, the Self does not dissolve into itself. He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "Which one?
through three *vārtikas*: "Even the determination 'This is your Self' would not truly be a resolution of the question, for these [questions] concern the Self by means of the Self through the Self."
Due to its arising from non-awakening, one Self is within the *piṇḍa*, and likewise another is within the *liṅga*.

"The witness of the intellect (buddhisākṣī) would be the third [option], since this one is likewise doubted; therefore, tell us which of these is intended here. [The opponent replies: "By the words 'directly' (*sākṣāt*) and so forth, the nature of the means of knowledge (*māna*) is determined as being distinct from the other [the object] by way of its 'this-ness' (*idantā*). [The author states:
"The meaning of the reply, beginning with 'He who [breathes] through prāṇa' and so forth..."

Yājñavalkya also speaks; he says, "He who [breathes] by means of breath," desiring to directly awaken [the student] to the inner Self (pratyagātman) through the indicative mark (liṅga) of breath and so forth. He clarifies the intention of one who wishes to awaken [the student] by means of that indicative mark through the inference of breathing and other such functions.

"Having first caused [the disciple] to grasp the intellects, I shall thereafter awaken him to that which possesses the specific attributes as they have been acquired"— keeping this in mind, Yājñavalkya spoke to him with the words "He who [breathes] by means of prāṇa. Thus, the awakening was not stated through a logical mark (liṅga), but rather by means of inference (anumāna).

Having purified the referent of the word "thou" (tvaṃpadārtha), he spoke thus with the intention: "I shall subsequently establish its identity with Brahman through specific attributes such as 'directly' (sākṣāt) and so forth. Now, one might object that even this [identity] is established from the indicative mark (liṅga) alone; however, this is not so, for it is not established by the sentence alone.
The meaning is that it is because [the goal] is to be attained by a single [means]. Having thus stated the intended purport (*tātparya*), he provides an explanation of the word-meanings (*padārtha*):
"By the breath moving through the mouth, that which is not seen by the breath."
"This very Self is the most inward of all, the ordainer within all" (p.
When this collection of instruments is asleep, that which is asleep therein is one whose vision has ceased.

"Seeing the forms of latent impressions, he breathes the vital breaths by means of the wind"— this is an elaboration of what was stated previously. Having thus provided the explanation of the individual words, he states the intended meaning once again:

Therefore, the non-selfhood of the vital breaths and so forth is established by their being described as instruments; and since the intellect and everything up to the physical body are of the nature of the vital breath, they too are non-self. Thus, he states another argument for the non-selfhood of the body and so forth: "Because it is an object of sight, like a jar, the body [is non-self], as are the vital breaths and so forth."
"Thus, by virtue of being an instrument, the non-selfhood of both the subtle body (liṅga) and the physical body (piṇḍa) is established.

Regarding the statement that the Self is the cause of activities such as breathing, this objection is raised: that the Self would then be a composite entity consisting of breath and so forth, and would possess activity. To this, he says:
"By means of the instruments of action such as the vital breaths, he, being himself uncomposite and solitary, performs their activities, just as a magnet [acts upon] iron. [Objection:
But surely, there is no self distinct from the aggregate of the body and its instruments, just as there is no proven patient; how [then can this be]?
"It is said that its immutability and lack of attachment [follow from this]. To this, he replies:

"In this world, no fixed movement of insentient objects such as chariots is ever seen unless they are presided over by some sentient being; yet, such fixed movement is observed in the body, senses, mind, intellect, vital breath, and so forth."
p.
614) Since activity proceeds by means of that [knowledge], one must accept that the Self is other than those [objects];
thus, he demonstrates the meaning of the passage beginning with "one might say" (*brūyāt*) by means of three *vārtikas*.

"Having previously promised, 'I shall show you the Cow directly,' one who is unable to do so should awaken [the disciple] by means of a symbol (*liṅga*). Just as someone might act in such a way, even though you have promised the direct manifestation of the Supreme Self (*parātman*), you have failed to accomplish it.
He makes known his liberation through a sign; therefore, it must be exactly as he promised, and just as his vision is, so too must be his reply to me. Otherwise, there would be a fault.
He states the intended meaning of the sentence of the reply beginning with "Not from vision" (*na dṛṣṭeḥ*) as follows: "Just as..."

"I have repeatedly spoken the proposition and the response to you; therefore, you are either satisfied with what has been said, or you are desirous of further knowledge. This is the meaning: "according to the proposition" means according to what was asked;
"the response" means the reply, which I have spoken precisely as it pertains to the subject matter.

It has been stated more than once that the Self cannot be known as an object; for instance, [it was said] "This is your Self which is within the vital breaths. Yet you desire to know it as an object. That is not possible.
Apart from the path already described, the reality of the self cannot be pointed out like a jar or other such objects, because it lies beyond the scope of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This is an elaboration of what preceded. To the question, "How can there be perception regarding that which is not an object? he says:

"By whose power one says 'I know,' and by whose power one also says 'I do not know'—having seen that very thing here through its respective perceptions, I say: 'Whatever fault you perceive, [it arises] from objects such as sound. It is born from objects such as sound.

The meaning is: by the grace of that immutable experience (kūṭasthānubhava) through which you say, "I know" or "I do not know," experience that very one— the immutable Self— by means of the vision that constitutes its own nature, and then tell me if you perceive any fault of being an object in the Self.

If it is argued that even though the Self is not an object, it is nevertheless made into an object, this is not sound. Just as an object cannot be made into an object, so too the commentary speaks of the nature of the thing (*vastusvābhāvya*) for the sake of its demonstration; for that thing which is immeasurable cannot be [made an object].
It is stated as follows, so that it may be specifically pointed out by means of a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa), just like a jar.

He explains the meaning of the term "the nature of reality" (*vastusvābhāvya*): the eternal witnesshood of the Self with respect to the seer, the seeing, and the seen—which are all conjoined—is called its "nature of reality. [Objection: But if the Self is a witness to the knower and so forth, does it not follow that the Self possesses activity?
He says "no"—prior to activity, the knower and so forth were uniform, neither risen nor set;
they remained as a non-agent, for the inward vision is indeed uncomposite. How then [is this so]?
He says that because the self possesses the nature of cause and effect, it does not have the state of being unattached (*asaṅgatva*):

"This true form of the self is without cause or effect; it is to be purified through a single division, which transcends the distinctions of sequential and simultaneous action. If that is so, how [can there be] such a thing?
Regarding the state of being a witness (*sākṣitva*), he says in that context: "It attains the state of being a witness due to its connection with delusion (*moha*).
If it is then asked whether this connection with ignorance (*ajñāna*) is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), he says "no":
"And the soul’s association with delusion has as its sole cause mere darkness (*tamas*). It is not [ultimately real].
Witnesshood alone is produced by ignorance, but [the text] says that causality and so forth are also produced:
"The immutable Seer, His delusion, and the semblance of vision therein—these are said to be the cause of the world, the Witness, and the Guide. Now, [one might ask: what is this causality?
He says that [the cause] is not ultimate, because causality does not exist due to immutability; it could only exist through the absence of delusion regarding that [cause].

And because the effect is insentient, he states that the insentient portion must be inferred in the cause: [The text continues: "Because the effect is insentient, the insentient aspect in the cause is to be inferred.
He says:

"Furthermore, because cognition and so forth follow from their own kind, it is logical to infer their cause [as being ignorance]. He states that it is not only the state of being a witness and so on that is produced by ignorance, but also the state of being distinct and so on:

"Even the distinction from the knower and so forth is appropriate for the object of knowledge (*prameya*), which is of the nature of consciousness, as long as it is unmanifested, and for that witness of its own darkness. He establishes that being a witness is produced by ignorance: "The state of being a witness for one whose vision is immutable is not possible, just as it is not for an insentient thing."
Because there is no connection with the objects of perception, even when that [reflection] exists, it does not possess the status of being a witness for another;

for the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) is connected to the relationship between cause and effect by way of the path of its own delusive appearance— this is the sense conveyed by the word "connection" (saṃbandha).

The dyad of cause and effect is denoted; in that relationship termed "cause and effect," witness-hood (*sākṣitva*) arises due to the entry of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) produced by ignorance (*avidyā*). This means that [the Self] is the witness.
To the objection that there may be a witness whose nature is the knower (*pramātṛ*) and so forth, and thus the absence [of such a witness] does not follow, he says "no":

Just as the relationship with the knower and so forth is established through the fact of experience, so too its absence is established merely through experience; thus it has been stated that being the witness, the inner ruler, and the cause is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*). But surely, it is not produced by ignorance, rather—
He says "no" to the claim that [the subject and so forth] are produced by merit (*dharma*) and the like:

"In this context, these two (the subject and the object) are said to be without other causes; however, entities such as the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) are caused by merit, demerit, and so forth. All of this will be stated as it pertains to the present subject matter.

This is not to be doubted, because the inherent nature of various kinds of objects is being elaborated upon. Is the intellect, when connected with the two consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*), [something else]?

Regarding the term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), he says therein: "In this world, the perspective of the subject (*pramātṛ-dṛṣṭi*)—which consumes objects such as sound and so forth, which depends upon numerous means, which yields results in the form of pleasure and pain, and which perishes in an instant—is [so] because its cause is fragile; thus it occurs for every body."
And this [reality], in the form of action and its factors, is differentiated by virtue of its uncommon causes.
If it is argued that such a vision is established by itself (*svataḥ*), he says "no"—
for it is indeed pervaded by that [vision] which consists of the nature of non-action and non-factors, since its true essence is solely that much.
Since the relationship of pervaded and pervader is accepted on the grounds that [the effect] is born, he says "there is no difference"—
for where there is an occurrence in its entirety between two things, the pervader and the pervaded,
only there can pervasion be primary, as in the case of the substance of a rope and a snake.
He states that pervasion (*vyāpti*) between two distinct things is not primary:

"Because of the separation of space, time, and so forth, pervasion does not directly occur between two unique realities, just as between the Himālaya and the Vindhya mountains. Now, [one might ask: is the perspective of the subject (*pramātṛ*) also [distinct]?
Because there is still a distinction here even from the ultimate perspective, [one might argue that] the pervasion is not primary. To this he says: "No;
this worldly view of the Self depends upon the subject and so forth.

"The vision of that inner self, however, is to be known as ultimate. Therefore, he states that here the pervasion is indeed primary: "In this way, by the vision of the ultimate Self, the worldly vision of the self undergoes the six modifications of being; it is pervaded [by the Self] just as a jar is pervaded by space."

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: "But since it is indeed all-pervasive, why is it that the pervasion of the Self, like the pervasion of objects perceived by worldly vision, is also perishable? To this he says "no," because with respect to the manifestation of consciousness, it is independent of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*).

Therefore, just like the appearance of a jar or other objects, even the non-existence of the Self is not perishable; thus, once again, he demonstrates the essential nature of the pervaded and the pervader by distinguishing them: "The conscious one is inactive and a witness; the insentient is active, external, and differentiated."
"The witness of the knower and so forth is established as residing in deep sleep. Now, [an objection may be raised]:
"It is untenable that consciousness resides in deep sleep, because there is an absence of consciousness in deep sleep.
To this, he says:

"If the pervasion by experience is not admitted for one in deep sleep, how could the cognition 'I did not know anything here in deep sleep' arise by its own force? This is the elaboration of the answer:
"Because the intellect and so forth have dissolved, and because the body and so forth are insentient, like a clod of earth."
"There would not even be the perception [of the form] 'I did not know'";
thus, the experience of ignorance in the form "I did not know" has the witness-consciousness as its witness.
Regarding what was stated there, this objection is raised: "Is [ignorance] established by means of the subject (*pramātṛ*)? He says, "No.
Ignorance is established solely by the appearance of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), not by means of the subject.
Because its very nature is ignorance, it is established merely through the appearance of the subject and so forth.

"It does not depend on ignorance. To this he replies: "The perceiver, whose nature is that of an agent, is directly evident as the reflection of consciousness, awareness, and the intellect. The meaning is that the subject (pramātṛ) is established through consciousness, its manifestation, and ignorance. [This constitutes] the definition characterized by the knower, the knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the fruit.
He explains this by means of four *vārtikas* in order to elaborate upon the inherent nature of the reality:

"That which persists as the form of 'I' within memory, certainty, recollection, passion, and so forth, as well as within the self that is afflicted by disease, is considered the supreme cognizer (*pramātṛ*). It is that which remains distinct within the single knower through the various divisions of memory and the rest."

That cognition, which has the knower as its agent, manifests with the appearance of manifold forms; it appears externally as distinct, possessing universals, forms, actions, and so forth. This object of experience, appearing separate from the knower’s cognition, is merely a delusive function of consciousness.

When the body and other such qualifiers appear here as belonging to the enjoyer, that is traditionally held to be the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*). If it is argued that these four are established by themselves (*svataḥ*), he says "no": agency, instrumentality, and objectivity [are established] through the witness-self (*ātmasākṣitah*). The fruit is also included here.
It should be observed. For this very reason, he states that the lack of selfhood (*anātmatva*) of the agent and so forth is established by way of exclusion (*vyatirekeṇa*): (p. 621) [agent etc.]...

"Because it is established that there is no selfhood [in these], therefore [it is not the Self]. Now, one might object: "The Mīmāṃsakas and others hold that the agent of cognition is the Self; the Buddhists hold that it is consciousness (*vijñāna*); and the Cārvākas hold that the body and so forth are the Self. Therefore, the Witness is not the Self. To this, he says "no":

The self is established as a witness by virtue of being distinct from the objects of cognition (*mātrādi*) and so forth; it does not possess agency, because the agency of the knower (*pramātṛ*) and others ceases precisely when they are [realized as] objects to be accomplished. Thus, the meaning is that the agency of the knower and others is non-self (*anātmatā*); the agent of knowledge is one thing, while the witness of that is another.
To the objection that this would result in the loss of non-duality (*advaita-hāni*), he says:

because the intellect and so forth arise from the delusion of the inward-facing Self and are primarily insentient (*jaḍa-rūpa*), it is logical that agency belongs to the Self; and because consciousness (*cit*) is predominant, enjoyment belongs [to the Self]. Thus, agency and enjoyment belong to the Self alone through its own ignorance (*svāvidyā*) consisting of the intellect and so forth.

The meaning is that [the Self] possesses the state of being an agent, instrument, and object primarily through the predominance of its manifestations (*ābhāsa*), while it possesses the state of being an enjoyer through the predominance of its manifestations, but is in itself (*svataḥ*) the immutable Self (*kūṭastha-ātman*).

This is for the sake of establishing the point stated starting from the passage "by the very nature of things" (*vastu-svābhāvyāt*) up to the verse beginning with "That indeed was this" (*tad dha idam*).

He says that what was stated by us here should be recollected: "Everything that was said regarding the explanation of the indeterminate (avyākṛta) should also be connected here for the sake of purifying the reality of things.
To the question, "What was stated there?", he says:

The meaning is this: an entity whose nature is not cognized by itself cannot be established through its own greatness; for it has been refuted that such an entity exists as either being or non-being, just as in the case of the Self. (p. 622)

An insentient object is not established by itself; precisely because of its insentience, it alone undergoes birth and destruction, whereas the self does not undergo existence or non-existence. Since both of those have been rejected by the self, therefore the eternally unchanging consciousness—the inner self—is the subject, and everything else is the object.
"Everything is imagined. Therefore, he says that birth and so forth are false with respect to the nature of experience:

"Therefore, consciousness—which is unborn and one—is perceived as if it were being born; likewise, although there is no other birth [of it], through the arising of the cause of cognition, and even upon its destruction, it appears to perish because of its similarity [to that cause]."

It is observed that, for this reason, even Īśvara cannot establish its status as an effect; thus it has been stated that the world is illusory (*mithyā*). To this, the following objection is raised: "But how can the world be illusory, since it possesses the nature of being an object of knowledge (*meya*)? To that, he says:

An object that has entered the domain of the unknown attains the status of a cognizable (*meyatva*) when it comes into contact with the mind; it does not attain anything else. Thus it is said that there are two grounds. Since the state of being unknown is possible only for the Inner Self (*pratīc*), that alone is the object of knowledge (*meya*), and not that which is negated as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).

The duality of cause and effect. Or rather, let it be that the self is not an effect, but let it be a cause. To this, he says: "Since the production of the effect from a cause is established, [the self must exist] even prior to consciousness."
"Therefore,
let consciousness be recognized as being devoid of the relation of cause and effect. Thus,
prior to the establishment of the cause and prior to the establishment of the effect, consciousness exists in states such as deep sleep.
Therefore, consciousness is established as being neither an effect nor a cause. [Objection:

But how can there be a "prior" to the establishment of the cause, since the cause itself is beginningless? [Response: This is not a fault; even the notion "it is a cause" is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) for one who has just awakened from sleep. [Objection: But if consciousness itself does not exist, how [can there be such a construction]?

It is said that [the nature of] being devoid of causes and so forth is considered when the substratum (dharmin) exists, according to the principle that attributes are examined only when there is a subject; regarding this, he says: "Even the emptiness of the empty is seen by its witness while it exists. Now, if it is argued that there is no other establisher for the empty, then [it must be established] by itself.
He says that it must be self-luminous:
"If emptiness were without a witness, it would be like something without a witness. Now, one might object: "Emptiness is not self-luminous; nevertheless, it is established by itself."
He says "no" [to this objection]:

"The witness and the witnessed would both be established because they have their own intrinsic nature (svārthatva), but emptiness (śūnyatā) does not [establish itself] because it exists for the sake of another (pārārthya); lacking its own intrinsic nature, it would be like the object of the sixth [sense]. This is the meaning.

Even if the witness lacks external means of proof, it may be established by itself due to its self-luminous nature; however, this is not possible for that which is born of emptiness or is insentient. Therefore, let consciousness (saṃvit), though immutable (kūṭastha), also exist in the state of the goal (upeya).
Anticipating the objection that "consciousness is differentiated," [the author says:]
He shows its fivefold state for the purpose of elaborating upon the intrinsic nature of things: [p. 624]—

This inner self within the body is understood to be fivefold, as stated [in the following]: "By way of being the single cause, the witness, the agent, and the one who experiences suffering. Among these, its oneness is ultimate; the others depend upon the functioning of ignorance. Among these, its state as the cause...

He establishes [the cause] through scripture, through indicative marks, and through direct perception of the connection between cause and effect; since this is experienced, therefore the Supreme Self possesses causality. He establishes its nature as a witness:

"Even non-existence (abhāva) is not established apart from the direct witness (pratyak-sākṣin); how much less so, then, existence (bhāva) in this world? Thus, [the author] says that [the Self] is established by the Sāttvika [state] as "self-established" (svayaṃ-siddha), for the Witness (sākṣin) is not established by anything else; even its status as the knower (pramātṛtva) and so forth belongs to that [Witness] alone.
He says "by one's own ignorance":

even that which is at the end of the intellect becomes established when it has ascended to the experience as described; through the knower, the act of knowing, and the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge becomes established—as one who is happy, fair-complexioned, wealthy, or possessing cattle.

"Relying upon external objects of cognition while remaining on the level of the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), all this that has been stated is established. Thus, causality and so forth—all of it—depends upon the functioning of ignorance (avidyā) with respect to the inner self (pratyak) alone;
therefore, the inner self is non-dual. [Objection: But let it be so.
At the time of the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the self is established in the form of being a cause and so forth;
but prior to that, in states such as deep sleep, how is the self established, given the absence of any means of valid cognition?

Regarding this, he says: "Prior to the emergence of the knower and so forth, that which is the cause of the knower and so forth—namely, the ignorance consisting of non-apprehension of the non-dual—is always the means of knowledge for the Seer. The meaning of this is as follows:
ignorance, first of all, manifests in states such as deep sleep; otherwise, for one who has awakened from sleep, [there would be no recollection of that state].

Because of the reflective awareness, "I did not know," the self is established as the prover of that [ignorance] through the impossibility of its establishment otherwise. Now, if ignorance is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the self, then there ought to be a distinction within the self such as that of the knower (*pramātṛ*) and so forth. To this he says, "No": *naivam; yataḥ—* (It is not so; because—) [The text continues: "The self is indeed the locus of ignorance, for it is the substrate of the notion 'I do not know. And since the notion 'I' is the very nature of the self, the self is established by the very fact of its own existence, even without the operation of a means of valid cognition. Thus, the self is established as the locus of ignorance, and therefore there is no requirement for a further distinction such as that of the knower and so forth. This is the meaning.

In that state, the distinction between the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the knower is not admitted, because [reality] is encompassed solely by the true nature of the inwardly directed consciousness, which is pure being. Now, one might ask: "How is it not seen?
For the fruit of knowledge and so forth are accepted there. To this, he says: "The fruit is precisely of such a kind."
"And likewise, how could there be room for distinction between the means of knowledge,
the object of knowledge, and so forth, within the non-dual, single self that is the knower? By the phrase 'because of the further emergence of another knower, etc.',
this objection is answered by stating that it is the very knowledge of one's own nature that is called the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the Self."
Even the designation of [the Self] as the cause of the knower and so forth during states such as deep sleep is consistent,
because it is admitted that even the immutable witness (kūṭasthadṛṣṭi) possesses causality through its own ignorance (svāvidyā).
They consider that the two subsequent *vārtikas* should also be introduced in accordance with this [point].

Or rather, let it be thus: "Surely, because the reality of the Self is self-luminous (*svayaṃprabha*), it would remove its own ignorance by itself; what need is there for a means of knowledge (*māna*)? To this, he says:
"This [teaching], arrived at by the path of valid cognition, is not sufficient for the destruction of delusion according to the actual state of things,
because of the attachment to not beginning the treatise";
and because all worldly transaction is preceded by experience, experience cannot exist without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

He says that it does not remove ignorance: "By not abandoning the stated meaning, the conventional usage of the knower and so forth within the stages born of that ignorance is like a dream, an illusion, or a magician’s trick. Now, one might object: "The world is not equal to a dream and the like."

He says "no" to this: "The entire world arises from the darkness of the unreal, which is established without inquiry"; thus he states the consequence of its being imagined. Therefore, when delusion is destroyed, it is destroyed, and there remains only consciousness.
If it is then argued that, as before, non-duality does not exist, he replies:

"In the case of the causal relationship between entities such as the cognizer and so forth, which are merely divided, the cognizer, the means of cognition, and so on, are non-distinct; the Self alone is one and non-dual by its very nature. Now, an objection is raised:
"But surely, like non-self entities, the Self also depends upon space and other factors; therefore, it is not non-dual. To this he replies: "No."
p.

627) There is no dependence on space, time, state, and so forth, for the Self, because it is established by itself without depending on anything else; whereas space and the rest depend upon that [Self]. Thus ends the discussion on dependence on space and so forth.

If so, to whom does [the property] belong? He says: "to that which is not the Self. That is to say: whatever object may exist in dependence upon space, time, causes, and so forth, that alone would be dependent upon them, but not [the Self] which bestows the establishment of space and the rest.
[Objection: Since some objects depend on space and so forth while others do not, there is no loss of non-duality (advaita). To this he replies:

Whatever object whatsoever is perceived by virtue of the factors of action (*kāraka*) and so forth, that should be understood as the fruit of an action (*kriyāphala*), being independent [of anything else]. Since every effect is merely conceptualized (*kalpita*), there is no loss of non-duality (*advaita*); this is the meaning. Now, let it be so.

To the claim that the fruit of action and the agent of action are ultimately real even though their true nature is not perceived, he says "no": since knowledge depends upon reality, while all actions depend upon an agent;
and since the notion of an agent and so forth arises from delusion regarding the Self, it is established that reality is by its own nature non-dual.

The meaning is that because the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is in accordance with reality, and because action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*) are unreal—being born of ignorance—the non-dual Self (*advayātman*) is established as the reality. It has been stated that knowledge depends upon reality; let it be so, but that knowledge which depends upon reality, when practiced repeatedly, [leads to liberation].
Regarding this, he says:
"The causal factors, such as the seed and so forth, turn back [from their effects], just as knowledge [turns back] from saline soil.

Since it destroys its own cause, let knowledge be the subverter of ignorance by the very fact of its birth; yet, while that knowledge has the Self as its substrate and is indicated by its fruit, if it were not established by the Witness (sākṣin), then he says:
The establishment of valid cognition occurs through the transformation of the cognizer;

for the cognizer, it is established by consciousness alone through the mediation of the cognizer, and not by means of mental modifications (*vṛtti*). The meaning is that both the knower and the means of knowledge are established by experience. He states the refutation regarding their being established by the mind (*māna*):

For, if one were to posit another cognizer (mātrantara), it would be impossible to avoid the fault of infinite regress (anavasthā), since the need for a further cognizer immediately following the [first] cognizer would persist;
thus, starting from the words "only by the excellence of the cognizer" up to "or a modification of the internal organ" (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti).

By means of the preceding collection of Vārttika passages, he demonstrates the system of valid cognition established during the state of avidyā. Primarily for the purpose of elaborating upon the inherent nature of reality, the intended meaning has been stated thus far; now—
The *Prativārtika* is explained as follows:

"The cause would exist by means of the subject and the object; the subject also would achieve a pre-eminent state of consciousness, and likewise, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would possess certainty. This is its meaning.
The excellence of the cognizer is the "cognizer-excellence" (*pramātratiśaya*), which is something to be inferred from its effect, as otherwise a changeless entity could not function as a cause;
it is by means of that very excellence [that cognition occurs].
The cause would be the nature of the cognizer; that which follows [as] the cause of cognition is the excellence of consciousness— that [consciousness] whose excellence is that nature of the cognizer.
Immediately following that, the excellence of consciousness in the form of the knower becomes the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
which is determinate and culminates in a result. He states that the very form of the result is also the form of the cognition itself:
Just as a determination possessing the form [of the object] arises for the purpose of apprehending the object of measurement— such that,

while the external is primary, there is a cognition of the non-common object— as when the determination possessing the form of a jar arises as "this is a jar," so too [it occurs] by virtue of the primacy of the external object of measurement.

When cognition exists as an awareness directed toward objects such as a jar by way of establishing them, then that cognition becomes specific; for at that time, the cognition takes on the very form of the object, such as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth. Thus it is then.
He states that knowledge has external objects as its primary focus:

"At the time of the operation of the means of knowledge (*māna*), the external object of cognition (*meyopasarjana*)—such as a jar and so forth—is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it arises as a result qualified by that [object]. This is when the means of knowledge is determining its own power.

It functions, which means it produces a fruit. At that time, those three— the means of knowledge (*māna*), the knower who is its agent (*kartṛ*), and the reflection residing therein (*tadgatābhāsa*)— become dominated by the object of knowledge (*prameya-pradhāna*),
being inclined toward the object of knowledge by virtue of having the object of knowledge as their primary focus.

630) Because the fruit arises [from that], at that time there is both the predominance of the object and the predominance of the cognition. Thus it is said: "After the cessation of the means of valid cognition..."

"Because it is the cause for depositing a latent impression (*vāsanā*), the cognition—which has the object of knowledge as its subordinate element—is directly perceived by memory. Thus, immediately after the operation of determining its own object, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) deposits a latent impression within its own substrate, which remains there in the form of a mental trace (*saṃskāra*). And that...
Knowledge, which exists in the form of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) as something unseen, is awakened by Rudra;

having the object of cognition as its subordinate element—meaning, "of what is the object of cognition subordinate?"—it arises in the form of memory. Since this is so, therefore, at the time of recollection, [there is the cognition] of the object.

"The knowledge of being subordinate [to the Self] possesses primacy. Now, one might object: "In this way, for one who establishes the process of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there would be a loss of duality. To that he replies:
"When, directly realizing its own Self, it attains the state of being the objective support (*ālambanatā*)."

"That very [object] consisting of cause and effect is considered the objective support. Regarding the phrase "by means of the excellence of the cognizer" (*pramātratiśayenaiva*), the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) indicated here by the word "cognizer" is said to be "directly perceiving" (*sākṣātkurvat*); that is, the internal organ together with its mental modification (*savṛttika*).

When one realizes one's own self directly through the grace of the immutable consciousness (kūṭastha-caitanya), that which becomes the object of support—namely, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) together with its mental modifications (vṛtti)—becomes established as the object of support.

"That which has [something] as its support" (yad-ālambana) refers to the internal organ accompanied by its modifications. When it attains the state of being such an object of support, it becomes perfected.

The meaning is that when its state—that is, the internal organ together with its modifications—becomes the object [of consciousness], it rests upon immutable consciousness; for that [internal organ] is a manifestation of ignorance. And that very [consciousness]...

Immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-caitanya*) is the support and substratum (*ālambana*) of the manifold of cause and effect; therefore, there is no loss of non-duality (*advaita*).
