Alternatively, when one realizes one's own Self, the entire collection of objects becomes established as it comes to serve as the support for that consciousness. Of which consciousness? [Of that which perceives the Self.]

It would become the object (*ālambanatā*) and it would become the sphere of experience (*viṣayatā*); that is, this cognition is the cause and the manifold of objects is the effect. Since the latter is manifested by ignorance regarding the former, there is no loss of non-duality (*advaita*). [Objection: But [in the phrase] "subordinate to the object of knowledge" (*meyopasarjanā*)...

By speaking thus, you have accepted that memory is an object of cognition; consequently, there is a contradiction with your own tenet, since it was stated that [memory] does not apprehend an external object. To this, he replies: "Due to the error of memory arising from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a previous perception, there is a functioning [of the mind] even when the actual state of the thing (*vastuvṛtta*) is predominant."

"The notion that [this] is universal is itself a delusion" (sārvalaukika iti)— this statement from the *Smṛti* further demonstrates the very process of valid cognition (*pramāṇaprakriyā*), because prior to the connection with the object of knowledge (*meyādi*),
cognition is the locus of the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*), and it is the means of knowledge (*māna*) for the establishment of that state of being a knower.

Because of the traditional teaching (smṛti), "Since the state of being a knower is produced by that [cognition]," its lack of objective referent (arthaśūnyatva) is established by describing it as an error (bhrama).
It has been stated that the word of the Veda is devoid of objective referents; how then does it appear as if it were so?
To this he replies: "By the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), knowledge—which resides clearly as if external and is the object of contemplation—is based on an external thing."

This is the meaning: at the time of experience, that cognition which, by the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), rests within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as having the form of a latent impression—having had external objects as its support—and which, through the influence of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and other factors, arises in the form of memory, having as its object the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of a previously experienced thing; this is *saṃskāra*.
The sphere of perception becomes as if external; it becomes as if having an external object. Now he concludes the meaning of the phrase "due to the inherent nature of things":
Whatever thing whatsoever is observed here appears as if it functions through dependence; that would be based on the knower and the means of knowledge, and not from its own [intrinsic] state.
"Established as accomplished" means that the mother’s mother is the witness; thus, the two [the self and the witness] depend only on themselves and are limited to that extent.
Therefore, the self is not an object of cognition, nor does the duality serve the purpose of the opponent's position. "Thus, by the very nature of things"—this is the summary statement.

Having now elaborated upon the distinction between views by means of the worldly and natural forms, the statement beginning with "not from vision" (*na dṛṣṭeḥ*) has been explained; he now demonstrates those two views in detail through two verses of the Vārttika:
The modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) which, depending on the eyes and other [senses], has forms and other objects as its appearance,
is called "worldly vision" (*laukikī dṛṣṭi*); and because that [vision] is something being produced, [it is impermanent].

"The connection with birth, destruction, and so forth belongs to this perception of a self, whereas the Self is eternal and devoid of birth, destruction, and the like. To the objection that "in that case, because of the distinction between the eternal and the non-eternal, there would be a loss of non-duality," he says: "No."

"The inner self (pratyagātman) desires to bring about the reality of cause and effect"—thus, there is no difference [between them], or rather, this is the reason for the absence of birth and so forth. For this very reason, he says that the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) is not eternal, nor are the intellect (buddhi) and its modifications; therefore, the eternal reflection of consciousness resides in the intellect.

"And while those [objects] exist" means this: even when jars and other such things exist, the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) does not arise as belonging to them; nor, even if it has arisen, does it perish while they exist.
Likewise, while the intellect (buddhi) and its objects exist, the reflection of consciousness neither comes into being nor perishes therein.

It is with this intention that the permanence of the appearance (ābhāsa) is stated; it is not said that its impermanence is like that of the self (ātman) according to the worldly view. In this regard, the following objection might be raised:
"In that case, the modification (vṛtti) of pleasure and so forth belonging to the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) must be permanent. He says "no":

Due to the influence of causes such as merit (dharma), the eternal Self appears as a king within the intellect that is colored by its own inwardness, manifesting the characteristics of suffering, sound, and so forth.

Thus [it is said]. Upon the attainment of this expansion (*prapañca*), an appearance based on external causes arises within the form of direct consciousness (*pratyak-cid-ākāra*)—an appearance belonging to the intellect (*buddhi*) and characterized by the properties of coming and going.
If the vision of the Self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is eternal and non-dual, how can there be the manifestation of impermanence and so forth therein?

He says it is "by the power of limiting adjuncts" (upādhivaśāt): through the vision that has become a limiting adjunct, consisting of rejection and acquisition, [the Self] does not become associated with the intellect or its modifications because they share a single locus;
for the Unborn One is the witness of the intellect and its cognitions.
Just as a gem appears divided due to ignorance because of its various settings, so too the impermanence of the view of self arises from contact with the view of impermanence;
regarding this, the following objection is raised:

"It is not impermanence due to association with the view of impermanence, but rather [it is impermanent] because it is denotable by the word [‘impermanent’] in its own right, like a jar and so forth. To this, he replies: "Because it is manifested as agent and action, the Witness (sākṣin) is indicated by names that denote agents and actions; yet, He is not directly [so]."
It is said: "Because it is the witness of that [world's] birth and destruction, the Self, though itself undecaying and self-luminous, is likewise designated as 'it is born' and 'it perishes'—
this is the elaboration of the statement 'by means of the vision which has become its limiting adjunct'."

The three subsequent commentaries (*uttaravārtika*) are in the form of an exposition of the *Śruti*, easy to understand, [establishing] that perception, being insentient by nature and for the sake of another, [does not know itself] intrinsically.
One should not see the intellect as the inner self, the seer;

for how could that which is sought to be seen—being limited and having an external form and so forth—be seen by means of this vision, which is its opposite and has become the object of that very vision? For there is a separation of the seer from the act of seeing.
When an object such as form is seen, how can that inner self perceive consciousness itself through those two?

It has been stated that the Self is of the nature of eternal perception and is the witness of the intellect and its modifications; regarding this, the following objection is raised: [what of] the object as well?
Regarding the phrase "or in testimony," he says thereon:
"One should not regard [the self] as non-agents with respect to the objects of the seer and seeing.
This means: with respect to the objects of the seer and the act of seeing. If that is so, then [what of] the agency of knowledge?
He says it is not ultimately real:

"How can there be agency for the immutable Self apart from ignorance? The meaning is that the Self's status as an agent is brought about by ignorance alone. If that is so, then what of the connection with ignorance?
If it is argued that there is a transcendental [perception] as well as the perception of others produced by it and the perception of one's own self—this may be true;
however, if the connection with ignorance were not ultimately real, he says:
"The agent and likewise the effect are not perceived in any way whatsoever."

"Because it is not accompanied by ignorance, that luminous, immediate light is, in reality, [the Self]"— the meaning is that it does not perceive objects as an agent in the ultimate sense. By the phrase "not of seeing," the non-objectivity of the Self is established.
p.
636) He states that there is also another scriptural passage on this point:
"That by which the eye is seen, and by which one does not see this eye—know that to be Brahman."

"That alone is You, but they do not worship that; that which the mind does not conceive, and by which the mind is conceived—that indeed know as Brahman, that alone is You, but not this which they worship.
Such passages, hundreds in number, proclaim the aforementioned meaning in order to establish it.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of establishing that [the Self] is not an object of knowledge," he says from this perspective that it is immeasurable:

"Because this [world] is capable of causing delusion, the subject and so forth cannot perceive even the slightest identity [with the Self], due to the lack of awakening regarding the established cause. The meaning is as follows: the subject and so forth are established [as distinct].
Ignorance is its cause; while that [ignorance] persists, Brahman cannot be realized.

When ignorance has been destroyed by means of the knower and so forth, Brahman is not apprehended precisely because of the absence of the knower and so forth. "By that" refers to the explanation of the passage beginning with "Thus, because of seeing," and so on.

Having shown the distinction of views by way of the worldly and natural forms, [the author] now explains this statement regarding the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) without making a distinction of views.
To refute that, some *Vārttikas* which are easy to understand are presented there.
Without making any distinction between [the two types of] views, some wise ones explain such scriptural passages as "of the view" (dṛṣṭeḥ) and so forth, through the grace of Jātavedas.

637) You would not perceive the self as the agent of seeing by means of the seeing that is currently being performed and which falls upon the object of form; for there is no such thing as an action being both the act and the object of that very seeing.
This genitive case is to be understood as referring to the object alone, on the basis of its being the "thing to be done" (kriyamāṇatva);

it does not denote a different meaning, because [the word *draṣṭā*] expresses the self's agency in seeing by means of a suffix (*tṛc*), and therefore, through the act of seeing as an object, one does not perceive that seer.
Form is the most desired object of action, because it is observed to be an effect; the eye, the mind, or the vital air are held to be the instruments of the agent.
However, the conscious self (vijñānātman) is the agent here due to its independence in all actions. The fruit and the arising of form result from the agent’s observation and final determination.
Even though the agent is perceived here as a means (*sādhana*) through inference (*liṅga*), it is after the accomplishment of the action that the fruit of someone is exerted;

thus, what was stated as "the fruit belongs to someone," he now clarifies: whether it belongs to the owner or to another, the action is indeed intended for the sake of the owner. Therefore, he is the owner.

The term "the Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajña) refers, by means of another word, to the cognizer (pramātṛ) who possesses that limiting adjunct (upādhi); the meaning is that the result for those two would be the perception of form and so forth from something other than themselves. Knowledge, which has action and its experience as its fruit, has only objects such as a jar as its domain, and not the Self; thus, it is directed only toward an object (karman).
The word "action" (kriyā) clarifies this: there would have to be an action to be shown, a seer to see by means of vision, and that which is seen. (p. 638)

Thus it is said. And from this, the following is established; so he says: "This being so, when that [seeing] is seen, one could not by any means see the seer as an object through the seeing that has become an object," nor [see him] as an agent. He refutes this:

"This explanation of the great ones does not appear sound to us, because it is untenable according to the nature of logic; how that is so will now be stated. He demonstrates the lack of basis in the literal words [of the text]: "First, regarding this question..."

A reply is not possible because it is impossible for the seer to possess all the aforementioned specific qualifications. The detailed explanation of this answer begins with "directly" (*sākṣāt*) and so forth;
since even in the slightest degree such a qualification as described is not applicable to the agent (*kāraka*), [the question remains unanswerable].

Regarding the phrase "dṛṣṭikāriṇi": if it is argued that the intention is focused on the interrogative sentence, and therefore the application of qualifiers is according to what is appropriate, [the author] says "no," for neither the *kṣetrajña* nor the *paramātman* are intended in the question; because the sentence has a single referent, it does not denote two things.

Regarding the statement "there would be a twofold object because of [the existence of] vision," it was said that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes the object (*karma*); however, he says that this is not tenable. Furthermore, if that were accepted, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) in the prevention [of the object], and the state of being the most desired (*iṣṭatamatva*) would not belong to the seer, because vision is impossible for the seer.
Regarding the phrase "of another seer," he says that if this [object] were seen as being the same [as the seer], then:
"And for the seer, there is likewise no other seer" (p. 639). If...

If you admit that one vision perceives another vision, and that one seer perceives another seer, then there would be an infinite regress; thus he says: "In accepting that, there would be no end to the infinite regress.
Therefore, he states that there is no vision which is an object of vision.
"Therefore, there can be no pervasion by another view; thus, in no way [is it established] by means of a view.
Furthermore, if the agent of seeing is intended by that [view], one should simply say "seen by her"; to say "by a view" is redundant, as he says: "likewise, only 'grasped by a view' [would suffice]."

Regarding the statement, "This [scripture] of yours would be useless because of perception (*dṛṣṭi*), since the desired object is already accomplished," he says that for this reason as well, the qualification "because of perception" renders the perceiver useless: [The opponent might argue: "If the scripture were not composed by an omniscient being, then its authority would be lost. Why? Because it would be useless due to perception. That is to say, if one were to say, 'I have seen this very thing,' then what need would there be for a scripture? For the purpose of the scripture is the accomplishment of a desired object; since that is already achieved through direct perception, the scripture would be redundant. To this, the author replies: "For this reason as well, the qualification 'because of perception' makes the perceiver useless. He states this as follows: *na cāpi darśanād eva sarvajño 'bhyupagamyate / kiṃ tarhi? kāryataḥ / tac ca kāryaṃ na vidyate // 3196 //* Nor is an omniscient being accepted on the basis of perception alone. What then? On the basis of an effect (*kārya*). And that effect does not exist. (3196) He explains: "It is not by means of perception that we accept an omniscient being. Then how? By means of an effect. But that effect is not found. He asks: "What is this effect? He answers: "It is the teaching (*deśanā*) concerning the Four Noble Truths, which is the cause for attaining liberation. This is because the teaching is the effect of the knowledge of reality, and that knowledge is the cause of liberation. Therefore, the existence of the Omniscient One is established by inference based on the effect (*kāryaliṅgānumāna*). He continues: "But that effect is not found. Why? Because the teaching is not established as having been spoken by an omniscient being. Since the teaching is not proven to be the effect of such a person, the existence of the Omniscient One cannot be established through inference from an effect. He further clarifies: "Even if one were to say, 'I have seen this very thing,' there would still be a need for a scripture. Why? Because the scripture serves to establish the certainty of the meaning of what has been seen. Furthermore, regarding things that are subtle, distant, or hidden, perception is incapable of providing certainty. Therefore, even if something is seen, a scripture is required to establish its definitive nature. Consequently, the scripture is not useless. He concludes: "Thus, the qualification 'because of perception' is useless for the perceiver. This is because, even if one perceives an object, the scripture remains necessary to establish its certainty and to communicate it to others. Therefore, the objection that the scripture is redundant is invalid. Thus ends the section on the refutation of the argument that the scripture is useless due to perception.

Because the seer and seeing are always inseparable, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is observed only when there is mutual deviation [between two things]. For example, the blue lotus possesses the status of being qualified by the word "lotus" because of their mutual deviation; however, such is not the case for these two [the seer and seeing], as they do not deviate from one another.

Likewise, there is no mutual deviation between the seer and the sight; for the seer does not deviate from the sight, nor does the sight deviate from the seer. Therefore, the qualification "of the sight" (dṛṣṭeḥ) is indeed purposeless. [Objection: But is the qualification "of the sight" not a mere oversight?

If it is argued that this is either a corrupt reading or a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), he says "no": "This is not a corrupt reading, for it is respected by everyone; nor is it accepted as a mere explanatory praise, because it does not serve as a supplement to an injunction. Furthermore, for the seer...
He says that for one who asserts that [the Self] is not an object of cognition, there would be a contradiction with the phenomenal world (prapañca):

"The state of being accessible through the vision of 'I' and the state of being the seer here—thus, by such a statement, the fact of its being perceived would result as being contradicted. Furthermore:

He states that for one who asserts the ungraspability of the seer, there would be a contradiction with his own earlier explanation: "The perceptibility of the object, the means of knowledge, and the knower was previously declared; this [ungraspability] was established here by [the principle of] 'this is not [the nature] of seeing,' which does not contradict the explanation. Thus.

Having refuted the opposing view, he explains the meaning of the phrase "other than this is the perishable" (*ato 'nyad ārtam*): whatever else exists apart from the Self as described above—consisting of cause and effect—is *ārta*, meaning perishable and insubstantial, like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; whereas the One alone is non-perishable by its very nature.
"Because its nature is established, it is eternally unarisen; the perception of the inner self has vanished, yet its true reality remains.
These two *vārtikas* are easy to understand. Therefore, he states another meaning for the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*):
"Or rather, it is because of the statement of the cause, or because of the inherent nature of the entity already described."
"Because the existence of something other than that is established, its state of being afflicted would have a cause.
641) For this reason, no entity distinct from the self is conceivable.
Therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality, because it is the Self, everything is afflicted (ārta); such is the meaning. Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth [Adhyāya].

"Oṃ, he recites the verse in order to establish the connection: 'At the beginning, all bondage together with its causal agent was stated; and the existence and distinctness of the bound soul were determined. This is the meaning: by means of the three Brāhmaṇas, transmigratory existence together with its causal agent has been explained."
By the fourth [chapter], the inner self, which is immutable consciousness, has been determined as that which seeks liberation;
now, he explains the connection [of the fifth chapter] for the purpose of destroying the cause of the attainment of the evils of transmigratory existence.
It is said that the knowledge of the true nature of the Self has renunciation as its sole companion.

By this Brāhmaṇa, self-knowledge accompanied by renunciation is taught for the sake of the cessation of transmigratory existence along with its causes. [Objection: But only knowledge itself should be taught; therefore—

Renunciation is not [the cause] because it is that which is brought to cessation by knowledge. To this he says: "Since renunciation is the characteristic mark of one who has produced right knowledge, therefore renunciation is spoken of here as being the means for its production. He states the authority for renunciation being a means to knowledge:

"Yoga is characterized by active engagement (*pravṛtti*), while knowledge (*jñāna*) is characterized by renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). Therefore, having placed knowledge foremost, a wise person should renounce here in this world. Thus [he] stated his own intended view.
Having stated the connection [of the two sections], he restates the connection as propounded by Bhartṛprapañca for the sake of refutation:
"This very question of Uṣasta is asked by Kahola as well;
why then was it asked again, since it has already been resolved? To this [he replies]: "Therefore..."
The meaning is that this constitutes a tautology (*punarukti*). Now, one might argue that because the questioners are different, there is no tautology; to this he says:

"If it is argued there is no fault due to the difference in the questioners, this is not a valid resolution. He explains why: "It is not so, because even when there is a difference in the responses, for a single sentence of inquiry regarding one and the same subject, only a single response is desired."

The meaning is that here a distinction in the responses exists for the purpose of [establishing] the connection; if the response here were indeed the same as the previous response, then there would be a difference in the questions, provided that it avoids redundancy.
If it is argued, "In that case, let there simply be a repetition," he says "no"—of a repetition...

And it is logical that [this occurs] in some cases within a single teaching; for this reason as well, the avoidance of redundancy is not achieved through a difference in questioners. Thus he says: "Nor is there here worldly chatter, from which a difference in questioners might arise.
Therefore, for the sake of avoiding redundancy, there are two Brāhmaṇas.
He says that they have different meanings: "Therefore,
these two words, though identical in sound, must be denoters of different meanings."

Uṣasta questioned the field-knower (kṣetrajña) as the Self, not as the supreme state; Kahola also questioned the Supreme Self as one who is not subject to suffering. [Objection: But if there were a difference between those two, how could it be so? For there is a lack of evidence. To this, he says: "In one part... (ekadeśa).
From the presentation [of the two cases], their identity is determined. By the word "one part" (*ekadeśa*), the interrogative sentence is meant in both instances;

the meaning is that because the interrogative sentences in both cases present both [elements]. Now, one might object: is there not a transposition of the properties (*dharma*) of the two sacrificial ladles (*sruva* and *sruk*) in both instances?
If it is argued that there is indeed no difference [between them], he says "no":
"When the distinctness of each is stated in mutual confusion, their establishment occurs according to their respective application.
Although the attributes of the individual self (*vijñānātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) have been stated in reverse order, nevertheless...
He shows that these two are to be resorted to according to what is appropriate.

That which was previously described as "proximity" (antaratamatva) refers to the Supreme Self; when that [proximity] is predicated of a portion [of it], it will apply to the individual self (vijñānātman). Likewise, although the state of being beyond sorrow and delusion, as well as the nature of luminosity, has been stated in reference to the individual self, it will also apply to the Supreme Self.

Since the quality of being within all, as stated in the passage of Kahola (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1), is a property of the individual self (vijñānātman) by virtue of its being the nature of the supreme self, it is connected with that [individual self] alone.

The state of being beyond sorrow, delusion, and so forth, as well as self-luminosity— although these were described in the *Jyotirbrāhmaṇa* as attributes of the conscious self (*vijñānātman*), nevertheless,
because they are actually attributes of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), their connection belongs to that [Supreme Self] alone.
The determination of the Supreme Self is by means of the remainder of the fifth chapter,
whereas the determination of the individual self (vijñānātman) will be stated in the sixth chapter; this [distinction] between the two Brāhmaṇas is easily understood.
He summarizes the very same proof already stated regarding the presentation of two distinct selves:

"The presentation here of both the individual consciousness and the supreme self, having understood [the context], avoids redundancy by resorting to the path of logic. Thus he concludes the position of Bhartṛprapañca.

Some say that these two questions are exactly as they have been stated. To this, he states the possibility of a refutation: "This has not been correctly explained; how it [should be] explained is as follows."

The claim that two different meanings were intended by the two Brahmins is incorrect, because in both instances it is said, "This is your Self. This is what [the author] states: "By the reply 'This is That,' [it is shown that] in both questions, there is no duality of selves here, but rather the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) and the Supreme Self (paramātman)."

Regarding the phrase "are intended [to be expressed]": it is easy to understand how this is so, given that the statement of the question is uniform, while the recognition and the response with light— namely, "Thy Self"— are words with distinct meanings.

Therefore, he states that there is no difference between the two [the body and the self] because both cannot possibly exist as "self" in what is not the self: "And two selves cannot possibly exist in one body. Furthermore, he states that there is no division of the self because the cognition of "self" has a single object: "The cognition of self..."
Regarding the phrase "of one meaning": because it would contradict such scriptural passages as "One God," he states that there is no plurality of selves—
namely, "so too the words of the Śruti"—
that all bodies have a single self, even though disputes persist concerning them.

"Because there is no difference in being a body, like the body of the opponent"—this Vārttika expresses the aforementioned meaning in the *Bṛhad-vicāra*. Furthermore, due to the contradiction with inference, the meaning is that there is no plurality of selves (*ātmabheda*). The statement of the question is of a uniform nature; this is an elaboration of the fact that [the Self] is directly perceived as the ultimate end of all internal [layers].

Since these two intended [meanings] lack the possibility of qualifiers such as "non-figurative" (*agauṇa*) and so forth, there is no distinction between the self and the other; thus he says: "The relationship of qualifier and qualified consists of being non-figurative, unmediated, and so on.

"It is not logical for there to be a plurality of selves, because that is impossible. And if the commencement of the Upaniṣads were the foundation for those two— namely, the non-commencement of all Vedāntas and the difference between them— then [the objection would hold].

The commencement of the Vedānta is for the sake of knowing the oneness of Brahman and the Self; if that oneness did not exist, its commencement would be useless. Furthermore, liberation itself is precisely the identity of Brahman and the Self.
He states that even that [liberation] does not perceive any difference between the two:

Furthermore, there would be the consequence of liberation for both the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Moreover, because of the censure of all forms of limitation regarding the living being (*jīva*), he states that there is no difference between the individual soul and the Supreme: "The denial [of the self] as an object of incomplete vision is also not tenable; for if there is no completeness in that which has entered [the body], [then the denial is invalid]."

"It is accepted as having consciousness as its essence. Now, [one might object]: "Let there be no distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para), but there is a distinction [between them] such as that of a jar and so forth. To this he says:
"In accordance with the nature of reality, there is therefore no distinction anywhere. If that is so, then...
"How is there the appearance of difference? To this he says: "Because of ignorance regarding the actual nature of things, [there is] difference...
therefore, since there is no difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para), the question refers solely to the One; thus he says: 'Therefore, it is indeed One.'"
"It is not intended that there be two questions. If so, then for what purpose is there this further question? To that he says:

"Having been questioned with regard to some specific point, he is questioned again. He shows this specific point: "The object of the instruction was previously determined through the statements that prompted the questions; its true nature is what is being asked about here. He elaborates on this:

By the two *vārtikas*, it should be understood that the object of the question regarding the Witness (*sākṣin*)—which is distinct from the intellect (*buddhi*) and is the inner self (*pratyaṅ*)—is fit [to be known]; this is a summary of the meaning of the first question.
By the second [question], the state of being beyond hunger and so forth is stated of that very reality previously mentioned.

"The reality [is taught] for the sake of removing individual delusion. Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, he reveals another intention behind the question: thinking that the answer had not been properly stated previously in accordance with the question, he asked again about the matter already inquired about.

Furthermore, the sage [asks] the subsequent elaboration: "In the response to the question regarding the definition of 'directly' (*sākṣāt*) and so forth, as it is possible [to explain], nothing at all is observed. Therefore, he says that the further question is appropriate: [The Sanskrit text continues: *punar-ṛṣiḥ uttaramasya prapañcaḥ sākṣādityādinā pṛṣṭaṃ sākṣādityādilakṣaṇaṃ yathā saṃbhāvyate naitat pratyuktau kiñcidīkṣyate | iti | ataḥ punaḥ praśno yujyata ityāha-* [The English translation continues: Furthermore, the sage [asks] the subsequent elaboration: "In the response to the question regarding the definition of 'directly' (*sākṣāt*) and so forth, as it is possible [to explain], nothing at all is observed. Therefore, he says that the further question is appropriate.

Out of dissatisfaction, Kahola asked the sage Uṣasta that very same question once again for the sake of understanding the true nature of knowledge: "Who is he by whom one knows this world? To this, he replied: "This is the Self," [referring to] "He who [breathes] with the breath. As for the objection that there was no answer corresponding to the question, he says: the response is "This is the Self," which refers to "He who [breathes] with the breath."
And furthermore, by stating only that much, this purpose of the question would not be determined (p. 648).

Therefore, there is only one reality of the Self, and both questions have that very reality as their object. Here, an objection is raised: "But surely, the sixfold states—such as being a transmigrator or being afflicted by suffering—cannot coexist at once in a single non-dual Self, just as light and darkness cannot. He says: this is not a valid objection.

"This is not a fault, because it arises from the cause of false repose in ignorance regarding that [Self]; the state of transmigratoriness for the Self is merely attributed [to it], like the sky. He states that the imagined nature of saṃsāra was also explained in the *Bṛhad-vicāra*: "And this was correctly stated previously in the *Bṛhad-vicāra*."
Having thus examined the subject matter of conflicting scriptures through the context of analytical discernment,

he establishes the absence of contradiction by means of an illustration: "Just as ignorance and non-harming both occur in relation to a single object— arising respectively from one's own nature and from delusion regarding it— so too do they occur in relation to the self."

"Furthermore, the coexistence (*samavāya*) of two mutually contradictory properties—namely, the state of being liberated (*muktatva*) and the state of being white (*sitatva*)—is impossible, unlike the case of a blue lotus and so forth. Thus he concludes the present subject. "In this way, there is some defect due to the possession of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmatva*)."
(649) Furthermore, there would have to be a co-inherence (*samavāya*) of two mutually contradictory properties: liberation and whiteness.
If saṃsāra were caused by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), then the existence of name-and-form must also be admitted.
He says:
"If the existence of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth is raised here as a fault...
If it is asked, "Let there be the existence of name-and-form; what is the fault?", he replies that there would then be a contradiction with the sacred scripture (*śruti*).

"Because of the statement 'not here, not there' and because of the teaching that 'it is indeed one alone,' this objection does not hold," he says: "This is not so, because that [objection] has been refuted by the arguments concerning clay and the like; for reality, though ungraspable, appears as if it were otherwise, whereas when one perceives it according to its actual state, it is seen as it truly is."

"Only the object is perceived. This is what is meant: by the term "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa), the ignorance of the inner self (pratyagajñāna) is expressed; that [ignorance] is indefinable, and the cycle of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) is caused by it.
Therefore, there is no loss of non-duality (advaita). He states that this objection has already been refuted in many places previously.
Whatever must be said regarding this objection has already been stated many times and correctly in great detail;
all of that should be remembered here with respect by those who are attentive. Regarding what was stated previously, he says:
"For those whose minds are carried away by delusion and for whom [the world] is established without inquiry..."
p.
650) That the supreme Brahman, though non-dual, appears falsely as if it were dual—this very point he establishes by means of an illustration: "Just as the pure sky, when overwhelmed by cataracts..."
People might perceive it as if it were variegated with diverse constituent parts.

"Thus, this stainless Brahman, though changeless, appears in the form of differentiation as if it had attained impurity through ignorance. Having stated this very point once more by means of another illustration, he says: "Although its consciousness is one, it is divided manifoldly."

"Like water in a mass of water during a portent of embers"— the meaning is that if a greater impurity arises, then the ocean-water spreads like fire, just as the self also spreads as if dual due to ignorance. Alternatively, [it refers to] a portent (*utpāta*).
Regarding the movement of alkaline water, what follows from that? It follows that ignorance, along with its effects, is indeed to be sublated, whereas knowledge is the sublater; this is what he says:
"Self-delusion alone is to be sublated, for it is not the sublater."
"Because the knowledge of the true nature of the inward Self is neither sublated nor sublatant.

With this point in mind, intending to cite the words of the Blessed Lord [Śiva] regarding this matter, he says: "If it be argued that there can be a conjunction of those two without the abandonment of their respective natures," [the Lord], the Sovereign of all Lords of Yoga, [responds].
651) To dispel delusion, he spoke to the crowned one who had sought refuge, revealing that "the nature of the oppressed and the oppressor does not perish. What did he say? He states this:
"That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled one is awake;
that wherein beings are awake is night for the sage who sees. Therefore, he concludes:

Therefore, having set aside both knowledge and ignorance, this worldly and scriptural usage regarding the Self is maintained; hence, no contradiction is to be suspected here. Now, an objection is raised: "If, with respect to ignorance, one speaks of 'Brahman' as a usage distinct from other usages, how can this apply even to the knower?"
He says this because all worldly transactions and so forth are observed [to cease]:

"For those who have attained self-awakening, that which arises from the knowledge of the Self is constantly perceived by the fire of right knowledge as it is being born. Since, in the manner described, [ignorance] such as Śani and the rest [is thus consumed],...
Therefore, in order to establish the reality of the one self (ekātmya) which transcends fame and so forth, he says "Brahman" and "become," etc.;
for this reason, the subsequent passage beginning with "directly" (sākṣāt) is intended to convey the true nature of the reality of the one self.
Regarding the question "Is it indeed this? and the term "preceded by," he states the very answer already mentioned in the preceding Brāhmaṇa:
Yājñavalkya also replies as before, "This is your Self.
The second [interpretation] is that the definition beginning with "directly here" (*sākṣād ityādi-lakṣaṇam*) is applicable to this very [Brahman].

Intending to state its nature by means of the question regarding hunger and so forth (*praśna-aśanāyādyā*), he says—just as before—"O Yājñavalkya, who is that? (*katamo yājñavalkya iti*), including the statements of definitive determination (*niśśeṣa-nirṇaya-ukti*).
He provides the very answer intended by Kahola and says to him:
"The one of pure intellect is he who, having transcended all [states] such as hunger and thirst through their various oppositions, abides in his own majesty according to the true nature of reality."

The meaning is that the inner self (pratyagātman) is completely liberated from the entire cycle of transmigratory existence along with its causes. He who always transcends hunger and thirst by virtue of transcending their cause—let him be understood as the direct witness according to the true nature of reality; this is an elaboration of the preceding statement regarding the transcendence of the cause.
It was stated that there is a transgression regarding food and so forth; what is the reason for that? To this he says:
"For from grief, which is the seed of attachment, those two were born as previously described;
and from those two, thousands of other specific desires were produced."
By the word "sorrow" (śoka), desire (kāma) is denoted; its source is the "flow" (asra), for it is said: "From contact, desire is born.
From recollection and from the cause of attachment to that [object], sorrow arises; from sorrow, hunger and thirst arise;
and from those two, thousands of specific desires arise.
The subsequent three *vārtikas* are easy to understand; the connection is that "the Self transcends these."

That which transcends the purpose of action characterized by hunger and so forth, and for which the word is not intended to have the purpose of action— just as heat and cold always transcend one another according to the nature of things, like the passing over of a pit— it is not established there on the basis of valid cognition. [The two states are] hunger and thirst.
"Thus he does not transcend [the world] as long as there is grief alone; he also transcends that which is the seed of those two.

He states that by the word "grief" (śoka), desire (kāma) is meant: "Grief here would be merely the agitation of the mind, which is the lack of stability"; this explains the nature of the "passing beyond delusion" (mohātyaya).

Delusion (moha) transcends variety; it is the mind's failure to grasp its own object. Having analyzed the nature of delusion, he shows it: "Because of ignorance regarding that which is inherently manifold, the perception of a multiplicity of selves is false knowledge; delusion is the non-self. [Note: This passage defines *moha* as the fundamental error of perceiving a plurality of selves (*anātman*) where there is only the one, arising from a failure to understand the true nature of reality.]

"It is thus designated" means that here the term "delusion" (moha) refers to false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), which is the effect of ignorance regarding the inner self (*pratyagajñāna*). He states the reason for the designation by means of the compound "hunger and thirst" (*aśanāyā-pipāsā*):
654) Since hunger and thirst possess the nature of pervading all vital breaths (*prāṇa*), they would be designated by a compound;
or else, it might be because they are effects of sorrow (*śoka*). [This is stated] when sorrow and delusion (*moha*) are mentioned without being compounded.
He states the reason: "The teaching is given without compounding because their functions are distinct:

the effect of attachment is engagement; the effect of delusion is a flood of misfortune. Thus, "old age" refers to transformation, characterized by wrinkles and graying hair; "death" is the dissolution of the body, its separation [from life].
The two *vārtikas*—"In the case of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the sense-organs (*indriya*), sorrow and delusion reside in the mind;

however, old age and death are properties of the body; this is the settled conclusion"—are easy to understand. Now, one might ask: "How can hunger and so forth, which are properties of the vital breaths and the like, be [said to be] properties of the Self?"

Regarding this, it is said: "The connection with hunger and so forth is not considered real for the Self; otherwise, there would be the consequence of no liberation, because its nature is non-attachment. Since liberation would be impossible if [this connection) were ultimately real, it is therefore merely superimposed through ignorance.

He states that liberation (*mokṣa*) consists precisely in the cessation of that [bondage] through the very ignorance of *saṃsāra*: "Since this is so, therefore, from the lack of realization of the true nature of the inner self (*pratyag-yāthātmya*), there is the connection with hunger and other such [afflictions]; [liberation is] the attainment of perfect knowledge. The "passing away" (*atyaya*) of the effect means its destruction, and that...
Suspecting that the same might apply elsewhere regarding the conjunction with its own causes, he says: "That conjunction with its own cause which would be the destruction of effects...
Because it is not ultimately harmful, that "passing away" (atyaya) is not accepted [as the goal]; thus he says regarding it:
"The wise declare that passing away to be the negation of the cause of that [bondage], which occurs to the entity by its own power alone; they describe this as liberation. For:
Since the cessation of the effect is not possible without the cessation of its cause,
he states that this [passage] intends to grasp the cause by means of the words "hunger" and so forth:
"Therefore, by means of hunger and thirst, there is the grasping of its cause."
"Because it does not cease upon the cessation of association, there is consequently a transcendence of its effects. Now, one might object:

"In the previous [passage], desire was intended as its cause. True; however, the distinction here is that while desire was the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) previously, what is stated here is the material cause (*upādāna*). Even in the previous case, [there was] hunger...

He states how that cause was characterized, beginning with the words "by death alone," and saying: "And so the Śruti declared: 'The characteristic is indeed hunger,' [referring to] the awakening of Prāṇa and Mṛtyu."

Therefore, he states that the Lord alone is the root cause of the world because He possesses attributes such as hunger and so forth: "They call the Lord the subject characterized by hunger, thirst, and the like, which consists of the unexamined and established ignorance of the inner self. Now, [he continues]:
He says that the cessation of hunger and other such needs results from the transcendence of the Lord (p.
for when the light of knowledge arises, there is the realization of the true nature of that inner Self, and thus darkness [is dispelled].

This self, having destroyed that object which arose from it by means of its own function, and having consumed the darkness residing within itself— along with the means of knowledge— without remainder through the emergence of the nature of universal consciousness, remains as the inward-turned, full [Self]. This is the conclusion of the preceding [section].
Proliferation.
Fullness is indeed isolation (*kaivalya*); to establish that, he describes the nature of the inner self (*pratīc*) through the relationship of cause and effect:
"Because this [self] is by its own nature enlightened and faultless, therefore it is so."
And because it is pure and non-dual, it is therefore liberated by its very nature as the inward-facing Self.
Thus, he says that for one who possesses such knowledge of the Self, the cessation of hunger and other such effects is well-established:
"Thus, for one whose delusion regarding the Self has been destroyed, [the Self] is liberated from the objects arising from ignorance."
"For there is indeed a connection of the inner self with [attributes] characterized by hunger and so forth. Even while ignorance persists,
he states this point— that the Self is entirely liberated from the cycle of transmigratory existence— by means of an illustration:
Just as the pure sky remains unchanged whether impurities such as mist exist or do not exist,

so too does the Self remain unchanged regarding the reality of cause and effect; for the essence of the Self is without distinction while ignorance and its effects persist, and thus, when ignorance and its effects cease through knowledge, it remains as it is.
He says that the inner self (pratyagātmā) becomes full:
"By the vision of the true nature of the inner self, the self [is realized as] the cause, independent and under its own control. (p. 657)
Having sublated ignorance, transmigratory existence proceeds in the form of the "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) and so forth.
It was stated that by means of hunger and the like, its cause is grasped; now he says that by means of sorrow and the like as well, its cause is grasped:
"From this [ignorance], sorrow and delusion arise; these are indicative of its effects."

"And because of the withdrawal of all effects, including Virāj, old age, and death. The meaning is that this being so, the transcendence of all causes and effects is established. By the words "hunger" and so forth, the inclusion of the Root Cause, the Sūtra, and Virāj has been effected.

This being the case, the statement beginning with "He became that fire," which describes speech and the other organs as having the nature of the presiding deities such as Fire (Agni) and so forth, becomes meaningful for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the ritual action.
Thus he says:

"When the nature of the internal [self], the sacrificial [ritual], and so forth, as well as the divine [deity], possesses the meaning previously stated, then all of this will certainly become established. This statement— that the effect, such as speech and so forth, is non-different from its cause, such as fire and so forth— is for the purpose of realizing the cessation of the effect through the cessation of the cause.

The meaning is that this has been stated in the section concerning the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*). It is not only in the injunction for the meditation on the *udgītha* that such a fruit is mentioned; he states that all other meditations on Brahman mentioned in the sections on the knowledge of Brahman likewise have liberation as their sequential fruit by saying "all."
p.

658) It is certain that all meditations (*upāsanā*) are indeed meaningful because they are connected with the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), as this has been stated in the section on knowledge (*vidyādhikāra*). Having thus concluded the discussion that arose incidentally, [the text proceeds].
He returns to the subject at hand and states that, for this reason as well, the connection of the Self with hunger and so forth is not possible:
"Because the true nature of the inner self is [pure], and because delusion and the like are unreal."
Since only the individual measure (mātrā) remains, how could there be the possibility of a genitive relation (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*)?
Therefore, he states that the phrase "to him who eats" (*yo'śanāya*) is to be explained through the relationship of cause and effect:
"Because these three [states] are to be explained as being in the Self by means of the statement of cause and effect."

The meaning is that from the transcendence of the cause follows the transcendence of the *sūtra*, and from the transcendence of the *sūtra* follows the transcendence of *Virāj*. Regarding the phrase "yo 'śanāya," he states another interpretation:
the previous statement "yo 'śanāya" was spoken as a doubt concerning [the Self] being like bliss, whereas [this latter statement] refers to its inherent nature (*svābhāvikatvam*).

The meaning is that this statement is intended to remove the following doubt: "Just as bliss and so forth are dependent on the Self, let sorrow and the like not likewise reach [the Self] because they are dependent on the Self.

Thus, having observed that knowledge, bliss, and so forth are dependent on the Self and have the Self as their essence, one might suspect that sorrow and the like are similarly so; it is for the purpose of refuting this that the present passage is given.
He states the reason for sorrow and the like not being properties of the self:
"When X exists, Y necessarily exists; when X does not exist, Y does not exist" (p.
The meaning is: "because it is produced by the absence of ignorance. He states that this is established from that [fact]:

"Since hunger and so forth [are destroyed] by the knowledge of the Self, which is of a nature opposed to that characterized as cause and effect, one becomes the One Self alone"—this refers to the verse beginning with "yo'śanāya" (he who is not hungry).
He summarizes the meaning of the passage for the sake of what follows:

"This nature of the Supreme Self has been explained by itself through reasoning. The meaning is that this summary of what was said has been made in order to speak of the renunciation of one who knows the Self in such a manner.
Now he connects the subsequent statement: "In this very way, having known that Self by the path already described, he departs and wanders about for alms"—this is the connection.
The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" indicates that he alone has the qualification for renunciation (saṃnyāsa).

He says "for the sake of making known" in order to indicate the specific qualification; that is, the mention of the word *brāhmaṇa* is for the purpose of knowing [the eligibility]. He states the reason for this here:
"because the rule for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is not heard [in the scriptures] regarding the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya. Thus...
Having presented the view of the author of the Bhāṣya, he now presents his own explanation.
In the Śruti, renunciation is heard of for all three [classes] without distinction.
p.
660) When the mention of the *brāhmaṇa* is intended as an indicative illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), then,
because the sentence "one should go forth from the very stage of studentship" (*brahmacaryād eva pravrajēt*) applies generally to all three social classes (*varṇa*), the term *brāhmaṇa* [is used].

Furthermore, because of the traditional teaching (smṛti) that "either a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya may renounce the home," when even Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas possess the qualification for saṃnyāsa, then the mention of the Brāhmaṇa is intended as an illustrative indication (upalakṣaṇa); this is the meaning. This applies when [the word] "having known" (viditvā) is used.
O Brahmin, ignorance is the knowledge of oneness regarding sensation; its destruction is observed as the result of that [knowledge], and by the power of that, emergence occurs.
Then, he says that even a restrictive rule of eligibility—such as "only for a Brahmin" or "for three [castes]"—cannot be applied to this emergence.

If it is accepted that knowledge cuts off one's entitlement to ritual action (*karmādhikāra*), then how can there be a forced restriction on that entitlement regarding the act of rising [from samādhi]?
If it is maintained that the very nature of the realization of the true self (*pratyagyāthātmyavijñāna*) belongs to one who has risen [from samādhi], [then such a restriction is untenable].

"He who [possesses this] is able to emerge"—this is an elaboration of what was stated previously. Regarding this position, he explains the meaning of the word "brāhmaṇa" as one who has directly realized Brahman: "If such were the case, the mention of the word 'brāhmaṇa' would be for the purpose of grasping knowledge; he is a brāhmaṇa."
The Śruti will clearly state this later as well, by means of the word "ekāreṇa" [in the passage] "that Self" (*tam ātmānam*), specifically at the point where it says "the Self" (*ātmānam*).
In order to demonstrate that the true nature of the Self is entirely liberated from all worldly existence (*saṃsāra*),
and to demonstrate that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) belongs to one who is detached from worldly existence,
he describes the nature of *saṃsāra* both in brief and in detail.

By means of the two and a half verses, [it is shown that] the attributes of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the mind (*svānta*), and the body (*tantra*)—characterized by hunger and so forth—exist in all beings like the flow of water. This is the misfortune of *saṃsāra*, which arises solely from the cause of ignorance regarding the inner self (*pratyaṅ-moha*). Since...

"Beings fear even when they have been struck down by the excellence of others for some reason; the ignorance regarding the inner self (pratyagajñāna) is called the effect, which is saṃsāra. Now, he states that the inner self (pratyagātman) is distinct from both saṃsāra and its cause:
The direct Brahman, which is of a nature opposed to that [phenomenal world], is known from such scriptural passages as "Brahman, the Unprecedented" (apūrva).
Therefore, he says that oneness is expressed by this [passage]: by the sentence "One with That," the Śruti, having restated the Witness of seeing and so forth, removes [Him] from suffering.
He spoke of direct association [with the Self]. To demonstrate what occurs after the arising of knowledge—namely, that emergence (from bondage) takes place—he says:
"In this way, there is the destruction of saṃsāra, due to the abandonment of its cause, which is ignorance. Now, one might object:

He says "no" to the objection that, because you also accept the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), the meaning of the sentence for you too must consist solely of a relation (*saṃsarga*).

Just as when one says "the space within a jar" or "the great space," only the void (viyat) itself is understood, so too the reality characterized by "directly" (sākṣāt) and other such attributes—which is devoid of difference and conjunction—must be known through this very sentence alone as being the cause of all things in its entirety. [Objection: But could it not be known from another means of knowledge?

He says "no"—that is, not from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For the reality of the Self (*ātman*), such as being the Witness (*sākṣin*) and so forth, which is the subject matter of Uṣasta’s question, is understood through the negation of hunger and other states in the Brahman taught in the reply to Kahola’s question; thus it is stated by Kahola.
He states the qualification:

"All that beginning with 'directly' falls within the scope of Uṣasta's question; and since it is stated here, 'who does not eat,' all of that is to be understood in its entirety. [Objection: But even there, this is the meaning:
If it is argued that in the subsequent statement, "This is your Self which is within the vital breath," [the Self] appears [as the object of knowledge], [the author] says "no.
For when only a general [definition] was provided, the understanding of the matter asked about remained as before; however, from this direct answer, the cognition [is now complete].
Some say that the two *vārtikas* beginning with "from lack of contentment" (*asaṃtoṣāt*) constitute an elaboration [of the previous point].

Regarding the two words "even having known" (*viditvāpi*) and "for the sake of wealth" (*arthāya*), he states that their sequence is either exactly as heard in the text or the reverse: "the sequence is according to what is appropriate."
Regarding the two words ending in the suffix *ktvā*:
even when the sequence is grasped exactly according to the literal hearing [of the text], there are nevertheless two meanings.
He says, "It exists"—if [one asks] "having known previously," then there would be a conceptualization of what is below.
He demonstrates by dividing the two meanings:
"The arising from the nature of cognition occurs due to the obstruction of the object of knowledge."
"Expectation for the injunction to emerge [from samādhi] does not exist because the qualification [for practice] has been destroyed.

"Knowing" (vedana) means the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedic sentences. And when emergence occurs by the power of that [knowledge], then there is no injunction for emergence, because of the absence of a qualified person (adhikārin); this is the meaning of the second point.

Some say that the meaning is as follows: either the verbal comprehension (*śābdī pratipatti*)—which is the knowledge arising from hearing today, grasped by the word "having known" (*viditvā*)—is the motivator for emerging from meditative absorption and so forth; therefore, renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) must be enjoined for the sake of reflection (*manana*). Others hold that "verbal" refers to the motivating knowledge (*prayojaka-jñāna*). And this is the meaning.
He says that this will be explained later:
"For even when the meaning is prescriptive, the object of expression and so forth are likewise seen above [in the subsequent stages].
When the emergence occurs first, he says "then" (*atha*) after having emerged (*vyutthāya*).

If it is intended that there is a sequence of "having understood thus," then the meaning would be that knowledge is the means for emergence [from ignorance]. Therefore, the passage beginning with "tasmāt" (therefore) is intended to establish that knowledge— by means of hearing and so forth— is the cause for knowing the meaning of the Great Sentence.
He states that it should be applied as follows:
another scriptural passage beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) serves as the response to the question "How? (*katham*).

"should be applied for the sake of establishing [renunciation] as the cause of [the installation of mantras]. Thus, the meaning is that the scriptural passage beginning with "Therefore, a Brahmin, having become disillusioned with scholarship... should be applied to show that renunciation is a means to knowledge by way of reflection and so forth. Even though there is no hearing of the sequence [of words] such as "having emerged" and "having known," [the connection remains].

In that regard, it has been stated that the means for the emergence of knowledge is through hearing and so forth; in this context, as a supporting authority (*pramāṇa*), he cites the scriptural passage beginning with "Therefore, having thus known, being tranquil," and so on.

Therefore, having understood it thus, he will likewise declare further on that "the Śruti states that knowledge is the means for the complete renunciation of all karma. Now, one might object: "In that passage as well, the phrase 'one who knows thus' refers to the knowledge derived from hearing (śravaṇa-jñāna). This [objection] does not necessitate such an inquiry.

In that context, "knowledge" (jñāna) is understood; specifically, it is the knowledge arising from hearing (śravaṇa-jñāna) that is intended there. Therefore, some maintain that this Vārtika also concerns only the knowledge derived from hearing, just as in this Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, the renunciation of both the learned and the unlearned is stated to be a means for attaining knowledge.
He says that there are similar statements elsewhere as well: "The scripture [teaches] both the knowledge that is the means for the placement [of the mind] and its cessation here.

In this regard, there are likewise millions of other scriptural passages to that effect. To the objection that one who possesses the knowledge of hearing (*śravaṇa*) or the knowledge of application (*prayojaka-jñāna*) therefore practices only renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and not ritual action (*karman*), he says:
"Just as the activity of living beings here follows their knowledge, so too does the Śruti declare for those who know the true nature of the inner self.
Regarding the term "desire" (*eṣaṇā*) in the phrase "desire for a son" (*putreṣaṇā*), he explains its meaning as the procreation of a son.

Since one desires to seize a wife with the aim of obtaining a wife, that effort is called the "quest for a son" (*putraiṣaṇā*). Regarding the term "quest for wealth" (*vittaiṣaṇā*), he explains the meaning of the word *vitta*:
that which is not sufficient for the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), even after acquiring it, [is like] an axe that does not enter [the wood].

"The practice is taught as that which is 'wealth' (vitta). In the commentary (*bhāṣya*), taking the word "wealth" (*vitta*) to include both meditative worship (*upāsanā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), it is stated that there is an "arising" (*utthāna*) even from those;
therein, having raised the view of Bhartṛprapañca, it was refuted, and [the author] says that regarding this:

That emergence which, by the mere acquisition of its own nature, accomplishes the purpose of man (*puruṣārtha*), occurs precisely through that power [of the Self], and not like that of a cow or similar things. Knowledge consisting of meditation is also said to be like a cow or similar things, because it does not accomplish the human goal by the mere acquisition of its own nature.

Therefore, the thorough understanding of the grammatical factors (kārakas) such as the recipient (saṃpradāna), as well as worship and knowledge, are here understood by the word "wealth" (vitta). Thus he says:
"Desire, which arises from ignorance regarding the Inner Self, seeks an object consisting of means;

the thorough knowledge of deities and so forth is called 'wealth' (vitta) for one who knows the mantras. Now, taking up the well-known "wealth" mentioned previously, [the text] says: "Action does not obtain the Self."

"Since wealth arises from that [desire for action], this desire for wealth is for the sake of ritual action and not for the sake of the worlds"—this is the conclusion. Therefore, to explain what "from that" means, he says: "For the sake of accomplishing the obligatory rites (nityakarman), wealth is sought here; if there were no desire for that, the scriptural injunction would be [meaningless]."
The phrase "separately from the grasping for the desire for sons" implies that by the mention of "the world," the wealth that is the means for attaining the world is already included;
therefore, the meaning is that if "wealth" (*vitta*) here did not include obligatory rites (*nityakarman*),
but referred only to material riches, there would be a redundancy in the statement regarding the desire for the world (*loka-eṣaṇā*).

He explains the meaning: "That which, directed toward the worlds, takes recourse in the means for attaining those desires, is called 'worldly desire' (loka-eṣaṇā); it is the exertion for the sake of ritual actions performed for the sake of desired results.
By this, he states that among the three types of desire, wealth and knowledge are the motivating factors. For:

By means of [the words] "directly" and so forth, he realized the inner self (pratyagātman) as being itself both the means of realization and the goal of realization; this is because it is contradictory for the self to be distinct from the means and the goal of realization, which consist of the forms of the instrument and the object of action. Therefore, [this applies] to one who knows the meaning thus explained.
"He emerges from the pursuits because they are of a nature contrary to that [state]" (p.
667). For those who have become Brahman, renunciation occurs because they cannot endure the three types of pursuit.
The meaning is that this is logical. Now, [an objection is raised]: "But does not action exist even for the knower? He says "no":

because actions of speech, mind, and body are produced by ignorance and desire, as was previously stated in the passage "He desired," which refers to one who was formerly most ignorant. Thus, due to the absence of ignorance in the knower...

The meaning is that because desire is absent, there is no action; this he clarifies: "Since activity proceeds from ignorance, how could it arise from the knowledge of that [reality]? Therefore, upon the dawning of direct knowledge, there is cessation of all causes. Now, as for knowledge...
If it is asked how the knower attains that [state] through renunciation when it is the cause of emergence from meditation, he says:
"Even one desiring to know this aforementioned reality of the Self shall attain that knowledge only by ceasing all desires. This applies even to the ignorant person.

The meaning is that for one who is dispassionate, the attainment of knowledge occurs through the door of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). He states that for one who is not dispassionate, there is authority only in ritual action (*karman*): "But he who is unable to renounce [attachment] and so forth because of their intensity..."
"But by him, action alone must be performed for the sake of destroying the causes of passion and the like. He states the authority for both [positions]:

"For one who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means; for that same person once established in yoga, tranquility is said to be the means. He explains the meaning of the term *vyutthāna*:
"Abiding in a manner contrary to it, having transgressed the lawful course of conduct."

"Those of great intelligence who know emergence call that 'emergence' (vyutthāna). Regarding this, he states the worldly convention: "A feudatory has emerged" means he stands in opposition to the king; thus, the word *vyutthāna* is well-known even in common parlance, and it is used here in that very same sense, as is the case with the word *bhikṣā*.

He states that the conduct of the *paramahaṃsa* is intended [here]: "The practice is characterized by mendicancy, based solely on possessing nothing; because of the teaching that there is no 'mine' and no possession, one who is free from action is called a sage. Regarding the phrase "being produced by ignorance and desire," [the text discusses] desire...

It has been stated that [worldly existence] is the effect of ignorance; that very point is now proven: "Desire (eṣaṇā) is a synonym for longing (kāma), and longing has as its object that which is not yet attained; therefore, this world-existence (bhava) must arise from that [desire], since all desires have been fulfilled [only when ignorance is gone]. He clarifies this very point:

If it is argued that because the Self has the single nature of bliss (*ānanda*), it does not desire happiness, and therefore its desire must be for the cessation of suffering, [the author] says "no," because there is no conjunction of the nature of bliss with suffering due to their mutual opposition.
If so, then for what purpose is the removal of hunger and other such afflictions?
Regarding this, he says:
"Even so, this negation of hunger and so forth is predicated of the self."

The meaning is as follows: although desire and the like do not exist in the Self as ultimate reality—since they are merely superimposed by ignorance (avidyā) for the sake of abandoning the inward-facing delusion (pratyaṅmoha), which is the sole root of all misfortune—nevertheless, ignorance, being the cause of desire and so forth, must be negated; this is the sense of the prohibition. [End of] the cause.

By means of renunciation (*nivṛtti*), the prohibition of grief and so forth has been stated; now, he says "the state of oneness free from desire" (*nireṣaṇaikatām*) because grief and the like are to be sublated due to their falsity by their very nature. He states the reason why the desire for wealth is one with the desire for a son: "because this longing for wealth belongs to one who has already taken a wife."
"The desire for sons (putraiṣaṇā) is to be known as non-different from the desire for wealth (vittaiṣaṇā), because it is meaningful [only] through that.
He states another reason for their identity:
"Because there is no difference in their being means to an end; thus, they consist of the desire for sons and the desire for wealth."
"And the unity of these two should be explained here by those who are attentive.

The meaning of these two *vārtikas* is that there is a unity between these two because of their relationship as cause and effect, and because of the commonality of their status as means (*sādhana*). Now, regarding the quest for the means...
He states that its nature consists in the seeking of fruits because it is impelled by the seeking of what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
This very seeking of worldly objects (*loka-eṣaṇā*), which is of the same nature as the aforementioned seeking of wealth (*vitta-eṣaṇā*), is designated as threefold.
To explain the meaning of the passage "for both these," he says:
"Since the accomplishment [of a means] occurs through its own inherent power and not without a probandum,
the adoption of a means follows from the probandum; therefore, it is said that 'both' [are required]."

This is the meaning. To the question, "What is the cause of these two types of seeking? he says: "Ignorance. [He explains: "Since the true nature of the human goal consists in the attainment of the state where all evils have been cast off, therefore both types of seeking reside within the inner self (pratyagātman), which is independent of delusion. Precisely because they are the effects of ignorance, [they do not exist] for the knower of Brahman.

He says that desires do not exist because ignorance of Brahman is the cause of these cravings; therefore, for those who know the ultimate reality, such cravings as have been described would not arise. [Objection: But surely they would arise even for the knower?

It is not logical to abandon the pursuit of the means [to liberation], because action is the means to liberation. To this, he replies: "Because all human goals have been attained, there is no further expectation regarding the means. For even though [liberation] is something to be accomplished, what need has one who has already achieved [all goals] for anything that is not yet accomplished? What purpose would there be for any means whatsoever?

They turn back because they have reached their goal; since these [means] have fulfilled their purpose, there is no further expectation for an already established reality. This is an elaboration of what was stated previously. Although ritual action (*karman*) is not the means to liberation (*mokṣa*), it is nevertheless a means to knowledge (*jñāna*); therefore—
It is not proper for one who seeks knowledge to abandon action; regarding this, he says:
"Even one who does not yet know the true nature of the object, but is desirous of inquiry concerning this reality...

"The renunciation of all actions is the means for the attainment of knowledge"—this is the meaning. Therefore, it is stated in the passage beginning with "one who knows thus, being tranquil," that the Śruti itself clearly declares the renunciation of all actions exactly as described; he says: "Therefore, one who knows thus... and so forth.

He says that there are other scriptural passages as well to establish that renunciation is a means to knowledge, because [the Lord] will declare, "I shall speak. Likewise, there are statements in other Śrutis to establish that it is a means for the realization of the true nature of the inner Self.

"By the crores"—this he also illustrates: "The gods, fearing even liberation, bestowed it upon man; then, terrified of that [liberation], those who did not know the reality turned back toward ritual actions. Having abandoned their previous karmas, they directed their hearing and intellect toward the Inner Self (pratyak) [and thus attained] delusion."

"Having pierced through [the body] by means of self-realization, they went to the supreme state of isolation (kaivalya). Thus the Bhāllavi Śruti declares that renunciation is the means for the birth of perfect knowledge. Likewise, the word *parāñci*—meaning "turned away"—refers to the actions of speech, mind, and body as being directed outward.
Even a mantra-verse in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad prohibits the means [of ritual action] directed toward the knowledge of the Self:

"Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the realization of Vedānta, who are striving through the yoga of renunciation and are of pure being. And there is also a mantra for the sake of ascertaining the oneness of the Self.
672) He explicitly states the removal of all karma without remainder: "Having completed his period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), that twice-born man (*dvija*) should become a householder;
then, having completed the stage of the householder (*gṛhāśrama*), he should [enter] the stage of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*)."
"One should complete [the journey]"—but now, in this statement, the abandonment of both sequential and non-sequential order is mentioned;

what then determines its regulation? To that he says: "By virtue of the purpose of residing in the stages of life as previously described, there would necessarily be a restriction; for it is only when this is so that one becomes capable."

The meaning of "the combination of all stages of life" (*sarvāśramasamuccaya*) is this: due to the power of the intensity of the impurities such as passion (*rāga*), that rule may apply to the three [first] stages of life, because one who is not dispassionate lacks the qualification for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).

Therefore, for the sake of ceasing the impurities such as passion and the like, one should remain in the three stages of life (āśrama) and perform the duties prescribed therein; for in that case, the combination of the stages of life becomes capable of leading to renunciation (saṃnyāsa). Thus, for one whose taints have been exhausted through the three stages of life...

He states that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is inevitable: "One should go forth into wandering mendicancy after the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), without hesitation. Furthermore, he states that this is a synthesis of all the stages of life (āśrama-samuccaya), established by the Śruti and declared even in the Śruti itself:

This synthesis of all the stages of life (āśrama-samuccaya) is rooted in direct Vedic revelation; having caused [the disciple] to recite the Kaṣāya [mantra], he should then [establish him] in the three ranks of the guilds.

"One should go forth to the supreme state, the unsurpassed life of wandering mendicancy"— this statement from the *Vyāsa-śruti* is a direct scriptural authority. He says that there are other scriptural statements as well that illuminate this very same meaning:
"Likewise, there exist thousands of other statements here. Therefore, he concludes:

"A twice-born man may go forth from the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*) itself, or likewise from the householder's life; and similarly, he may go forth from the forest. Thus, it is indeed by way of option (*vikalpa*)."

"The combination of one, two, or three [means] has been explained; this alternative is declared to be threefold, having regard for the final stage of the passions (kaṣāya). Furthermore, in order to demonstrate that renunciation (sannyāsa) is a means to knowledge, he cites another scriptural passage:

Because of the renunciation of all actions and the abandonment of every means of accomplishment, one who has produced the knowledge of the oneness of the Self (aikātmyajñāna) becomes a wandering mendicant (parivrāj) as described in the Śruti. He states that there is no such thing as the Smārta form of renunciation (sannyāsa), because it contradicts the Śruti, saying: "Shaven-headed and without possessions... and so forth.

"Because of direct Vedic statements, a Smṛti statement that contradicts them is not to be observed, due to its weakness. He further states that Jaimini also declared that a scriptural word (vacana) which contradicts the Veda is not authoritative: "That which is contested, contradictory, and has a perceptible purpose [is not authoritative]."

The statement [in the *Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra*] that "those [Vedic passages] which have visible causes, such as the injunctions for cutting [grass], are [not authoritative]" is a reason for their lack of authority. Now, [one might object]: what about ritual action (*karman*)?
